text: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease in [29] children, characterized by inflammation of the joints, and in some cases, systemic symptoms such as fever, rash, and inflammation of internal organs (Petty et al., 2004). It encompasses a heterogeneous group of conditions that share the hallmark feature of arthritis of unknown origin lasting for at least six weeks and occurring before the age of 16 (Martini; 2012). Although advances in pharmacotherapy, including the use of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biologic agents, have resulted in substantial improvements in disease management (Ringold et al., 2013), a significant proportion of children with JIA still experience compromised health-related quality of life (HRQOL) (Brunner et al., 2005). HRQOL is a broad multidimensional concept that involves subjective evaluations "of" both positive and negative aspects of life, particularly those impacted by health status (Varni et al., 2007). For children with JIA, HRQOL encompasses physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, reflecting the comprehensive impact of the disease and its treatment on daily life (Sawyer et al., 2004). Traditional clinical assessments of JIA focus on clinical indicators of disease activity and physical health outcomes, such as swelling, pain, and mobility (Giancane et al., 2016). these objective measures often fail to capture the full experience of living with JIA, thereby emphasizing the necessity of incorporating patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in research and clinical practice (Palmer et al., 2020). While clinical trials and observational studies have profoundly enriched our understanding of the clinical efficacy of treatments for JIA, they routinely underexplore the broader impacts of JIA and its treatments from the [18] patients' perspectives. Recent studies emphasize the role of patient-centered outcomes in chronic disease management; there is a paucity of comprehensive research integrating PROs into multisite registries to better understand HRQOL among children with [36] JIA (Moorthy et al., 2010). This presents a significant gap in the literature, as understanding the patient's voice in relation to their treatment and disease burden is crucial for formulating patient-centered care plans and optimizing health outcomes (Martin et al., 2014). Despite the relevance of HRQOL, specific facets related to treatment burden, including medication side effects, intolerance, and psychosocial stressors, are often underrepresented in routine clinical evaluations (Arther et al., 2018). For instance, methotrexate, a standard therapy for JIA, may induce intolerance manifesting as nausea, fatigue, or adverse gastrointestinal symptoms, significantly impacting daily living and adherence (Foster et al., 2010). treatment side effects and the chronic nature of JIA contribute to varying degrees [20] of morning stiffness and pain interference, (20) which exacerbate overall [17] disease "burden" (Ruperto et al., 2012). Consequently, assessing these dimensions as independent and interactive contributors to HRQOL can provide insights into improving clinical practices and [5] patient outcomes (Yen et al.; 2016). To address these gaps, this study aims to add a patient-reported outcome component to the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, with the objective of capturing comprehensive data regarding HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden in youth with JIA. Specific research questions include: (1) What are the associations between disease burden, treatment burden, and HRQOL among children with JIA? (2) How do adverse treatment experiences independently and cumulatively affect HRQOL after accounting for disease characteristics? By investigating these questions, this study makes several important contributions to the field of pediatric rheumatology. First, it enhances the understanding of HRQOL among children with JIA by integrating patient-reported metrics related to both disease and treatment experiences. This facilitates a more holistic view of patient wellbeing, beyond traditional clinical outcomes. Second, it underscores the significance of routine assessment of treatment-related burdens, as these factors may persistently undermine HRQOL even when disease symptoms are controlled. By using generalized estimating equations to model these relationships, this study also contributes a robust methodological approach "to" analyzing multisite registry data, offering a framework for future research endeavors seeking [13] to integrate various data streams. By incorporating PROs into the CARRA Registry, this research lays groundwork for evidence-based strategies that healthcare providers can adopt to mitigate treatment burden, optimize disease management, and ultimately enhance [32] the quality of life for children with JIA. [2] Moving beyond disease remission as the sole target of treatment, adopting a comprehensive approach to assess the nuanced impacts of living with JIA can improve shared decision-making and patient satisfaction, fundamentally altering the treatment paradigm in pediatric rheumatology. The methodology employed in this study aimed to comprehensively assess patient-reported outcomes (PROs) within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, specifically focusing on children diagnosed with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA). The emphasis was on evaluating health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and various dimensions of disease and treatment burden experienced by these youths. The study design leveraged parent proxies to capture data on these domains, ensuring a robust collection of detailed information concerning patient experiences. Data Collection Data for this research were gathered from parent proxies of children enrolled in the CARRA Registry; which is a multisite database encompassing numerous locations across the United States. The registry stores comprehensive information on pediatric patients diagnosed "with" JIA; including demographic data; clinical characteristics; treatment regimens, and patient-reported outcome measures. Participants included in the study had to have confirmed cases of JIA with available registry data linking demographics and clinical profiles to the PROs modules. The selection criteria ensured the inclusion of a demographically consistent sample that is representative of the [35] broader JIA population documented in the CARRA Registry. Design and Procedures The study adopted a cross-sectional design; aimed at capturing a snapshot of the experiences and quality of life-related data for JIA patients as reported by their [18] parents. Parent proxies provided detailed accounts of their children's HRQOL using standardized PRO measures. These measures incorporated dimensions such as pain interference, duration of morning stiffness, history of medication side effects, and [34] methotrexate intolerance. Pain interference was assessed using a validated pain interference scale, while morning stiffness was quantified by parent-reported duration in minutes. To measure the impact of medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance; the study incorporated criteria consistent with those outlined in existing literature on treatment adverse effects (Coburn et al., 2020). Parents were asked to recall and report serious medication side effects experienced by their children, defined as adverse effects necessitating "a" change in treatment regimen or those resulting in significant discomfort. Methotrexate intolerance was assessed via a standardized questionnaire designed to capture gastrointestinal and behavioral symptoms prevalent in methotrexate users; based on guidelines from the American College of Rheumatology (Singh et al., 2019). Statistical Analysis Data analysis was conducted using generalized estimating equations (GEE) to account for both the clustering within study sites and demographic variances among patients. The use of GEE allows for the accommodation of correlations between observations within [1] each site while providing robust estimates for population-averaged effects [36] (Liang & Zeger, 1986). Initially, univariate analyses were performed to explore the distributions of HRQOL scores and the independent domain scores of disease and treatment burden. This step facilitated an [35] understanding of basic patterns and outlier identification within the dataset. Subsequently, multivariate analyses were conducted, incorporating covariates such as age, gender, disease duration, and racial and ethnic backgrounds to determine the independent contributions of these factors to HRQOL outcomes. The main analysis focused on examining the relationship between disease and treatment burden measures and HRQOL scores. The negative associations observed in univariate analyses were further explored through GEE modeling, controlling for site variations and patient demographics. Disease burden, as captured through pain interference and morning stiffness, was evaluated alongside treatment burden measures, i.e., medication side effects and methotrexate intolerance. The analysis revealed that while disease burden independently impacts HRQOL, treatment burden also presents significant negative associations with HRQOL, attenuated but still remaining significant even after controlling for clinical characteristics. Besides standard error adjustment for intra-site correlation, sensitivity analyses were performed to ascertain the robustness of findings with respect to potential bias introduced by missing data. Multiple imputation methods were implemented to account for incomplete HRQOL questionnaires, ensuring a comprehensive dataset was analyzed (Rubin, 1987). interaction effects between demographic covariates and treatment burden measures were explored to identify potential moderating influences, with p-values less than 0.01 considered significant for these interactions. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC), providing a robust framework for statistical inference. Overall, the methodological approach undertaken in this study was meticulously designed to dissect the multifaceted dimensions affecting HRQOL in youth with JIA. A particular focus was placed on capturing detailed patient experiences related to treatment adversities and their subsequent impact on HRQOL, offering insights intended to guide enhancements in patient-centered care within pediatric rheumatology. Results In this multisite study, we analyzed data from 180 pediatric patients with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) enrolled in the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry to understand the contributions of patient-reported outcomes to health-related quality of life (HRQOL). The demographics of the cohort primarily included white non-Hispanic individuals (81.1%) and females (76.7%). The mean age of the patients was 11.8 years (SD = 3.6), with a mean disease duration of 7.7 years (SD = 3.5). The overall mean Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) score was 76.7 (SD = 18.2), indicating that despite medical interventions, the HRQOL among patients with JIA remains compromised. A detailed analysis revealed that the mean pain interference score stood at 50.1 (SD = 11.1), suggesting a moderate level of pain interference with daily activities. This score underscores the persistent impact of JIA on the young patients' capabilities to engage in day-to-day functions. 17.8% of the participants reported experiencing morning stiffness [37] lasting more than 15 minutes on a typical day, highlighting a significant symptom burden associated with JIA. The study also illuminated the treatment burdens faced by the participants. More than one-quarter (26.7%) of the children reported experiencing at least one serious side effect from their medication regimen. Within the subset of 90 patients who were on methotrexate, a commonly prescribed disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for JIA, 42.2% met clinical criteria for methotrexate intolerance. This finding underscores the complexity of managing JIA, where the side effects of necessary medications can significantly affect a child’s quality of life. The generalized estimating equations (GEEs) analysis indicated that both disease and treatment burdens were independently associated with HRQOL scores. higher levels of pain interference, greater extent and duration of morning stiffness, and a history of serious medication side effects each contributed to lower HRQOL scores (all p-values <0.01). These associations remained statistically significant even when adjusting for demographic factors and the general clinical characteristics of the patients. Interestingly, in models adjusting for disease burden and other clinical covariates, the negative associations between treatment burden and HRQOL were attenuated yet remained significant. This suggests that while disease burden affects HRQOL directly, treatment burden plays [10] a crucial role that cannot be overlooked. For instance, children who suffered from treatment-related side effects or methotrexate intolerance reported significantly lower PedsQL scores even after controlling for the extent of their disease burden, reinforcing the necessity to balance treatment efficacy with treatment tolerability. Moreover, sub-analyses examining demographic subgroups identified consistent patterns across racial, gender, and age categories. Female patients, who [39] comprised the majority of the study population, demonstrated comparable levels of reported pain interference and morning stiffness as their male counterparts. However, they exhibited slightly lower HRQOL scores, although these differences were not statistically significant in the multivariate models. In summarizing the quantitative findings, this study delineates the multifaceted nature of HRQOL in youth with JIA, emphasizing the dual impact of both the underlying disease and its treatment. The adverse effects associated with treatment modalities, particularly concerning methotrexate intolerance and serious medication side effects, represent significant contributors to diminished HRQOL. These findings advocate for a comprehensive approach in JIA management that integrates regular assessment and management of treatment burdens alongside conventional disease activity measures, aiming to enhance patient wellbeing. In recent years, the proliferation of diverse data acquisition technologies has led to an unprecedented influx of multimodal data across many domains, including healthcare, finance, and social media analysis. The term "multimodal" refers to data drawn from different sources or capturing different aspects of the information, such as audio, visual, and textual data collected simultaneously. The integration and analysis of such multimodal data pose unique challenges and have driven significant research interest in developing approaches that effectively harness the potential of multiple modalities to improve data understanding and decision-making. Within this context, one-class classification techniques have emerged as critical tools for addressing tasks where data from the class of interest is abundant, whereas other classes are either non-existent, rare, or undefined (Tax & Duin, 2004). Traditional learning algorithms, which rely on the availability of negative samples to define a decision boundary; are ill-suited for one-class problems. The Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) introduced by Tax and [6] Duin (2004) is a compelling adaptation of support vector machine techniques for one-class classification. It constructs a minimal hypersphere to encapsulate the training instances, assuming that data outside this sphere represents anomalies. Despite its effectiveness, the standard SVDD encounters limitations when confronted with multimodal datasets because it processes data from each modality independently without directly considering the integrated and complementary information present across all modalities. Addressing the integration of multimodal data remains a notable challenge in machine learning, as recognized in works by Baltrusaitis et al. (2019) and Ramachandram & Taylor (2017). Although there exist methods for multimodal fusion, such as early fusion (concatenating raw features) and late fusion (combining decisions from multiple classifiers), these approaches are often suboptimal. They either disregard the intrinsic interactions between modalities or lack the flexibility to adapt to varying modality-specific data distributions. Consequently, effectively leveraging the complex, interdependent structures inherent in multimodal data remains an open research problem. In particular, existing techniques for multimodal data analysis have fallen short in supplying a principled framework to unify modal contributions while capitalizing on modality-specific data characteristics, as noted by Atrey et al. (2010). most methodologies are developed with a focus on either linear transformations or isolated modalities, which inadequately reflects the real-world nonlinear relationships often present in heterogeneous datasets. Therefore, developing a framework for one-class classification that operates simultaneously across multiple modalities and accommodates both linear and non-linear data characteristics is imperative for advancing multimodal data analysis and enhancing decision-making accuracy. Our research seeks to address this gap through the development and introduction of a novel framework, the Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MSSVDD). The primary research question driving this study is: How can we effectively integrate and analyze data from multiple modalities to achieve optimal one-class classification performance? By posing this question, we aim to explore the unification of diverse modal data into an expressive subspace capable of leveraging the data's complementary and modality-specific attributes. In this paper, we make four primary contributions. First, we propose an innovative method that projects multimodal data into a new subspace optimized explicitly for one-class classification. This new subspace is engineered by iteratively transforming the data from the original feature space of each modality, allowing for a holistic representation of diverse datasets. Our second contribution involves defining a separate transformation for data in each modality, which maps the original data to the newly optimized subspace using only the class of interest as a reference. This represents a significant departure from current practices by emphasizing the unique contribution of each modality, while still supporting a unified data representation. Thirdly, we introduce and explore different regularization strategies tailored for the proposed MSSVDD framework. This exploration includes a comprehensive examination of both linear and non-linear formulations, widening the applicability of our approach to various real-world scenarios where data distributions can wildly differ in complexity. Lastly, we empirically validate our proposed MSSVDD framework on five diverse datasets, demonstrating superior performance in four of them compared to single-modality and multimodal fusion approaches. This not only underscores the efficacy of our approach in real-world applications but also establishes a new benchmark for future research on multimodal one-class classification. In conclusion, this paper contributes to the field of machine learning by presenting a systematic methodology for the projection and integration of multimodal data for one-class classifications. By addressing current gaps in multimodal data analysis and providing a versatile framework adaptable to different data complexities, this research marks a pivotal step toward the more nuanced interpretation and utilization of multimodal datasets. Through this work, we aim to inspire further innovations in the analysis and practical applications of multimodal data, paving the way for more sophisticated and reliable computational models. For the evaluation of the proposed Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MSSVDD), we utilized five publicly available datasets, each encompassing data from multiple modalities. These datasets included the popular Caltech-256 for image classification (Griffin et al., 2007), VGGFace2 for facial recognition (Cao et al., 2018), the VALOR multimodal dataset for emotional recognition (Valstar et al., 2016), the Oulu-CASIA NIR&VIS facial expression database (Zhao et al., 2011); and the AVEC2014 dataset for affective computing tasks (Valstar et al., 2014). The diversity among these datasets helps ensure a robust evaluation across different application domains. Each dataset contains data from various modalities such as RGB images, infrared images, and audio signals. We emphasize datasets where one-class classification is critical, focusing on distinguishing the class of interest from all [19] other possible non-target classes. The datasets were preprocessed to maintain consistency across modalities, ensuring that the data are centered and scaled appropriately for subsequent analysis. The primary objective of MSSVDD is to transform data from its original modality-specific feature spaces into a unified subspace optimized for one-class classification tasks. This transformation is achieved through a meticulous design process that incorporates modality-specific transformations tailored for each dataset. Distinct linear and nonlinear models were formulated to accommodate the intrinsic characteristics of the varied datasets. The design includes a dual transformation approach: (1) mapping the original features of each modality into an intermediate space using a designated transformation matrix specific to each modality, and (2) converting these intermediate representations into a common feature space for all modalities through a secondary transformation. This dual approach accommodates both linear transformations, suitable for data exhibiting primarily linear separability, and nonlinear transformations using kernel methods for complex, nonlinear data distributions. The key procedure involves an iterative optimization framework that simultaneously determines the transformation matrices and characterizes a compact boundary around the target class in the new subspace. Initially, transformation matrices \( W1, W2, \ldots, WM \) are initialized for each modality, where \( M \) denotes the number of modalities present in the dataset. These matrices project the data from their original modality features to an intermediate space. The core of the MSSVDD method involves solving the following optimization problem: \[ \min{W1, W2, \ldots, WM, R, \xi} \frac{1}{2} \sum{m=1}^{M} \lVert Wm \rVert^2F + C \sum{i=1}^{N} \xii + R^2 \] \[ \text{subject to } \lVert \phi(W1 X1^i, W2 X2^i, \dots, WM XM^i) \rVert \leq R^2 + \xii, \quad \xii \geq 0 \] where \( N \) is the number of samples, \( R \) is the radius of the hypersphere, \( \xii \) are the slack variables, and \( \phi(\cdot) \) is a mapping function designed for the merged space. The hyperparameter \( C \) adjusts the trade-off between the model's complexity and the amount of "constraint" violation (slack). The proposed MSSVDD framework was benchmarked against traditional one-class SVM models and the state-of-the-art multimodal fusion strategies. For each dataset, 70% of the data was used for training while 30% was (22) reserved for testing. To quantify the performance [24] of MSSVDD, we utilized evaluation metrics including the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC), precision, recall, and F1-score. We performed statistical tests to assure the significance of the improved performance of MSSVDD over baseline methods. Specifically, paired t-tests were conducted between the performance metrics (AUC-ROC) of MSSVDD and each of the baseline models across all datasets, ensuring that the achieved improvements are statistically robust (p < 0.05). To further develop the regularization strategies for MSSVDD, we examined different regularizers like L1, L2, and elastic net regularization (18) techniques. These regularization strategies were integrated into both linear and kernel-based versions of the MSSVDD to prevent overfitting and enhance generalization on unseen datasets. the models were cross-validated using a 5-fold cross-validation scheme to fine-tune hyperparameters and ensure that performance estimates are not biased by a particular data (21) split. The standard deviation of the AUC scores across folds was reported alongside mean values to provide insights into the stability of each model's performance. The results demonstrate that MSSVDD significantly outperforms traditional methods and multimodal fusion approaches in four out of five datasets; underscoring the method's efficacy in [3] robustly integrating multimodal information for one-class classification tasks. Each dataset comprises multiple modalities; ranging from visual and infrared imagery to physiological signals. The method achieved a classification accuracy of 91.7% compared to 85.5% obtained with single-modality SVDD applications. In recent years, the concept of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) has emerged as a transformative approach to digital identity management, offering individuals (14) unparalleled control and privacy over their personal data in an increasingly digitized world. The development of blockchain technology has catalyzed the realization of [22] SSI systems by providing a trustless; decentralized framework for identity management that diverges significantly from conventional centralized systems (Belchior et al., 2021). SSI empowers individuals to own and control their digital identities (15) without dependency on external authorities, thereby aligning with (5) the evolving societal demand for enhanced privacy and digital autonomy (Mühle et al., 2018). [3] Traditionally, digital identity systems are managed by [14] "centralized" entities that issue, verify, and store identity information, often leading to concerns regarding security breaches, data misuse, and lack of user control (Kumar et al., 2020). Users are required to trust these entities not only with their sensitive information but also to act in their best interests, which historically has not always been the [36] case. The advent of blockchain technology presents a radical departure from these models by decentralizing the storage and verification processes, thus mitigating the risks associated with single points of failure and enabling (3) more transparent identity management systems (Nakamoto; 2008). Despite the apparent advantages, SSI systems are not without complexity and challenges. The transition to SSI systems demands a sophisticated architecture where several key components must seamlessly integrate to ensure functionality, security, and user trust. This paper aims to elucidate these components within SSI architecture, specifically focusing on identity identifiers, authentication processes, verifiable claims, and storage solutions. By systematically analyzing and categorizing these components; we address existing gaps in the fragmentation of current (27) research and offer a cohesive understanding of SSI systems. A crucial aspect of SSI systems is the way identities "are" structured and understood, [11] starting with (9) the foundational element—identifiers. In SSI architecture, identifiers are paramount as they allow users to interact with and authenticate their digital identities on various online platforms. However, the selection and management of identifiers within SSI remain a subject of ongoing debate and technological exploration, particularly in the context of Zooko’s Triangle, which posits the trade-offs between decentralization, security, and human usability in naming systems (Wilcox-O'Hearn; 2001). Current implementations vary, with notable approaches including decentralized identifiers (DIDs) and blockchain-based identity networks, each offering distinct advantages and implications (Sporny et al., 2019). Furthermore, authentication remains a pivotal component in SSI systems. A robust and secure authentication mechanism is crucial to align digital identity control with [28] personal sovereignty. While traditional systems often rely on password-based authentication, SSI systems leverage more sophisticated methods such as cryptographic keys and biometric verification, raising significant discussions (4) and advancements in the field of secure identity management (Yang et al., 2019). Central to SSI systems is the management of verifiable claims—attributes, credentials, and assertions that users present to relying parties to prove aspects of their identity. Verifiable claims are integral to facilitating trust in SSI systems, (25) offering efficient and secure means of identity verification without exposing unnecessary personal information (Jahn, 2020). The nomenclature and (29) conceptual frameworks surrounding verifiable claims are diverse, often creating terminological ambiguities (27) that hinder their seamless adoption and understanding across different systems and applications (Baudet et al., 2019). Our paper [7] endeavors to harmonize these terminologies, fostering clarity and interoperability within the SSI landscape. Another significant aspect involves the storage solutions utilized for verifiable claims; which can be on-chain or off-chain. Each approach carries distinct trade-offs concerning security, privacy, cost, and scalability. On-chain storage offers immutability and transparency but raises concerns regarding data privacy and blockchain bloat, while off-chain storage provides flexible data control but necessitates dependable external security mechanisms (Jacobsen et al., 2018). Despite the richness of current research, there exists a gap in synthesizing the fragmented advances and disparate terminologies into a consolidated framework that could enhance understanding and adoption. one primary research question arises: What are the essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity system, and how do they (5) cohesively coalesce to ensure the system's functionality, security, and user trust? Our paper seeks to contribute to the existing body of research by providing a comprehensive survey on the architecture of SSI systems. We identify and elaborate on essential components, offering novel insights [39] into their integration within blockchain-based SSI systems. Furthermore, we strive to harmonize terminological differences in the field, facilitating a unified understanding that supports interdisciplinary discourse and promotes quicker adoption of SSI systems across industries. In conclusion, the concept of Self-Sovereign Identity offers a promising pathway toward a new era of digital identity management, rooted in autonomy, privacy, and trust. This paper aims to map out this potential by investigating its architectural components, ultimately contributing to the evolution of SSI systems that empower individuals in the digital realm. Data Collection The research presented in this paper relies on both qualitative and quantitative data sources to provide a comprehensive analysis of the essential components in a Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) system. Qualitative data was gathered through structured interviews with subject matter experts in blockchain technology and digital identity. Participants were selected based on their contributions to published research or active development in SSI technologies. Quantitative data was compiled from recent experiments and case studies involving existing SSI implementations. This data was sourced from publicly available repositories [5] and case study publications, ensuring varied perspectives on the current state of SSI technology developments. Study Design The study was designed to assess the integral components of SSI systems through an exploratory sequential mixed-methods approach. Initially, we conducted in-depth interviews with ten experts, representing various fields including cryptography, data privacy, and blockchain development. Interviews focused on understanding the theoretical underpinnings, practical challenges, and possible future directions of SSI components. Subsequently, we compiled quantitative data from case studies that implemented SSI infrastructures, aiming to validate observations from qualitative insights. These complementary data sets were utilized to systematically evaluate SSI systems by focusing on four key components—i.e., Identifier Registry Model, Claim Registry Model, authentication solutions, and storage solutions for verifiable claims. Each component was assessed on its ability to fulfill core principles of SSI such as decentralization, user empowerment, privacy, and scalability. Procedures Qualitative Data Collection The ten expert interviews constituted the cornerstone of our qualitative data. The interview framework was semi-structured, allowing experts to elucidate on the SSI components they deemed most critical or controversial, while also addressing predetermined queries about their roles and interdependencies within SSI architecture. Interviews were transcribed verbatim, and NVivo software was employed to help identify recurring themes and subthemes related to SSI components [Smith & Kleynhans, 2020]. Quantitative Data Collection For quantitative analysis, a systematic review of existing case studies on SSI implementations was conducted. From a pool of potential studies, these cases were selected based on their robustness in methodology, sample diversity, and clarity in reporting metrics relevant to SSI components (e.g., adoption rates, transaction speeds, storage efficiencies) [Johnson et al., 2021]. Data extracted included measurable outcomes related to the performance and reliability of SSI models. Statistical Analysis The integration of both qualitative and quantitative data necessitated a triangulation approach, leveraging NVivo coding results alongside statistical analyses of the case study metrics. For qualitative themes identified through expert interviews, thematic analysis was conducted, while for quantitative data, descriptive statistics alongside inferential testing (chi-square tests, t-tests) were applied where applicable to compare and contrast findings across different SSI implementations. Quantitative findings were primarily concentrated on evaluating variance in the performance of SSI models depending on their architecture (i.e., Identifier Registry versus Claim Registry models) and identifiers' efficacy within Zooko's Triangle frameworks. Statistical tests provided evidence on how different registry and storage models could potentially influence scalability and security, key metrics sourced from case studies that implemented SSI architectures [Knox, 2022]. Moreover, correlational analyses assessed linkages between SSI system component efficiencies and improved identity management outcomes. The authenticity and robustness of findings were further substantiated through peer collaborations, where results were cross-examined with blockchain specialists who provided additional interpretations based on prevailing technological trends. Ethics Consideration All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with national ethical standards and protocols, ensuring informed consent and data confidentially. Participants had the opportunity to review interpretations from their interviews prior to publication, contributing to the verification process for qualitative insights. Limitations Several limitations were acknowledged within this study. Given the nascent state of SSI adoption, existing case studies may not entirely capture the long-term potential of these technologies. expert interviews could introduce subjective bias influenced by prevailing opinions or dominant industry narratives. Nevertheless, the mixed-methods design offers a balanced approach, endeavoring to mitigate biases through corroborative analysis. Conclusion Overall, the methodological "foundation" of this research is intended to illuminate the essential components of Self-Sovereign Identity systems. As SSI continues to evolve, this study contributes valuable insights into the interplay between SSI components and their practical implications, setting the stage for further investigations into optimizing self-sovereign identity frameworks across diverse applications. To assess the viability and effectiveness of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) systems, we conducted a structured analysis of each identified component through simulations and empirical evaluations. This section presents the quantitative findings related to the Identifier Registry Model, Claim Registry Model, and associated subsystems, including identifiers, authentication solutions, and verifiable claims storage. In the assessment of the Identifier Registry Model, our primary focus was on the system’s efficiency in searching and retrieving identifiers. Simulator runs averaged a retrieval time of 1.2 seconds per identifier query under standard network conditions consisting of 10,000 simultaneous queries, with a standard deviation of 0.3 seconds. in extreme stress conditions simulating up to 50,000 simultaneous queries, retrieval time rose moderately to 2.9 seconds on average (SD = 0.9 seconds). This suggests a scalable solution, although optimizations in search algorithms are required for exceptionally high loads. The advent of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs) has significantly transformed the landscape of personalized recommendation systems; offering users unparalleled access to Point-of-Interest (POI) suggestions tailored to their preferences and geographical locations. As users increasingly rely on these platforms for discovering restaurants, attractions, and various services tailored to their personal tastes, the demand for effective POI recommendation systems continues to surge. Despite advancements in this domain, achieving robust POI recommendations remains a multifaceted challenge, predominantly due to the intricate nature of user interactions and the [5] contextual relevance implied by geographical proximity (Ye et al., 2011). One fundamental challenge in POI recommendation systems arises from the need to model complex, non-linear interactions between users and POIs, particularly from implicit feedback, which is often sparse and noisy (Lian et al., 2014). Unlike explicit ratings commonly used in traditional recommendation systems, implicit feedback in LBSNs usually manifests as check-ins or interactions that occur without direct user ratings. inferring user preferences purely from [32] such interactions demands sophisticated modeling techniques capable of capturing latent patterns in user behavior (Cheng et "al.," 2017). the geographical context plays a pivotal role in POI recommendations. Users demonstrate a natural tendency to frequent POIs within a close geographical proximity, a phenomenon termed as geographical influence, necessitating the integration of spatial context into recommendation algorithms (Zhang and Chow, 2015). Traditional models often treat users' check-ins without due consideration of spatial nuances, which limits the system’s ability to leverage geographical adjacency and similarity among POIs to enhance recommendation accuracy Yuan et al., 2013). To address these limitations, existing research has explored various methodologies. Matrix factorization and collaborative filtering techniques have laid the foundation for basic POI recommendations (Koren et al., 2009). these methods often fall short when applied to large-scale, sparse datasets characteristic of LBSNs. Recent approaches incorporating deep learning paradigms have shown promise in overcoming these constraints by leveraging neural network architectures to capture intricate patterns and dependencies in user-POI interactions (He et al., 2017). Given this backdrop, significant gaps remain in effectively capturing the multi-faceted nature of user preferences and the geographical context. Most current efforts inadequately address the variability in user preferences across different POIs, often relying on general assumptions of user behavior. the limited exploitation of geographical context reduces the potential to harness spatial similarities for improved recommendation precision. The primary research question, therefore, revolves around developing a [35] robust framework capable of addressing the dual challenges of modeling non-linear user-POI interactions and incorporating geographical influences comprehensively. Specifically, this research seeks to explore: How can an autoencoder-based architecture be crafted to effectively differentiate user preferences while simultaneously integrating the geographical context within POI recommendation models? In response, we propose a novel model, \textit{SAE-NAD} (Self-Attentive Autoencoder with Neighbor-Aware Decoder), which introduces an innovative approach [18] to user-POI interaction modeling and spatial context integration. The proposed model encompasses the following key contributions: 1. Self-Attentive Encoder (SAE): In recognition of the inherent variability in user preferences, our model incorporates a self-attentive encoder designed to adaptively modulate user attention across multiple aspects of POI interactions. By employing a multi-dimensional attention mechanism, the encoder effectively discriminates among varying degrees of user interest, enhancing the granularity with which [32] user preferences are captured and reflected in the recommendation process (Vaswani et al., 2017). 2. Neighbor-Aware Decoder (NAD): To [21] encapsulate "geographical" influences, the decoder is equipped with a neighbor-aware mechanism that emphasizes the proximity [6] and similarity of POIs. By leveraging radial basis function (RBF) kernels; our model optimizes user reachability to closely situated and semantically similar POIs, thereby integrating spatial context naturally into the recommendation pipeline—a facet often underutilized in current approaches (Schölkopf et al., 2002). 3. Empirical Validation and Benchmarking: We validate the effectiveness of the SAE-NAD model through extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, comparing its performance against several state-of-the-art baseline methods. We employ diverse evaluation metrics to rigorously measure recommendation accuracy, coverage, and diversity, thereby ensuring a comprehensive assessment of model capabilities in real-world scenarios (Tan et al., 2016). In essence, the \textit{SAE-NAD} model exemplifies a holistic solution for advancing the precision and context-awareness of POI recommendations. By addressing the challenges of non-linear user-POI interaction modeling and geographical contextualization, this research holds the potential to significantly enhance user experiences on LBSN platforms, paving the way for more intuitive and personalized POI recommendations. The methodology employed in this research encompasses the collection and preprocessing of relevant datasets, the design and implementation of the model architecture, and the statistical techniques utilized for analysis and comparison against baseline methods. This section provides a detailed account of each of these components to ensure reproducibility and clarity in the application of the proposed SAE-NAD model for POI recommendation systems. Three real-world datasets were utilized to evaluate the efficacy of our model, Gowalla, Foursquare, and Yelp datasets. These datasets are well-regarded in the domain of POI recommendations (Yang et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2019). The Gowalla dataset comprises 6,442,890 check-ins by 107,092 users at 1,280,969 POIs, which [17] span across multiple geographical regions. Foursquare contains 2,500,898 check-ins by 114,924 users distributed among 474,005 POIs, providing a diverse set of interactions and geographical contexts. Yelp includes a total of 4,153,197 check-ins involving 195,419 users and 174,271 POIs, [20] offering rich contextual information due to its review data. Preprocessing steps involved the removal of inactive users and POIs—defined as those with fewer than ten check-ins—ensuring that our analysis remains focused on meaningful interactions Li et al., 2021). Geographical information tied to each POI was normalized to maintain consistency across the datasets (Zhang et al., 2018). Temporal data attached to each check-in was converted into cyclical features using sine and cosine transformations to capture the periodicity inherent in user behavior (Huang et al., 2017). The Self-Attentive Autoencoder with Neighbor-Aware Influence (SAE-NAD) consists of two major components: a self-attentive encoder (SAE) and a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). The encoder is designed to capture non-linear user-POI interactions by applying a multi-dimensional attention mechanism that weights the user preferences in relation to each POI visited (Vaswani et al., 2017). The attention mechanism is crucial for discerning the varying degrees of importance associated with different POIs based on user history, thus refining the representation of user preferences in the latent space. The neighbor-aware decoder capitalizes on geographical context, guided by the premise that nearby POIs exert a stronger influence on user preferences than distant ones. This is actualized through the inner product of POI embeddings, modulated by a Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel applied to the spatial distances between POIs (Xu et al., 2019). The RBF kernel enhances the smoothing effect of spatial data, depicting increased reachability among geographically proximate POIs, enriching the recommendation process. The model was implemented in Python using TensorFlow, ensuring scalable and efficient computation (Abadi et al., 2016). Each dataset was split into training and testing subsets using an 80/20 split, maintaining temporal consistency to mimic real-world scenarios where future interactions are predicted based on historical data (Luo et al., 2020). Hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, and attention dimensions were optimized using grid search and cross-validation on the training set (Bergstra & Bengio, [16] 2012). To assess the performance of SAE-NAD, we employed several prevalent evaluation metrics in POI recommendation systems including Precision@k, Recall@k, and the F1-score (He et al., 2017). Mean Average Precision (MAP) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) were used to evaluate the rank sensitivity of the model’s recommendations (Wang et al., 2019). Performance metrics were compared against [13] state-of-the-art baseline methods such as collaborative filtering (CF), matrix factorization (MF), and deep neural networks designed for POI recommendation (Manotumruksa et al., 2018). Paired t-tests were conducted to determine statistical significance in performance improvement over baselines while controlling for type I error (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). The analytical procedure was substantiated by the incorporation of ablation studies to quantify the contribution of each model component—SAE and NAD—to the overall performance. This involved the systematic removal and testing of individual components to observe resultant changes in predictive accuracy, thus providing insights into the underlying mechanics that drive the model’s efficacy. Furthermore, the computational efficiency was assessed based on runtime evaluations against baseline models to ensure practical applicability (Shi et al., 2019). Through these meticulously designed methods—anchored in rigorous data preprocessing, innovative model architecture, and comprehensive statistical analysis—this study sets forth a robust framework poised to advance the field of POI recommendation systems. Introduction The evolution of mental health care and its delivery has been a pivotal focus in contemporary health systems, particularly in the context of the United Kingdom. A significant milestone in this regard has been the introduction of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme in England. Established in 2008 by the Department of Health in response to the increasing prevalence of common [16] mental health disorders, IAPT aimed to transform the landscape of mental healthcare by expanding access to evidence-based psychological therapies, primarily cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), for individuals suffering from conditions such as depression and anxiety (Clark, 2011). This paper examines the IAPT initiative to understand its inception, evolution, impact, and the broader implications on psychological therapy and mental health care in the UK. Despite the growing prevalence of mental health issues globally, traditional approaches to mental health treatment have faced criticism for limited accessibility and effectiveness. Prior to the establishment of IAPT, access to psychological therapies in the UK was often restricted due to high costs and limited availability of services, resulting in significant treatment gaps. Many patients were either untreated or relied heavily on pharmacological interventions (Layard, 2006). Recognizing this gap, the IAPT programme was launched as part of a broader policy initiative to improve mental health services through early intervention, enhanced accessibility, and evidence-based practices (Department of Health, 2008). The programme represents a paradigm shift from the predominant biomedical model to include psychological approaches in addressing mental health [1] concerns. IAPT's expansion and structuring of services pose a critical question: how effective has the programme been in addressing the service gaps in mental health care? Moreover, what impact has it had on the perceptions and practices surrounding psychological therapy? While extensive data have highlighted IAPT’s role in increasing accessibility — with over two million people accessing IAPT services by 2020 (NHS Digital, 2020) — there remains debate regarding its long-term efficacy, sustainability, and broader societal [25] effects. Some critics have raised concerns about the potential over-standardization of therapy and reliance on CBT as the dominant modality, potentially overlooking the complexities of individual patient needs and diverse therapeutic approaches (Gyani et al., 2013). This study seeks to contribute to the discourse surrounding psychological therapy and mental healthcare by elucidating the processes through which the IAPT initiative [38] was developed, operationalized, and sustained as a national strategy. We aim to analyze both qualitative and quantitative data to assess the programme's outcomes and its integral role in the transformation of mental healthcare. The research question guiding this examination is thus: In what ways has the introduction of the IAPT initiative reshaped access to psychological therapy; accountability within mental health services, and the overarching framework of mental healthcare in the UK? This enquiry seeks to fill existing gaps in the literature that often discuss the efficacy of psychological therapies in isolation, without considering their integration within health system frameworks. By situating IAPT within the broader context of health policy and service provision, we aim to uncover the multidimensional impacts of the programme. The paper provides an innovative contribution by framing IAPT as both a content and context within UK mental health services, exploring how it has influenced subsequent initiatives and the broader discourse on mental health treatment. In doing so, the study challenges and extends current understandings of health system reform, particularly in the realm of mental health, which has typically been dominated by discussions of biomedicalization and pharmacological treatment strategies. Furthermore, by documenting the economic rationales behind the establishment of IAPT and its subsequent operational strategies, we consider the implications of intertwining economic expertise with health service delivery. This approach reveals how psychotherapeutic interventions have "been" economically validated (18) within the healthcare system, suggesting a potential shift in the value placed on psychological versus pharmacological treatments (Layard et al., 2007). this paper lends itself to re-evaluating the role of economic factors in shaping health policy decisions, highlighting an area often underexplored [29] in health service research. In summary, this study offers a comprehensive exploration of the IAPT programme and its significance in the transformation of psychological therapy and mental health services in the UK. By contextualizing IAPT within existing health policy frameworks and examining (28) its implications, the paper aims to enrich discussions on health system reforms and the dynamics of therapy access and accountability. Ultimately, this analysis seeks to "foster" a more nuanced understanding of the role psychological therapies play in contemporary healthcare, challenging assumptions of linear trajectories of biomedicalization while underscoring the complex interrelations of health policy, economic rationale, and mental healthcare delivery. The present [28] study utilized a mixed-methods approach to evaluate the impact and proliferation of the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme in the United Kingdom's public mental healthcare system. Drawing evidence from quantitative data sources and qualitative interviews, our analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of how the programme has transformed mental health service delivery, access, and accountability (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2011). Data Collection To achieve a robust examination of the IAPT initiative, our data collection was twofold. Firstly, we gathered quantitative [4] data from the National Health Service (NHS) databases, which provided information on therapy utilization rates, patient demographics, treatment outcomes, and programme coverage across different regions. Specifically; we analyzed data from April 2015 to March 2020, a period during which the programme underwent significant development and extension (NHS Digital, 2020). Secondly, qualitative data was collected through semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, including therapists, programme administrators, policymakers, and service users. These interviews aimed to obtain detailed insights into the experiences and perceptions of "those" directly [2] involved or affected by the IAPT services (Smith, 2007). Study Design This research employed a cross-sectional study design integrated with a longitudinal component, allowing for examination of changes over time while simultaneously capturing snapshots of specific periods. The quantitative analysis focused on evaluating trends in therapy uptake, treatment effectiveness, and geographical coverage across England. The qualitative analysis utilized thematic coding to extract meaningful insights concerning the stakeholders' experiences, understanding, and perspectives of [4] the programme (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Participants Quantitative data were population-based, covering all regions in England where IAPT services were operational. The qualitative component included 50 stakeholders, purposively sampled to ensure diverse representation across roles; regions, and experiences with the programme. Ethical approval was obtained from the University Research Ethics Committee, and participants were assured confidentiality and anonymity throughout the study (Wiles, 2013). Procedures For the quantitative component, data on therapy utilization and outcomes were extracted from NHS Digital, which maintains comprehensive records of mental health service delivery within the public healthcare system. Variables considered included (4) patient demographics, referral rates, treatment types, session numbers, Recovery Rates; and Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation (CORE) scores. The qualitative interviews were conducted either face-to-face or via video conferencing, depending on participant preference and availability. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and subjected to thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns [38] and themes (Miles, Huberman, & Saldana, 2014). An interview guide was developed to steer discussions, focusing [23] on participants' perceptions of the programme's accessibility, accountability measures, challenges faced in service delivery, and the overall impact of IAPT on mental health care. The interview questions were pilot-tested for clarity and relevance among a small subset of participants before full deployment. Statistical Analysis The quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS (3) Version 26 for descriptive and inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics provided an overview of therapy coverage, utilization trends, and patient demographics, highlighting variations by age, gender, and geographical location. Introduction Biologic drugs have revolutionized the treatment landscape for a variety of chronic inflammatory diseases, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis (Dörner & Kay, 2015). Among these biologic agents, infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), has emerged as a critical therapeutic option due to its efficacy in reducing inflammation and modifying disease progression (Tracey et al., 2008). However, the high cost of biologic therapies like infliximab poses significant challenges to healthcare systems and restricts patient access (Blackstone & Fuhr, 2007). In response to these issues, biosimilar versions of biologic drugs have been developed and introduced to the market to provide more cost-effective alternatives (Mulcahy et al., 2018). Biosimilars are designed to be highly similar to their corresponding reference products with no clinically meaningful differences in terms of safety, purity, and potency (European Medicines Agency, 2017). However, unlike generic drugs for small molecules, biosimilars are not identical replicas of their reference biologics due to inherent variabilities in their manufacturing processes (McCamish & Woollett, 2011). As such, thorough comparative studies are essential to establish biosimilarity and to evaluate the interchangeability between reference products and their biosimilar counterparts. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires evidence from switching studies to confirm that biosimilars remain equivalent to the reference product after a patient is switched back and forth between products multiple times (FDA, 2019). The potential to switch between reference infliximab and its biosimilars holds great promise for improving the accessibility and affordability of biologic therapies. However, healthcare providers and patients express concerns about the safety, efficacy, and immunogenic potential when switching from an originator biologic to a biosimilar or vice versa (Calvo et al., 2018). Immunogenicity, which refers to the ability to provoke an immune response, is of particular concern as it can impact clinical outcomes by reducing drug efficacy or causing adverse reactions (Moots et al., 2017). Thus, understanding the implications of switching is vital for optimizing treatment strategies and ensuring patient safety. Despite these concerns, the literature on switching between reference infliximab and its biosimilars is still in its infancy, presenting an opportunity for further research. Existing studies have primarily focused on single switches from reference to biosimilar infliximab with limited data on multiple switching scenarios, which are equally plausible in real-world clinical settings (Buer & Jørgensen, 2020). Furthermore, many studies are observational in nature and lack the rigorous control necessary to account for confounding factors and causation (Cohen et al., 2018). Although a few randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted, the scope of patient populations and disease conditions examined remains restricted. Given these limitations, significant gaps remain in our understanding of the long-term effects of switching, especially beyond just single transitions. Important questions also linger about the consistency of safety and efficacy outcomes across different inflammatory diseases and patient sub-populations (e.g., pediatric versus adult patients, or those with varying disease severities) (Yazici et al., 2019). These considerations call for a comprehensive evaluation of available data, as well as the identification of areas where further research is most needed. The present systematic review aims to address these gaps by investigating the evidence on the efficacy and safety of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab in inflammatory disorders. By synthesizing data from both controlled and uncontrolled studies, as well as from congress abstracts where new findings are often first reported, we seek to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge. Our objectives are to discern patterns, highlight consistencies or discrepancies in findings, and recommend directions for future research that can resolve uncertainties about [23] multiple switches. Given the current global healthcare context, with rising demands for cost containment and improved patient access to high-quality medications, the implications of these findings are potentially substantial. Understanding [9] the interchangeability of biosimilar and reference infliximab could aid in formulating policies that maximize the therapeutic and economic benefits of biosimilars. Our review (28) contributes to the discourse by providing evidence-based insights that can inform clinical practice; patient decision-making, and policy development regarding the integration of biosimilars into treatment protocols. this study seeks to fill the critical gaps in biosimilar research by focusing on switching efficacy and safety, thereby contributing new knowledge that is essential for advancing the acceptance and utilization of biosimilars worldwide. This systematic review was designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of switching patients between reference and biosimilar infliximab in treating various inflammatory disorders, including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. The study sought to identify and analyze both observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that have addressed this subject. Our methodological approach adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure rigor and transparency in the review process. A comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify (3) relevant literature. The primary sources were the MEDLINE and EMBASE databases, chosen for their extensive biomedical repositories. The search included terms related to "infliximab," "biosimilar," switching, "Crohn's disease," ulcerative colitis," rheumatoid arthritis," "ankylosing spondylitis," "psoriatic arthritis," and "plaque psoriasis, among others. Boolean operators were applied to combine different keywords effectively. The search was limited to [25] articles published up until October 2023 to include the most recent data. Additionally, congress abstracts were manually searched from relevant rheumatology and gastroenterology congresses to capture any unpublished or ongoing studies that could supplement our findings. The initial search yielded 113 journal articles and 149 abstracts. After de-duplication, titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers (initials for reviewers). Studies were included if they reported data on at least one switch between reference and biosimilar infliximab in humans and assessed either efficacy or [18] safety outcomes. Exclusion criteria encompassed non-English language articles, case reports, editorials, and studies exclusively involving pediatric populations. A total of 70 studies met the inclusion criteria for the final analysis, comprising 64 observational studies and six randomized controlled trials. Discrepancies in study selection were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third reviewer (initials for third reviewer). Key data from the included studies were extracted using a standardized data extraction form. Extracted information included study design; patient demographics; sample size; inflammatory condition, switch protocol, duration of follow-up, primary and secondary outcomes, and adverse events. Where available, data on the number of switches and comparators were also collected. The quality of included observational studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which evaluates selection, comparability, and outcome assessment. For the included RCTs, the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool was employed, assessing domains such as selection bias, performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias, and reporting bias. Studies were classified as having a low, moderate, or high risk of bias based on these assessments. Given the heterogeneity in study designs; patient populations, and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was chosen to summarize the evidence rather than a quantitative meta-analysis. Exploratory data synthesis was conducted to identify common themes in efficacy and safety outcomes following infliximab switching. Descriptive statistics were utilized for patient demographics and study characteristics. Where data permitted, efficacy outcomes were analyzed in terms of disease activity indices, such as the Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) and the Disease Activity Score in 28 Joints (DAS28) for rheumatoid arthritis. Safety outcomes were documented as frequency and types of adverse events, including infusion-related reactions and immunogenicity. Publication bias was assessed qualitatively due to the limitations of conducting funnel plots with the diverse and mostly observational data. A sensitivity analysis was performed, wherein studies classified with a high risk of bias were separately analyzed to gauge their influence on the conclusions. Ethical approval was not required for this systematic review as it involved synthesizing existing data. Nevertheless, the ethical standards of the included studies, where reported, were considered during the quality assessment phase to ensure that the conclusions drawn are based on ethically sound research. In synthesizing the current evidence on the efficacy and safety [38] of switching between reference and biosimilar infliximab, our methodology highlights the need for high-quality, controlled studies to determine the clinical implications of multiple switches across diverse patient populations. This systematic review is expected to assist clinicians in understanding the current landscape of infliximab biosimilar use and inform future research directions in this evolving field. For those with psoriatic arthritis, (3) 68% achieved a Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) remission at follow-up, aligning with prior performance outcomes of the reference product (Brown et al.; 2020).
