The rigorous evaluation of pharmaceuticals through clinical drug trials is a cornerstone of evidence-based medicine, aiming to ensure that new medications are both safe and effective before (16) they reach patients. While internal validity—guaranteeing that the trial's results are applicable to the experimental conditions—remains a primary focus, the external validity, or generalizability; of these trials is equally vital. External validity assesses the extent to which the findings can be applied beyond the controlled conditions of the study, particularly to real-world settings such as general practice. The ability of healthcare providers [27] to extrapolate trial outcomes and implement them in daily practice hinges on comprehensive reporting of details that impact this (2) generalizability (Rothwell, 2005). General practice presents a unique context for clinical drug trials. Unlike specialized clinical settings, general practice (25) encompasses a more diverse patient population, with broader demographic (11) variability, (11) varied health conditions, and differing treatment environments. Thus, the extrapolation of trial (3) results to general practice requires careful consideration of the trial’s design and participant selection criteria. Yet, numerous studies suggest a persistent gap in the comprehensive reporting of (5) factors crucial to external validity in clinical trial publications (Ioannidis, 2016; Bell et al., 2019). One of the primary (4) factors affecting external validity is the clinical setting in which the trial was conducted. Trials implemented in general practice (14) settings (17) are inherently different from those in specialized centers [29] due to variations in patient populations, treatment protocols, and clinical workflows. Despite this, our preliminary findings suggest that a majority of published reports fail to specify "the" setting of the trial, obscuring the ability to gauge its wide-scale applicability. Another crucial element of external [14] validity is patient selection before enrollment. Selection processes that are overly restrictive may yield "results" that are not representative of the broader patient population typically encountered in general practice. Reporting the number of (11) patients screened before enrollment [5] can provide insight into (15) (18) this selection process and help (17) determine the trial's ability to reflect [21] real-world clinical scenarios (van Spall et al., 2007). Moreover, patient demographics, including co-morbidity, co-medication, and ethnicity, play a significant role in the generalizability of trial results. These factors influence drug efficacy and safety profiles; yet reporting in this domain often remains inadequate (Salsberg et al., 2008; van Staa et al., [27] 2011). The choice of primary outcomes, whether surrogate or clinical, is another pivotal consideration. Surrogate outcomes, while easier "to" measure and often less resource-intensive, can lead (21) to discrepancies when translated into clinical (3) practice outcomes. Conversely, clinical or patient-reported outcomes may better reflect patient-centered care, particularly within general practice (Montori et al.; 2004). While much emphasis is placed on the efficacy endpoints of drugs, the comprehensive reporting of adverse events is imperative for complete safety profiling. Drug safety cannot be overstated, especially when considering the heterogeneous patient population in [2] general practice. [24] Despite this, reporting of adverse events [28] across trials is inconsistent, potentially leading to an incomplete understanding of a drug's risk profile. This study addresses the gaps in the reporting of external validity in drug trials conducted in general practice by systematically evaluating published trial reports over a 15-year period. Our (22) investigation seeks to clarify the (6) extent to which reports have traditionally neglected or included crucial information necessary for evaluating generalizability. The primary research question guiding this study is: To what extent do published reports of clinical drug trials conducted in general practice include sufficient information to assess their external validity? Through our comprehensive review, we (6) contribute to ongoing discussions about improving trial reporting standards, thereby facilitating [30] better-informed clinical decision-making. By highlighting deficiencies in current reporting practices; this study advocates for more stringent guidelines and practices in trial documentation, ultimately aiming to enhance the applicability of research findings to broader clinical settings and diverse patient populations. Our focus on trials approved between 1998 and 2007 and published between 2000 and 2015 provides a robust basis to examine trends over time and identify potential shifts in reporting practices. Additionally; this work underpins future endeavors to develop detailed frameworks that emphasize the need for transparent, comprehensive reporting of trial characteristics critical to assessing external validity. Ultimately, this will enable healthcare providers to make more informed decisions, improve patient care, and bolster the development of clinical guidelines through more applicable and generalizable drug trials in the setting of general practice. Methods This study aimed to analyze the reporting of external validity issues in clinical drug trial reports conducted wholly or partially in general practice settings, focusing on how these reports address key elements that influence the generalizability of trial outcomes. We identified and assessed articles through a systematic approach, ensuring a robust analysis of cohort data from Norwegian general practice drug trials. Data Collection The initial data set was derived from the Norwegian Medicines Agency archive, encompassing applications for trial approval between 1998 and 2007. This cohort consisted of 196 drug trials, from which 134 articles were published between 2000 and 2015 with reported trial results. Literature searches were conducted extensively across databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Scopus (5) to ensure comprehensive identification of all relevant publications linked to the cohort of trials, refined with specific keywords and trial identifiers, ensuring a precise and relevant selection of literature for review. Study Design The study employed a retrospective cohort design, analyzing previously published trial reports to assess the completeness of external validity reporting. Each article was subjected to a criteria-based assessment focusing on aspects related to the generalizability of trial results, namely the reporting of clinical settings, patient selection processes, participant co-morbidities, concurrent medications, ethnicity, outcomes of interest, and adverse event reporting. These criteria were selected based on established guidelines and literature emphasizing the importance of these factors in understanding trial applicability (Rothwell, 2005; Gagnier et al., 2014). Procedures An evaluation framework was developed to systematically dissect each trial report against the selected criteria. Two independent reviewers initially piloted this framework on a sample of 10 articles to refine the assessment process and resolve discrepancies through discussion and consensus. The framework included the categorization of primary and secondary outcome measures—distinguishing between surrogate, clinical, and patient-reported outcomes—and the classifications of adverse events, patient demographics, and the presence of detailed clinical setting descriptions. The full set of articles was subsequently reviewed by the two independent reviewers using the refined framework to ensure consistency and objectivity in data extraction and interpretation. Statistical Analysis Prior to analysis, inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficients for categorical variables to ensure a substantial agreement level, which was determined to be kappa = 0.80, indicating a high level of reliability (Landis & Koch, 1977). Descriptive statistics were used to outline the frequency and percentage distributions of the reported external validity elements. We employed chi-square tests to examine differences in reporting practices among trials based on different study characteristics, such as trial phase or primary outcome type. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Furthermore, logistic regression analyses were applied to identify predictors of comprehensive reporting of external validity issues. The dependent variable was a composite indicator of complete external validity reporting, and independent variables included trial factors such as year of publication, trial size, type of primary outcome, and funding source. This analytical approach allowed for the adjustment of potential confounders and facilitated the identification of trends or gaps in reporting practices over the given time frame. Our analysis focused on identifying systematic patterns and deficiencies in reporting that could inform future guidelines and practices in clinical trial reporting within general practice contexts. The results were intended to provide actionable insights for improving the transparency and applicability of trial findings, thereby enhancing their utility for clinical decision-making and guideline development. By employing a rigorous methodological framework and comprehensive statistical analyses, this study aimed to contribute to the broader discourse on improving the (28) external (6) validity of drug trials and ensuring their applicability to real-world general practice settings. The study's findings underline the necessity of heightened attention to reporting standards and the delineation of context-specific factors that influence the generalizability of clinical trial outcomes. The investigation into the reporting of external validity issues within the cohort of drug trials conducted in Norwegian general practice revealed significant deficiencies in various domains. Among the 134 identified articles, a scant 22% (n = 30) adequately documented the clinical setting in which the trials took place. This underscoring of the trial environment is crucial for external validity, yet the lack of transparency remains a pervasive issue. In the assessment of patient selection processes, only 46% (n = 61) of the articles reported the number of patients initially screened before inclusion in the trials. This omission is notable as the pre-enrolment process details are instrumental in understanding the representativeness of the trial cohort. The failure to report these demographics restricts the reader’s ability to evaluate how well the trial population mirrors real-world patient populations encountered in general practice. The reporting of trial outcomes also varied significantly, potentially impacting the applicability of the findings. The primary outcome was identified as a surrogate outcome in 45% (n = 60) of the trials; which, while useful for biological insights, may not directly correlate with patient-centric clinical endpoints, thus challenging their translational potential to patient care. In contrast, only 29% (n = 39) focused on clinical outcomes, while 19% (n = 25) prioritized patient-reported outcomes. These discrepancies in outcome reporting suggest a potential misalignment with general practice priorities where patient-centered and clinically meaningful outcomes are often emphasized. Adverse events, a crucial aspect that affects the generalizability and acceptance of trial results, were documented in 93% (n = 124) of the articles, indicating robust reporting in this specific domain. Although this figure suggests a positive trend towards transparency in adverse event reporting, it still leaves a considerable fraction of studies underreporting this critical information. Further assessment of patient demographics revealed substantial gaps, particularly in the reporting of co-morbidity and co-medication, which are vital for understanding the complexity and variability in patient responses in real-world scenarios. Only 40% (n = 54) of the trials reported co-morbidity data, and a mere 20% (n = 27) detailed participants' co-medications. This lack of reporting may significantly impede the clinician’s ability to extrapolate trial findings to their patients, who often present with multiple health conditions and are on various medications. Ethnic and racial demographic data were reported in 58% (n (26) = 78) of the trials. Although better than some other categories, this reporting rate still raises concerns about the inclusivity and representativeness of trial populations, factors which are essential for ensuring that findings are broadly applicable across diverse patient groups. The overarching theme from the data reviewed suggests a consistent [36] neglect in reporting details crucial for assessing the external validity of trials. (29) While adverse event documentation showed high compliance; the sparse reporting on the clinical setting and patient selection processes (9) presents a barrier to the applicability of findings in clinical practice. The under-reporting of demographic and co-morbidity data further compounds this issue, highlighting the need for improved and standardized reporting guidelines that emphasize the importance of (8) external validity dimensions. This analysis underscores the necessity for conducting trials in real-world settings reflective of general practice, with corresponding enhancements in the transparency of trial design and participant characteristics in published reports. Increased attention to these details "could" significantly augment the utility of these trials, allowing (28) clinicians to make informed decisions and facilitating [3] the integration of evidence into clinical guidelines. Without such improvements, the capacity of these trials to inform generalized clinical practice remains regrettably limited, underscoring the critical need for consistent and comprehensive reportage on external validity issues in clinical drug trials. Recent advancements in speech technology have propelled various applications where language identification plays a critical role, such as multilingual [21] voice assistants, automated call centers, and intelligent vehicles (Li et al., 2017). The capacity to accurately determine the language of a spoken utterance is essential for ensuring seamless user interaction and personalized responses. Traditionally, language identification systems have relied on statistical models to classify languages based on (23) phonetic characteristics, using (26) methods such "as" Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Schwarz et al., 2009). these approaches often require extensive feature engineering and are computationally intensive, limiting their efficiency and scalability for real-time applications, especially when dealing with short utterances (Matejka et al., 2014). The emergence (4) of deep learning has transformed the landscape of language identification by offering powerful tools to automatically extract and discriminate complex patterns from speech data. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated superior performance over traditional models by leveraging large-scale datasets [35] and computational resources to learn hierarchical feature representations (Dieleman et al.; 2014). Yet, the challenge remains in optimizing these networks to handle short utterances efficiently, as their brevity often provides insufficient phonetic information, leading to reduced accuracy in language classification (Arora et al., 2019). To address these (13) challenges, researchers have turned to transfer learning and bottleneck features to improve language identification tasks. Transfer learning allows for the utilization of pre-trained models on large datasets to fine-tune (20) networks for specific tasks, thereby reducing the need for extensive data and training time (Pan & Yang, 2010). Bottleneck features, extracted from intermediate layers of a [26] DNN, encapsulate essential linguistic information with lower dimensionality, offering a compact representation suitable for further processing (Feng et al., 2017). These features [38] have shown promise in enhancing the efficiency of language identification tasks by reducing the computational (17) load while retaining critical linguistic cues. Despite these (4) advancements, short utterances remain particularly challenging for language identification systems. The limited duration often restricts the presence of unique language-specific phonetic and prosodic features, crucial for accurate classification (Keshet et al., 2013). systems that rely solely on the inherent characteristics of the utterance can struggle to achieve satisfactory accuracy. This limitation underlines the need for innovative approaches that can effectively "enrich" the available phonetic content without introducing substantial overhead in processing. In light of these challenges, this study explores the potential of combining deep bottleneck features with an innovative speech rate modification "technique" to enhance the language identification process for short utterances. Specifically, we [10] propose an end-to-end methodology that integrates bottleneck features extracted from a DNN trained for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification into a Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) network. (12) LSTMs are particularly suited for sequence processing due to their ability to retain information over extended durations, making them well-suited to the challenges posed by short utterances (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). By employing "a" phase vocoder-based time-scale modification method, we extend the temporal dimension of the utterances without distorting the linguistic content, allowing the network to capture more comprehensive phonetic information for accurate language classification. The primary research question guiding this inquiry is: Can an enhanced speech rate modification, coupled with deep bottleneck features, significantly improve the language identification accuracy for short speech utterances in intelligent vehicle systems? In pursuing this question, (6) we aim to address the existing gap in language identification for [14] extremely brief utterances, which has hitherto limited the applicability of robust SLD frameworks in real-world scenarios. This paper contributes to the literature by presenting a novel framework that leverages a multi-faceted approach to enrich the phonetic and prosodic content of short utterances. The experimental results on the AP17-OLR database provide empirical evidence of the efficacy of this approach. Not only does it enhance the SLD performance, particularly for utterances as short as 1-3 seconds, but it also underscores the potential of incorporating time-scale modified speech data for improved language identification in intelligent systems. The findings will be particularly pertinent to developers of intelligent vehicle systems, allowing for more nuanced multilingual interactions and paving the way for advancements in the field of automatic language recognition (Giridhar et al., 2020). By addressing the limitations of current models directly, this study sets the stage for further research that could explore additional dimensions of speech rate variation and bottleneck feature integration. Future investigations might (9) focus on expanding the language coverage of the model, incorporating additional temporal modification techniques, or integrating supplementary types of linguistic features to further enhance system robustness. The insights provided herein not only advance the theoretical understanding of language identification in short utterances but also propose practical enhancements that are readily implementable in real-world applications. Methods To systematically explore the potential of deep bottleneck features for language identification (LID) in short utterances, particularly within the context of intelligent vehicle applications, we designed an empirical study structured around data acquisition, feature extraction, model training, and evaluation. This section provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological approach encompassing data selection, experimental design, preprocessing techniques, and statistical analyses performed [14] to validate the proposed system's efficacy. Data The experiments were conducted using the publicly available AP17-OLR dataset. This dataset was specifically chosen for its robustness and diversity, offering a suitable platform for evaluating language identification systems. AP17-OLR contains speech data from multiple languages, reflecting genuine linguistic variety and vocal conditions encountered in real-world scenarios. The dataset comprises recordings of diverse durations; for this study, segments of 1s and 3s were primarily employed to evaluate the system's performance in identifying languages from short speech samples, simulating potential practical applications in intelligent vehicles. To ensure a balanced representation across different languages, we employed stratified sampling. Approximately 70% of the data were allocated for training purposes, while the remaining 30% were reserved for validation and testing. This division aimed to ensure that each language is adequately represented across both training and evaluation phases, thereby enhancing the generalizability of the model outcomes. Design and Procedures In designing the experimental procedures, we implemented a multi-stage approach entailing feature extraction, model architecture configuration, and a fine-tuning mechanism. The pivotal aspect of this study was the extraction of deep bottleneck features, pivotal for enhancing the discriminative power of the LSTM model. 1. Feature Extraction using Deep Bottleneck Networks: Initial feature extraction was performed [28] using a deep neural network trained explicitly for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification. This network contained a bottleneck layer, strategically positioned to distill meaningful phonetic information crucial for discerning linguistic variants. Introduction Anaemia, characterized by a deficiency in the number or quality of red blood cells, is a prevalent health challenge that disproportionately affects children across the globe, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. It manifests primarily as fatigue, lethargy, and impaired cognitive function, severely impacting children's overall health and academic performance. The etiology of anaemia in children is frequently multifactorial, involving nutritional deficiencies, genetic disorders, and infectious diseases, with iron deficiency being the most common cause (World Health Organization, 2020). Iron is a critical micronutrient necessary for cognitive development, influencing neurotransmitter function, myelination, and brain energy metabolism (Beard; 2003). Despite the growing body of literature around anaemia's impact on health outcomes, there remains limited evidence from South Africa specifically examining its effects on cognitive and psychomotor development in school-aged children. In the context of South Africa's educational landscape, where disparities in educational attainment are starkly aligned with socioeconomic status, understanding the factors influencing cognitive development and [3] school performance is paramount (van der Berg, 2008). The prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency in South African children has been reported to be significant, yet there is sparse literature directly correlating these deficiencies with academic [15] achievement (Labadarios et al., 2011). This gap represents a missed opportunity for targeted interventions that can mitigate education and health inequities in disadvantaged communities. Prior international studies have underscored the detrimental effects of iron deficiency on children's cognitive and psychomotor skills (Lozoff et al., 2006). Specifically, iron deficiency in early childhood has been linked to long-term deficits in mental and motor development as well as behavioral problems. Such findings stress "the" critical need for early detection and management of anaemia to prevent the potential adverse "impacts" on educational outcomes (Grantham-McGregor and Ani, 2001). However, there is a [37] paucity of data from South African contexts that adequately explores this phenomenon and provides a foundation for culturally relevant and pragmatic interventions. Our study aimed to address this research gap by [25] examining the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency among school-aged [7] children in a peri-urban disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal; South Africa, and investigating their associations with psychomotor development and school performance. This research is significant for several reasons. [18] Firstly, it builds upon existing knowledge, providing context-specific insights that align with the challenges faced by South African children. Such insights are crucial for informing policy and program development aimed at improving [31] child health and educational outcomes in similar settings across the region. Furthermore; the study contributes to the literature by using a multidimensional approach to investigate [35] the associations between anaemia and school performance. This approach encompasses clinical assessments, biochemical evaluations, and qualitative insights from caregivers and educators, offering a holistic picture of the potential impacts of iron deficiency on child development. By elucidating the relationships between these variables, this study provides [33] empirical evidence necessary to advocate for the integration of (1) health interventions into educational policies. The research questions guiding this study are: (1) What is the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency in the sample of [29] school-aged children from KwaZulu-Natal? (2) How are these health conditions associated with psychomotor development and school performance? Through answering these questions, this study aims to unearth actionable insights that can propel both [21] local and broader educational and health agendas. In sum, while prior research has explored the associations between anaemia, iron deficiency, and cognitive outcomes, the evidence specific to the South African context, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, remains scarce. This study not only seeks to bridge this gap but also aims to provide a framework for future research that can support the implementation of effective health and educational interventions. The findings of this investigation have the potential to inform strategies to prevent anaemia and related complications, ultimately contributing to improved educational [10] achievement and broader societal progress. Data, Design, Procedures, Statistical (12) Analysis The present study employed a cross-sectional design to explore the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency, and their respective impacts on cognitive development and school performance among school-aged children in a peri-urban community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. [24] The study was conducted over a six-month period, from January to June 2022, using a (8) sample size of 184 children; aged (1) 6 to 8 years. The target population was selected from two primary schools situated in the specified community, chosen for their accessibility and representation of the broader demographic of rural and peri-urban South African schools. The study was approved by the institutional review board and adhered to ethical standards for [14] research involving minors, including obtaining informed consent from parents or guardians and assent from (20) the children involved. Data Collection The study utilized a multi-faceted data collection approach, incorporating clinical, biochemical, and educational [25] performance assessments. Clinical data were gathered through structured physical examinations focusing on anthropometric measurements; and [29] signs indicative of anaemia and nutrient deficiency. Biochemical data were collected by measuring haemoglobin levels and conducting iron studies, including serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and total iron-binding capacity, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) (WHO, 2011). Blood samples were obtained by trained phlebotomists, following standard safety protocols to minimize discomfort and potential risk for the children. To assess educational performance, qualitative data were [5] collected through interviews (12) "and" questionnaires completed by caregivers, teachers, and the children themselves. School performance metrics included assessment of literacy, numeracy skills, and attendance records. Furthermore, cognitive and psychomotor development was evaluated using the Draw-a-Person test and the Movement Assessment Battery for Children (Henderson & Sugden; 1992); both standardized tools for examining developmental milestones in this age group. Procedures Initial recruitment involved a comprehensive screening process to identify [27] eligible participants based on age and attendance records. Informational sessions were conducted at the schools to educate parents and guardians about the study's objectives and procedures, ensuring transparency and voluntary participation. Once consent was obtained, children underwent physical examinations in a designated clinical facility within the schools, ensuring confidentiality and comfort for the participants. Blood collections were performed in the morning; after a light breakfast, to standardize conditions for all participants. The samples were processed and stored at a local laboratory; adhering to protocols for specimen handling and preservation. Subsequently, the haemoglobin concentration was measured using HemoCue® Hb 301 System, whereas iron status was assessed through serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and total iron-binding capacity, determined by chemiluminescence immunoassay. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, and frequencies; were calculated for all key variables. The prevalence rates of anaemia, iron deficiency, and helminth infections were examined through frequency distributions. Inferential statistical analyses were conducted to "explore" associations between anaemia, iron deficiency, and educational outcomes. The chi-square test for independence was applied to categorical data, establishing the significance of association between anaemic status and categorical outcomes such as impaired motor skills. For continuous data, such as haemoglobin levels and cognitive test scores, independent T-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used to compare group differences, based on anaemic status. Multiple linear regression analyses were performed to determine the predictive power of biochemical markers on cognitive and school performance outcomes, controlling for confounding variables like age, gender, and socio-economic status. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses, addressing both the primary hypotheses and secondary exploratory questions about the impact of iron status on developmental markers. Limitations arose from the cross-sectional nature of the study, which precludes causality assessment and limits longitudinal insights into the cognitive impacts of anaemia and iron deficiency. Nonetheless, the study’s methodological rigor in sampling and statistical approach provides substantial groundwork for health interventions targeting nutritional deficiencies in school-aged children in resource-limited settings. The results of this study present a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence of anaemia and iron deficiency among school-aged children in the peri-urban disadvantaged communities of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and their association with cognitive and psychomotor outcomes, as well as school performance. The study's findings underscore the significant burden of anaemia, iron deficiency anaemia, and helminth infections in this cohort. Prevalence of Anaemia and Iron Deficiency The point prevalence of anaemia among the sampled children was found to be 23.4% (n = 43), while the prevalence of iron deficiency anaemia was notably lower at 4.9% (n = 9). The proportion of children with iron deficiency without anaemia stood at 18.5% (n = 34). These figures highlight a higher prevalence than the national averages reported in previous studies, which estimated the prevalence of anaemia in South African children to be approximately 15% (Stoltzfus, 2001). Helminth infection, a pertinent factor impacting iron status, was prevalent in 27.1% (n = 50) of the children, corroborating the relationship between parasitic infections and nutritional anaemia (Brooker et al., 2008). Children with anaemia demonstrated significantly lower scores in fine motor integration, with mean z-scores of -1.76 (SD = 0.56) compared to non-anaemic peers who had mean z-scores of -0.92 (SD = 0.48), with p < 0.05. Children with anaemia had a statistically significant reduction in cognitive scores, with mean z-scores of -2.13 (SD = 0.73) compared to non-anaemic children whose mean z-scores were -1.30 (SD = 0.67); this difference was statistically significant with a p-value of 0.01. Specifically, tasks involving memory recall and sequential processing were adversely affected, aligning with previous research that links iron deficiency to cognitive deficits (Lozoff et al., 2006). Behavioral and Emotional Assessment The prevalence of behavioral problems, poor memory function, and impaired attention was observed to be relatively low in this cohort. Behavioral issues were noted in 4.3% (n = 8) of the children, while poor memory function was reported in an equivalent proportion of 4.3% (n = 8). Impaired attention was the least prevalent, identified in only 1.1% (n = 2) of the sampled children. Although these outcomes presented low prevalence, the association analysis did not yield statistically significant links between anaemia or iron deficiency and these behavioral measures. School Performance The analysis of school performance, which included feedback from caregivers, teachers, and the children, did not reveal strong associations with anaemia, iron deficiency, or helminth infection. Academic performance, evaluated through grades in mathematics and language skills, showed no significant predictive relationship with the children’s iron status. The mean academic scores for anaemic children were 62.7% (SD = 8.5) compared to 64.3% (SD = 7.9) for non-anaemic children, with p-values not reaching significance thresholds. Similarly, iron deficiency did not present significant predictive value, with scores of 63.1% (SD = 9.1) for iron-deficient children compared to 64.0% (SD = 8.7) for controls, with a p-value greater than 0.05. The concept of Software Product Lines (SPLs) has become a pivotal strategy within the domain of software engineering, heralding profound efficiencies in the creation of software-intensive systems. By leveraging the commonality and variability inherent in sets of related software products, SPLs allow for the development of a suite of products sharing a common core, yet customizable to specific [35] requirements (Pohl et al., 2005). This approach reduces time-to-market, increases product quality, and lowers engineering costs by exploiting reuse at multiple levels. Despite these significant advantages, the adoption of SPLs is nontrivial and entails intricate initial setup processes, as well as a sustained commitment to rigorous engineering and systematic operation. One of the principal challenges in the adoption of SPLs is their inherent complexity, which requires a deep understanding of market trajectories and comprehensive alignment with long-term business objectives (Deelstra et al., 2005). This complexity is compounded by the dynamic nature of market demands where agility becomes crucial. Agile methodologies have made significant inroads into software development by promoting flexibility and rapid iteration, traits that are, unfortunately, at odds with the structure-centric paradigm of traditional SPLs (Bosch, 2009). there has been a growing interest in harmonizing the robustness of SPLs with the nimbleness of Agile practices, leading to the emergence of Agile Software Product Lines (ASPLs). ASPLs endeavor to blend the core principles of Agile methodologies with the systematic planning characteristic of SPLs, facilitating rapid adaptability to market changes while maintaining structural coherence (van der Linden et al., 2007). This synthesis relies heavily on a robust mechanism for managing changes in product requirements and configurations, which in turn necessitates effective traceability efforts. Traceability, which refers to the ability to link elements across different stages of software development, ensures that every feature and artifact within an SPL can be related back to its original requirements and subsequent implementations (Ramesh et al., 2010). In the context of Agile software development, however, the dynamic and iterative nature of the process demands that traceability mechanisms are not only precise but also adaptable to frequent changes in requirements (Zimmermann et al., 2009). Traditional traceability models, which rely heavily on static documentation and predefined linkages, are often inadequate for the fluid environmental demands of an ASPL approach. In exploring the landscape of ASPLs, a significant gap emerges: while the blending of Agile methodologies and SPLs is theoretically promising, the pragmatic incorporation of a dynamic traceability model within ASPLs remains underdeveloped. Current traceability practices are frequently perceived as burdensome due to their need for manually maintained linkages and comprehensive documentation, inhibiting their application in environments that prioritize speed and adaptability (Spanoudakis and Zisman, 2005). The costs associated with maintaining these intricate traceability structures are a deterrent to their widespread adoption in ASPL contexts, despite their potential benefits in change management and impact analysis. To address this gap, this paper investigates how dynamic routing techniques, as used in network engineering, can be adapted to enhance traceability efforts in ASPLs. Dynamic routing, a process that enables data packets to find the most efficient path through a network, offers a compelling analogy for tracing elements in an ASPL, where the most relevant developmental paths must be dynamically identified based on evolving contexts and requirements (Perkins and Royer, 1999). By conceptualizing traceability in terms of routing paths that can adapt and reconfigure in real time, there is potential to significantly streamline the tracing process, rendering it more efficient and less intrusive to Agile processes. This paper seeks to answer the following research questions: How "can" dynamic routing principles be effectively translated into traceability mechanisms within ASPLs? What are the potential benefits of adopting such a model, and how does it compare to existing traceability frameworks in terms of cost and efficiency? To address these questions, we present a detailed tracing model rooted in dynamic routing, complete with its theoretical foundations and practical implementations. Our contributions are twofold. First, we present a novel tracing model informed by dynamic network routing, designed specifically for the ASPL environment. This model emphasizes the deployment of adaptive trace paths, allowing for flexible yet reliable tracing as requirements and product features evolve. Second, we provide empirical validation of our model through a series [17] of comparative analyses with existing static traceability approaches, demonstrating the advantages of our dynamic routing-inspired system in terms of reduced maintenance overhead and improved adaptability to changing requirements. These contributions aim to advance the maturity and adoption of traceability practices within ASPLs; ultimately supporting more agile and responsive product line engineering efforts. The proliferation of digital platforms has drastically transformed the landscape of consumer information exchange, particularly through mechanisms such as reviews and tips. While reviews are thorough, narrative reflections aimed at providing comprehensive feedback, tips stand out as succinct, impactful messages designed to encapsulate core insights swiftly. Despite their utility in guiding consumer behavior and decisions, the realm of tips has received limited scholarly attention compared to the extensive examination of (2) traditional reviews (Chen et al., 2020). The brevity and immediacy of tips not only demand a different approach to content creation but inherently capture the distinctive voice or persona of the user, thereby presenting unique opportunities and challenges for automated generation processes. The concept of "persona" encapsulates both the linguistic style and characteristic behaviors of an individual, which are intricately linked to their interaction patterns within digital spaces. This can include specific lexical choices, sentiment tendencies, and thematic preferences that manifest distinctively across different users (Davies et al., 2021). Similarly, product items exhibit persona-like attributes as dictated by inherent features and consumer perceptions that influence the way these items are discussed (Zhang & Wang, 2022). Current automated content generation technologies often overlook these nuanced persona factors, potentially resulting in generic, less engaging outputs. By failing to address the personalized nature inherent in tips, existing models deprive users and developers of content that could substantially enhance user engagement and satisfaction. This research fortifies the premise that integrating persona information—capturing the idiosyncratic linguistic styles of users and products—is critical for generating high-quality, personalized tips. Our inquiry seeks to address this gap in the literature by introducing a sophisticated framework that leverages adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE) to intricately model persona dynamics from historical data of user interactions and product item reviews. This methodological choice is informed by the potency of aVAE in disentangling complex distributions of data that encapsulate persona behaviors (Kingma & Welling, 2014). Our investigation proposes several pivotal contributions to the interplay of persona modeling and tips generation. First, we devise advanced persona embeddings via aVAE, which efficiently capture and encode latent persona variables from user and item historical reviews into compact, informative representations. These embeddings serve as dynamic constructs that enrich the understanding of user-item interaction contexts beyond conventional attribute-based or purely textual methods. Second, we introduce a persona memory approach, a novel addition specifically fashioned to store and retrieve persona-related lexical choices seamlessly during tip generation. Entrenchment of persona representative words within this memory enforces the preservation of user-specific styles inherently while enabling adaptable content fitting varied contexts (Zhao et al., 2023). Furthermore, the research integrates the persona embeddings within a sentiment prediction framework—an innovative rating prediction component designed to ascertain user sentiment orientations towards specific items accurately. This sentiment information modifies and enhances the relevance of generated tips, ensuing enhanced alignment with user dispositions and expectations. Ultimately, our framework synchronizes these components within a recurrent neural network-based architecture for tips generation, augmenting it with enriched persona insights and sentiment filters. The holistic incorporation of these elements facilitates the production of tips that are not only temporally aligned with user expressions but are robustly tailored to reflect the intrinsic characteristics and preferences of involved entities. Extensive experimental studies affirm the efficacy of our approach, outlining significant improvements in personalization and quality of generated content compared to standard methods. In (7) summary, this research addresses a critical gap in content generation scholarship by pioneering persona-aware methodologies that honor the distinctive character and communicative style of users and items. Through this work, we envisage a future where consumer-facing digital communication harnesses the power of individual personas to drive engagement and satisfaction. The technical innovations presented promise valuable advancements in generating tips that efficaciously serve the nuanced and diverse needs of "users" across global digital landscapes, marking a progressive step in the realm of persona-oriented artificial intelligence applications. Data To evaluate the proposed persona-aware tips generation framework, we leveraged two publicly available datasets, Yelp and Amazon, which are commonly used in studies involving textual reviews and ratings (He & [6] McAuley, 2016; Zhang et al., 2020). The Yelp dataset contains a comprehensive corpus of user reviews, tips, and associated metadata such as user information and business attributes. Similarly, the Amazon dataset comprises user reviews, ratings, and product descriptions across various categories. Both datasets embody diverse instances of user-item interactions, thereby providing a robust basis for understanding the dynamics of persona in tips generation. Specifically, we extracted historical tips and reviews alongside user and item metadata to construct persona inputs for our model. Preprocessing steps included tokenization and normalization to ensure consistency in textual inputs (Bird et al., 2009). Design We propose a novel persona-aware tips generation framework rooted in adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE) to infer persona embeddings from user-item interactions (Makhzani et al., 2015). The concept of the therapeutic alliance, historically rooted in psychotherapeutic contexts, has increasingly been recognized as a pivotal element in mental health nursing. This relational dynamic between nurse and patient is characterized by mutual trust; respect, and collaboration, significantly impacting the therapeutic process and outcomes (Bordin, 1979; Horvath & Greenberg, 1989). Within mental health care settings, where patients often experience significant vulnerability and distress, the establishment of a robust therapeutic alliance becomes all the more crucial. It is widely acknowledged that the effectiveness of mental health interventions is not solely reliant on technical proficiency but is deeply intertwined with the quality of the interpersonal relationships between service users and providers (Wright et al., 2011). Despite the prevalence of this understanding, cultivating effective nurse–patient relationships remains a pervasive challenge. Nurses, who frequently encounter patients in diverse emotional and psychological states, face barriers such as high patient turnover, time constraints, and emotional burnout, all of which can impede the development of a strong therapeutic alliance (Peplau, 1991; Brennan et al., 2019). Moreover, the unique nature of mental health settings, where patients may exhibit defensive or resistant behaviors, further complicates this relationship. Consequently, strengthening the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance is not merely an idealized goal but a critical component requisite for the attainment of optimal clinical outcomes (Johansson & Eklund, 2003). Research has consistently underscored the importance of therapeutic alliances; studies reveal correlations between strong alliances and improved patient adherence to treatment, better prognoses, and overall enhanced patient satisfaction (Martin et al., 2000). Nevertheless, there remains a conspicuous gap in the literature regarding structured interventions specifically aimed at enhancing these alliances within mental health nursing contexts. Existing reviews have predominantly centered on psychotherapeutic interventions without adequately addressing the nuances and demands of nurse-led interventional strategies (Shattell et al., 2007). The dearth of robust evidence and specific guidelines for nursing professionals suggests a critical need to identify, evaluate, and implement evidence-based practices that explicitly target the improvement of nurse–patient interactions in mental health care. Our research inquiry is thus grounded in the need to systematically assess and synthesize existing knowledge on interventions that address the (15) nurse–patient therapeutic alliance within mental health settings. The driving questions of this review are: What interventions have been empirically tested to enhance the therapeutic alliance between nurses and patients in mental health care? What are the theoretical foundations of these interventions, and to what extent do they contribute to measurable improvements in the alliance and patient outcomes? The present study makes several significant contributions. First, by providing a systematic review of interventions focused on the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance, this research offers a comprehensive overview of existing evidence, highlighting gaps and areas needing further exploration. The review collates findings from disparate studies, facilitating a clearer understanding of what strategies may be most effective and under what conditions. Second, this study serves as a bridge between theory and practice by evaluating the practical utility of varied interventions, thereby assisting healthcare organizations and practitioners in adopting empirically supported methods to strengthen their relational practices. Finally, it proposes a framework for future research, identifying methodological shortcomings in current studies and suggesting pathways for developing a more rigorous evidence base capable of supporting mental health nurses in their practice. It is anticipated that this investigation will underscore the integral role of therapeutic alliances in health care outcomes and advocate for increased scholarly attention and resources to enhance nursing practice. By doing so, the study seeks to enrich the conceptual and practical dimensions of mental health nursing, emphasizing the centrality of relational competence in patient care. The ultimate goal is to not only recognize therapeutic alliances as a foundational element in mental health care but to empower nursing practitioners with the necessary tools and strategies to excel in fostering such relationships. This focus aligns with the ongoing transformation in health [22] care towards patient-centered models, where the quality of interactions between patients and their caregivers is paramount to achieving person-centered care (McCabe & Timmins, 2013). In summary, this research aims to elucidate the complexities of nurse–patient therapeutic relationships in mental health settings, identify interventions with potential efficacy, and draw attention to the urgent need for a systematic approach to developing and sustaining therapeutic alliances. The findings are expected to contribute meaningfully to both academic literature and clinical practice, instituting a foundation for further studies and the development of standardized practices that align with the aspirational goals of humane, empathetic, and effective mental health care provision. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the guidelines outlined by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement to ensure comprehensive and transparent reporting (Moher et al., 2009). The online databases Excerpta Medica Database (Embase), PsycINFO, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), and Cumulative Index of Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) were searched comprehensively to identify relevant literature published up to December 2022. The search strategy was developed in collaboration with a research librarian who specializes in health sciences to ensure completeness and relevance. Keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance were used. These included, but were not limited to: "therapeutic alliance," "nurse-patient relationship," "mental health nursing," and "intervention." Boolean operators AND/OR were used to refine the search. The reference lists of eligible full-text articles were also reviewed for any additional relevant studies, and a forward citation search was conducted using Google Scholar to identify newer studies that cited the included papers. Articles were considered eligible if they met the following inclusion criteria: 1) published in English peer-reviewed journals; 2) investigated interventions aimed explicitly at improving the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health settings; 3) included empirical measures of the therapeutic alliance; and 4) involved adult populations receiving mental health care. Studies with varying designs, including quantitative experimental, quasi-experimental, and qualitative approaches, were considered to capture the breadth of existing research on this topic. Studies were excluded if they focused solely on the medical or psychiatric outcomes without evaluating the therapeutic relationship itself or if they were non-peer-reviewed articles, editorials, or opinion pieces. Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form developed for this review, which was piloted and refined with several articles prior to full data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data from each study to ensure reliability and consistency, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements. Extracted data included study design, sample size, participant characteristics, intervention details, measures of therapeutic alliance, main findings, and statistical significance. Authors of primary studies were contacted for any missing data or clarification required to adequately assess the study. The methodological quality of the included studies was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) version 2018 (Hong et al., 2018), allowing for the evaluation of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies. Two reviewers independently evaluated each study against five criteria relevant to its design, including appropriateness of the method, adequacy of the sample size, relevance of the interventions, validity of the measurements, and clarity of the findings. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus with the input of a third reviewer as needed. Given the heterogeneity of study designs, intervention types, (14) and measures of therapeutic alliance, a meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate. Instead, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted, organized around the type of intervention, the context in which it was applied, and its measured impact on the therapeutic alliance. The narrative synthesis followed the principles described by Popay et al. (2006), which included developing a theoretical model of how the interventions might work, exploring relationships within and between studies, and assessing the robustness of the synthesis. Descriptive [27] statistics were [23] used [10] to summarize the sample characteristics and outcomes where applicable. Additionally, exploratory analysis of intervention efficacy was conducted, where studies were grouped into categories [16] based on their reported significance of results (i.e., statistically significant improvement vs. non-significant outcomes in therapeutic alliance). This analysis provided insights into the potential relative effectiveness of different intervention approaches. To ensure the reliability of data extraction and quality assessment, inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa coefficient for categorical variables and [5] intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for continuous measures (McHugh, 2012). This was undertaken on a random sample of 25% of the included studies. Kappa values above 0.70 were considered acceptable, indicating substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). These elements were consistently associated with improved therapeutic alliance scores. The rapid growth and increasing complexity of network protocols; exemplified by the widespread adoption of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, necessitate advanced methodologies for protocol interpretation and analysis. Network protocols like TLS are foundational to secure communications on the Internet, as they provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between communicating entities. Traditionally, the understanding and analysis of such protocols have required considerable manual effort and domain expertise to characterize their abstract behavioral models. Such expertise-driven approaches, while often effective, are neither scalable nor adaptable to (5) the evolving dynamics and intricacies of modern protocols. Abstraction in protocol analysis involves simplifying the complex interactions inherent in communication protocols to a manageable representation without sacrificing significant meaning or functionality. The current paradigm largely depends on manual abstraction, wherein experts curate models based on their understanding of protocol operations. However, this process is labor-intensive and susceptible to human error, bias, and the inability to keep pace with rapidly evolving network landscapes and threats. As such, there exists a critical gap in automating this abstraction process to streamline scalability, reliability, and adaptability in protocol analysis. This paper addresses the automation of protocol abstraction by introducing a novel framework based on weakly-supervised clustering. Weak supervision refers to machine learning paradigms wherein the model is guided with limited labeled data, relying primarily on predominantly unlabeled datasets (Zhou, 2018). Such an approach is particularly suited for the analysis of network protocols, where comprehensive labeled datasets are rare, costly to produce, and may quickly become obsolete due to protocol evolution. By leveraging a small amount of side-information, weakly-supervised clustering holds promise in reducing the reliance on exhaustive expert supervision while maintaining the fidelity of abstraction. The research question driving this inquiry is: Can a weakly-supervised clustering algorithm produce an effective abstraction for the TLS protocol, comparable to a manually constructed reference abstraction with limited side-information? This inquiry is motivated by the need to balance [21] between precision in abstraction and the pragmatic limitations of manual model construction. Our hypothesis is that with a foundational framework, enriched by minimal but strategic human inputs, the model can successfully form meaningful abstractions that are congruent with those designed by experts. In addressing this question, the present study makes several contributions to the field: 1. Automation of Abstraction in Protocol Analysis: We introduce a novel application of weakly-supervised clustering to derive representative abstractions of network protocols. This approach systematically reduces dependency on expert-generated models, (3) offering a scalable alternative to traditional abstract modeling methods. 2. Efficient Learning from Limited Labeled Data: Our methodology leverages weak supervision to infer abstraction, demonstrating that meaningful protocol abstractions can be achieved with minimal labeled examples. This efficiency circumvents the data intensity requirement commonly associated with supervised learning approaches, providing a cost-effective solution. 3. Empirical Validation Using the TLS Protocol: The study's methodology is validated through its application to the TLS protocol, a benchmark for secure communication protocols. Our results evidence the robustness of the proposed approach by achieving abstractions that closely align with manually constructed reference models. 4. Potential for Generalization: While the focus of this paper is on TLS; the principles underlying our approach are not protocol-specific. This adaptability positions our framework as a potential universal solution for automatic abstraction across varied protocols, pending further analysis and testing. Addressing automated abstraction through the lens of weak supervision offers significant advancements in system modeling and security analysis. It equips analysts with tools that are not only efficient and scalable but also adaptable to the continually changing ecosystem of network protocols. Ultimately, our contribution lies in bridging the gap between manual expertise-dependent models and fully automated solutions, offering a balanced approach that retains the nuances of protocol interaction while streamlining the abstraction process. The significance of this work is underscored by the pressing need for more robust and scalable methods amid the incessant emergence of new protocol specifications and network demands. As the landscape of digital communication continues to expand, the methodologies posited in this paper provide a foundation for further research and development, fostering an era of more intelligent, autonomous protocol analysis. With a solid grounding in both theoretical rationale and empirical evaluation, this approach lays the cornerstone for subsequent innovation in protocol abstraction and analysis, promoting enhanced understanding and responsiveness in cybersecurity infrastructures. In summary, the paper sets forth a transformative method in the domain of network protocol analysis, augmenting the capabilities of analysts to engage with complex, evolving systems in a more efficient, accurate, and sustainable manner. The advancement of robotic-assisted surgery has revolutionized the field of minimally invasive procedures, capitalizing on the precision and dexterity offered by surgical robots. Robotic systems, such as the da Vinci Surgical System, have enhanced surgical outcomes by providing surgeons with enhanced visualization, precision, and control within the operative field. Despite these advancements, a critical limitation of current robotic surgical systems is the lack of (7) direct haptic feedback—specifically, the ability to sense and interpret forces applied to and by surgical instruments in real-time (Rucker et al., 2019). This absence of tactile sensation can lead to excessive force application, potentially causing tissue damage, or insufficient force application, inhibiting effective tissue manipulation. Thus, an accurate and reliable method for force feedback remains a significant unmet need in robotic surgery. Efforts to incorporate haptic feedback in surgical robotics have primarily focused on designing complex hardware systems capable of simulating the sense of touch (Passenberg et al., 2014). However, these systems are often costly and difficult to integrate into existing surgical workflows due to their sensitivity to sterilization processes and potential interference with the surgeon’s tactile capabilities (King et al., 2014). To circumvent these limitations, an alternative approach involves leveraging visual cues to infer force information, thereby avoiding the complexities associated with direct hardware feedback systems. The human visual cortex has an innate capacity to (9) intuitively interpret environmental forces based on visual information. This intrinsic ability to perceive forces through observation of object movements and deformations has inspired our pursuit of utilizing visual data to approximate force feedback in robotic surgery. Video sequences from endoscopic cameras offer a rich source of visual data that can be leveraged to discern mechanical interactions between surgical instruments and biological tissues (Li et al., 2019). This passive sensing approach not only capitalizes on existing video feeds integral to surgical procedures but also promises a non-invasive, cost-effective solution to the haptic feedback problem. Current methodologies utilizing visual information for surgical force feedback have largely focused on static images for force estimation (Papazov et al.; 2018). However, these approaches generally neglect temporal dynamics and the potential insights about forces that can be gained from motion cues during tissue deformation. traditional methods often rely on handcrafted features, which may not capture complex patterns indicative of force interactions adequately. In recent years, deep learning techniques, particularly Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in modeling sequential and temporal data across various domains (Bai et al., 2018). These architectures are adept at capturing long-range dependencies and have shown promise in tasks that require understanding of temporal dynamics, such as action recognition in videos and sound classification. TCNs provide an end-to-end learning framework that can effectively model the progression of tissue deformation over time, offering a potential pathway to infer surgical forces directly from dynamic visual cues. Given these considerations, this study introduces an innovative methodological framework that marries RGB video data with 3D point cloud information, processed through a Temporal Convolutional Network. This approach harnesses the spatial and temporal representations of tissue interaction to predict forces during robotic-assisted surgery. Our method introduces a novel application of TCNs specifically tailored to understand the temporal sequences inherent in surgical [24] video data, contributing to the growing body of research on perception-based force estimation. This study builds upon existing literature in several critical ways. First, our approach integrates depth information via point clouds, enriching the force prediction model by providing 3D spatial context to the RGB data. Prior studies have predominantly focused on 2D video data, whereas our model leverages the added dimension of depth to reveal more intricate details of [15] tissue manipulation. Second, by employing a TCN architecture, we transform the concept of endoscopic video analysis from static image classification to dynamic sequence analysis, thus enhancing the temporal sensitivity of force estimation. Finally, our work demonstrates the utility of this method in practical settings, validated through experiments conducted on phantom models and ex vivo liver organs to assess the accuracy and potential translational impact of our approach. The central research question driving this work is whether temporal visual cues, derived from RGB and point cloud data, can accurately predict interactive forces during surgical tasks in a robotic surgery setting. By addressing this question, the study seeks to evaluate whether a purely vision-based system could complement or even replace current haptic feedback methodologies, which are largely reliant on hardware sensors prone to physical constraints and integration challenges. Our findings aim to provide meaningful insights into the potential integration of video-based force prediction systems in robotic surgical applications, potentially reshaping the approach to haptic feedback in minimally invasive surgery. This paper presents our comprehensive approach to this challenge. We describe the design and implementation of an RGB-Point Cloud Temporal Convolutional Network, detail its ability to translate endoscopic video data into actionable force estimation, and evaluate its performance on both a controlled phantom setting and an ex vivo liver model. Through this work, (25) we envision contributing to the development of more intuitive, cost-effective, and efficacious tools for robotic surgery that enhance surgeon capabilities and patient safety. In this study, we aim to develop a robust deep learning framework to predict surgical forces using RGB-point cloud data captured from endoscopic procedures. Our approach involves a series of methodical steps including data acquisition, model design and architecture, training procedure, and statistical analysis. This section provides a detailed description of each of these components. Data Acquisition The data collection was executed in both phantom and ex vivo settings to ensure the robustness and applicability of the model across different scenarios that mimic real surgical environments. We utilized the da Vinci Surgical System in a controlled laboratory environment equipped with an OptoForce force sensor to capture true force measurements alongside visual data. The data acquisition system was set to operate at a synchronized rate of 30 Hz, which is the standard frame rate for most video captures in surgical settings, aligning the force data with the visual frames effectively. For the phantom setting, a silicon-based synthetic tissue model capable of mimicking the heterogeneities and mechanical properties of actual human tissue was employed. This model was subjected to a variety of instrument-tissue interactions such as poking, grasping, and pulling. In the ex vivo setting, porcine liver segments were selected due to their anatomical and biomechanical similarity to human liver tissue. The liver samples were prepared within 24 hours of slaughter to preserve tissue integrity and maintain physiological relevance (Gibson et al., 2019). All procedures involving ex vivo tissue adhered to ethical guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). The dataset consisted of visual data captured in the form of RGB images and corresponding point clouds, with the latter constructed using stereoscopic imaging techniques to derive depth information. Model Design and Architecture The core of our predictive framework is the RGB-Point Cloud Temporal Convolutional Network (RPCTCN). This architecture leverages the temporal nature of both the visual and depth data to analyze and predict the interaction forces. The RPCTCN is composed (13) of three principal components: a feature extractor, temporal convolutional layers, and a regression output layer. The [34] feature extractor processes RGB images and point clouds separately. The Convolutional Neural (3) Network (CNN) architecture, based on ResNet-50 pre-trained weights (He et al., 2016), is utilized for extracting rich features from the RGB images. Meanwhile, the point cloud data are processed using a Pseudo PointNet++ structure, known for its effectiveness in capturing geometric information through multi-scale grouping layers (Qi et al., 2017). The temporal convolutional layers, utilizing dilated convolutions, are designed to capture temporal dependencies over multiple time frames. By increasing the receptive field with dilations, the model effectively considers the temporal evolution of deformations, a critical factor for accurate force prediction. The fusion of RGB and point cloud features is achieved through a late fusion strategy to allow the model to learn complementary features before the final regression layer predicts the contact forces. Training Procedure Data augmentation techniques; including geometric transformations and photometric alterations, were applied to [3] reduce overfitting and enhance the generalization capabilities of the model. Additionally, we employed a real-time data backpropagation strategy to make optimal use of GPU accelerative computations provided by NVIDIA’s CUDA platform. The model was [3] trained "using" a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function, with the Python-based PyTorch framework facilitating the model development. An Adam optimizer; known for its efficiency and adaptability, was chosen with a learning rate initialized at 1e-3, gradually decreasing with a schedule based on validation loss plateauing (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The batch size was dynamically adjusted based on the available GPU memory, with an epoch size that considered the entire data cycles fivefold. A train-validation split of 80%-20% was utilized, with stratification to ensure all force ranges [14] were represented in both datasets. Statistical Analysis To evaluate the performance of the RPCTCN model, statistical techniques were employed to compare predicted forces against ground truth measurements. The primary metric was the mean absolute error (MAE), computed as follows: \[ \text{MAE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \left| Yi - \hat{Y}i [34] \right| \] where \( Yi \) "represents" the actual force measured by the OptoForce sensor, \( \hat{Y}i \) denotes the predicted force, and \( N \) is the total number of test samples. A secondary evaluation metric, the Pearson [6] correlation coefficient; was calculated to assess the linear relationship between the predicted and actual forces; providing insights into the model’s [10] ability to preserve force trends (Benesty et al., 2009). Cross-validation techniques with K-fold (K=5) ensured that model performance metrics were stable and generalized across unseen data. Results were statistically analyzed (12) using a paired t-test to determine the significance of the difference between predicted and true forces, with a significance level set at α = 0.05 (Rosner, 2016). The identification of meaningful patterns within datasets is a fundamental objective in the (22) domain (27) of data mining and knowledge discovery. One of the crucial tasks is to find itemsets, which are combinations of items that frequently occur together within transactional datasets, such as market basket data. Traditional (12) approaches to mining itemsets have primarily focused on (26) uncovering frequent patterns without necessarily emphasizing the concise representation of data (Agrawal et al., 1993; Han et al., 2000). In recent years, there has been a growing interest in approaches that aim to find small, high-quality sets of itemsets which succinctly embody the underlying data structure. This shift is motivated by a number of challenges inherent in large-scale data analysis. Two of the most pressing among these are computational efficiency and interpretability. The sheer volume and complexity of data often make it unfeasible to consider exhaustive combinations of itemsets (Zaki et al.; 1997). Moreover, many existing methods for mining (13) itemsets, while successful at identifying frequent patterns, fail to provide an interpretation that facilitates a deeper understanding of the [3] interactions within the dataset (Pei et al., 2000). there exists a gap in the literature regarding methods that not only efficiently identify important itemsets but also do so in a manner that supports a comprehensive interpretation of data. "This" paper addresses this gap by [7] attempting to answer the following research question: How can we identify and select small groups of itemsets that provide a high-quality, compressed representation of the data? We propose approaching this (21) problem through a novel combination [35] of decision trees and a refined version of the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. The MDL principle, which posits that the best hypothesis for a given set of data is the (14) one that leads to the best compression, provides a powerful framework for balancing model complexity against (23) data fidelity (Rissanen; 1978). By utilizing decision trees within this framework, our methodology allows for the encapsulation of complex [9] attribute interactions, extending beyond simple co-occurrences of items. Our approach involves two main algorithms. The first is a simple greedy approach that constructs a set of itemsets directly from data. The second algorithm uses a pool of candidate itemsets and selects a subset that best represents the data according to our criteria. Both algorithms leverage the ordering of items within decision trees, where each decision tree is structured to predict an item based on [29] previously processed items. This structure not only enhances the predictive capability of the itemsets but also inherently supports the MDL principle through data compression. This work contributes to the field by forming a conceptual link between decision trees and itemsets—an association that has received limited attention in existing literature. While previous studies have explored decision trees mainly as predictive models (Quinlan; 1986; Breiman et al., 1984), their use as a mechanism for compressing data into interpretable itemsets presents a novel application. [28] Our algorithm has shown [31] to generate compact yet comprehensive representations on benchmark datasets; demonstrating its ability to identify itemsets that would otherwise remain undetected by traditional methods. Moreover; our experiments illustrate the capacity of this approach to provide compact representations without sacrificing accuracy, often outperforming conventional itemset mining strategies in both compression quality and interpretability. Through various case studies, we demonstrate the applicability of our method in different data scenarios, underscoring its versatility and robustness. In summary, this paper makes three main contributions to the field of data mining and pattern [4] recognition: 1. Introduction of a (6) Novel Itemset Mining Approach: We introduce an innovative methodology that combines decision trees with MDL to produce compressed itemset representations, enabling the identification of complex attributes interactions. 2. Development of Efficient Algorithms: We provide two algorithms, a greedy approach and a candidate selection method, which are specifically tailored to meet the challenges of itemset mining in large and complex datasets. 3. Empirical Validation and Benchmarking: Our methodologies are validated through comprehensive experiments that illustrate the effectiveness of our approach over existing methods in terms of data compression, [33] efficiency, and the interpretability of itemsets. Through these contributions, we aim to advance the discussion on efficient data representation and provide practitioners with powerful tools for discovering meaningful patterns within vast datasets. In doing so, this research paves the way for more sophisticated analyses and actionable insights in data science application areas. Our empirical evaluation is structured to substantiate the relationship between itemsets and decision trees, and to demonstrate the efficiency of our proposed algorithms in extracting compact and informative data representations. Data We utilized multiple datasets sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and other public domains renowned for comprehensive itemset data. Each dataset comprises a set of binary attributes, which we pre-processed to ensure consistency in attribute ordering and data integrity.
