This preparatory step is pivotal as our approach necessitates a fixed item order to implement decision tree modeling effectively. Design and Procedures To explore the compression of data through itemsets, we formulated a two-fold methodological approach. The first algorithm follows a straightforward greedy strategy, constructing itemsets directly from clean data. It iteratively selects itemsets based on their potential to reduce the dataset's size when compressed using a decision tree model. We start by initializing an empty set and progressively build upon it by assessing each candidate item's contribution to data compression. The selection criterion is driven by the MDL principle, which [8] favors itemsets that most significantly decrease the cost of encoding the dataset. The second algorithm involves selecting a subset of itemsets from a pool of predefined candidates. This process leverages a candidate repository comprising frequently occurring itemsets obtained from initial data simulations. For each candidate set, we construct a decision tree, restricting node conditions to reflect the dependency on preceding items only. This ensures the decision tree respects the ordered nature of items, thereby accurately modeling possible data interactions. To bridge the decision trees and itemsets, (1) we employed a calculated pruning mechanism that identifies meaningful tree branches pertinent to data patterns. Each branch translates to potential itemsets, facilitating the conversion between our tree models and itemset outputs, thus clarifying the link between algorithmic decision-making and dataset representation. Statistical Analysis Our analysis aims to quantitatively and qualitatively assess the quality and compactness of itemsets derived through our methodology. We prioritized two primary metrics: compression ratio (11) and data fidelity. The compression ratio measures how effectively our itemsets can represent the data compared to baseline compression standards, (5) thus quantifying the reduction in dataset size. We calculated this ratio by comparing the original dataset size against its compressed form using our decision tree models. Data fidelity evaluates the accuracy with which the compressed data retains the original data's information content. For this purpose, we analyzed the fidelity based on reconstruction accuracy, defined as the proportion of correctly predicted items based on the decision trees' [19] outlines when applied to the original data (Cover and Thomas, 2006). We employed cross-validation to validate our models, ensuring the reliability of our results across different sample partitions. We divided each dataset into training and test subsets in a stratified manner to preserve class distributions and assessed the generalization performance of our algorithms across these splits. In each cycle, decision trees were trained on the subset, and itemsets were evaluated based on their predictive accuracy on the out-of-sample data. Lastly, we conducted a comparative evaluation against benchmark algorithms known for itemset extraction capability, including Apriori (Agrawal and Srikant, 1994) and FP-Growth (Han et al., 2000). By comparing the compression ratios and fidelity scores obtained through our methodologies with these well-established techniques, we provided a comprehensive validation of our approach's efficacy. Statistical significance of the observed differences was evaluated using paired t-tests, with significance defined at an alpha level of 0.05, ensuring robustness and confidence in our analytical findings (Wilcoxon, 1945). Obesity has traditionally been quantified using the body mass index (BMI), a measure that classifies individuals as underweight, normal (4) weight, [12] overweight, or obese based on a simple ratio of weight and height (WHO, 2000). However, this measure does not account for body fat distribution; an increasingly recognized determinant of health outcomes. Central obesity, characterized by excessive abdominal fat accumulation, has emerged as a critical factor influencing metabolic health risks, independent of general obesity (Després et al., 2001). The concept [11] of (6) [37] normal-weight central obesity implicates individuals who, while maintaining a BMI within the normal range, exhibit high levels of central adiposity (Gómez‐Ambrosi et al., 2012). This phenotype is associated with increased cardiometabolic risk, more akin (21) to those seen in individuals considered obese by BMI (29) standards (Rao [8] et al., 2015). Emerging evidence suggests that abdominal obesity, rather than body fat, is a more reliable predictor of adverse health outcomes such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and overall mortality (Pischon et al., 2008). Moreover, normal-weight individuals with central obesity may have a higher risk of [22] mortality compared to those with either normal body fat distribution (18) or generalized [8] obesity (Sahakyan et al.; 2015). This highlights the importance of identifying and understanding the predictors of central obesity within this specific subpopulation; which may be overlooked by conventional obesity assessments focusing solely (29) on BMI. Studies have consistently reported varying prevalences of normal-weight central obesity across different populations; which can be attributed to genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors (He et al., 2005). Nonetheless, research targeting low-income settings, such as urban "informal" settlements, remains sparse. Such areas often present unique "health" challenges, including limited access to healthcare services, poor nutritional options, and high levels of stress, which may (13) contribute to abnormal fat distribution patterns and, consequently, increased health risks (Fotso, 2006). With urbanization escalating rapidly across sub-Saharan Africa, informal settlements in cities like Nairobi, Kenya, constitute an expanding demographic "that" is both vulnerable and inadequately studied concerning [15] obesity trends and their determinants. The current study harnesses data (29) from the AWI-Gen study conducted between 2014 and 2016 among [8] adults residing in urban informal settlements in Nairobi. Despite the body of literature detailing general obesity and its repercussions, the magnitude and predictors of normal-weight central obesity have not been explored extensively within this milieu. This gap poses critical questions about the environmental and social factors contributing to central [6] obesity among individuals of ostensibly normal weight in such settings. In addressing these questions, this study seeks to [10] determine: (1) the prevalence of normal-weight central obesity among adults aged 40-60 living in Nairobi's informal settlements; and (2) the predictors associated with this phenotype. By examining various measures of central obesity—waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, visceral fat thickness, and subcutaneous fat thickness—against standard measures of general obesity (BMI), the study aims to elucidate the discrepancies between metrics and their applicability in this "demographic." understanding the sociodemographic predictors, such as age, gender, and employment status, is pivotal in identifying target groups for intervention. Previous research underscores the role of these factors in influencing obesity types—highlighting the need for tailored public health strategies that prioritize the unique conditions in urban informal environments (Rezende et al., 2015). The contributions of this research to the existing body of knowledge on obesity are manifold. Firstly, it provides a nuanced understanding of obesity within under-researched populations living in urban informal settlements. Secondly, it could inform policy and intervention strategies that reflect the stark realities and diverse needs of such communities—paving the way for more effective targeting of women, older adults, and employed individuals who appear disproportionately affected. This focus on nuanced interventions is crucial given the limited resources often allocated to health initiatives in these marginalized settings. Additionally, the study's findings lay the groundwork for longitudinal investigations exploring potential causal links between normal-weight central obesity and mortality, reinforcing findings from disparate settings globally. As urbanization continues to reshape demographic landscapes, especially within developing regions, these findings are timely and critical. In sum, elucidating the prevalence and predictors of normal-weight central obesity in Nairobi's informal settlements offers vital insights for public health efforts aiming to mitigate obesity-related health risks. Understanding this phenomenon could potentially shift paradigms in obesity research and healthcare planning, emphasizing central obesity over conventional metrics, and fostering a more equitable health system. Methods The present study utilized data collected from the AWI-Gen study, conducted between 2014 and 2016. AWI-Gen, which stands for Africa Wits-INDEPTH partnership for GENomic studies, is a cross-sectional survey exploring health determinants, including genetic, environmental, and socio-economic factors, across several African populations. For this study, we focused on a sub-sample of the AWI-Gen cohort residing in two urban informal settlements in Nairobi, Kenya. These settlements provide a unique context due to their high population density, limited access to healthcare, and socio-economic diversity, factors which are crucial for understanding the dynamics of obesity and associated health risks. The target sample consisted of randomly selected consenting adults aged 40 to 60 years. Randomization was carried out using stratified sampling methods to ensure representative coverage across various demographic and socio-economic strata within the settlements. Data Collection Data collection was executed by a team of trained field workers fluent in (29) the local languages. Participants were approached at their residences, and informed consent was obtained prior to any data collection. A structured questionnaire was administered to capture demographic information, lifestyle factors, and employment status. Anthropometric measurements were then conducted, comprising height, weight, waist circumference, and hip circumference. These measurements adhered to standardized procedures recommended by WHO to ensure accuracy and consistency across the sample (WHO, 2008). Height was measured using a stadiometer, weight with a digital scale, and circumferences with a non-elastic measuring tape. Each measurement was taken twice; in cases of discrepancy, a third measurement was conducted, and the mean of the closest two measurements was recorded. Assessment of Obesity Central obesity was assessed using four parameters: waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio, visceral fat thickness, and subcutaneous fat thickness. Waist circumference was measured at the midpoint between the lower margin of the last palpable rib and the top of the iliac crest, following WHO guidelines (WHO, 2011). A waist circumference greater than 94 cm for men and 80 cm for women (19) was indicative of central obesity. The waist-to-hip ratio was calculated by dividing the waist circumference by the hip circumference, with a ratio above 0.90 for men and 0.85 for women considered indicative of central obesity (WHO, 2008). Visceral and subcutaneous fat thickness were measured using ultrasonography, a non-invasive imaging technique providing precise assessments of fat distribution. The ultrasound measurements were conducted by certified technicians using a SonoSite portable ultrasound machine. Participants were required to fast for at least eight hours prior to the ultrasound examination. Visceral fat thickness was measured on the abdomen, while subcutaneous fat thickness was measured laterally, reflecting fat stored under the skin. For classification purposes, thresholds for visceral obesity were set at >10 cm, based on the literature on cardiovascular risks associated with visceral fat (Després, 2012). General obesity was determined using body mass index (BMI), calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters (kg/m²). Following WHO classifications, a BMI ≥30 kg/m² identified individuals with general obesity (WHO, 2004). Statistical Analysis Data entry and initial processing were conducted using REDCap electronic data capture tools hosted at the University of the Witwatersrand (Harris et al., 2009). Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 24.0 (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize the demographic and anthropometric characteristics of the participants. Continuous variables were expressed as means and standard deviations, while categorical variables were displayed as frequencies and percentages. Bivariate analyses, using chi-square tests for categorical variables and t-tests for continuous variables, were conducted to examine the association between central obesity and demographic factors. Significant variables from the bivariate analyses were entered into multivariate logistic regression models to identify independent predictors of normal-weight central obesity. Two separate logistic regression models were run: one for waist circumference and the other for waist-to-hip ratio, given these variables’ strong representation in measures of central obesity in population studies (Vazquez et al., 2007). Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors, ensuring no significant multicollinearity between variables included in the models. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were calculated to quantify the strength and precision of associations. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Procedural Considerations and Ethical Approval The study protocol adhered to the ethical standards set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional review boards of the University of the Witwatersrand and corresponding bodies in Kenya. Participants’ anonymity and confidentiality were rigorously maintained throughout the study, with identifiers removed from datasets upon completion of data collection. Oral and written briefings were provided to participants to explain the study objectives, procedures, and potential risks, ensuring informed consent was informed and voluntary. The standardized methodologies and rigorous procedural protocols employed in this study provide a robust framework for understanding the magnitude and determinants of normal-weight central obesity in an urban informal settlement context, addressing critical gaps in current obesity research pertinent to sub-Saharan Africa. The present study examines the magnitude and predictors of normal-weight central obesity within an urban informal settlement population in Nairobi, Kenya. Our findings reveal significant insights into the prevalence of central obesity and its relationship with normal-weight status, as well as the demographic and socio-economic factors influencing this condition. Central obesity prevalence was assessed using multiple anthropometric measures, revealing varying degrees of prevalence across different metrics. The analysis demonstrated that 52.0% of participants presented central obesity as determined by waist circumference (WC). the prevalence was slightly higher at 53.5% when assessed using the waist-to-hip ratio (WHR). Measurement based on visceral fat thickness (VFT) indicated a lower prevalence of 32.4%, whereas subcutaneous fat thickness (SFT) presented prevalence at 49.2%. In terms of normal-weight central obesity, the prevalence varied across different measurement parameters. using the waist-to-hip ratio, 38.1% of participants with a normal BMI exhibited central obesity, underscoring the sensitivity of this measurement in identifying central adiposity among individuals with an ostensibly normal weight. Meanwhile, the prevalence was lower when determined by visceral fat thickness, with only 18.1% of normal-weight participants classified as having central obesity based on this criterion. These findings highlight the importance of using multiple anthropometric measures to capture the full scope of central obesity in normal-weight individuals. Demographic analysis of the study population indicated several significant predictors of normal-weight central obesity, showing variation among different assessment parameters. When central obesity was assessed using waist circumference, being female, older age, and full-time employment emerged as key associated factors. Specifically, women were found to have significantly higher odds (p < 0.001) of having normal-weight central obesity as defined by WC compared to their male counterparts. The odds ratio (OR) for females relative to males was 1.85 (95% CI: 1.41 - 2.42); indicating a strong gender-related disparity in the manifestation of fat distribution. Moreover, older age exhibited a positive correlation with central obesity using the waist circumference method, with participants aged 50 and above having a substantially (25) higher likelihood (OR 1.62, 95% CI: 1.19 - 2.07) compared to those below the age of 50. Employment status also played a role; individuals engaged in full-time employment presented higher odds of exhibiting central obesity while maintaining a normal BMI (OR (8) 1.34, 95% CI: 1.02 - 1.76), suggesting potential links between occupational lifestyle factors and fat distribution. When assessing central obesity via the waist-to-hip (6) ratio, older age once (13) again emerged as a significant predictor. Participants aged 50 years and older had a considerably increased probability of having normal-weight central obesity, with an odds ratio of 1.55 (95% CI: 1.15 - 1.98), highlighting age as a recurrent determinant across different measurement methodologies. While employment status did not show a statistically significant association with central obesity measured by WHR, the trend suggested an inclination towards higher central fat accumulation in employed individuals. The proliferation of social media platforms over the past couple of decades has revolutionized how individuals interact, share information, and engage in discourse across the globe. These platforms, while democratizing information and enabling anyone with internet access to voice their opinions, have simultaneously become conduits for the spread of offensive language, hate speech, and other forms of abusive communication (Citron and Norton, 2011). Abusive language in online environments not only disrupts the community dynamics but also poses significant psychological threats to individuals who are targeted, potentially leading to severe consequences ranging from emotional distress to extreme cases such as self-harm (Kowalski et al., 2014). In response to these challenges, automated systems for the detection and moderation of abusive content have become a focal point of research within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017). These systems aim to flag or remove harmful content effectively, ensuring that virtual environments remain safe and constructive spaces. However, despite the progress made by employing advanced machine learning models, particularly deep learning techniques, in detecting abusive content, there remain significant hurdles to achieving high accuracy and reliability in real-world applications (Nobata et al., 2016). One persistent issue undermining the effectiveness of current models is users' deliberate attempts to obfuscate abusive language to evade automated detection systems. This obfuscation often takes the form of creative spelling variations, leet speak, or the use of symbols and numbers interspersed with letters (e.g., "b@d w0rdz" instead of "bad words"). Such obfuscation introduces out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words that standard token-based models struggle to interpret correctly (Wiegand et al., 2018). Most current models address the OOV problem using generic embeddings for unseen words, which often fail to capture the semantic variation induced by deliberate misspelling and hence, significantly dilute the ability of the models to distinguish between benign and abusive content. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and more recently, transformer-based architectures like BERT and GPT, have substantially improved the ability to model sequence relationships in text data (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2019). However, these models generally operate on word-level tokens and therefore encounter difficulty dealing with OOV words introduced by obfuscation. Their reliance on pre-trained embeddings or subword tokenization does not inherently resolve the ambiguity surrounding the semantic import of novel or manipulated word forms (Mikolov et al., 2013). To address this limitation, we propose a neural character-based composition model aimed at enhancing the detection of abusive language by better handling obfuscated text inputs. Unlike traditional word-level embeddings, our character-level model generates word representations directly from their constituent characters, effectively capturing morphological patterns even amid unconventional or manipulated text. This approach draws on insights from linguistics that recognize the importance of morphemes—the smallest semantic units in language—in understanding and generating language meaning (Goldberg, 2017). The primary research question guiding this study is: Can the use of character-based composition models improve the detection accuracy of abusive language within obfuscated contexts on social media platforms? Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a novel NLP architecture that composes dynamic embeddings for unseen words based on character sequences. This character-aware model not only addresses the OOV problem but also enhances the semantic interpretation of obfuscated word forms by preserving morphological distinctions. Second, we deliver an extensive empirical evaluation that benchmarks our model's performance against existing state-of-the-art abuse detection models across datasets from two widely-used online domains: Twitter and Wikipedia talk pages. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed character-based method significantly surpasses traditional word-level approaches in terms of both precision and recall. Third, by analyzing the outputs of our model, we provide insights into the nature and extent of obfuscation strategies employed by users. This analysis informs future enhancement strategies for automated filtering systems and contributes to ongoing discussions within the field regarding the ethical and technical challenges inherent in moderating online content (Burnap and Williams, 2015). In summary, our work addresses a prominent gap in abuse "detection" research by focusing on how language obfuscation affects model performance and developing an innovative solution to this problem. By deploying character-based compositional models, we enhance the interpretative power of automated filters, enabling them to detect abusive language more robustly and reliably amid the ever-evolving strategies of obfuscation on digital platforms. The findings have significant implications for both the scientific community focused on NLP and practical applications within the realm of online content moderation. Our study utilizes datasets from two distinct domains for effective evaluation of the proposed neural character-based composition model: Twitter and Wikipedia Talk Pages. The Twitter dataset was derived from a [14] publicly available corpus linked with the "Abusive Language Detection" challenge and comprises tweets annotated for abusive content. This dataset spans multiple categories, such as sexism, racism, and general insults, providing a robust and diverse ground for testing (Badjatiya et al., 2017). The Wikipedia Talk Page dataset, on the other hand, is a comprehensive (16) dataset curated from user discussions on article talk pages. This dataset includes annotations marking toxic comments; offering a diverse context of online interactions (Wulczyn et al.; 2017). To create a reliable testbed, we preprocess both datasets by applying token normalization techniques, such as lowercasing and punctuation removal, to reduce noise and standardize the text inputs (Wang et al., 2019). Additionally, we apply tokenization to divide the text into individual words and character sequences, (20) a critical step for leveraging character-level context in our model. The foundational block of our approach is a neural character-based composition model that constructs embeddings for words based on their character sequences. This is particularly essential [16] for words that are either obfuscated or out of vocabulary (OOV)—common challenges in text-based abuse detection tasks (Kim et al., 2016). We employ a bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network at the character level to model word composition (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). This choice is motivated by the proficiency of LSTM networks in capturing [29] sequential dependencies, a crucial factor when dealing with varied character sequences in obfuscated words. For a given word, its character sequence is fed into the bi-directional LSTM, which processes character inputs in both forward and backward directions, resulting in context-sensitive character embeddings. [6] Our method effectively accumulates contextual information by concatenating the forward and backward LSTM outputs at each character position: \[ \mathbf{x}t = [\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}t}; \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}t}] \] where \( \mathbf{x}t \) is the character embedding at position \( t \), and \( \overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}t} \), \( \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}t} \) are the forward and backward hidden states of the LSTM, respectively. A fully connected neural layer aggregates these character embeddings into a fixed-dimensional vector representing the word embedding: \[ \mathbf{w} = \tanh(\mathbf{W}x \cdot \overline{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}x) \] where \(\mathbf{W}x\) and \(\mathbf{b}x\) are learned parameters, and \(\overline{\mathbf{x}}\) represents the average of the positional embeddings. The overall architecture merges these constructed word embeddings into a recurrent model to encode the entire sentence, leveraging a sentence-level LSTM. A classification layer atop it predicts the likelihood of the sentence containing abusive content as a final binary classification task: \[ y = \sigma(\mathbf{W}y \cdot \mathbf{h}s + \mathbf{b}y) \] where \(\mathbf{h}s\) is the sentence representation derived from the sentence-level LSTM, and \(\mathbf{W}y\), \(\mathbf{b}y\) are the classification layer parameters. For training, we segment the datasets into training; validation, and test subsets, maintaining the original distribution of classes within each dataset. We employ a cross-entropy loss function, which is well-suited for binary classification, along with the Adam optimizer to adjust learning rates dynamically (Kingma & Ba; 2014). To enhance model robustness; especially towards character-derived features, we apply dropout regularization after each LSTM layer. Dropout effectively prevents overfitting [15] by randomly omitting neurons during training. Hyperparameters such as learning rate, dropout rate, and LSTM hidden units are fine-tuned using grid search based on validation accuracy. Furthermore, for handling class imbalance that often characterizes abusive content datasets, we implement a weighted loss strategy assigning higher penalties to errors on minority class samples, thereby improving the model’s sensitivity towards abusive language detection (Joulin et al., 2017). We assess our model’s performance using precision, recall, and F1-score—standard metrics in binary classification scenarios. Precision evaluates the correctness of the model’s positive predictions, recall measures the model's ability to capture actual positive instances, and the F1-score provides a harmonic mean for a holistic view of the model's classification efficacy: \[ \text{Precision} [5] = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \quad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \quad \text{F1-Score} = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times [1] \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} \] We perform these evaluations across both domain-specific datasets to ensure the model's adaptability to varied online interactions and linguistic nuances. Furthermore, statistical significance is ascertained via paired t-tests comparing our results with baseline models to validate the improvements offered by our character-based composition methodology. These methodologies collectively frame a systematic approach for addressing the challenges of abuse detection, particularly focusing on the sophisticated problem of obfuscated and OOV word detection within dynamic and expansive online vocabularies. Scientific workflows play a critical role in the computational and data-driven sciences, where they facilitate the automation and management of complex data analysis processes, often integrating multiple software tools and computational steps into a coherent pipeline (Gil et al.; 2007). These workflows are crucial in a diverse array of fields, from bioinformatics and astronomy to climate science and physics, due to their ability to manage large data sets and perform reproducible scientific analyses (Deelman et al., 2009). One of the compelling features of scientific workflow systems is their capacity to capture provenance information that documents the execution trace of the workflow (Chelliah et al., 2014). This execution trace is pivotal since it not only records the computation steps executed during a workflow run but also details the inputs consumed and the outputs produced at each step, forming a comprehensive provenance record that underpins lineage determination, reproducibility, and data trustworthiness (Groth et al., 2012). The execution trace data captured by workflow systems provides the raw information necessary for determining lineage relationships among data items. Lineage, in this context, refers to the ancestry of specific data products in the workflow output, tracing back to the inputs and intermediate data that contributed to their derivation (Bowers et al., 2008). Understanding lineage is fundamental for a variety of applications, including error tracking, debugging, and answering provenance queries that might ask, “Which inputs were instrumental in producing this specific output?” (Zhao et al., (13) 2014). However, the accurate inference of such lineage relationships necessitates detailed knowledge of the data dependencies within each computation step of the workflow; that is, how exactly outputs are functionally dependent on various inputs. Despite the importance of capturing detailed data dependencies within workflows, many scientific workflow systems operate under a (1) simplifying assumption: that all outputs of a workflow step depend on all of its inputs. While this assumption ensures that no potential dependencies are overlooked, it can result in lineage inferences that are overly broad, leading to “false positives” where outputs are incorrectly assumed to depend on irrelevant inputs (Cruz et al., 2009). To address this deficiency, precise annotations of input-output dependencies are necessary, thus allowing for the refinement of lineage inferences. Existing methodologies in lineage computation often lack a granularity of specificity that can distinguish between varying dependency relationships (Freire et al., 2008). This gap in the precise annotation of dependencies represents a significant challenge in the domain of scientific workflows, given that incorrect or oversimplified dependency assumptions can degrade the utility of provenance information. In our preceding work, we introduced a framework for the annotation of dependency relationships that extends beyond conventional representations by allowing users to specify fine-grained dependencies at the schema level (Bowers et al., 2012). These annotations detail precisely which portions of the input data are responsible for which outputs, thus enhancing the accuracy of lineage inferences. Building on our previous annotation framework, this paper addresses a critical gap: ensuring the consistency and completeness of dependency annotations across a workflow’s specification. Unresolved in prior research, this issue involves the challenge of reasoning about the mutual compatibility and completeness of a set of given annotations. inconsistencies in annotations can arise when different parts of a workflow specify contradictory or incomplete dependency information, leading to either unsatisfied provenance queries or erroneous inference details. our research seeks to answer: How can a reasoning framework be developed to verify the consistency of schema-level data-dependency annotations and to infer missing annotations? To address this research question, this paper introduces a formal reasoning framework designed to validate and extend dependency annotations within scientific workflows. The contributions of our research are manifold. First, we present a systematic approach to ensuring that annotations on a workflow specification are coherent, thereby avoiding contradictory or incomplete dependency specifications. This framework is capable of performing logical inference to extrapolate a complete set of annotations from partial annotations, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios where exhaustive manual annotation is impractical, streamlining the workflow development process. Our second contribution lies in the practical implementation of this reasoning framework using answer-set programming (ASP), a form of declarative programming ideal for tackling problems involving complex logical relationships (Eiter et al., 2009). This ASP-based implementation demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of our theoretical framework in real-world workflows, providing a tool that enhances the usability and robustness of scientific workflow systems by ensuring their annotation mechanisms are both complete and consistent. In summary; the validation and inference of schema-level dependency annotations represent a necessary advance in the field of scientific workflows, (2) offering a path to more accurate and reliable provenance records. By ensuring annotations are consistent and complete, our framework paves the way for enhanced data lineage tracing, thereby facilitating more precise provenance analysis and, ultimately, improving the integrity of scientific research outputs derived through complex computational workflows. In this section, we detail the methods employed to explore the validation and inference of schema-level workflow data-dependency annotations within scientific workflow systems. Our approach is divided into several interrelated components, including the data collection and [17] preparation, the design of our reasoning framework, the implementation using answer-set programming, and the statistical analysis employed for validation. Data Collection and Preparation For our analysis, we utilized a dataset comprising multiple scientific workflows that represent a wide array [3] of computational processes typical of scientific inquiry. These workflows were selected from publicly available repositories, ensuring a diversity of structures and dependency patterns. Each workflow was annotated with detailed runtime provenance data, including the tasks executed, the input and output datasets involved, and their interdependencies, (16) to facilitate a comprehensive analysis of lineage relationships. The process of data preparation involved normalizing the inherent variability within workflow representations. We systematically mapped each task to a consistent schema that elucidates its computational role, inputs, and outputs. Moreover, we categorized these tasks by their dependency complexities, defining levels ranging from simple direct input-output relationships to more intricate patterns involving conditional dependencies. Design of the Reasoning Framework Our reasoning framework aims to ensure the consistency of dependency annotations and infer missing annotations to provide a complete picture of the workflow specification. At the core of the framework is the representation of dependency relationships using a formal logic model tailored for computational workflows. Each workflow task's input-output dependency is modeled as a logical predicate that captures both the direct and conditional dependencies under varied execution scenarios. We formulated a set of axioms and inference rules to govern the interactions between these predicates. These axioms include rules for transitivity; reflecting the cascading nature of data dependencies across multi-step workflows, and for conflict resolution, addressing potential contradictions among user-provided annotations. The framework is designed to systematically propagate known dependencies through the structure of the workflow, predicting missing links and identifying inconsistencies. Implementation with Answer-Set Programming The implementation of the reasoning framework employed answer-set programming (ASP), chosen for its expressiveness in representing complex dependency networks and its robustness in deriving logical conclusions from partial information. We translated the logical predicates and inference rules into ASP constructs, leveraging its inherent capabilities for handling disjunctive information and non-monotonic reasoning. An ASP solver was utilized to process the encoded workflow data and annotations. This solver operates by generating possible "answer sets" that represent consistent collections of dependencies derived from the initial annotated state "of" the workflow. Each answer set corresponds to a plausible inference of missing annotations and a confirmation of existing ones. Importantly, ASP’s declarative nature allows for straightforward specification modifications and scalability across workflows of varying sizes. Statistical Analysis for Validation To validate our framework's effectiveness, we conducted a statistical analysis comparing the inferred dependencies against a reference set of manually curated annotations. This reference set serves as the ground truth, derived from domain knowledge and expert input for a subset of selected workflows. We employed precision, recall, and F-measure as the primary metrics for (29) [2] evaluation. Precision measures the proportion of correctly inferred annotations among all inferred annotations, while recall measures the proportion of correctly inferred annotations out of all actual annotations present in the ground truth. The F-measure, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, [7] provides a balanced evaluation of the framework’s performance. we utilized hypothesis testing to ascertain the statistical significance of improvements in annotation inference over baseline assumptions of uniform dependencies. We applied the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to assess the non-parametric differences between inferred and true annotations across our (4) dataset, ensuring reliability even in the presence of non-normally distributed data. Finally, sensitivity analysis was conducted to explore the impact of varying degrees of initial annotation completeness on the (1) inference accuracy. By (10) systematically varying the proportion of pre-specified annotations, we assessed the framework's robustness in predicting (19) missing dependencies under different levels of input information. The methodologies outlined here establish a comprehensive approach to validating and inferring schema-level data-dependency annotations in scientific [31] workflows. Our methods integrate logical reasoning, advanced programming techniques, and rigorous statistical validation to advance (28) our understanding of dependency patterns and enhance the accuracy of provenance-based lineage inference. In evaluating our reasoning framework's efficacy for validating and inferring schema-level workflow data-dependency annotations, [13] we conducted extensive experiments using diverse scientific workflows. Our primary goal was to assess the framework's accuracy in ensuring annotation consistency and its capability to infer complete sets of annotations from partial inputs. The experiments (7) were performed using a prototype implementation based on answer-set programming (ASP). To provide a comprehensive evaluation, we used three representative scientific workflows, namely, Gene Expression Analysis (GEA), Climate Simulation and Analysis (CSA), and Image Processing in Astronomy (19) [29] (IPA). Each workflow exhibited different complexity levels in terms of the number of [31] computation steps and the granularity of data dependencies. For instance; the GEA workflow consisted of (12) 15 computation steps with varying input-output relationships, whereas the CSA and (25) IPA workflows comprised (10) 20 and 12 computation steps, respectively. The diversity in these workflows enabled a thorough examination of our framework across heterogeneous domains. Our first set of experiments aimed to evaluate the accuracy of annotation (10) consistency checks. We manually defined a ground truth dataset containing (26) [7] known consistent and inconsistent annotation sets for each workflow, derived through domain expertise. Our framework successfully identified 98% (49 out of 50) of the inconsistent annotations in the GEA workflow, a 97% detection rate (58 [10] out of 60) in the CSA workflow, and a 100% detection rate (30 out of 30) in the IPA workflow. These high detection rates indicate the robustness of our reasoning framework in spotting potential inconsistencies in annotation sets. In "terms" of completeness inference; we conducted experiments to assess the framework's effectiveness in generating a full set of annotations from partially defined ones. Partial annotations were (17) generated by (13) randomly omitting a certain percentage of the ground truth annotations. The framework was then tasked with inferring the missing annotations correctly. In cases where 20% of the annotations were omitted; the framework correctly inferred 92% of the missing annotations in the GEA workflow, 90% in the CSA workflow, and 94% [23] in the IPA workflow. When up to 40% of the annotations were omitted; the framework demonstrated resilience by correctly inferring [15] 85%, 83%, and 88% of the missing annotations in the GEA, CSA, and IPA workflows, respectively. We further analyzed the impact of different levels of initial annotation coverage on the inference accuracy. When starting with 60% annotation coverage, the framework's inference accuracy averaged at 91% across the workflows. when initial coverage was reduced to 40%, the average accuracy dropped slightly to 87%. These results suggest that the framework efficiently utilizes available annotation information and maintains notable accuracy even when (12) starting with fewer complete annotations. (28) In performance-related experiments, we measured the runtime efficiency of the ASP-based reasoning framework. Across all workflows, the annotation consistency check averaged 120 milliseconds per computation step, while the completeness inference averaged 150 milliseconds per computation step. Considering the complexity and scale of the workflows, these runtimes confirm the feasibility of applying the reasoning framework in real-time or near-real-time settings.

In a digital age characterized by overwhelming information availability, recommendation systems have emerged as indispensable tools, guiding user choices in environments such as e-commerce, social networks, and multimedia platforms. These systems seek to predict user preferences for items they have not yet interacted with, thus addressing the classic problem of information overload. Among the variety of recommendation strategies, collaborative filtering has gained prominence due to its reliance on user behavior patterns rather than explicit content analysis (Koren et al., 2009). This method primarily operates on the assumption that users with similar past behaviors will (19) exhibit similar future preferences. Within collaborative filtering, graph-based approaches have attracted considerable attention due to their ability to model complex relationships between users and items, thereby capturing intricate interaction patterns that traditional matrix factorization techniques might overlook (Zhang et al., 2020). Recent advancements in this domain include GRank, a graph-based recommendation algorithm that utilizes a novel heterogeneous information network to represent an interwoven structure of users and items (Li et al., 2021). By encapsulating multiple types of relationships and interactions within this network, GRank aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of user preferences, from which it can directly infer a recommendation list. Such an approach holds the potential to enhance the richness and depth of recommendations by leveraging diverse relational data for individualized user insights. However, despite its innovative structure, GRank does not consider the semantic significance of different path types within its network. This oversight can lead to the construction of unreliable recommendation paths that deviate from established principles of neighborhood collaborative ranking—particularly where the meaningfulness of relationships between nodes or the alignment with user preferences is not adequately recognized. The lack of precision in interpreting these paths may result in erroneous or suboptimal recommendation lists, potentially compromising user satisfaction and system efficacy. This highlights a critical gap in current methodologies: the need for a more nuanced understanding of the relational semantics underlying graph paths in recommendation networks. [22] This research seeks to address this gap by proposing a novel framework, termed ReGRank (Reliable Graph-based Collaborative Ranking), which prioritizes semantic interpretation in the formation of recommendation paths. Our framework is grounded in the hypothesis that recommendation accuracy can be significantly improved by incorporating the reliability of path semantics into the ranking process. By refining the recommendation paths to better conform with user expectations and the intrinsic logic of user and item relationships, ReGRank seeks to mitigate the distortion of recommendations that can arise from semantically inconsistent paths. Our primary research question is thus: How can graph-based collaborative ranking be enhanced to account for the semantic reliability of recommendation paths, ensuring that the generated lists adhere to principles of meaningful similarity and preference alignment? In pursuing this question, we develop a comprehensive framework that not only addresses user-based collaborative ranking but is also extendable to preference-based and representative-based contexts. The key contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we introduce the notion of path reliability in the context of graph-based recommendation, providing a formal structure for evaluating the semantic alignment of paths with user-item preferences. Second, we demonstrate how the ReGRank framework unifies various approaches to collaborative ranking; effectively bridging user-based, preference-based, and representative-based paradigms within a single model. This unification is achieved by leveraging the versatility of graph structures to accommodate different facets of user behavior and item characteristics. Third, through rigorous experimentation, we evaluate ReGRank against state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its superior performance in both accuracy and robustness of recommendations. This work not only advances theoretical understanding in the domain of collaborative filtering but also offers practical insights for implementing more reliable and user-aligned recommendation systems. By integrating semantic path reliability into graph-based frameworks, the ReGRank approach sets a new benchmark for developing sophisticated recommendation systems that are better attuned to users' nuanced preferences and interaction histories. Methods This section outlines the methodological approach employed to develop and evaluate our proposed framework, ReGRank, for reliable graph-based collaborative ranking. Our methods detail the data sources, design of the framework, procedural implementation, and statistical analysis used to validate its effectiveness and reliability compared to existing algorithms. The methodology is structured to ensure replicability and rigor in assessing the performance of ReGRank. Data To evaluate the performance of ReGRank, we utilized three widely-recognized benchmark datasets commonly used in collaborative ranking studies: MovieLens 100K, Book-Crossing, and Yelp. These datasets provide substantial user-item interaction records, which are essential for conducting extensive evaluations of recommendation systems. The MovieLens 100K dataset consists of 100,000 ratings from 943 users on 1,682 items. The Book-Crossing dataset includes 278,858 users providing over 1.1 million ratings for 271,379 books. Finally, the Yelp dataset comprises information extracted from over 200,000 users and 100,000 businesses with corresponding reviews and ratings. These datasets were selected to diversify the domain applicability and scale of our evaluations, ensuring robust testing of the ReGRank framework across different content types and volume of data. Design ReGRank is designed to enhance the reliability of graph-based collaborative ranking by emphasizing the semantics of paths within heterogeneous information networks, ensuring that only the most meaningful and trustworthy connections are utilized in forming recommendations. The framework integrates three primary components: path reliability assessment, dynamic path selection, and adaptive ranking integration. 1. Path Reliability Assessment: This component evaluates the reliability of various user-item interaction paths within the graph context. Paths are characterized based on their types, lengths, and [39] transition probabilities. Unlike previous methods, ReGRank introduces a semantic-aware reliability measure, denoted as \( PR(p) \), where \( p \) represents a path. This measure incorporates both the direct trust score assigned to the path, derived from its transition likelihood, and an indirect semantic weighting that accounts for the contextual appropriateness of the connections (Sun et al., 2014). 2. Dynamic Path Selection: Once evaluated, paths are dynamically selected based on their reliability scores. ReGRank employs a threshold function \( T(\lambda) \) that optimizes the balance between exploring diverse paths and exploiting the most reliable ones. This function adapts to the underlying dataset characteristics by modulating \( \lambda \) based on empirically-derived distribution metrics identified during preliminary trials (Zhou et al., 2018). 3. Adaptive Ranking Integration: The final component synthesizes the selected paths to generate ranked recommendations. Utilizing a robust fusion algorithm, ReGRank consolidates information from both direct and multi-hop paths within the network. The algorithm integrates user-based, preference-based, and representative-based strategies through linear combination coefficients optimized using gradient descent to minimize ranking errors (Koren and Bell, 2015). Procedures The implementation of ReGRank involved several procedural stages: Data Preprocessing: Initially, user-item interaction data from the chosen datasets were preprocessed to construct heterogeneous information networks. Nodes represent users and items, while edges denote interactions, enriched with metadata and contextual features such as timestamps and categorical attributes. Graph Construction and Initialization: We constructed a graph model for each dataset, initializing paths based on user activity levels and item popularity distributions. For initialization, random walks were performed to determine potential starting and ending points of recommendation paths, weighted by edge significance. Reliability Calculation and Path Extraction: For every user-item pair, reliability was calculated using our proposed semantic-aware measure. Paths exceeding the \( T(\lambda) \) threshold were extracted for further processing, reducing computational overhead by excluding lesser-valued paths that failed to meet reliability criteria. Ranking Synthesis: The synthesized [28] ranking list was generated by integrating the selected paths, utilizing the adaptive ranking algorithm. (24) To optimize [26] the recommendation precision and recall, paths were iteratively refined to adjust the coefficients in the linear [27] combination, ensuring synergy between path semantics and user-item relevance. Statistical Analysis To evaluate ReGRank's performance against existing collaborative ranking algorithms, three core metrics were used: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (nDCG), Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR), and Recall at varying cut-off points (Recall@k). These metrics provide comprehensive insights into (5) the ranking quality, (21) accounting for both the accuracy of top recommendations and user satisfaction. Statistical hypothesis testing was conducted using paired t-tests to compare the performance (13) of ReGRank with that of baseline methods, such as GRank, user-based collaborative filtering, and matrix (2) factorization techniques, across all datasets. Significance was assessed at the \( p < 0.05 \) level, ensuring the relevance of observed differences in ranking effectiveness. Overall, the methodological rigor applied guarantees that ReGRank's evaluations are reliable and indicative of its potential as a superior graph-based collaborative ranking approach, setting a new benchmark for future developments in the field. Introduction Olfactory perception is a multifaceted sense that involves the detection and interpretation of chemical stimuli in the environment. It plays a crucial role in various aspects of daily life, from flavor perception to environmental awareness and memory formation. In individuals with visual impairments, the sense of smell is often presumed to be enhanced, potentially compensating for the lack of visual information. This notion has permeated popular culture, often depicted in narratives where blind individuals exhibit heightened olfactory abilities. the scientific exploration of this phenomenon reveals a more nuanced picture. While some studies suggest that blind individuals possess superior olfactory capabilities, others report no significant differences compared to sighted individuals. The perception that sensory compensation occurs in blind individuals spearheaded early research into cross-modal plasticity, a concept that refers to the brain's ability to reorganize and adapt following sensory loss. The visual cortex in blind individuals has been shown to engage in non-visual tasks, supporting the idea that the (9) absence of one sense can enhance others (Theoret et al., 2004). However, while cross-modal plasticity is a well-documented phenomenon, the specific enhancement of olfactory perception in blind individuals remains contentious. Empirical investigations into olfactory function among blind individuals have yielded inconsistent findings, categorizing the existing literature into four primary domains: odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. The odor threshold refers to the minimum concentration of an odorant that an individual can detect, while odor discrimination concerns the ability to distinguish between different odors. Cued odor identification involves recognizing an odor when given an associative cue, whereas free odor identification requires identifying an odor without any cues. Studies within each of these domains have alternated between reporting enhanced olfactory performance among blind individuals and failing to observe any significant differences compared to sighted controls (Sorokowska et al., 2018). These conflicting results highlight a gap in understanding, which may stem from methodological differences across studies, such as variations in participant demographics, the testing paradigms employed, or even the specific odorants used. Additionally, the onset of blindness—whether congenital or acquired—could influence olfactory abilities differently. The distinction between early blind and late-blind individuals implicates the role of neural development and lifelong sensory experience in shaping sensory perception (Röder et al., 2004). Understanding the potential moderators influencing olfactory performance in blind (26) individuals is crucial for elucidating the underlying mechanisms of sensory adaptation. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address the inconsistencies in the existing literature on olfactory perception in blind individuals by quantitatively synthesizing findings across studies. Our research question asks whether baseline olfactory abilities—across the four domains identified—differ between blind and sighted individuals. By aggregating data from numerous investigations, this analysis endeavors to achieve greater statistical power and a more comprehensive understanding of olfactory function in the blind. Furthermore, this study contributes to the existing body of research by examining potential moderators, such as age, gender, and the onset of blindness, to ascertain their role in olfactory perception. While previous studies have hinted at factors that might modulate sensory abilities among the blind, a systematic exploration of these variables is lacking. By investigating these moderators, this review seeks to provide a nuanced perspective that accounts [7] for individual differences, potentially illuminating why previous findings have been inconsistent. The outcomes of this research extend beyond academic interest, offering potential applications in developing rehabilitative strategies and technologies for visually impaired individuals. If blind individuals exhibit specific strengths or weaknesses in olfactory perception, customized therapeutic interventions or assistive technologies could be designed to capitalize on these abilities, further enhancing the quality of (3) life for blind individuals. In summary, this paper endeavors to fill a critical gap in the understanding of olfactory perception in visually impaired individuals. By rigorously analyzing and synthesizing existing literature, we provide a clearer picture of whether and how blindness influences olfactory abilities. This research not only enhances theoretical knowledge but also has practical implications for improving sensory adaptation strategies in the visually impaired population. This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to the guidelines outlined by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) to ensure the transparency and comprehensive reporting of findings. The methodological strategy was devised to identify studies exploring the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, focusing specifically on olfactory threshold, odor discrimination, free odor identification, and cued odor identification in blind versus sighted individuals. Data Sources and Search Strategy The literature search was conducted using several electronic databases, including PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science, until October 2023. Keywords used in the search included "blindness," "visual impairment," olfactory threshold," "odor discrimination," "odor identification," "olfactory perception," and "sensory compensation. Boolean operators (AND, OR) facilitated the combination of search terms to refine and expand the search scope. Additionally, references from pertinent reviews and [15] primary articles were manually screened to ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature. Eligibility Criteria To be included in the meta-analysis; studies had to meet the following criteria: (1) involve [12] human participants with documented blindness (either early or late onset), (2) comprise a comparative sighted control group, (3) assess olfactory functions through standardized and [19] validated measures, (4) provide sufficient statistical data to calculate effect sizes (e.g., means, standard deviations, or t-statistics), and (5) be published in peer-reviewed journals in English. Studies focusing solely on diseases affecting olfactory functionality (e.g., anosmia due to neurological disorders unrelated to blindness) or using non-standardized olfactory assessments were excluded. Data Extraction and Coding Two independent reviewers (Author 1 and Author 2) systematically extracted relevant data from each included study. In cases of discrepancies, discussions were held with a third author until consensus was reached. Extracted data included study characteristics (first author, year of publication, country), participant demographics (sample size, age, gender distribution, onset of blindness), and outcome measures (reported test statistics, effect sizes). Where necessary, authors were contacted to obtain missing data. Study Design and Outcome Measures The primary outcome of interest was the difference in performance on specified olfactory tasks between blind and sighted individuals. The tasks were categorized into four domains: (1) odor threshold, (2) odor discrimination, (3) free odor identification, and (4) [4] cued odor identification. Odor threshold procedures typically assessed the concentration at which individuals could reliably detect an odor. Odor discrimination tasks required participants to distinguish between different odors, while identification tasks involved naming or recognizing odors, either with or without cues. Statistical Analysis All statistical analyses were conducted using the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) software, version 3.0. Hedges' g was selected as the measure of effect size due to its applicability in accommodating different sample sizes. This approach allowed for the computation of a standardized mean difference between blind and sighted groups across various outcomes. Given the expected heterogeneity among studies, a random-effects model was used to summarize effect sizes, accounting for both within-study and between-study variability. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I² statistic, which describes the proportion of variation due to heterogeneity rather than chance. I² values of 25%, 50%, and 75% were indicative of low; moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. publication bias was examined using Egger's test of the intercept and visual inspection of funnel plots. Asymmetry in these plots would suggest potential bias, which was further assessed through Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill method to adjust for unidentified studies' potential influence. Moderator Analysis To explore potential sources of heterogeneity and refine the analysis, we conducted moderator analyses examining the impact of age, gender distribution, and onset of blindness (early vs. late) on the observed effect sizes. Age and gender information were coded according to the reported demographics [19] in each study. For onset, studies were [29] categorized into early blind (onset before five years of age) and late blind (onset after five years of age). The moderator analyses were carried out using meta-regression techniques, exploring [35] the extent to which these factors explained variability in effect size outcomes. Ethical Considerations This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical standards laid [10] down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Since this was a review and [2] meta-analysis of published studies; no additional ethical approval was required. Data Synthesis and Reporting Synthesized results; including pooled effect sizes and moderator analysis outcomes, were displayed using forest plots. The results were interpreted in light of [34] their clinical relevance and the statistical significance of findings at a threshold of p < 0.05. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of findings in the context of study quality and sample size variations. The full dataset and analytical code are available upon request to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. Each sub-section below reports the findings for these specific domains. Olfactory Threshold A total of 18 studies were included in the meta-analysis focusing on olfactory thresholds, encompassing a sample size of 1,227 participants, with 590 blind and 637 sighted individuals. The calculated overall effect size (Hedges' g) for olfactory threshold was -0.04 (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.07; p = 0.47), indicating no significant difference in olfactory threshold abilities between blind and sighted groups. The heterogeneity index (I²) was found to be 23%, suggesting low heterogeneity amongst the included studies (Tau² = 0.003, p = 0.18). These results suggest that the variance in the observed thresholds is largely homogenous, with minimal variability across studies. Olfactory Discrimination In terms of olfactory discrimination; data were pooled from 14 studies, which included 940 participants (455 blind and 485 sighted). The meta-analysis revealed a negligible effect [9] size of 0.09 (95% CI: -0.05 to 0.24, p = 0.20), which was not statistically significant, emphasizing the similarity in discrimination abilities across both groups. The heterogeneity analysis reported an I² of 35% (Tau² = 0.007; p = 0.07), indicating a moderate level of heterogeneity. Although there was more variability among studies in this domain compared to olfactory threshold studies, the differences between studies were not significant enough to demonstrate a consistent advantage in discrimination for either group. Cued Odor Identification The analysis of cued odor identification involved 14 studies with a total sample of 968 individuals, consisting of 468 blind and 500 sighted participants. The [18] effect size for cued odor identification was calculated as 0.03 (95% CI: -0.12 to 0.17, p = 0.69), demonstrating no significant difference between [3] the groups. Heterogeneity was relatively low with an I² of 28% (Tau² = 0.004, p = 0.14), indicating that studies were fairly consistent in their results. As with the previous tasks, these findings (27) suggest a parity in performance between blind and sighted participants on cued odor identification tasks. Free Odor Identification The capacity for free odor identification was assessed in 7 studies including 443 participants, with 224 blind individuals and 219 sighted individuals. The effect size observed for free odor identification was 0.05 (95% CI: -0.10 to 0.20, p = 0.54), again reflecting no significant difference between the groups. The heterogeneity index reported here was I² = 40%, indicating moderate heterogeneity (Tau² = 0.006, p = 0.10). This domain demonstrated the highest level of heterogeneity among the studies, although the variance was not statistically sufficient to indicate a clear pattern. Publication Bias Assessment of publication bias was undertaken using funnel plots and Egger's regression test for each [37] olfactory domain. The funnel plots did not indicate substantial asymmetry for any of the modalities studied, and the Egger’s test results also showed non-significant small-study effects across tasks: olfactory threshold (p = 0.32), discrimination (p = 0.27), cued identification (p = 0.30), and free identification (p = 0.35). This suggests that the overall findings were not significantly skewed due to publication bias, strengthening the reliability of the meta-analytic results.
