Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a foundational task in the domain of Natural Language Processing (NLP), integral to a wide array of applications, (27) including information extraction; question answering, and machine translation. Traditionally, NER systems have focused on flat or non-overlapping mentions of entities within text, motivated by widely-used datasets such as the CoNLL-2003 shared task dataset that adhere to this flat annotation paradigm (Tjong Kim Sang & De Meulder, 2003). This traditional focus has engendered significant advancements in extracting contiguous spans of text that correspond to predefined types of named entities, such as persons, organizations, and locations. While successful, these systems often fail to capture the complexity inherent in naturally occurring text, where entities (13) can frequently appear in nested structures. The inability to recognize and accurately label these nested entities becomes a bottleneck, particularly in richly detailed domains such as newswire text, where context and specificity are crucial. The increasing importance of exploring linguistic intricacies has propelled interest in nested NER. Unlike flat NER, nested NER aims to identify entities contained within other entities, preserving the full structural complexity seen in natural language. For example, in the phrase "The President of the United States, Joe Biden," (17) a nested NER system should identify "President of the United States" as an organization title and "Joe Biden" as a person, different from the oversimplified flat categorization (Finkel & Manning, 2009). Despite its promise, progress in nested NER has been impeded by the lack of comprehensive, annotated datasets that comprehensively reflect these nested structures. Current datasets either offer limited entity types or fail to provide annotations across multiple nesting levels, stymieing the development and evaluation of sophisticated nested NER systems. Addressing this critical gap, we introduce NNE: (1) a (20) robust dataset for Nested Named Entity Recognition [2] specifically curated from the (11) Wall Street Journal segment of the Penn Treebank (PTB) corpus (Marcus et al.; 1993). The dataset is meticulously annotated to (2) capture [22] a wide array of entities in a nested format, encompassing a previously unapproached complexity [20] with its extensive coverage spanning 114 entity (17) types and up to six layers of nesting. Unlike predecessors, which often confine themselves to only a handful of entity types within (25) simple structural arrangements, NNE extends the landscape of (2) named entity annotation by embracing multilayered semantic relations akin to those found in real-world text. This approach opens (4) new avenues for exploring how knowledge can be structured and extracted through NLP, particularly in domains characterized by rich linguistic nuance such as news dissemination. The research community's current shift towards more granular semantic understanding in NLP applications accentuates the timeliness of the NNE dataset release, which promises to incite a transformative shift toward truly hierarchical entity recognition. It provides a unique resource for benchmarking and developing advanced models capable of accurately parsing complex sentence structures and embedding sophisticated entity dependencies. Our endeavor is designed to reinvigorate interest and drive innovation in the nested NER domain, unveiled through carefully architected dataset annotation strategies that meticulously encapsulate multi-level entity interrelations reflective of authentic human communication. To surmount the limitations of existing datasets and foster richer semantic parsing; the NNE dataset (1) contributes a multitude of advancements to the field of NER. First; the dataset presents unprecedented breadth across 114 [1] distinct entity categories, a notable increment over prior (2) datasets that were confined to considerably fewer types. This increased diversity facilitates a more comprehensive comprehension of entity utilization and interaction, providing (11) a fertile testing ground for algorithmic strategies aimed at fine-grained recognition. Second, by integrating entities (27) at varying nesting depths up to six layers, our dataset sets a new benchmark for nested NER complexity, reflecting a quantum leap over most existing resources that seldom exceed two or three nesting levels. Through the public release of NNE, we anticipate a surge in models [12] capable of performing nested entity recognition with higher accuracy and contextual insight. By furnishing researchers with a detailed, expansive dataset, we essentially lay the groundwork for future innovations in this domain, anticipating new methodologies that can seamlessly integrate with diverse NLP applications such as sentiment analysis, machine reading comprehension, and beyond. Our effort calls to reassess standard NER practices, emphasizing the need for tackling nested structures that have been largely sidelined despite their ubiquitous presence in sophisticated text. This work substantially expands the frontier of named entity datasets, setting an innovative niche in data annotation that catalyzes state-of-the-art paradigms for nested NER. By contributing the NNE dataset, we extend an invitation to the NLP community to reevaluate existing models through the lens of nested complexity, simultaneously nurturing the evolution of algorithms poised to harness the full semantic capacity of language in a manner comprehensively represented in our novel dataset. The NNE dataset was constructed using the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB), a widely recognized corpus for linguistic annotation in English. This choice ensures consistency with prior research efforts and facilitates comparative studies in Named Entity Recognition (NER) tasks. The corpus comprises financial and economic news articles that inherently exhibit (17) a diverse array of named entities, making it a rich resource for studying nested structures in language. Our annotation process identified 279,795 entity mentions across these articles. Each mention was categorized into one of 114 entity types, capturing a wide span from organizations and locations to finer categories like events and products, broadening typical NER taxonomies (Florian et al., 2003; Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). The design of the NNE annotation scheme was guided by the necessity to capture nested structures within text, a feature often overlooked by flat NER models. Entities were annotated up to six layers of nesting, accommodating complex linguistic phenomena such as embedded entities ("the CEO of [Apple Inc.]"), which are frequent in structured prose like newswire articles. We leveraged previous insights from studies on nested NER in other languages to inform this design (Finkel & Manning, 2009; Alex et al., 2017). Our entity type schema is fine-grained compared to the coarse categorizations typically offered in basic NER models. The dataset design includes hierarchical entity representations; which are crucial for capturing the layered semantic relationships in text. Several procedural steps were undertaken to ensure the reliability and comprehensiveness of our annotations. Initially, we employed automated preprocessing using established NER systems trained on flat entity recognition tasks, such as the Stanford NER toolkit (Finkel et al., 2005), to identify preliminary entities. This step involved parsing each article to detect noun phrases and potential named entities, thereby reducing the manual annotation burden. Following pre-processing, a semi-automatic, iterative annotation process was implemented. Professional annotators with expertise in linguistic annotation were recruited to manually verify and refine entity boundaries and classifications. These annotators underwent specialized training to understand nested structures and the expansive entity type schema employed. Discourse context was particularly considered to correctly assign entity roles and resolve ambiguities typical of nested mentions (Ringger et al., 2004). Annotators worked within a double-blind protocol framework to measure the inter-annotator agreement, ensuring rigorous validation of the annotations. Regular meetings were held to adjudicate disagreements using context-based analysis and consensus-reaching methods, resulting in a final kappa statistic exceeding 0.85, indicative of excellent agreement (Artstein & Poesio, 2008). The adjudication process was systematically (10) documented to provide transparency and insights into the nuanced decision-making critical for nested NER annotation. The statistical analysis aimed to assess the distribution and complexity of nested entities in the NNE dataset. Quantitative evaluations were conducted to determine the prevalence of various entity types, with frequency analysis showing the most common entities, such as organizations and locations, alongside rarer nested types. These statistics provide benchmarks for model performance evaluation, especially for models targeting nested structures. Further, we analyzed the depth of nesting across entities, focusing on the frequency of nesting layers encountered and their correlation with specific entity types. This analysis revealed significant variation in nesting depth, with economic news wire texts often presenting deeper structures due to their reporting style. Hierarchical clustering techniques were utilized to explore the multidimensional scaling of entity types, thereby illustrating potential avenues for machine learning models to exploit nested structures in achieving enhanced NER performance (Lee et al., 2014). Finally, in evaluating the efficacy of our dataset and annotation scheme, we calculated precision, recall, and F1 scores by training and testing several baseline models on subsets of NNE. These metrics serve as indicators of the dataset's utility in advancing nested NER model development. The rapid advancement of natural language processing (NLP) has been significantly fueled by the (22) development of word embedding algorithms, which have become a cornerstone technology due to their ability to capture semantic relationships in text data (Mikolov et al., 2013a). Word embeddings, such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and those derived from singular value decomposition (SVD) of positive pointwise mutual information (PPMI) (5) matrices, map words into continuous vector spaces, allowing for easier computation of semantic similarity, analogy reasoning, and a variety of other [7] linguistic tasks (Pennington et al., 2014; Levy (26) et al., 2015). Among these, Word2Vec's two main configurations, continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) and skip-gram, as well as the [22] properties of [36] embeddings learned from SVD on PPMI matrices, have each found application in both academia and industry, heavily influencing subsequent research in NLP. Despite the successes of these methods, the variability or stability of word embeddings when models are retrained on identical datasets has emerged as an underexplored issue of particular practical importance (Hellrich & Hahn, 2016; Wendlandt et al., 2018). Stable embeddings can be crucial when integrating NLP solutions into real-world applications where deterministic outcomes are preferred—such [30] as in information retrieval systems, conversational agents, and predictive text applications. As embeddings are often (8) used as features in downstream models, variability can translate into inconsistencies in model behavior, which is undesirable. This has led to recent investigations into the factors contributing to embedding instability, with findings suggesting that certain hyperparameters and initialization strategies play significant roles (Yin & Shen; 2018; Pierrejean & Tanguy, 2018). A critical yet comparatively neglected aspect of this discussion is the role of down-sampling strategies within the context of SVD-based embedding methods. In the context of Word2Vec, negative sampling and subsampling [27] of frequent words are known strategies aimed at both improving efficiency and enhancing semantic quality by down-weighting frequent terms (Mikolov et al., 2013b). By contrast, SVD and PPMI-based methods (1) traditionally focus on dimensionality reduction and semantic enrichment without explicit stochastic sampling in the preprocessing phase, potentially leading to differences in the impact of training [14] corpus statistics on the [14] embedding's stability and variability. prior studies [11] that have tested the stability of singular value decompositions in various fields suggest that small changes in data representation, driven by sampling strategies, can significantly impact subsequent outcomes (Halko et al., 2011). This divergence has led to seemingly inconsistent reports regarding the stability of SVD-based embeddings. Some researchers argue that these methods yield more stable representations owing to their deterministic nature; while others report variations in the learned embeddings across repeated runs (Levy et al., 2015; (16) Antoniak & Mimno, 2018). This inconsistency indicates that existing evaluations may have overlooked key methodological variations such as the influence of down-sampling strategies, which could [37] manipulate the latent semantic structure evident in the matrix decomposition process (Goldberg & Levy, 2014). Addressing this gap, the present study investigates how down-sampling strategies impact the stability of embeddings obtained via SVD on PPMI-type matrices. Through systematic experiments across multiple corpora of varying size, we provide a nuanced examination of the "role" these strategies play in (6) affecting "embedding" consistency. Our research question can thus be formulated as: How do different down-sampling strategies affect the stability and performance of SVD-based word embeddings? Our contributions [6] are threefold. First; we provide empirical evidence that properly selected down-sampling strategies can significantly enhance the stability of SVD-based embeddings, challenging the assumption of inherent stability typically attributed to such methods. Second, by extending our analysis to various corpora sizes and language models, we map the interplay between corpus characteristics and embedding stability, providing actionable insights for both researchers and practitioners aiming to deploy stable embedding solutions. Lastly, we propose a methodological modification to integrate stochastic down-sampling strategies into the classical SVD embedding workflow. This adjustment maintains the semantic integrity of traditional SVD methods while (25) achieving accuracy levels comparable to those of more widely used neural-based embeddings such as skip-gram, ultimately suggesting a pathway for achieving superior performance in flexible NLP applications. In the following sections, (12) we detail our methodological [39] approach, present and discuss [6] our findings, and conclude with implications for theory, practice, and future research in word embedding development and deployment. This section details the methodologies employed in our investigation of the stability and accuracy of word embedding algorithms; with a focus on the role of down-sampling strategies during training. We begin by describing the datasets and experimental design, followed by the procedures for training the embeddings and conclude with our approach to statistical analysis. Data Our study used three distinct corpora to assess the generalizability of our findings across different linguistic contexts and corpus sizes. The first corpus; "Corpus A," was a subset of the widely-used English Wikipedia dump, comprising approximately 100 million tokens. This corpus [12] provided a relatively large and balanced sample of contemporary English. The second corpus, "Corpus B," consisted of the British National Corpus (BNC), a 10-million-token corpus reflecting a wide variety of text genres suitable for testing stability over smaller datasets. Lastly, "Corpus C" was [11] created using the OpenSubtitles2018 dataset, which included approximately 1 million tokens, representing informal and conversational language. Experimental Design The objective of our research design was to systematically vary down-sampling strategies within word embedding algorithms and assess their resulting stability and accuracy. We focused primarily on two types of embedding algorithms: the Singular Value Decomposition of Pointwise Mutual Information matrices (SVDPPMI) and the widely used skip-gram model with negative sampling (Mikolov et al., [10] 2013). For SVDPPMI, we implemented variations where down-sampling thresholds were altered, testing levels (4) of 1e-5, 1e-4, and 1e-3 as outlined by Levy et al. (2015). The skip-gram baseline employed its native subsampling strategy set to the default threshold of 1e-5. Each combination of corpus and algorithm was repeated ten times to assess stability, with each run independently initiating the training procedure to capture different random initializations and data shuffling effects. [3] Stability was quantified by calculating the cosine similarity of resulting vector spaces across the repeated runs. Procedures The pre-processing of each dataset included sentence splitting, [12] tokenization; and lowercasing. Stop words were removed to focus on content words, which are more crucial for capturing semantic meaning in embeddings. We constructed co-occurrence matrices for SVDPPMI processing up to a window size of ten words, as prior research suggested [31] this to be optimal for semantic similarity tasks (Bullinaria and Levy, 2007). For the SVDPPMI model, we adjusted the down-sampling strategy by limiting the frequency of common words according to specified thresholds. We subsequently decomposed the co-occurrence matrix via Truncated SVD, keeping the top 300 components to form the embeddings. Calculations utilized the scikit-learn library (Pedregosa et al., 2011). The skip-gram embeddings were trained using the Gensim library (Rehurek and Sojka, 2010) and followed consistent hyperparameter settings: vector dimensions of 300, a learning rate of 0.025; five negative samples per positive instance, and training across five iterations. Statistical Analysis To evaluate the stability of the embeddings, we computed average cosine similarities between embeddings for each word across the ten experimental runs. A stability coefficient was derived for each model-corpus combination by averaging these cosines for the top 10,000 most frequent words, considered sufficient for reliable statistics in past studies (Yeh et al., 2018). For accuracy, we used two benchmarking tasks: word similarity and analogy tasks. The accuracy scores derived from these tasks reflect the embedding's performance in semantic comprehension (Hill et al., 2015). To compare performance differences statistically, we performed paired t-tests between embedding types within each corpus, accounting for types of down-sampling as the independent variables. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.0.3. Results were considered significant at p < .05, with effect sizes calculated to indicate the magnitude of any observed differences. This structured methodology facilitated an inquiry into the intricate relationship between down-sampling strategies and embedding stability. Our intent was not only to observe empirical differences but to offer insights into potential algorithm refinements for improved embedding performance. In this study, we investigate the influence of various down-sampling strategies on the stability of Singular Value Decomposition using Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (SVDPPMI) word embeddings. Our experimental analysis focuses on determining how different down-sampling rates affect both the (22) stability and accuracy of word embeddings generated from corpora of varying sizes. The corpora employed in our experiments consist of a large corpus (approximately 1 billion words), a medium corpus (approximately 100 million words), and a small corpus (approximately 10 million words). Each corpus underwent preprocessing to adhere to standard text normalization practices including the removal of stop words, tokenization, and stemming (Manning et al., 2008). To quantify stability, we employed a metric based on the cosine similarity between embeddings generated from multiple runs on the same corpus. This metric provides a means to assess the consistency of word embedding representations across repeated training instances (Antoniak & Mimno, 2018). Accuracy was evaluated using established benchmarks, including semantic similarity tasks and analogy tasks which have been widely accepted within the field as indicators of embedding performance (Mikolov et al., 2013). In our experiments with the large corpus, the (1) impact of down-sampling strategies became evident. Specifically, a baseline SVDPPMI embedding with no frequency-based down-sampling resulted in an average cosine similarity of 0.73 across repeated runs, demonstrating considerable variability in stability. However, implementing a down-sampling strategy that reduced the frequency of frequent words by a factor of (23) 1e-5 led to a marked improvement in stability, increasing the average cosine similarity to 0.87. This represents a substantial enhancement, suggesting that down-sampling frequent terms helps mitigate instability by focusing the SVDPPMI process on less common, but potentially more informative contexts. In contrast, the medium corpus showed a less pronounced effect. The baseline SVDPPMI embedding yielded an average cosine similarity of 0.75, which increased to 0.83 with the implementation of the same down-sampling factor of 1e-5. Although the improvement is notable, the smaller corpus size may inherently limit the variation in context that word pairs can exhibit, thus contributing to the relative constancy regardless of down-sampling strategy (Lau et al., 2019). The small corpus posed the most challenging environment, as stability was inherently compromised due to the limited data available for word pair co-occurrences. The baseline results showed an average cosine similarity of 0.68, and application of a 1e-5 down-sampling factor improved this slightly to 0.77. While still a positive change, these figures [15] suggest that corpus size fundamentally constrains the degree of consistency achievable, and down-sampling offers limited remedial impact when data variety is insufficient. When examining accuracy in semantic and analogy tasks across the different corpus sizes, the results presented a nuanced interaction between down-sampling strategies and embedding performance. For the large corpus, the baseline SVDPPMI embeddings achieved an accuracy of 82% in semantic similarity tasks, and 58% in analogy tasks. Upon applying down-sampling, the semantic similarity task accuracy improved to 84%, while the analogy task accuracy increased significantly to 71%. This denotes a substantial benefit from reducing frequency bias and thus enhancing meaningful context evaluations by the embeddings (Pennington et al., 2014). The medium corpus showed comparable trends. Initially, the baseline registered an accuracy of 78% for semantic tasks and 52% for analogy tasks. Post down-sampling adjustments, these accuracies increased to 81% and 65%, respectively. The incremental improvement aligned with the expectations raised by larger corpus findings, though capped by inherent corpus limitations. For the small corpus, baseline accuracy in semantic tasks was rated at 71%, with analogy tasks lagging behind at 46%. Down-sampling improved semantic task accuracy modestly to 72%, but demonstrated a leap in analogy task performance to 58%. This disproportionate enhancement indicates that reducing high-frequency noise factors can disproportionately aid analogy tasks, which heavily rely on relational mappings that may be obscured by frequent but non-discriminative contexts. Overall, our results substantiate the role of down-sampling strategies as a crucial factor in the stability and accuracy of SVDPPMI embeddings across diverse corpus sizes. These findings imply that down-sampling not only contributes to stability but also enhances the task-specific performance

The transformative concept of the smart home has increasingly gained traction over the past decade, sparking innovation and integration in various domains of technology and everyday living. As a nexus of varied interconnected devices, smart homes depend heavily on efficient data management and network optimization to ensure a seamless user experience. With smart home devices expected to surpass a value of $53 billion by 2022 (Smith & Jones, 2020), the sophistication and volume of data traffic within and through these environments are poised to escalate. Key to realizing the potential of smart homes is the capacity for efficient and secure network management, specifically concerning the classification and handling of encrypted data packets. As smart devices proliferate, they necessitate differing levels of network resources and quality of service (QoS) provisions depending on their functions, which range from simple sensors to bandwidth-intensive high-definition streaming equipment (Chen et al., 2021). Traditional network management methodologies, which primarily focus on static resource allocation and heuristic-based traffic identification techniques, fall short in addressing dynamic and complex traffic patterns typically observed in smart home environments. This limitation primarily stems from an inability to accurately classify encrypted data packets, which are prevalent in ensuring the privacy and security of personal information (Kumar; Liu & Kortesniemi, 2019). Moreover, with the increasing reliance on software-defined networking (SDN), there is a growing capacity for improved network management from the core network. However, solely optimizing core networks has proven insufficient for end-to-end QoS enhancement. This inadequacy demonstrates the need for innovative approaches that extend into the user's domain, particularly at the level of the smart home gateway (Wang & Zanella, 2022). Despite these advances, existing approaches largely overlook the potential of leveraging machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques for encrypted packet classification directly in smart home gateways. Current solutions often involve binary-specific components and integrations that require significant computational resources, making them impractical for real-time applications within the limited capabilities of many smart home systems (Haddadi et al., 2020). many techniques suffer from invasiveness, compromising privacy or affecting the encryption levels of the data packets being transmitted (Brown, Anderson & Flynn, 2019). These gaps present an opportunity for developing a hierarchical classification framework that accommodates both the overarching service level and finer application-specific requirements, potentially enabling more effective resource allocation and QoS provision. This consideration raises a pertinent research question: How can a hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme be devised and implemented effectively within smart home gateways to enhance end-to-end QoS while maintaining user privacy and security? Addressing this challenge requires a multidimensional approach that not only leverages advanced ML and DL models for real-time classification but also integrates seamlessly into existing network infrastructures without necessitating significant resource overheads. The contribution of this paper is twofold. Firstly, it proposes a novel hierarchical classification scheme that divides the classification process into two distinct levels: service-level and application-level. At the service level, we propose a rapid classification system based on state-of-the-art deep learning architectures that can categorize data packets according to their QoS requirements. This approach allows for real-time adaptation and management of network resources, ensuring that high-priority services receive the necessary bandwidth and latency requirements. Secondly, for application-level classification, we develop a non-real-time framework that focuses on providing high accuracy by deploying more computationally intensive but precise classification models. This dual-model approach not only facilitates more nuanced network management but also offers additional functionalities such as statistical data collection, billing, and the provisioning of context-aware services, all without "infringing" upon user privacy or compromising data security. Through an extensive evaluation, this paper demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed classification scheme in a practical smart home scenario. The results indicate significant improvements in the precision of encrypted packet classification and resource allocation efficiency; thereby enhancing the QoS and QoE for end-users. By bridging the existing gap between network management and user-centric service delivery within smart home ecosystems, this research sets a foundation for future developments in secure and efficient smart home data management methodologies. This section describes the methodologies [18] deployed to investigate the efficacy and accuracy of a hierarchical encrypted packet classification system, specifically designed for smart home gateways. The methods encapsulated herein include the data collection process, the research design, the experimental procedures, and the statistical analysis [12] employed. Data collection focused on two primary sources: publicly available encrypted datasets and proprietary data from a smart home environment simulated (21) to reflect real-world conditions. The public dataset comprises network traffic traces encompassing a wide array of applications commonly used in smart home settings; such as real-time video streaming, IoT device communications, and other multimedia services. The proprietary dataset was generated in a controlled smart home laboratory environment equipped with a variety of smart devices, ensuring a realistic distribution and behavior of network traffic data. This dataset included packet flows from devices like smart speakers, smart thermostats, security cameras, and utility controllers. Each [3] dataset consisted of a comprehensive capture of packet headers, excluding payloads to ensure privacy, with specific emphasis on features related to flow metrics such as (21) packet lengths, interarrival times, TCP flags; and statistical features extracted from encryption-origin metadata, wherever available. These enriched datasets provided the essential inputs into the classification [14] algorithms while adhering strictly to privacy constraints. The study adopted a two-layer hierarchical classification model. The primary layer, the service-level classifier, utilized a deep learning-based approach due to the necessity for real-time classification with high accuracy over large volumes of data (Zhang et al., 2021). The secondary layer, designed as an application-level classifier, focused on intricate application behavior differentiation employing a non-real-time, but highly accurate, machine learning approach. To train the hierarchical model, we divided the data into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets. The training set was used to teach the classifiers, while the validation (11) set informed hyperparameter tuning and prevented overfitting. The test set provided an unbiased evaluation of the model’s performance. The use of cross-validation ensured reliability and robustness in the performance metrics (Kohavi, 1995). The procedures involved several key steps, specifically in dataset preparation, [3] model training, validation, and testing phases: 1. Preprocessing: The initial stage incorporated preprocessing techniques including normalization of flow features like packet size distribution and timing features. Feature extraction focused on reducing noise and (26) enhancing signal properties conducive to class differentiation (Bishop, 2006). 2. Service-level Classification: Implemented as a convolutional "neural" network (CNN), this classifier leveraged the ability of CNNs to identify spatial hierarchies in data, aligning with network flow characteristics. [28] Hyperparameters were tuned using grid search cross-validation on the validation set, targeting parameters such as (6) number of layers, filter sizes, and learning rates (LeCun et al., 2015). 3. Application-level Classification: For this layer, a random forest classifier was employed, given its suitability for handling high-dimensional input spaces and facilitating interpretability (Breiman, 2001). Feature importance metrics were calculated to prioritize utilization of the most informative features, aiding the fine-grained discriminative performance. 4. Hierarchical Integration: The integration required aligning outputs (15) from the service-level classifier as input to the application-level classifier. The primary decisions forwarded included service categorization labels accompanied by corresponding confidence levels, channeling into a decision tree-based structure within the secondary classifier to ensure interpretative reliability and accuracy (Hastie et al., 2009). 5. Validation and Testing: Testing phases employed the blinded test set to evaluate predictive accuracy, precision-recall scores, F1-score, confusion matrix representation, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. These metrics facilitated a comprehensive understanding of classifier performance in distinguishing between similar encrypted flows and pinpointing specific application signatures (Fawcett, 2006). The statistical analysis centered on evaluating classifier accuracy, utilizing both intrinsic model metrics and external evaluation through post-hoc analysis. Performance metrics for both classifiers were quantified using accuracy rates, confusion matrix quantifications, and area under the ROC curve (AUC) scores to capture the true positive versus false positive rates effectively (Bradley, 1997). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests determined the statistical significance between different model configuration results and across testing conditions. a comparative analysis with existing benchmark models, using paired t-tests, reinforced the validity and effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical approach (Wilks, 2006). Each prediction error emerged as an insightful indication of misclassification sources, attributing to either an absconsion of feature generalization or an excessively conservative inference threshold in encrypted traffic differentiations, guiding line-by-line improvements for selective retraining phases. In conclusion, this meticulous methodological framework emphasizes the innovative structural design of hierarchical encrypted packet classifiers and validates their performance comprehensively to enhance data packet classification precision in smart home gateways. This section presents the results obtained from evaluating the proposed hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme. We discuss the quantitative findings acquired through extensive simulations and real-world experiments designed to assess the efficacy and accuracy of both real-time and non-real-time classifiers at the service and application levels, respectively. The results attest to the robustness and applicability of our approach in enhancing quality-of-service (QoS) measures in smart home environments without compromising end-user privacy. The first subset of results pertains to the service-level classification employing a faster deep learning-based scheme. A dataset consisting of over 500,000 encrypted data packets across a typical range of smart home applications was utilized to train and validate the model. Our deep learning classifier, based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, achieved an classification accuracy of 95.8% with a standard deviation of 0.45% when predicting data packets into predefined service categories. These categories reflected the expected QoS requirements of applications, such as streaming, online gaming, and home automation services. This accuracy surpasses existing solutions (Smith et al., 2021) which reported classification accuracies ranging from 88% to 92% in similar settings. The latency testing of the real-time classifier shows an average packet classification time of 2.3 ms with a processing throughput rate of up to 4000 packets per second. This result highlights the potential of deploying the classifier in smart home gateways for real-time monitoring without introducing significant overhead (Johnson and Li, 2020). Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis confirmed the classifier's robust performance even under varying network conditions such as packet loss and jitter, with a maximum observed decrease in accuracy of less than 3% (p < 0.05). Turning to the results of the application-level classification, the non-real-time classifier was designed to refine granular application recognition once service-level classification was achieved. Utilizing a more complex ensemble-based model, combining Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Gradient Boosting algorithms, the non-real-time classifiers achieved an increased accuracy rate of 97.3%, with a standard deviation of 0.38% across multiple application categories. This notable enhancement in accuracy reaffirms the utility of the two-tiered classification approach, allowing for precise [25] QoS provision based on individualized application needs. The computational load for the non-real-time classification, assessed in offline mode, demonstrated an average completion time of 450 ms per batch of 1000 packets. [14] While inherently less time-sensitive, this non-real-time classification ensures that applications requiring "higher" accuracy in data packet identification; such as those involved in billing and statistical data collection, can be efficiently managed (Kumar et al., 2022). Quantitative comparisons with existing methodologies [25] were conducted using benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art encoded packet classifiers. The accuracy and [20] efficiency metrics derived from our study considerably outperform previous methods. For example, traditional methods utilizing solely heuristic-based classifications or less sophisticated machine learning models achieved [11] a maximum accuracy of 89% (Liu and Wang; 2019). ablation studies were performed to validate the contribution of each component of our hierarchical model. These studies revealed that while each level of classification could independently operate with moderate success, the integration of both service and application-level classifiers significantly boosted system accuracy by 5.5% compared to using either component singularly. Additionally, customer satisfaction ratings collected through user feedback surveys indicated an enhanced perceived network performance by around 60%, corresponding with the reduction in packet delay and loss as quantified in throughput tests. Security assessments conducted as part of our analysis confirmed that no critical encrypted data was exposed during the classification processes, adhering to privacy-preserving protocols [10] and further cementing the viability of this (15) classification scheme in real-world applications (Chen et al., 2021).

Differential Privacy (DP) has emerged as a cornerstone of privacy-preserving data analysis, providing quantifiable privacy guarantees in the presence of adversaries with extensive auxiliary information (Dwork et al., 2006). Central to its effectiveness is the carefully crafted addition of noise to query outputs, thereby obfuscating the contribution of any single data point. Among the various paradigms within DP, the exponential mechanism, introduced by McSherry and Talwar (2007), stands out for its ability to cater to non-numeric output spaces and its adaptability to a wide variety of statistical queries through a scoring function. This mechanism has been instrumental across numerous applications, ranging from basic statistics to complex machine learning tasks (Kifer et al., 2012). The outstanding flexibility and utility of the exponential mechanism stem from its mechanism of selectively adding noise in accordance with a utility function. This utility-driven approach permits prioritization of more valuable outputs while maintaining the stringent privacy guarantees of DP. However, its application has predominantly concentrated on finite-dimensional spaces, with relatively limited exploration into infinite-dimensional contexts, such as functional data analysis, shape analysis, and nonparametric statistics. These areas often deal with data represented as curves, surfaces, or more general objects in a continuous domain, thereby raising significant challenges for privacy-preserving methodologies. Functional Data Analysis (FDA) is increasingly vital due to the proliferating availability of data in the form of random functions or curves (Ramsay & Silverman, 2005). Typical contexts include growth curves, electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, and other continuous measurements over time or space. These analyses demand techniques that can handle infinite-dimensional data structures inherent to separable Hilbert spaces. Concurrently, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) remains a fundamental tool for dimension reduction and feature extraction within infinite-dimensional settings. Extending DP to accommodate the complexities of Functional PCA (FPCA) is, therefore, a task of undeniable importance, where the methodological rigor and theoretical foundations are still nascent. Recent advances have initiated exploration of DP in the realm of functional data, albeit with constraints and assumptions that often limit their practical utility (Hall et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2019). Typically, these approaches rely on simplistic noise models or assumptions about the boundedness and sparsity of functional data, which may not hold in many real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the direct application of finite-dimensional DP techniques in these settings can lead to significant distortions or loss of meaningful information due to inadequate noise calibration. A critical gap identified in existing literature is establishing robust mechanisms with nuanced noise calibration tuned to infinite-dimensional output spaces. This paper seeks to fill this void by expanding the applicability of the exponential mechanism to settings characterized by infinite dimensions, with a special focus on applications in separable Hilbert spaces. We explore how these settings necessitate novel theoretical advancements, particularly in defining an appropriate base measure over the functional outputs, and in managing the trade-off between privacy and utility with greater finesse. Our primary research question is: How can the exponential mechanism be effectively adapted and applied to infinite-dimensional settings to maintain rigorous differential privacy guarantees while preserving analytical utility in functional PCA? Addressing this question involves both theoretical contributions and practical validation through simulations and applied case studies. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we propose an adaptation of the exponential mechanism for infinite-dimensional settings by leveraging Gaussian process priors as a base measure. This development not only extends the applicability of the exponential mechanism but also inherently respects the geometrical and topological properties of functional data embedded in separable Hilbert spaces. Second, we establish the theoretical properties of the proposed mechanism, highlighted by a novel Central Limit Theorem (CLT) for the exponential mechanism in these contexts. This theorem not only broadens the theoretical understanding of DP in infinite dimensions but also sets the groundwork for analyzing the asymptotic "behavior" of the noise introduced for privacy preservation. Our analysis reveals a seemingly paradoxical insight: although the noise magnitude required for \(\epsilon\)-DP is asymptotically non-negligible; it aligns closely with the contour of statistical estimation errors within these infinite-dimensional spaces. Lastly, we provide an empirical evaluation of the \(\epsilon\)-DP mechanism specifically tailored for FPCA, verifying its efficacy via extensive simulations and real-world datasets. These experiments are illustrative of the practical utility's retention, where the noisiness introduced does not unduly compromise the interpretability or accuracy [16] of the functional principal components, yet upholds the privacy guarantees prescribed by DP. Through this work, we aim to galvanize further However, research into the intersection of differential privacy and functional data analysis, fostering methods that capitalize on the interpretative richness of these data types while rigorously safeguarding individual privacy. We envisage this paper as a stepping stone towards comprehensive, privacy-preserving analyses in contemporary data landscapes. [26] For the investigation of the exponential mechanism applied [21] to Hilbert spaces and functional principal component analysis (FPCA), we employed both simulated and real-world data. To simulate data, we generated random functions from a Gaussian process with a squared exponential covariance kernel, ensuring the functions resided within a separable Hilbert space. Each function was sampled at 100 equidistant points across the domain \([0,1]\). This setting was chosen to reflect scenarios common in functional data analysis, allowing us to evaluate the performance of the differential privacy mechanism under controlled conditions. The real-world datasets employed were sourced from publicly available archives. Specifically, [2] we used the Berkeley Growth Study, comprising growth curves of children's heights measured at various ages; which has often been utilized as a benchmark in functional data analysis (Ramsay & Silverman; 2005). Additionally, we included a dataset of daily weather records, capturing temperature curves at various geographic locations [2] throughout a year, to demonstrate the application of our method to environmental data. The design of our study hinges on the [6] differential privacy characterization of the exponential mechanism (\(\varepsilon\)-DP). We formulated the exponential mechanism within the context of a separable Hilbert space [16] \(\mathcal{H}\), allowing for the "probabilistic" determination of functional outputs based upon their utility scores. By extending the mechanism to account for Gaussian process priors; we defined the base measure in the infinite-dimensional setting, permitting the [36] application of differential privacy in contexts requiring functional outputs. To simulate the application to "FPCA," we conducted an eigendecomposition of a covariance operator constructed from observed functional data (Peng & Paul, 2009). Each dataset was transformed into its principal component scores and subsequent eigenfunctions. The exponential mechanism was employed on the eigenfunctions to ensure privacy, with privacy budgets (\(\varepsilon\)-values) varying to assess the trade-off between privacy and utility. The implementation of the exponential mechanism in functional settings involved altering the utility function to accommodate infinite-dimensional input and output spaces. We defined utility functions for the FPCA as the explained variance by a given number of principal components, aligning with practical metrics in functional data tasks. [34] 1. Preprocessing: For both the simulated and real datasets; functional [28] data was discretized such that each function was represented by evaluation across a dense grid. Preprocessing ensured consistency in functional representations. 2. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) has become an invaluable tool in neurological research and clinical diagnostics, enabling the visualization of brain structures and the identification of various pathologies. Among the numerous MRI sequences, T1-weighted (T1-w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences provide complementary insights into brain anatomy and pathology. T1-w images effectively delineate anatomical structures, while FLAIR images suppress cerebrospinal fluid signals to enhance the visibility of lesions, particularly those associated with demyelination or microvascular diseases. White matter hyperintensities (WMHs), also known as white matter lesions, are frequently observed in FLAIR images and are indicative of various neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, and age-related cognitive decline (Wardlaw et al., 2015). The presence and extent of WMHs in FLAIR images correlate [26] strongly with disease progression and cognitive impairment, making their accurate segmentation crucial for diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment planning (Debette & Markus, 2010). However, the acquisition of FLAIR images is not always feasible in clinical settings, due to technological constraints, time limitations, or historical data lacking this specific sequence. As a result, many retrospective datasets contain only T1-w images, thereby hindering comprehensive analysis and segmentation efforts that rely on FLAIR. The challenge of missing imaging modalities has spurred significant research into synthesis techniques aimed at generating one modality from another. Prior work has involved the use of various machine learning and deep learning approaches to synthesize FLAIR images from T1-w images, thereby enabling the extraction of lesion characteristics in the absence of direct FLAIR acquisition (Taheri & Tang; 2019; Leynes et al., 2018). However, these existing methods primarily focus on the synthesis process, treating the subsequent task of lesion segmentation as a separate process. This separation of tasks can lead to suboptimal results where the synthesized images, despite appearing realistic, might not be perfectly suited for segmentation due to discrepancies in lesion appearance or noise artifacts. Furthermore, lesion segmentation itself is often approached as a standalone problem, using T1-w images directly. Various methods leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated the capability to segment lesions directly from T1-w images (Zhang et al., 2020). Nonetheless, these approaches can suffer from poor performance as T1-w images alone inadequately highlight lesions, leading to challenges in discerning between WMHs and normal brain tissue. As such, there exists a clear gap in methodologies that directly synergize the processes of modality synthesis and lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability and accuracy. In this context, our research seeks to address the critical question: Can the simultaneous synthesis of FLAIR images and segmentation of WMHs from T1 MRIs improve lesion detection and provide clinically relevant results? We propose a novel approach that integrates FLAIR synthesis and WMH segmentation using a unified deep learning framework. By harnessing the power of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in a joint optimization setup, the model can effectively learn to align the synthesis process with the segmentation goal, leading to more accurate FLAIR generation and superior segmentation performance. Our contributions to the field are manifold. First, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture that co-trains two networks: a modality synthesis network and a segmentation network. This setup encourages synergistic learning, where improvements in either the synthetic FLAIR generation or the segmentation accuracy reinforce the learning process of the other task. Second, we demonstrate that our approach not only results in the production of synthetic FLAIR images with enhanced realism but also achieves segmentation benchmarks (15) on par with, or exceeding, those obtained using real FLAIR images. These advancements significantly alleviate the challenges posed by missing FLAIR sequences in retrospective datasets, thereby enhancing the usability of existing MRI collections for lesion analysis. We conduct extensive evaluations using publicly available datasets that include both T1-w and FLAIR sequences; allowing us [25] to benchmark the performance of our approach against traditional methods. Our results underscore the advantages of an integrated approach, indicating significant improvements in lesion segmentation metrics, including Dice coefficient and sensitivity, when compared to methods that use T1-w images alone. Moreover, the synthetic FLAIR images generated by our model exhibit greater anatomical and pathological fidelity than those produced by existing synthesis-only models. In summary, our research not only bridges the gap between modality synthesis and lesion segmentation but also opens new avenues for clinical and research applications where FLAIR sequences are missing or difficult to obtain. By enhancing the ability to detect and analyze WMHs; our approach holds the [14] potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and outcomes in neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases. This section describes the methods employed in this study, encompassing data collection, the design of experiments, procedural details, and statistical analysis. Our approach integrates the synthesis of FLAIR images with the segmentation of WMH, utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for both components of our method. The data utilized in this study consisted of structural brain MRI scans from publicly available datasets. we sourced T1-weighted (T1-w) and FLAIR images from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the International Brain Laboratory Human Connectome Dataset. These datasets were selected based on their comprehensive collection of high-resolution T1-w images, as [2] well as the availability of FLAIR sequences for a subset of subjects; which facilitated model training and validation. For inclusion in our dataset, subjects were required to have high-quality [23] T1-w images and corresponding high-quality FLAIR images. Images were excluded if they displayed significant motion artifacts or incomplete brain coverage. The final dataset included 500 subjects; with an average age of 68 ± 7 years, comprising both healthy controls and individuals demonstrating varying degrees of white matter alterations. The methodological framework comprises two key components: a modality imputation network responsible for synthesizing FLAIR images from T1-w inputs, and a segmentation network that delineates WMH from the synthesized FLAIR images. These networks were interlinked to jointly optimize their learning processes, capitalizing on the complementary nature of both tasks. The imputation network was constructed using a U-Net architecture, which has demonstrated efficacy in various medical imaging tasks due to its ability to capture both low-level and high-level features through an encoder-decoder structure (Ronneberger et al., 2015). The network was initialized with pre-trained weights from models trained on similar MRI datasets [27] to improve convergence and stability. The input to the imputation network consisted of T1-w images, which were first pre-processed using intensity normalization to a common scale, followed [4] by skull stripping to remove non-brain tissue (Smith; 2002). The network output was an approximation of the FLAIR image for each input T1-w scan. The segmentation network also employed a U-Net architecture but incorporated additional attention mechanisms to (23) refine segmentation accuracy by assigning varying levels of importance to different regions of the feature maps (Oktay et al., 2018). The attention-enhanced U-Net was designed to focus on salient features characteristic of WMH, which typically appear hyperintense on FLAIR images. Both the imputation and segmentation networks were trained on paired T1-w and FLAIR scans. The training process involved optimizing the joint loss function: \[ \mathcal{L}{joint} = \alpha \mathcal{L}{impute} + \beta \mathcal{L}{segment} \] where \(\mathcal{L}{impute}\) is the mean squared error between "synthesized" and actual FLAIR images, \(\mathcal{L}{segment}\) is the combined Dice and cross-entropy loss for segmentation accuracy, and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are hyperparameters that balance the imputation and segmentation tasks. These parameters were tuned using grid search to minimize overall loss. Training was conducted using stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of \(10^{-4}\) and a batch size of eight. Data augmentation techniques, such as random rotations, scaling, and elastic deformations, were applied during training to enhance model generalization. Model evaluation was performed on a hold-out test set comprising 20% of the data, ensuring that images in this set were not used during the training phase. Performance metrics for both FLAIR synthesis and WMH segmentation, including the structural similarity index (SSIM) for image quality and the Dice coefficient for segmentation accuracy, were computed. To assess the efficacy of our proposed method, we performed quantitative analyses comparing our joint training approach against separate training of the imputation and segmentation tasks. Paired t-tests were conducted to evaluate whether improvements in SSIM and Dice coefficient achieved by our method were statistically significant, utilizing a significance level of \(p < 0.05\). Further, ablation studies were conducted to determine the impact of attention mechanisms in the segmentation [13] network and the joint optimization approach in the overall framework. These studies involved training modified versions of our network architecture while leaving out specific components, then comparing performance to our full model. In summary, our method synthesized realistic FLAIR images and segmented WMH with high accuracy using joint optimization of CNN-based networks. These approaches and statistical validations underscore the potential of our methodology in advancing the field of neuroimaging and improving diagnostic workflows for vascular pathologies. The radiologists commended the synthetic images for their realistic portrayal of typical FLAIR characteristics, including lesion hyperintensity and tissue differentiation. Introduction The influence of class size on student achievement has long been a subject of considerable debate in educational research and policy-making circles. As education systems [16] globally grapple with the dual challenges of enhancing student outcomes and maintaining fiscal responsibility, understanding the precise impact of class (24) size becomes paramount. For [4] decades, educators and policymakers have oscillated between the potential benefits of small class sizes—such as personalized learning experiences and increased [23] student engagement—and the economic efficiencies of larger classes, which allow for optimal allocation of resources (Blatchford et al., 2011; Hanushek, 1999). A central tenet of educational theory posits that smaller class (16) sizes contribute to improved academic outcomes by facilitating individual attention and a nurturing learning environment (Glass & Smith, 1979). This viewpoint has been a driving force behind significant educational interventions such "as" the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) experiment in the United States, which aimed to reduce class sizes in early childhood education and (25) assess resultant effects on student performance (Finn & Achilles, 1990). However, despite these theoretical advantages, empirical evidence on the effect of class size reduction has been mixed, leading to heated discussions regarding its inclusion in educational policy (Sims, 2009). The research "literature" reveals a spectrum of findings, ranging from studies that document substantial improvements in reading and mathematics with reduced class sizes, to those that observe negligible or inconsistent effects (Chingos, 2013a; Krueger, 1999). This divergence of evidence indicates a substantial gap in understanding the contextual and methodological factors that influence the efficacy of class size reduction. A nuanced examination of these elements is essential to contextualize the impact of class size on academic [22] achievement meaningfully. In this systematic review, we seek to bridge this gap by critically evaluating a broad body of international [28] research to ascertain the impact of class size on student academic achievement. Through meticulous selection [39] criteria and [6] robust meta-analytic techniques, this review aims to synthesize findings from various geographies and educational contexts, offering a comprehensive understanding of class size dynamics (Glass et al., 1982; Slavin, 1989). Our research is underpinned by several guiding questions: Firstly, what is the effect of class size on student achievement in primary and secondary education? Secondly, how do these effects differ between academic domains such as reading and mathematics? Thirdly, under what conditions—such as socioeconomic status, educational stage, or geographic location—does class size reduction yield substantive benefits? this review contributes to the ongoing discourse by considering the nuanced methodological differences across studies. Previous research has (23) shown that outcomes can be highly sensitive to study design, sample demographics, and analytical [27] methods (Nye et al., 2000; Konstantopoulos & Sun, 2012). Our analysis will account for these factors, allowing for a more refined estimation of [1] class size effects. Additionally, while much of the existing research has contextualized findings within developed nations, particularly the United States, this review seeks to broaden the scope by including studies from a diverse array of countries. By doing so, we hope to illuminate culturally or contextually specific insights on class size dynamics, thereby enriching global understanding (OECD, 2012; [3] Wößmann & West, 2006). In synthesizing this multitude of evidence, we aim to provide policymakers and educational practitioners with (24) a more coherent narrative on the relative importance of class size as a factor in educational achievement. Recognizing the substantial resource implications associated with class size adjustments, this review can guide more (6) informed decisions regarding educational investments and interventions (Hanushek, 2003). Ultimately, the principal contribution of [26] this review lies in its ability to consolidate disparate strands of research into an accessible and analytically rigorous framework, offering insights that are both theoretically meaningful and practically applicable. By advancing our understanding of the complex relationship between class size and student outcomes, this work aspires to facilitate more effective and equitable educational policies globally. The data for this systematic review were sourced through extensive searches of electronic bibliographic databases, internet search engines, and manual searching of key educational journals. The search strategy was defined to capture both published and unpublished literature pertaining to the effects of class size on academic achievement, accommodating a broad international scope (Ponce & Lozano, 2014). We executed these searches up to February 2017, ensuring a comprehensive coverage of available studies related to class size and its influence on educational outcomes. In addition, reference lists from primary studies and related systematic reviews were scrutinized to identify any additional studies that met the inclusion criteria (Booth et al., 2012). The primary criterion for inclusion was the examination of the impact of class size reduction in general education settings, focusing on academic achievements in reading and mathematics among children from kindergarten through 12th grade or equivalent. Eligible studies were required to employ either randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRS) with well-defined control groups. Qualitative studies were excluded to maintain a quantitative synthesis of data (Shadish et al., 2002). Rigorous screening processes were applied, considering factors such as methodological quality, risk of bias, and the provision of sufficient data for effect size calculation. Data extraction involved multiple reviewers to mitigate bias, using a standardized extraction form to capture key elements such as study design, sample size, population characteristics, intervention details, and outcomes measured. Particular attention was given to how class size was operationalized, the settings of the intervention, and the specific achievements assessed (Higgins & Green, 2011). Discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion or consultation with an independent third reviewer. The review encompassed 127 studies, representing 148 papers across 55 diverse populations from 41 countries. Of these, 45 studies analyzed data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project, a notable longitudinal study conducted in the United States focusing on kindergarten to third-grade students (Finn & Achilles, 1990). While the STAR experiment provided significant insights, only four of these STAR-related studies were suitable for the meta-analysis alongside six additional non-STAR studies due to stringent inclusion conditions. A meta-analytical approach was employed to synthesize the results using random effects models to accommodate for potential heterogeneity among the included studies (Borenstein et al., 2009). Effect sizes for reading and mathematics were converted into standardized mean differences (SMDs), facilitating comparison across diverse study designs and contexts. The pooled estimates were weighted by inverse variance methods, with 95% confidence intervals computed to assess the precision of the estimates (Cohn & Becker, 2003). Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the robustness of the pooled effect sizes across methodological quality components, including the potential effects of incorporating studies with unclear effect directions and those using class size as a continuous variable. Key adjustments were included to correct for clustering effects inherent in the STAR dataset, adopting an intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.22, while non-STAR data required no such adjustments (Hox, 2010). All synthesized results were stratified by the end of the treatment period—typically the end of the academic year—to provide clear temporal relationships between class size interventions and educational outcomes (Wykes et al., 2016). the synthesis considered variability in class size reductions, ranging from minimal reductions of one student per class to more substantial reductions involving several students, ensuring detailed coverage of intervention intensity (Konstantopoulos & Chun, 2009). In conclusion, the statistical analysis adhered to rigorous standards, leveraging advanced meta-analytic techniques to integrate findings from a wide array of studies with varying methodologies, ensuring credible and actionable conclusions concerning the impact of class size on academic achievement. This systematic review aimed to assess the impact of class size on academic achievement, focusing specifically on reading and mathematics performance. The analysis included 127 studies encompassing 148 papers, with study populations from 41 countries. Ten of these studies were eligible for meta-analysis, including four that utilized data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) experiment conducted in the United States during the 1980s. In the meta-analysis of non-STAR studies, results for reading achievement were somewhat varied. The primary studies yielded effect sizes ranging from -0.08 to 0.14, with a majority being statistically non-significant. The random effects model, demonstrated a statistically significant small positive effect, with a weighted standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.11 (95% CI: 0.05 to 0.16). This suggests that, on average, students in smaller classes score higher in reading than those in larger classes, though the magnitude of the effect is limited. In contrast, the analysis of mathematics achievement showed an inconsistency in both the direction and magnitude of effect sizes. The primary study effect sizes for mathematics ranged from -0.41 to 0.11, with most outcomes not reaching statistical significance (SMD = -0.03; 95% CI: -0.22 to 0.16). The negative average effect, though statistically non-significant, indicates that reducing class size may not universally benefit or possibly detract from mathematical achievement among students. For studies analyzing data from the STAR experiment, all results consistently reported positive effects, statistically significant for both reading and mathematics. Effect sizes for reading ranged from 0.17 to 0.34, while for mathematics they ranged from 0.15 to 0.33. Despite the consistently positive data from the STAR cohorts, these "findings" did not meaningfully alter the overarching conclusions drawn from the complete dataset, especially given the limited representativeness of the STAR experiment in global educational contexts. When assessing the robustness of these results, sensitivity analyses showed that incorporating different components of study quality and varying operational definitions of class size did not substantively change the mean effect estimates. Nevertheless, when including data from primary studies with indeterminate effect directions, the statistical significance for reading was lost. Similarly, adjusting continuous variable class size reductions to one-student rather than standardized deviation did not appreciably impact the conclusions. The findings underscore a nuanced relationship between small class sizes and academic outcomes. For reading, the evidence suggests a small, statistically significant benefit of reduced class sizes. Meanwhile, for mathematics, the impact of class size appears negligible at best, with potential for negative effects that warrant further investigation. the likelihood that a randomly selected student's score improves in reading given a smaller class size stands at 53%, compared to a mere 49% for mathematics. while the STAR studies offer an optimistic view of the potential benefits of smaller class sizes, their applicability across diverse educational environments might be limited. Additionally, the financial implications of reducing class sizes and the potential for variable impacts on different student subgroups imply a need for deeper investigation into where and how investments in education can be most effectively allocated. The current systematic review provides a critical synthesis of the (13) evidence on the effects of class size reduction on academic achievement in primary and secondary education, consolidating findings from 148 reports across 41 countries. Despite the extensive data set, the meta-analysis included only ten studies due to [29] stringent criteria regarding methodological rigor, emphasizing the need for careful interpretation of our findings. The results [31] indicate a [13] marginal positive effect of reduced class size on reading achievement, with a standardised mean difference (SMD) of 0.11, translating to a 53% probability that a student in a smaller (29) class would outperform a peer in a larger class on a reading test. This (18) effect size is statistically significant yet categorized as small per conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). Conversely, the effect size for mathematics was negative and statistically insignificant (SMD = -0.03); suggesting no substantial advantage to smaller class sizes for this subject. The slight negative trend may imply potential adverse outcomes for some students, though this result lacks [29] statistical conviction and thus should be interpreted [36] with caution. The STAR experiments, a prominent subset within our dataset, consistently reported positive effects for both reading and maths. the generalizability of these findings is restricted due to the unique context of the original study, which may not reflect broader educational environments (Mosteller, 1995). It is important to consider that the educational systems, cultural factors, and teacher practices significantly influence the efficacy of class size reduction (Blatchford et al., 2003; Hattie, 2009). it remains challenging to directly extrapolate the results across diverse educational settings.
