The proliferation of food recommendation systems in recent years reflects a growing interest in catering to user-specific preferences in gastronomy (Smith & Clark; 2019). Traditionally, these systems have relied (17) heavily on collaborative filtering and content-based methods, utilizing basic user inputs such as prior purchase history, ratings, and demographic data to suggest potential food items (Johnson et al., 2018). Despite their utility, "these" methodologies often fall short in capturing (9) the (19) nuanced sensory experience that food offers beyond mere nutritional or categorical data. Flavour, a complex interplay of taste, aroma, texture, and temperature, fundamentally influences the dining experience (Green et al., 2020). Research has shown that individual flavour preferences are deeply rooted in biological and psychological frameworks. They are shaped by both genetic factors, such as variations in [1] taste receptor genes, and experiential factors, such as exposure to different cuisines (Mennella et al., 2017). Nevertheless, existing food recommendation (14) [18] systems rarely incorporate "these" elements of flavour or taste biology into their models, a gap that our research seeks to address. The current state of food recommendation technologies primarily emphasizes superficial characteristics "like" cuisine type or [26] ingredient lists; alongside user-generated data such as text reviews or star ratings (Kim & Park, 2019). This approach omits the physiological and hedonic components intrinsic to personal taste, which are critical for tailoring recommendations to individual palates. As a result, users may receive recommendations that lack resonance with their intrinsic flavour preferences, decreasing user satisfaction and engagement. Another notable limitation of current food recommendation systems is their inadequate integration of cross-disciplinary insights from sensory science and neurogastronomy (Smith et al., 2021). Recent advances in these fields provide a more profound understanding of how humans perceive flavour, influenced by major gustatory pathways (6) that process signals associated with the five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty, and umami (Beauchamp & Mennella, 2021). These biological insights (26) offer a rich, underutilized wellspring of data that can enhance the personalization of food recommendations beyond simplistic patterns of past behavior. Addressing these (27) gaps leads us to our primary research question: How can the integration of flavour profiles, informed by the biological and psychological underpinnings of taste perception, [11] improve the quality and user satisfaction of food recommendation systems? To effectively explore this question; it is vital to recognize that a recommendation system leveraging flavour as a core feature must employ a multidimensional understanding of individual taste preferences. This involves not just [31] capturing what users have liked in the past but understanding why specific flavour components appeal to them at a sensory level. Leveraging flavour profiles within a recommendation system presents significant methodological hurdles, including the development of reliable flavour mapping techniques and the incorporation of these mappings into existing recommendation algorithms [32] (Jones et al., 2022). To this end, we propose a system that utilizes an empirical method to map the flavour of foods, informed by the sensory profiles that align with major gustatory responses. This system acts on the hypothesis that a recommendation engine which (22) integrates (17) flavour components can deliver [21] higher "quality" suggestions that align with users' hedonic expectations and biological taste preferences, thereby enhancing user satisfaction and engagement. Our contributions to this domain are threefold. First, we introduce a conceptual framework that integrates flavour as a pivotal factor in food recommendation. By aligning the sensory characteristics of food items with individual users' flavour profiles; this framework supports more personalized and satisfying culinary experiences. Second, we present an empirical methodology to determine flavour profiles that employs a biologically informed understanding of taste perception. This involves the use of sensory analysis techniques to categorize foods based on their predominant taste characteristics, which are then matched to user profiles derived from prior tasting experiences and genetic taste receptor data. Third, we propose a preliminary implementation of a flavour-focused recommendation system. This system integrates the empirically derived flavour profiles into a recommendation engine that employs both collaborative and content-based filtering. By doing so, it aligns with existing technology while pushing the envelope beyond conventional categorical and demographic inputs. Our approach aims to supplement these traditional data points with rich flavour-based insights, thus opening new avenues for enhancing the accuracy and enjoyment of food recommendations. In conclusion, the present work seeks to spark more robust mechanisms by which flavour influences food choices, advocating for its consideration as a major feature set within food recommendation (9) systems. Flavour's integration into these systems represents not merely an incremental improvement, but a paradigm shift toward holistic, biologically informed personalization. As such, our framework lays the groundwork for future advancements in gastronomic technology that incorporate both hedonic and health-related factors to recommend foods that are not only enjoyable but also conducive to improved quality of life. The methodological framework encompasses data collection, design and implementation of the recommendation engine, and statistical analyses to validate the efficacy of incorporating flavour-based features. Data Collection Data harnessing constituted two central components: flavour profiling of food items and user-reported taste preferences. We sourced the flavour data from the comprehensive flavour database of the Food Flavourist Association (FFA), which catalogues thousands of food items characterized by their relative prominence in sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami components (Smith et al., 2019). Each food item's profile is quantified into a five-dimension vector (Fi), representing the intensities of these taste dimensions normalized to a scale of 1 to 10. To determine user taste preferences, we employed a purposive sampling technique, recruiting participants (N=500) [2] from varying demographics to ensure a representative sample. Participants were asked to rate their liking for a curated selection of 70 diverse dishes on a ten-point Likert scale, designed to encapsulate broad culinary genres and delicate flavour nuances—ranging from common dietary staples to distinct regional delicacies (Johnson et al., 2020). Design and Implementation The design phase involved developing the flavour-centric (7) recommendation engine. The algorithm operates by matching user taste vectors with food item vectors to maximize alignment between user-reported preferences and potential dish recommendations. The user taste vector (Ui) is calculated as a cumulative weighted average derived from the Likert scale ratings provided by each participant across the selected dishes. This vector captures an individual's propensity towards each of the primary taste dimensions. Incorporating biological insights, we specifically anchored the algorithm on the neural representations of taste processed by the gustatory nerves—namely, the chorda tympani, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves—which encode different aspects of taste perception (Bartoshuk, 1991). By mapping users' taste profiles to these neural processing trends, we hypothesized increased precision in matching algorithm outputs with user preferences. The algorithm adopts a collaborative filtering approach modified with content-based mechanisms. We used Pearson correlation coefficients to assess the similarity between user profiles and the existing database items (Resnick et al., 1994). Each user's historical ratings were leveraged to infer missing preferences through a weighted average of peer preferences, while similarity matrices based on flavour vectors facilitated the content-based component to override biologically implausible predictions. Procedures Participants underwent an introductory briefing outlining the objectives and procedures, followed by the consent process. Each participant was then guided through a web-based platform where they completed the dish rating task. Additionally, participants provided demographic details and previously experienced any dietary restrictions to ensure personalized recommendations. Following the data collection phase, participants engaged with the recommendation system curated specifically for this study. The engine supplied a personalized list of food items, which participants scored based on perceived alignment with [1] their flavour preferences. We hypothesized that the flavour-enhanced recommendations would yield significantly higher satisfaction scores owing to closer alignment with participants' taste preferences (Raghunathan et al., 2010). Finally, regression analyses examined the predictive power of our algorithm in explaining variance in user satisfaction. Multiple linear regression models with satisfaction as the dependent variable were constructed, incorporating flavour matching scores as independent predictors, while controlling for demographic covariates and their interactions. Overall, the statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.0.4), and all hypotheses were tested at α = 0.05. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have become indispensable tools in synthesizing research evidence, offering comprehensive insights into specific research questions and informing healthcare policies and clinical practices (Moher et al., 2009). The robustness of these syntheses depends heavily on the accurate identification and inclusion of relevant data from available studies. However, one common challenge faced by researchers is the existence of multiple sources of data for single trials, which can potentially influence the outcomes of systematic reviews. This issue arises because individual trials are often disseminated through various publications, such (25) as journal articles, conference proceedings, trial registries, and corporate reports, each potentially containing different aspects of the trial data (Page et al., 2020). The presence of multiple data sources for singular trials adds complexity (15) to the systematic review process, as it necessitates the identification and reconciliation of data discrepancies between different reports. Such data discrepancies could result from updates in trial data, differences in reporting standards, selective reporting of outcomes, or varying levels of detail provided across sources (Chan et al., 2014). Systematic reviewers are thus tasked with discerning the most reliable and complete data among multiple sources to ensure the validity of their findings. The challenge is compounded by the potential for conflicts in the data, which can lead to bias if not adequately addressed. Despite the prevalence of this issue, there is limited guidance available on how to effectively manage multiple data sources within systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Existing guidelines, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, focus on the reporting of systematic reviews but do not specifically address the complexities of extracting data from multiple sources for the same trial (Shamseer et al., 2015). As a result, researchers are often left to navigate these challenges without a clear, systematic approach, increasing the risk of biased results and incomplete evidence synthesis. The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was undertaken to investigate these challenges and to develop practical guidance for incorporating multiple data sources effectively (Example et al., 2021). Our study highlights the intricacies involved in identifying, linking, and reconciling data from different sources, and emphasizes the need for a structured approach to ensure the transparency and reproducibility of systematic reviews. In this paper, we address the critical gap in existing methodologies by offering practical guidance for using multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Our recommendations are based on the insights gained from the MUDS study and supplemented by evidence from existing literature. We propose a comprehensive framework for managing multiple data sources, which we believe will improve the accuracy and reliability of systematic reviews. We outline [22] six key recommendations: (1) the specification of source selection criteria; (2) the process of linking individual trials with multiple sources; (3) the implementation of a prespecified protocol for extracting trial characteristics; (4) the prespecification of outcomes and results to be examined; (5) the identification and documentation of data sources included in the review; and (6) the importance of sharing data to reduce bias and enhance reproducibility. Firstly; we propose that systematic reviewers should clearly specify which sources they will use before initiating their review. This involves anticipating where the most comprehensive and reliable data might be found and striving to include all relevant reports related to the trials of interest. In doing so, researchers can mitigate the risk of selection bias and ensure that their review is exhaustive and balanced (Higgins et al., 2019). Secondly, our guidance emphasizes the importance of linking reports from multiple sources for the same trial. This can be achieved by contacting study authors to confirm which documents pertain to the same trial and documenting this process using a modified PRISMA flowchart. This step is critical for maintaining accuracy and preventing the duplication of data (2) (Liberati et al., 2009). Thirdly, we advise the use of a prespecified protocol for data extraction, which involves noting and reconciling any differences among sources. When discrepancies arise, contacting study authors for clarification can aid in resolving conflicts and ensuring accurate data synthesis (Tugwell et al., 2010). Fourthly, prespecifying the outcomes and results to be examined in the review helps mitigate bias associated with selective outcome reporting. By clearly defining outcomes of interest in advance, reviewers can more effectively assess all eligible sources for the data they require (Saldanha et al., 2014). Fifthly, we recommend that systematic reviewers document which data sources were included in their analyses to provide transparency and allow others to evaluate potential influences on their findings. This documentation aids in the reproducibility of the review and assists future researchers in understanding the decision-making process regarding data source selection (Gøtzsche et al., 2007). Lastly, we highlight the importance of data sharing as a means of reducing research waste and enabling future endeavors in the field. Sharing the data used in systematic reviews fosters transparency, allows for verification of results, and facilitates secondary analyses (Van Valkenhoef et al., 2012). In summary, this paper contributes to the ongoing discourse on improving systematic review processes by presenting practical, evidence-based guidance for managing multiple data sources. By adopting these recommendations, researchers can enhance the quality and rigor of their systematic reviews, ultimately leading to more reliable evidence syntheses and better-informed decision-making in clinical and policy contexts. This section details the methodology employed in the Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study to develop practical guidance for using multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The methods encompass the design of the study, data collection, procedures for integrating and analyzing data from various sources, and statistical analyses conducted to ensure robust findings. Data Collection The MUDS study aimed to investigate the impact of using multiple data sources on the outcomes of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. We focused on identifying and integrating data from multiple publications related to individual clinical trials. The trials included for analysis were identified through an extensive literature search using databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, using a predefined search strategy tailored to ensure comprehensive retrieval of relevant publications. Keywords for searching included combinations of "multiple data sources," "systematic review," "meta-analysis," "clinical trials," "duplicated reports," and other relevant terms. Publications related to clinical trials were included if they met the following criteria: (1) the publication reported on clinical trial data; (2) the trial was reported in multiple sources, such as journal articles, conference abstracts, or online trial (28) registries; and (3) the primary or secondary outcomes pertinent to the research question of the systematic review were reported. Reports were excluded if they were narrative reviews, editorials, or commentaries without original data. Design Our study was structured in two phases. The first phase involved identifying discrepancies across multiple reports of the same clinical trials, documenting differences in trial characteristics, outcome measures, and results. In the second phase, we developed a set of guidelines for authors of systematic reviews to effectively manage data from multiple sources, aimed at minimizing bias and improving data transparency. Procedures Linking trials across multiple data sources began with extracting trial identifiers from each publication, such as trial registration numbers, author names, and institutional affiliations, which helped pair different publications to single trials. We reached out to corresponding authors via email for confirmation [10] and [16] clarification on discrepancies across reports when necessary. Each publication was evaluated for methodological quality using predefined criteria adapted from the [21] Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing risk of bias, further informing decisions about inclusion and data extraction. Data from all identified sources for each clinical [27] trial were systematically extracted using a standardized data-extraction form. The data collected included information on (19) trial design, participant characteristics, interventions, outcomes measured, and the results thereof. This information was used to assess consistency across sources and to determine the most reliable data for inclusion in meta-analyses. When discrepancies were noted in trial outcomes or results between sources, we employed a decision tree to guide resolution of conflicts. Outcomes were prioritized based on source reliability, such as peer-reviewed journal articles being favored over conference abstracts. (24) Authors were contacted to clarify (27) issues arising from conflicting data, and if unresolved, data were presented with noted discrepancies in the results section of the systematic [6] review. Statistical Analysis We performed statistical analyses on two levels: within [33] and across individual trials. Across [6] individual trials, pooled analyses were conducted using fixed-effect or random-effect models depending on the heterogeneity of the included data, assessed by the I² statistic. Fixed-effect models were applied when heterogeneity was low (I² < 30%), while random-effects models were used in [33] cases of [9] substantial heterogeneity (I² > 50%). Within the analysis of individual trials, sensitivity analyses were employed to evaluate the impact of selecting different data sources on effect estimates. We compared outcomes using (15) data solely from the primary publication versus including multiple sources, evaluating the degree of confidence in effect estimates through confidence intervals and examining potential publication bias using funnel plots. For meta-regression analyses, covariates such as the type of data source, trial size, and publication year were (8) included to explore factors associated (18) with discrepancies in trial data across sources. Significance was evaluated at a level of p < 0.05. Analyses were performed using RevMan (27) (Review Manager) for meta-analyses and STATA for statistical modeling (9) and meta-regression. In conclusion, our methodological approach in the MUDS study offers a comprehensive framework for integrating multiple data sources, emphasizing transparency and accuracy in systematic reviews to enhance the reliability of synthesized evidence. This methodology underscores the importance of rigorous data collection, critical appraisal, and robust statistical analysis in producing high-quality, evidence-based conclusions. The analysis included data extracted from multiple sources for individual trials, as demonstrated in the MUDS study. Our study focused on 150 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) identified from five (19) key medical databases and over 300 supplementary records from conference proceedings and clinical trial registries. We [31] found that, on average, 2.8 individual sources per trial were located, ranging from a minimum of one source to a maximum of eight sources per trial. The reliance on multiple sources facilitated comprehensive data extraction and contributed significantly to the robustness of the findings across the review. The integration However, of various data sources led to enhanced completeness in identifying key trial characteristics and outcomes. For instance, we found that 64% of the trials had discrepancies in the reported sample sizes across different sources. In 48% of these cases, the discrepancies were notable enough to potentially affect the outcomes and conclusions of a meta-analysis. By contacting study authors, we were able to resolve 70% of these discrepancies, leading to a mean correction in (26) sample size that ranged from -15 to +10 participants per study. This suggests a significant impact on the data completeness and reliability attributable to the verification and triangulation process. Using multiple data sources also affected the reported results in the included trials. Approximately 35% of the trials [11] displayed variations in the reported effect sizes (e.g., However, mean differences or odds ratios) [30] across [11] different sources. In most instances, peer-reviewed journal articles provided the most consistent estimates, (28) while conference abstracts occasionally reported exaggerated effect sizes or failed to provide detailed information, such as confidence intervals or p-values. [36] When only the most complete (11) and coherent datasets from peer-reviewed articles were incorporated, the pooled risk ratio for the primary outcome was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78, 0.90), reflecting a statistically significant effect. Inclusion of a broader set of data adjustments from all sources modified the pooled risk ratio slightly to 0.82 (95% CI: 0.76, 0.88), demonstrating that broader data integration leads to minor, though potentially meaningful, refinements in effect estimates. Differences were also noted in the reporting of primary versus secondary outcomes. Among the trials that [1] reported both primary and secondary outcomes, 20% featured divergent primary outcome reporting between journal articles and other sources. For secondary outcomes, 37% of trials showed variability across sources regarding the measures used or the statistical significance of findings.

Helminth infections, particularly soil-transmitted helminths (STH), remain a significant public health concern, predominantly affecting children in tropical and subtropical regions. These infections, caused by intestinal nematodes such as Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworms, have been linked to various adverse health outcomes, including malnutrition, anemia, and impaired cognitive and physical development in children (WHO, 2020). The substantial burden of these infections is [28] attributed to their high prevalence in environments with inadequate sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, leading to a cycle of transmission and reinfection (Pullan et al., 2014). Despite the global recognition [15] of these infections' impact, the most effective and sustainable interventions to mitigate their effects remain debated. Mass deworming, whereby entire populations at risk are treated with anthelmintic drugs irrespective of their infection status, has been a cornerstone of public health strategies aimed at controlling and eventually eliminating helminth infections. This approach [36] has [21] been primarily driven by the availability of safe and effective drugs such as albendazole and mebendazole (Montresor et al., 2020). the long-term benefits of mass deworming programs, particularly concerning health and cognitive outcomes in children, have been questioned by [38] some researchers, thereby generating a contentious discourse within the scientific [25] community (Hawkins et al., 2017). Existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses on the subject have predominantly utilized aggregated data to assess the impacts of mass deworming programs. These studies have produced mixed results, with some indicating modest improvements in health and educational outcomes, while others suggest that the benefits may be negligible or context-dependent (Taylor-Robinson et al., 2019). A critical limitation of these aggregated analyses is their inability to capture individual variability in responses to deworming, which can be influenced by host factors (e.g., nutritional status, immunity), environmental exposures, and socio-economic conditions. Consequently, there remains a need for more nuanced analyses that utilize individual participant data (IPD) to elucidate the heterogeneous effects of mass deworming interventions. The present research aims to address these limitations through a systematic review and individual participant data network meta-analysis, focusing on evaluating the impact of mass deworming on health and cognitive outcomes in children residing in helminth-endemic [37] areas. This approach enables the examination of treatment effect modifiers and allows for a comprehensive [6] assessment of deworming's efficacy across different subpopulations and settings. It also facilitates the construction of a more accurate and reliable evidence base that can inform policy decisions and resource allocation within affected regions. By conducting an IPD network meta-analysis, this study will contribute to the literature in several key ways. Firstly, it will provide a more granular understanding of the variability in individual responses to mass deworming interventions. This understanding has the potential to refine and optimize treatment protocols by identifying specific subgroups of children who may benefit the most from deworming efforts. Secondly, the study will explore the network of available interventions and their relative effectiveness, thus offering insights into the most effective anthelmintic drugs and delivery strategies. Thirdly, the research will expand the evaluation of outcomes beyond immediate health benefits by incorporating cognitive and educational metrics, which are [21] crucial for assessing the long-term impacts of deworming on child development. Furthermore, this study aligns with global health priorities, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those aimed at ending epidemics of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and improving child health and education (United Nations, 2015). By leveraging robust statistical techniques and a comprehensive dataset, the findings of this research have the potential to significantly influence public health strategies targeting STH infections and contribute to global efforts in reducing health disparities and promoting sustainable development. In conclusion, the proposed systematic review and IPD network meta-analysis represents a significant advancement in the study of mass deworming's impacts on children in helminth-endemic areas. By addressing critical methodological gaps in previous research and employing a rigorous analytical framework, this study seeks to provide policymakers and health practitioners with actionable insights [37] to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of deworming programs worldwide. The anticipated results are expected to offer evidence-based recommendations that are responsive to the diverse needs of affected populations, ultimately supporting international efforts toward the elimination of STH as a public health problem. The methods section of this systematic review and individual participant data (IPD) network meta-analysis follows the guidelines established by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) for conducting IPD reviews (Liberati et al., 2009). This protocol was pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, registration number: CRD42021234567). Data Sources and Search Strategy The literature search aimed to identify all relevant studies on mass deworming interventions targeting children in helminth-endemic areas. A comprehensive search strategy was developed under the guidance of a professional librarian and implemented across multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science from their inception to October 2021. The search string combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to "deworming," "helminths," "parasitic worms," children, "health," and "cognitive outcomes. In addition to electronic database searches, reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were screened to ensure the comprehensiveness of the retrieval process. authors of identified studies were contacted to request unpublished data, particularly concerning raw IPD that may not have been reported in the published manuscripts. Eligibility Criteria We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that examined the effect of mass deworming on health and cognitive outcomes among children aged 2-18 years in areas where helminth infections are endemic. Studies needed to provide, or be able to provide upon request, extractable IPD that included baseline and follow-up measurements for relevant outcomes. Trials that used single-, double-, or triple-drug deworming strategies were included. Exclusion criteria comprised studies targeting adult populations, interventions focusing on other health measures unrelated to deworming, and studies lacking adequate outcome measures relevant to this analysis. Study Selection and Data Collection Two independent reviewers (Author A and Author B) screened titles and abstracts identified through the search. Full texts were retrieved for studies deemed potentially eligible, and decisions regarding inclusion were made independently by the same reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by discussion or in consultation with a third reviewer (Author C). A bespoke data extraction form was developed and piloted, capturing key details such as study design, intervention characteristics, participant demographics, and outcomes. For eligible studies, corresponding authors were contacted for IPD and were asked to provide de-identified data sets. Data management followed ethical guidelines pertinent to IPD handling, ensuring confidentiality and data security. Outcomes The primary outcomes of interest were health improvements, assessed through standardized measures of physical health (e.g., hemoglobin levels, nutritional status), and cognitive outcomes, assessed through validated tests of cognitive function appropriate for age (e.g., Raven's Matrices, Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children). Secondary outcomes included school attendance rates and infection reinfection rates. Outcomes extraction focused on obtaining sufficient detail to allow comparative analysis across intervention types and populations. Risk of Bias and Quality Assessment Risk of bias in individual studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 for randomized trials (Higgins et al., 2011). This assessment characterized study quality across various domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, and outcome assessment. Two reviewers independently performed quality assessments, with disagreements settled through discussion or recourse to a third reviewer. The quality of evidence (QoE) across studies for each outcome was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) criteria, with QoE rated as high, moderate, low, or very low. Statistical Analysis The primary analysis involved an IPD network meta-analysis using a Bayesian framework to compare the effects of different deworming regimens on the outcomes of interest, allowing for the inclusion of both direct and indirect evidence. This approach offers a more precise estimate by incorporating all available data and accounts for the correlated nature of outcomes within trials. A hierarchical model was fitted using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques, executed in WinBUGS (Lunn et al., 2000). Model convergence was assessed through inspection of trace plots and the Gelman-Rubin statistic, with adequate convergence indicated by values close to 1. For each primary outcome, summary relative effects were estimated and presented as odds ratios or mean differences with 95% credible intervals. Sensitivity analyses examined the [17] robustness of results regarding assumptions such as missing data mechanisms and heterogeneity across studies. We also conducted [6] subgroup analyses investigating variations in effect sizes based on geographic location, baseline infection intensity, and the age of participants. The potential for publication bias was explored using comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger’s test for asymmetry where applicable. All analyses adhered to an intention-to-treat principle, where feasible, and all statistical tests were two-sided with a significance threshold set at a p-value of less than 0.05. Data synthesis and statistical analysis [34] were independently reviewed by a senior statistician (Author D) to ensure the robustness of the findings. The systematic review and individual participant data network meta-analysis (IPD NMA) included data from 35 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) encompassing 120,487 children across endemic helminth areas. Based on the comprehensive dataset, the analysis revealed significant findings pertaining to health outcomes and cognitive improvements attributable to mass deworming interventions. Health Outcomes: The primary metric for assessing health outcomes was the prevalence of helminth infections post-intervention. The pooled prevalence of helminth infection in the deworming group showed a substantial decline compared to the control group, demonstrating an odds ratio (OR) of [10] [30] 0.35 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.29 to 0.41; p < 0.001). the reduction in the intensity of infections, measured in eggs per gram (EPG) of feces, exhibited a notable mean difference of -275 EPG (95% CI, -318 to -232; p < 0.001). This indicates that children receiving deworming therapies were significantly less burdened by parasitic infections. The dissemination of health science research findings is a critical component in the advancement of public health and scientific literacy among the general population. In this process, journal editors and media professionals play pivotal roles in determining which research findings are communicated to broader audiences through press releases and subsequent media coverage. Health science articles encompass a wide spectrum of topics, each with varying degrees of relevance to public interest and policy implications. The decision-making process underlying the selection of articles deemed newsworthy by journal editors for press release issuance or by journalists for media coverage remains underexplored (Dunwoody et al., 2015). Understanding what characterizes the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles is crucial for researchers and communication practitioners seeking to optimize the dissemination and impact of scientific findings. The issue of newsworthiness is particularly salient in the context of health sciences, where reliable information can guide public health decisions (Viswanath et al., 2008). Despite the acknowledged importance, the evaluative criteria used by editors and journalists [23] are often implicit and can vary widely across different stakeholders (Nelkin, 1995). The subjective nature of these assessments can be attributed to multiple factors, including the scientific rigor of the study, the novelty of findings, and the potential societal impact. While prior studies have examined the criteria influencing editorial decisions (Kline et al., 2016), a systematic, data-driven characterization of what specifically renders a health science article newsworthy has not been conducted. The existing literature on media coverage selection processes suggests key thematic areas that generally align with increased coverage likelihood. Themes such as those relating to epidemiology, public health crises, and behavioral studies are noted as particularly appealing to journalists and the public (Schwitzer et al., 2005). Furthermore, content analysis of press releases has traditionally identified elements like sensational language, direct relevance to substantial portions of the population, and clear implications for health outcomes as influential in media uptake (Seale, 2003). However, these insights are often derived from qualitative analyses or limited case studies that do not capture the breadth or variance of content across diverse health topics and journal practices. To address this gap in our understanding of what constitutes newsworthiness in health science, we employ a robust data-driven approach leveraging statistical machine learning methods. We propose that elements within the text of published health science articles, particularly those contained in abstracts, could serve as indicators of their potential to be selected for press releases or media coverage. These components can be analyzed quantitatively to delineate predictive patterns and themes. The primary research question guiding this study is: What attributes of published health science articles are predictive of (1) the likelihood of press release issuance by journal editors and (2) the probability of mainstream media coverage? By scrutinizing the textual content of articles through advanced computational techniques, this study aims to pinpoint specific linguistic features and latent topics that correlate strongly with perceived newsworthiness. Our contributions are multifaceted. First, we introduce an empirical methodology employing machine learning to systematically evaluate large corpus datasets comprising health science articles, including those that did not receive press releases or media coverage. (18) Through this methodology, we generate predictive models capable of discerning patterns that are suggestive of press release and media coverage likelihoods. Second, we present a comparative analysis of the predictive accuracy across datasets differing in size and context, underscoring the robustness of our approach in the characterization of newsworthy content. This empirical validation offers insights into editorial and journalistic selection processes, potentially guiding new communication strategies for researchers and (24) institutions aiming to enhance the visibility of their work. Third, we report on the specific words and topics most predictive of press release (23) issuance and media coverage, thus contributing to the broader discourse on public engagement with (8) science. Such findings implicate not only the thematic but also [2] the linguistic attributes that enhance the appeal of health science articles. Our results highlight; for example, the prominent media attention garnered by epidemiological papers focusing on common behavioral topics, such as alcohol consumption, (23) delineating pathways through which researchers might strategically communicate their work to resonate with public interests. In conclusion, our study offers a pioneering, data-driven perspective on the factors influencing the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles, presenting implications for both theoretical understanding and practical communication within the scientific community. This work serves as a foundational contribution to future research exploring the intersections of health science, communication studies, and information dissemination strategies. This study employed a robust methodological framework to analyze the attributes of health science articles that influence their newsworthiness, particularly in relation to press release issuance and mainstream media coverage. We incorporated both quantitative and qualitative methods, leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to decipher complex patterns within the datasets. Introduction Systematic reviews are fundamental tools in evidence-based disciplines, serving [17] as comprehensive syntheses of research literature to inform practice, policy, and future research. The growing dependency on systematic reviews necessitates rigorous "methodologies" to ensure their [1] validity and reliability. The inclusion of [27] diverse data sources is a critical component of this methodology, with discussions often centered on whether to incorporate data from conference abstracts. Conference abstracts are brief summaries of studies presented at academic and professional conferences, and they represent a wealth of preliminary research findings. Despite their apparent importance, the inclusion of conference abstracts in systematic reviews [16] remains a contentious issue within the research community. The rationale for considering conference abstracts within systematic reviews is founded on several conceptual and empirical grounds. Primarily, the publication bias, a well-documented concern in systematic reviews, suggests that studies with positive outcomes are more likely to be published in peer-reviewed journals as full-length articles compared to those with negative or [22] null results (Song et al., 2010). As a consequence, excluding conference abstracts may inadvertently contribute to an overestimation of treatment effectiveness due to the underrepresentation of less favorable or equivocal findings. By contrast, "including" conference abstracts in systematic reviews could help mitigate publication bias, providing a more balanced view of the available evidence and enhancing the credibility of the review findings (Hopewell et al., 2007). the time-lag bias is another aspect where additional data from conference abstracts may prove beneficial. Studies with significant results often reach publication faster than those with non-significant findings (Stern & Simes, 1997). Within this context, conference abstracts could provide early insights into emerging research that has not yet undergone the lengthy process of full publication, thereby reflecting the current state of research in a timely "manner." The prospect of accessing this body of evidence contemporaneously is particularly pressing in fast-evolving fields, such as biomedical research and technology, where timely information can have immediate implications for clinical decisions and policy-making (Egger et al., 2003). Despite these potential benefits, the inclusion of conference abstracts in systematic reviews also [21] presents notable challenges and limitations. The core argument against their inclusion [1] hinges on the quality of the information contained within the abstracts themselves. Frequently, conference abstracts provide limited methodological detail and are inherently brief, raising concerns about their methodological rigour, validity, and reproducibility (Bielefeldt et al., 2009). Further compounding this issue is the fact that the process of peer review (20) for conference submissions can vary significantly in stringency compared to that of journal articles, potentially affecting the dependability of the findings reported (Sandhu et al., 2016). In addition to (19) questions of quality, the practicalities of systematically searching for and incorporating conference abstracts into reviews are not trivial. The process can be resource-intensive, requiring time-consuming searches across numerous conference proceedings databases that may not be well-indexed or maintained (Royle & (23) Waugh, 2003). There is also no standardized method for the identification and retrieval of abstracts, unlike the more streamlined processes available (7) for full-text journal articles, which could increase the risk of incomplete or inconsistent data inclusion (Hopewell et al., 2002). Given the potential for conflicting assessments of treatment effects and variability in meta-analytic results when conference abstracts are included, the question of when and how to include these abstracts calls for more nuanced consideration. Emerging research implies that shifts in the pooled estimate of treatment effects can occur when abstracts are included in (16) a meta-analysis; although these shifts typically affect the precision rather than the magnitude [22] of the effect size (Scherer & Langenberg, 2007). Therefore, rather than applying a blanket policy towards inclusion or exclusion, systematic reviewers need to weigh the necessity of conference abstracts on a case-by-case basis, considering the availability of higher-quality evidence and the specific context of the review. The primary objective of this paper is to provide systematic reviewers with pragmatic guidance on how to handle conference abstracts within the broader framework of systematic reviews. We aim to contribute to the discourse by examining the advantages and disadvantages of including conference abstracts and by proposing strategies to enhance the robustness of reviews that incorporate them. By advocating for conditional inclusion based on the context and aims of the review, we offer an approach that balances the need for comprehensive data coverage with the demands for methodological rigor. In particular, we suggest that when evidence is especially sparse or conflicting, reviewers should actively seek out conference abstracts and employ complementary strategies such as author contact for additional data and performing sensitivity analyses to evaluate the impact of including these abstracts on review outcomes. In summary, this paper addresses a significant methodological gap in systematic review practices by evaluating the role of conference abstracts in evidence synthesis. Our recommendations are informed by the examination of existing empirical studies, methodological considerations, and practical constraints, contributing an informed perspective to this ongoing debate. By equipping researchers with actionable guidelines, we aim to enhance the quality and reliability of systematic reviews in diverse research environments. This section outlines the methodology employed to investigate the handling of conference abstracts in systematic reviews, with a focus on the rationale behind their inclusion or exclusion. The methods encompass data sources, study design, procedures, and statistical analyses to support the conclusions drawn. Data The primary data utilized in this study included conference abstracts and their corresponding full-length publications, where available. [33] The sample was obtained through a systematic and structured search of various databases such as PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, focusing on a selection of medical and scientific conferences that were known for their rigorous peer-review processes. registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) were consulted to identify any registered trials that had reported preliminary results in conference abstracts. Relevant guidelines and position papers from organizations such as the Cochrane Collaboration and PRISMA were reviewed to gain insight into current standards and practices (Smith et al., 2018; Jones and Williams, 2020). Design A retrospective cohort design was employed to evaluate the consistency between conference abstracts and their subsequent full-length publications. This involved comparing the methodological details, results, and conclusions presented in abstracts to those in final articles. We constructed two cohorts: one comprising studies that were initially reported in conference abstracts and later published as full articles, and another containing studies that remained unpublished beyond the abstract stage. This design allowed for a direct assessment of the influence of including conference abstracts in systematic reviews, particularly in terms of reported outcomes and methodological robustness (Brown et al., 2019). Procedures The selection of conference abstracts and their paired full-length articles followed a stringent inclusion and exclusion criterion. Abstracts included were those reporting clinical trials or observational studies, containing quantitative data that could impact meta-analytic outcomes. Exclusion criteria encompassed non-empirical abstracts, such as narrative reviews, discussion papers, or editorial comments, and abstracts lacking sufficient detail for analysis. Once identified, abstract-full article pairs were analyzed for congruence in key domains, including participant characteristics, intervention descriptions, outcome measurements, and statistical analyses. Discrepancies between the abstract and full publication were cataloged, with emphasis on changes in sample sizes, statistical significance, and effect sizes that could alter systematic review conclusions (Taylor and Adams, 2021). To further enhance the comprehensiveness of the included data, attempts were made to contact the authors of abstracts seeking additional information such as trial protocols or unpublished data. Where possible, supplemental information obtained from trial registries or through direct communication with authors was integrated to improve the reliability of data extracted from abstracts (Harrison et al., 2020). Statistical Analysis To quantitatively assess the impact of including conference abstracts in systematic reviews, meta-analyses were conducted with and without the incorporation of abstract data. We employed random-effects models to account for heterogeneity among studies. The primary metrics assessed included pooled treatment effects and confidence intervals; changes in these metrics were attributed to the inclusion of abstract data, highlighting the contribution of abstracts to systematic review outcomes (Anderson et al., 2018). Sensitivity analyses were performed to (1) evaluate the robustness of meta-analysis results when abstracts contributed unique data not available in full articles. This involved re-running meta-analyses excluding the abstracts to determine if their inclusion altered the outcome or merely enhanced the precision of estimates. Meta-regression was utilized to ascertain whether study characteristics, such as the year of publication and study size, influenced discrepancies between abstract and full article data (Clark and Lewis, 2019). Further statistical evaluation involved calculating the inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) for the assessment of data consistency between pairs of conference abstracts and full articles, thereby ensuring the reliability of the data extraction process (Wilson et al., 2021). In summary, the methods deployed allowed for a rigorous examination of the role conference abstracts play in systematic reviews. By focusing on methodological congruence and the statistical importance of abstract data, this study provides insights into whether conference [28] abstracts can validly contribute to evidence synthesis efforts. To quantify the impact, we conducted a comprehensive examination of data across multiple systematic reviews where conference abstracts were considered. However, impact on treatment effect estimates was observed in 28% (n=39) of the systematic reviews incorporating conference abstracts. In the realm of bibliometric analysis, the accurate identification and matching of identical publications across diverse databases are paramount to ensuring data reliability and integrity in research assessments. Unique Identifiers (UIDs), such as Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), have emerged as critical tools in this regard, providing a standardized mechanism to identify and link identical publications across various bibliometric repositories. The implementation of UIDs simplifies the process of data integration across databases, enhances data retrieval accuracy, and mitigates the risk of duplication (Haunschild et al., 2019). With the advent and proliferation of complex multi-database systems in health sciences, databases like Pure and SciVal have increasingly relied on UIDs for matching identical publications. However, the efficacy of UIDs in this context remains under-examined, especially concerning their role in bibliometric methodologies. The field of bibliometrics, particularly within health sciences, heavily relies on comprehensive and integrated data for assessing research outputs and impacts (Bornmann & Leydesdorff, 2013). Health sciences also demonstrate a significant overlap in publications across various databases, necessitating precise matching to avoid discrepancies in bibliometric indicators, such as citation counts and publication metrics (Moed, 2005). While UIDs such as DOIs offer a streamlined approach for linking data, literature indicates several potential pitfalls and error types that may undermine their effectiveness. These include duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOI indexing, and missed DOI registrations (Peters et al., 2018; López-Illescas et al., 2012). These errors could lead to either the inflation or underestimation of bibliometric indicators, impacting the accuracy of analyses that underpin research evaluations, funding decisions, and policy-making. Despite the recognized importance of UIDs in bibliometrics, there is a notable gap in rigorous studies exploring the specific challenges and limitations associated with their use as match keys between databases like Pure and SciVal. Existing literature often acknowledges the utility of UIDs but falls short of providing a detailed examination of their practical efficacy and the errors that may arise during their application in large-scale bibliometric studies (Sugimoto et al., 2017). This gap is particularly pronounced in the field of health sciences, where research output is voluminous and often overlaps across multiple platforms and repositories. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating how effectively UIDs serve as match keys in integrating [10] publications between Pure and SciVal, focusing on health science publications. The primary research question guiding this study is: How accurately and effectively do UIDs function as match keys for identifying and linking identical health science publications between the Pure and SciVal databases? To address this; we examine the coverage and precision of UIDs, exploring the characteristics of matched and unmatched publications and identifying prevalent errors that impact the matching process. Our study focuses on health sciences due to the field's significant bibliometric demands and the critical role of accurate publication data in advancing research and healthcare policies (Börner et al., 2010). This study makes several contributions to the literature on bibliometric data integration and UID functionality. First, it provides empirical insights into the strengths and limitations of UIDs as tools for database integration, offering evidence-based analysis of how these identifiers function in real-world scenarios involving widely-used academic databases. Second, our investigation into error types enhances understanding of common pitfalls in DOI usage and provides practical recommendations for improving bibliometric practices. Third, by focusing on health science publications, this research highlights domain-specific challenges and contributes to the development of refined methods for bibliometric analysis within this critical research area. Lastly, this study discusses the implications of [6] using UIDs for calculating bibliometric indicators, such as publication counts and citation metrics, offering a nuanced understanding of how errors in UID implementation can distort research evaluations. Through a combination of literature review and a case study approach, this research advances our understanding of how UIDs operate as match keys, identifying areas where existing methodologies may [30] be improved. Given the increasing reliance on cross-database bibliometric analyses in evaluating research impact; the findings from this study are expected to aid in refining data integration techniques, ultimately contributing to more accurate and reliable research evaluations in the health sciences [21] and beyond. Methods In this study, we implemented a mixed-methods approach to evaluate the effectiveness of unique identifiers (UIDs) as match keys for aligning identical publications between the databases Pure and SciVal, focusing particularly on publications in the health sciences. The methodology comprised data collection, study design, detailed procedures for matching, and statistical analysis. Each component was systematically designed to address the research questions and objectives. Data were obtained from the Pure and SciVal databases; two platforms widely used for research management and bibliometric analysis, respectively. The dataset focused on journal publications in the health sciences discipline, "written" in English, (6) published between 2015 and [20] 2020. This timeframe was selected based on the expectation of comprehensive DOI utilization, a prevalent UID, during these years. Each publication record from both databases included the following information: title; author(s), publication year, journal name, DOI, and other relevant metadata where available. The design of the study [37] involved both a literature review (4) and a case study. Our case study aimed to empirically test and analyze the hypothesized effectiveness of UIDs, primarily DOIs, in matching publications accurately between databases. Inclusion criteria were set to filter records based on the presence of a DOI, ensuring that only publications with this form of UID were considered for detailed analysis. Publications without a DOI or with erroneous [15] entries that led to a failure in (28) preliminary matches were excluded from further analyses. For the matching procedures, we commenced by aligning each publication in Pure with a corresponding entry in SciVal using the DOI as the primary "match" key. The process involved cross-referencing DOIs, given their near-universal endorsement as a [2] digital [2] identifier, meant to be unique for each [35] publication. A custom script was developed to facilitate batch processing and automate the match identification; utilizing the Python programming [31] language (25) due to its robust capacity for handling large datasets and text processing. Following the primary matching procedure, the results were subjected to manual (23) verification to identify and resolve discrepancies. This step included reviewing mismatches and duplicates flagged by the script; as well as cross-referencing other publication details such as title and author information to ensure data fidelity and [1] to discern errors in DOI assignment or entry. Particular attention was given to duplicate DOIs, as these were "hypothesized" to affect bibliometric indicators. Statistical analysis was conducted to (6) evaluate the effectiveness of UIDs in the matching process. [9] The analysis focused on three main areas: coverage, precision, and impact on bibliometric indicators. Coverage was assessed by calculating the proportion of publications with DOIs that were successfully matched between the two databases. Precision was evaluated by determining the correctness of matches, specifically the ratio of true matches to the total number of matches identified. To ascertain the nature and impact of errors detected, comparative analyses were employed to [9] examine characteristics between (25) publications that were successfully matched and those that were not. Error-specific analysis (19) delved into the types noted during the literature review: duplicate DOIs, incorrect DOIs, non-registered DOIs, and any other systematic failures. Hypothetical datasets were simulated, introducing controlled errors to contrast potential bibliometric outcomes versus clean datasets, (19) thereby quantifying the effectivity and reliability of exact matches. The implications of mismatches on bibliometric indicators—number of publications, number of citations, and average citations per publication—were statistically evaluated. Paired t-tests and chi-square tests were utilized to compare bibliometric measures before and after error corrections to assess the statistical significance of differences attributable to mismatched or duplicated publications. The statistical computations were performed using R, chosen for its comprehensive suite of statistical packages and graphical capabilities. The final phase involved synthesizing the findings to derive insights into the robustness of UIDs as match keys in bibliometric analyses and the potential implications for research assessment and database management. This included recommendations for database managers and researchers on addressing UID-related errors, underscoring the need for improved UID utility and error management in bibliometric evaluation processes. Through this methodical approach, our study critically assessed the utility of UIDs in efficiently and accurately matching publications across databases, offering valuable contributions to improving bibliometric practices and research management. In this [9] study, we evaluate the effectiveness of unique identifiers (UIDs) as keys for matching identical publications [39] across the Pure and SciVal databases. Our analysis focuses on publications in the health sciences, highlighting coverage, precision, and discrepancies. Coverage analysis revealed that UIDs demonstrate a high level of applicability as match keys for journal publications. Specifically, our data set consisted of 10,000 health sciences publications extracted from both Pure and SciVal. After exhaustive matching, 8,700 publications (87%) were successfully matched based on existing UIDs, primarily leveraging digital object identifiers (DOIs). This implies that UIDs effectively match the majority of publications across databases, ensuring comprehensive coverage. However, examining precision uncovered some deficits. Among the publications with matched UIDs, 3% (261 publications) revealed misalignments in their metadata between the two databases. Specifically, these discrepancies were categorized as follows: 142 publications had slight author name inconsistencies, such as variations in the use of initials; 87 publications exhibited title discrepancies due to alternate spellings or punctuation variations; and 32 instances showed year of publication differences, typically due to delays in issues publication dates or advance online releases versus print versions. These findings indicate that while UIDs effectively bind the publications, the precision of metadata remains slightly compromised at times. Over the past decade, microservice architecture has emerged as a pivotal shift in the design and deployment of software applications, aligning seamlessly with the increasing adoption of cloud-based solutions. Unlike traditional monolithic architectures, which bundle all of an application’s components into a singular, often cumbersome unit, microservices disaggregate functionality into independently deployable, modular services. This architectural paradigm facilitates greater agility in development processes, allowing for the incremental enhancement of discrete components without necessitating wholesale changes to the entire system (Dragoni "et" al., 2017). As organizations strive to enhance scalability and increase the fault tolerance of their applications, microservices have been widely adopted, driving the need for platforms that effectively manage these distributed systems. Despite the clear advantages, the complexity introduced by a multitude of operationally independent services presents significant challenges, particularly in regard to performance management and resource distribution. This is compounded by the diverse and dynamic environments typical of public and private cloud infrastructures, which host these microservice platforms (Newman, 2015). to facilitate continuous integration, deployment, and scaling of microservices, platforms such as Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, and Amazon ECS have emerged. These platforms streamline the deployment processes across various cloud environments and offer orchestration capabilities crucial for maintaining service reliability and performance. Existing literature has explored various aspects of microservice platforms, focusing extensively on the benefits they confer in terms of scalability and resource efficiency (Balalaie et al., 2016). there remains a notable gap in understanding the provisioning performance of these platforms at scale, especially when intersected with complex cloud architectures (Reyes-Cortez et al., 2020). Most studies have traditionally concentrated either on the micro-level—delving into the internal workings of individual microservices—or on the macro-level—examining broad infrastructure considerations without sufficiently connecting insights from both dimensions. There exists a dearth of integrated performance modeling that comprehensively analyzes the interactions and dependencies across these layers to inform efficient resource management and capacity planning. This paper seeks to address this gap by "posing" the following research question: How can a unified performance model be developed to evaluate and optimize the provisioning performance of microservice platforms across both micro-level service operations and macro-level cloud infrastructure? By exploring this question, the research aims to elucidate the intricate relationships between containerized application performance and underlying infrastructure dynamics, thereby advancing the state-of-the-art in microservice platform performance management. The contributions of this study are multi-faceted. First, we develop and implement a microservice platform atop Amazon EC2, one of the most prominent cloud computing services, (19) known for its flexibility and broad adoption. This foundation serves as a practical basis for our performance modeling, rooted in real-world application scenarios. Second, we propose an innovative performance model that factors in both micro and macro layers, offering a dual perspective that captures the nuances of containerized microservice deployment and resource allocation across cloud environments. This model is designed to facilitate what-if analyses and rigorous capacity planning exercises by enabling a systematic examination of platform elasticity and provisioning performance. Third, we conduct empirical evaluations to validate our model, applying it to various deployment scenarios to simulate and measure the elasticity of the microservice platform. These evaluations help to identify bottlenecks and inefficiencies within microservice operations, providing actionable insights to optimize resource consumption and improve runtime performance. The findings from these simulations will inform stakeholders on the potential trade-offs between service granularity and infrastructure allocation, guiding decision-making in cloud-native application design and deployment. In summary, this paper contributes to the ongoing discourse on cloud-native application management by providing an integrated framework that enables the in-depth; holistic performance evaluation of microservice platforms. Through this work, we aim to offer practical insights and tools that empower organizations to make data-driven decisions in managing and scaling their microservice deployments, ultimately enhancing both the operational and economic efficiencies of cloud-based software systems. Hypertrophic scarring is a common complication following dermal injury, characterized by the excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) components leading to raised, erythematous, and often pruritic scars. These scars can cause significant physical [3] discomfort and psychological distress, making their management a crucial aspect of post-injury care (Jimi et al., 2017). Among the various mechanisms [34] implicated in the pathogenesis of hypertrophic scars, [22] the matrix [6] metalloproteinases (MMPs) have received significant attention. MMPs are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases responsible for the degradation of various components of the ECM, thus playing a critical role in tissue remodeling and homeostasis (Brew & Nagase, 2010). Matrix metalloproteinases are known to participate in numerous (23) physiological and pathological processes, including embryonic development, reproduction, and tissue regeneration, as well as in inflammatory and degenerative diseases (Sternlicht & Werb, 2001). During normal wound healing, MMPs help "to" remove damaged matrix structures and facilitate the influx of new matrix proteins; enabling tissue repair and remodeling. However, dysregulation of MMP activity can lead to pathological conditions, including fibrosis and hypertrophic scarring (Verhaegen et al., 2009). Despite extensive research on MMPs in wound healing, the specific roles and regulatory mechanisms of individual MMPs during hypertrophic scarring remain inadequately characterized. Compression therapy is among the most widely employed conservative interventions for managing hypertrophic scars, with its efficacy attributed to several proposed mechanisms, such as reduction in blood [29] flow, collagen synthesis modulation, and changes in cytokine expression (O'Brien et al., 2017). However, the impact of compression therapy on the regulation and expression of MMPs within hypertrophic scars has not been thoroughly investigated. Understanding how compression influences MMP [5] activity could unveil new therapeutic targets and strategies for managing problematic scarring. The current research aims to address this gap by exploring the transcriptional and translational regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy using a red Duroc swine model. The swine model is particularly [39] advantageous due to the similarity of its skin structure and wound (12) healing processes to those of humans; making it a robust model for investigating scar formation and treatment (Gallant-Behm et al., 2008). Our study's primary research question is: How does compression therapy influence the expression and activity of matrix metalloproteinases during the progression of hypertrophic scar formation? To explore [9] this question; we employed a comprehensive approach to profile the expression of all 26 known MMPs in swine hypertrophic scar tissue, both with and without compression therapy. Utilizing a combination of microarray analysis, reverse transcription-polymerase (26) chain (27) reaction (RT-PCR), Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry, we systematically examined the transcription and protein [32] expression levels of MMPs. This approach enables a thorough understanding of the nuanced regulatory dynamics involved. Our findings reveal that out of the 26 known MMPs, 13 were differentially transcribed during the wound healing process. Interestingly, the upregulation of these MMPs observed during the early stages of wound healing gradually declined as healing progressed. However, the introduction of compression therapy altered this pattern, attenuating the decline in 10 of the 13 differentially regulated MMPs. MMP7 was highlighted as a critical enzyme whose regulation under compression therapy was substantiated at both the transcriptional and protein levels. These findings carry several significant implications. First, they provide insight into the molecular responses of hypertrophic scars to mechanical interventions, underscoring the therapeutic potential of modulating MMP activity in scar management. Second, they raise important considerations regarding the timing and application of compression therapy to maximize its benefits in scar reduction. Third; they identify specific MMPs, such as MMP7, as promising targets for drug development aimed at mitigating hypertrophic scars. In conclusion, this study advances our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of hypertrophic scar modulation under compression therapy, highlighting the complex interplay between mechanical forces and biochemical pathways. The identification of MMPs as key mediators in this process opens new avenues for therapeutic interventions in hypertrophic scar management. Future research should focus on elucidating the signaling pathways involved in MMP regulation under varying mechanical stress conditions and further validating these findings in human clinical settings to enhance translational applicability. By "addressing" the previously unexplored intersection of compression therapy and MMP regulation, "this" study contributes to the broader field of wound healing and scar management. The knowledge gained here underscores the potential for tailored therapeutic strategies that leverage the mechanobiological aspects of scar formation and resolution; ultimately improving patient outcomes in the management of hypertrophic scars. The study was meticulously designed to investigate the regulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in hypertrophic scars and their response to compression therapy using a Red Duroc swine model. The "animal" model was selected due to its close resemblance to human cutaneous wound healing; particularly in terms of collagen deposition and scar formation (Mast et al., 1992). This study adhered to the ethical guidelines for animal experimentation and was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Data were collected from 16 adult Red Duroc pigs. Full-thickness excisional wounds, sized 4 cm by 4 cm, were created on each pig's dorsum using a standardized surgical procedure to simulate hypertrophic scar formation. Prior to surgery, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane to ensure optimal analgesia and immobility. The wounds were allowed [38] to heal spontaneously without any intervention for the initial two weeks to enable uniform scar formation across all subjects. Subsequently, the [18] pigs were randomly divided into two groups: one serving as a control with no further treatment, and the other receiving controlled compression [39] therapy. Compression therapy was delivered to the assigned group using custom-fabricated silicone gel sheets with a compression garment providing approximately 15–20 mmHg pressure, verified using manometry (Heath et al., 2020). The therapy (22) was initiated two weeks post-surgery [5] and continued for another two weeks. Compliance with the compression regimen was rigorously monitored; and adjustments were made as necessary to maintain consistent pressure application. Biopsy specimens were harvested at four designated time points: pre-surgery (baseline), two [24] weeks post-injury (prior to compression therapy), and at four and six weeks post-injury. At each time point, biopsies from both treated and untreated sites were taken. Specimens were immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C for molecular analysis or fixed in formalin for histological evaluation. Multiple methodologies were employed to evaluate MMP transcriptional and translational responses. Microarray analyses were initially performed to profile [6] the expression of all known 26 MMPs across different time points. RNA was extracted from the frozen tissue samples using the TRIzol reagent method; with purification using an RNeasy kit (Qiagen). RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer; and cDNA was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Affymetrix porcine [35] genome array was used for microarray analysis following the manufacturer’s instructions. Differential gene expression was calculated using the robust multiarray average (RMA) method for normalization, with significance determined using the false discovery (12) rate (FDR) approach to adjust for multiple comparisons (Benjamini & Hochberg; 1995). Genes with an FDR-corrected p-value <0.05 were considered significantly differentially transcribed. To validate microarray findings; quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was used with primer sets specific for selected MMPs, focused on those showing notable transcriptional changes. Expression levels of MMP7, identified as a key responsive gene, were quantified using the SYBR Green dye on an ABI 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) with GAPDH as an internal control. The comparative CT method (ΔΔCT) was applied for relative quantification. At the protein level, Western blotting was conducted for a subset of MMPs, particularly MMP7, to confirm translational regulation. Proteins were extracted from tissue samples using a radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by the Bradford assay. Equivalent amounts of protein from each sample (30 µg) were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. Membranes were blocked in 5% skim milk and probed with primary antibodies specific to MMP7, followed by horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies. Bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence kit and quantified with ImageJ software. Immunohistochemistry was conducted on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections to localize MMP7 expression within tissue architecture.
