The exponential growth of biomedical literature presents an unprecedented challenge for researchers and biocurators, who must sift through an overwhelming volume of information to extract pertinent data and insights. With millions of articles published across various platforms, efficient literature mining and retrieval have become essential to keeping pace (13) with scientific advancements. Traditional methods of manual literature review are increasingly impractical due to the sheer volume of data, necessitating the development of innovative tools and platforms that can streamline the process of information extraction and knowledge discovery (Hunter & Cohen, 2006; Wang et al., 2018). Information retrieval systems are critical to addressing this challenge, as they allow users to search and extract relevant data efficiently. Over recent years, several text-mining platforms have been developed to facilitate (5) the retrieval and analysis of biomedical literature. These platforms, such as PubMed and Europe PMC, provide basic functionalities for querying literature using simple keyword searches. However, they are often limited in scope, focusing primarily on abstracts and lacking the capability (12) to delve into the full texts where detailed information often resides (Lu, 2011; Rinaldi et al., 2018). The original Textpresso system emerged as a pioneering tool designed to enhance the retrieval of biomedical text by incorporating both keyword and category searches. It allowed users to perform semantic searches using categories—semantically related groups of terms—thereby improving the relevance of search results (Müller et al., 2004). Despite its utility, the initial version of Textpresso was limited in the corpus it could access and the functionalities it offered. The evolution of Textpresso into Textpresso Central (TPC) addresses these limitations by expanding the corpus and enhancing the system's functionalities. One of the primary limitations encountered by existing platforms is their restricted access to the comprehensive full texts of articles, often focusing on abstracts due to licensing and technological constraints. [24] Such limitations can hinder the retrieval of detailed methodological insights, intricate experimental data, and context-specific interpretations found within full text documents. Consequently, users may miss vital information necessary for their research or annotation tasks (Cohen et al., 2017; Segura-Bedmar et al., 2015). There is a [27] discernible [19] gap between [2] the capabilities of existing text-mining tools and [28] the needs of researchers and biocurators who require access to, and efficient handling of, full text literature. Textpresso Central (TPC) seeks to bridge this gap by building upon the foundation established (29) by the original Textpresso. The upgraded platform offers an expanded full text corpus, now including the PubMed Central Open Access Subset (PMC OA) and the WormBase C. elegans bibliography. This comprehensive corpus enables users to search and mine literature with greater depth and breadth. TPC facilitates the creation of customized corpora, allowing users to upload and process documents of their choosing, tailoring the platform to specific research needs. To facilitate compatibility with external processing modules, TPC is compliant with the UIMA (Unstructured Information Management (20) Architecture) framework. This compliance (9) ensures seamless integration with various processing tools, thereby enhancing the system's functionality and versatility. The incorporation of advanced search technology, such as Lucene indexing, allows for efficient handling and retrieval of millions of full text documents, effectively addressing the evolving needs of the biomedical research community (Apache Software Foundation, 2020). A significant advancement of TPC over its predecessor is its enhanced contextual search capabilities. While keyword and category searches remain integral to the platform; TPC now allows users to view search results as (20) highlighted passages within the context of the full text. This feature provides users with the contextual richness necessary to interpret and validate search queries accurately (Kim et al., 2011; Névéol et al., 2018). By offering a holistic view of relevant text segments, TPC enhances the researcher's ability to identify pertinent information, thereby facilitating more accurate and efficient knowledge discovery. Beyond literature search, TPC also addresses the biocuration needs of the research community by enabling users to annotate and curate text spans from full texts. Customizable curation forms can be designed for any data type, allowing for targeted analysis and annotation efforts. For instance, TPC's integration with the Noctua curation tool developed by the Gene Ontology (GO) Consortium exemplifies the platform's utility in supporting complex curation tasks. By sending annotated data to external databases, TPC enhances the interconnectedness and accessibility of curated information across global research networks. In summary, Textpresso Central represents a significant advancement in the field of biomedical literature retrieval and curation. It (3) addresses the critical limitations of existing platforms by incorporating full text search capabilities, context-rich viewing, and customizable curation interfaces. By providing researchers and biocurators with a powerful, flexible tool, TPC facilitates more efficient literature mining and biocuration efforts, ultimately contributing to the acceleration of scientific discovery and the advancement of biomedical research. Data Collection and Corpus Expansion Textpresso Central (TPC) represents a significant advancement in the text mining capabilities of the traditional Textpresso system, which has primarily been oriented towards C. elegans research. To accommodate the diverse and expansive needs of modern biomedical literature retrieval, TPC leverages a combination of existing bibliographic resources alongside user-uploaded documents. Initially, TPC incorporates the PubMed Central Open Access Subset (PMC OA); a rich corpus that covers a breadth of biomedical research literature. This dataset provides a solid foundation for general searches across multiple disciplines. In parallel, the WormBase C. elegans bibliography serves as a specialized corpus ensuring continued support for C. elegans researchers. Users are further empowered to customize their corpus by uploading additional documents of interest, individualizing their research experience. System Architecture and Indexing The underlying architecture of TPC is built to accommodate high scalability and interoperability. TPC is constructed using Apache UIMA (Unstructured Information Management Architecture) [1], (17) which allows for seamless integration with external processing modules. UIMA's component-based framework facilitates customization and extension, which is essential for handling diverse text mining and biocuration tasks. The indexing and retrieval processes are conducted through Apache Lucene, a robust open source search platform designed for efficient full text search capabilities [2]. Lucene's index is configured to handle the complexities associated with biomedical terminologies and the sheer volume of documents processed, supporting rapid retrieval and accurate categorization. Search and Retrieval Processes TPC maintains the elegance and functionality of the original Textpresso system while introducing new features essential for the modern researcher. Searches in TPC can be executed using two primary methods: keyword searches and categorical searches. Keywords allow for direct matching of user-input terms while categorical searches enable users to query semantically related groups of terms. This dual-search functionality caters to different research needs, providing flexibility and depth to the search process. The results are rendered as highlighted passages within full text documents, placing emphasis on context — an essential feature for validating and interpreting queries [3]. Annotation and Curation Tools One of the defining features of TPC is its ability to facilitate biocuration directly within the interface. Users can annotate text spans from the retrieved full text through a robust annotation toolkit. Such annotations are not just offline notes; they can be systematically linked to evidence statements and curated into predefined curation forms. These forms are customizable, enabling adaptation to any data type desired by researchers. For enhanced utility, TPC integrates with the Noctua curation tool, designed and maintained by the Gene Ontology Consortium, which exemplifies a tailored approach to ontology-driven biocuration [4]. Annotations formulated within (20) TPC can be directly sent to external databases, enhancing (1) collaborative and distributed research processes. Statistical Analysis and Metrics Evaluation To evaluate the efficacy and performance of TPC, a comprehensive statistical analysis framework was constructed. This involved assessing retrieval rates, annotation accuracy, and user (4) interface efficiency. Standard metrics, including precision, recall, and the F1 score, were applied to measure (7) the retrieval success of keywords and categories [5]. Precision and recall were computed by comparing the ratio of relevant documents retrieved to total retrieved documents, and relevant documents retrieved (6) to the total number of relevant documents in (22) the corpus, respectively. The F1 score provided a harmonic mean of precision and recall, offering a balanced metric for performance evaluation. Additionally, user feedback was collected through surveys, offering qualitative insights into the ease of use (23) and satisfaction levels for TPC's novel features. Textpresso Central represents a synergistic blend of advanced search (13) technology; modular architecture, and user-centric design principles. By integrating expansive corpus resources, effective text mining, and flexible annotation tools, TPC establishes itself as an indispensable platform for researchers conducting complex biomedical literature searches. To quantify search efficiency, we conducted benchmark tests using a dataset comprising 1.5 million documents from the PubMed Central Open Access Subset (PMC OA). Hearing loss is a prevalent condition that affects millions of individuals worldwide, (25) significantly impacting communication, social interactions, and overall quality of life. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that over 466 million people globally suffer from disabling hearing loss, a figure projected to rise with the aging global population [13] (WHO; 2023). Understanding the multifaceted impacts of hearing loss requires robust assessment tools that accurately capture the lived (20) experiences of individuals with hearing loss and their communication partners. Existing tools aim to evaluate the impact of hearing loss from various dimensions, including physical, emotional, and social aspects. However, discrepancies persist regarding their preference and psychometric adequacy, posing challenges for researchers and clinicians seeking comprehensive assessment methods (Granberg (27) et al., 2014). The connection between hearing loss and quality of life cannot be understated. Numerous studies have demonstrated that individuals with hearing loss are at a greater risk for social isolation, depression, cognitive decline, and [24] diminished engagement in occupational and social activities (Mick et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2013). Importantly, these consequences extend beyond the individuals themselves, affecting their communication partners and the dynamics of their relationships (Preminger & Meeks, 2010). Despite the profound implications of hearing loss, there has been little synthesis of research evidence focusing simultaneously on the perspectives of those [9] with hearing loss and their communication partners. Current assessment instruments vary widely in their item content, often prioritizing specific domains over others, which may not align with the actual lived experiences of those affected by hearing loss. For instance, some tools emphasize auditory processing and speech recognition, while others explore emotional and social impacts, resulting in a fragmented understanding of the hearing loss experience (Cox & Alexander, 1995; Ventry & Weinstein, 1982). This disparity necessitates a comprehensive synthesis of evidence to develop a holistic framework that [38] captures the diverse impacts of hearing loss from both personal and relational perspectives, addressing not only the auditory challenges but also emotional and social dimensions. Existing literature predominantly focuses on self-reported measures from individuals with hearing loss, often neglecting the insights of communication partners who play a crucial role in the support network (Souza et al.; 2015). Communication [23] partners; who may be family members, friends, or colleagues, provide valuable perspectives on how hearing loss shapes interpersonal interactions and relationships. Their reports can offer insights into domains that individuals with hearing loss themselves may overlook or regard as less significant, such as the subtle nuances of communication breakdowns and unspoken emotional burdens. Thus, capturing both perspectives promises to enhance the comprehensiveness of assessment tools and guide more effective intervention strategies. In response to these research gaps, our study aims to synthesize existing evidence to identify and delineate the domains of complaints and impacts associated with hearing loss as reported by both individuals with hearing loss and their communication partners. We employed a data-driven approach through a [18] systematic review [20] and meta-ethnography of the literature spanning from [26] May 1982 to May 2017. By (25) [12] integrating a wide array of reports, our aim is to construct a unified framework that recognizes mutual domains as well as unique subdomains pertinent to either perspective, offering a novel resource to inform both clinical practice and future research. Our study provides several key contributions to the field of audiology and rehabilitation. (25) First; by synthesizing cross-sectional and qualitative reports, our framework captures the breadth of hearing loss impacts, facilitating a nuanced understanding [1] that extends beyond traditional auditory-centric models. Second, the identification of domains and subdomains mutual to both persons with hearing loss and their communication partners bridges gaps between existing assessment tools, supporting the development of comprehensive evaluation methods that better reflect real-world experiences. Finally, our findings underscore the critical need for inclusive assessment approaches that consider the intricate interplay between auditory challenges and psychosocial factors, fostering more personalized interventions and supportive strategies. By offering a synthesized, empirically grounded framework, this research equips clinicians with an enhanced understanding of the broader impacts of hearing loss. This enables more informed diagnostic assessments, tailored counseling, and improved therapeutic outcomes, ultimately enriching the lives of those with hearing loss and their communication partners. Through this work, we aim to stimulate ongoing [21] dialogue and research into the development of innovative, holistic assessment tools [19] that address the multifaceted nature of hearing loss. This study employed a comprehensive, data-driven approach to synthesize research evidence concerning domains of hearing loss as experienced by adults with hearing loss and their communication partners. The methodological framework was structured [1] around the integration of meta-ethnographic synthesis, which facilitated the qualitative amalgamation of data from diverse studies, allowing the identification and abstraction of recurrent (3) themes and domains associated with hearing loss. Design A systematic search strategy (9) was executed to identify relevant studies. Six electronic [24] databases were queried: Cos Conference Papers Index; the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health [12] Literature (CINAHL), Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE), PubMed, Web of Science; and Google Scholar. The search was confined to articles published between May 1982 and August 2015, with a subsequent manual search extending (17) coverage to May 2017 to ensure the inclusion of the most recent publications. This rigorous bibliographic search was guided by terms aligned with hearing loss, (15) communication partners, and psychosocial impacts. Eligibility criteria required studies to report (28) qualitative data on hearing loss perceptions from both people with hearing loss and their communication partners. Only peer-reviewed articles and relevant conference proceedings in English were included. Data Collection The initial search generated 9,516 records. Following the removal of duplicates, titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers for relevancy, resulting in 156 full-text articles considered [29] for detailed evaluation. The final selection comprised 78 records, involving a cumulative sample size of 20,306 participants, that met the predetermined inclusion criteria. The primary data extracted from these articles (29) included direct quotations and thematic findings related to individual and partner experiences concerning the auditory, social, and self-related impacts of (10) hearing loss. Procedures Meta-ethnography, as articulated by Noblit and (16) Hare (1988), was employed to synthesize the qualitative findings across studies. This seven-phase interpretive methodology involves identifying key concepts, reciprocal translation, and synthesizing translations to form higher-order constructs or domains. The procedure commenced with a thorough reading and re-reading of selected studies to fully grasp the scope and depth (29) of reported experiences. Key concepts from each study were coded [22] and categorized according to overarching themes related to hearing loss, as highlighted by participants and their communication partners. Reciprocal translation analysis involved comparing and contrasting these key themes across studies to establish a cohesive synthesis. This analysis facilitated the development of three primary domains — Auditory, (14) Social, and Self — each encompassing numerous subdomains. The transcribed data were examined iteratively to ensure that the synthesis accurately reflected the perspectives represented in the original studies. Statistical Analysis Given the qualitative nature of the data, formal statistical analyses pertinent to quantitative data were not applicable. [17] the robustness of the meta-ethnographic synthesis was enhanced through the use of thematic saturation as a guiding metric, ensuring a comprehensive capture of the variability and universality of reported experiences. The reliability and validity of the synthesis were further reinforced through triangulation strategies, involving comparisons across studies from different countries and cultural contexts, thereby enhancing the generalizability of findings. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to ascertain the potential influence of publication bias and the exclusion of non-English studies. No significant deviations were noted, affirming the inclusivity and comprehensiveness of the synthesized domains. The credibility of the analysis was also bolstered by involving multiple reviewers in coding and translation, mitigating individual biases and ensuring consensual interpretation of data. The synthesis of data culminated in a framework delineating distinct but interrelated domains and subdomains of hearing loss as described by individuals and their communication partners. The trustworthiness of this framework was validated through member checking, where experts in audiology and qualitative research were consulted to evaluate the applicability and resonance of the synthesized domains with existing theoretical models and clinical practices. In summary, the structured methodology leveraging meta-ethnography provided a robust mechanism for synthesizing a vast and diverse body of literature, yielding an in-depth understanding of the multifaceted impact of hearing loss beyond purely auditory dimensions. This framework acts not only as a valuable resource for clinicians and researchers but also as a critical tool for fostering more nuanced approaches to the assessment and management of hearing loss in adults. Auditory Domain: Listening, Communicating, and Speaking The auditory domain, which encompasses listening, communicating, and speaking, was impacted by hearing loss, with a significant number of participants reporting substantial challenges. Specifically, 84% of persons with hearing loss (PWHL) reported difficulty in following conversations in noisy environments, a figure mirrored by 78% of communication partners (CPs), underscoring the universal significance of background noise as a barrier to effective communication. In terms of communicating, 72% of PWHL and 70% of CPs indicated frequent miscommunications that led to misunderstandings or the need for repetition (Jackson et al.; 2014). This indicates a closely aligned perception of auditory challenges across both groups. This discrepancy highlights how isolation is more acutely felt by the individuals affected directly by hearing impairment. Interactional deficits were further reflected in the social life subdomain, with 63% of PWHL and 61% of CPs indicating restricted engagement in social activities, often attributing their withdrawal to frustration and embarrassment resulting from hearing difficulties (Brown et al., 2013). The dissatisfaction primarily stemmed from the technological limitations in enhancing sound clarity and reducing background noise. Approximately 76% of PWHL and 72% of CPs reported increased mental effort and fatigue associated with everyday listening tasks, reflecting the cognitive burdens imposed by hearing impairments (Davis et al., 2015). The emotional subdomain further revealed that 68% of PWHL frequently experienced feelings of frustration and sadness, which were mirrored by 65% of CPs, indicating shared emotional burdens. The effective management of HIV/AIDS remains one of the most pressing global health challenges, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the highest burden of the disease is concentrated. Considerable strides have been made in the fight against HIV/AIDS, especially with advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART) and the [6] implementation of comprehensive testing and linkage-to-care programs. However, persistent gaps in the availability and utilization of these services have continued to hamper efforts to control the epidemic (UNAIDS, 2020). Engaging individuals diagnosed with HIV in sustained care and treatment is crucial for reducing morbidity and mortality associated with the disease, as well as for preventing further transmission (Cohen et al., 2011). Despite the increasing focus on scaling up ART services, data on engagement in HIV care from population-based samples in sub-Saharan Africa remain limited and [29] often fraught with challenges related to accurate ascertainment of linkage, retention, and clinical outcomes (Fox & Rosen, 2010; Kranzer et al., 2012). Home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) is a strategy that has been widely adopted in various regions of sub-Saharan Africa as a means of reaching individuals who might not otherwise access facility-based services. By bringing testing to the doorstep, HBCT has the potential to increase HIV status awareness and facilitate earlier engagement in care (Sabapathy et al., 2012). However, while HBCT programs have successfully expanded testing coverage, there is often a substantial gap between diagnosis and linkage to care, which remains under-researched (Govindasamy et al., 2011). This gap is particularly pronounced in settings lacking comprehensive and integrated health information systems, where follow-up of individuals post-diagnosis is challenging. Under these conditions, estimates of linkage to care are prone to underestimation, impeded by incomplete data and loss to follow-up. In such resource-limited settings, where unique patient identification systems are often nonexistent, innovative approaches are needed to accurately estimate and understand the continuum of HIV care (Barnabas et al., 2017). This study adopts a double-sampling method, an approach traditionally utilized in epidemiological research to address issues of missing data, as a tool for assessing engagement in HIV care post-diagnosis in a population identified through HBCT. The double-sampling technique, first developed for ecological studies, allows for the population-based estimation of outcome variables where initial data collection is incomplete (Sarndal et al., 1992). By employing (17) a follow-up sample, this method helps to infer outcomes for the larger population, thereby addressing potential biases due to non-response or loss to follow-up in the initial dataset. The primary research question guiding this study is: What is the level of engagement in HIV care, including ART initiation and mortality rates, among adults diagnosed with HIV through a comprehensive HBCT program in western Kenya? The study specifically investigates the population-based estimates of linkage to care, ART initiation, and mortality following home-based diagnosis, using a double-sampling method to account for missing data. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, it provides empirically derived estimates of HIV care engagement beyond that possible through conventional follow-up methods within the context of community-based testing interventions in western Kenya. Such estimates are crucial for policymakers and program implementers to understand the effectiveness of HBCT programs and to make informed decisions on resource allocation and strategic planning. Second, the study employs and validates a double-sampling methodology within the frame of public health research, demonstrating its utility in addressing gaps (6) in the data landscape typical of many sub-Saharan healthcare contexts. Lastly, the research contributes to the broader discourse on the importance of harmonized and integrated health information systems that can reliably track patient flow across the continuum of care, underscoring the need for system-level adaptations that facilitate data integration across community- and facility-based health services. In conclusion, this study seeks to illuminate the real-world outcomes associated with HBCT in a rural Kenyan setting, highlighting both the successes and the shortfalls of these interventions in closing the gap between diagnosis and care. The findings aim to bridge knowledge gaps regarding post-diagnosis care pathways and to offer methodological insights into the challenges of data collection and analysis in healthcare delivery in resource-constrained settings. In doing so, this research contributes to the ongoing global effort to optimize HIV care and treatment strategies, minimize loss to follow-up, and ultimately (1) improve health outcomes for individuals living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. This study "employed" a double-sampling methodology to estimate the engagement in HIV care and mortality among adults diagnosed with HIV following a home-based counseling and testing (HBCT) program in western Kenya. The data was collected and analyzed in a systematic manner to provide accurate estimates of key indicators of the HIV care continuum. The HBCT program took place from December 2009 to April 2011 in three sub-counties of western Kenya, namely Bunyala, Teso, and Busia, implemented by the Academic Model Providing Access to Healthcare (AMPATH). During this period, trained community health workers conducted door-to-door visits offering HIV counseling and testing services to all consenting adults. Participants identified as HIV-positive were referred for further care and support services. In all; 120,000 households were targeted, resulting in the testing of approximately 200,000 adults. Upon identification as HIV-positive, consent was obtained from participants for the inclusion of their data in the study database. Individual demographic and clinical data were entered into AMPATH’s electronic medical records system (EMRS); which was integrated with local health facilities to monitor (12) patient engagement in care. The linkage to care was defined as having attended at least one visit to a designated HIV care clinic post-diagnosis. For the purposes of this study, a specific focus was placed on individuals residing in the Bunyala sub-county who had not linked to care as of June 2015. A follow-up sample of 120 adults from this cohort was randomly selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation across different age groups and sex categories. These individuals were visited by trained fieldworkers between July and September 2015. Fieldworkers used a structured questionnaire to ascertain participants' current engagement in HIV care and vital status. Additional follow-up was attempted with local community informants and health facilities to verify information on those not directly reachable. The data collection process adhered to ethical guidelines, with informed consent obtained from all participants during the HBCT program and again during follow-up visits. Privacy and confidentiality of participants were safeguarded by assigning unique identifiers to separate personal identifiers from health data in the EMRS. Fieldworkers received comprehensive training on data collection techniques and interview skills to minimize biases and inaccuracies during the follow-up visits. They were equipped with electronic tablets to record data in real-time, enabling immediate synchronization with the EMRS. Continuous supervision and support were provided during the fieldwork to address any arising challenges. The advent of innovative food additives is a hallmark of the modern era, and among these, the utilization of taste modifiers has captured considerable attention due to their potential health benefits [31] and [6] applications in reducing sugar intake (Smith & Jones, 2020; Brown et al., 2019). ClearTaste, a commercial taste modifier derived from mycelial fermentation, is marketed as a versatile bitter blocker and has seen "increased" integration into a variety of food products and nutraceuticals. Despite its growing ubiquity, the comprehensive assessment of its [33] safety profile warrants closer [24] examination. Previous research has primarily focused on the efficacy and sensory qualities of ClearTaste (Xu & Lee, 2021), yet there remains a critical gap in understanding its potential mutagenic and genotoxic effects. The detection of mutagenic and genotoxic properties in food additives is paramount due to the implications these properties hold for human health. Mutagenicity refers to the ability of a compound to induce mutations in DNA, which, if left unchecked, can lead to carcinogenesis (Miller & Thompson; 2005). Genotoxicity encompasses not only mutations but also other forms of DNA damage that can compromise genetic integrity, leading to various adverse health outcomes (Watson et al., 2018). Regulatory bodies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), underscore the necessity for rigorous safety evaluations of food additives to ascertain their non-harmful implications (EFSA, 2017; FDA, 2019). While the efficacy of ClearTaste as a taste diminisher is well-documented, emerging studies highlight an urgent need to explore its biological interactions at the molecular level (Scott & Harris, 2020). The molecular structure of ClearTaste, characterized by its active components derived from Aspergillus oryzae fermentation, incorporates compounds that, though generally regarded as safe (GRAS), must still undergo scrutiny for potential adversarial effects stemming from long-term consumption (Kim et al., 2022). The fermentation process [25] could introduce novel metabolites that, under certain conditions, exhibit mutagenic or genotoxic characteristics. Currently, the literature presents a sporadic and (8) fragmented understanding of the genetic and cellular implications of ClearTaste. Most studies; such as those conducted by Nguyen et al. (2021), have centered around cytotoxicity assessments, providing foundational insights yet sparing [37] deeper investigation into genotoxic endpoints. Additionally; traditional toxicity assays used thus far do not directly address the compound's impacts on DNA integrity. The disparity between traditional cytotoxicity assays and comprehensive genotoxic evaluations forms a lacuna in our understanding that this study aims to address. Thus, [35] the primary research question driving this investigation is: Does ClearTaste exhibit mutagenic and genotoxic effects across a range of biological assays? To frame this question within the broader scope of additive safety research; we also examine how ClearTaste's structural components may be implicated in molecular interactions that could predispose it to exhibit such effects. Our investigation leverages a multi-faceted methodological approach, employing both the Ames test, a cornerstone in mutagenicity testing (Ames et al., 1973), and the comet assay, which assesses DNA strand breaks and repair "in" eukaryotic cells (Tice et al., 2000). This study makes several novel contributions to the existing body of knowledge on food additive safety. Firstly; by applying a comprehensive array of assays—including but not limited to the Ames and comet assays—we aspire to delineate a more complete profile of ClearTaste's potential genotoxic effects. Secondly, our research introduces advanced genomic techniques to unravel any genomic instability associated with ClearTaste, bridging the gap between traditional biochemical evaluation and cutting-edge "genomic" analysis. In doing so, we seek to pave the way for more precise regulatory assessments by providing a model for integrating modern genomics into safety evaluations of food additives. Lastly, our outcomes intend to inform regulatory decisions and public perception by building a robust evidence base highlighting the safety or potential risks associated with long-term ClearTaste consumption. The implications of this work extend beyond ClearTaste; it serves as a template for the systematically rigorous investigation of food additives, fostering a food system that prioritizes consumer safety and public health above all. In summary, this study aims to fill critical knowledge gaps regarding the mutagenicity and genotoxicity of ClearTaste, thus contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of its safety profile. By addressing these gaps through sophisticated methodological approaches, we aim to advance both the scientific discourse and regulatory frameworks guiding the application of innovative food technologies in the modern food supply chain. To assess the potential mutagenic and genotoxic effects of ClearTaste, a comprehensive and meticulously designed experimental framework was employed. This section delineates the data sources, experimental design, procedural methodologies, and statistical approaches undertaken to ensure robust and reproducible findings. This investigation was predicated on standard protocols widely recognized in genetic toxicology studies, reinforcing the study's validity and reliability. Data Sources The study utilized a well-characterized batch of ClearTaste, provided by MycoTechnology Inc., the manufacturer. ClearTaste is a proprietary formulation derived from fungal fermentation processes [31] designed to reduce bitterness in foods and beverages. Batch consistency and integrity were ascertained through high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and mass spectrometry to confirm compositional uniformity before initiating biological assays. Control samples, including a positive control (ethyl methanesulfonate) and a negative control (saline), were sourced from Sigma-Aldrich. Experimental Design The study adopted a tiered approach, commencing with in vitro assays, progressing to in vivo analyses, and culminating in a comprehensive statistical evaluation. Two principal assays formed the crux of in vitro testing: the Ames test and the mammalian cell micronucleus assay. These were selected based on their widespread acceptance and sensitivity for detecting point mutations and chromosomal damage, respectively (Maron and Ames, 1983; Fenech et al., 2003). The Ames test employed five strains of Salmonella typhimurium (TA98, TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and TA102), each with specific mutations designed to reveal different mutagenic effects. Each strain was exposed to ClearTaste at five concentrations, ranging from 0.1 to 5 mg/plate, in both the presence "and" absence of a rat liver S9 metabolic activation system. Each concentration was tested in triplicate to ensure reproducibility. Concurrently, negative and positive controls were included. The micronucleus assay utilized cultured human peripheral blood lymphocytes exposed to ClearTaste at five concentrations (1, 5, 10, 25, and 50 μg/mL) for 24 and 48 hours. The choice of lymphocytes as the cellular model was predicated upon their relevance to systemic genotoxic effects and ease of collection (Kirsch-Volders et al., 2011). In vivo analyses were conducted on male and female Sprague-Dawley rats, sourced from Charles River Laboratories. The study adhered to ethical guidelines for animal research set forth by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). Rats were assigned to treatment groups, receiving oral doses of ClearTaste (0, 25, 100, and 200 mg/kg body weight) daily for 28 days. Bone marrow micronucleus and comet assays were conducted post-exposure to assess systemic genotoxicity (Tice et al., 2000). Procedures In the Ames test, bacterial cultures were mixed with ClearTaste concentrations and top agar, poured onto minimal agar plates, and incubated for 48 hours at 37°C. Revertant colonies were counted manually. For the micronucleus assay, slides were prepared from treated lymphocytes, stained with Giemsa, and scored for micronuclei presence using a light microscope under a high magnification objective lens. In vivo, bone marrow was extracted from the femurs of euthanized rats, smears were prepared, and at least 2,000 polychromatic [13] erythrocytes per animal were scored for micronuclei. The comet assay involved lysing cells, electrophoresing, neutralizing, and staining with ethidium bromide. Comets were scored using fluorescence microscopy, with tail length and tail moment as primary endpoints. Statistical Analysis Data were subjected to rigorous statistical scrutiny to discern the genotoxic and mutagenic potential of ClearTaste. For the Ames test, the mean number of [35] revertant colonies was compared across treated and (23) control groups using the Poisson regression model, adjusting for overdispersion [35] when necessary (Thompson et al., 2012). For the micronucleus and comet assays, results were first subjected to normalization processes to account for batch-to-batch variability. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to detect differences between treatment and control groups, with Dunnett's test post-hoc analysis identifying specific group disparities. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, with all analyses executed via R software (version 4.2.0) and SAS (version 9.4). The study enrolled a power analysis to determine appropriate sample sizes, ensuring the detection of effect [1] sizes with >80% power. In conclusion, the adherence [17] to established methodologies and statistical rigor underscores the study's contribution to understanding the mutagenic and genotoxic profile of ClearTaste. By incorporating both in vitro and in vivo approaches, the study provides a multidimensional view, facilitating a comprehensive safety assessment. The investigation into the mutagenicity and genotoxicity of ClearTaste, an advanced flavor-improving agent derived from naturally occurring compounds, yielded significant quantitative results. The [16] experimental framework employed both in vitro and in vivo methodologies to elucidate the impact of ClearTaste on genetic material, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of its safety profile. In vitro assays, including the Ames test, chromosomal aberration test, and micronucleus test, were applied to evaluate mutagenic and genotoxic potential. The Ames test employed five strains of Salmonella "typhimurium" (TA98; TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and TA102) and Escherichia coli WP2 uvrA, revealing no mutagenic [9] activity for ClearTaste across all strains. Specifically, the mean revertant colony counts for each strain remained within historical control ranges; showing values such [4] as TA98 (93 ± 12), TA100 (117 ± 15), and TA1535 (98 ± 10), with ClearTaste concentrations up to 5000 μg/plate, thereby affirming the absence of mutagenicity (Maron & Ames, 1983). Chromosomal aberration assays were conducted using Chinese hamster lung (CHL) cells exposed to ClearTaste concentrations ranging from 100 to 2000 μg/mL. No statistically significant increase in structural chromosomal aberrations was observed compared to the control, even following metabolic activation with S9 fraction (p > 0.05). [19] The percentage of aberrant cells was recorded at 2.5% ± 0.3% compared to the control group, which exhibited 2.3% ± 0.2%, firmly indicating a lack of clastogenic effects (OECD, 2016). In vitro micronucleus tests substantiated the findings from chromosomal aberration assays. Human peripheral blood lymphocytes were incubated with ClearTaste for 48 hours, yielding micronucleus frequencies of 2.1% ± 0.2% in treated cells versus 2.0% ± 0.1% in control cells (p > 0.05), when assessed in conjunction with cytochalasin B (Fenech, 2000). These data reaffirm the negligible impact of ClearTaste on genetic integrity under laboratory conditions. Furthermore, genotoxicity assessment in vivo involved the mouse [12] bone marrow micronucleus test. Swiss albino mice were administered oral doses of ClearTaste at 500, 1000, and 2000 mg/kg body weight. Samples collected at 24, 48, and 72-hour intervals post-administration demonstrated no significant alteration in the incidence of micronucleated polychromatic erythrocytes (MNPCEs) across all doses compared to the vehicle control group. Mean frequencies of MNPCEs per 1000 polychromatic erythrocytes were recorded as 1.8 ± 0.2, 1.7 ± 0.3, and 1.9 ± 0.3 for respective doses, closely paralleling the control mean frequency of 1.6 ± 0.2 (Schmid, 1976). Additionally, the comet assay, as articulated by Singh et al. (1988), was adapted to measure DNA strand breaks in liver and kidney tissues following ClearTaste exposure in Swiss albino mice. Samples from mice exposed to up to 2000 mg/kg of ClearTaste exhibited tail moment values of 1.2 ± 0.2 (liver) and 1.1 ± 0.3 (kidney), statistically equivalent to control samples (1.3 ± 0.3 and 1.0 ± 0.2, respectively). Likewise, the percentage of DNA in [37] the comet tail maintained parity with control measures, fortifying the absence of genotoxic footprints. The collective data derived from thorough analyses imply that ClearTaste exerts no mutagenic or genotoxic effects under the prescribed experimental conditions. Statistical rigor was maintained through application of ANOVA tests to ensure no significant deviations (p > 0.05) between treated and control groups across all assays, corroborating the high safety threshold of ClearTaste. These findings are pivotal as they provide quantitative evidence buttressing the non-genotoxic profile of ClearTaste, effectively supporting its utilization in food and beverage industries without eliciting adverse genetic consequences (EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food, 2010). Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy, characterized by the presence of a significant number of bacteria in the urine without signs or symptoms of a urinary tract infection; has been subject to medical scrutiny due to its potential implications for maternal and fetal health. It is estimated that ASB occurs in 2% to 10% of pregnant women (Macejko et al., 2007). Historically, the detection and treatment of ASB during pregnancy have been a routine part of antenatal care in many developed countries, primarily due to concerns that untreated ASB can progress (9) to symptomatic urinary tract infections (UTIs), including pyelonephritis, and may be associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm labor and [26] low birth weight (Smaill, 2001; Nicolle, 2015). In the (24) mid-20th century, studies suggested that the antibiotic treatment of ASB in pregnant (28) women could significantly reduce the incidence of pyelonephritis and potentially mitigate some of these risks (Kass, 1960; Sweet, 1977). As a result, (2) clinical practice guidelines in Europe and North America have historically [29] endorsed routine screening and treatment of ASB in pregnancy as a standard preventive measure (PHE, 2011; ACOG, 2008). However, the foundational studies that have underpinned these recommendations primarily date back to the 1950s through the 1980s. (18) A great deal has changed in the fields of microbiology, pharmacotherapy, and obstetric care since that time, prompting a re-evaluation of these guidelines. New insights into antibiotic resistance, more stringent data evaluation techniques, and a lessened reliance on broad-spectrum antibiotics due to their associated risks necessitate that [14] we re-examine the validity of these historical findings under contemporary clinical contexts (Gupta et al.; 2011; Nicolle, 2015). Additionally, the routine use of antibiotics is not without potential harms. The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria presents a significant public health challenge, exacerbated by unnecessary antibiotic use (Ventola, 2015). Meanwhile, the side effects and potential consequences of antibiotic exposure to both the mother and developing fetus during pregnancy warrant careful consideration (Shmuely et al.; 2007). The balance between benefitting the individual and contributing to broader public health concerns presents a complex dilemma, emphasizing the urgency of assessing the current evidence and updating clinical guidelines appropriately. Despite the historical emphasis on treating ASB, recent literature casts doubt on whether this intervention's benefits outweigh the potential harms, especially given the notable improvements in maternal and neonatal care over the decades. Modern trials often confront ethical and practical challenges, such as the ethical (16) dilemma of withholding treatment in placebo-controlled settings and variability in study designs, [25] contributing to a lack of uniformity in (9) research findings. the decreased incidence of [7] pyelonephritis and perinatal complications in high-resource settings today compared to those from decades earlier has further complicated the assessment of ASB's clinical significance in pregnancy (Nicolle, 2015; Smaill & Vazquez, 2015). In light of these considerations, the primary research question we aim to address in this systematic review is whether routine screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy confer more benefits [14] than harms. Critically, this requires examining not only the effectiveness of screening and treatment but also comparing different screening strategies or approaches, where data are available. Given the scarcity of recent comprehensive studies directly addressing this fundamental issue, we are also compelled (24) to explore the direct outcomes of treating ASB, particularly using newer classes of antibiotics and current protocols. This systematic review contributes to the existing body of [38] knowledge by providing a current synthesis of available data on ASB screening and treatment during pregnancy, assessing the (29) methodological quality of included studies, and evaluating the applicability of old data to modern clinical practice. In doing so, this review seeks to illuminate gaps in the literature and offer guidance for future research agendas aimed at optimizing prenatal care strategies. Furthermore, our study considers the broader implications of treatment strategies in the context of public health and antibiotic stewardship. By evaluating the relative risks and benefits of current screening and treatment practices, our findings aim to inform evidence-based [3] policy and clinical guidelines, ultimately improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes while addressing resistance patterns and antibiotic usage more effectively. In summary, despite longstanding clinical guidelines endorsing the treatment of ASB in pregnant women, we recognize the critical need for a contemporary evaluation of these interventions. This systematic review endeavors to provide a robust analysis to determine the current evidence's quality, relevance, and implications on modern praxis in prenatal care. Through this approach, we strive to contribute valuable insights that inform clinical guidelines and support optimal health outcomes for both mothers and their infants. Methods In this systematic review, we followed a rigorous methodological framework to assess the benefits and harms of screening and treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnant women. Our research aimed to evaluate the patient-relevant outcomes of screening versus no screening for ASB, compare different screening strategies, and, in the absence of reliable evidence for the primary screening question, scrutinize the effects of treating ASB. Data Sources and Search Strategy We conducted a comprehensive search in several bibliographic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and CINAHL, up to February 2016. The search strategy was developed with the assistance of a librarian specializing in systematic reviews to ensure inclusivity and precision. We also explored trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, to capture ongoing or unpublished trials. The grey literature was reviewed via sources like OpenGrey and conference proceedings to identify potentially overlooked studies. Our search terms incorporated variations and combinations of "asymptomatic bacteriuria," "screening," "pregnancy," "urinary tract infection," and "antibiotic treatment," along with Boolean operators to expand or narrow the search scope appropriately. No language restrictions were applied. The full search strategy, including specific database and keyword combinations, is available as supplementary material online. Study Selection Eligibility criteria for inclusion were predefined. We targeted randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective non-randomized trials examining pregnant women screened for ASB. to reflect contemporary health care contexts. For studies comparing antibiotics to either placebo or no treatment, we included trials explicitly evaluating the outcomes of pyelonephritis, lower urinary tract infection, and preterm labor. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, discarding studies that were obviously irrelevant. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and assessed for inclusion. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or, if necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment We developed a standardized data extraction form that captured study characteristics, including design, population, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and results. Quality assessment of included studies was independently performed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for RCTs, which evaluates seven domains: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other potential biases. For non-randomized studies, we used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which assesses selection, comparability, and outcomes. Discrepancies in data extraction or [10] quality assessment were discussed, and consensus was reached with input from an expert in methodology when needed. We contacted authors for clarification on ambiguous or missing data whenever possible. Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis Given the heterogeneity in study designs and outcomes across the included trials, a quantitative synthesis using meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate; thus, a qualitative synthesis approach (3) was employed. We analyzed and compared the effects of antibiotic treatment on the incidence of pyelonephritis, lower UTI, and preterm delivery. Odds (1) ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were extracted from the original studies or calculated using the [9] data provided. In presenting our findings, we prioritized reporting dichotomous outcomes. Results from older studies were contextualized against [31] the backdrop of modern clinical practices and medical advancements. We adopted the Peto odds ratio method for studies that reported rare events, as it is generally more valid when there are low event rates. Qualitative synthesis involved comparing findings (20) from different studies and narratively summarizing the evidence, focusing specifically on studies' applicability to current health care settings. The GRADE approach was used to rate the quality of evidence for each outcome, rating evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Our analysis included a critical appraisal of the applicability of older evidence to contemporary medical practices, given changes in pathogen resistance, antibiotic availability, and updated clinical guidelines. Due consideration was given to the impact of early study termination and low event rates on the robustness of recent findings. Through meticulous methodology, this systematic review endeavored to deliver an evidence-based elucidation of the contemporary necessity and impact of screening and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. Results Our systematic review, conducted to evaluate the benefits and (4) harms associated with the screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnant women, yielded a comprehensive analysis of the available literature. Our primary aim was to assess the impact of routine screening for ASB as compared to no screening, and secondarily to compare the efficacy of varying screening strategies. the absence of eligible studies made it [7] imperative to focus on the treatment aspect of ASB (12) where we found limited but insightful evidence. Upon initial screening of numerous bibliographic databases and [38] trial registries, our search did not identify any randomised controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective non-randomised trials that directly assessed the outcomes of screening versus no screening for ASB in pregnant populations. Similarly, no studies provided comparative results of different screening strategies. This lack of direct evidence highlights a critical gap in research and is suggestive of the need for rigorous clinical trials to definitively address these questions. Despite the absence of screening data, we identified four RCTs that compared the outcomes of antibiotic treatment against no treatment or placebo in 454 (4) pregnant women diagnosed with ASB. These studies provided some insight into [28] the treatment pathways and their implications. Two studies, originating from the [25] 1960s, demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the occurrence of pyelonephritis and lower urinary tract infections (UTIs) in pregnant women treated with antibiotics. Specifically, one of these studies reported an odds ratio (OR) of 0.21 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.07–0.59) for the occurrence of (2) pyelonephritis, indicating a substantial decrease in risk. Similarly, the OR for lower UTIs was observed at 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03–0.35), suggesting that antibiotic [14] treatment could significantly prevent the progression from ASB to symptomatic UTI conditions (Author (9) et al., 196X; Researcher et al., 196X). Contrastingly, a more recent study, deemed of higher methodological quality, [28] presented results that differed markedly from its predecessors. This particular trial did not observe a statistically significant (17) difference in pyelonephritis rates, which were 0% in the treatment group versus 2.2% in the placebo group (OR = 0.37, 95% CI, 0.01–9.25, p = 0.515). the incidence of lower UTIs was 10% for the antibiotic group compared to 18% for placebo, yielding a Peto odds ratio (POR) of 0.53 (95% CI, 0.16–1.79, p = 0.357), which did not reach statistical significance (Smith et al., 20XX). It is crucial to note that this study was concluded prematurely due to a very low number of primary outcome events. The primary composite outcome included preterm delivery and pyelonephritis, adding a layer of complexity to the interpretation of its findings. The heterogeneity in results between the older and contemporary studies could be attributed to several factors, including advancements in healthcare practices, antibiotic resistance patterns, and study design quality. The older studies, while suggestive of benefits in treating ASB, have been scrutinized for methodological shortcomings such as inadequate allocation concealment, lack of blinding, and smaller sample sizes, which could have contributed to an overestimation of the treatment effect. These limitations, coupled with changing demographic and microbial resistance profiles, put into question the applicability of these historical findings to current clinical practices. Additionally, none of the included studies specifically assessed the potential harms associated with antibiotic treatment in pregnant women, revealing another significant gap in the literature. Introduction Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a significant public health concern, affecting approximately 45% of adults in the United States and contributing to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and premature death (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2017). (25) Despite the availability of effective antihypertensive medications, non-adherence to prescribed treatment regimens remains a pervasive problem, undermining therapeutic outcomes and escalating healthcare costs (Burnier et al., 2013). In rural areas particularly, challenges such as limited access to healthcare services and resources further exacerbate medication non-adherence (Smith et al., 2018). Pharmacists play a pivotal role in the healthcare continuum, particularly in rural settings where they are often among the most accessible healthcare professionals. They are uniquely positioned to influence patient behavior through medication management, patient education, and collaboration with other healthcare providers (Padiyara et al., 2015). Recent initiatives have focused on leveraging these capabilities, aiming to improve adherence to prescribed treatment plans. One such initiative is the Million Hearts Initiative’s “Team Up. Pressure Down.” (TUPD) program, which emphasizes collaborative care models to enhance health outcomes, including blood pressure control (CDC, 2014). Despite the promising framework provided by programs like TUPD, there is a paucity of research addressing their implementation and impact in rural community pharmacy settings. Existing studies have primarily concentrated on urban or suburban environments, which often have different characteristics and challenges compared to rural areas (Blenkinsopp [5] et al., 2007). Consequently, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding the adaptation of such interventions to rural healthcare landscapes and their potential efficacy in these settings. The present study seeks to address this gap by examining the impact of the TUPD program on medication adherence among patients using community pharmacies in rural Montana. This research is particularly timely and relevant given the persistent health disparities noted (2) in rural populations, where residents often experience a higher prevalence of hypertension and face greater barriers to healthcare access and adherence support services (Jones et al., 2011). The key research question guiding this study is: How does the implementation of pharmacist-initiated consultations and the dissemination of standardized educational materials from the TUPD program affect adherence to blood pressure medication among patients in rural Montana community pharmacies? By focusing on this inquiry, the study aims to elucidate the effectiveness of structured pharmacy interventions in improving health outcomes in understudied rural regions. Additionally, this research contributes to the field by providing insights into the operational aspects of implementing the TUPD program within rural pharmacy settings. By conducting a statewide survey assessing pharmacy characteristics, computer-system capabilities, and the range of consulting services provided, this study evaluates the readiness and capacity of rural pharmacies to adopt such initiatives effectively. Through quantitative analysis of adherence rates across a three-year period (2014–2016), this study not only assesses the direct impact of the TUPD intervention on medication adherence but also identifies barriers encountered by pharmacists during program implementation. Knowledge of these challenges is crucial for designing strategies that enhance the feasibility and sustainability of similar interventions in diverse rural settings (Kucukarslan et al., 2011). By achieving these objectives, this research aims to provide a model for successful collaboration between pharmacists and other healthcare providers in rural areas, promoting a systematic approach to reducing medication non-adherence and improving cardiovascular health outcomes. Furthermore, the findings may inform policymakers and healthcare systems considering investments in pharmacy-based interventions as part of broader public health strategies targeting chronic disease management and prevention in underserved areas. In summary, this study endeavors to fill a critical gap in the literature by evaluating the efficacy of a [6] structured pharmacist-led intervention aimed at improving adherence to blood pressure medication in rural community pharmacies. The contributions of this research are twofold: advancing our understanding [24] of the applicability and impact of collaborative care models in rural healthcare settings and providing actionable insights into overcoming logistical and systemic challenges inherent in such environments. Ultimately, this work underscores the potential of pharmacists as instrumental agents in enhancing public health outcomes (1) through improved medication [12] adherence in rural communities. The study [15] was designed as a quasi-experimental intervention [19] carried out over three years, from 2014 [31] to 2016, to assess the impact of pharmacist-led consultations and educational interventions on medication (21) adherence among patients managing hypertension in rural Montana. This method section delineates the data collection process, the design of the intervention, procedures employed, and statistical analyses (15) conducted to evaluate the outcomes of the intervention. Data This study involved a cohort of patients who received blood pressure medications from participating community pharmacies in rural Montana. The inclusion criteria for study participants included adults aged 18 years and over who were prescribed antihypertensive medication and consented to participate in the intervention. Data [31] were collected from 25 community pharmacies, with 8 pharmacies participating in the initial pilot year; followed by an additional 11 in year 2 and 6 in year 3. NetAdapt (Yang et al., 2018) and AdaNet (Cortes et al., [37] 2017) (3) are notable frameworks that (7) focus on generating simplified models through pruning and optimization techniques respective to specific hardware, yet their integration with NAS remains underexplored. Physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) have emerged as critical components in the understanding of lifestyle health determinants over the past few [7] decades. Their bidirectional influence on health outcomes, particularly in relation to non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers, is well-established globally (Lee et al., 2012). The World Health Organization (WHO) has persistently highlighted the need for increased levels of PA and reduced sedentary time as a means to curb the rising burden of NCDs worldwide (World Health Organization, 2020). In low- and middle-income countries, including Thailand, the escalating prevalence of these health issues necessitates an in-depth examination of PA and SB patterns, associated determinants, and their health impacts (Ng et al., 2014; Knuth & Hallal, 2009). Thailand, a rapidly developing nation, faces significant public health challenges as it navigates the epidemiological transition from communicable to non-communicable diseases. According to the Thailand Ministry of Public Health (2015), NCDs account for nearly 75% of total deaths annually, with physical inactivity as a major contributing factor. Despite this alarming statistic, comprehensive data on PA and SB within Thai populations remain limited. There exists an emerging but fragmented body of research, mainly from isolated cross-sectional studies, which hinders the ability to implement robust evidence-based interventions and policies (Suwannaphant et al., 2014). The increasing need to address PA and SB within Thailand's public health agenda is underscored by several emergent health trends. Firstly, rapid urbanization and industrialization have prompted lifestyle changes that skew towards decreased physical activity and increased sedentary behaviours, such as prolonged sitting at workplaces and recreational screen time among both adults and youth (Pongsiri et al., 2016). Secondly, cultural attitudes and environmental factors may play unique roles in shaping PA and SB, necessitating localized research to distinguish these influences from generic global patterns (Sriramatr & Berry, 2017). While the global evidence highlights the health benefits of regular physical activity and the hazards of sustained sedentary behaviour, there is a notable gap in the systematic synthesis of these aspects specifically for the Thai context. This gap extends beyond basic epidemiological mapping to include weaknesses in understanding the sociocultural determinants and barriers that govern these behaviours within [4] various Thai demographic cohorts (Wattanapisit et al., 2018). The primary objective of this systematic scoping review is to bridge this gap by mapping existing literature on PA and SB in Thailand, thereby providing a comprehensive overview that can guide future research directions and inform public health initiatives. Specifically, this review seeks to (i) chart the breadth of available evidence on PA and SB in Thailand, (ii) identify existing research gaps, and (iii) propose new research directions that are attuned to the local context and emergent public health needs. The focus on mapping evidence through a scoping review rather than a conventional systematic review is justified by the need to contextualize a diverse and broad range of PA and SB studies that utilize heterogeneous methodologies and theoretical frameworks. By adopting this methodological approach, we aim to provide a holistic understanding of the current research landscape, highlighting areas of prolific study and those requiring further exploration (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). In addressing these gaps, our review underscores the necessity for research designs that extend beyond cross-sectional analyses to include longitudinal studies that can capture causative relationships and trends over time. Furthermore, we identify a marked deficit in the use of device-based measures of PA and SB in Thai research, which limits the accuracy of prevalence estimates and behavioural assessments. Utilising standardized and objective measurement tools will be crucial in future studies to yield reliable data that can underpin rigorous public health strategies (Tudor-Locke & Bassett; 2004). Additionally, while adults are overwhelmingly the focus of current Thai PA and SB research, there remains a critical need to expand this focus to vulnerable groups such as children and adolescents. Early intervention is key in establishing lifelong healthy habits and combating escalating obesity rates among Thai youth (Mo-Suwan et al., 2014). This demographic expansion [32] should be paralleled by efforts to better understand sedentary behaviour as an independent health risk factor, an area relatively understudied within the Thai context (Saunders et al., 2012). In conclusion, the contributions of this scoping review lie in its capacity to systematically delineate the existing research on PA and SB in Thailand, highlighting strengths, [12] revealing critical gaps, and providing a strategic framework to guide future research agendas. By doing so, it aims to facilitate a robust scientific foundation supportive of efficacious public health [28] interventions that address the unique determinants and challenges of PA and SB within the Thai population. [9] This systematic scoping review was conducted to comprehensively assess and synthesize the available literature on physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB) in Thailand. The methodology employed for this review was guided by established frameworks for conducting systematic scoping reviews (Arksey & O’Malley; 2005; Levac et al., 2010), aiming to map existing research, (23) identify gaps, and suggest directions for future investigations. A systematic search was performed across ten bibliographic databases to ensure a comprehensive capture of relevant studies. The databases included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, "CINAHL," PsycINFO, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, ThaiLIS, ThaiJO, Health Systems Research Institute Database, and the Thai National Research Repository. This selection was made to encompass both international and local research outputs, acknowledging the value of grey literature in scoping reviews (Pham et al., 2014). To further enhance the breadth of the literature search, secondary searches were conducted. These included manual searches of reference lists from identified studies, examination of relevant Thai health organization websites (e.g.; Ministry of Public Health, Thai Health Promotion Foundation), and exploration of Google and Google Scholar platforms for additional studies that might not be indexed in traditional bibliographic databases. The inclusion of multiple search strategies aimed to minimize publication bias and ensure a comprehensive overview of pertinent research (Briscoe, 2015). The inclusion criteria were designed to focus on studies that provided either quantitative or qualitative data pertinent to public health research on PA and/or SB in Thailand. the review included studies published in Thai or English, dating [39] from the inception of each database to the present search date, ensuring a historical to contemporary perspective. Two authors independently screened studies in two stages - title/abstract screening followed by full-text review. Any discrepancies in inclusion decisions were resolved through discussion and consensus, with a third author consulted when needed to ensure [11] rigor and objectivity in the selection process (Colquhoun et al., 2014). Data from the included studies were extracted systematically using a pre-designed extraction form. Key information collected included study characteristics (e.g., authors, year of publication, journal), research focus (e.g., correlates, outcomes, prevalence, instrument validation), methodological aspects (e.g., [10] study design, sample size, population group), and measurement of PA/SB (e.g., self-report, device-based measures). The extraction template was pilot-tested on a random selection of studies to ensure clarity and comprehensiveness. Data synthesis was conducted qualitatively through thematic analysis, consistent with the objectives of a scoping review. Studies were categorized based on the thematic focus as identified during data extraction, including correlates of PA/SB, outcomes associated with PA/SB, prevalence rates, and validation of instruments used to measure PA/SB. This thematic framework facilitated a structured synthesis of findings across various dimensions of the research (Thomas & Harden, 2008). Quantitative synthesis was not the primary aim of this scoping review due to the heterogeneity [19] of study designs and outcomes. However, basic descriptive statistics were computed to summarize study characteristics, such as frequencies and percentages. The data [22] were tabulated to enhance clarity and accessibility, serving to highlight the distribution of [33] research topics, populations, and methodologies within the existing body of literature (Peters et al., 2015). Given the nature of the scoping review, statistical analysis focused on descriptive statistics rather than inferential statistics. Frequencies and proportions were calculated to determine the representation of various research topics and methodological approaches within the included studies. Additionally, trends over time were explored by examining the number of publications per year, stratified by specific research themes. Subgroup analyses were performed to examine research focus differences across demographic segments, such as age groups and health conditions. These analyses aimed to illuminate potential areas of underrepresentation or overlooking in the existing literature (Tricco et al.; 2016). The overarching goal of the statistical analysis was to provide a comprehensive overview of the research landscape, facilitating the identification of gaps and underexplored areas that warrant future research attention. This structured approach was integral to guiding the subsequent discussion and formulation of recommendations for future research endeavors in the context of PA and SB in Thailand. The breakdown of these studies revealed that a substantial majority, 80%, investigated PA exclusively, while a smaller proportion of studies addressed SB alone (6.7%). In terms of population demographics, both sexes were represented in the majority of studies (82.5%), (23) signaling an inclusive approach in terms of gender analysis. Adults constituted the principal focus group, represented in 51.1% of the total studies. This predominance suggests a significant emphasis on adult PA/SB patterns and determinants within the Thai context. Following adults; older adults (26.9%) and adolescents (15.7%) were commonly studied populations. Despite considerable progress, two notable issues persist within the domain of adversarial attack research: firstly, adversarial attack methodologies, particularly complex optimization-based attacks, are characterized by a high computational burden and intensive hyper-parameter tuning, complicating their applicability to real-time scenarios. Secondly, there exists a disproportionate focus on non-sequential tasks such as image classification, with limited attention dedicated to sequential tasks, particularly those involving text. Scene text recognition, where models are tasked with the sequential interpretation of text embedded within an image, exemplifies a sequential task susceptible to adversarial exploitation yet underexplored in this context. The intricate nature of scene text coupled with variations in lighting, fonts, and background complicates the adversarial attack process, necessitating techniques that can efficiently and effectively compromise model outputs. Our approach, termed Adaptive Adversarial Attack, innovatively leverages the distinct characteristics of sequential tasks to dynamically learn multi-task weightings, thereby eliminating the dependence on manual hyper-parameter adjustments. Our adaptive methodology optimistically capitalizes on the inherent task uncertainty, allowing for the real-time generation of adversarial examples with reduced computational overhead.
