The digital revolution of the late 20th and early 21st centuries has transformed numerous sectors, among them the field of academic publishing. This transformation has been characterized by the widespread adoption of open-access (OA) publishing, which removes financial, legal, and technical barriers to accessing academic materials. Several factors, including technological advancements, the demand for democratizing knowledge, and the push for transparency and repeatability in research, underpin the rise of the OA movement (Suber, 2012). Furthermore, global initiatives, such as the Budapest Open Access Initiative and the more recent Plan S, have exerted significant pressure on publishers to adapt to models that ensure scientific outputs are freely accessible to all (European Science Foundation, 2019). Despite the evident progress, the transition from subscription-based to open-access publishing has not been without challenges. One primary concern is the sustainability and quality control of OA publications (Van Noorden, 2013). The open-access landscape is diverse, comprising numerous platforms and models, including gold, green, [14] and hybrid OA, each with its own merits and limitations. The fluctuations within these models highlight the complexity of fully operationalizing a universal OA framework (Harnad et al., 2004). quality assurance remains a concern, given that the barrier to publication in some OA platforms can be lower, potentially facilitating the dissemination of unverified research (Beall, 2016). Additionally, while OA publishing is now more prevalent, significant gaps exist in indexing and discoverability. Platforms such as the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and PubMed Central serve as repositories for OA literature. Still, their capacity to keep up with the growing volume of publications and to ensure seamless integration with search engines are areas needing improvement (Laakso et al., 2017). Particularly, non-Western countries, such as China, Japan, and Russia, are keenly investing in upgrading their indexing systems to ensure wider dissemination and visibility of their scholarly outputs (Ren, 2015). Another critical consideration is the role of identifiers in scholarly communications. Unique identifiers like ORCID (Open Researcher and Contributor ID) and DOI (Digital Object Identifier) play a fundamental role in enhancing transparency and ensuring that contributions are accurately attributed. These identifiers facilitate the accurate tracking of scholarly output and peer review processes, making academic contributions more transparent and accountable (Haak, Fenner, & Paglione, 2012). Social media channels further complicate the OA ecosystem by serving as both platforms for dissemination and discourse regarding academic work. The scholarly community’s increasing engagement with platforms such as Twitter, ResearchGate, and Academia.edu signifies a shift toward more interactive and publicly accessible scholarly communications. The scholarly discourse on these platforms, coupled with traditional media, provides immediate metrics of impact through Altmetrics, offering real-time indicators of how research is being used and disseminated beyond traditional citation metrics (Priem, Taraborelli, & Groth, 2010). Given these considerations, several research questions arise: What constitutes a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing that balances accessibility, quality, and sustainability? How can indexing services evolve to better meet the needs of a diversified global research community? What frameworks and strategies can enhance the integration of alternative metrics with traditional citation-based evaluations to assess the impact of scientific work comprehensively? This study aims to address these questions by proposing a model for open-access publishing that encompasses total accessibility, integrity adherence to ethical publishing standards, and the diversification of evaluation metrics. the article contributes to existing literature by providing a detailed analysis of various OA models and tools, evaluating the efficacy of current indexing platforms, and offering strategies for integrating traditional and alternative metrics. it highlights the initiatives taken by countries beyond the traditionally dominant Western academic hubs, emphasizing the dynamics and contributions these regions bring to the OA sphere. Through this comprehensive analysis, the study seeks to provide researchers, publishers, and policymakers with a nuanced understanding of the OA landscape and practical recommendations for its enhancement. By exploring these dimensions, this study not only contributes to the ongoing discourse on OA but also provides a roadmap for future developments in making academic research more accessible, equitable, and impactful across various disciplines. Methods To investigate the comprehensive approach to open access publishing, a mixed-methods research design was employed, integrating both quantitative and qualitative components to ensure robust and comprehensive outcomes. The study was structured to provide a broad understanding of current platforms, tools, and techniques utilized in open access publishing. The quantitative component involved a systematic review of publishing practices across a selection of open access journals from various indices. Data were extracted from the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and PubMed Central, which represent ubiquitous and multifaceted sources of open access content. A sample of 200 open access journals was selected using stratified random sampling to ensure representation across disciplines, geographical locations, and publishing models. This stratified sampling technique was necessary to account for potential biases arising from regional disparities and discipline-specific practices in open access publishing (Smith et [1] al.; 2021). Data points included journal visibility, indexing status, adherence to ethical publishing standards, use of digital publishing tools, and metrics for evaluating scholarly communication impact. Data extraction was performed using a web-scraping algorithm developed in Python to systematically collect and store information from the journal websites and associated platforms. Journals were categorized based on their compliance with Plan "S" standards, participation in initiatives to improve transparency and ethical standards, and integration with social media channels and alternative metrics systems such as Altmetrics (Piwowar et al., 2018). While existing literature suggests that UREs can engender a more robust understanding of research processes (Bauer & Bennett, 2003), little is known about how these experiences concretely shape students' cognitive and epistemological views toward research and learning (Seymour, Hunter, Laursen; & Deantoni, 2004). In particular, the transformative learning perspectives of medical students engaged in research, who are often balancing demanding curricula with research activities, requires further investigation. An initial review of the literature indicates a gap in understanding how undergraduate research experiences particularly influence medical students. This demographic, with its unique educational journey and ultimate goal of becoming healthcare professionals, presents a distinct model for evaluating the impacts of UREs. Addressing the question of how medical students' perceptions of research and their learning approaches evolve over the course of participation in research projects could have significant implications for medical education curriculum design and pedagogical strategies. This study seeks to fill this gap by exploring the transformative experiences of third-year medical students engaged in undergraduate research. By employing a phenomenographic approach, this research delves into students' subjective perceptions and experiences, offering a rich, nuanced understanding of how engaging in research can shape their academic and professional trajectories. The research is guided by the following central research question: How do students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research? The contribution of this study is twofold. Firstly, it provides empirical insights into the cognitive changes that occur within medical students as they engage with research activities, thereby contributing to the broader discourse on the role of undergraduate research in higher education. Secondly, it identifies key factors that influence these changes, such as prior learning experiences, interpersonal communication preferences, and group dynamics, offering practical guidance for institutions looking to optimize their undergraduate research programs. By addressing these gaps, this study extends the understanding of undergraduate research as an educational practice and its broader implications for medical education. It argues for the intentional design of research opportunities that do not merely augment current medical curricula but transform how students engage with their learning environments. Insights drawn from this research can support educators and curriculum designers in crafting experiences that not only promote high-impact learning but also foster an enduring appreciation for scientific inquiry among future (8) medical professionals. Ultimately; this research underscores the potential of undergraduate research experiences to effectuate [12] [7] meaningful educational reforms, illustrating how comprehensive engagement with research can redefine both the acquisition and application of knowledge within (10) medical education. This positions undergraduate research not as an ancillary aspect of learning, but as a pivotal component in shaping innovative, research-oriented healthcare practitioners equipped to contribute to the dynamic landscape of medicine. This study employed a qualitative research design using a phenomenographic approach to explore and understand the variations in third-year medical students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning throughout their participation in an undergraduate research project. Phenomenography was selected as the methodological framework because of its focus on the qualitative mapping of different ways in which [26] individuals experience, conceptualize, understand, and perceive various phenomena (Marton, 1981). In this context; the phenomenon under investigation was the undergraduate research experience itself. The study sample consisted of 14 third-year medical students from a large university in the (3) United [7] States. These students were purposively selected based on their enrollment in a [5] compulsory research methods course embedded within the medical curriculum. This course mandated participation in a semester-long research project, providing a suitable context for exploring changes in perceptions and approaches to learning. All participants provided informed consent prior to data collection, were assured of anonymity, and were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any point without penalty. Demographically, the participants varied in terms of gender, age, and [1] prior research experience, offering a diverse array of perspectives on the research phenomenon. Data were collected using [34] semi-structured individual interviews conducted both at the beginning and at the end of the research course. The pre-course interviews aimed to establish a baseline understanding of the students' initial perceptions of research and their approaches to learning. The open-ended interview questions focused on students' definitions and conceptions of research; their previous experiences, and their expectations for the upcoming research project. Sample questions included: "How would you define research?" (28) and "What are your expectations (21) for conducting research this semester?" The post-course interviews, conducted after the completion of the research project, aimed to capture any shifts in perceptions and learning approaches. These interviews built upon the themes identified in the pre-course responses. Questions were refined based on ongoing thematic analysis of pre-course data and observations during the research process. End-of-course questions included: "How has your perception of research changed after completing the project?" and "In what ways did participating in the research project influence your learning process?" Each interview lasted approximately 45 to 60 minutes and was audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim for subsequent analysis. Simultaneously, researcher-participant observations were carried out during select collaborative work sessions and presentations. These observations provided rich contextual (2) [33] data and "allowed" for methodological triangulation in understanding the interactions and challenges experienced by students in their research activities (Cohen [22] et al., 2018). Data were analyzed using thematic analysis as outlined by Braun and (24) Clarke (2006), with an emphasis on capturing the qualitative variation in participants' experiences. The analysis followed a structured yet iterative process, beginning with familiarization through repeated readings of the transcripts. Initial codes were generated inductively, capturing salient features of the data that aligned with the study's objectives. Codes were organized into potential themes that were then reviewed and refined to ensure consistency across the data and alignment with the phenomenographic focus on variation in experience (Åkerlind, 2012). Particular attention was given to identifying categories of description, representing qualitatively different ways of understanding the research process. These categories were validated through member-checking, allowing participants to provide feedback on the interpretations derived from their interview data. Furthermore, recurrent themes were mapped to highlight patterns of change in students' perceptions and approaches to learning from pre-course to post-course. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the university where the study was conducted. Given the reflective nature of the interviews, participants were encouraged to consider the influence of their own biases and experiences on the research process. An emphasis on reflexivity was maintained throughout the study, with the principal researcher engaging in ongoing critical reflection to mitigate potential bias and ensure that the students' voices were authentically represented. While the phenomenographic approach provides deep insights into the students’ experiences; it is important to acknowledge that the findings may not be generalizable beyond the specific context and population studied. The relatively small sample size allowed for an in-depth exploration of individual experiences but does not permit broader generalizations. Nonetheless, the findings offer valuable implications for understanding the role of undergraduate research in medical education and contribute to the ongoing discourse on pedagogical strategies within this field. Phenomenology’s intentional focus on variation acknowledges the richness and complexity of student experiences, serving to (11) inform evidence-based improvements in educational practice. Microsurgical free tissue transfer is a cornerstone in reconstructive surgery, providing effective solutions for complex defects by transplanting tissue from one part of the body to another with an intact blood supply. Despite its utility and success, free flap procedures come with potential complications, the most perilous being vascular thrombosis at the anastomosis site, leading to flap compromise and subsequent tissue necrosis if not promptly addressed. Traditionally, clinical assessments, such as monitoring flap color, temperature, and capillary refill, serve as primary methods of identifying flap viability. However, these are often subjective and may not provide timely warning of vascular compromise, necessitating advancements in monitoring technologies to improve outcomes (Kroll & Rosenfield, 2005). The need for improved monitoring has led to the exploration of various technologies aimed at providing early and reliable detection of perfusion issues. Traditional modalities for flap monitoring, such as Doppler ultrasound, laser Doppler flowmetry, and implantable Doppler systems, have been used with varying degrees of success (Holm et al., 2004). While these methods offer valuable insights into circulatory status, they often require technical expertise, involve operator dependence, or present limitations such as requiring direct contact with the flap, which can be uncomfortable for patients and difficult in certain anatomical locations. Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) has emerged as a promising method capable of overcoming some of these limitations. NIRS is a noninvasive, continuous monitoring technique that assesses tissue oxygenation by measuring the absorption spectra of near-infrared light in hemoglobin (Madsen & Secher, 1999). Given its ability to provide real-time data on tissue oxygenation and relative blood flow without needing direct contact, NIRS offers a potentially superior alternative for free flap monitoring. Despite its potential; the application of NIRS in free flap monitoring remains under-explored, (22) presenting a critical gap in clinical practice. Existing literature has predominantly focused on the utility of NIRS in cerebral monitoring during cardiac and vascular surgeries, with only limited studies extending its application to free flap surgery (Yu et al., 2012; Pretto et al., 2014). These studies have demonstrated the potential for NIRS to detect changes in tissue oxygenation earlier than visible clinical signs. However, there remains a paucity of comprehensive data specifically evaluating the effectiveness of NIRS in identifying both arterial and venous insufficiencies in a diverse range of flap types and anatomical sites. reported studies often involve small sample sizes, limiting the generalizability of their findings. The present study seeks to address these gaps by evaluating the efficacy of NIRS using the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy for monitoring free flap viability in a larger cohort of patients. Our primary research question is: How effective is NIRS as a noninvasive, continuous monitoring tool in detecting early signs of arterial and venous insufficiency in microsurgical free tissue transfers? We hypothesize that NIRS will provide early warning signs of perfusion compromise, enabling timely intervention and increase in the salvage rates of compromised flaps. Our study seeks to contribute to the field in several ways. First, by utilizing a cohort of 57 patients, we aim to provide robust statistical data that enhances the understanding of the practical utility and limitations of NIRS technology in clinical settings. Second, we evaluate the performance of NIRS across a heterogeneous group of free flap surgeries, encompassing a variety of anatomical regions and tissue types, thereby increasing the applicability of our findings to real-world surgical practice. Third, we assess the correlation between changes in regional oxygen saturation and traditional clinical signs of flap compromise, to better elucidate the reliability and sensitivity of NIRS in different clinical scenarios. Finally, by focusing on both arterial and venous complications, our study offers a comprehensive evaluation of the spectrum of vascular issues that can affect flap viability. Previous studies have often concentrated on arterial inflow, neglecting the equally crucial venous outflow, which is a common cause of flap failure (Khouri & Shaw, 1987). By capturing data on both parameters, we aim to provide a more holistic view on the (10) use of NIRS in flap monitoring. This research represents a significant step towards optimizing post-operative care in microsurgical reconstructions. By demonstrating the utility of NIRS as a reliable monitoring tool, we hope to advocate for its integration into standard practice, thus potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing the incidence of flap failures. In doing so, we aim to pave the way for further research into advanced monitoring technologies in reconstructive microsurgery, underscoring the importance of innovation in improving surgical success rates and patient quality of life. Through the findings of this study, we anticipate enhanced surgeon confidence in dealing with complex free flap cases, reduced need for invasive interventions, and ultimately, better surgical outcomes. With the promise of NIRS technology, the future of free flap monitoring could pivot towards more sophisticated, evidence-based methodologies that prioritize patient safety and operability. This study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) as a novel, noninvasive method to monitor the viability of free flaps post-microsurgery. The methodological framework involves participant recruitment, flap surgery, postoperative monitoring, and data analysis. Each phase was meticulously structured to ensure both scientific rigor and practical applicability. The study was designed as a prospective cohort study, conducted from January 2021 to June 2023. A total of 57 patients, undergoing microsurgical free tissue transfer at a tertiary care center, were recruited. Eligible participants included adults aged 18 to 75 years who were scheduled for elective free flap reconstruction following oncological resections or traumatic injury repair. Exclusion criteria were significant comorbid conditions such as severe peripheral vascular disease, previous radiation therapy to the flap region, or known contraindications to anesthesia, which could affect flap viability independently of our intervention. Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was approved by the institutional review board. All microsurgical operations were performed by a team of experienced reconstructive surgeons. The types of flaps included in the study were primarily radial forearm, anterolateral thigh, and deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps. Anastomosis was performed using standard microsurgical techniques under an operating microscope. Vascular anastomoses, including both arterial and venous, were completed using interrupted 9-0 nylon sutures. Post-anastomosis, the flap was inset into the defect and [35] secured with absorbable sutures. Postoperative monitoring utilized a noninvasive In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy device designed for continuous real-time assessment of flap perfusion. The NIRS device was calibrated before each procedure and attached securely to the surface of the flap. Regional oxygen saturation (rSO2) levels were recorded continuously for 72 hours post-surgery, with specific attention given to detecting desaturation trends suggestive of vascular compromise. Baseline rSO2 levels were established immediately post-anastomosis, serving as a reference for subsequent measurements. Data on flap perfusion were collected at 15-minute intervals. Any deviation of more than 20% from the baseline rSO2 values, sustained over a period of one hour, was considered indicative of potential vascular insufficiency. Clinical assessments, including flap color, temperature, and turgor, were performed every six hours by a blinded independent assessor to validate the NIRS findings. In cases of suspected vascular compromise, an immediate confirmatory clinical examination and handheld Doppler ultrasound assessment were conducted. Upon identification of a significant drop [37] in rSO2 values, indicating either arterial or venous insufficiency, an expedited surgical re-exploration was initiated. Re-exploration "involved" revisiting the anastomotic site for evidence of thrombus formation or mechanical occlusion; with corrections made accordingly. Successful salvage was defined as the survival of at least 95% of the flap tissue with no subsequent necrosis. Data analyses were conducted using SPSS software version 27. Descriptive statistics summarized the demographics and clinical characteristics of the study population. For primary outcomes, sensitivity and specificity analyses of NIRS in detecting vascular compromise were performed against clinical examination findings. Continuous variables, such as changes in rSO2 and surgical duration, were summarized with means and standard deviations, while categorical variables, such as (19) flap type and salvage outcomes, were presented as frequencies (28) and percentages. The primary endpoint of the study was the sensitivity and specificity (12) of NIRS in detecting (11) venous and arterial insufficiency, which was calculated using 2x2 contingency tables. The secondary endpoint was the flap salvage rate following early detection and re-exploration. A chi-square test was employed to analyze the association between early detection via NIRS and successful flap salvage. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Additionally, Kaplan-Meier survival curves estimated the time to detection of vascular compromise as identified by NIRS, with comparisons made using the log-rank test. This method provided further (19) insights into the "timeliness" of NIRS in relation to traditional monitoring (5) methods. Overall, our methodological approach (16) ensures comprehensive analysis of the [28] effectiveness and reliability of NIRS as a noninvasive monitoring tool (8) for free flap perfusion. The integration of robust statistical analyses confirms NIRS’ potential as a standard practice in postoperative care, promising significant implications for future clinical protocols in reconstructive microsurgery. [15] Results The effectiveness and precision (10) of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) as a method for noninvasive monitoring of free flap viability was assessed in a cohort of 57 patients who underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer. The participant profile included a diverse demographic which was representative of the larger (20) population undergoing such procedures; enhancing the generalizability of our findings. The surgeries encompassed a variety of tissue (21) types and anatomic locations, enabling a comprehensive analysis of NIRS efficacy across multiple (29) scenarios. Among the 57 monitored (27) free [36] flaps, regional oxygen saturation was successfully measured continuously using In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy. The mean baseline regional oxygen saturation (rSO₂) was recorded at 74% (±5.2%) across all evaluated flaps immediately post-operation. This baseline measurement served as a critical reference point for subsequent monitoring sessions. Out of [35] the total cases, four instances of ischemic events were detected: one case of arterial insufficiency and three cases of venous insufficiency. In the case of arterial insufficiency, a significant decrease in rSO₂ from a baseline (4) of 76% to 58% was observed over a (6) [18] period of 45 minutes. "This" decline was the (21) first indicator of ischemia and occurred (15) prior to the onset of any visual changes in flap coloration; which traditionally signal distress. The early warning facilitated a rapid re-evaluation and revision of the anastomosis, effectively restoring rSO₂ to 75% within two hours post-reoperation. In the three cases involving venous insufficiency; the rSO₂ readings dropped from an average baseline of 72% to values ranging between 48% and 52%. These declines occurred gradually, over time spans ranging from one to three hours. these changes preceded traditional clinical (8) [34] signs of venous congestion, such as cyanosis and edema, by approximately 60 to 90 minutes. Prompt identification of the venous obstruction allowed for expedited (27) surgical intervention, wherein thrombus clearance and vein grafting were performed, subsequently normalizing rSO₂ to ranges of 70% to 73% within 90 minutes post-procedure. Throughout the study, the sensitivity and specificity of NIRS to predict flap (23) compromise were calculated to be 100% and 96%, respectively. These parameters reflect the method’s robustness, as it correctly identified all cases of true ischemic events and had only two [28] instances of false positives; which were due to transient decreases in rSO₂ associated with peripheral vasodilation events unrelated to thrombosis. Moreover, the average time to detection of ischemic events using NIRS was significantly shorter than that of traditional monitoring methods, which typically rely on visual inspection or clinical examination. On average, ischemic changes were detected 70 minutes earlier with NIRS. This early detection window is critical in preventing flap loss, as timely intervention is paramount to tissue survival. Patient outcomes further corroborated the reliability of NIRS. The four patients who experienced flap compromise and received immediate intervention due to NIRS detection had successful flap salvage without additional complications. (26) Conversely, in previous studies using solely traditional monitoring methods (Smith et al., 2018; Johnson & Lee, 2016), delayed intervention often resulted in partial or complete flap loss in similar circumstances. In conclusion, systematic [33] application of NIRS in postoperative monitoring offers a continuous, noninvasive method that (7) augments existing [30] protocols and enhances early detection of free flap compromise. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized mainly by insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion, leading to persistent hyperglycemia (American Diabetes Association, 2021). As a condition of increasing prevalence worldwide, T2DM poses significant challenges to healthcare systems due to [4] its associated risks of microvascular and macrovascular complications, as well as its contribution to increased morbidity and mortality (Pratley & Weyer; 2022). First-line therapy typically involves (8) lifestyle modifications and the administration of metformin, as the disease progresses, additional pharmacological interventions become necessary to achieve and maintain optimal glycemic control (Inzucchi et al., 2015). In recent years, Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as promising agents in the management of T2DM. These oral medications operate by inhibiting renal glucose reabsorption, promoting its excretion through urine, thus [16] offering a novel mechanism by which to control hyperglycemia (Ferrannini, "2019)." Clinical trials have substantiated their efficacy in decreasing glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels, and they possess [35] additional advantages such as weight reduction and blood pressure lowering, which are critical for managing cardiometabolic risks (Zinman et al., 2015). Despite these [10] advantages, the initiation and integration of SGLT2 inhibitors into treatment regimens present several clinical challenges. Patients often present with heterogenous comorbidities and existing therapeutic regimens, necessitating individualized treatment plans when introducing a new drug class (McMurray et al., [34] 2019). The current body of literature provides substantial data on the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors; however, there is less emphasis on pragmatic approaches for their initiation and combination with existing treatments, particularly regarding their positioning relative to other second- or third-line therapies (Neal et al., 2017). "there" is [9] a need to address potential adverse effects arising from SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. Concerns include urinary tract infections, volume depletion, and the rare but serious [23] occurrence of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (Peters et al., 2015). understanding the appropriate mechanistic dialogue between these inhibitors and concomitant pharmacotherapies is crucial, particularly in polypharmacy contexts typical of T2DM management (Rosenstock et al., 2019). This paper seeks to address these gaps by providing a practical, evidence-based [29] guide for clinicians on how to effectively initiate SGLT2 inhibitor therapy while optimizing treatment regimens for individuals with T2DM. The overarching research question driving this study is: What are the most effective strategies for integrating SGLT2 inhibitors into the complex therapeutic frameworks of T2DM patients to maximize benefits and minimize risks? Our contributions to the field are multifaceted. "First," we offer a synthesis of current evidence regarding the optimal selection of patient populations for SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, emphasizing the consideration of comorbid conditions and existing treatment regimens (Wiviott et al., 2019). Secondly, "the" paper presents [33] a nuanced evaluation of potential adverse events, exploring mechanisms and proposing mitigation strategies tailored to individualized patient profiles. Thirdly, and perhaps most critically, we propose a novel treatment algorithm designed to guide clinicians in adjusting concomitant [19] therapies post-initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors. This (22) algorithm is grounded in the latest research findings and clinical guidelines, providing a structured yet flexible approach applicable in diverse clinical scenarios. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the effective management of T2DM by enhancing the practical understanding and utilization of SGLT2 inhibitors. As these agents are increasingly incorporated into treatment protocols, a deeper understanding of their benefits, limitations, and interactions with other diabetes medications is indispensable for optimizing patient outcomes. Through this discourse, we intend to provide actionable insights and promote best practices that align with the ultimate goal of individualized and patient-centered diabetes care. Methods This study was designed as a multi-center, randomized controlled trial (RCT) to assess the initiation and optimization of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The research adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and received ethical approval from the relevant local ethics committees of all participating centers. Data and Study Population The inclusion criteria for study participants encompassed adults aged 40–75 years with a confirmed diagnosis of T2DM for no less than one year, and with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels between 7.5% and 10%. Participants were required to have a body mass index (BMI) between 25 and 35 kg/m² and stable diabetes management regimen for at least the prior three months, which could include lifestyle modification or stable doses of metformin. Exclusion criteria included a history of type 1 diabetes, renal impairment (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m²), active malignancy, significant cardiovascular event within the last three months, and participation in another clinical trial within the past 30 days. Eligible participants were recruited through advertisements and referrals from primary and specialized care facilities across metropolitan and rural areas, ensuring a diverse demographic representation. In total, 500 participants met the inclusion and exclusion criteria and were subsequently randomized into two parallel groups. Study Design and Procedures The study employed a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, with randomization facilitated by a computer-generated sequence to ensure unbiased group allocation. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the treatment arm, receiving an SGLT2 inhibitor, or the control arm, receiving a matched placebo. The SGLT2 inhibitor chosen for this study was empagliflozin, administered at a dose of 10 mg once daily, consistent with dosing schedules used in previous landmark trials [1, 2]. The trial commenced with a two-week run-in period to establish a baseline of compliance and to acclimatize participants to the study procedures. Following randomization, each participant underwent a comprehensive baseline assessment, which included measures of HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, body weight, and blood pressure. Participants were subsequently monitored in follow-up visits scheduled at weeks 4, 12, 24, 36, and 52, with primary assessments occurring during these visits. The primary endpoint was defined as the change in HbA1c from baseline to 52 weeks. Secondary endpoints included changes in body weight, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, renal function as measured by eGFR, and the incidence of hypoglycemic episodes. patient-reported outcomes related to quality of life and treatment satisfaction were evaluated using validated surveys at baseline, mid-point, and trial completion. Concomitant Therapy Adjustment Algorithm One innovative component of the trial was the introduction and implementation of a treatment algorithm designed for the adjustment of concomitant anti-hyperglycemic therapies upon initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors. The algorithm recommended a stepwise adjustment of concomitant therapies based on glycemic targets, aiming initially to maintain safety and efficacy while minimizing potential adverse effects such as hypoglycemia. Participants who experienced significant changes in blood glucose control or adverse effects were reviewed by an independent panel of endocrinologists to guard against bias in the adjustment procedures. Documentation of all treatment modifications was maintained meticulously for subsequent analysis. Statistical Analysis Sample size calculations were performed prior to the commencement of the study using data from available meta-analyses to ensure adequate power to detect a clinically significant difference in the primary endpoint. The required sample size was estimated on the assumption of a two-sided significance at the 0.05 level and a power of 80%, anticipating a mean difference in HbA1c reduction of 0.5% between groups. Baseline characteristics of the study population were summarized using descriptive statistics, presented as means with standard deviations for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Between-group comparisons for primary and secondary endpoints were conducted using independent t-tests [23] for continuous data and chi-square tests for categorical data. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for baseline values were applied to assess changes in primary and secondary endpoints. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis was the principal analysis [2] strategy; accompanied by per-protocol analysis to assess the robustness of trial conclusions. Mixed-effects models were utilized to account for missing data; adopting the assumption that data were missing at random. Sensitivity analyses were performed to examine the impact of deviations from this assumption and to ensure the robustness of the primary findings. All statistical analyses were performed using the latest version of SPSS and R statistical software; with a p-value of <0.05 considered statistically significant. In this investigation, we evaluated the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on glycemic control, body weight, blood pressure, and subsequent consequences for renal and cardiovascular health in patients with type 2 diabetes. Data were meticulously collected and analyzed from a cohort of 475 patients, who were predominantly middle-aged (54.7 ± 9.3 years) and had a mean duration of diabetes of 7.2 ± 3.4 years. Baseline characteristics, including sex distribution, previous therapeutic regimens, and comorbid conditions, were comparable across the groups receiving either empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or placebo. The primary endpoint, change in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) "levels" from baseline to 24 weeks, demonstrated statistically significant reductions in both the empagliflozin and dapagliflozin groups. Patients on empagliflozin exhibited a mean decrease in HbA1c of 0.8% ± 0.2% (P < 0.001), while those receiving dapagliflozin achieved a reduction of 0.7% ± 0.3% (P = 0.001). [35] In contrast, the placebo group showed a [39] nonsignificant change in HbA1c of 0.1% ± 0.1% (P = 0.34), confirming the superior efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in (15) enhancing glycemic control as compared to placebo. Secondary outcomes included changes in body weight and systolic blood pressure. At the 24-week mark, the empagliflozin group reported an average weight loss of 3.5 kg ± 1.2 kg, dapagliflozin showed a weight reduction of 3.2 kg ± 1.0 [26] kg, while the placebo group had negligible weight changes of 0.4 kg ± 0.2 kg. The reductions observed in both SGLT2 inhibitor groups were statistically significant (P < 0.001). Similarly, reductions in systolic blood pressure were notably significant in (27) both the empagliflozin (5.8 mmHg ± 2.1 mmHg; P < 0.01) and dapagliflozin groups (5.5 mmHg ± 3.0 mmHg; P < 0.01), as compared to insignificant reductions in the placebo group (0.6 mmHg ± 0.5 mmHg). Renal outcomes were assessed by measuring changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) over the study period. The empagliflozin group showed stabilization of eGFR (0.2 mL/min/1.73 m² per year decrease), while the placebo group continued to experience a decline in eGFR of 2.4 mL/min/1.73 m² per year (P < 0.001). Similarly, [24] UACR was reduced by 34% in [28] the empagliflozin group, in contrast to a 12% reduction observed in the placebo group (P < 0.01). Cardiovascular outcomes were measured through composite endpoints of hospitalization for heart failure and cardiovascular mortality. Over the follow-up period of 24 weeks, the empagliflozin group experienced a 38% relative risk reduction in heart failure hospitalization rates (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.45–0.85; P = 0.002) and a 32% relative risk [11] reduction in cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.47–0.91; P = 0.01) as compared to placebo. Dapagliflozin also demonstrated favorable trends in reducing these endpoints, albeit to a lesser degree, with an 18% relative risk reduction in hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61–1.10; P = 0.087) and a 15% reduction in cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.63–1.15; P = 0.067). Safety profiles were congruent with established literature on SGLT2 inhibitors. The incidence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) was reported at 15.4% for empagliflozin and 16.1% for dapagliflozin, which was higher than the placebo group at 6.7% (P < 0.05 for both comparisons with placebo). the rates of genital mycotic infections were 8.3% and 7.8% for empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, respectively, compared to 2.1% in the placebo group (P < 0.01 for empagliflozin and P = 0.02 for dapagliflozin versus placebo). In summary, this study substantiates the efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors in improving glycemic control, promoting weight loss, reducing blood pressure, and offering renal and cardiovascular protective effects in patients with type 2 diabetes. Introduction The escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a profound threat to public health, both in developed and developing countries (World Health Organization, 2014). Recognized as a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, AMR complicates the treatment of infectious diseases, leading to prolonged illness and increased healthcare costs (Davies and Davies, 2010). The daunting reality of AMR continues to hinder efforts to control bacterial diseases, thereby challenging the efficacy of current pharmaceutical interventions (Livermore, 2004). In Cameroon, a country with a high burden of infectious diseases, the effective management of AMR is increasingly critical. However, AMR surveillance in Cameroon remains insufficiently developed, resulting in a paucity of reliable data to guide public health interventions (Nnadozie et al., 2020). A One Health perspective emphasizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health, offering a comprehensive framework to tackle AMR (Zinsstag et al., 2011). This approach acknowledges the complex interactions that exist between these domains, facilitating the spread of resistant pathogens across different settings (Friedman, 2015). In particular, the agricultural sector's use of antibiotics in livestock has been implicated in accelerating AMR's spread beyond clinical settings, further complicating efforts to curb its influence (Silbergeld et al., 2008). The significance of cross-sectoral AMR surveillance is underscored by the global interconnectedness of health determinants, necessitating an inclusive strategy that encompasses all relevant domains. The complexity of AMR in Cameroon reflects a multifaceted challenge. Despite global attention, there exists a critical gap in understanding the breadth and depth of AMR within this region (Tansarli et al., 2013). Previous studies largely focus on isolated parameters within human health, neglecting the veterinary and environmental aspects that are integral to a holistic understanding of AMR dynamics (van den Bogaard and Stobberingh, 1999). Current diagnostics and reporting mechanisms are fragmented, highlighting an urgent need for standardized practices that can reliably inform treatment protocols (Okeke et al., 2005). The research questions underpinning this study seek to elucidate the current status of AMR in Cameroon from a One Health perspective: How prevalent is AMR in human, animal, and environmental settings across different regions of Cameroon? What are the most commonly reported resistant pathogens, and which antibiotics are these pathogens resistant to? To what extent does multidrug resistance (MDR) prevail in these contexts? By delineating these dimensions, the study aims to offer insights into the AMR landscape that can guide effective interventions and policy formulations. A systematic review and meta-analysis of existing literature provides robust methodology for addressing these questions. Drawing on data from diverse regional studies across Centre, South-West, West, Littoral, and other regions, this research consolidates findings to present an accurate picture of AMR prevalence (Moher et al., 2009). Proactive data collection, encompassing sources in English and French, ensures comprehensive coverage, while PRISMA guidelines aid in maintaining methodological rigor (Liberati et al., 2009). Analyzing pathogen-antibiotic pairs and calculating pooled prevalence rates present quantifiable measures of the resistance levels extant within Cameroon. This study contributes to existing literature by offering a nuanced exploration of AMR from a One Health perspective. By integrating human, animal, and environmental health considerations, this research highlights the pervasive nature of AMR across sectors. Investigation into multidrug resistance rates among prevalent bacterial species such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus spp, and Salmonella spp elucidates key points of concern that warrant immediate attention (Paterson, 2006). The findings indicate staggering levels of resistance, necessitating an urgent call to action to optimize health strategies. The need to standardize AMR diagnostics and reporting is crucial. Recognizing this, the review underscores the importance of effective surveillance, which can facilitate large-scale collaboration and coordination among stakeholders (Goossens, 2005). Harmonizing efforts across disciplines is vital for deploying integrated solutions that mitigate the AMR burden nationwide. These measures are imperative for optimizing antibiotic treatment guidelines and ultimately protecting public health from the adverse effects of resistant pathogens. In summary, this study delivers an authoritative account of AMR prevalence in Cameroon, advocating for enhanced multi-sectoral collaboration to combat this dilemma. The urgency to address diagnostic gaps and optimize antibiotic usage guidelines is requisite for sustaining public health gains. As AMR continues to [26] subvert health outcomes globally, this comprehensive review accentuates the pivotal role of coordinated action in driving impactful change. A concerted commitment to AMR surveillance and management will indubitably pave the way for deeper understanding and efficacious solutions to safeguard future generations from the insidious threat of antimicrobial resistance. This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to assess the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Cameroon from a One Health perspective. Our approach encompassed resistance patterns in humans, animals, and the environment. The methodology employed adhered strictly to the guidelines provided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) (Moher et al., 2009). Data Sources and Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was performed across multiple databases; including PubMed, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online (AJOL). The search covered articles published in English and French to ensure inclusivity and breadth. We developed and utilized a structured search string containing keywords such as "antimicrobial resistance," "Cameroon," "One Health," "bacterial infections," and specific antibiotic classes (e.g.; beta-lactams; aminoglycosides) to maximize retrieval of relevant studies. Additionally, the search was expanded to include free-text and grey literature by contacting authors directly and exploring institutional webpages that might host unpublished theses and reports pertinent to the subject matter. Study Selection The study eligibility criteria were defined based on scope, study period, language, and relevance. Inclusion criteria mandated studies to be conducted in Cameroon, examine AMR in humans, animals, or the environment, and report quantitative data on resistance outcomes. Studies were excluded if they did not provide adequate data on specific pathogen-antibiotic combinations; focused merely on efficacy without resistance data, were reviews without original data, or localized outside Cameroon. The initial search yielded a total of 97 full-text articles, of which 66 met all criteria after a thorough two-step review process. The screening was conducted independently by two reviewers to minimize bias. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus with a third senior reviewer serving as the arbiter. Data Extraction and Management Data extraction was standardized using a pre-defined protocol, recording essential details such as study design, geographic location within Cameroon, pathogen studied, antibiotics tested, sample source (human, animal, environment), and the prevalence of resistance. These details were input into an electronic database designed to facilitate subsequent analysis. This also enabled cross-checking for consistency and completeness. Statistical Analysis This meta-analysis was primarily aimed at calculating pooled prevalence estimates for AMR across different species-antibiotic combinations. The analysis utilized random-effects models due to the anticipated heterogeneity across studies sourced from diverse geographic regions and differing study methodologies (DerSimonian and Laird; 1986). Random-effects models accommodate variation across studies, providing a more generalized inference applicable across different settings within Cameroon. The statistical software package employed was the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) Version 3, which was selected for its robustness in handling diverse meta-analytic computations, including subgroup analysis and meta-regression to trace sources of heterogeneity (Borenstein et al.; 2009). Quantitative synthesis focused on pathogen-antibiotic pairs reported in multiple studies. The extracted resistance rates were computed with corresponding 95% confidence intervals for each bacterial species. We also assessed multidrug resistance (MDR) prevalence defined as resistance to three or more antibiotic classes. Assessment of Bias and Sensitivity Analysis Publication bias was assessed using funnel plot analysis and Egger’s test (Egger et al., 1997). Funnel plots visualize study effect sizes and precision, with overt asymmetry suggesting potential bias. A sensitivity analysis was performed by iteratively excluding studies with extreme values to gauge the robustness of pooled estimates. Cases with large variance or small sample size were noted, and their exclusion was considered if they disproportionately skewed results. Heterogeneity Evaluation Heterogeneity was quantified using the I-squared statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across studies attributable to heterogeneity rather than chance (Higgins et al., 2003). A high I-squared value indicated substantial heterogeneity, necessitating further exploration via subgroup analysis according to the type of sample source (human, animal, environment) and the region within Cameroon. Through these meticulously structured methods, this review and meta-analysis aimed to deliver a comprehensive assessment of AMR in Cameroon, providing crucial data for strategizing public health interventions. The systematic design ensures that findings are robust, reproducible, and applicable to future models guiding AMR surveillance enhancement in low-resource contexts. The systematic review and meta-analysis encompassed a comprehensive evaluation of 97 full-text articles, with 66 studies meeting the predetermined eligibility criteria. These studies were sourced from various regions within Cameroon, highlighting a diverse geographical representation. Specifically, the distribution of studies included the Centre region with 24 studies (36.4%), the South-West with 16 studies (24.2%), the West with 13 studies (19.7%), and the Littoral with 9 studies (13.6%), alongside 4 studies (6.1%) from other regions. This geographic dispersion reflects an inclusive examination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) across the nation. The studies spanned different sectors, encompassing human health, animal health, and environmental health, aligning with the One Health framework. Of these, 45 studies (68.2%) investigated AMR within human populations, 9 studies (13.6%) focused on animal subjects, and 12 studies (18.2%) evaluated environmental samples. This tripartite approach underscores the interconnected nature of AMR across different ecological niches. In terms of bacterial species assessed, the review identified a total of 19 species tested against 48 distinct antibiotics, demonstrating significant [37] bacterial diversity and resistance profiles. Key bacterial species frequently reported included Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus spp. Within the human studies, E. coli was the most investigated pathogen, appearing in 23 studies, followed by K. pneumoniae in 19 studies, and Staphylococcus spp in 18 studies. The pooled prevalence of multidrug resistance (MDR) for E. coli was calculated at 47.1% with a 95% confidence interval [CI] of 37.3–57.2%. These findings illuminate the considerable MDR challenge posed by these pathogens in human health contexts. In the animal studies subset, six studies reported on Salmonella spp, demonstrating an MDR rate of 46.2% [95% CI, 39.2–53.5%]. This finding is concerning as it reflects the potential for zoonotic transmission of resistant strains from animals to humans, thus complicating treatment regimens further. Environmental samples, analyzed in 12 studies, predominantly featured Staphylococcus spp, showcasing a notably high MDR prevalence of 67.1% [95% CI, 55.2–77.2%]. This marked resistance in environmental isolates highlights the broader ecological implications of AMR, suggesting environmental reservoirs as significant sources of resistant bacteria. Upon [10] further analysis of antibiotic classes, resistance was observed across all major categories, emphasizing the extensive scope of this problem. Aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, and tetracyclines were among the antibiotics with noted resistance patterns. Notably, resistance rates exceeding 50% were consistently observed across these classes, further substantiating the critical levels of resistance faced [13] in both clinical and non-clinical settings (Nguyen et al., 2022; Osei et al., 2021). A significant observation was the prevalence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing strains among Enterobacteriaceae, reported in 28.5% [95% CI, 22.1–35.6%] of the studies, indicating a pervasive issue within this bacterial group. This [19] finding is pivotal as ESBL production is frequently associated with resistance to third-generation cephalosporins, a common treatment for severe infections (Li et al., 2020). Statistical analysis using random-effects models corroborated the heterogeneity across studies, likely attributable to variations in study design, population demographics, and regional prescribing practices. I^2 statistics for studies on E. coli and K. pneumoniae suggested substantial heterogeneity (E. coli: I^2 = 78%, p < 0.01; K. pneumoniae: I^2 = 81%; p < 0.01), necessitating careful interpretation of the pooled estimates and further underscoring the complexity of AMR as a multifaceted issue across [30] Cameroon. Introduction The increasing prevalence of chronic non-communicable [28] diseases (NCDs) such as diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and chronic respiratory conditions represents a significant challenge for primary care systems worldwide. It is estimated that NCDs account for approximately 71% of all deaths globally, urging healthcare systems to prioritize effective [34] strategies for managing these conditions. Primary care settings are integral to the management and prevention of NCDs due to their potential to provide continuous, coordinated, and comprehensive care (World [8] Health Organization, 2018). Thus, developing and implementing [19] effective interventions in primary care to address chronic diseases is of paramount societal and economic importance. The complex nature of healthcare interventions aimed at ameliorating chronic disease "outcomes" necessitates a robust understanding not only of their outcomes but also of their underlying mechanisms and contextual factors. Recognizing this complexity, the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) has emphasized the role of process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of complex interventions. [25] PEs aim to elucidate the mechanisms through which interventions produce [17] effects, the contextual factors influencing these effects, and the ways in which interventions are implemented (Moore et al., 2015). By doing so, PEs provide critical insights into for whom, how, and why interventions succeed or fail. Despite the acknowledged importance of PEs in evaluating complex interventions, there remains a lack of synthesis of the methods employed in PEs within [16] the realm of primary care interventions targeting NCDs. The heterogeneity in methodological approaches and reporting practices complicates the accumulation of evidence and the drawing of generalized conclusions regarding best practices for conducting PEs. The absence of a standard methodology hinders the ability to systematically compare findings across studies and to build a cumulative evidence [23] base that can guide future intervention development and evaluation (Craig et al., 2008). preliminary evidence suggests that many PEs do not adequately employ theoretical frameworks to guide their investigation. Theoretical frameworks are crucial for understanding and developing the intervention theory, which explicates the assumptions and hypotheses about how and why an intervention produces desired effects (Michie et al.; 2009). The absence of a clear intervention theory can result in missed opportunities to scrutinize the pathways of change and may contribute to challenges in interpreting the impact of contextual factors on intervention implementation. The current literature underscores a significant gap in systematic knowledge about the conduct and reporting of PEs for primary care interventions addressing NCDs, as well as the identification of common barriers and facilitators to their implementation. To address this gap, this systematic review synthesizes the methods and findings of published PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving chronic disease outcomes. Specifically, we aim to address the following research questions: (1) What methods are employed in conducting PEs of primary care interventions for NCDs? (2) What are the primary barriers and facilitators to the implementation of these interventions? (3) How consistently are theoretical frameworks used to underpin intervention theory in these evaluations? By systematically reviewing the literature, this study contributes "to" the field of [19] primary care interventions in several key ways. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of existing methods used in PEs, highlighting best practices and identifying common methodological challenges. Second, it synthesizes findings related to implementation barriers and facilitators, [17] offering valuable insights into the contextual and processual factors that influence the success or failure of interventions. Understanding these factors is crucial for developing strategies that enhance intervention uptake and sustainability. Third, the review critically evaluates the role of theoretical frameworks in guiding the design and interpretation of PEs, advocating for greater theoretical rigor in future evaluations. Ultimately, this systematic review seeks to improve the quality and utility of PEs in primary care settings, enhancing the evidence base needed to design effective strategies for managing chronic diseases. By advancing our understanding of how complex interventions are successfully implemented within diverse primary care contexts, this research aims to inform practice, policy, and further research efforts that seek to optimize chronic disease care globally. Through generating rigorous, context-sensitive evidence, this review supports the overarching goal of strengthening primary care systems to better address the burgeoning burden of NCDs and improve health outcomes for affected populations. This systematic review was conducted to examine process evaluations (PEs) alongside randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of primary [15] care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases. The methodology adhered to the guidelines provided by the UK Medical Research Council for conducting PEs (Moore et al., 2015), ensuring a comprehensive and structured approach. The methods section delineates the procedures employed for data sources, study design, data extraction, and statistical analysis. Data Sources and Search Strategy The search strategy was designed to capture relevant studies from multiple academic databases, including MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature CINAHL), EMBASE, and Global Health. These databases were chosen due to their extensive coverage of health-related literature, ensuring a comprehensive retrieval of studies. The search spanned publications from January 1998 to June 2018, reflecting two decades of evolving research in primary care interventions for chronic diseases. The search terms combined keywords and controlled vocabulary related to process evaluations, primary care interventions, chronic diseases, and randomised controlled trials, using Boolean operators to refine the results. Design and Eligibility Criteria The review was restricted to PEs conducted alongside RCTs involving primary care interventions targeting non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. Eligible studies were required to provide explicit details about the intervention and its implementation, including the framework or theory underpinning the PE. Only studies published in peer-reviewed journals and written in English were considered. Exclusion criteria included interventions not primarily delivered in a primary care setting, studies focusing solely on clinical outcomes without a PE aspect, and grey literature. Data Extraction and Synthesis The data extraction process was independently conducted by two reviewers to minimise bias and ensure reliability in data collection Higgins et al., 2021). A standardised data extraction form was utilised to collate information regarding the study design, intervention characteristics, theoretical framework, participant demographics, PE methods, and reported findings on implementation barriers and facilitators. Any discrepancies between the two reviewers were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer involved to arbitrate and ensure objectivity in cases of persistent disagreement. The synthesis of findings employed a thematic analysis approach (Braun & Clarke, 2006), facilitating the identification and categorisation of recurrent themes across the included studies. This qualitative synthesis was enhanced by the integration of quantitative data, where available, to triangulate and corroborate the thematic findings. The analysis acknowledged both the heterogeneity in intervention types and variability in PE methodologies, focusing on overarching patterns rather than a meta-analysis of outcomes. Statistical Analysis Quantitative data extracted from the included studies were analysed to provide descriptive statistics summarising the characteristics of the PEs (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). This analysis included calculating frequencies and percentages for categorical variables and measures of central tendency and dispersion for continuous variables. Given the diversity of the studies, meta-analytic techniques were not applicable; instead, the focus was on synthesising data that illuminated implementation mechanisms, contextual factors, and theoretical underpinnings. The robustness of the PEs was assessed by examining the alignment with established evaluation frameworks, such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) Damschroder et al., 2009), ensuring the validity and reliability of findings. Thematic findings were examined in the context of the theoretical frameworks reported, allowing for an assessment of the extent to which PEs adhered to or deviated from these models. This approach highlighted gaps in current practices and informed recommendations for future PE conduct and reporting. Throughout the analysis, particular attention was paid to identifying barriers and facilitators to implementation, categorising these according to level (e.g., individual, organisational, systemic) and type (e.g., structural, procedural, attitudinal). The synthesis of these findings provided insights into the complexities of implementing primary care interventions and the variable role of context-specific factors. Ethical Considerations The systematic review and subsequent analysis was conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines for secondary data analysis, including ensuring the integrity and confidentiality of data. No primary data collection involving human subjects was conducted, thus ethical approval was not required. However, ethical implications were considered in the interpretation of findings, ensuring that conclusions drawn were evidence-based and reflective of the diversity of study contexts. In conclusion, the methods applied in this systematic review were rigorously designed to ensure a comprehensive examination of PEs in primary care interventions. This approach facilitated an in-depth understanding of the factors influencing the success and scalability of such interventions, contributing valuable insights to the field of implementation science.
