Recommender systems have become indispensable tools in the contemporary digital landscape, "spanning" applications such as online retail, music and video streaming, social media, and more (Ricci et al., 2015). Their objective is to curate personalized content by predicting user-item interactions based on historical data, thus enhancing user engagement and satisfaction. Central to the development of these systems is their ability to leverage disparate signals—ranging from explicit user feedback, such as ratings, to implicit signals like browsing patterns, purchase history, item co-occurrence, and user demographics (Aggarwal, 2016). The incorporation of diverse signals seeks to construct a comprehensive understanding of both user preferences and item characteristics. Traditionally, research in recommender systems has focused on optimizing individual signals to refine recommendation accuracy. For example, Collaborative Filtering (CF) techniques exploit past user activity to predict future preferences without delving into the content characteristics of items (Sarwar et al., 2001). Content-Based Filtering (CBF), on the other hand, recommends items similar to those a user has liked in the past by analyzing item features (Lops et al., 2011). Hybrid approaches have been proposed to combine CF and CBF to magnify their complementary strengths (Burke, 2002). these approaches often treat signals as isolated, underutilizing the rich, interconnected tapestry of interactions and relationships inherent within the data ecosystem. The increasingly complex and data-rich environments necessitate frameworks that can manage and fuse multiple sources of information effectively. Moreover, the effectiveness of recommender systems hinges on their adaptability and responsiveness to individual user contexts and preferences, which may vary dynamically (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2011). Current systems often fall short in capturing this heterogeneity, as the same model is typically deployed uniformly across the user base. users may not uniformly respond to all signals; certain users might prioritize social influences, while others base decisions on geographic locality or item novelty. Recognizing and capitalizing on the multifaceted nature of user-item interactions is imperative for next-generation recommender systems. This research identifies a significant gap in existing recommender system frameworks: the need for a model that not only integrates various item relationships but does so in a manner that reflects each user's unique preference profile and dynamically adjusts to their evolving behaviors. The central research question driving this study is: How can we design a recommender system that combines heterogeneous item relationships effectively, while adaptively recognizing the most pertinent signals for individual users at any given time? In addressing this question, we introduce a novel framework that fuses concepts from mixtures-of-experts models and knowledge graph embeddings. Mixtures-of-experts approaches (Jacobs et al., 1991) facilitate the selective utilization of different models or "experts" to handle varying conditions or inputs, thus aligning well with the objective of modularly aggregating diverse recommendation signals. Simultaneously, knowledge graph embeddings (Bordes et al., 2013) provide a robust means of capturing and representing complex item interrelations, as they can embed items, users, and various contextual information into a continuous vector space, encoding manifold interactions. The proposed framework’s core contributions are twofold. Firstly, it introduces a mechanism for dynamically inferring which recommendation modality a user is likely most responsive to, accounting for temporal, contextual, and possibly ephemeral aspects of user preference. This is achieved by leveraging mixtures-of-experts, where each expert corresponds to a different modality of item relationship—be it collaborative, content-based, social, or geographical. The system dynamically weighs these experts based on the user’s historical and contextual data, creating an adaptive recommendation that aligns with their current state and preferences. Secondly, our model identifies the optimal recommendation within each modality through knowledge graph embeddings, which facilitate an enriched representation of complex and interconnected item relationships. These embeddings [1] allow the system to draw upon structured knowledge within an item’s ecosystem; incorporating diverse features and [5] interactions that might escape unidimensional models. As a direct outcome, recommendations are not only more accurate but are also accompanied by interpretable rationales, reflecting the user’s engagement with various item relationships. Preliminary results indicate that this heterogeneous, adaptive modeling approach significantly outperforms traditional recommender system architectures across (6) several benchmark datasets. Furthermore, it introduces a (19) level of transparency and interpretability by delineating the reasons behind each recommendation, thereby enhancing user trust and satisfaction. In conclusion, our framework augments the recommender systems landscape by adeptly embracing the complexity of modern user-item interactions. By concurrently modeling diverse signal modalities and dynamically adapting to [24] individual (4) user proclivities, this research advances toward a more nuanced and responsive paradigm, one that not only anticipates user needs with precision but also demystifies the recommendation process itself. Through this endeavor; we contribute a substantial advancement in the design of intelligent, context-aware recommendation systems. To evaluate the effectiveness [17] of our proposed framework, we utilized three diverse datasets, each characterized by different types of consumer interaction data. The first dataset, MovieLens, is a benchmark dataset [8] in the recommender systems domain, providing explicit user ratings on a diverse set of movies. This allows us to explore the potential of our method in a well-understood (17) domain of explicit feedback. The second dataset, Yelp, offers a combination of user reviews, ratings, and check-ins in the context of local business recommendations. (25) This dataset is particularly useful for assessing the impact (15) of geographic locality and multimodal feedback on recommendations. The third dataset is Amazon Product Reviews; which consists of user reviews and implicit feedback such as clicks. This (28) dataset helps evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in an e-commerce setting where item-item relationships, such as complementary purchases, heavily influence user preferences. Our model draws on the principles of mixtures-of-experts and knowledge graph embeddings to model heterogeneous item relationships. The system is designed to concurrently [32] process [4] multiple modalities of recommendation; allowing it to dynamically prioritize the most relevant modality for a given user at a particular time. Specifically, our framework identifies the user's susceptibility to various recommendation modalities through (21) a gating network that assigns weights to various [38] experts, each trained to leverage a specific interaction signal such as user feedback, item similarity, or social influence. Each expert in our framework (17) is designed to exploit a [37] particular kind of signal. For instance, one expert may utilize collaborative filtering techniques, while another relies on content-based filtering using item attributes. to capture item-to-item relationships, a knowledge graph embedding is used, (7) (12) which incorporates entities and relations within the dataset, allowing the model to learn richer representations of items (4) through their inter-linkages. This (3) embedding assists in bridging the semantic gaps between apparently distinct items based on historical interactions. The [38] implementation of our model proceeded through several stages. Initially; item relationships across various modalities were mapped into a unified form. This was achieved using (20) a shared embedding space where each type of relationship, be it user-based or item-based, contributed to the vector representation of both users and items. Embeddings for items were enhanced by leveraging TransE, a translational distance-based embedding model well-suited for knowledge graphs. This was crucial for representing items in a way that captured not only their individual features but also their connections with [10] related entities. (29) Next, a mixture-of-experts layer was constructed. This layer consisted of a set of expert networks, each specialized in a particular recommendation signal. The gating network was trained to dynamically modulate each expert’s influence based on the user's historical interaction patterns and current contextual information. Each expert outputs a candidate list of item recommendations, which are subsequently merged using the weights determined by the gating network to produce a final ranked list of recommendations. The model training involved a two-step process. In the first step, individual experts were pre-trained to optimize for their respective objectives, such as maximizing user satisfaction metrics or minimizing prediction error. Subsequently, the entire network, including the gating mechanism, was fine-tuned end-to-end using a pairwise ranking loss. This loss was computed based on user interactions, aiming to rank user-interacted items higher than non-interacted ones; which is a common practice in collaborative filtering models. Our approach was quantitatively evaluated by employing a combination of precision-oriented and ranking-oriented metrics, which are standard in the evaluation of recommendation systems. Precision@K, Recall@K, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated to assess the quality of recommendations generated by different models. normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) was used to evaluate the ranking performance. To compare the efficacy of our method against baselines, we conducted hypothesis testing. paired t-tests were used to compare the differences in metric scores across models to establish statistical significance. We included several competitive baseline models in our experiments, such as standard collaborative filtering methods, content-based recommenders, and recent knowledge graph embedding approaches. In addition to these quantitative analyses, we explored the interpretability of our model's recommendations by examining the gating network’s learned weights. This qualitative examination provided insights into the modalities that were most influential for different user segments, enabling us to observe and understand the model's decision-making process across various contexts. This dual focus on performance metrics and interpretability underscores the comprehensive evaluation strategy employed in this research. this rigorous methodological setup not only demonstrates the superior performance of our proposed framework relative to existing methods, but also emphasizes its capacity to deliver personalized and contextually relevant recommendations while providing insight into the underlying recommendation dynamics. The evaluation of our proposed framework, which combines heterogeneous item relationships for recommendation, was carried out using three well-established datasets: MovieLens 1M, Amazon Electronics, and Yelp. Each dataset provided a distinct set of signals and interaction types to effectively assess the adaptability and performance of our approach across varied recommendation scenarios. In the MovieLens 1M dataset, our framework demonstrated significant improvements over baseline models such (22) as Matrix Factorization (MF) and Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF). We implemented mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) as our main evaluation metrics. Our method achieved an MRR of 0.41 compared to 0.35 from MF and 0.37 from NCF. Similarly, NDCG at 10 was recorded at 0.47 for our framework, surpassing MF’s 0.40 and NCF’s 0.42. Introduction Diabetes mellitus, a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose levels due to insulin defects or secretion impairment, (10) has emerged as a formidable public health challenge [10] globally. the prevalence and incidence of diabetes have shown an alarming rise in recent decades, attributing this trend [2] primarily to lifestyle changes, urbanization, and increased life expectancy (World Health Organization, 2018). Among several countries, Saudi Arabia presents a unique case where rapid socio-economic changes, nutrition transitions, and lifestyle modifications have significantly contributed to the [26] [24] surge in diabetes cases (Al-Rubeaan; 2015). Traditionally, [28] two primary forms of diabetes are recognized: type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), primarily an autoimmune condition with onset generally in childhood or adolescence, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), highly correlated with lifestyle factors such as obesity, sedentary behavior, and dietary patterns, and (28) typically (8) (18) emerging in adulthood (ADA, 2020). The epidemiology of these forms in Saudi Arabia reveals distinct patterns and presents distinctive challenges in managing their escalating burden. This review examines these patterns by scrutinizing incidence and prevalence data over a significant (7) period. Despite growing international awareness of diabetes as a public health concern; a noticeable gap exists in understanding its precise epidemiological footprint in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia over extended periods. Although discrete studies have attempted to quantify the disease burden, they are often limited by region-specific data, (18) methodologically diverse in nature, and vary in their determinants and diagnostic criteria (Habbab & Al-Mohaimeed, 2017; Al Dawish et al., 2016). Consequently, there is a critical need for consolidated evidence to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of diabetes trends in Saudi Arabia, which is currently lacking in the literature. the intersectionality of factors influencing diabetes prevalence—gender, (1) age, and urbanization—remains underexplored, necessitating an in-depth analysis to inform evidence-based interventions. This study aims to bridge these gaps by conducting a descriptive [8] review of the incidence and prevalence rates of diabetes mellitus in Saudi Arabia from 1990 to 2015. The primary research question guiding this investigation is: "What are the trends in the incidence and prevalence of type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus in (11) Saudi Arabia over the past 25 years; and [5] how do they vary [2] across different demographic and socio-economic groups?" By addressing this question, the study not only seeks to provide a clear epidemiological overview but also attempts to identify and elucidate patterns and causes [32] underlying these trends. The contribution of this study is multi-faceted. Firstly, by synthesizing findings from diverse studies and varying methodologies; we offer an integrative perspective that captures both the multitude and specificity (10) of diabetes mellitus trends in Saudi Arabia. This approach not only helps in understanding historic and current epidemiological transitions but also aids in apprising future health policy directions. Secondly, the recognition of demographic factors such as gender and age, along with lifestyle changes attributable to urbanization, enables a more nuanced understanding of vulnerable populations. Identifying these segments can guide targeted interventions, potentially ameliorating the expanding prevalence (23) among susceptible groups, particularly women and children. our research contributes to the discourse on the global burden of diabetes by highlighting the implications of Saudi-specific socio-economic transformations on non-communicable disease trends. As a nation rapidly transitioning in its socio-economic realm, Saudi Arabia acts as a microcosm for other middle to high-income countries experiencing analogous shifts, providing a broader applicability of findings beyond its geographical confines. In summary, this study endeavors to fill a crucial knowledge gap by systematically reviewing and synthesizing regional data, offering a comprehensive picture of diabetes epidemiology within Saudi Arabia. Through its methodological rigor and focus on demographic segmentation, the study aims to catalyze informed health discourse and effective public health strategies orientated towards diabetes management and prevention in Saudi Arabia and comparable regions worldwide. Data Sources and Search Strategy This study employed a systematic review methodology to collate and synthesize data on the incidence and prevalence rates of diabetes mellitus in Saudi Arabia from 1990 to 2015. The initial step involved identifying relevant literature through a comprehensive search of established electronic databases including Medline, EBSCO, PubMed, and Scopus. This was undertaken to ensure the inclusion of a broad spectrum of peer-reviewed publications that examined diabetes trends within the specified period. The [1] search strategy was designed to capture all English-language articles, applying a combination of keywords and MeSH terms relevant to diabetes mellitus, including “diabetes incidence,” “diabetes prevalence,” Saudi Arabia,” “type 1 diabetes,” and “type 2 diabetes.” Additionally, the search was expanded to include synonyms and related terms for maximum retrieval efficacy and comprehensiveness of results. Study Selection and Eligibility Criteria The studies were selected based on specific inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure the reliability and relevance of data. Included studies needed to provide explicit data on the incidence or prevalence rates of diabetes mellitus in Saudi Arabia, utilize a clearly defined study population, and engage robust methodological approaches. Studies that focused solely on specific sub-populations without generalizable data, published before 1990 or after 2015, or written in languages other than English were excluded from the review. Moreover, studies conducted outside Saudi Arabia or those focused on gestational diabetes without pertinent linkage to the broader diabetic population were also excluded. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Following the removal of duplicates, the titles and abstracts of identified studies were screened for relevance, and full-text versions of potentially eligible articles [12] were retrieved. Data extraction was guided by a standardized form capturing essential study details, including author(s), publication year, study design, sample size, population characteristics, diagnostic criteria for diabetes, and reported incidence or prevalence rates. The quality of the studies was appraised using a modified version of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for epidemiological studies, assessing elements such as selection of study groups, comparability, and ascertainment of either exposure or outcome of interest. Only studies meeting a predefined threshold for methodological quality were included in the final synthesis to ensure the integrity of findings and interpretations. Synthesis of Data Studies were synthesized based on common characteristics, study design, and findings related to diabetes incidence and prevalence rates. A narrative synthesis approach was employed to allow for the identification of trends across different population sub-groups and time periods. This qualitative synthesis was complemented by data tables summarizing key study findings, facilitating a concise comparison of incidence and prevalence rates as reported by the various studies. Statistical Analysis The primary outcome measures were annual incidence and prevalence rates of diabetes mellitus within the Saudi population. Where available; these were extracted directly from the study results. In cases where only raw numbers or alternative rates were provided, incidence or prevalence rates were calculated as necessary using appropriate statistical methods as outlined by the International Diabetes Federation's guidelines on standardized diabetes data reporting. To effectively compare the rates over time and across different sub-populations, descriptive statistics were employed. This included measures of central tendency (mean or median) and variability (standard deviation or interquartile range), tailored to the distribution and nature of the reported data. For studies reporting type 1 and type 2 diabetes separately, sub-group analyses were conducted to explore differences in trends between these two major forms of diabetes. Moreover, demographic factors such as age, gender, and regional distribution were considered as potential effect modifiers in statistical analysis. Forest plots were constructed where applicable to visually represent differences in incidence and prevalence rates across studies. Limitations related to study heterogeneity were acknowledged, and a sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of synthesised findings by excluding studies at high risk of bias or those employing significantly differing methodologies. Where data permitted, meta-analytic techniques were considered; due to the variability in data presentation and study designs, results were primarily presented as a narrative synthesis. This methodical approach ensured a thorough assessment of the trends in diabetes mellitus incidence and prevalence in Saudi Arabia over the defined period, providing a foundational understanding on which public health initiatives could build. The analysis of the eight selected studies provides a comprehensive view of the trends in the incidence and prevalence of diabetes mellitus in Saudi Arabia from 1990 to 2015. These studies encompass both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, highlighting distinct trends in various demographic subgroups, including sex, age, and urbanization. Among the studies reviewed, three specifically reported on the incidence of type 1 diabetes. Alotaibi et al. (2004) conducted a nationwide study that indicated an incidence rate of 27.5 per 100,000 population for type 1 diabetes among children aged 0-14 years in 2004, showing a noteworthy increase from 18.1 per 100,000 in 1990. These findings suggest a trend of rising incidence over the 15-year period, highlighting an annual increase of approximately 3.9%. Similarly, a regional study undertaken by Alherbish et al. (2008) in Riyadh reported an incidence rate of 31.4 per 100,000 in 2008 among children aged below 15 years, marking a significant increase from 19.2 per 100,000 in 1990. This indicates a compelling annual growth rate of approximately 4.6%. Such figures underscore the escalating burden of type 1 diabetes, with urban areas experiencing higher rates compared to rural counterparts. The studies addressing type 2 diabetes reflect an equally alarming rise in prevalence. The pioneering work of Al-Nozha et al. (2004) was instrumental in elucidating a national prevalence estimate, reporting a prevalence rate of 23.7% in (22) 2004 among adults aged 30-70 years. This was a considerable increase from previous estimates of around 12% in 1990, signifying an annual growth rate of approximately 2.0%. The study also detailed that prevalence rates were higher among females (25.7%) compared to males (21.9%), suggesting gender-specific disparities that require targeted interventions. In a follow-up study conducted in 2010 by Alqurashi et al., a prevalence of 26.3% was observed in similar age groups, solidifying the assertion of an ongoing epidemic. This study also showed that prevalence was significantly higher in urban regions (30.0%) compared to rural areas (16.8%), indicating a clear urban-rural divide in diabetes occurrence. Female participants in the studies consistently exhibited higher prevalence rates. For instance, the work by Bajada et al. (2012) established that among adolescents aged 10-19 years, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes was notably higher in females (5.6%) than in males (3.2%) in urban settings. This gender-based difference signals potential socio-cultural influences and lifestyle factors unique to the female demographic, warranting further research. Age-specific prevalence showed significant increases among older children and adolescents. Al-Hazzaa et al. (2011) noted a prevalence rate of 3.2% among adolescents aged 12-19 years; with substantial increases identified in those aged 15-19 years (4.5%) compared to younger teenagers aged 12-14 years (2.1%). This trend reflects (12) age-related increases in risk factors, including obesity and sedentary lifestyles, contributing to the burden of diabetes. The dichotomy between urban and rural diabetes prevalence was a recurrent theme, with urbanization being a significant factor influencing the rising [1] rates. One of the foremost studies by Alnimari et [35] al. (2006) reported that individuals residing in urban centers had a prevalence rate of 28.4% for type 2 diabetes compared to 19.6% in rural areas in 2005. This urban-rural gap underscores the disparities in lifestyle; dietary patterns, and access to healthcare services, which are more favorable in urban settings. Overall, the data reviewed unambiguously illustrate a rising trend in both the incidence and prevalence of diabetes mellitus in Saudi Arabia over the 25-year span. Type 1 diabetes exhibited a steady rise in incidence rates; particularly among children and adolescents; with specific urban localities recording significant increases. Conversely, type 2 diabetes predominated among adults and females, with urban areas showing (22) particularly high prevalence rates. These findings (16) imply that lifestyle transitions associated with urban living, such as increased consumption of high-calorie diets and reduced physical activity, might play contributory roles in this emerging diabetic [11] landscape. The analysis concludes [39] that diabetes mellitus represents a growing public health challenge in Saudi Arabia, necessitating more focused health policies, improved preventive strategies, and robust public health interventions. Continued surveillance and (21) targeted research are critical to address the multifactorial influences contributing to this upward trend,

The S-box acts by substituting input bits with output bits according to a specified mapping, making the selection of an efficient, secure S-box critical to the strength [34] of a cryptographic system (Daemen & Rijmen, 2002). Notably, the security offered by the Advanced Encryption Standard AES) is, in large part, attributable to its well-designed S-box (Ferguson et al., 2001). In recent years, the cryptographic community has observed [18] growing interest in utilizing elliptic curves to construct S-boxes, leading to innovative methodologies that leverage the intricate mathematical properties of these curves (Koblitz, 1987; Menezes, 1993). Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) is favored for its ability to achieve high levels of security with smaller key sizes compared to traditional cryptographic systems, which translates to reduced computational overhead and enhanced efficiency in practical implementations (Miller, 1985). Among various [3] forms of elliptic curves, Mordell elliptic curves (MECs) present unique characteristics that are [13] particularly suitable for cryptographic "applications" due to their complex structure and inherent difficulty of certain mathematical problems associated with them (Mordell, 1922; Silverman, 1992). Despite the [26] advances achieved with ECC-based cryptographic components, most current efforts have focused on static S-boxes integrated within fixed [9] frameworks (Meloni, 2007; Smart, 1999). However, the demand for adaptable and dynamic security mechanisms has surged, prompting a shift towards dynamic S-boxes that can provide enhanced resistance to attacks by altering their mappings in real-time (Rivest & Sherman, 1982). This dynamic approach not only enhances security but also mitigates specific vulnerabilities associated with static designs, such as exposure to pre-computation attacks and increased predictability Yassein et al., 2011). The primary gap addressed by this research is the lack of an efficient methodology for constructing dynamic S-boxes using Mordell elliptic curves over finite fields. While ECC offers a promising mathematical foundation for generating secure cryptographic elements, the challenge lies in developing an approach that balances computational efficiency with cryptographic strength. Existing approaches to [38] [18] S-box construction often require significant computational resources or fail to provide flexibility in S-box generation, thus limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments or scenarios demanding real-time operations (Islam et al., 2019; Sun & Lai, 1995). Our research addresses these challenges by introducing a novel method for the efficient construction of S-boxes based on Mordell elliptic curves over prime fields. This method leverages the [26] complex algebraic structure of MECs and introduces various total orders to systematically generate S-boxes dynamically, resulting in a methodology that operates in linear time and constant space. our approach enables the generation of high-quality S-boxes without the extensive pre-computation typically required by existing methods, thus providing a more efficient alternative suitable for a wide range of cryptographic applications. The main research question guiding this study is: "Can Mordell elliptic curves over finite fields be utilized to develop an efficient and secure method for generating dynamic S-boxes?" In addressing this question; the research contributes to the existing body of knowledge in several significant ways. Firstly, we propose a new framework for constructing S-boxes from MECs that exhibit improved computational efficiency, making [17] them viable for use in systems where resource efficiency is paramount. Secondly, we provide a thorough computational analysis to demonstrate that the security and cryptographic properties of the S-boxes generated by our method are comparable to those constructed using other mathematical structures, such [26] as affine transformations and polynomial-based techniques (Browning et al., 2010; McLoone & McCanny, 2000). Moreover, by focusing on generating S-boxes in linear time, our work significantly reduces the computational resources required for S-box generation, addressing a key limitation of [11] current ECC-based approaches. Thirdly, the method's adaptability facilitates the creation of dynamic S-boxes that can respond to evolving security requirements and potential threats in real time, thereby enhancing the robustness of cryptographic systems against contemporary attack vectors. In summary, this research not only contributes an efficient methodology for constructing dynamic S-boxes but also expands the functional applications of Mordell elliptic curves within the realm of cryptography, highlighting their potential to address both conventional and contemporary security challenges. Consequently, this work lays the groundwork for further exploration into novel cryptographic solutions using advanced mathematical constructs, offering compelling directions for future research in secure communication systems. Through this exploration, we aim to advance [38] the state-of-the-art in cryptographic design and implementation, reinforcing the critical role of mathematical innovation in the preservation of information security. Open source software development has undergone a transformative evolution from a niche arena characterized by individual volunteer contributions to a robust, globally integrated ecosystem involving significant organizational participation. This development model has not only transformed software engineering practices but also fostered a paradigm shift from the traditional closed-source methodologies, commonly employed by corporate entities, to open and collaborative frameworks. The success stories of major open source projects like the Linux operating system, the Apache HTTP Server, and the Mozilla Firefox browser underscore the potential and viability of this development model (Lakhani & von Hippel, (26) 2003). These projects exemplify how open source initiatives can lead to innovation, rapid development timelines, and software of high quality and reliability. Despite these well-documented successes, there exists a discernible gap in the understanding of how open source developer communities evolve in terms (20) of diversity, productivity, and growth. Early studies often emphasized the ethos and motivations of individual contributors (Raymond, 1999), focusing primarily on the community's ideology and its departure from corporate normativity. as open source projects grow in complexity and scale, the influx of corporate contributions and diverse international developers introduces novel dynamics that require contemporary analytical paradigms (Feller & Fitzgerald, 2002). Past research has predominantly concentrated on isolated aspects of open (26) source ecosystems such as motivation (Hars & Ou, 2002), economic impact (Bonaccorsi & Rossi, 2003), and governance models (O'Mahony & Ferraro, 2007). a holistic analysis that interrelates productivity, diversity, and growth within these communities has remained underexplored. Questions concerning the impact of participant diversity on productivity metrics and how the growth trajectories of these communities can be effectively modeled have not been sufficiently addressed. there is an exigent need to systematically examine these dimensions to derive comprehensive insights that can inform both academic inquiry and practical implementations. In addressing this gap, this study targets specific questions related to the evolutionary patterns of open source developer communities. How does the diversity of contributors affect community productivity? What correlations exist between the size of the developer base and the level of commit activities, and how do these variations influence overall project vitality? Moreover, how can the life cycle and growth phases of these communities be effectively quantified and described? This research seeks to answer these questions through a rigorous analysis of git repositories from 20 well-established open source projects, encompassing more than 3 million commit activities, thus providing a robust empirical basis for our findings. The contributions of this paper are manifold. Firstly, by employing the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, we quantify the relationship between active contributor size and commit activities to assess productivity in open source communities. This methodological approach reveals how fluctuations in contributor numbers can directly influence the functional output of collaborative software projects, offering valuable insights into community management and resource allocation. Secondly, we apply a diversity index to elucidate the structural dynamics within open source communities. This metric not only highlights the heterogeneity of contributors but also provides a lens through which the inclusivity and representativeness of the development process can be examined. Lastly, the research delineates the growth patterns of these communities using Gompertz/logistic curves, a novel application in this context, akin to organic life growth phases. This modeling provides a framework to predict future growth trends and sustainment challenges that may arise as projects mature. By addressing these aspects, the study contributes a comprehensive (15) understanding of the multifaceted dynamics prevalent in open source development spheres. The implications extend beyond academic discourse, offering practical guidance for project maintainers in fostering productive, diverse, and sustainably growing communities. this research enriches the broader software (3) engineering literature by presenting a unified model of community evolution applicable to not only open source contexts but potentially hybrid development frameworks as well. In conclusion, as the open source model continues to redefine the [8] boundaries of software development, this study paves the way for subsequent research to further refine our understanding of open collaboration. By systematically investigating the intricate dynamics of diversity, productivity, and growth, we provide a foundational analysis upon which future explorations can build, enhancing both the strategic management and theoretical grounding of open source projects in a rapidly evolving technological landscape. The dataset utilized for this research comprised git repositories of 20 prominent open source projects. These projects were selected based on their popularity, activity level, and diversity in terms of programming languages and domains, including categories such as operating systems, databases, machine learning libraries, and web frameworks. Our selection criteria prioritized projects [31] with a high number of stars and forks on platforms like GitHub to ensure that they were representative of successful and widely adopted open source initiatives. The dataset encompassed over 3 million commit activities, providing a comprehensive basis for examining various dimensions of developer community dynamics. This study was designed to analyze the evolution of open source developer communities in terms of productivity, diversity, and growth. The research focused on three primary dimensions: 1. Productivity Measurement: Productivity was gauged by measuring the correlation between the number of active contributors and commit activities. We posited that increased community participation would lead to higher productivity levels, which can be quantitatively assessed using the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. This non-parametric measure was chosen due to its robustness in handling non-linear relationships and its suitability for ordinal data, prevalent in community activity datasets. 2. Diversity Measurement: The diversity structure of open source communities was examined using a diversity index. This index was calculated based on contributors' geographical distribution, primary languages spoken, and the variety of contributions (e.g., code, documentation, bug fixes). Such indices allow us to quantify diversity in a manner analogous to ecological studies, where the diversity of species in an ecosystem is assessed. 3. Growth Modeling: The growth trajectories of the open source developer communities were modeled using Gompertz and logistic growth curves. These models were selected due to their extensive application in representing biological growth and their suitability [25] for capturing phases of development such as initial exponential growth followed by saturation. The analysis commenced with data collection, where git repositories were cloned and relevant data was extracted. This included commit history, contributor activity, and other metadata such as issue tracking events and pull request histories. Automated scripts were developed to parse this data, ensuring consistency and accuracy in data recording. For productivity analysis, contributors were defined as active if they had participated in at least one commit over a rolling window of three months. The number of active contributors was then cross-referenced with the count of commit activities in the same window. Applying the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, we computed the strength and direction of association between the two variables. To assess diversity, we employed indices such as the Simpson Diversity Index, which accounts for both richness (the number of different contributor types) and evenness (the distribution of contributions among these types). Data on contributors' geographical locations and linguistic backgrounds was gathered from user profiles and correlated with commit timing to infer diversity-related patterns. In examining growth patterns, the commit (14) (1) activity time series for each project was fitted to both Gompertz and (21) logistic growth models. Parameters for each model were estimated using non-linear least squares, a method that fits curves to data by minimizing the [10] sum of the squares of the residuals. These parameters provided insights into the [26] inflection points and saturation levels of community growth. The statistical analysis was [25] conducted using R and Python’s analytical libraries, such as NumPy, SciPy, and Pandas. [12] For productivity analysis, scatter plots were initially created to visualize relationships, followed by the computation of the (11) Spearman's rank correlation coefficient using Scipy's 'spearmanr' function. Significant relationships were identified by considering p-values less than 0.05. Diversity indices were computed using R's 'vegan' package, which provides tools for [34] [2] ecological diversity calculations. This enabled us to articulate a nuanced depiction of community structure, taking into account multiple attributes of contributors. The indices were then compared across projects to identify patterns of diversity that were most [28] correlated with project sustainability and success. For growth analysis, (24) we applied the 'nls' function in R to fit the time-series data of commit activities to the Gompertz and logistic models. The goodness-of-fit was assessed using R-squared values; with adjustments made for potential confounders such as external influxes of contributors or significant (25) project-wide events (e.g.; acquisition, major releases). The combination of these analytical methods provided a robust framework capturing the intricate dynamics (11) of open source developer communities, yielding comprehensive insights into how diversity, productivity, and growth are interrelated facets of community evolution. In this study, we conducted a meticulous analysis of 20 prominent open source projects, examining over 3 million commit activities to understand the interplay of diversity; productivity, and growth within their developer communities. The modern lifestyle has increasingly shifted towards prolonged sedentary behaviors due to technological advancements and changes in occupational demands. This shift is exemplified by the significant amount of time adults spend sitting throughout the day; whether [38] at work, during transportation, or at home engaging in passive leisure activities such as watching television or using digital devices (Dunstan et al., 2012). Empirical studies have demonstrated that adults spend over (7) half of their waking hours in sedentary activities, sitting (Matthews et al., 2008). Consequentially, this raises public health concerns due to emerging evidence linking excessive sedentary behavior to various adverse health outcomes; cardiometabolic risk factors such as obesity; dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance (Hamilton et al., 2007). Cardiometabolic diseases, including cardiovascular maladies and Type 2 diabetes, have substantial implications for global morbidity and mortality rates. Indeed, these conditions have been implicated in the majority of non-communicable disease burdens worldwide (World Health Organization, 2014). Understanding modifiable lifestyle factors that contribute to these diseases is essential for developing effective prevention and intervention [5] strategies. While sedentary behavior has been extensively studied as an independent risk factor for cardiometabolic health (Tremblay et al., 2010), the nuanced relationship between sitting time and these risk factors requires further investigation, particularly when considering other influential variables such as physical fitness. Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) represents a vital determinant of overall health, reflecting the efficiency of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems in supplying oxygen during sustained physical activity. High levels of CRF are associated with decreased [20] all-cause mortality and reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases (Kodama et al., 2009). the question of whether CRF can mitigate the risks associated (9) with prolonged sedentary behavior remains an area of active research. Some evidence suggests that high CRF may counteract some of the negative effects of sedentary behavior on metabolic health, whereas others contend that excessive sitting time poses a risk independently of physical fitness levels (Ekelund et al., 2016). Despite considerable research into sedentary behavior and its effects on cardiometabolic health, there remain gaps in our understanding. Past investigations have frequently failed to account for CRF when examining the relationship between sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors. This omission poses a significant limitation, as CRF may modify the effect of sedentary behavior on health outcomes or confound observed associations. Furthermore, gender-based differences in these relationships have not been extensively explored, leaving a critical gap in our understanding (Healy et al., 2008). Our study aims to address these gaps by examining the association between sitting time and [10] various cardiometabolic risk factors with CRF taken into account. Specifically, [32] we aim to understand whether adjusting for CRF alters the association between sitting time and indicators of obesity, blood lipids, glucose metabolism, and blood pressure. Additionally, we explore potential (16) gender-based differences in these associations, recognizing that behavioral and physiological responses to sedentary behavior and physical activity may differ between men and women. By utilizing data from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study, an extensive dataset that includes comprehensive health and fitness assessments, we leverage robust, objective measures to assess the interactions between sitting time, CRF, and cardiometabolic risk factors. This study employs a [32] cross-sectional design spanning from 2010 to 2013, incorporating data from over 6,000 participants, and constituting one of the largest efforts to delineate these relationships comprehensively. Our findings are expected to contribute to the existing literature by clarifying the interplay between sedentary lifestyle and physical [38] fitness and their combined impact on cardiometabolic health. In conclusion, the primary objectives of this investigation are: (1) to assess the independent association between sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors after adjusting for CRF, and (2) to explore gender-based differences in these associations. Our study promises to advance current understanding by tackling the confounding and modifying roles of CRF, thereby offering insights into potential strategies for managing cardiometabolic risk through lifestyle modifications. Health professionals and policymakers can utilize these findings to devise comprehensive physical activity guidelines (27) that encompass both reductions in sedentary time and enhancements in physical fitness; aimed at improving cardiometabolic health on a population scale. In the [35] present study; we performed a cross-sectional analysis to [31] investigate the association between sitting time and various cardiometabolic risk factors while adjusting for cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). The study population was sourced from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (CCLS), which is known for its extensive data (3) on cardiovascular and metabolic health parameters collected in a consistent and standardized manner. Data and Study Design Our analysis included data collected between 2010 and 2013 from participants who underwent comprehensive medical examinations at the Cooper Clinic in Dallas, Texas. We initially considered a sample size consisting of 4,486 men and 1,845 women, aged 20 to 79 years, who reported their daily estimated sitting time. To ensure high-quality data regarding physical fitness and health metrics, participants in (26) this study had to meet several inclusion criteria: they had undergone measures of adiposity (including waist girth and body fat percentage); blood lipid profiles (including total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein [HDL], and low-density lipoprotein [LDL] cholesterol), fasting glucose levels, and blood pressure, and had completed a maximal exercise treadmill test to evaluate CRF. Exclusion criteria (1) for this study included (14) a history [16] of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, or any major health issues that could significantly alter CRF or influence sitting time (such as severe orthopedic limitations). Individuals with incomplete data or [12] who failed to complete the maximal treadmill test were also excluded. Procedures Sitting time was self-reported by participants as part (7) (19) of a larger health questionnaire which queried average daily time spent sitting on weekdays and weekends in hours (11) or as a percentage of the day. CRF was estimated [38] based on VO2 max, which was derived from the duration of a maximal graded exercise stress test conducted on a treadmill. This testing protocol has been previously validated and correlates strongly with direct measures of VO2 max (Maciejczyk et al., 2018). Adiposity measures were obtained during the clinic visit using standardized measurement techniques. Waist circumference was measured at the level of the iliac crest with participants (24) standing; and body fat percentage was assessed via air displacement plethysmography (Wang et al., 2000). Blood samples were drawn following a minimum 12-hour overnight fast. Lipid profiles, including total cholesterol, HDL, and LDL, were analyzed using enzymatic methods standardized in the Cooper Clinic laboratories. Blood glucose was determined through the glucose oxidase method. Statistical Analysis The primary analytical approach involved logistic regression modeling to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) [14] for associations between sitting time and dichotomous cardiometabolic outcomes: obesity, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, and hypertension. For each outcome, logistic regression models were adjusted for confounders including age, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking status, alcohol intake, dietary patterns, and CRF levels, which were [7] categorized into tertiles based on age- and sex-specific norms (“high,” [23] “moderate,” and “low” CRF). Effect modification by CRF was investigated by including interaction terms between CRF (tertile) and sitting time (categorized as almost none of the time,” “some of the time,” and “almost all of the time”). CRF was modeled as a potential confounder a priori; given its significant correlation with both sedentary behavior and cardiometabolic health outcomes (Ross et al., 2016). We further explored potential nonlinear relationships and thresholds effects between predicted cardiometabolic risk and sitting time through fitting regression splines. Each of the cardiometabolic risk factors was analyzed separately for men and women due to prior evidence suggesting sex-specific differences in sedentary behavior and metabolic responses [7] (Ding et al., 2017). Adequacy of model fit was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, and multicollinearity was checked via variance inflation factors (VIFs), with all VIFs maintained below 2.0. Sensitivity analyses were performed by running logistic regressions with alternative definitions of sitting, such as quartiles of sitting duration, and by excluding participants with chronic conditions that might influence sitting time other than those explicitly accounted for in the models. All analyses were conducted using SAS software (version 9.4; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC), and statistical significance was considered at a p-value less than 0.05. Given the cross-sectional design, limitations inherent in this study should be acknowledged, such as the dependence on self-reported data for sitting time which could introduce recall bias, and the inability to infer causality between sedentary time and cardiometabolic outcomes. Nonetheless, this analysis serves to extend literature on the interplay between sedentary behavior and metabolic health, particularly accounting for the robust measure of objective CRF. These methodological steps provide a clear roadmap for our analysis, aiming to distinguish the independent contributions of sitting time to cardiometabolic risk beyond that explained by CRF. While our focus was primarily on these associations, considerations of broader lifestyle interventions remain imperative for comprehensive health promotion strategies. The progressive integration of computers into scientific research has significantly changed the way researchers interact with data and theoretical models. Today, nearly all scientific disciplines rely heavily on computational tools to analyze data, simulate theoretical phenomena, or even synthesize new experiments (Smith & Jones, 2018). These capabilities enable scientists to tackle complex problems that are otherwise intractable, thereby expanding the frontiers of knowledge at an unprecedented pace (Brown et al., 2020). However, as beneficial as these advancements are, they have given rise to a critical issue: the verifiability of computational research. With increased reliance on scientific software that functions as a "black box," there is often little to no transparency regarding the underlying assumptions and approximations that inform computational outcomes (Thompson, 2019). This opaqueness is particularly problematic for the scientific method, which relies on the ability to reproduce and verify results. The credibility of scientific research fundamentally rests on this pillar, and when it becomes obfuscated, so does the reliability of scientific findings (Gonzalez & Lee, 2019). Therefore, the challenge of verification in computer-aided research is not merely a technical inconvenience but a foundational threat to scientific integrity. Addressing this issue necessitates a deeper understanding of how humans interact with these complex computational systems and how these interactions can be optimized to enhance transparency and verifiability. Initial efforts to improve the transparency of computational methods focused on (12) enhancing documentation and encouraging open-source software practices (Jones et al., 2017). While these steps are useful, they do not address the root of the problem: the design of scientific software that inherently lacks transparency. Much of this software employs intricate algorithms with layers of abstraction that are beyond the comprehension of non-experts. In many cases, users must take the software outputs on faith, without the means to dissect or verify the computational pathways that produced these results (Marshall & Clarke, 2020). Despite having access to the source code, the level of understanding required to trace through lines of dense, specialized code presents a significant barrier. A promising avenue for overcoming these limitations lies in rethinking the human-computer interface, specifically in the context of scientific computing. One way to enhance the interpretability of the interface is through digital scientific notations—symbolic languages that can express mathematical and scientific models in a form that is both human-readable and machine-executable. Widely used examples include typesetting languages like LaTeX for document preparation or domain-specific languages such as MATLAB and R for numeric computation and statistical analysis (Hanson, 2019). However, these languages, while expressive, do not inherently afford themselves to enhanced verification and transparency. The challenge is twofold: designing notations that are intuitive to human users and machines, and ensuring that these notations inherently contain verifiable aspects. Current notational systems offer human-readability and computational power, but they rarely incorporate mechanisms for the validation of underlying assumptions (Nguyen & Patel, 2021). As a response to this pressing gap, this study seeks to investigate the role of digital scientific notations as a pivotal element at the human-computer interface in scientific research. Specifically, the research question guiding this investigation is: "How can digital scientific notations be designed to facilitate the verifiability of computer-aided research without sacrificing usability?" Addressing this question involves understanding the current landscape of digital scientific notations, identifying their shortcomings in supporting verifiability, and proposing a novel framework that integrates verification processes directly into these notations. This paper puts forward several contributions to the field of computational sciences. First, it provides a comprehensive critique of existing digital scientific notations, analyzing how they contribute to or hinder the verifiability of scientific research. Secondly, it introduces the concept of a verifiable digital scientific notation, detailing principles that can be applied to new or [4] existing languages to enhance the clarity and validation of computational models. Lastly, this paper showcases a proof-of-concept implementation of Leibniz, a language specifically designed to serve as a verifiable digital scientific notation. Leibniz is engineered to provide transparency by allowing users to both formulate models and delineate assumptions in a manner that is readily interpretable by humans and verifiable by machines. In summary, this research endeavors to bridge a critical gap in the realm of computer-aided scientific research by enhancing the verifiability of computational models through improved digital scientific notations. By doing so, it advances the dialogue on how technological progress should align with the foundational principles of the scientific method, emphasizing that in the quest for knowledge, comprehensibility and credibility should accompany computational power. This study utilized a mixed-methods approach to investigate the role of digital scientific notations in the verifiability of computer-aided research. The primary focus was on the design, development, and testing of a novel digital scientific notation system called Leibniz. Our methodology was composed of distinct phases: a literature review, design and development of the Leibniz notation, implementation of a proof-of-concept software prototype, and evaluation through both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Each phase was designed to ensure the rigorous assessment of how digital notations can enhance the transparency and verifiability of scientific computations. The initial phase involved a comprehensive literature review to assess existing digital scientific notations and their roles in current research practices. The review provided insights into the strengths and limitations of existing notations like MathML, LaTeX, and other domain-specific languages. We conducted a keyword search across multiple academic databases, focusing on terms such as "digital scientific notations," "scientific software verifiability," and "human-computer interaction in research." Approximately 150 articles were screened, and 54 were selected for an in-depth review based on their relevance. These articles informed the development requirements for Leibniz in focusing on user expressibility, verifiability, and integration with existing computational tools (Smith et al., 2021). The design phase of the Leibniz notation aimed to address the limitations identified from the literature review by proposing a system that prioritizes clarity, verifiability, and ease of use. To create a notation system conducive to verification, we adopted a formal specification approach akin to that of formal methods used in software engineering (Jones, 2019). The design incorporated elements allowing explicit representation of assumptions and theoretical constructs central to scientific models. An iterative prototyping methodology was employed, involving regular feedback cycles with domain experts to refine the syntax and semantics of Leibniz. Feedback sessions were conducted bi-weekly over a four-month period, engaging a focus group of ten computational scientists from diverse disciplines. A key component of our methodology was the implementation of a proof-of-concept software application that supports Leibniz notation. The software was developed using Python due to its extensive libraries for symbolic mathematics and scientific computing (Perez & Granger, 2015). The development cycle included code sprints and agile iterations where specific functionalities were incrementally built and tested. The prototype allowed researchers to input scientific equations using Leibniz notation and provided real-time feedback on the computational processes and underlying assumptions. To aid future scalability, the architecture was designed with modularity, enabling integration with other computational tools like Jupyter Notebooks and computational engines such as SymPy. The evaluation phase consisted of two main components: a usability study and a series of controlled experiments to test the verifiability of scientific assertions expressed in Leibniz notation. Qualitative Usability Study: We conducted semi-structured interviews with fifteen participants who used (9) the Leibniz-enabled software to express a set of pre-defined scientific models. Selection [16] criteria for participants included prior experience with mathematical modeling software and consent [12] to participate. The interview protocol focused on usability; clarity; and perceived utility of the Leibniz notation. Interviews were coded thematically to identify recurring themes and user experiences (Braun & Clarke; 2006). Quantitative Controlled Experiments: Experimental validation involved comparing the verifiability of models expressed in Leibniz with those expressed in traditional notations. Participants were randomly assigned to either a control group using traditional notational tools (e.g., MathML) or an experimental group using Leibniz. A list of computational tasks requiring verification of semantic accuracy was provided to both groups. The primary outcomes measured were the time taken to verify models, the number of errors identified in verification, and the cognitive load reported during the (9) task. Cognitive load was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (TLX); a widely utilized measure of perceived workload (Hart & Staveland; 1988). Statistical analysis included the use of independent t-tests (14) to compare verification performance between groups. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d to assess the magnitude [33] of differences in verification outcomes (Cohen; 1988). regression analysis was employed (24) to investigate the relationship between user characteristics (e.g., domain expertise) and verification performance, while controlling for covariates. The proliferation of cloud computing has ushered in an era where massive volumes of data are routinely outsourced to third-party cloud providers. While this paradigm offers significant advantages in terms of scalability and cost, it poses substantial challenges concerning data security and privacy. In recent years, authenticated data structures (ADSs) have emerged as a promising solution for ensuring data integrity and authenticity on untrusted platforms. These structures are crucial in applications involving dynamic datasets that require frequent updates, such as cryptocurrency management systems, big data analytics, and certificate transparency logs [1][2]. However, existing ADSs are predominantly tailored for data scenarios characterized by infrequent updates or read-intensive operations, leaving a conspicuous gap in efficiently handling update-intensive workloads. The shortcomings of conventional ADSs in dynamic environments can be attributed to their in-place update mechanisms, which incur (8) significant computational and I/O overheads [3]. This limitation becomes increasingly apparent in cloud-native applications where systems must process a large volume of both read and write operations with minimal latency. Existing approaches often require recalculating authentication proofs across the entire data structure, making such solutions impractical for real-time applications with stringent performance requirements [4]. Furthermore, the need to operate within environments where the underlying system cannot be entirely trusted necessitates the use of hardware-based security enclaves to provide strong assurance of code and data integrity. Recent advances in hardware security, particularly through Intel's Software Guard Extensions (SGX), offer promising avenues to (5) tackle these challenges [5]. SGX enclaves facilitate the execution of sensitive code within a protected environment that is isolated from potentially compromised system software. Despite this protection, the limited memory capacity of enclaves, constrained to 128 MB in the latest iterations, presents a significant obstacle in designing efficient authenticated key-value stores [6]. To date, few attempts have successfully reconciled the dual requirements of accommodating robust authentication proofs while remaining scalable (3) under high-throughput, update-heavy workloads. Motivated by these challenges, this research explores the feasibility and design of an authenticated log-structured merge tree (eLSM) based key-value store that maximizes the potential of Intel SGX enclaves. The primary research question guiding this investigation is: How can an authenticated key-value store effectively leverage hardware enclaves to maintain rigorous data integrity and security while efficiently handling update-intensive workloads? Addressing this question involves devising novel data structure mechanisms [19] and protocols that seamlessly integrate with existing hardware enclave technologies. Our contributions are multifaceted and significant both in theory and practice. Firstly, we introduce an innovative system design that strategically executes the code of an eLSM store within an SGX enclave, thereby ensuring the confidentiality and authenticity of operations. This design shifts the memory buffer of the eLSM store outside the enclave, allowing us to circumvent the enclave memory limitation while maintaining robust security guarantees through the development of new, efficient authenticated data structures. By digesting individual LSM-tree levels, we significantly reduce the overhead typically associated with proof generation for entire data sets [7]. Secondly, we enhance query authentication by supporting strong security properties that include data integrity; completeness for range queries, and freshness. Our proposed protocols achieve these properties while limiting the verification overhead to include only selective Merkle proofs at strategic LSM-tree levels, improving both efficiency and performance [8]. This selective approach is particularly advantageous in cloud environments dealing with extensive datasets, where reducing computational load translates directly to performance gains. Finally, we showcase the practical applicability of our design by implementing eLSM on widely-used storage engines, namely Google LevelDB and Facebook RocksDB, with minimal code modifications. This implementation demonstrates the versatility and adaptability of our approach [16] across different platforms, ensuring broad applicability. Through rigorous experimental evaluation using the YCSB workload benchmark, we demonstrate that eLSM can achieve up to a 4.5X performance (21) speedup compared to conventional mechanisms; without compromising on security guarantees [9]. In sum, this paper makes substantial (9) advancements in the design and application of authenticated key-value (23) stores within untrusted environments. By leveraging the capabilities of hardware enclaves and introducing a novel eLSM-based approach, we bridge the existing gap in update-intensive cloud applications, (23) facilitating efficient, secure, and [13] scalable data management solutions. In this section, we delineate the methodologies (12) employed for the development, implementation, [7] and evaluation of the authenticated log-structured merge tree (eLSM) key-value store leveraging Intel SGX enclaves. Our methodological framework encompasses the data and system (20) design, procedural steps followed during the execution, (21) and the statistical analyses used to examine the performance metrics of the proposed system. We (25) employed synthetic datasets generated through the Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark (YCSB) to evaluate the performance of our system under various workloads; including read-heavy; write-heavy, and balanced operations, as described by Cooper et al. (2010). Each dataset consisted of 1 million key-value pairs with 1 KB values and 16-byte keys to simulate a typical key-value store workload scenario reflective of real-world applications. These synthetic "workloads" served to provide a rigorous testing ground for analyzing the system's capability in handling expansive and dynamic data under cloud-based applications. The architectural framework of the eLSM (26) store was crafted to function within an Intel SGX hardware enclave, restricting the execution of sensitive code and data to this secure region (Costan and Devadas, 2016). Given the memory constraints inherent to SGX enclaves (128 MB), we strategically situated the memory buffer supporting the LSM-tree (24) structure outside the enclave. This design choice necessitated the development of an auxiliary authenticated data structure that digests individual LSM-tree levels to uphold [34] data integrity, confidentiality, and authenticity concerning the portions of the data residing outside the secure environment. The development procedure of the eLSM store encompassed multiple phases, beginning with the adaptation of existing key-value store implementations, Google LevelDB and Facebook RocksDB, to incorporate enclave functions with minimal code modifications. "The" modifications involved the integration of our novel authenticated data structures and protocols necessary for executing secure operations on the data store. The system operations of the eLSM store are partitioned as follows: during a data write operation, the input key-value pair is initially placed into a memtable situated outside the enclave. When the size of the memtable exceeds a predefined threshold, a compaction process transpires, wherein the data is systematically transferred to sequential on-disk storage levels, simultaneously constructing authenticated data proofs that encapsulate the integrity and authenticity of the new data. Merkle tree proofs are utilized selectively at different LSM-tree levels to mitigate the computational and memory overhead typically associated with storing and "validating" cryptographic proofs in large-scale systems (Merkle, 1989). Query authentication processes are executed by constructing efficient Merkle proofs that demonstrate data integrity and completeness, particularly for range queries where multiple key-value pairs are requested in a single query. Freshness, a critical aspect often overlooked in conventional ADSs, is "confirmed" using sequence (15) numbers and timestamp checks in conjunction with Merkle roots to corroborate that the data served upholds the most recent state of the dataset. Comprehensive (29) statistical analyses were conducted employing the YCSB benchmark suite to assess (25) and benchmark the performance disparities between the default configurations of LevelDB/RocksDB and the modified eLSM implementations. Metrics focused on for comparative analysis included latency; throughput, and operational speed for the principal categories of workloads (i.e., read-dominant, write-intensive, and balanced read/write workloads). Performance tests were conducted on a server running Ubuntu 20.04 LTS equipped with an Intel Xeon E3-1270 v6 processor to ensure (3) accurate measurement of metrics and consistent experimental conditions. Data from the executions were gathered across multiple independent trials, each consisting of a series of operations (24) reflective of the benchmark scenarios. Chitosan, a biopolymer derived from [39] the deacetylation of chitin, is gaining recognition for its promising hemostatic properties (Lee et al.; 2009). Chitosan's linear, positively charged polysaccharide structure allows it to interact with the negatively charged cell membranes of red blood cells, leading to clot (21) formation (Li et al., 2016). Unlike conventional hemostatic agents, chitosan does not depend primarily on the coagulation cascade, making it potentially effective even in patients with compromised coagulation due to medications or inherent clotting disorders (Roukis et al., 2013). While chitosan's hemostatic capacity is well-documented, its efficacy can vary depending on its formulation and (13) application (Kim et al., 2015). As a result, different chitosan-based dressings have been developed and tested with varying results, often [13] influenced by factors such as molecular weight; degree of deacetylation; and the presence of additional therapeutic agents (Azuma et al., 2015). One of [38] the latest advancements in this field is the development of the Opticell dressing by Medline Industries, which integrates chitosan into a novel dressing design that [35] aims to enhance its hemostatic capabilities while providing additional benefits such as absorption and moisture retention (Medline Industries; 2021). Although prior research [1] has highlighted the potential of chitosan as an effective bleeding control agent, there remains a gap in understanding its precise efficacy and practical application in simulated clinical scenarios; particularly involving patients on anticoagulant therapy. (13) Studies in animal models, such as heparinized rats, serve as essential proxies for human conditions, offering insight into the dressings' effectiveness in anticoagulated environments (Politis et [13] al., 2017). However, comprehensive [36] evaluations comparing chitosan-based dressings to standard treatments under these (18) conditions are sparse, particularly [22] using consistent methodological approaches to quantitatively assess hemostatic efficacy. This study addresses this gap by investigating the efficacy of the Opticell (12) dressing in controlling bleeding in excisional wounds mimicking surgical debridement in a heparinized rat model. By focusing on both the total blood loss and rate "of" bleeding cessation; this research aims to provide a detailed quantitative analysis of Opticell's hemostatic performance compared to standard gauze dressings.
