By leveraging the unique properties of chitosan, this study holds the potential to significantly impact wound management practices, offering a novel solution that could alleviate a common and persistent challenge in the field of surgery and wound care. This experimental study aimed to evaluate the hemostatic efficacy of chitosan-based Opticell dressings compared to standard gauze in the management of bleeding from excisional wounds in heparinized laboratory rats. The study was conducted following the ethical guidelines for animal research and was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The animal model consisted of male Sprague-Dawley rats, each weighing approximately 600 grams. These rats were chosen due to their physiological parallels to human hemodynamics, in blood clotting mechanisms, making them ideal for this hemostatic investigation (Nair et al., 2020). A total sample size of 12 rats was utilized, allocating six rats to each of the experimental (Opticell dressing) and control (standard gauze) groups, contributing to a total of 72 wounds evaluated across two different trials. Rats were administered an intraperitoneal injection of heparin at a dosage of 800 IU/kg two hours prior to the wound induction to simulate systemic anticoagulation, a condition that complicates hemostasis in clinical settings (Smith et al., 2018). Heparin acted as a blood thinner to increase bleeding propensity, thereby testing the efficacy of the dressings under challenging conditions. Following anticoagulation, three uniformly spaced, paired 12-mm excisional wounds were created on the dorsal surface of each rat using a sterile biopsy punch. This method ensured that each wound was identical in size and depth; which is crucial for consistency in the evaluation of the dressing's efficacy (Jones et al., 2017). For the intervention, Opticell or standard gauze dressings were randomly assigned to the wounds on each rat. Dressings were applied with a standardized pressure of 3 seconds, closely mimicking potential clinical practice with minimal handling (Brown and Patel, 2019). The primary outcome measured was total blood loss, determined by recording the weight of each dressing before and after application, with the difference representing the amount of absorbed blood. To assess total bleeding, the dressings were left in place on the wounds until bleeding cessation, with a designated maximum time of 10 minutes. Post-application, the dressings were removed and weighed using a high-precision electronic scale (±0.01 mg accuracy), comparing pre- and post-application weights to quantify blood absorption. Both intervention groups reached hemostasis within the 10-minute maximum period. Blood loss comparisons were then made between the Opticell and gauze dressings. A secondary aim of the study was to evaluate the rate of bleeding over a shorter time frame. This was accomplished by applying and removing the dressings at one-minute intervals, immediately reapplying them with the standardized gentle pressure of 3 seconds for three consecutive minutes. The rationale was to capture temporal changes in hemostatic capacity, particularly the initial moments of bleeding, which are often critical in surgical and emergency settings (Cheng and Zhao, 2021). Dressings from each time point were weighed identically to the total blood loss procedure, ensuring continuity in measurement precision. Descriptive and inferential statistics were employed to analyze (11) the data. The primary endpoint, total blood loss at 10 minutes, was presented as mean ± standard deviation, with a non-parametric Mann-Whitney test applied to assess differences between the two dressing groups. This test was chosen due to its robustness in handling small sample sizes and non-normal data distribution, which was confirmed through preliminary normality tests (Kruskal and Wallis, 1952). For the secondary endpoint, rate of bleeding at minutes 1, 2, and 3, data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test for pairwise comparisons. This analysis facilitated the identification of statistically significant differences in bleeding rates over time between the two groups, as evidenced by a threshold of P < .05 considered statistically significant (Garcia, 2019). All statistical analyses were executed using SPSS software version 25.0, ensuring rigorous data management and analysis integrity. Through these meticulous methodologies, the present study endeavored to contribute towards evidence-based practices in wound management, specifically targeting improved hemostatic interventions in patients subjected to anticoagulation therapy. The primary outcome of this study was to evaluate the hemostatic efficacy of Opticell, a chitosan-based dressing, compared to standard gauze in heparinized rats with excisional wounds. Our quantitative analysis focused on two main parameters: total blood loss and rate of bleeding cessation over a standardized time interval. In the assessment of total bleeding volume, both dressing types were left in place until hemostasis was achieved, which required 10 minutes in each case. Blood loss was significantly different between groups. the total blood loss measured with standard gauze dressings averaged 627 ± 47 mg over the 10-minute duration, whereas Opticell dressings resulted in a significantly reduced total blood loss of 247 ± 47 mg during the same period. During these repeated interventions, the gauze group's bleeding rate demonstrated a decline over the 3-minute measurement period, but remained substantially higher than that observed in the Opticell group. The statistically significant reduction in bleeding rates across all measured intervals (P < .05) was confirmed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test, emphasizing the efficacy of Opticell in rapidly achieving and maintaining hemostasis. These findings, based on a sample size of six wounds for the total bleeding assessment and twelve wounds for the rate of bleeding analysis per group, illustrate the functional benefits of chitosan's positive charge and unique polymeric structure in enhancing hemostatic outcomes. The reduced blood loss and more rapid achievement of hemostasis with Opticell highlight its potential as a valuable tool in managing bleeding during surgical procedures and wound care, especially in patients with impaired coagulation due to anticoagulant medications. Moreover, the standard deviation values indicate a consistent outcome across the experimental group, underscoring the reliability of [6] Opticell's performance in this controlled setting. (20) These robust quantitative results support the hypothesis that chitosan-based dressings may offer significant clinical advantages over (11) traditional gauze in contexts where enhanced hemostatic control is critical. In summary, the overall reduction in blood loss and prolonged hemostatic maintenance observed in the Opticell group suggest a promising adjunctive role for chitosan-based dressings in the management of surgical and trauma-related bleeding, reinforcing the need for further research to [28] explore clinical applications beyond experimental "animal" models. Discussion and Conclusion The findings of this study underscore the significant hemostatic potential of [32] chitosan-based Opticell dressings in the management of bleeding in patients under anticoagulation treatment. The comparative analysis between [7] Opticell and traditional gauze dressings demonstrates a clear advantage of the former in both total blood loss and the rate of bleeding cessation in heparinized rat models with excisional wounds. In the realm of spoken dialogue systems, disfluency poses significant challenges that impact the effective interpretation of speech. Disfluencies, which include phenomena such as pauses, hesitations, self-corrections, and false starts, are inherent aspects of spontaneous spoken dialogue. These elements are indicative of natural human conversation and reflect the dynamic and often unpredictable nature of spoken language (Shriberg, 2001; Clark & Wasow, 1998). As dialogue systems become increasingly prevalent, enhancing their ability to manage and interpret disfluent speech is paramount for developing more natural and responsive interactions between humans and machines. Traditionally, dialogue systems have aimed to process speech by first converting it into text, then applying natural language processing (NLP) techniques for interpretation (Jurafsky & Martin, 2009). this approach can be impeded by disfluency, which disrupts the flow and clarity of spoken language. identifying and addressing disfluencies are essential for accurately decoding a speaker's intended meaning and ensuring smooth conversational exchanges (Brennan & Schober, 2001). Furthermore, the need for dialogue systems to be incremental — processing speech word-by-word as it is spoken — is increasingly recognized as crucial for real-time applications (Schlangen & Skantze, 2009). Incremental processing enables immediate system responses, thus mimicking human conversational behavior more closely. The field has witnessed various attempts to address disfluency detection through a spectrum of methodologies. Early efforts mainly focused on rule-based systems or traditional machine learning models leveraging hand-engineered features (Heeman & Allen, 1999; Johnson & Charniak, 2004). While these approaches laid the groundwork, they often struggled with the variability and unpredictability inherent in disfluent speech. More recently, deep learning methodologies, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have gained prominence due to their ability to model temporal dependencies effectively (Graves, 2013). These models have demonstrated impressive performance in tasks such as speech recognition and syntactic parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Amodei et al., 2016) and are now being explored for disfluency detection. Despite these advances, a significant gap remains in developing domain-general systems capable of detecting disfluencies robustly across diverse dialogue contexts. Most existing approaches are domain-specific and require substantial amounts of annotated disfluent data for training, which limits their applicability and scalability (Liu et al., 2017). A system that can be trained on relatively clean data yet generalize well to various domains would be of tremendous value, providing both data efficiency and robustness. The central research question addressed in this paper is: How can we design a multi-task learning framework based on LSTMs for domain-general spoken disfluency detection that efficiently generalizes (25) across different datasets without losing accuracy? Multi-task learning, which involves training a model on multiple related tasks simultaneously, has shown promise in various NLP applications by leveraging shared representations to improve performance across tasks (Collobert & Weston, 2008; Ruder, 2017). By integrating multi-task learning with LSTM architectures, we hypothesize that it is possible to improve not only the accuracy of disfluency detection but also the generalization potential across different dialogue settings. This paper contributes to the ongoing discourse in three significant ways. First, we introduce a multi-task LSTM-based model designed to incrementally detect disfluency structures in spoken language. The choice of LSTMs is motivated by their proven capability in capturing long-range dependencies and temporal dynamics necessary for processing sequential data, while the multi-task framework aims to enhance generalization by learning shared patterns across tasks. Second, we present empirical results demonstrating the model's performance on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus, a challenging benchmark for dialogue systems. Our approach achieves a notable improvement of approximately 10 (19) percentage points over prior neural network-based methods, showcasing the effectiveness of our model architecture. [30] Finally, to evaluate the generalization potential of our model, we conduct a cross-domain assessment using the bAbI+ dataset. This dataset provides a controlled environment with synthetic goal-oriented dialogues and varying types of disfluencies. The performance of our model on bAbI+ without additional (26) training underscores its robustness and ability to handle diverse disfluent phenomena, shedding light on which types of disfluency may be universally addressed through domain-general processing strategies. Our findings suggest that by focusing on shared features across dialogue contexts; it [39] is possible to achieve both high accuracy in known domains and robust (3) generalization to new ones. This advancement holds promise for the broader application and scalability of spoken dialogue systems across diverse real-world scenarios. In recent decades, the issue of school exclusion, also commonly referred to as suspension, has garnered considerable attention from educational researchers, policy makers, and practitioners alike. School exclusion is a disciplinary measure imposed on students for [23] breaches (25) of conduct, resulting in their temporary removal from classroom instruction and; in some cases, from school premises altogether (Whitford & Levine‐Donnerstein, 2014). As schools are critical socialization agents—second only to families in their influence—they bear the dual responsibility of fostering academic achievement and upholding social discipline. Hence; the effects of exclusionary policies not only impact immediate educational outcomes but also have long-term implications for students' social and economic trajectories (Maimon, Antonaccio, & French, 2012). The prevailing corpus of research unequivocally indicates the adverse fallout of (26) school exclusions. Students who experience suspensions are more susceptible to academic failure, diminished graduation rates, (13) and subsequent involvement in antisocial or criminal activities (Arcia, 2006). Moreover, the suspension is often a precursor to entanglement with the juvenile justice system, thereby enmeshing young individuals in cycles of punitive control that restrict future opportunities for gaining skills and employment "(Townsend," 2000). Economically, the repercussions extend beyond the individual, imposing substantial costs on taxpayers and society at large (17) due to the increased likelihood of future social service needs and lower lifetime earnings potential among excluded students (Hemphill et al., 2006). Concurrently, school exclusions reveal profound (18) inequities entrenched within educational systems. Empirical evidence underscores that such disciplinary actions disproportionately affect males, ethnic minorities, and students from economically disadvantaged or special [3] educational needs backgrounds (Skiba et al., 2002). These disparities not only violate principles of educational equity but potentially exacerbate existing social inequalities; further marginalising (2) already vulnerable groups. Despite these insights, school exclusion persists as a disciplinary measure, highlighting a pressing need for effective interventions. Several programs have been implemented over the years with the aim of mitigating school exclusion rates. These initiatives, which range from enhancing academic skills to providing counseling and mentoring, and skills training for teachers, have demonstrated varying degrees of success. to date, there has been a lack of comprehensive syntheses regarding their overall efficacy. Previous [24] reviews have often been fragmented, focusing on localized interventions without appraising the broader landscape of preventative measures across different educational contexts (Wilson, Lipsey, & Derzon, 2003). Against this backdrop, the present systematic review seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by assembling evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating school-based interventions aimed at reducing exclusion rates. Our approach prioritizes a methodologically rigorous design to ensure reliable estimation of intervention impacts. As (11) the first systematic review of its kind, this study will not only quantify the efficacy of various intervention types but will [4] also explore moderating factors that potentially influence intervention outcomes, such as participant demographics, the theoretical underpinnings of interventions, and implementation quality. The central research question driving this review is: “Do school-based interventions reduce the use of exclusionary sanctions in schools?” In examining this, the study also seeks to discern the relative [6] effectiveness of different intervention approaches. (29) To this end, we will compare the impacts of interventions such (1) as the enhancement of academic skills, counselling, and mentoring/monitoring, as well as skills training for teachers. we [28] aim to delineate the role of contextual factors such as age, gender, and ethnicity of participants in shaping intervention efficacy. this review aspires to address the methodological heterogeneity observed across studies by evaluating whether characteristics specific to intervention design, implementation fidelity, and evaluator involvement consistently affect outcomes. For example, concerns have been raised that independent evaluators may report lower effect sizes compared to those involved in intervention design, highlighting potential biases needing empirical clarification (Lipsey, 1990). In terms of contributions, this review holds significant promise for both theoretical development and practical application in educational settings. Theoretically, it seeks to challenge and refine prevailing assumptions regarding the universality and translatability of intervention efficacy by situating its findings within a broader sociocultural context. Practically, the study provides policymakers and educators with evidence-based recommendations that can inform the design and implementation of future disciplinary practices, steering them toward interventions proven to be effective at reducing school exclusion. Ultimately, the findings aim to aid the development of more equitable and effective educational policies and practices, contributing to a reduction in exclusion-related disparities and ameliorating long-term adverse outcomes for at-risk student populations. This endeavor not only advances the scholarly discourse on school discipline but also holds implications for broader social justice endeavors within the educational system. The methodological framework for this systematic review was designed to rigorously evaluate the efficacy of school-based interventions in reducing disciplinary school exclusions. This process consisted of several key components, including data sources and inclusion criteria, study design and procedures, and statistical analysis methods. The initial phase of this research involved a comprehensive search for relevant studies that were published from 1980 onwards. Twenty-seven databases, including both published and unpublished literature repositories such as ERIC, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically explored. Searches were conducted from September 1 to December 1, 2015. In addition to database searches, targeted efforts were made to identify further studies through expert consultations, assessments of citation lists from previous reviews, and searching conference proceedings (Higgins & Green, 2011). This extensive search strategy yielded a total of 42,749 references. Studies were deemed eligible for inclusion if they met specific pre-established criteria. They needed to evaluate school-based or school-supported interventions aimed at reducing suspension rates and should target school-aged children between four and 18 years of age; regardless of nationality or social background. only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with at least one experimental group and one [37] control or placebo group were considered for inclusion, as these provide the highest quality evidence for intervention efficacy (Borenstein et al., 2009). The identification and selection of studies followed a rigorous two-stage screening process. Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) remains a formidable challenge in oncology, representing a heterogeneous disease with varied prognoses and diverse therapeutic responses. The advent of novel therapeutic strategies, including chemotherapy and targeted therapies (TT), has revolutionized the treatment landscape for MBC, offering patients improved survival outcomes and a better quality of life (Cardoso et al., 2019). Despite these advancements, the financial burden associated with cancer treatment has prompted an imperative for rigorous economic evaluations to ensure that novel interventions offer value for money (Purushotham [27] et al., 2012). Such evaluations [3] are essential to inform healthcare policy and reimbursement decisions, particularly in settings of resource limitation. Model-based economic evaluations have become a cornerstone in assessing the cost-effectiveness of cancer therapies, wherein they integrate data on clinical effectiveness, costs, and utilities derived from various sources (Briggs et al., 2006). Over the past two decades, researchers have increasingly utilized such models to evaluate existing and emerging chemotherapy and TT interventions "for" MBC. The focus on these (21) therapies is particularly noteworthy, given their diverse mechanisms of action. Chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells indiscriminately, whereas TT offers precision [31] by targeting specific molecular [2] pathways implicated in tumor growth and survival (Slamon et al., 2001). the clinical and economic outcomes of these interventions can vary significantly, necessitating a nuanced understanding of their value proposition. Despite these efforts, there remains a notable lack of transparency and variability in the quality of model-based economic evaluations. A previous review by Neyt et al. (2013) highlighted considerable discrepancies in methodological rigor among published studies, impeding the comparability and transferability of findings across different settings. These inconsistencies are exacerbated by the diversity (9) in model structures, included perspectives, and assumptions regarding disease progression and treatment effect (Gold et al., 1996). Moreover, the increasing trend of industry-sponsored research introduces a potential bias towards reporting more favorable cost-effectiveness ratios, as highlighted by Sorenson et al. (2009). The need for a standardized approach to enhance the transparency and validity of economic evaluations is therefore apparent. In light of these challenges, the primary aim of this paper is to critically review and synthesize the quality, health benefits, and value for money of chemotherapy and targeted therapy for MBC; through an analysis of model-based economic evaluations published between 2000 and 2014. Our review will provide a comprehensive overview of the characteristics and outcomes of (29) these models, identifying key trends and gaps in the literature. we aim to assess the relationship between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, thereby offering insights into factors that underpin high-quality economic evaluations. This analysis is underpinned by several research questions: (1) What are "the" prevailing model structures and assumptions employed in economic evaluations of chemotherapy [7] and TT for MBC? (2) How does the quality of these studies, as assessed through a standardized checklist, vary across different model characteristics? (3) "What" is the relationship between study sponsorship and reported cost-effectiveness outcomes? Our contributions are fourfold. First, we provide an updated synthesis of the economic evaluations [27] of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, highlighting changes in treatment paradigms and methodological innovations over time. This will enable researchers and policymakers to better understand the current state of evidence and guide future research and reimbursement decisions. Second, by applying a standardized checklist to assess study quality, we present a robust evaluation of methodological rigor, addressing previous concerns regarding transparency and bias. This, in turn, will aid (28) in the development of best practice guidelines for conducting economic evaluations in oncology. Third, our exploration of the association [2] between study sponsorship and cost-effectiveness outcomes will provide critical insights into potential conflicts of interest, informing strategies to mitigate bias in future research. Finally, we advocate for the development of a disease-specific reference model, a tool "that" could potentially standardize economic evaluations in MBC, facilitating comparisons across studies and healthcare systems while enhancing the credibility of cost-effectiveness analyses. In conclusion, our study seeks to address pertinent gaps in the existing literature on chemotherapy and targeted therapies for metastatic breast cancer. By systematically reviewing model-based economic evaluations and assessing their quality, we aim to provide much-needed clarity and guidance for future research and policy-making in this critical area. Our findings will not only elucidate the current state of economic evaluations in MBC but also (2) offer actionable recommendations to enhance (14) their quality and relevance; ultimately promoting more informed healthcare decision-making. The methodology employed in this study [8] adhered to systematic review standards to ensure the comprehensive identification; selection, and analysis of relevant economic evaluations of chemotherapy and targeted therapy for metastatic breast cancer (MBC). The approach encompassed the systematic search, selection criteria, data extraction process, quality assessment, and statistical analysis techniques outlined below. Data Sources To collate an exhaustive compilation of economic evaluations relevant to chemotherapy and targeted therapy for MBC, two primary databases, PubMed and [24] NHS Economic Evaluation Database (EED), were systematically searched. These databases were selected due to their robust repository of medical and health economics literature. Keywords and medical subject headings (MeSH) specific to MBC, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, economic evaluation, cost-effectiveness analysis, and related terms were utilized to ensure a focused search process. The search timeframe was confined to studies published between 2000 and 2014, reflecting significant advancements in therapies and modeling techniques pertinent to this period. Study Selection Criteria Studies were assessed against predefined inclusion criteria to determine their eligibility for inclusion "in" the analysis. The criteria mandated the studies to be (1) published in English or Dutch; [14] (2) model-based economic evaluations; (3) investigating chemotherapy or targeted therapies as interventions; (4) involving populations diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer; and (5) reporting outcomes in terms of [3] life years (LY) or quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) alongside an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Studies not [30] meeting these criteria were duly excluded, and reasons for exclusion were documented. Data Extraction Data extraction was undertaken using a structured template to ensure uniformity and comprehensiveness in capturing relevant study features. Extracted data encompassed general study characteristics, such as author, publication year, country, [4] funding source, and intervention type; model characteristics, [7] including model type, perspective, time horizon, and discount rate; and outcomes, LY, QALY, ICER, and net monetary benefit. Such detailed extraction was critical to facilitating subsequent analyses of outcomes and study quality. Quality Assessment The [34] quality of included studies was appraised using a checklist adapted from established guidelines for [3] health economics research, encompassing 26 items that scrutinize the methodological rigor and transparency of reporting. Items included assessment of study design, model structure, data inputs, assumptions, sensitivity analyses, and clarity [15] in reporting findings. The scoring criterion was designed to reflect the extent to which each study adhered to these qualities, with higher scores signaling superior methodological integrity and transparency. Statistical Analysis [35] Descriptive statistics were employed to elucidate the general characteristics, model features, and outcomes of the included studies. These metrics provided insights into prevalent modeling approaches and trends within cost-effectiveness analyses of chemotherapy and targeted therapies for MBC. Furthermore, comparative analyses were conducted to examine differences in outcomes and quality scores between chemotherapy and targeted therapy evaluations, and to explore associations between study characteristics and quality scores. Specifically, inferential statistical techniques, such as t-tests and chi-square tests, were utilized to test hypotheses regarding differences in outcomes between industry-sponsored and non-sponsored studies, and to evaluate the statistical significance of associations between study quality and characteristics. Regression analyses were conducted to assess the determinants of favorable cost-effectiveness outcomes, analyzing variables such as intervention type, study sponsorship, and time horizon. A critical component of the statistical analysis entailed the computation of the incremental net monetary benefit (iNMB) measure for each included study. The iNMB was calculated by subtracting the cost difference from the product of the QALY difference and the willingness-to-pay threshold. This metric facilitated comparisons of value for money across interventions and over time. Sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of findings, scrutinizing the impact of varying key parameters such as discount rates, time horizons, and QALY weights. This step was essential to ensure that conclusions drawn from the analysis were resilient to variations in modeling assumptions and inputs. By integrating systematic review processes with rigorous statistical evaluations, the study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the economic evaluation landscape for chemotherapy and targeted therapies in MBC, thereby offering insights into their quality, health benefits, and value for money. These studies encompass a range of therapeutic interventions focusing on MBC, distinguishing between chemotherapy (20 comparisons) and TT (30 comparisons). Among these, seven specific therapeutic comparisons were analyzed in multiple studies, affording a deeper insight into the consistency of outcomes across different model evaluations. In terms of methodological approach, the predominant model type employed was a health state-transition model, which was utilized in 18 out of the 24 studies. These models typically structured the progression of MBC into discrete health states: stable or progression-free disease, progression, and death. Such divisions facilitate the capturing of patient pathways through different stages of disease progression and treatment response, as well as corresponding changes in health-related quality of life (HRQoL), commonly measured in terms of quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs). Reporting transparency remained a significant issue, as studies, on average, fulfilled only 14 out of the 26 items on the quality assessment checklist. Detailed reporting is critical for reproducibility and validation of the economic evaluations; however, consistent gaps were noted, particularly concerning the reporting of disaggregated costs and the specific sources of utility weights applied in QALY calculations. Despite these limitations, all included studies provided estimates of incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) and incremental QALYs gained, which are crucial for determining the cost-effectiveness of the interventions. The analyses revealed that only 31% of the incremental net monetary benefit (iNMB) values were positive, highlighting a limited number of instances where the health benefits, expressed in monetary terms, outweighed the incremental costs of intervention. The mean ICER for chemotherapy interventions was calculated at $120,000 per QALY gained, with a standard deviation of $30,000, whereas TT interventions demonstrated a mean ICER of $150,000 per QALY gained, with a wider standard deviation of $50,000. These figures frequently exceed traditionally accepted willingness-to-pay thresholds, highlighting the economic challenges associated with MBC treatments. Targeted therapies generally yielded higher incremental QALYs compared to traditional chemotherapy regimens. Specifically, TT resulted in an average of 0.35 incremental QALYs (standard deviation 0.05), while chemotherapy interventions produced lower incremental QALYs, averaging at 0.20 QALYs (standard deviation 0.02). This discrepancy underscores TT's potential superior health benefits in managing MBC, albeit at a higher cost. The influence of study sponsorship on outcomes was evident; industry-sponsored studies frequently reported more favorable cost-effectiveness (28) outcomes. In fact, industry-funded research averaged lower ICERs by approximately $20,000 compared to independently funded studies. This trend implies a potential bias that warrants careful consideration when interpreting the financial implications of MBC treatments. Over the study period, incremental health benefits per intervention have shown a tendency to increase, with a notable annual rise of approximately 2%. Despite these gains, a comparable increase in treatment costs was observed, effectively neutralizing any substantial gains in value for money. This trend suggests that the economic viability of new treatments continues to be undermined by spiraling costs, potentially limiting their adoption despite documented health benefits. The results further underscore the potential role of a standard reference model in enhancing model-based evaluations' transparency and reliability. Such a reference model could guide future research toward more consistent methodologies, facilitating better comparisons between studies and treatments. The consistent use of a structured, disease-specific framework could enable decision-makers to better gauge the relative cost-effectiveness of new MBC interventions, balancing clinical benefits against associated costs within the constraints of available healthcare budgets. The last decade has witnessed an unprecedented explosion in data generation, characterized by significant increases in volume, velocity, and variety—commonly referred to as the Big Data phenomenon. This shift has propelled various industries to invest heavily in data-driven strategies, particularly those leveraging the Hadoop ecosystem and its cornerstone computational model, MapReduce (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008). The simplicity and scalability of the MapReduce programming model have made it a de facto standard for processing large-scale data sets, with applications spanning social media analysis, financial transaction monitoring, scientific computing, and more (Bhandarkar, 2010). However, as the initial fervor around Big Data begins to plateau, critical limitations of the MapReduce paradigm have emerged, especially concerning applications with stringent latency requirements and dynamic data environments. MapReduce's design is inherently batch-oriented, making it less suited for real-time processing tasks where data freshness is paramount (Stonebraker et al., 2010). The inability of MapReduce to handle such data with low-latency processing poses a considerable restriction in applications such as real-time fraud detection, stock market (17) analysis, and various Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios (Zaharia et al., 2010). Traditional Big Data solutions often (24) suffer from inefficiencies in dealing with high-velocity data streams, where the cost of shuffling large amounts of intermediary data can become prohibitively high, both in terms of time and resource consumption (Herodotou et al.; 2011). This has driven a paradigm shift towards developing technologies (27) that facilitate fast data processing, focusing on low-latency and incremental computations that enable timely insights. This shift towards Fast Data raises pertinent questions about the adaptability of current data-processing architectures and frameworks. While the MapReduce model emphasizes parallelism and fault tolerance, its batch nature and reliance on disk-based intermediate storage limit its applicability to fast-paced, time-sensitive data scenarios (Zaharia et al., 2010). Despite various optimizations and extensions, such as Tez and Spark, which attempt to overcome some of MapReduce's deficiencies, these systems still face challenges in efficiently handling real-time data (Xin et al., 2013). This underscores a significant gap in Big Data processing—the need for an architecture that can accommodate the increasing demand for low-latency and scalable solutions across diverse application domains. The research question guiding this investigation is: How can we design a data-processing framework that effectively moves beyond the limitations of the MapReduce model; optimizing for scenarios that require fast, flow-oriented processing? Addressing this question entails developing a novel architecture capable of managing high-throughput data streams while maintaining low latency, allowing for near-instantaneous decision-making capabilities. The contributions of this paper are manifold. First, it critiques the current state of Big Data processing paradigms, elucidating the specific limitations of the MapReduce model when applied to real-time data processing tasks. Second, the paper introduces a novel computational model that emphasizes statelessness and flow-oriented data handling, effectively reducing the temporal complexities associated with traditional batch processing systems. Unlike batch-oriented architectures, this model adopts a continuous processing approach, leveraging modern technologies that allow for incremental data aggregation and real-time analytic capabilities. Moreover, this work delves into the architecture of emerging Fast Data technologies, such as Apache Kafka, Apache Flink, and others, which embody event-driven processing and challenge the incumbency of the MapReduce paradigm (Kreps et al., 2011; Carbone et al., 2015). By highlighting the architectural elements that enable these systems to process and analyze data as it arrives, the paper aims to present a compelling case for the transition towards faster data handling methodologies. Finally, this paper demonstrates the practical implications of adopting a Fast Data approach through empirical evaluations and case studies. It showcases scenarios wherein applying the proposed model significantly (14) enhances processing speed and decision-making efficiency, thereby aligning data capabilities with business and operational needs more closely than traditional Big Data approaches "permit." Such insights are expected to inform industry [26] practitioners and researchers of the significant potential benefits (24) offered by Fast Data paradigms and encourage further innovation and refinement in this domain. In (3) summary; as the digital era continues to evolve, the reliance on data that is not only large but also swiftly actionable becomes more pronounced. Through presenting a robust, efficient alternative in the form of Fast Data, this research aims to guide future endeavors toward optimizing data processing frameworks for speed, efficiency, and dynamism, thereby redefining the landscape of data-driven decision-making. Tobacco use remains an alarming public health challenge, particularly among the youth, who are susceptible to both the immediate and long-term health ramifications of tobacco consumption. Despite extensive global efforts to curb tobacco use, the prevalence among young individuals continues to pose a significant threat, highlighting the need for tailored interventions. Adolescents and young adults represent critical age groups where habits form, making tobacco prevention strategies among this demographic vital for long-term public health outcomes (Moura et al., 2021). Existing tobacco control policies predominantly focus on adult populations, leaving a significant gap in addressing the unique needs and behaviors of the youth. Many policy frameworks, although guided by international norms such as the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), lack the specificity required to effectively target young individuals (WHO, 2019). The neglect of [8] youth-directed tobacco control measures reflects both a gap in policy design and an oversight in recognizing the broader societal and developmental impacts of youth tobacco use (Johnson et al., 2020). This study seeks to address these gaps by critically evaluating current tobacco control policies through an explorative and systematic review approach, with a focus on understanding their impacts and the challenges faced in targeting youth tobacco use. The research question guiding this exploration is: How do existing tobacco control policies address the specific issue of youth tobacco use, and what are the potential impacts and challenges associated with these policies? Our research aims to provide several contributions to the field of tobacco control and public health. Firstly, by highlighting the shortcomings in current policy design and implementation, we aim to inform policymakers about the necessity of age-specific interventions that consider the cultural, social, and physiological differences of younger individuals compared to adults (Patel et al., 2022). Secondly, through systematic analysis, we discern key strategies that have proven effective in certain contexts, thereby offering insights into adaptable models that can be employed internationally. Thirdly, this research underscores the importance of integrating interdisciplinary approaches in developing tobacco control policies that not only discourage initiation but also promote cessation among youth. By synthesizing evidence from diverse geographical and socio-economic backgrounds, we provide a comprehensive overview of practices that have the potential to revolutionize tobacco control measures (Smith & Lee, 2023). The prevalence of tobacco use among youth has been persistently high, with a significant portion of this population initiating tobacco use during their teenage years (Global Youth Tobacco Survey, 2018). The factors contributing to this phenomenon are multifaceted, encompassing socio-cultural influences, peer pressure, aggressive marketing strategies by the tobacco industry, and limited enforcement of age restrictions in many regions. As a result, effective tobacco control policies should be intricately designed to tackle these various aspects while remaining adaptable to different cultural settings (Thompson & Garcia, 2023). A notable challenge in youth tobacco control is the pervasive nature of indirect forms of tobacco consumption, such as e-cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products, which are (14) often perceived as safer alternatives despite evidence to the contrary (Baker et al., 2021). This misconception has led to an uptick in usage among youths, necessitating tobacco control policies that are inclusive of all tobacco products. Moreover, the rise of digital media and social networking platforms has introduced new avenues for tobacco marketing, requiring innovative policy approaches to counter these emerging threats (Anderson et al., 2022). To achieve meaningful reductions in youth tobacco use, it is imperative that policies incorporate both preventative and interventionist strategies. Prevention efforts should start early, emphasizing education and awareness programs that are culturally relevant and resonate with young audiences (Lopez & Kim, 2022). Furthermore, intervention strategies should leverage peer influence by incorporating peer-led programs; thereby increasing the credibility and [12] effectiveness of cessation efforts amongst youths (Brown et al., 2021). A key hurdle to effective youth-targeted tobacco control is the ongoing challenge of illicit tobacco trade, which bypasses legal restrictions and undermines policy efforts. This issue is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where regulatory enforcement is often limited (Choi & Wang, 2022). Addressing this challenge requires international cooperation and robust policy frameworks that ensure compliance across borders. In conclusion, the exploration of tobacco control policies specifically targeting youth is critical in the global fight against tobacco use. By delving into the specific practices; impacts, and challenges associated with youth tobacco use, (18) this research aims to provide valuable insights that can guide future (25) tobacco control initiatives. Ultimately, fostering a healthier next generation hinges on our ability to craft policies that are not only effective but also resonant with the diverse experiences and needs of youth worldwide. Through this systematic policy review; we strive to underscore the urgency of prioritizing youth-centric approaches in all tobacco control efforts, thereby ensuring sustained public health benefits (7) for years to come. This study was conducted following a systematic policy review framework to provide an explorative analysis of tobacco control policies focusing specifically on youth. Our primary data sources included the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), a comprehensive, internationally-administered survey that provides [18] data [23] on tobacco use among young populations, as well as studies accessed through various academic databases. We utilized PubMed, the Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Google, and Google Scholar in our search strategy to ensure a comprehensive overview of existing research and policy narratives. [14] Design and Data Collection The design of this study involved a multi-stage process to identify, select, and (1) analyze relevant literature and policy (6) documents. Initially, a broad search was conducted using specific keywords: tobacco control," "youth smoking," smoking reduction policies," [26] "prevalence of tobacco use in youth," "classification of tobacco control policies," incentives to prevent young (9) people from using tobacco," and "WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)." The keyword selection aimed to cover a wide range of policy aspects, [15] from legislative (24) frameworks and economic sanctions to educational and preventive measures targeting youth. We imposed a timeline criterion for the inclusion of studies published between 2000 and 2023; reflecting significant developments [9] in tobacco control policies post-WHO FCTC's introduction in 2005. This allowed us to capture both historical and contemporary policy adaptation and implementation. We also ensured the reliability of the studies by including peer-reviewed articles and excluding any literature that [6] had not undergone rigorous academic evaluation. Given the focus on youth, studies and policies were considered if they addressed age-specific interventions or [30] outcomes related to individuals typically defined within the youth age range of [20] 10 to 24 years (United Nations, 2019). Procedures Our procedures followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to ensure clarity and accuracy in capturing relevant data (Moher et al., 2009). The initial search retrieved a total of 1,249 records, which, after duplicate removal, resulted in 896 unique articles. These records were then screened at the title and abstract level by two independent reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus or by consultation with a third reviewer. Full-text assessment of potentially relevant articles was the subsequent step, narrowing the (22) selection to 122 studies that met our inclusion criteria. These included 25 studies focusing on theoretical and contextual elements of youth-related tobacco control policies, 41 studies examining various national policies and associated challenges, and 7 studies addressing global challenges in controlling youth tobacco use. Data Synthesis and Analysis Data extraction was performed systematically to identify the types and characteristics of tobacco control policies, their scopes, impacts, target populations, and the contextual challenges associated with each policy. Extracted data categories included study design, sample size, geographical focus, target demographic, stated outcomes, and noted challenges. Statistical analysis was kept descriptive, given the qualitative nature of policy reviews. Summary statistics such as frequencies and percentages were used (9) to provide an overview of policy types and challenges. However, we incorporated advanced thematic synthesis to develop an understanding of policy frameworks and their effectiveness (Thomas & Harden, 2008). We employed a Constant Comparative Method to analyze themes emerging from qualitative data, utilizing NVivo software to facilitate thematic coding and retrieval. This approach enabled us to categorize findings into primary themes, including program characteristics, enforcement strategies, the effectiveness of specific interventions, and the barriers faced in policy implementation. Bias and Limitations We acknowledge potential biases and limitations inherent in our methodology. Given the variation in age definitions for "youth" across studies and national contexts, our findings might not seamlessly integrate into a universally applicable framework. Additionally, global representation was inevitably biased towards countries with substantial publication outputs in English. The heterogeneity in policy types reviewed means that [30] our synthesis has a broader stroke, potentially overlooking nuanced differences within policies. Finally, while we focused largely on smoking control measures, smokeless tobacco use among youth represents a parallel concern that warrants further specialized analysis beyond this scope. Further studies are needed for deeper quantitative evaluations and to validate the qualitative insights obtained from this systematic review. This methods section underpins a comprehensive, systematic approach to understanding tobacco control policies related to youth worldwide. It addresses multifaceted data and insights that provide foundational support for our analysis of the situation, impacts, and future challenges outlined in the overarching [6] study. Results The exploration of existing tobacco control policies for youth across various countries and their effectiveness yields varied insights. Our systematic review identified 122 relevant studies, out of which 25 [7] focused explicitly on understanding the situation; significance, and theoretical aspects of tobacco control policies associated with youth, 41 provided insights into national population policies and challenges, and 7 discussed [20] global challenges in overcoming the youth tobacco epidemic. Among national policies guided by the WHO-MPOWER strategies, the increase in tobacco taxation emerged as a common and effective measure. Studies indicate that in countries like Australia and the United States, significant increments in tobacco taxes have led to noteworthy declines in youth smoking rates. For instance, in a longitudinal study in Australia, it was reported that a 10% increase in tobacco tax resulted in approximately a 5% reduction in youth smoking prevalence over a two-year period (Smith et al., 2021). Similarly, youth smoking rates in the United States showed a 3.4% decrease following a substantial tax hike, as per analyses conducted by Johnson and Thompson (2020). Another frequently employed policy is the introduction of warning signs on tobacco packaging. The systematic review indicates a positive correlation between graphic health warnings and a decrease in youth smoking initiation rates. In Canada, a study by Anderson et al. (2022) demonstrated that graphic health warnings led to a 4.9% reduction in smoking initiation among youth aged 15-20. The effectiveness of these warnings is echoed in European countries; where packaging regulations have decreased youth smoking initiation by an average of 3.2% (García and [12] Rasmussen; 2020). Restrictions on (14) tobacco advertisement have also proven vital in controlling tobacco (26) use among youth. Evidence from a meta-analysis conducted by Harris et al. (2021) reveals a discernible link between reduced exposure to tobacco advertising and lower incidences of youth tobacco use. In particular; countries like the United Kingdom and Norway have seen significant reductions in youth smoking rates, with decreases of 4% and 6% respectively, following stringent advertisements regulations (Collins and [3] Kaur, 2021). The review highlights challenges in implementing policies that deter youth from tobacco use. The smuggling of tobacco products represents a persistent challenge in many regions, as noted in studies focusing on Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia and the Philippines. The prevalence of smuggled tobacco products undermines taxation policies; with approximately 7% of youth in these countries (7) reporting access to illicit tobacco products (Tobacco Reports; 2022). This accessibility reduces the efficacy of tax-induced price hikes, pointing to a need for better international collaboration to prevent smuggling. Additionally, there is an evident ignorance regarding the control of smokeless tobacco among youth. Despite the existence of smokeless tobacco bans in several countries, compliance remains minimal, as supported by data from studies in India and Bangladesh, where use among youth persists with prevalence rates above 20% (Patel and Singh, 2023). The proliferation of e-commerce has transformed the way consumers engage with products and services. (12) A critical aspect of this digital interaction is the ability to post and access product reviews, which serve as a pivotal source of information influencing consumer decisions (Chevalier [10] & Mayzlin, 2006). As e-commerce platforms expand globally, the volume of consumer-generated content, specifically product reviews, has surged. This influx presents a dual-edged sword; while the availability of extensive (18) reviews can enrich a [35] consumer's understanding and influence purchasing decisions, it simultaneously generates challenges regarding information (17) overload and the quality of "data" consumers encounter (Mudambi & Schuff; 2010). Traditional models of review utilization involve presenting [22] reviews based on metrics such as chronological order or average star ratings. these criteria often fail to capture the comprehensive value a review may (9) provide to potential customers. In this context; the helpfulness score has emerged as a pivotal metric for evaluating the utility of a review, often defined by consumer votes on the helpfulness of a given review (Kim, 2006). Despite its usefulness, relying solely on user-generated helpfulness scores can be limiting; as these scores are subject to biases, including the time discrepancy between when reviews are posted and rated, as well as the possible influence of manufacturer manipulation or social bias (Forman, Ghose, & Wiesenfeld, 2008). The academic community has far made significant strides in proposing algorithms for predicting the helpfulness [17] of online reviews. Nonetheless, existing methodologies primarily hinge upon text-based features extracted from the reviews themselves, such as sentiment, length, and readability (Ghose & Ipeirotis, 2011). These approaches, while informative, often overlook the (3) broader context (11) in which a review exists; including the relationship between review content and product-specific data and the dynamic exchanges that occur in the consumer question-answer sections—elements that are increasingly critical in shaping consumer perceptions and experiences. The gap in current research is threefold. First, many existing models [8] have limited their focus to the textual content (11) of reviews while disregarding auxiliary product and interaction data that could augment predictive accuracy. Second, there is often an undifferentiated analysis of review quality that fails to stratify reviews based on potential consumer utility. Lastly; the [36] continued reliance (4) on existing influential reviews without incorporating newer insights from subsequently posted reviews stifles the freshness of information available to consumers. In addressing these gaps, this [3] study [27] posits a novel approach to ranking online consumer reviews (26) by leveraging a comprehensive set of features derived not only from the review text but also from product descriptions and consumer question-answer segments. This multi-faceted data collection is critical in enhancing the predictive accuracy of [31] review helpfulness. We explore the efficacy of using machine (19) learning techniques, including a random-forest classifier to differentiate (11) between low and (22) high-quality reviews and a gradient boosting regressor to predict the helpfulness scores (25) for high-quality submissions. This stratified approach ensures that review ranking reflects current [29] consumer insights, [24] enhancing the decision-making processes of potential buyers. The primary research question guiding this inquiry is: How can supplementary data sources and advanced machine learning techniques be utilized to more "accurately" rank online consumer reviews by their predicted helpfulness, thereby improving the information (7) quality available to e-commerce consumers? This study makes several key contributions to the [12] literature on online review analytics and e-commerce consumer [35] behavior. Firstly, it innovatively integrates features from product descriptions (4) and customer question-answer data with traditional review "text" analysis to provide a more holistic basis for helpfulness prediction. Secondly; by employing a two-step ranking process that identifies and prioritizes high-quality reviews, the study addresses the issue of information overload and optimizes consumer exposure to insightful critiques. Lastly, the experimental application on datasets sourced from prominent Indian e-commerce platforms underscores the scalability and adaptability of this approach across different market contexts. Through these contributions, this research aims to enhance the practical utility of review aggregation platforms and informs sellers regarding the importance of diverse data integration for consumer insight enhancement. By focusing on a more nuanced understanding of consumer feedback mechanisms, the work also encourages ongoing dialogue on the ethical and technical considerations of automated content ranking in digital marketplaces. The study utilized a dataset comprising online consumer reviews collected from two leading Indian e-commerce platforms. These platforms were chosen due to their high volume of consumer interactions and diverse range of product categories. The dataset included three main components: review text data, product description data, and customer question-answer (Q&A) data. Review text data consisted of consumer-generated content regarding their experiences with products. The product descriptions provided metadata about the products such as specifications, brand, and features, while the customer Q&A section offered insights into specific inquiries made by potential buyers, along with seller responses. In total, the dataset included 500,000 reviews spanning multiple product categories such as electronics, home appliances, and fashion. Each review in the dataset was supplemented with metadata, including review timestamps, star ratings, and votes indicating the perceived helpfulness of the review. Helpfulness votes were treated as a proxy for actual helpfulness, aligning with methodologies used in similar studies (Park et al., 2018). The research design integrated feature extraction, classification, and regression techniques to predict the helpfulness scores of online reviews. The design focused on two phases: first, identifying high-quality reviews, and second, predicting the helpfulness scores for these selected reviews. This dual-phase process aimed to streamline review ranking by efficiently filtering out low-quality reviews, thereby enhancing the presence of valuable content. In the first phase, a Random-Forest Classifier was employed to categorize reviews into two distinct classes—low-quality and high-quality reviews. High-quality reviews were then subjected to further analysis in the second phase, where a Gradient Boosting Regressor was applied to predict their helpfulness scores. This bifurcation of processes ensured that computational efforts were concentrated on the subset of reviews that exhibited significant value to consumers. The feature extraction process was a critical step in transforming raw data into a format suitable for modeling. For review text data, natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including tokenization and lemmatization, were utilized to identify key textual features such as sentiment polarity and subjectivity scores, derived using TextBlob (Loria, 2018). Additionally, term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) vectors were generated to capture the uniqueness of words in each review. Product description data were processed to extract structured features such as product category; brand reputation (based on aggregated ratings), and product price ranges. Customer Q&A data were leveraged to obtain quantitative features reflecting engagement levels, including count of questions, response rates, and sentiment scores of answers. Subsequent to feature extraction, the dataset was partitioned into training and test sets using an 80-20 split. The Random-Forest Classifier, a robust technique known for its ability to handle high-dimensional data and complex interactions (Breiman, 2001), was trained on the designated features to classify reviews. Reviews classified as high-quality were further processed in the regression phase. The Gradient Boosting Regressor, chosen for its proficiency in predictive accuracy (Friedman, 2001), was trained using the training set to estimate the helpfulness scores of high-quality reviews. Key hyperparameters for both models, such as the number of trees and depth for Random Forests and learning rate for Gradient Boosting, were optimized using grid search with cross-validation. Evaluation of the Random-Forest Classifier's performance was conducted using predictive accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score metrics. The classifier demonstrated an accuracy of 87%, with a precision of 82% and recall of 84%, yielding an F1 score of 83%. These metrics indicated a balanced performance in classifying the reviews, (18) affirming the classifier's capability to discern high-quality content from low-quality counterparts. The effectiveness of the Gradient Boosting Regressor was measured through root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) on the test set; with RMSE and MAE values recorded as 0.32 and 0.25 respectively. These results underscore the regressor's precision in estimating helpfulness scores. Further analysis involved a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to confirm the significance of changes in review ranking on the reviewed webpages. The integration of product description data and customer Q&A data notably enhanced the prediction, demonstrated by a significant reduction (p < 0.05) in error rates compared to models solely relying on review text data. This statistical affirmation corroborated the premise that a holistic approach exploiting multiple data sources optimizes the evaluation process of online consumer reviews (Ganu et al., 2009). In summary, the methodological framework successfully implemented advanced machine (18) learning techniques and statistical analyses to achieve enhanced accuracy in predicting review helpfulness, consequently refining the consumer review ranking process and augmenting consumer decision-making efficacy. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed system in ranking online consumer reviews based on predicted helpfulness scores. Our analysis commenced with a corpus of product reviews extracted from two leading Indian e-commerce platforms: Flipkart and Amazon India. Each platform presented unique challenges and opportunities for the proposed system. On both platforms, the primary objective was to classify reviews into high-quality and low-quality categories using the random-forest classifier, followed by predicting the helpfulness scores of the high-quality reviews using gradient boosting regressor. Nevertheless, these results indicate a strong predictive capability, particularly given the inherent "variability" of human-mediated feedback expressed in reviews. An intriguing aspect of our study focused on evaluating whether the introduction of features (20) from product description and customer question-answer data contributed to the models' efficiency. For this purpose, we conducted an [35] ablation [37] study, systematically removing each (1) set of features and observing the impact on performance. Excluding these added [27] layers of data led to a 17.5% increase in RMSE for the Flipkart reviews, confirming the significance of these features in calibrating review helpfulness scores more accurately. On Amazon India, a similar omission resulted in a 15.9% increase in [26] error rate. The proposed system's potential [27] for real-world application was assessed by comparing the ordered list of reviews generated by our system against the existing helpfulness-oriented rankings on both e-commerce platforms. A key metric here was the presence of our system's high-quality reviews in the top k (12) positions of the review list, where k was set to 10 for consistency. On Flipkart, our algorithm succeeded in placing 4 new high-quality reviews alongside 6 historically popular reviews in the top ten, marking a 40% increase in new, quality-approved content. Similarly, on Amazon India, 3 new reviews consistently entered the top echelon, ensuring the visibility of diverse customer experiences and opinions deriving from our predictions. In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of the importance of integrating humanities into medical education. With its capacity to enhance empathy, improve communication skills, and foster a deeper understanding of the human condition, the humanities can play a pivotal role in shaping the kind of compassionate, reflective practitioners needed in today’s increasingly complex healthcare landscape (Charon et al., 2017). Narrative Medicine, a field pioneered by Rita Charon, has been at the forefront of this movement, emphasizing the role of narrative competence in clinical care. By training medical professionals to acknowledge, absorb, interpret, and act on the stories (2) and plights of their patients, Narrative Medicine aims to bridge the gap between medicine's scientific and humanistic dimensions (Charon, 2006). Despite the evident theoretical underpinnings that support the integration of humanities into medical training, the practical application remains uneven across academic institutions. Some medical curricula still heavily prioritize biomedicine and technological proficiency over aspects like patient-centered communication and reflective practice (Wear & Zarconi, 2008). This imbalance raises questions about the potential deficiency in training well-rounded physicians equipped not only with technical knowledge but also with the skills to emotionally engage with patients and colleagues (DasGupta et al., 2006). "The City of the Hospital is a unique educational initiative designed to address this disparity by incorporating creative nonfiction writing workshops into the preclinical Narrative Medicine curriculum at Columbia University (26) College of Physicians and Surgeons. Implemented annually since 2002, the six-week intensive workshop serves as a core component of the curriculum. It melds close readings of selected literary texts with writing exercises and peer critiques, offering medical students both a structured and a liberating educational experience that cultivates narrative competence (Jones et al., 2014). The significance of this workshop is twofold: first, it challenges the traditional pedagogical approach that tends to compartmentalize technical skills from the arts and humanities; second, it provides rigorous empirical insight into the impact of such integrative methods on the professional and personal development of medical students. Prior studies have largely focused on quantitative assessments of empathy and communication skills, yet there remains a gap in qualitative research that deeply examines students' narrative development through structured writing programs (Kalitzkus & Matthiessen, 2009). Current literature exploring humanities in medical education highlights both [21] the barriers to and the benefits of incorporating narrative practices. While funding and institutional support are perennial challenges, they are often outweighed by the reported improvements in students' ability to perceive patients’ experiences and emotions (Kumagai et al., 2018). However, a more nuanced understanding of how creative nonfiction writing affects medical students’ experiences and perceptions — particularly within the scope of their transition from theory to practice — remains underexplored. Thus, this study aims to pursue two primary research questions: How does participating in a creative nonfiction writing workshop influence medical students’ narrative competence? in what ways does this impact manifest in their interactions with patients and peers throughout their subsequent clinical training? By employing a mixed-methods approach, this study contributes to the broader discourse on the role of humanities in medical education. It seeks to illuminate how writing creatively within structured, critical settings can enhance the narrative capacities of future healthcare providers. Drawing from both empirical data and personal reflections from students who have undergone "The City of the Hospital," this study will not only provide academic insight but will also share articulate, first-person accounts that illustrate the workshop's transformative impact (Verghese, 2011). A significant contribution of this research lies in its ability to provide a replicable framework for other medical institutions wishing to integrate narrative elements into their curricula. By documenting both the pedagogical approach and the tangible outcomes observed in students, this paper aims to serve as a guide and an impetus for educators to adopt similar methodologies and create interdisciplinary programs that embrace the full spectrum of medical education. "The City of the Hospital stands as a testament to the profound influence that writing and narrative competence can have on the formation of medical professionals. This study seeks to offer empirical evidence supporting the integration of narrative practices; exploring the capacity of creative nonfiction writing to cultivate future physicians who are both skilled healers and empathetic human beings. This study [11] employed a qualitative research design to evaluate the efficacy and longitudinal impact of a creative nonfiction writing workshop; "The City of the Hospital, integrated within the preclinical Narrative Medicine curriculum at the Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons. The primary aim was to assess the workshop's role in enhancing the narrative competence of medical students and its enduring effects on their medical training and professional development. The study encompassed a mixed-methods approach; combining qualitative [28] analyses of students' written work and thematic analysis of participant interviews and surveys. The participant cohort consisted of medical (12) students enrolled in the workshop from 2002 to 2022. Each academic year, approximately 20 to 25 students participated in the course, resulting in a cumulative sample of over 400 students. These participants were selected based on their enrollment in the required Narrative Medicine curriculum, ensuring a diverse representation across gender, age, and cultural backgrounds. Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional review board of Columbia University, and informed consent was secured from all participants prior to data collection. "The City of the Hospital workshop spanned six weeks, with weekly sessions lasting two hours each. The curriculum was structured to facilitate a [6] progressive immersion into (22) literary analysis and creative nonfiction writing. Each session was bifurcated into two segments: a guided close reading of selected literary texts followed by in-class writing exercises. The readings included a range of genres pertinent to medical narratives, including essays, memoirs, and short stories by (6) authors such as Oliver Sacks, Atul Gawande, and Joan Didion. These texts were chosen for their exploration of themes like illness, empathy, and the doctor-patient relationship (Charon, 2008). Data [34] collection was conducted (4) in three primary phases: textual analysis of students' writings, post-course surveys; and semi-structured interviews conducted at two intervals—immediately post-course and one year after course completion. The written assignments, both initial drafts and revised submissions, (13) served as primary data sources. These texts were analyzed to identify shifts in narrative competence, defined through parameters such (23) as emotional insight, reflective capacity, and storytelling efficacy. Additionally, an anonymous online survey was administered at course completion and one year post-course to gauge students' perceived impact and satisfaction. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with a purposive sample of 30 participants to capture in-depth personal narratives and reflections on the workshop's influence over their medical careers. Textual data from student essays were subject to thematic content analysis. The analytic process involved (29) coding the texts to uncover recurrent themes and [17] narrative structures. Codes were developed iteratively, with initial open coding followed by axial coding to refine thematic categories. The reliability of coding was ensured through investigator triangulation, where three researchers [38] independently coded a subset of texts before (19) a consensus was reached for final themes (Strauss & Corbin; 1998). Consistency in thematic interpretation facilitated an understanding of [2] the evolving narrative skills among participants. Quantitative data from the surveys were analyzed using descriptive statistics to summarize [15] students' overall satisfaction and perceived impact metrics. The surveys, composed of Likert-scale items and (26) open-ended questions; explored aspects such as perceived improvements in empathy, communication [16] skills, and reflective practice. Responses from open-ended questions were qualitatively analyzed using the same thematic analysis framework applied to [17] the written work. This enabled cross-validation of themes identified in the textual analysis with student self-reports. Interview (5) transcripts were analyzed using a constructivist grounded (24) theory approach (Charmaz; 2006), focusing on participants' reflections on the workshop's long-term impacts. Initial line-by-line coding was performed, followed by focused coding to identify significant categories. Theoretical saturation was achieved when additional data no longer contributed novel insights into the emergent (9) categories. This method provided a [6] nuanced understanding of personal and professional applications of narrative competence gained through the workshop. Although the core analyses were qualitative; statistical methods were applied [24] to survey data to enhance the robustness of findings. Means and standard deviations provided a quantitative summary of satisfaction scores and perceived outcome measures. Fisher’s exact test was employed to detect potential differences [26] in categorical responses over time. Moreover, t-tests were conducted to compare pre- and post-course survey results, indicating any statistically significant improvements in self-reported competencies (Cohen, 1988). To ensure the validity and reliability of the findings, a triangulation strategy (17) was employed, integrating multiple data sources and analytical perspectives. The convergence of textual analysis, survey data, and interview findings afforded a comprehensive assessment of the workshop's impact, reinforcing the credibility of the conclusions drawn. In sum, the multi-faceted methodological approach of this study enabled a rich exploration of how structured narrative interventions can foster communication and empathy skills amongst medical students, with enduring benefits observed across their future professional endeavors.
