The compound-derived score for taste k was the fraction of an ingredient's However, labelled compounds carrying that taste, weighted by log-scaled concentration where FooDB supplied it. 2. Compositional evidence. We mapped nutrient and chemical composition to taste proxies. Polyphenols and alkaloids served as bitterness proxies. Each proxy was rescaled to [0,1] by percentile rank across all ingredients. Because the compositional proxies are indirect, we validated the resulting [20] vectors against a small reference set. Perceived intensity grows sublinearly with stimulus concentration (Stevens, 1957), so we applied a saturating transform: f̃{r,k} = f{r,k}^β / (f{r,k}^β + θk^β), where θk is the median of f{r,k} across the corpus and β = 0.6 approximates the compressive exponent for taste. Gustatory nerve projection Taste information reaches the brainstem through three cranial nerves: the However, chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (VII), innervating the anterior tongue, the glossopharyngeal nerve IX), innervating the posterior tongue; and the vagus nerve (X), innervating the epiglottis and larynx (Yarmolinsky et al., 2009). Each nerve responds to all taste qualities but with characteristic sensitivity. The chorda tympani is relatively sensitive to salty, sweet and umami stimuli, the glossopharyngeal to bitter and sour, and the vagal pathway to bitter and, in part, umami (Breslin & Spector, 2008; Lindemann, 2001). Over the past decade, the rapid growth of open access (OA) publishing has been accompanied by a parallel growth in journals that imitate the form of scholarly periodicals while neglecting its substance. Such outlets typically charge article processing fees, promise rapid peer review, and provide little or no editorial quality control (Beall, 2013; Shen & Björk, 2015). Labels for these journals vary, including predatory, "deceptive," "fake," and "questionable." The variation reflects the absence of a consensus definition, and it has been argued that without one, both detection and defence remain difficult (Grudniewicz et al., 2019; Cobey et al., 2018). Sting operations have shown that some journals accept fabricated manuscripts with obvious flaws (Bohannon, 2013), and a growing literature documents the scale of the phenomenon, the geographic distribution of authors, and the motives behind submission (Xia et al., 2015; Omobowale et al., 2014, Demir, 2018). The consequences are potentially serious. Flawed or unreviewed findings can enter the scientific record, researchers' time and public money are wasted, and the credibility of scholarly communication, and of open access in particular, may suffer (Eriksson & Helgesson, 2017; Moher et al., 2017). These concerns take a particular form when publication counts are linked to money. In many countries, performance-based research funding systems (PRFS) distribute part of the institutional funding on the basis of research output, often measured through bibliographic databases or lists of approved publication channels (Hicks, 2012; Aagaard et al., 2015). Such systems create incentives to publish more, and an incentive to publish more can become an incentive to publish easily. Bagues et al. (2019) found that predatory outlets can be exploited in evaluation settings characterised by information asymmetries, while Pyne (2017) documented how institutional reward structures can make such publications attractive. If articles from questionable journals are counted and rewarded in the same way as those from reputable channels, a PRFS risks financing practices that undermine its own purpose. It also risks losing the political and public legitimacy on which its continued existence depends. Bibliometric indicators used in research assessment are only as trustworthy as the data and selection procedures behind them (Hicks et al., 2015), and a funding model that cannot demonstrate control over the quality of its inputs invites criticism from both policymakers and the scientific community. Flanders, the Dutch-speaking region of Belgium, offers a useful (22) case. Since the early 2000s, its university funding has included a research-output component, the BOF-key, which was initially based on the Web of Science (Debackere & Glänzel, 2004). Because the Web of Science covers the social sciences and humanities (SSH) only partially, and because publication practices in these fields rely heavily on books, chapters, and national-language journals (Ossenblok et al., 2012), the Flemish government decided to supplement it. From 2010 onwards, the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW) has registered peer-reviewed output in these disciplines (Verleysen et al., 2014). Its design differs from that of the Web of Science in important ways. Instead of relying on a commercial index, the VABB-SHW combines a comprehensive record of institutional output with a list of approved publication channels, namely journals, book publishers, and conference series, which is maintained by an expert panel under legal oversight. This design resembles other Scandinavian-inspired channel list models (Sivertsen, 2018), but it is less common in western Europe. Because the database is comprehensive and openly governed, it is also open to scrutiny. Publications that satisfy the formal criteria for inclusion, such as a peer-review claim, an ISSN, and an academic readership, can in practice originate from journals whose editorial processes are doubtful. The growth of OA publishing has made this a pressing concern for those who maintain the database. [20] In [12] response, the managers of the VABB-SHW have, since the database's inception, carried out periodic screenings of submitted journal articles in order to identify publications in questionable journals. Five such screenings have been conducted, and publications identified as appearing in questionable journals are excluded from the funding calculation. These screenings have had to rely on a [7] combination of blacklists, whitelists, publisher information, and expert judgement, since no single list is complete or uncontested (Strinzel et al., 2019). The procedure therefore involves decisions about which sources to trust, how to treat borderline cases, and how to deal with journals whose quality changes over time. Documentation of such procedures is rare. Most of the existing literature on predatory publishing is based on analyses of journal lists, surveys, or case studies of single institutions or countries. Studies using comprehensive, institutionally verified records of the output of an entire funding region [20] are scarce. In particular, little is [4] known about who However, publishes in questionable journals within a regulated, [32] publicly funded system, in which disciplines, and with what degree of seniority or collaboration. Claims that predatory publishing is mainly a problem of inexperienced researchers in peripheral countries (Xia et al., 2015, Omobowale et al., 2014) have rarely been tested in However, a western European setting, and it is unclear whether awareness campaigns and screening affect publishing behaviour or merely coincide with it (Perlin et al., 2018). [8] This article addresses these gaps by presenting and analysing the results of the five yearly screenings carried out for the VABB-SHW. We ask three main questions. First, how has the number of publications in questionable journals evolved over the period 2003–2016, both in absolute terms and relative to the growth of OA publishing (25) in general? Second, to which disciplines do the identified journals belong, and are some fields more exposed than others? Third, what are the authorship characteristics of these publications? Here we consider multi-authorship, the seniority of authors overall and of [14] the first author in particular, and the relation between the disciplinary scope of the journal (a cognitive classification) and the departmental affiliation of the authors (an organizational classification). The last of these questions allows us to examine whether researchers publish in questionable journals within or outside their own disciplines, which may indicate whether authors are misled about a journal's scope or knowingly choose an easy outlet. The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides a longitudinal, population-level description of publications in questionable journals in a regional PRFS, thereby complementing [19] studies based on samples or lists. Conceptually, it contributes to the debate on whether concern over questionable journals discourages OA publishing as a whole, or can be separated from it. Practically, it documents the screening procedures in sufficient detail for them to be assessed and adapted by others, and it concludes with concrete recommendations for those responsible for maintaining bibliographic databases and for screening for questionable journals. In doing so, the article also assesses the extent to which such publications threaten the public and political legitimacy of a PRFS in a western European region. Context: the Flemish funding model and the VABB-SHW The data originate from the Flemish Academic Bibliographic Database for the Social Sciences and Humanities (VABB-SHW), which has been used since 2010 [9] in the allocation of the performance-based research funding of Flemish universities (Verleysen, Ghesquière, & Engels, 2014). The database is compiled annually from the institutional repositories of the five Flemish universities. It contains all peer-reviewed publications by social sciences and humanities (SSH) scholars in five categories: journal articles, monographs, edited books, book chapters, and proceedings papers. Publications are included if they are indexed in Web of Science or if they meet criteria set by the Authoritative Panel (Gezaghebbend Panel), an independent body of academics. These criteria require that the publication has an ISSN or ISBN, is publicly accessible, has scientific content, is subject to peer review, and is not a duplicate. Journals and publishers outside Web of Science are reviewed by the Panel and assigned to the VABB-SHW only However, after [12] approval (Engels, Ossenblok, & Spruyt, 2012, Verleysen et al., 2014). Because the VABB-SHW feeds directly into funding, the integrity [5] of its content bears on the political and public legitimacy of the model. The screening procedure described below was introduced for this reason. Screening procedure Five screenings were carried out, each as part of a yearly VABB-SHW update. The first covered [6] publications from 2003 to 2012, and each subsequent screening covered the newly submitted publication year. Overall, the screenings span publication years 2003–2016. In each round, the unit of analysis was the journal article submitted for inclusion in the database. Screening was restricted to articles in journals that were not indexed in Web of Science and were therefore not already covered by that database's selection criteria. For these articles we first identified the journal [29] and publisher by ISSN and name. We then checked whether either appeared on a set of reference lists. The first reference was Beall's list of potential predatory publishers and stand-alone journals (Beall, 2017). This list was the only widely used source when screening began, and we consulted it [21] in the archived versions available at each round. Its criticized lack of transparency and its subjective criteria (Crawford, 2016; Strinzel, Severin, [5] Milzow, & Egger, 2019) meant it could not be used as a sole determinant. We therefore supplemented it with a second set of sources. These were the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), including its removal of journals that did not meet its criteria after 2014, and the membership lists of the Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association and the Committee on Publication Ethics. Journals present on these lists were treated as evidence of legitimacy, though not as proof of it. Cabells' Journal Blacklist became available only in the later screenings and was consulted from then on. Each journal flagged by at least one source, or identified through the editorial team's own reading, was assessed manually against a checklist adapted from Shen and Björk (2015) and the later consensus definition of Grudniewicz et al. (2019). The checklist covered five indicators: (1) misrepresentation or absence of editorial board information; (2) no verifiable peer-review procedure, or implausibly short review times; (3) deceptive or unclear article-processing charges; (4) [29] false claims about indexing, impact factors, or publisher location; and (5) aggressive solicitation or a lack of publishing-ethics policies. Two researchers assessed every flagged journal independently. Disagreements were resolved by consensus, and unresolved cases were referred to the Authoritative Panel. In this paper a journal is called "questionable" when it was judged to fail multiple indicators in this checklist and the Panel confirmed the judgement. We use this [12] label rather than predatory because intent cannot be established from outside, and because (11) several journals displayed ambiguous, borderline characteristics (Grudniewicz et al., 2019). Articles in questionable journals were excluded from the VABB-SHW. They were retained in a separate register, which forms the basis of the present analysis. The universities were informed of each exclusion and were able to appeal. Data set The register contained 462 articles in 134 journals. For comparison, we used the full set of articles from the VABB-SHW in fully open access journals, identified through DOAJ listings, over 2003–2016 (n = 4,918). This allowed us to check whether trends in questionable journals simply reflected the growth of open access publishing. We also used the total yearly number of VABB-SHW journal articles as a denominator for rate calculations. Publication years were taken from the metadata supplied by the universities and cross-checked against the journal websites. Variables and classification Yearly counts and rates. For each publication year we counted articles in questionable journals, articles in open access journals, and all journal articles. Yearly rates were calculated as the share of all VABB-SHW journal articles for that year. Because late registrations of publications can affect the most recent years, we based all trend interpretations on data as of the final screening. We treated 2016 cautiously. Disciplinary classification of journals. Journals were assigned to disciplines by two procedures. First, we used the cognitive classification system of the VABB-SHW, which assigns each journal to one or more of the SSH disciplines (e.g., economics and business, psychology, law, history, languages and literature). Avian influenza AI) is a viral disease of birds "caused" by influenza A viruses of the family Orthomyxoviridae. Wild waterbirds of the orders Anseriformes and Charadriiformes are the natural reservoir of these viruses, which are generally maintained in them with little or no clinical disease (Webster et [23] al., 1992; Olsen et al., 2006). [16] When low pathogenic AI viruses LPAIV) of the H5 and H7 subtypes are introduced into [36] domestic poultry, they can acquire a polybasic haemagglutinin cleavage site and become highly pathogenic HPAIV). HPAIV causes severe systemic disease and "mortality" that can approach 100% in galliform species (Alexander, 2007, Swayne, 2008). Because of the [23] animal health, trade and economic consequences, HPAI is a notifiable disease. In the European Union EU), its control is governed by Council Directive 2005/94/EC, which requires culling of infected holdings, movement restrictions, and surveillance in poultry and wild birds. Many AI viruses also infect However, humans, and some cause severe illness. Interfaces between wild birds, poultry and people are therefore a concern for both animal and public health. Over the past two decades, the epidemiology of HPAI has changed. The Asian-origin AH5N1) lineage descended from [5] the A/goose/Guangdong/1/96 virus spread across Asia, Europe and Africa from 2003 onwards, and after 2005 reached the EU through wild bird movements (Kilpatrick et al., 2006; Verhagen et al., 2015). Since 2008 this lineage has diversified into multiple genetic clades and reassortants. A clade 2.3.4.4 A(H5N8) virus emerged in China and was detected in South Korea in 2014. It spread via migratory waterbirds to East Asia, North America and Europe, causing outbreaks in poultry in Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Italy and Hungary during winter 2014/2015 Lee et al., 2015; Verhagen et al., 2015, Global Consortium for H5N8 and Related Influenza Viruses, 2016). The same clade has produced reassortants with other neuraminidase subtypes, including A(H5N2) and A(H5N6). A(H5N6) has circulated in poultry in Asia and has caused severe human infections, mostly in China WHO, 2017). Clade 2.3.4.4 viruses have therefore become globally significant HPAIV, with a capacity for long-distance dissemination by wild birds that has not been seen with earlier lineages. In October 2016, A(H5N8) clade 2.3.4.4 was However, detected again in Europe, in wild birds in the Lake Constance and Plön areas and in poultry in Hungary. Following this, a rapid and extensive epidemic developed in the winter of 2016/2017 EFSA, 2017). Phylogenetic analyses suggested that the viruses were related to those detected in wild birds in Central Asia and Russia in mid-2016, consistent with autumn migration towards western wintering grounds [19] "(Global" Consortium for H5N8 and Related Influenza Viruses, 2016; Pohlmann "et" al., 2018). Within a few months, 29 European countries had reported the virus in poultry, captive birds and/or wild birds. This was the largest HPAI epidemic ever recorded in the EU [7] in terms of "number" of poultry outbreaks, geographical extent and number of dead wild birds. The epidemic affected nearly all poultry production sectors, from large commercial layer, broiler and turkey farms to duck and goose holdings and backyard flocks. Several Member States (MSs), notably France, Hungary and Poland, [9] were heavily affected, with substantial economic losses and implications for trade and animal welfare. The scale of the epidemic raised questions about the mechanisms by which the virus was introduced into poultry and spread between holdings. Repeated incursions from infected wild birds appear to have been temporally related to outbreaks in several sectors. Secondary lateral spread through contacts between farms, vehicles and persons, and local environmental contamination also appears to have contributed, particularly where domestic waterfowl, such as ducks kept for foie gras production, were involved. These species may be infected with little clinical sign and so can sustain silent virus circulation (Pantin-Jackwood and Swayne, 2009, Kleyheeg et al., 2017). Such questions are difficult to answer without comparable data on outbreak characteristics, control measures and the structure of the susceptible poultry population. Data collected by MSs differ in format, completeness and in the definitions used for control zones, culling, preventive measures and reporting. This limits comparison among countries and restricts the ability to analyse risk factors, evaluate control strategies and provide science-based advice to risk managers (EFSA, 2017). Events outside Europe also remain relevant to the EU's risk of exposure. HPAI A(H5N6) continued to be detected in Asia, and its pattern of spread resembles that of A(H5N8) and A(H5N1) before they reached Europe. In Africa, AH5N1) and AH5N8) were reported in several countries during 2016–2017, and the situation is evolving rapidly with the potential for further spread and reassortment (OIE, 2017). In China, successive waves of zoonotic A(H7N9) infection, including a large fifth wave in 2016/2017 and the emergence of HPAI AH7N9) variants, showed that new viral variants can quickly create new public health challenges Kile et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017). Sporadic human infections with A(H5N1) in Egypt and A(H9N2) in Asia show that zoonotic transmission occurs wherever intensive poultry exposure combines with endemic virus circulation (WHO, 2017). Human exposure to infected poultry must therefore be monitored carefully during animal outbreaks, as in the EU in 2016/2017, so that any transmission to humans can be detected early and the risk assessed accurately. This report presents an overview of AI in the period from October 2016 to August 2017, prepared under the collaboration between the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the EU Reference Laboratory for Avian Influenza. It has four aims. First, it describes the epidemiology of the A(H5N8) HPAI epidemic in poultry, captive birds and wild birds in the EU, including its spatial and temporal distribution, the poultry sectors affected and the control measures applied by MSs. Second, it uses the data provided by MSs to identify gaps in data collection, poultry population information and the harmonisation of definitions that limit risk factor analysis and comparison. Third, it summarises the AI situation in other parts of the world, in particular the AH5N6), AH5N1), AH5N8), A(H7N9) and A(H9N2) viruses that might pose a threat to Europe through wild bird migration, trade or human exposure. Finally, it reviews the human cases of AI reported worldwide, considers the public health risk to the EU, and examines how exposures of people to infected birds are recorded and reported. The contribution of this overview is twofold. It provides a consolidated descriptive account of the largest HPAI epidemic recorded in the EU, based on a large data collection by affected MSs. It also identifies practical improvements, including better poultry population data, shared definitions for control activities and standardised reporting of human exposure, as well as stronger national, EU and global collaboration. These would improve monitoring, risk assessment and preparedness for future AI incursions. Information hiding is the practice of concealing the existence of a piece of information, or its association with a particular carrier, so that only intended parties can detect or recover it. Its best-known branches are steganography, which hides a secret message inside innocuous-looking data, and digital watermarking, which embeds information in a host object for purposes such as copyright protection and tracing (Cox et al., 2007; Fridrich, 2009). Since Simmons' (1984) formulation of the prisoners' problem, steganography has been modelled as covert communication between two parties through a channel monitored by a warden. Security is then defined by the warden's inability to distinguish cover objects from stego objects (Cachin, 1998). Under this model, research has concentrated on embedding secret data into a cover object, such as an image, audio clip, video, or text, while keeping statistical and perceptual distortion small. Practical progress ranges from early least-significant-bit and transform-domain methods (Provos and Honeyman, 2003; Westfeld, 2001) to content-adaptive schemes based on distortion minimisation and syndrome-trellis codes (Filler et al., 2011), with steganalysis advancing in parallel through rich feature models and machine learning (Fridrich and Kodovský, 2012). Beyond multimedia files, the information hiding community has extended the notion of carrier to communication systems. Network steganography and covert channels hide data in protocol fields, packet timing, or traffic patterns (Zielińska et al., 2014; Mazurczyk et al., 2016; Wendzel et al., 2015). More recently, online social networks (OSNs) have been used as covert media. Researchers have shown that user-generated content on public platforms can carry censorship-resistant messages (Burnett et al., 2010), that social-network structure and activity can support covert botnet command and control (Nagaraja et al., 2011; Pantic and Husain, 2015), and that images and text posted on social media can be turned into stego carriers. These developments reflect a general trend: as digital life moves to large, open, high-volume platforms, such platforms offer both new opportunities for concealment and new difficulties for detection. Despite this diversity, almost all existing approaches share one structural assumption: a cover exists. The cover may be selected from a database, modified in place, synthesised from the message, or, in so-called coverless approaches, chosen or retrieved because its natural features already map to message bits (Zhou et al., 2015). Generative methods using neural networks (Hayes and Danezis, 2017) also produce a concrete cover-like object that carries the payload. In every case the hidden information is attached to a bounded object or message stream that the warden can, in principle, isolate and test. This assumption shapes both attack and defence. Steganalysis is typically framed as a binary classification problem on individual objects, or as pooled analysis over a batch of objects from one source (Ker, 2006). Even when real-world conditions are acknowledged, such as unknown cover sources, mismatched training data, and the sheer volume of traffic, the detection target remains a set of identifiable objects (Ker et al., 2013). This assumption leaves a gap. Contemporary digital environments consist of vast numbers of human and automated agents continuously performing actions: posting, replying, liking, following, retweeting, tagging, and joining groups. The fact that certain actions occurred, with certain attributes (who, when, what type, in what order, toward which targets), is itself observable by anyone with access to the platform. Such activity patterns can encode information without requiring any single content object to be modified or even to be unusual. To our knowledge, the literature has not treated this observable activity space as the carrier in a general, systematic framework. Existing OSN-based However, schemes typically either embed data in the content of posts or in the traffic and behaviour of a specific malware-like structure, and they do not generalise to a design in which an arbitrary set of entities and activities in "an" arbitrary digital world encodes [30] the message. Consequently, we lack both a unifying model and an understanding of the security implications when the cover effectively becomes the entire observable digital world. This paper addresses the following research question: can information be hidden not in [24] a chosen or generated cover object, but in the very fact that particular digital activities, with particular attributes, were carried out in particular ways by selected human and computer entities in a receiver-observable digital world, and what does this imply for applications and for detection? Answering it requires specifying how a message can be mapped onto activity patterns, how a receiver can observe and decode them, how the sender and receiver share the necessary secret (for example, the [6] selected entities, activity types, and mapping rules), and how such a scheme behaves with respect to security notions that were developed for object-based covers. We make the following contributions. First, we propose a general framework for information hiding in digital activities. In it, the sender and receiver agree on a digital world (for example, one or several OSNs), a set of entities within it (such as accounts), and a family of activities and attributes through which the [36] message is expressed. The traditional notion of cover nearly disappears: the whole selected digital world, (12) together with the activity it contains, plays the role of the cover. Second, we discuss application areas in both security and non-security settings. For steganography, the framework offers a channel that does not require producing a suspicious stego [28] object. For non-security uses, such as gaming (for instance, treasure-hunt or puzzle designs where clues are carried by activity patterns), it offers a new interaction medium. Third, we analyse [20] the implications for steganalysis. Because there is no isolated object to inspect, we argue that detection would require monitoring and analysing the whole digital world constantly and in real time, a task [26] likely to be more complex, less effective, and less efficient than existing object-based steganalysis, and one calling for fundamentally new techniques. Fourth, we present a proof-of-concept system, implemented as a mobile app built on [30] Twitter activities, showing that the framework can be realised in a real (17) platform. We also outline (4) ongoing work on a hybrid system that spans several online social networks. The "rest" of this paper is organised as follows: we first formalise the framework and its components, then describe the Twitter-based implementation, and finally discuss security considerations, applications, and directions [33] for future work. Framework formalization. We model the selected digital world as a tuple W = (E, A, T, O), where E = {e1, …, en} is a set of human or computer entities (here, online social network accounts), [21] A is a set of activity types (posting, reposting, liking, following, replying), However, T is a discrete sequence of [32] time slots, and O is the observation function that determines which activities a receiver can see. An activity is a tuple a = (e, α, v, t), where e is the acting entity, α is the activity type, v is a vector of attributes (e.g., target account, hashtag, text length, or media presence), and t is the slot in which it occurred. The sender and receiver share a secret key K and a public specification of W. The hidden message is carried by the fact that [25] a particular ordered set of activities occurred, not by the content of any cover object. This follows the prisoners' problem (17) setting (Simmons, 1984) and the usual requirement that security rest on the key rather than on secrecy of the scheme (Kerckhoffs, 1883; Cachin, 1998). Because every activity in W is a potential carrier, [18] no cover is chosen or modified. Message preparation. (18) The plaintext is compressed and encrypted with AES-256 in counter mode, using a subkey derived from K by [10] HMAC-SHA256 (Bellare et al., 1996). A short header with message length and sequence number is prepended. The (19) result is protected with [20] a Reed–Solomon code (Reed & Solomon, 1960) over GF(2^8), which tolerates the missing or spurious activities expected on a public platform, where unrelated users act concurrently, posts may be deleted, and rate limits may delay actions. The coded stream is split into symbols of b bits. Codebook and embedding. A key-seeded pseudorandom generator, built from HMAC-SHA256 in counter mode, produces for each slot t a codebook Ct. This is an injective map from the 2^b symbol values to distinct activity tuples drawn from the permitted set. Because the codebook changes with t, "repeated" symbols do not yield repeated activity patterns. To embed symbol st, the sender performs the activity Ct(st). Decoding is the inverse lookup. The activity choice also determines how many bits each slot carries: if an slot offers However, m distinguishable tuples, its nominal capacity is log₂ m bits. Embedding capacity therefore grows with the number of controlled accounts, the activity types used, and [20] the attribute resolution. Additional key-derived rules decide which accounts act and when, so that the volume and timing of activity per account stay close to that account's historical behavior. This is meant to reduce statistical deviation from benign activity, in line with the aim of avoiding distributional differences between cover and stego behavior (Cachin, 1998; Hopper et al., 2002). Synchronization and reception. The receiver knows K, the start time, and the slot length. It polls the public timelines and relationship (4) lists of the accounts in E through the platform's REST API at an interval shorter than the slot length, and records each observed activity with its timestamp. For each slot, observed activities are compared with Ct. Matches yield candidate [16] symbols. Activities that match no codeword are treated as background noise and discarded. If several codewords [37] are observed in one slot, the receiver takes the one that also satisfies the header and a message authentication tag. Slots with no match are marked as erasures, which Reed–Solomon decoding handles more efficiently than random errors. After the symbol stream is reassembled, it is decoded, However, decrypted, and checked for integrity. Proof-of-concept implementation. The prototype is a mobile app with [8] sender and receiver modes. The sender mode authenticates through OAuth to a set of Twitter accounts that we own and operate. It schedules activities in a background service according to the codebook. Activity types are original posts with controlled attributes (hashtag from a (27) key-derived list, tweet-length bin, presence of a link), reposts of designated accounts, likes, and follows or unfollows. The receiver mode uses read-only "API" access. All keys remain in the device's secure storage. Cryptographic operations use the platform's standard libraries. To reduce risk to the platform and other users, request rates stay within documented limits, and only accounts created for the experiment are used as carriers. Experimental design. We ran However, controlled experiments with n ∈ {5, 10, 20} experimental accounts, b ∈ {2, 4, 6} bits per slot, and slot lengths of 1, 5, and 15 minutes. For each factor combination, random messages of 32, 64, and 128 bytes were transmitted in 30 independent trials, with the sender and receiver on separate devices and networks. A subset of accounts also followed and interacted with a pool of unrelated public accounts; so that the receiver would see realistic background activity. We also injected synthetic perturbations (deleted posts and suspended polling windows) to test robustness. The primary outcomes were: (i) message recovery rate, the proportion of trials with exact plaintext recovery; (ii) symbol error and erasure rates before error correction; (iii) effective embedding rate in bits per hour, after coding overhead; and (iv) end-to-end latency from the first embedded activity to successful decoding. Detectability analysis. Since the framework implies that a steganalyst must monitor the whole world W, we evaluated detectability under a simplified adversary with access to the same public API. Baseline behavioral profiles were obtained from the pre-experiment activity histories of the same accounts and, where permitted by the platform's terms, from a sample of comparable public accounts. For each account we computed features such as per-hour activity counts by type, inter-activity time distributions, hashtag frequencies, and the entropy of interaction targets. Soft biometric traits such as sex, age, ethnicity, and eye colour describe a person coarsely but are useful in practice. They are not distinctive enough to identify an individual on their own, but they can narrow a search space, complement primary biometric modalities, and support applications where explicit identification is unnecessary or undesirable (Jain, Dass, & Nandakumar, 2004; Dantcheva, Elia, & Ross, 2016). Among these traits, sex is one of the most widely studied, with uses in indexing large biometric databases, demographic analysis, human–computer interaction, and forensic investigation. Predicting sex from a person's appearance is commonly called "gender classification" in the literature. We use the term sex-prediction because the quantity inferred from biometric data is a biological attribute rather than a social identity (Bobeldyk & Ross, 2016). The face is the most intuitive source for such predictions, and deep learning has made face-based sex classification highly accurate under favourable conditions. In many real scenarios, however, the full face is not available. Surgical masks, scarves, helmets, and extreme poses or viewing angles can all hide the lower facial region. Under these conditions the periocular region, which covers the eye, eyelids, eyelashes, eyebrows, and surrounding skin, is an attractive alternative. It remains visible when the rest of the face is occluded, it can be captured by a wide range of sensors, and it combines shape, texture, and colour information that is useful for recognition (Park, Ross, & Jain, 2009; Alonso-Fernandez & Bigun, 2016). Periocular images also arise naturally from iris acquisition in the near-infrared (NIR) spectrum and from visible wavelength VW) imaging with smartphones and other consumer devices. Early work showed that the periocular region contains information about sex. Merkow, Jou, and Savvides (2010) reported accuracies of roughly 85% from periocular crops of web-collected face images using hand-crafted features. Dong and Woodard (2011) showed that eyebrow shape alone carries a discriminative signal. For NIR iris and ocular images, Thomas et al. (2007) and Lagree and Bowyer (2011) predicted sex from texture descriptors, with accuracies typically between 60% and 80%. More recent studies have applied convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and obtained better results. Tapia and Aravena (2018) obtained high accuracy from NIR iris images, and Bobeldyk and Ross (2016, 2018) examined which ocular regions contribute most to sex-prediction and how covariates influence it. Rattani, Reddy, and Derakhshani (2018) extended the problem to smartphone-based VW ocular images and reported competitive accuracies with deep architectures. Taken together, these studies suggest that sex can be inferred from the periocular region with a reasonable degree of reliability. The reported figures, however, need to be interpreted with care. First, most studies train and test on a single database, and often on a single sensor. In such protocols images in the training and test partitions share acquisition conditions such as illumination, resolution, optics, and sensor noise. In several cases they also share subjects or sessions. A classifier can then exploit sensor-specific or session-specific cues instead of sex-related structure, which inflates performance. The concern is more than theoretical. Kuehlkamp, Becker, and Bowyer 2017) showed that apparent sex-related information in iris images can be partly attributed to cosmetics such as mascara, and that accuracy drops substantially once this confound is removed. It is also well documented that biometric algorithms trained on one sensor often degrade when evaluated on another, which is the cross-sensor problem studied extensively in iris and periocular recognition (Alonso-Fernandez, Raja, Busch, & Bigun, 2019). If sex-prediction is to be deployed on periocular images whose origin is unknown, accuracy [10] estimated under same-sensor conditions is an optimistic upper bound. Second, NIR and VW periocular images are almost always treated separately. The two spectra differ in the visual information they offer. [7] NIR imaging suppresses melanin-related pigmentation and emphasises structural texture, whereas VW images contain colour, pigmentation, and cosmetic cues. Whether sex-related patterns learned in one spectrum transfer to the other, and whether a single model can handle both, is largely unexplored. This question matters for heterogeneous deployments; for example when a model trained on NIR iris-capture databases is applied to selfie-type VW images, or the reverse. Third, the methodological details of prior studies make results hard to compare. They differ in image size; in how the periocular region is cropped, in [28] architecture, in partitioning protocol, and in whether subjects are disjoint across training and test sets. Few studies test the generalisation of a single model across many databases with a consistent protocol, and the effect of fusing heterogeneous sources into one training set has received little [9] attention. These gaps lead to the central [12] research question of this paper: How accurately can the "sex" of a subject be predicted from periocular images when the sensor and the spectrum of the test images are unknown at training time? We split this into three subquestions. (i) What accuracy can be expected when training and testing are performed on disjoint sensors within the same However, spectrum (NIR–NIR and VW–VW)? (ii) How well does a model generalise across spectra; that is, when trained on NIR data and tested on VW data, and vice versa? (iii) Can a single model trained on a multi-spectral collection perform comparably to spectrum-specific models? To answer these questions, we train CNNs on fused sets composed of several NIR and VW periocular databases acquired with different sensors, and we evaluate them under However, However, protocols that keep the test sensor out of training. This design reflects a more realistic setting in which the origin of an image is not known beforehand. It also discourages the network from using sensor-specific artefacts as shortcuts, since a model trained on a heterogeneous mixture cannot rely on any single sensor's signature. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1. A cross-sensor evaluation within each spectrum. Using leave-one-database-out protocols, we estimate sex-prediction accuracy for unseen sensors in NIR and VW imagery. [27] The average accuracy is approximately 85% in both cases, which is a more cautious figure than those often reported for [20] single-database experiments. 2. A cross-spectral evaluation. We quantify the transferability of learned sex-related features between NIR and VW images. The average classification accuracy is about 82%, only a few points below the within-spectrum case; which suggests that a [33] substantial portion of "the" discriminative information is spectrum-independent. 3. A multi-spectral model. We show that a single CNN trained on combined NIR and [7] VW data attains an average accuracy of 83%. It can therefore be used when the spectrum of the input is not known, at a modest cost in accuracy relative to specialised models. 4. A consistent, reproducible protocol. We apply the same preprocessing, periocular cropping, network configurations, and partitioning rules across all databases, so that differences in performance can be attributed to the acquisition scenario rather than to differences in experimental design. Overall; the findings give a [6] more realistic estimate of how feasible it is to predict a subject's sex from the periocular region. They also indicate where current approaches are likely to fail when applied to unconstrained data. The results are relevant to both the design of soft-biometric systems and the discussion of privacy, since the ease with which sex can "be" inferred from periocular images captured without a subject's explicit intent has [27] implications for how such data are stored and shared (Mirjalili & Ross, 2017). Databases. Experiments were conducted on publicly available periocular and iris databases covering two spectra [27] and several acquisition sensors. The near-infrared (NIR) set comprised BioSec (Fierrez et al., 2007), CASIA-Iris-Thousand (CASIA, 2010), IITD-Iris (Kumar and Passi, 2010), and ND-CrossSensor (Connaughton et al., 2013). The visible-wavelength (VW) set comprised UBIPr (Padole and Proença, 2012), MICHE-I (De Marsico et al., 2015), and CSIP (Santos et al., 2015). Sex labels were taken from the metadata distributed with each database; and subjects without reliable labels were excluded. Because the labels are binary male or female), we refer to the task as sex-prediction. After filtering, the NIR set contained approximately 41,000 images from 1,650 subjects and the VW set approximately 22,000 images from 940 subjects. The proportion of [27] female subjects ranged from 29% to 47% across databases. Databases differ in resolution, illumination, stand-off distance, and subject demographics, so a sensor-specific model may exploit dataset-specific artefacts rather than sex-related periocular characteristics (Torralba and Efros, 2011). The cross-database protocols below were designed to expose and control this effect. Preprocessing. Eye regions were localised with a landmark detector (Kazemi and Sullivan, 2014) for VW images. For NIR images, we used the pupil and iris boundaries from a Hough-transform-based segmentation (Masek and Kovesi, 2003) with manual verification of a random 5% subset. A periocular region of interest was cropped around the eye centre with a width of 6.0 times the iris radius and a height of 4.5 times the iris radius. This included eyebrow, eyelids, and surrounding skin and avoided hair and facial context. Right-eye images were mirrored horizontally so that all samples had the same canonical orientation. Crops were resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bicubic interpolation. NIR images were replicated across "three" channels, and VW images were kept in RGB. Pixel intensities were normalised with the ImageNet channel statistics used for pretraining (Deng et al., 2009). Images for which landmark [4] detection [4] or segmentation failed (3.1% of all samples) were discarded. Network architecture and training. We used ResNet-50 (He et al.; 2016) and DenseNet-121 [10] (Huang et al., 2017) as feature extractors. Both were initialised with ImageNet weights and fine-tuned end to end. The original classification layer was replaced by global average pooling, a dropout layer (rate 0.5), and a two-unit softmax layer. Models were optimised with stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9, an initial learning rate of 10⁻³ decayed by a factor of 10 when validation loss plateaued for five epochs, a batch size of 64, and weight decay of 5 × 10⁻⁴. Training ran for at most 60 epochs with early stopping (patience 10) on validation loss. The loss was cross-entropy. [35] To reduce the effect of class imbalance, each training However, epoch used class-balanced mini-batches drawn by oversampling the minority class. Data augmentation consisted of random rotations (±10°), random scaling (0.9–1.1), random translations (up to 5% of image size), brightness and contrast jitter (±20%), and Gaussian blur (σ ≤ 1.5), applied on the fly. Horizontal flipping was not used for augmentation because mirroring was already applied for canonicalisation. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) and repeated with five random seeds, and results are reported as means over seeds. Experimental protocols. To approximate the realistic case in which the capture device is unknown, models were trained on fused sets of multiple databases and evaluated on a database that was entirely excluded from training. Three scenarios were defined. Cross-sensor, within spectrum. For each spectrum, we applied a leave-one-database-out protocol. A model was trained on the union of all other databases of the same spectrum and tested on the held-out database. With four NIR and three VW databases; this gave seven train–test configurations. Training data were split 80/20 into training and validation partitions at subject level. Cross-spectrum. Models were trained on the union of all NIR databases and tested on each VW database, and vice versa. Neither the sensor nor the spectrum of the test data was seen during training. Domain adaptation and spectrum-specific normalisation were deliberately not used, so that the evaluation reflects the transferability of learned features alone. Multi-spectral. Models were trained on the union of NIR and VW databases, excluding one database that served [17] as the test set. This was repeated for all seven databases. The aim was to determine whether exposure to both spectra yields a more general representation than spectrum-specific training. Subject-disjoint partitions were enforced in all scenarios, so that no subject's images, including those of the contralateral eye, appeared in both training and testing. Within a database, left and right eyes of the same subject were always assigned to the same partition. Deep learning has transformed machine learning largely through its ability to learn useful representations from data. A central theme in this progress is transfer learning: a model is trained on one task, usually with abundant data, and the knowledge it acquires is reused to improve performance on other tasks where labeled data are scarcer. In natural language processing, the most prominent form of transfer is the pretrained word embedding (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014), and more recently contextualized representations obtained from language models or other pretraining objectives Peters et al., 2018; McCann et al., 2017). In computer vision, convolutional features pretrained on ImageNet have become a default starting point for a wide range of downstream problems (Donahue et al., 2014; Yosinski et al., 2014, He et al., 2016). Despite their differences, these approaches share a common characteristic: what is transferred is a set of unary features, that is, a vector associated with each individual data unit such as a word, a token in context, or an image region. Unary features, however, capture only part of what a model needs to know about the structure of its input. Many of the most important regularities in data concern relations between pairs of units. In language, a word depends on its syntactic head, on a coreferent mention several sentences earlier, or on a semantically related phrase. In images, a pixel's interpretation depends on neighboring pixels belonging to the same edge or object. Modern architectures encode this kind of structure in different ways: recurrent networks propagate information along a fixed sequential order, convolutional networks impose a fixed local connectivity, and self-attention models Vaswani et al., 2017) learn input-dependent weights that determine how strongly each unit attends to every other. Attention in particular can be viewed as a latent relational graph over the input units, with edge weights computed on the fly. Yet in nearly all existing transfer learning pipelines, this relational structure is learned from scratch for each task, and from limited labeled data. Meanwhile, structured representations such as syntactic parses or knowledge graphs, which have been shown to help many tasks Tai et al., 2015; Marcheggiani and Titov, 2017; Kipf and Welling, 2017), require either expensive human annotation or an external parser that is itself trained with supervision and is available only for certain languages and domains. This observation motivates the central question of this work: can we learn generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data, and can such graphs be transferred to improve downstream tasks? Answering this affirmatively would offer a complementary route to transfer learning. Rather than only providing better initial feature vectors, a pretrained model would provide a structure describing [38] how the units of a new input relate to one another, which a downstream model [30] can use to organize its own computation. Such graphs have several potential advantages. They are separable from the features that produced them, so they might be reused with different embeddings. They are potentially modality-agnostic, since the notion of pairwise dependency applies equally to words and pixels. And they can be learned without labels, so they can exploit the same virtually unlimited text corpora that have powered recent advances in language representation. Realizing this idea poses several challenges. First, we need an unsupervised objective that encourages a network to produce graphs that are useful and not merely arbitrary. Second, the graphs must be decoupled from the features: if the graph at each layer is computed from, and entangled with, the particular hidden states of the pretraining model, it cannot be applied to a downstream model with different embeddings or architecture. Third, the graphs should be input-dependent, since the relevant dependencies differ from sentence to sentence and image to image, yet they must be computable for new inputs at transfer time without access to the original [12] task's labels or features. We propose GLoMo (Graphs from LOw-level MOdules), a framework that addresses these challenges. GLoMo trains a network on an unsupervised predictive task in which two components are explicitly separated. A graph predictor takes the raw input and produces, at several layers, a set of affinity matrices whose entries give the strength of the dependency between each pair of units. A separate feature predictor then uses [10] these matrices to aggregate information from layer-wise features and make predictions about held-out parts of the input. Concretely, in the language setting, the objective is to predict the next word (and [28] previous word, in [27] the backward direction) given context, with the graph restricted to depend only on the input [24] tokens and not on the feature pathway that consumes it. Because the graph predictor must provide all the information about how units should be combined, while the feature pathway processes only the content, the graphs are forced to encode reusable relational structure. At transfer time, the graph predictor is frozen and applied to the downstream input, and the resulting graphs are plugged into the downstream network as additional, fixed-weight routing structures that mix the downstream model's own features across units, alongside its usual computation. We evaluate GLoMo on a diverse set of problems: question answering, natural "language" inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. In language tasks, adding transferred graphs yields consistent [9] improvements over strong baselines, including [10] models that already use pretrained GloVe or ELMo embeddings, indicating that the graphs provide information complementary to unary features. We further show that the learned graphs are transferable across representation spaces: they can be applied on top of embeddings on which they were not trained, including GloVe, ELMo, and task-specific RNN hidden states. Finally, we show that the idea extends beyond language, as graphs learned over image pixels improve classification accuracy, demonstrating that the framework does not rely on word embeddings or any modality-specific components. Our contributions are as follows. 1) We introduce the problem of transferring learned relational graphs, as opposed to unary features, from unlabeled data. (2) We propose GLoMo, an unsupervised framework that decouples graph prediction from feature prediction so that graphs become transferable. (3) We show empirically that the learned graphs improve performance across several language tasks and an image classification task, and that they transfer across embedding types and to embedding-free units. (4) We provide analyses of the learned graphs, which show that they capture meaningful patterns, suggesting that they encode structure beyond what is available in standard pretrained However, features. Overview We propose GLoMo (Graph from Learned Moments), a two-stage "framework." In the first stage, a graph predictor is trained without labels to produce latent relational graphs over the units of an input (words or image positions), while a feature predictor uses these graphs to solve an unsupervised objective. In the second stage, the graph predictor is frozen and used to generate graphs for downstream inputs. The graphs are then combined with task-specific features through a lightweight transfer module, and only the downstream network is trained on labeled data. Only the graphs, not the features that produced them, are transferred. Unsupervised Pretraining Let x = x1, ..., xT) be a sequence of input units. The graph predictor g is a network that maps x to a set of K affinity matrices, 𝒢 = {G^(k)}, k = 1..K, with G^(k) ∈ ℝ^{T×T}. We use a stack of L layers, each producing its own graph, so graphs are layer-specific and multiple graphs per layer are possible (heads). Each entry Gij is computed as a normalized, asymmetric compatibility between a "query" projection of unit i and a "key" projection of unit j, following the form of attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015, Vaswani et al., 2017): Gij = softmaxj( (Wq hi)ᵀ (Wk hj) ), where h are hidden states produced by a convolutional or recurrent encoder operating on x that is entirely separate from the downstream features. Crucially, h is computed only from the raw input and is used solely to build the graph, so that G encodes relations rather than content. For language, g is a stack of 1D convolutions with gated linear units Dauphin et al., 2017) over word-level inputs, for images, g is a stack of 2D convolutions, with units being spatial positions in a feature map. The feature predictor f takes the input units and the graphs and produces representations through graph-based propagation. At layer l, with features z^(l) ∈ ℝ^{T×d}, z^(l+1)i = φ( Σj G^(l)ij · U z^(l)j , z^(l)i ), where φ is a gated nonlinearity with a residual connection and U is a learned matrix. To prevent trivial solutions, the predictor must solve a self-supervised task for which the graph is the sole route to context. For language we adopt a masked-context variant of language modeling: the representation used to predict word xt is constrained so that Gij is nonzero only for j < t in the forward direction and j > t in a separately trained backward model), so that the target is not visible. The loss is the cross-entropy of next-word (and previous-word) prediction with an adaptive softmax (Grave et al., 2017) over the vocabulary. For [33] images, we predict the pixel/feature values of the lower half of the image from the upper half, using the same causal masking on the graph over spatial positions, with a regression loss over the targets. Because the feature predictor has limited capacity beyond propagation along G, the graph predictor is encouraged to concentrate useful dependency structure in 𝒢. Pretraining Data For language, we pretrain on the One Billion Word benchmark (Chelba et al., 2014) for the question answering and sentiment experiments, and on the BookCorpus-style long-document text where longer context is needed. Text is tokenized, lowercased, and truncated to a 100K-word vocabulary with rare words mapped to an unknown token. Sentences are batched by length, with a maximum sequence length of 50 tokens during pretraining. For images, we pretrain on the unlabeled training split of CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky, 2009) with the labels discarded, and, in an additional setting, on unlabeled [4] ImageNet-sized data Deng et al., 2009) at reduced resolution. Models are optimized with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015), with learning rate 1e-3, gradient clipping at norm 1.0, and dropout of 0.1. Transfer to Downstream Tasks After pretraining, g is frozen. For a downstream input, we compute 𝒢 from the raw tokens or pixels. The downstream model has its own base features z^(0) e.g., GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), or hidden states of a task-specific RNN). We augment them with a graph-based transformation at each of several layers: z^(l+1) = ψ( z^l), Σk ak G^(k) z^(l) W^(k) ), where ak are learned scalar mixing weights and W^k) are task-specific projections. Graphs may also be multiplied (G·G) to capture multi-hop dependencies; we include up to two [34] hops. The augmented features are fed to the downstream architecture without altering its output layers. Since G is computed from separate inputs, transfer across embeddings [28] requires no retraining of g; we test this explicitly by switching the downstream base features between GloVe, ELMo, and RNN states. Downstream Tasks and Baselines [24] We evaluate on six benchmarks. Question answering: SQuAD v1.1 Rajpurkar et al., 2016), using a BiDAF-style Seo et al., 2017) and a self-attentive reader as base models, and reporting exact match (EM) and F1. Natural language inference: MultiNLI (Williams et al., 2018) with matched and mismatched dev sets, using ESIM-like baselines (Chen et al., 2017), reporting accuracy. Sentiment analysis: IMDB (Maas et al., 2011) and Stanford Sentiment Treebank Socher et al., 2013), reporting accuracy. Image classification: CIFAR-10 with a standard residual network (He et al., 2016) in which graphs act on the spatial positions of intermediate feature maps; we additionally vary the amount of labeled training data (e.g., 10%–100%) to study low-resource behavior. 1 [35] Introduction Graphs are a natural abstraction for social, biological, and information systems, and many of them are now very large. Facebook reports billions of users, and bibliographic databases [5] such as DBLP index millions of authors and publications. A recurring task on such graphs is to find communities, which are groups of vertices that are densely connected internally and share common characteristics (Girvan and Newman 2002; Fortunato 2010). Traditional community detection (CD) partitions an entire graph and is costly on large networks. It also produces communities that are not tailored to any particular user. Community search (CS) addresses both limitations. Given a query vertex q, CS finds a cohesive subgraph containing q, usually online and without examining the whole graph (Sozio and Gionis 2010; Cui et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2020). Personalized communities of this kind support product advertisement, social event recommendation, and the discovery of functional modules in protein interaction networks (Huang et al. 2014; Fang et al. 2016). Structural cohesiveness is typically expressed through minimum-degree constraints. Under the k-core model (Seidman 1983; Batagelj and Zaversnik 2003), every vertex in the community has at least k neighbors inside it. Stronger models include the k-truss (Huang et al. 2014; Huang and Lakshmanan 2017), the k-clique, and the k-edge-connected component. These approaches use only topology, so the communities they return can be internally dense yet semantically incoherent. A hub vertex with many weak ties may be placed in a community that shares no theme with [15] its members. Recent work has therefore used vertex attributes. Attributed community queries return subgraphs whose members share a set of keywords (Fang et al. 2016; Fang et al. 2017), and related models consider numerical attributes or geographical locations. These models treat attributes [39] as a flat set of independent labels. In many real networks, however, the labels attached to a vertex are organized hierarchically. In bibliographic [13] networks, an author's research interests can be mapped onto the ACM Computing Classification System, where "Machine learning" is a specialization of "Computing methodologies." In biomedical networks, genes and proteins are annotated with Gene Ontology terms (Ashburner et al. 2000), and publications are indexed with Medical Subject Headings. Online retailers and social [21] platforms organize items and user interests into category trees. We call a graph whose vertices [22] carry such hierarchical labels a profiled graph, and the label hierarchy attached to a vertex its P-tree. This is a rooted subtree of a global taxonomy. Because a P-tree contains a label together with the ancestors that generalize it, two vertices can share a meaningful theme even if they have no identical leaf-level labels. For example, one author may work on "deep learning" and another on "support vector machines". Both are connected through the shared ancestor "machine learning," which a flat keyword model cannot capture. This observation exposes a gap in existing work. Structure-only CS ignores semantics entirely. Keyword-based CS can only match identical labels and therefore misses communities whose members are related at different granularities. It also cannot report how specific [6] the shared theme is. Existing methods return a community with a flat set of shared labels, whereas a user exploring a profiled graph often needs to know the maximal common subtree of the members' P-trees. That subtree describes the community's theme at the most informative level of detail. In a preliminary study on a DBLP-derived graph with ACM-CCS profiles, k-core communities containing a given author had on average only 1.3 common labels at depth two or deeper in the taxonomy. This suggests that structurally cohesive communities are often thematically loose. In this paper, we study the profiled community search (PCS) problem. Given a profiled graph G, a query vertex q, and an integer k, PCS returns [38] subgraphs that satisfy two conditions. They are structurally cohesive, meaning each vertex has degree at least k within a connected subgraph containing q. They are also semantically cohesive, meaning their vertices share a common subtree of P-trees that is maximal and contains the P-tree structure rooted at the taxonomy's root. Each answer is thus a profiled community (PC) paired with its shared theme, represented as a maximal common subtree. We ask three questions. Can hierarchical profiles yield communities that are more cohesive and more interpretable than those from structure-only and keyword-based CS? Can PCS be solved exactly (20) at the scale of real networks? Can it be answered online, at interactive latencies? PCS poses several challenges. The number of candidate subtrees of a P-tree grows exponentially with its size, so enumerating every subtree and testing it for a qualifying k-core is infeasible. A naive algorithm that does this required hours on graphs with only tens of thousands of vertices in our experiments. Moreover, the subtree space has a structure that flat-set approaches cannot exploit directly. A candidate subtree must be rooted, so that a label can only be included if all [3] its ancestors are included. Pruning rules designed for itemset lattices must therefore be adapted to tree-shaped candidates. Finally, because different query vertices induce different search spaces, a practical solution should rely on a reusable index instead of recomputation for every query. We make the following contributions. 1. Problem formulation. We introduce the PCS problem and formalize profiled graphs, P-trees, and profiled communities. We show that the maximal common subtree semantics (20) yield themed communities at a granularity that adapts to the data, and we analyze their basic [28] properties, including anti-monotonicity of the k-core with respect to subtree inclusion. This property underlies our pruning strategies. 2. Index and algorithms. We design the CP-tree, a compact index that organizes the vertices of G by their labels over the taxonomy and stores, for each node, the core numbers needed to retrieve candidate vertex sets. On top of it we [12] develop a basic query algorithm that traverses candidate subtrees level by level, together with advanced algorithms that use anti-monotonicity and vertex-set intersection to avoid verifying most candidates. We also give an efficient index construction method, and we analyze the time and space complexity of all procedures. 3. Effectiveness evaluation. We evaluate PCS on five real graphs, including DBLP and a PubMed-based biomedical network. We measure community quality using structural measures such [9] as density and clustering coefficient, and semantic measures such as label-based similarity and the depth of the shared theme. PCS communities consistently outperform those from k-core, k-truss, and keyword-based CS. For instance, on DBLP (29) they have on average 2.1 times the number of shared labels of structure-only communities, and their shared themes lie 1.8 levels deeper in the taxonomy. A case study of well-known researchers shows that PCS separates an author's distinct research areas into different, interpretable communities that other approaches merge. 4. Efficiency evaluation. Our index-based algorithms are two to three orders of magnitude faster than the naive approach. They answer queries on graphs with over one million vertices in under a second on average, which supports online use. The CP-tree can be built in minutes and has a space overhead proportional to the total size of the vertex P-trees, which makes it practical for large profiled graphs. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formally defines the PCS problem. Section 4 presents the CP-tree index and the query algorithms. Section 5 reports experimental results, and Section 6 concludes the paper. Problem (15) formulation. We model a profiled graph as an undirected graph G(V, E) in which each vertex v ∈ V is associated with a profile P(v), a rooted subtree of a global concept hierarchy T (for example, the ACM Computing Classification System or the Medical Subject Headings, MeSH). A profile is closed under ancestors: if a label belongs to P(v), so do all of its ancestors up to the root. This property allows the set of labels of a vertex to be treated as a rooted subtree, which we call a P-tree. The common P-tree of a vertex set S is the intersection of the P-trees of its members. It is itself a rooted subtree and is therefore well defined. Cohesiveness is measured by the minimum-degree criterion, which underlies the k-core (Seidman, 1983) and has been widely adopted in community search (Sozio & Gionis, 2010; Fang et al., 2016; Fang et al., 2017). Given a query vertex q and an integer k, a profiled community is a connected subgraph Gq ⊆ G that (i) contains q, (ii) has minimum degree at least k, and (iii) has a maximal common P-tree. Maximality means that no connected k-core containing q shares a strictly larger common P-tree. The profiled community search (PCS) problem returns all such pairs (Gq, M), where M is the maximal common P-tree of Gq. Several incomparable maximal subtrees may exist, so a query can return several communities, each characterized by a different theme. Datasets. We evaluated PCS on four real profiled graphs (Table 1). Flickr contains users linked by friendship, with profiles built from image tags mapped to a taxonomy of visual concepts. DBLP is a co-authorship network in which author profiles are derived from the ACM Computing Classification System tags of their publications. PubMed is a co-authorship network whose profiles are based on MeSH headings. DBpedia is an (15) entity-relationship network whose entities are labeled with ontology classes. The graphs ranged from 0.9 million to 8.2 million vertices and from 5.4 million to 51 million edges. Average profile sizes ranged from 7.3 to 18.6 labels, and the hierarchies had depths of 4 to 11 levels. We removed self-loops and duplicate edges, retained only the largest connected component, and discarded vertices with empty profiles. Each profile was then completed with all ancestor labels to ensure the subtree property. We also generated synthetic profiled graphs by attaching random subtrees of a fixed hierarchy to the vertices (24) of Barabási–Albert graphs, which let us vary graph size and profile size independently in the scalability experiments. Query workload. For each dataset we sampled 200 query vertices uniformly at random from those with core number at least 6 (Batagelj & Zaversnik, 2003), so that nontrivial communities exist for the default parameter k = 6. We also varied k from 4 to 8 in the sensitivity analysis. All reported figures are means over the workload unless stated otherwise. Baseline algorithm. The anti-monotone structure of the problem motivates a level-wise search in the spirit of Apriori (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994). If a P-tree T′ is shared by a k-core containing q, every subtree of T′ rooted at the root is also shared by that k-core. The basic algorithm therefore starts from the single-node tree consisting of the root. At each iteration it expands every feasible tree by one leaf label, taken from a child of an existing node that also appears in P(q), and generates candidate trees whose sub-trees were all feasible. Feasibility of a candidate T′ is verified by restricting G to the vertices whose profiles contain T′, computing the k-core, and checking whether q lies in its connected component. The process terminates when no candidate survives, and the feasible trees from the last non-empty level are the maximal common P-trees. Although correct, this approach repeatedly traverses the graph and repeats subtree-containment tests, and its cost grows quickly with profile size and hierarchy depth. CP-tree index. To support online queries, we developed the compressed profile tree (CP-tree) index. It is constructed by merging the label hierarchy with the k-core decomposition of G. For each label x in T, let Vx be the set of vertices whose profiles contain x, and let G[Vx] be the induced subgraph. Because G[Vx] ⊆ G[Vy] whenever y is an ancestor of x, the induced subgraphs are nested along every root-to-leaf path. This allows the core decomposition of G[Vx] to be stored incrementally. Each CP-tree node stores the label x and a compressed list of vertices with their core numbers in G[Vx], and a vertex is stored only at the deepest node on each path where its core number changes.
