Modern autonomous systems, including self-driving vehicles, unmanned aerial platforms, robotic manipulators, and smart-grid components, depend on a [16] continuous flow of information from sensors through communication channels to estimation and decision modules. This dependence makes them vulnerable. Sensors degrade or fail, measurements are corrupted by noise, and wireless links drop or delay packets. A malicious party can also deliberately alter the data. Incidents such as Stuxnet (Langner, 2011) and the vulnerabilities documented for power-grid state estimation (Liu et al., 2011; Kosut et al., 2010) show that cyber-physical systems are realistic targets of attacks on data integrity. If a controller or decision maker acts on corrupted measurements, performance can degrade, and in safety-critical settings the consequences may be severe (Cárdenas et al., 2008; Mo & Sinopoli, 2016). Estimating the true system state from unreliable and possibly adversarial measurements is therefore a central problem in secure control. Classical state estimation offers well-developed tools but makes assumptions that attacks violate. The Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1966) and the Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960) are optimal or well-behaved when the dynamics are known and the disturbances are benign, typically zero-mean Gaussian noise with known covariance. Robust formulations, such as H-infinity filtering Nagpal & Khargonekar, 1991) and the minimax and dynamic game viewpoint of Başar and Bernhard (1995), treat disturbances as worst-case but bounded-energy signals. The security literature has studied attack detection and identification (Pasqualetti et al., 2013), secure estimation under sparse sensor attacks (Fawzi et al., 2014), and the limits of stealthy attacks (Mo & Sinopoli, 2016; Teixeira et al., 2015). These results give strong guarantees, but they usually require linear or otherwise tractable dynamics, structural assumptions on [13] the attack, such as sparsity or a known model class, and explicit analytical derivations. For nonlinear, high-dimensional, or partially unknown systems, these requirements are often not met, and the resulting designs can be conservative or intractable. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural alternative. Combined with neural function approximators, RL has produced strong policies in games and continuous control (Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Lillicrap et al., 2016; Schulman et al., 2017) without requiring closed-form solutions of the underlying optimization problem. Most RL work, however, is aimed at designing controllers, not observers, and typically assumes the agent observes its environment faithfully. Neural network policies are known to be fragile to small perturbations of their inputs (Szegedy et al., 2014; Goodfellow et al., 2015), and adversarial perturbations of observations can sharply reduce the return of trained agents (Huang et al., 2017). Robust RL has responded in several ways. Early work treated disturbances as a worst-case player (Morimoto & Doya, 2005). Robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) trains a [24] protagonist against an adversary that applies destabilizing forces. Subsequent work has considered robustness to adversarial state perturbations through state-adversarial Markov decision processes, regularization, and learned optimal attackers (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Oikarinen et al., 2021). These approaches mostly aim to make the policy insensitive to observation errors. They do not ask a different question: given a stream of possibly corrupted measurements, how should a dedicated observer combine them to reconstruct the state as accurately as possible when an intelligent adversary chooses the corruption? This is the gap we address. Treating the observer as a learned decision maker that selects estimates, or observation strategies, from corrupted measurement histories has received little attention in the adversarial setting. The problem is a game: [28] the adversary chooses errors to maximize the estimation or downstream performance loss, and the observer chooses its strategy to minimize it. Two difficulties arise. First, the observer sees only corrupted outputs, so the problem is partially observed, and a good strategy generally depends on the history of measurements Kaelbling et al., 1998; Hausknecht [32] & Stone, 2015). Second, a static or hand-designed adversary is a weak test, because a fixed attack pattern can be learned and discounted, whereas an adaptive adversary can exploit whatever [12] "weakness" the observer retains. Meaningful robustness requires training the observer against an adversary that is itself learning, as in the framework of Markov games (Littman, 1994) and multi-agent deep RL (Lowe et al., 2017). Without some restriction on the adversary, such as a bound on the magnitude or energy of the injected errors, no estimator can guarantee anything, since unconstrained corruption can make the measurements uninformative. Any credible framework must therefore specify the sense in which the adversary is bounded and show how performance depends on that bound. The research question of this paper is accordingly the following. Can adversarial deep reinforcement [8] learning be used to design observer strategies for autonomous systems that remain accurate when the information channel is corrupted by an adaptive, bounded adversary, and how well do such learned observers perform relative to the adversary's capabilities? We pose the design of the observer as a zero-sum, two-player sequential game between an observer and an attacker acting on the measurement channel, and we solve it with deep RL. We make three contributions. First, we develop a general framework that formulates robust observer design under adversarial measurement errors as an adversarial RL problem, in which an observer agent and an adversary However, agent are trained in alternation, or concurrently, with opposing objectives. The formulation "does" not rely on linearity of the dynamics, Gaussian noise, or a specific attack structure, and it accommodates sensor faults, noise, channel failures, and deliberate cyber-attacks within one error-injection model. Second, we implement the "framework" using neural networks as function approximators for both players, while noting that the framework is agnostic to the approximator class, and any other suitable family, such as kernel methods, tree ensembles, or basis expansions, could take its place. Third, we present simulation studies showing that the learned observation strategies perform remarkably [30] well when the adversary's injected errors are bounded in a suitable sense, and we characterize how performance varies with the bound. Together, these results suggest that adversarial RL is a practical route to observers that are robust by construction, rather than by analysis of a specific attack model. The rest of the paper formalizes the problem setting, describes the training procedure, and reports the numerical experiments. We consider a discrete-time stochastic linear plant, x{t+1} = A xt + B ut + wt, with state xt ∈ ℝⁿ, control ut ∈ ℝᵐ, and process noise wt ~ N(0, Q). The controller receives a measurement yt = C xt + vt + at, where vt ~ N(0, R) is ordinary sensor noise and at ∈ ℝᵖ is an additive error injected by an adversary. The injection represents sensor faults, channel corruption, or a false-data-injection attack, as in the cyber-physical security literature (Pasqualetti et al., 2013). The adversary is constrained by a per-step budget ‖at‖∞ ≤ ε. "We" call this the bounded-error assumption. The [35] budget is the main experimental variable, and we report results for ε ∈ {0, [5] 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0} in units of the standard deviation of the noiseless measurement. The controller is a fixed linear-quadratic regulator, ut = −K x̂t, computed for the nominal plant (Anderson & Moore, 1990). The observer is the only component that is designed or learned, so differences in closed-loop performance come entirely from the quality of x̂t. The observer design problem is formulated as a two-player zero-sum Markov game in the spirit of robust adversarial reinforcement learning (Pinto et al., 2017) and of classical minimax estimation Başar & Bernhard, 1995). The observer's observation at time t is a window of the last H measurements and past estimates, ot = (y{t−H+1:t}, x̂{t−H:t−1}, u{t−H:t−1}), with H = 10. Its action is the estimate x̂t. We parameterize it as x̂t = A x̂{t−1} + B u{t−1} + πθ(ot), so the network learns a correction to the model-based prediction rather than the full state. This residual structure follows the Luenberger observer (Luenberger, 1966), and it improves sample efficiency and keeps training stable. The adversary observes the true state, the observer's previous estimate, and the [11] current measurement. Its action is "at" = ε·tanhμφ(st)); which satisfies the budget by construction. The per-step reward for the observer is rt = −(xt − x̂t)ᵀ W xt − x̂t) − λ‖x̂t − x̂{t−1}‖², with W = I and λ = 0.01. The second term discourages jumpy estimates. The adversary receives −rt. The observer objective is therefore maxθ minφ E[Σt γ^t rt], with γ = 0.99 and episodes of T = 200 steps. Both policies are fully connected networks with two hidden layers of 128 units and ReLU activations. Critics have the same [26] architecture and take state–action pairs as input. Neural networks serve here as a convenient function approximator, and the formulation does not depend on them. Any other class that supports gradient-based or value-based policy improvement could replace them. We optimize with a deterministic actor–critic method with target networks and replay buffers (Lillicrap et al., 2016) and use twin critics to limit overestimation (Fujimoto et al., 2018). Training alternates between players. The observer is updated for No = 5 gradient steps against a frozen adversary, and then the adversary is updated for Na = 1 step against the frozen observer, as in other alternating minimax schemes. Each player's replay buffer holds 10⁶ transitions. Exploration uses Gaussian action noise with standard deviation decaying from 0.2 to 0.05. Optimization uses Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, [25] batch size 256, and soft target update coefficient 0.005. Training runs for 2×10⁶ environment steps. To reduce cycling and overfitting to the current adversary, the [2] observer is periodically trained against [27] a pool of earlier adversary checkpoints (Bansal et al., 2018). An adversary is sampled uniformly from the pool with probability 0.3. Early in training the adversary is held at zero or random attacks for 10⁴ steps so that the observer first learns a sensible nominal estimator. The primary simulation testbeds are two benchmark systems. The first is a linearized, discretized quadrotor-altitude/attitude model with n = [20] 6 states and p = 3 measured outputs. The second is a lower-dimensional cart–pole system linearized about the upright equilibrium n = 4, p = 2), which is open-loop unstable and therefore sensitive to estimation errors. Both are simulated at 50 Hz with noise covariances chosen to give a nominal signal-to-noise ratio of about 20 dB. Because the data are generated by simulation, no external datasets are used. Initial However, states are drawn from N(0, 0.1 I), and [38] each training and evaluation episode is generated by a distinct random seed. Training and test seeds are disjoint. We compare the learned observer with four baselines under the same controller and noise realizations. These are (i) a steady-state Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960), (ii) a Luenberger observer with poles placed at the Kalman filter's closed-loop locations, (iii) a Kalman filter with χ² innovation-based residual detection that rejects flagged measurements (Mo & Sinopoli, 2010), and (iv) a robust H∞ filter designed for the same budget ε. We also include an ablation in which the observer is trained with the same algorithm but against random bounded noise instead of a learned adversary, to isolate the effect of adversarial training. Evaluation uses four attack models. The first is no attack. The second is random bounded attacks, with at drawn uniformly from [−ε, ε]ᵖ. The third is a constant-bias attack at the budget limit. The fourth is a worst-case attack from a fresh adversary, trained from scratch for 10⁶ steps against the frozen final observer, which tests whether robustness reflects real minimax behavior or only coadaptation with the training adversary (Gleave et al., 2020). However, We also test robustness to model misspecification by perturbing the entries of A by up to 10% and to attacks above the training budget (εtest up to 2εtrain), to see how performance degrades beyond the bounded-error assumption. Contemporary veterinary graduates enter a profession in which technical competence is necessary but not sufficient. Veterinarians are routinely asked to navigate disagreements about animal welfare, euthanasia, the use of animals in research and production, breed-related disease, and the competing interests of animals, However, owners, employers, and society. These issues are often emotive, morally complex, and politically charged, and members of the public and the profession can hold sharply divergent views about them (Fraser, 2008, [18] Mellor, 2016). Accreditation bodies and professional organizations accordingly expect graduates to be able [1] to identify ethical problems, reason about them systematically, and engage respectfully with people who disagree (Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, 2020; American Veterinary Medical Association, 2019). Developing these capacities requires structured opportunities to practice discussing contested topics, yet such opportunities are not simple to create within crowded curricula and diverse student cohorts. Educators have long recognized that discussion-based and cooperative learning strategies can promote deeper engagement with controversial material. Cooperative learning, in which students work interdependently and are accountable for their own and others' contributions, is associated with improved achievement, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009, Slavin, 2014). Exposure to alternative perspectives can also prompt cognitive conflict, which in turn encourages students to re-examine and refine their reasoning (Piaget, 1985, Johnson et al., 2000). Structured academic controversy, role-play, and debate are therefore commonly used to teach ethics, sustainability, and [15] other socially [24] contested subjects (Oros, 2007; Kennedy, 2007). However, classroom discussion of polarizing issues carries risks. Students may be reluctant to speak when they fear judgment, social exclusion, or conflict with peers or instructors, and dominant voices can crowd out quieter ones (Hess, 2009; Hand & Levinson, 2012). Such reluctance may be amplified in professional programs where students are already managing performance pressure, emotional exposure to animal suffering, and concerns about how their views will be perceived by future colleagues. One established approach to structured, whole-class discussion is the human continuum exercise (HCE). In this activity, students are presented with a stimulus statement or question and asked to [27] position themselves physically along a line between two poles, such as strong agreement and strong disagreement. They then explain their reasoning to nearby peers and to those at other points on [4] the line, and may move as their views change. The HCE makes the distribution of opinion visible, demonstrates that positions are rarely binary, and requires each student to commit to a stance before discussion begins. These features support active learning, opinion formation, and perspective-taking, and the exercise has been used at both secondary and tertiary levels in disciplines including [32] science, health professions, and ethics education (Kagan & Kagan, 2009, Kolb, 2014). Nonetheless, the HCE has practical and psychological limitations. It requires physical space and synchronous attendance, which restricts its use in large, distributed, or online cohorts. Because students' positions are publicly visible to peers and teachers, those who hold minority or uncertain views may feel exposed, and may move toward perceived majority positions rather than express their own (Noelle-Neumann, 1974; Asch, 1956). Time constraints may also limit the depth with which individual students can articulate their reasoning. Digital technologies offer potential means of addressing such constraints. Online discussion environments can extend participation beyond the classroom, give students time to consider and compose responses, and reduce some social cues that inhibit contribution (Suler, 2004, Hrastinski, 2008). Anonymity or pseudonymity can encourage candor, particularly for sensitive subjects, and can lessen the effect of status differences among participants (Diakopoulos & Naaman, 2011, Peddle et al., 2016). At the same time, online discussion is not uniformly beneficial. Anonymity can enable incivility, asynchronous forums often suffer from low participation and superficial exchanges, and generic platforms rarely scaffold the specific cognitive moves that [2] make discussion educationally productive, such as taking a position, justifying it, and responding to counterarguments (Gao et al., 2013; Wise & Chiu, 2011). Existing [29] tools for online debate or polling typically either aggregate opinions However, without prompting dialogue, or provide open-ended discussion boards without a clear structure for committing to and revising a position. There is therefore a gap between established, pedagogically grounded discussion exercises such as the HCE and the digital tools available to deliver them in flexible, supportive, and scalable ways. This gap is particularly salient for veterinary education. Veterinary curricula increasingly include ethics, welfare, and professional communication, but students often report discomfort when discussing controversial issues, and educators have limited evidence-based tools for creating safe spaces in which differing views can be expressed (Magalhães-Sant'Ana et al., 2014, Batchelor & McKeegan, 2012). Moreover, the expansion of online and blended delivery, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has intensified the need for activities that preserve the interactive and reflective qualities of face-to-face teaching in virtual settings (Hodges et al., 2020). Evidence is needed on whether an online adaptation of the HCE can [39] retain the strengths of [28] the original [14] while mitigating its social risks. This paper addresses that need by describing the design of the virtual human continuum (VHC), an online platform that reproduces the core structure of the HCE. Students respond to a stimulus question by placing themselves on a continuum, provide a rationale for their position, view the reasoning of others, and engage with differing viewpoints in a virtual environment. We also report a first evaluation of the tool with first-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine students at the University of Sydney. The study was guided by the following research question: to what extent do students perceive the VHC as providing a non-threatening environment [10] in which they can express their views, learn how others form arguments, and consider alternative opinions on emotive [27] and challenging issues? The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a transparent description of an innovative educational tool and the pedagogical principles underlying its design, enabling other educators to adapt or replicate it. Second, it offers empirical data on student perceptions [2] of the platform, including comfort in expressing views relative to face-to-face discussion. Third, it contributes to the broader literature on technology-supported dialogue by showing how an established cooperative [35] learning exercise can be translated into an online format that supports engagement with potentially polarizing topics in professional education. Study Design and Context This study used a descriptive, cross-sectional design to document the development of the virtual human continuum (VHC) and to evaluate student perceptions of it following a single classroom trial. The work was conceived as an educational design and evaluation project, drawing However, on principles of design-based research in which a tool is created, implemented in an authentic setting, and refined using user feedback (Anderson & Shattuck, 2012). The pedagogical basis was the human continuum exercise (HCE), a cooperative learning strategy in which students physically position themselves along a line between two opposing statements in response to a stimulus question, and then explain or defend their position to peers (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). The VHC was designed to reproduce this exercise in an online environment. Platform Development The VHC was developed in collaboration with the university's educational technology staff. Design requirements were identified from the first author's experience of delivering the face-to-face HCE and from the literature on online discussion, which emphasises anonymity, low barriers to participation, and clear structure as features that support open dialogue on sensitive topics (Suler, 2004). The platform was required to: (a) present a stimulus statement or question with a response scale anchored by "strongly disagree" and strongly agree", (b) allow each participant to place a marker on the continuum, (c) require participants to provide a written justification for their position; (d) display the distribution of all positions and rationales to the group; and (e) permit participants to revise their position after reading others' contributions. Participants were identified by pseudonym within the activity, so that peers could not attribute positions to individuals, although instructors could access identifying information for administrative purposes. The platform was built as a web-based application accessible through standard browsers on laptops, tablets, and smartphones, and was integrated with the university's learning management system for authentication. Prototype versions were tested by teaching staff and two student volunteers not involved in the evaluation, and minor changes to the interface and instructions were made before implementation. Participants and Setting Participants were first-year students enrolled in the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program at the University of Sydney, Australia. The activity was embedded in a scheduled unit of study addressing professional and ethical issues in animal-related practice. All students in the cohort (N = approximately 40) were invited to take part in the VHC session and to complete an optional, anonymous evaluation survey. Thirty-eight students completed the survey. Because the cohort was small and participation was voluntary, the sample was one of convenience, and the design did not include a comparison group. Procedure The session was delivered during a timetabled class. Students first received a short introduction to the purpose of the exercise, the ground rules for respectful discussion, and a demonstration of the platform. Three stimulus statements concerning ethically contentious issues relevant to veterinary practice and animal use were then presented sequentially. The topics were selected because they were likely to elicit divergent views and emotional responses, consistent with the definition of potentially polarising issues as those on which reasonable people hold strongly differing values (Hess, 2009). For each statement, students (i) placed themselves on the continuum and wrote a brief rationale, (ii) viewed the distribution of positions and the anonymised rationales of their peers, (iii) took part in a facilitated whole-class discussion in which selected comments were explored, and (iv) were given the opportunity to adjust their position and record any change. Facilitators were academic staff experienced in teaching ethics. They did not express personal views on the topics and intervened only to maintain respectful conduct or to prompt deeper reasoning. At the end of the session, students were given a link to the evaluation questionnaire and encouraged to complete it immediately, while the experience was fresh. The survey remained open for one week, and one reminder was provided in class. Data Collection Instrument Student perceptions were collected using a short online questionnaire developed by the research team for this evaluation. Items were generated from the intended pedagogical aims of the VHC and from prior literature on the benefits of structured classroom debate and online discussion, including exposure to diverse perspectives, development of argumentation skills, and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999; Kennedy, 2007). The questionnaire comprised statements rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). Key items asked whether the VHC (1) provided a non-threatening environment for discussing emotive and challenging issues, (2) provided an opportunity to see how other people form their ideas; (3) made students think about how to express their ideas and construct arguments; (4) left students feeling more comfortable expressing their views than in face-to-face discussion; and (5) encouraged students to consider other opinions. Additional items addressed usability, and open-text fields invited general comments. Content [4] validity was checked informally by two colleagues in veterinary education, and the wording was refined for clarity. No formal psychometric validation was undertaken, which is acknowledged as a limitation. Ethical Considerations The project was approved by the University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee. Participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous, and no identifying information was collected. Students were provided with an information statement explaining the purpose of the study, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. Declining to participate had no bearing on assessment or progression. Because the topics could be distressing, students were reminded of available university counselling services, and they could leave the activity at any time. Data Analysis Survey responses were exported from the online survey tool to a spreadsheet and checked for completeness. Given the descriptive aims and small sample, analysis was limited to descriptive statistics. For each item, the frequency and percentage of respondents selecting each response category were calculated. Responses of "agree" and "strongly agree" were combined to report overall

The 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak was the largest and most complex filovirus epidemic recorded. It caused more than 28,000 reported cases and more than 11,000 deaths, mostly in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone WHO Ebola Response Team, 2016). Earlier outbreaks in Central Africa had typically been confined to remote rural areas and were contained within weeks or months by classical measures: rapid case detection, isolation, contact tracing, safe burials, and community engagement (Chowell & Nishiura, 2014). In 2014, however, the virus spread into densely populated urban settings and across porous borders, in health systems already weakened by decades of conflict and underinvestment. Health workers were infected at disproportionately high rates, and the supply of trained staff, laboratories, vehicles, and basic communication infrastructure was overwhelmed (Kieny et al., 2014, Gostin & Friedman, 2015). Under these conditions, the speed and quality of information flow, from the village to the district, the national command center, and international partners, became a decisive factor in the response. Paper-based reporting was the default in most affected areas. Case investigation forms, contact lists, laboratory request forms, and daily follow-up sheets were completed by hand, transported physically, and entered later into spreadsheets or databases. This introduced delays of days to weeks, transcription errors, duplicate records, and difficulty reconciling data from different sources (Fäh et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Incomplete contact lists and poor linkage between laboratory results and clinical records were widely reported as obstacles to timely control. The consequence was that decision makers often worked with outdated or inconsistent epidemiological pictures, which hampered resource allocation and the identification of transmission chains (Frieden et al., 2014). Mobile health (mHealth), defined by the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as phones, tablets, and other wireless equipment (WHO, 2011), was widely proposed as a way to address these gaps. Mobile phone penetration in sub-Saharan Africa had grown rapidly during the preceding decade, often outpacing access to electricity, roads, and fixed-line networks (GSMA, 2014). mHealth tools had already been used for disease surveillance, community health worker support, and data collection in low-resource settings, with growing evidence of improved data timeliness and completeness (Braa et al., 2012, Aranda-Jan et al., 2014). Previous outbreaks, including cholera in Haiti and Zimbabwe, H1N1 influenza, and Marburg and Ebola in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had also seen mobile or electronic systems deployed for [12] outbreak response, although generally at small scale and with limited evaluation (Freifeld et al., 2010; Black et al., 2013). The 2014-2015 outbreak thus offered both an urgent need and an unprecedented opportunity to apply these technologies at scale. During the epidemic, a large and heterogeneous set of mHealth initiatives emerged. Governments, ministries of health, international agencies, nongovernmental organizations, academic groups, technology companies, and volunteer developers built or adapted tools for many purposes. These included electronic case reporting, contact tracing and follow-up, laboratory result transmission, mapping of cases, mobile-based symptom checkers, health worker training, public messaging and rumor tracking, and monitoring of returning travelers (Sacks et al., 2015; Tom-Aba et al., 2015, Oluwafemi et al., 2015). Some were adaptations of platforms already used in other contexts, such as DHIS2, Open Data Kit, CommCare, [29] and Magpi, whereas others were developed specifically for the outbreak. Many reports describe rapid deployment, often within weeks, and several suggest that mobile data collection improved the timeliness of contact follow-up and shortened the delay between data capture and analysis (Tom-Aba et al., 2015, Fäh et al., 2015). Digital tools have been credited as a major contribution to improved control of EVD in the later phases of the epidemic Kamadjeu et al., 2015). Despite this enthusiasm, the evidence base on what was actually developed and used remains fragmented. Information about tools is scattered across peer-reviewed articles, conference abstracts, technical reports, press releases, and project websites, and the terminology used to describe functions varies widely. Existing overviews have generally been narrative or have focused on single projects, a single country, or a single functionality such as contact tracing (Sacks et al., 2015, Danquah et al., 2019). Moreover, rapid, parallel development by many actors raised concerns about duplication of effort, lack of interoperability, limited alignment with national information systems, unclear data governance, and low sustainability beyond the emergency period (Heeks, 2006, Kamadjeu et al., 2015). Without a structured overview, it is difficult for public health agencies and developers to know which tools exist, what core functions they cover, and which combinations of features appear most useful for outbreak response. This hampers the building on [29] earlier [28] experience and risks repeating fragmented development in future outbreaks, including recent resurgences of EVD and other epidemic-prone diseases. Outbreak control relies [24] on a chain of [7] linked activities that are not independent. Surveillance detects and reports suspected cases, case management ensures isolation, care, and clinical documentation; contact tracing identifies and follows people at risk of [32] developing disease; and laboratory data management confirms or excludes infection and feeds results back to clinicians and epidemiologists. A tool that addresses only one step may speed [6] up that step but leave bottlenecks elsewhere, and data silos can prevent the integrated view needed for decision making. Systems covering several of these functions within a single platform may reduce duplicate data entry and facilitate real-time linkage of cases, contacts, and test results (Tom-Aba et al., 2015). Whether such integrated tools were common during the 2014-2015 outbreak, however, has not been systematically assessed. We conducted a systematic review of mHealth tools developed or used in the context of the 2014-2015 West Africa EVD outbreak. Our research question was: what mobile tools were reported for EVD management in 2014 and 2015, and which core functionalities surveillance, case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management) did they support? Our objectives were to identify and describe the available tools, to characterize their functionalities and the extent to which they were integrated, and to highlight the most promising approaches to guide future mHealth development for infectious disease control. This review makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic inventory of mHealth tools from this outbreak, using a reproducible search of multiple databases and independent dual review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines Moher et al., 2009). Second, it offers a functionality-based classification that allows tools to be compared on the activities central to outbreak response rather than [2] on their technical architecture alone. Third, it identifies tools that combine several core functions and may therefore be priority candidates for further development, evaluation, and preparedness planning. Study design and reporting framework We conducted a systematic review of mobile health (mHealth) tools developed or deployed in response to the 2014–2015 West Africa Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009, Liberati et al., 2009). Because the objective was to describe and compare tool functionalities rather than estimate intervention effects, no meta-analysis was planned, and the review was not registered in a prospective protocol registry. We defined mHealth in accordance with the World Health Organization as medical and public health practice supported by mobile devices such as mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, and patient-monitoring devices (WHO, 2011). A "tool" was defined as a distinct software application, platform, or system with a named identity or a clearly described, reproducible set of functions, irrespective of whether it was developed de novo or adapted from an existing platform. Search strategy and information sources We searched Google Scholar, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web of Science for reports published between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2015. No language restrictions were applied. The following search string was used and adapted to the syntax of each database: (outbreak OR "epidemic") AND (mobile phone OR smartphone OR "smart phone OR tablet OR "mHealth") AND ("Ebola" OR EVD OR VHF OR Ebola virus disease OR "viral hemorrhagic fever") AND ("2014" OR 2015). Searches were run on titles, abstracts, and keywords where the database allowed; for Google Scholar, which does not support field-restricted searching to the same degree, the full-text option was used and the first 200 records, sorted by relevance, were screened, a pragmatic cut-off commonly applied for this engine (Haddaway et al., 2015). Because mHealth implementations are often documented outside indexed journals, we additionally screened the reference lists of included records and of relevant narrative reviews, and examined grey literature such as reports from the WHO, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and technology developers' websites when these were cited in or linked from retrieved records. Records in languages other than English or French were translated using machine translation and verified by a fluent colleague when available. Eligibility criteria Records were eligible if they (1) described one or more specific mHealth tools; 2) explicitly stated that the tool was developed, adapted, or used in the context of the 2014–2015 West Africa EVD outbreak (including pilot, preparedness, or neighboring-country settings linked to this outbreak); and (3) provided sufficient information to characterize at least one functionality. We included original research articles, implementation reports, conference abstracts, technical reports, and descriptive commentaries that contained primary information on a tool. We excluded records that (1) referred to mHealth only in general terms without identifying a specific tool, (2) addressed other outbreaks or diseases without reference to the 2014–2015 EVD epidemic; (3) were purely opinion pieces, editorials, or news items with no original description of a tool, (4) concerned non-mobile information technology solutions only (e.g., desktop-only software, call-center-only services without a mobile application component); or (5) were duplicates. Where a tool was described in several records, these were grouped under a single tool entry, and the most informative record was used as the primary source, with additional records used to complete missing data. Study selection All retrieved records were exported to a reference manager and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and independently assessed by the same two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, when consensus could not be reached, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the title-and-abstract stage was quantified using Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the proportion of agreement expected [23] by chance. Values above 0.60 were interpreted as substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977). The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram, indicating the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons), and included. Data extraction [21] A standardized data extraction form was developed in Microsoft Excel, piloted on [10] a random sample of five included records, and refined to resolve ambiguities. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled through consensus. For each tool we recorded: name, developer or implementing organization, type of developer (government, nongovernmental organization, academic institution, private sector, or international agency), country or countries of deployment, publication type and year, development stage concept or prototype, pilot, or field deployment), platform and hardware e.g., Android, iOS, basic feature phone with SMS/USSD, tablet), connectivity requirements (online, offline-capable with synchronization), open-source [21] status, and target users (e.g., health workers, laboratory staff, contact tracers, community members, the general public). The principal data of interest [33] were the functionalities of each tool. Based [17] on the epidemiological workflow of EVD response (WHO, 2014) and previous typologies of mHealth functions Labrique et al., 2013), we predefined four core functionalities: 1. Surveillance: collection, transmission, or analysis of data on suspected, probable, or confirmed cases and deaths, including event-based reporting, alert generation, and mapping. 2. Case management: support for clinical care of patients, including registration, triage, symptom assessment, monitoring of clinical progress, treatment documentation, and patient tracking within treatment facilities. 3. Rates of reoffending remain stubbornly high in most jurisdictions that measure them. A worldwide synthesis of recidivism studies found that a substantial proportion of people released from custody are reconvicted or returned to prison within a few years, and that follow-up periods and definitions vary so widely that cross-jurisdictional comparison is difficult (Fazel & Wolf, 2015). High reoffending carries costs for victims, communities, and the individuals concerned, and it places sustained pressure on correctional budgets. These pressures have encouraged policymakers to look for community-based sanctions that can hold people accountable and protect the public while avoiding the expense and collateral harms of incarceration. Evidence that custodial sentences do not reliably reduce reoffending, and may modestly increase it relative to non-custodial alternatives, strengthens this interest (Gendreau et al., 1999; Nagin et al., 2009; Villettaz et al., 2006). Day reporting centres (DRCs) are one such response. Although their form varies, DRCs are non-residential facilities that people under criminal justice supervision must attend regularly, often daily or several times a week, to receive structured supervision, monitoring, and services. In the United States, early programmes were adapted from British day training and probation day centres. They expanded rapidly from the 1980s as an intermediate sanction positioned between routine probation and incarceration (Parent et al., 1995). DRCs are used at several decision points: as a condition of probation, as a diversion from jail or prison, as a sanction for people who violate supervision conditions, and as a step-down for people released on parole or post-release supervision. Typical components include drug testing, curfew checks, electronic monitoring, cognitive-behavioural programming, substance-use treatment, education and employment assistance, and referral to housing and health services. The combination of surveillance and treatment makes DRCs a hybrid, and their theoretical rationale is correspondingly mixed. Incapacitation and deterrence arguments emphasise close monitoring and the certainty of detection. Rehabilitative arguments emphasise that centres can deliver, in one place, the criminogenic-need-focused services that research on effective correctional intervention identifies as important (Andrews & Bonta, 2010). The correctional literature offers reasons for both optimism and caution about whether DRCs reduce recidivism. The Risk-Need-Responsivity framework holds that interventions are most effective when their intensity is matched to the person's risk level, when they target dynamic criminogenic needs, and when delivery suits the individual's learning style and circumstances (Andrews et al., 1990, Lowenkamp et al., 2006). A DRC that concentrates structured programming on higher-risk people could therefore reduce reoffending. By contrast, evaluations of intensive supervision programmes that emphasise surveillance without treatment have generally found no reduction in recidivism and, because closer monitoring detects more infractions, sometimes higher rates of technical violations and revocations (Petersilia & Turner, 1993). Reviews of community supervision also suggest that supervision officers often devote little time to the targets of change that predict reoffending (Bonta et al., 2008). Whether DRCs resemble surveillance-oriented intensive supervision or treatment-oriented correctional programmes is thus an empirical question. The answer is likely to depend on how centres are designed and on whom they serve. Primary studies of DRCs have produced mixed findings. Some quasi-experimental evaluations report lower rearrest or reconviction among participants than among comparison groups. Others report no difference, and some find that gains disappear after adjustment for selection into the programme. Marciniak (2000) compared probationers receiving day reporting in addition to intensive supervision with those on intensive supervision alone, and Ostermann (2013) examined New Jersey's DRC and halfway-back programmes for people on parole. Boyle et al. (2013) evaluated a statewide parole DRC programme in New Jersey, using a design intended to address differences between participants and comparison cases. These studies differ in population, comparison condition, outcome definition, follow-up length, and the extent to which the programme delivers treatment. Most rely on observational designs in which people assigned to DRCs may differ systematically from those who are not, in ways that are only partly captured by administrative [15] data. Programme integrity is rarely reported in detail, and cost-effectiveness is seldom addressed. Taken together, the single-site, heterogeneous character of this literature makes it hard for decision-makers to judge whether DRCs work, for whom, and under what conditions. Despite a few decades of implementation, we [18] [3] are not aware of a systematic review that comprehensively identifies, appraises, and synthesises the evidence on the effects of DRCs on recidivism. Existing syntheses either address wider categories of community sanctions, intermediate sanctions, or intensive supervision, where DRCs appear as one element among many (Drake et al., 2009, Villettaz et al., 2006), or they are narrative overviews of programme descriptions and implementation rather than effectiveness (Parent et al., 1995). Because DRCs combine features of supervision, treatment, and structured time use, broader reviews cannot isolate their contribution. The absence of (10) a rigorous review leaves practitioners However, and policymakers to rely on a few individual evaluations of uncertain [9] quality, and it leaves researchers without a clear picture of where evidence is strongest and where it is missing. This review therefore asks: What is the effect of day reporting centres, compared with alternative sanctions or supervision arrangements, on subsequent offending among people involved in the criminal justice system? Secondary questions concern whether effects (26) vary by the stage at which (28) DRCs are used (for example, diversion, probation, or parole), by participant characteristics such as risk level, age, gender, and substance-use history, by programme features such as treatment intensity and duration, and by the type of recidivism outcome, including rearrest, reconviction, technical violation, and reincarceration. Where data permit, we will also examine effects [8] on intermediate outcomes such [7] [16] as employment, substance use, and programme completion. This protocol sets out the methods for a systematic review prepared in line with Campbell Collaboration standards and reported with reference to PRISMA guidance (Page et al., 2021). The review will make four contributions. First, it will provide the first systematic, transparent estimate of the effects of DRCs on recidivism, using explicit eligibility criteria, comprehensive searches including grey literature, [33] and structured risk-of-bias assessment. Second, through meta-analysis where studies are sufficiently comparable, and structured narrative synthesis otherwise, it will explore the sources of heterogeneity across programmes, populations, and comparison conditions. Third, it will document the methodological quality of the evidence base and identify design weaknesses that limit causal inference, thereby guiding future evaluations. Fourth, it will offer policymakers and practitioners an evidence-informed account of whether and under [15] what conditions DRCs are a useful tool for reducing (12) reoffending. This review follows the Campbell Collaboration's standards for systematic reviews of intervention effects (Campbell Collaboration, 2019) and the guidance in the Cochrane Handbook (Higgins et al., 2022). Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021). Any deviations from this [27] protocol will be documented and justified in the final review. Criteria for considering studies Eligible studies will evaluate day reporting centres (DRCs), defined as non-residential, structured programmes that require justice-involved adults or young people to attend a designated facility regularly, usually daily or several times a week. Attendance must be combined with supervision and with services such as treatment, education, employment support, or cognitive-behavioural programming. DRCs may be used as a pre-trial alternative, a condition of probation or parole, a sentencing alternative to custody, or a transitional step after release. Programmes that provide only electronic However, monitoring, routine probation reporting, or residential care will be excluded. The comparison condition may be incarceration, (26) standard probation or parole, other community supervision, or no [32] [21] programme. Eligible designs are randomised controlled trials and quasi-experimental (2) designs with a comparison group. Quasi-experiments must show baseline equivalence or use statistical adjustment, matching, regression discontinuity, or instrumental variables to address selection bias (Farrington & Welsh, 2005; Shadish et al., 2002). Single-group pre-post designs, qualitative studies, and studies without a comparison group will be excluded. The primary outcome is recidivism, measured as re-arrest, reconviction, reincarceration, technical violation, or self-reported reoffending, at any follow-up. Secondary outcomes include employment, substance use, and programme completion, which will [37] be synthesised only if enough data are available. Studies must report enough information [18] to calculate an effect size. We will include studies from any country and year, published in any language for which translation is feasible. Search strategy An information specialist will help develop the search strategy, which will be peer reviewed using PRESS (McGowan et al., 2016). Search terms will combine synonyms for day reporting (for example, "day reporting centre/center," "day treatment," "community resource centre," "attendance centre," non-residential programme") with terms for offenders and recidivism. We will search Criminal Justice Abstracts, NCJRS Abstracts, PsycINFO, Sociological Abstracts, ERIC, Social Services Abstracts, MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit, ProQuest Criminal Justice, the Campbell Library, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Grey literature sources will include ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, Google Scholar (first 200 hits), government and research agency websites such as the U.S. National Institute of Justice, the UK Ministry of Justice, and the Australian Institute of Criminology, and trial registries including ClinicalTrials.gov and the Open Science Framework. We will also screen the [3] reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews, conduct forward citation searching, and contact experts [30] and programme evaluators to identify unpublished studies. Screening and data extraction Records will be managed in reference software and screening software, and duplicates removed. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion or a third [6] reviewer. A pilot test However, on a sample of records will check consistency, and reasons for full-text exclusion will be recorded. Two reviewers will independently extract data using a piloted coding form and compare results. Extracted information will include publication (20) characteristics; country and jurisdiction, programme features (referral point, duration, intensity, services, supervision level, and staffing); participant characteristics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, risk level, and offence type); research design and allocation method, sample sizes, attrition, follow-up length; outcome definitions and data source; and effect size data. Where information is missing, we will contact study authors. Where several reports describe the same study, they will be combined into one study record. Risk of bias assessment Randomised trials will be assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019). Non-randomised studies will be assessed with ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016), which covers confounding, participant selection, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. Two reviewers will assess each study independently, resolving disagreements through discussion. Risk of bias judgments will be summarised in tables and figures and used in sensitivity analyses. The certainty of evidence for the main outcome will be assessed using GRADE (Guyatt et al., 2008). Effect size calculation Because recidivism is dichotomous, the primary effect size will be the odds ratio, analysed as the natural logarithm with its standard error (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). Odds ratios will be calculated from event counts, proportions, or test statistics. For adjusted estimates such as logistic regression coefficients, we will use the adjusted odds ratio and note it in moderator analyses. Where studies report only continuous outcomes, such as offence counts or time to failure, we will convert standardised mean differences to log odds ratios using the method of Chinn (2000) or Hasselblad and Hedges (1995). For interpretation, results will be transformed back to odds ratios and, where baseline rates allow, to differences in recidivism probability. Effects will be coded so that odds ratios below 1 indicate lower recidivism in the DRC group. Where studies report several effect sizes, whether from multiple outcome measures, follow-up periods, or subgroups, we will use robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights to handle statistical dependence (Hedges et al., 2010; Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). Aphasia is one of the most common and disabling consequences of left-hemisphere stroke, affecting roughly a third of stroke survivors and persisting into the chronic phase in a substantial proportion of them [13] (Engelter et al., 2006, Flowers et al., 2016). It is not a unitary disorder. Patients differ in which components of language are affected (e.g., phonology, semantics, syntax, fluency), in how severely, and in the [7] extent to which domain-general cognitive abilities such as short-term memory and executive function are also compromised Butler et al., 2014, Fridriksson et al., 2018, Lacey et al., 2017). Classical taxonomies (Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction, anomic aphasia and so on) capture some of this heterogeneity but are poorly suited to the graded, multidimensional [24] profiles seen in real patients, and many individuals are unclassifiable or shift between categories over time (Kertesz & Poole, 1974, Wilson et al., 2018). Data-driven approaches have therefore been used to derive the underlying dimensions of impairment directly from patients' performance on extensive behavioural batteries. Principal component analysis (PCA) and related methods have consistently identified a small number of latent [21] factors, [36] typically reflecting phonological, semantic, fluency/speech production and cognitive-executive abilities, which together explain most of the variance in aphasic performance (Butler et al., 2014, Halai et [35] al., 2017, Mirman et al., 2015; Ingram et al., 2020). These factors have, in turn, been related to lesion location and white-matter damage, providing a more graded and mechanistically interpretable account of brain–behaviour relationships than aphasia syndromes (Halai et al., 2017, Kümmerer et al., 2013, Schumacher et al., 2019). Alongside these impairment scores, the paraphasias that patients produce are central to the clinical description of aphasia. Errors in picture naming, in particular, are used to characterise the nature of the underlying disorder: semantic paraphasias (e.g., dog for cat) are typically taken to indicate disrupted semantic representation or lexical selection, phonological paraphasias and neologisms e.g., "cap" or "tat" for cat) to indicate disrupted phonological retrieval or encoding, and omissions, circumlocutions and dysfluent attempts to reflect other failures of retrieval or articulation (Dell et al., 1997, Schwartz et al., 2006; Kohn & Goodglass, 1985). Error types are explicitly included in the diagnostic criteria and classification of aphasia and form the basis However, of influential computational models, such as the interactive two-step model, in which the relative proportions of semantic and phonological errors are used to estimate the integrity of semantic-lexical and lexical-phonological mappings (Dell et al., 1997; Foygel & Dell, 2000, Schwartz et al., 2006). Lesion-symptom mapping studies of naming errors have reported that semantic errors are associated with damage to anterior temporal and middle temporal regions, whereas phonological errors are linked to damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus and However, the underlying arcuate fasciculus Schwartz et al., 2009, [16] Walker et al., 2011; Mirman et al., 2015, Halai et al., 2017; Pillay et al., 2017). Despite this, the field has largely treated language impairments and paraphasias as separate topics. Most studies of the neural basis of aphasia have focused on scores summarising deficits, whereas studies of paraphasias have often been conducted in isolation, with little reference to the patients' broader language-cognitive profile. This separation is problematic for several reasons. First, the relationship between impairments and errors is unlikely to be one-to-one. Semantic However, errors, for example, may arise not only from degraded semantic knowledge but also from impaired phonological retrieval, reduced executive control over competing alternatives, or limited speech output (Mirman et al., 2015; Schwartz [24] et al., 2006, Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). Similarly, omissions may reflect failures at multiple processing stages and are often excluded from analyses or considered uninformative. Second, previous studies of errors have typically examined a restricted subset of error categories, commonly semantic and phonological, or have collapsed errors into experimenter-defined composite scores or ratios. Such approaches presuppose a particular theoretical account, ignore the co-occurrence structure of the full range of errors patients produce, and may obscure the relationship between less-studied categories (e.g., circumlocutions, mixed errors, dysfluent responses) and underlying deficits. Third, because errors and impairment scores are rarely modelled together, the lesion correlates reported for each are difficult to relate, and it remains unclear whether error-based and deficit-based analyses converge on the same neural substrates or capture partially distinct aspects of the aphasic syndrome. An integrated, data-driven framework is needed to address these issues. Such a [31] framework should (i) derive the structure of paraphasias empirically, from the pattern of co-occurrence across a broad set of error types, rather than imposing a theory-driven selection or combination, (ii) align this error structure with the patients' multidimensional language and cognitive profile within a single model, and (iii) relate the resulting fused dimensions to lesion data, so that errors, deficits and neural correlates can be considered simultaneously, that is, "triangulated". Dimension-reduction techniques such as PCA are well suited to this purpose, as they identify orthogonal latent factors, permit the examination of cross-loadings (and thus many-to-many mappings between errors and impairments), and produce continuous factor scores that can be used in lesion-symptom mapping without the need for arbitrary categorisation (Butler et al., 2014, Halai et al., 2017, Mirman et al., 2015). In the present study, we applied this approach to a cohort of individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia who completed an extensive language and cognitive battery and a picture-naming task in which responses were coded into fifteen error types. In the first step, we used PCA to establish the pattern of co-occurrence among these error types. In the second step, we entered the resulting error components, together with the patients' scores from the neuropsychological battery, into an omnibus PCA to generate fused impairment-paraphasia factors. In the third step, we mapped these factors onto the patients' structural lesion profiles to identify their neural correlates. We asked three questions: (1) what are the latent dimensions underlying naming errors when [25] all error types are considered together, 2) how do these dimensions map onto language and cognitive impairments, and which relationships are one-to-one versus distributed across multiple factors; and (3) which lesion correlates are associated with the fused factors, and do they converge with the existing literature? This study makes three contributions. Methodologically, it offers a unified, theory-agnostic model that avoids selective focus on particular errors or experimenter-derived composites. Empirically, it clarifies the complex relationships between specific error types and underlying deficits, including those for omissions and circumlocutions that have been comparatively neglected. Neurally, it tests whether the lesion correlates of these combined factors align with established regions implicated in phonology, semantics and speech production, thereby providing a more complete characterisation of post-stroke aphasia. The maps were checked and, where necessary, manually corrected by an expert neurologist. Lesion volume was calculated for each patient and used as a covariate in lesion analyses. The number of components was determined by the Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1) in conjunction with inspection of the scree plot and parallel analysis (Horn, 1965). Insufficient physical activity is among the leading modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, and premature mortality. Globally, physical inactivity is estimated to [3] account (11) for 6% to 10% [8] of the burden of major noncommunicable [2] diseases and for roughly 9% of premature deaths (Lee et al., 2012). Despite the well-documented benefits of regular activity, only about one in four U.S. adults meets national guidelines for both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activity (Blackwell (13) & Clarke, 2018; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2018). The burden of inactivity is not distributed evenly. [5] Adults in rural areas report [2] less leisure-time physical activity and have a higher prevalence of obesity than their urban counterparts, with national estimates of obesity of approximately 40% in rural settings versus 33% in urban settings (Befort et al., 2012). Rural residents also face structural barriers to activity, including dispersed destinations, limited recreational infrastructure, fewer programs, and constrained public health (23) resources (Frost et al., 2010, Bauman et al., 2012). A substantial evidence base now exists on how to promote physical activity at the population level. The Community Guide for Preventive Services, developed by the Community Preventive Services Task Force, recommends a portfolio of strategies spanning three broad domains: informational approaches (e.g., community-wide campaigns), behavioral and social approaches (e.g., social support in community [29] settings and individually adapted health behavior change), and environmental and policy approaches (e.g., creation of or enhanced access to places for physical activity combined with informational outreach) (Kahn [12] et al., 2002; Community Preventive Services Task Force, 2016). Socioecological models further hold that sustained behavior change is most likely when individual-level support is combined with change in the social, physical, and policy contexts in which people live (Sallis et al., 2006; Sallis et al., 2012). Community-wide multicomponent interventions grounded in these principles are therefore a promising means (8) of shifting population activity levels. Evidence for such interventions, however, derives disproportionately from large urban and suburban settings, from clinical or school samples, or from rural communities with relatively stable and demographically homogeneous populations. Systematic reviews of rural physical activity interventions (3) have consistently noted the small number of well-evaluated studies, short follow-up (25) periods, and limited attention to implementation processes and contextual fit (Umstattd Meyer et al., 2016; Based on these gaps, rural communities (16) remain underrepresented in the dissemination literature). Moreover, "rural" is not a monolithic category. Micropolitan communities, defined by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget as having an urban core of 10,000 to 49,999 residents, occupy an intermediate position: they are larger and more service-rich than remote rural towns, yet they typically lack the public transit, parks and recreation departments, and philanthropic and academic infrastructure of metropolitan areas. How evidence-based However, recommendations should be adapted for mid-size rural communities is not well understood. This gap is compounded in micropolitan communities that have become new immigrant destinations. (26) Beginning in the 1990s, immigration from Latin America and elsewhere shifted away from traditional gateway states and cities toward the rural Midwest and South, often driven by labor demand in meatpacking, food processing, and agriculture (Massey, 2008; Lichter, 2012). Many Midwestern towns have However, consequently experienced rapid demographic change within a single generation, with linguistically and culturally diverse newcomers settling alongside long-term residents. Immigrant and [35] Latino adults in the United States often report lower rates of leisure-time physical activity than non-Latino White adults, and activity patterns tend to decline with acculturation and time in the United States (Crespo et al., 1996, Marquez & Bryan, 2011). Newcomers in However, new destinations may also confront language barriers, long and physically demanding work shifts, limited transportation, unfamiliarity with local resources, and strained institutional capacity to serve them (Lichter, 2012). Interventions developed elsewhere cannot be assumed to translate without modification into such settings, and the literature offers few examples of community-wide physical activity interventions designed for communities that are simultaneously rural and rapidly diversifying. Lay health advisor models, also described [7] as promotores de salud or community health workers, offer one plausible approach to bridging these gaps. Lay health advisors are trusted community members who receive training to provide social support, information, and navigation to peers, and they have been shown to improve health behaviors and outcomes in underserved and minority populations (Balcázar et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2014). Evidence from Latino and rural communities indicates that peer-led walking groups and other group-based activities can increase physical activity while building social capital and local capacity for sustaining programs (Ayala et al., 2011; Cleland et al., 2012). Because lay leaders are embedded in community networks, they can also serve as conduits for informational campaigns and as advocates for environmental and policy improvements. Yet few studies have integrated a lay health advisor approach with the full range of Community Guide recommendations in a single community-wide effort, and fewer still have done so in a micropolitan new destination. Closing this gap also requires attention to how evidence-based interventions are adapted and evaluated. Adaptation frameworks emphasize the systematic modification of intervention content, delivery, and context to improve fit while preserving core functions (Escoffery et al., 2018), and community-based participatory research principles stress shared decision-making between researchers and community partners throughout this process (Israel et al., 1998). Evaluation frameworks such as RE-AIM encourage assessment not only of effectiveness but also of reach, adoption, implementation, and maintenance, which are dimensions of particular relevance to resource-constrained settings (Glasgow et al., 1999). Community-wide interventions are difficult to evaluate with a single design, and combining population-level surveillance with longitudinal cohort data, observational measures of the environment, and qualitative and process data can yield a more complete account of what changes, for whom, and why. In this paper, we describe the design and early implementation of Active Ottumwa, a community-wide intervention to increase physical activity in Ottumwa, Iowa, a micropolitan city of approximately 25,000 residents in the rural southeastern part of the state. Ottumwa has experienced substantial demographic change linked to employment in meatpacking and related industries, and now has a sizable and growing Latino population. Active Ottumwa is part of a community-academic partnership in which local organizations and residents helped to shape the intervention. The initiative adapts strategies recommended by the Community Guide across behavioral and social, campaign and informational, and environmental and policy domains, using trained lay health advisors, referred to here as physical activity leaders, as the central delivery mechanism for group-based activities such as walking groups, tai chi, and yoga. The overarching research question is whether a multicomponent, lay health advisor–based intervention grounded in Community Guide recommendations can increase physical activity among residents of a micropolitan new destination community. Secondary questions concern the reach of the intervention across population subgroups, the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted strategies, and the contextual factors that facilitate or constrain implementation. This report makes three contributions. First, it extends the evidence base on physical activity promotion to a setting that is underrepresented in the literature: a mid-size rural community undergoing immigration-driven demographic change. Second, it documents a transparent process for adapting and integrating evidence-based, multilevel strategies through a community-academic partnership, including the training and deployment of 45 physical activity leaders and the execution of a five-channel communication campaign. Third, it presents a multi-method evaluation [4] design, combining a cross-sectional community (3) survey, a longitudinal cohort, observational [38] data, key informant interviews, and project (26) records, that may serve as a model for evaluating community-wide interventions in similar settings. By describing implementation in detail, we aim to inform practitioners and researchers seeking to translate evidence-based recommendations into the (7) diverse rural communities where they are most needed. Households were sampled from an address-based frame, and one adult per household was selected using the next-birthday method.
