Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture that cause activity limitation. It is attributed to non-progressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain and is frequently accompanied by disturbances of sensation, cognition, communication, perception, behavior, and epilepsy (Rosenbaum et al., 2007). It is the most common cause of physical disability in childhood. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated its pooled prevalence at about 2.1 per 1000 live births, with higher rates among preterm infants and in low- and middle-income settings (Oskoui et al., 2013). Because CP persists across the lifespan, it places a sustained burden on affected individuals, caregivers, and health systems. This burden includes pain, contractures, hip displacement, scoliosis, reduced participation, and substantial lifetime costs (Graham et al., 2016). Spasticity is the dominant motor feature in most children with CP. It is classically defined as a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes resulting from hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex Lance, 1980). Over time, spasticity combines with weakness, impaired selective motor control, and altered muscle growth. These changes lead to secondary musculoskeletal problems, including shortened muscle–tendon units, fibrotic change in muscle, and fixed contractures (Graham et al., 2016; Mathewson & Lieber, 2015). Contemporary management is multidisciplinary and includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses, oral antispastic drugs, intramuscular botulinum toxin A, intrathecal baclofen, selective dorsal rhizotomy, and orthopedic surgery. Evidence supports several of these interventions, particularly botulinum toxin, casting, and goal-directed training (Novak et al., 2020). However, their effects are often modest or transient, and they have limitations. Repeated injections can be costly and distressing, and antibody formation or waning response may occur. Oral agents are limited by sedation and weak evidence of functional benefit. Neurosurgical and orthopedic procedures are invasive and not suitable for all patients. Consequently, many families seek complementary and alternative therapies, and in East Asia traditional medicine approaches are widely used alongside conventional rehabilitation (Novak et al., 2020). Acupotomy, also called needle-knife therapy, is one such approach. It was developed in China in the 1970s by Zhu Hanzhang and integrates the principles of traditional acupuncture with those of modern minimally invasive surgery Zhu, 1992). The instrument is a stainless-steel needle with a flat blade at its tip. This allows the practitioner to puncture the skin, then cut, release, or dissect fibrotic or adherent soft tissue such as fascia, ligament, tendon sheath, or muscle insertion, while also stimulating acupoints. The proposed mechanisms are mechanical and biological. They include release of local tension and adhesions, improved local microcirculation, modulation of inflammatory mediators, and reduced abnormal mechanical stress on connective tissue Lee et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). In CP, the rationale is that releasing shortened or fibrotic muscle–tendon units and myofascial restrictions may reduce passive resistance to stretch, improve joint range of motion, and facilitate motor training. Clinicians in China and Korea have also proposed that acupotomy at selected sites could alter afferent input and reduce excitability of the spinal stretch reflex arc, although direct evidence is limited. Acupotomy is typically applied to the muscles and tendons most affected, such as the adductors, hamstrings, gastrocnemius–soleus, and cervical or paraspinal structures. It is usually delivered as a short course and combined with rehabilitation training. Clinical research on acupotomy has grown in the last two decades, mostly from China. Randomized and non-randomized studies have reported improvements in muscle tone, joint mobility, gross motor function, and activities of daily living when acupotomy is added to rehabilitation in children with spastic CP. Systematic reviews have synthesized acupotomy evidence in other musculoskeletal conditions, such as knee osteoarthritis, lumbar disc herniation, and myofascial pain syndrome. These reviews found potential benefit but noted important methodological limitations (Lee et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). For CP, earlier syntheses have focused mainly on acupuncture and However, its variants, including scalp, electro-, and laser acupuncture. Their [3] conclusions have been tempered by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, and a high or unclear risk of bias Zhang et al., 2018; Novak et al., 2020). Acupotomy involves cutting soft tissue and so differs from filiform needling in technique, tissue effect, and risk profile. Evidence on acupuncture therefore cannot be assumed to apply to acupotomy. Reported adverse events associated with acupotomy include bleeding, infection, nerve injury, and procedural pain, and these are particularly relevant in children. Safety [20] must [4] therefore be assessed together with efficacy. Despite the growing use of acupotomy for CP; several gaps remain. First, to our knowledge, no comprehensive systematic review has quantitatively evaluated randomized evidence for acupotomy in CP across outcomes. Second, the primary studies vary widely in participant age, CP subtype and severity, Gross Motor Function Classification System level, acupotomy technique, treatment frequency, comparators, and co-interventions. This makes it difficult for clinicians to interpret [1] the findings. Third, outcome measures differ. Some trials report spasticity with the Ashworth or Modified Ashworth Scale (Bohannon & Smith, 1987), others report motor function with the Gross Motor Function Measure (Russell et al., 1989), and others use range of motion, activities of daily living scales; or non-standardized clinical effectiveness rates. The methodological quality of these trials, [8] including randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and outcome reporting, has not been systematically appraised. However, Finally, safety data are inconsistently reported, and the certainty of the evidence has not been evaluated using a structured approach such as GRADE Guyatt et al.; 2008). Without such an appraisal, guideline developers and clinicians cannot judge whether acupotomy deserves a place in multidisciplinary CP care or further research investment. The present study therefore aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupotomy for CP. Specifically, we asked whether, in children and adults with CP (population), acupotomy alone or combined with conventional rehabilitation (intervention) is more [17] effective than rehabilitation alone, sham treatment, or other active comparators comparison) in improving spasticity, gross motor function, joint range of motion, and activities of daily living, and whether it is acceptably safe (outcomes). We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA) guidance (Page et al., 2021). This [7] study makes three contributions. It provides the first structured synthesis of randomized evidence on acupotomy for CP that covers both efficacy and adverse events. It assesses the risk of bias and the certainty of evidence for each outcome, and it explores sources of heterogeneity through prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses. It also identifies methodological shortcomings in the existing literature and offers recommendations for the design, conduct, and reporting of future trials of acupotomy in CP. Methods Study design and registration We conducted a systematic review [36] and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials RCTs) of acupotomy for cerebral palsy CP). The review followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins et al.; 2022) and is reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page [9] et al., 2021). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO before the searches were run, and the registration details and the PRISMA checklist are given in the Supplemental Digital Content. Because the analysis used only published data, ethical approval was not required. Eligibility criteria Eligibility was defined using the PICOS framework. Participants. We included children and adolescents aged 0–18 years) with a diagnosis of CP of any subtype (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic or mixed) and any Gross Motor Function Classification System GMFCS) level; based on established diagnostic criteria (Rosenbaum et al., 2007). Studies of motor impairment from other causes were excluded. Interventions. The experimental intervention was acupotomy (also called needle-knife or miniscalpel-acupuncture), a technique combining acupuncture with soft-tissue release, used alone or added to conventional rehabilitation. Studies in which acupotomy was combined with other traditional Chinese medicine modalities, such as herbal medicine, tuina or moxibustion, were excluded unless the other modalities were also given to the control group. Comparators. Controls received conventional rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, Bobath/neurodevelopmental therapy, or task-oriented training), pharmacological spasticity management, sham acupotomy, manual acupuncture, or no additional treatment. Named entity recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying mentions of real-world entities in text, is a core component of many natural (13) language processing pipelines. Its output feeds entity linking, relation and event extraction, question answering, and knowledge base population (Mintz et al., 2009; Ling et al., 2015). Progress on NER has been driven largely by a small number of shared benchmarks, most prominently the CoNLL-2003 shared task data (Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003) and OntoNotes (Hovy et al., 2006; Pradhan et al., 2013). Neural sequence labelling architectures, from BiLSTM-CRFs (Lample et al., 2016; Ma and Hovy, 2016) to contextualised pretrained representations (Peters et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019), have [34] pushed performance on these benchmarks to a level where remaining gains are small. This success is tied to the way the benchmarks represent the task. Each token belongs to at most one entity mention, and the label inventory is small, typically four to eighteen types. This flat, coarse-grained [35] view discards much of the semantic content of natural language. Entity mentions routinely contain other entity mentions. In "University of California, Berkeley", the organisation contains a state and a city. In "the Bank of [16] China", a financial institution contains a country. Such nested structure is pervasive in news, biomedical text, and other domains, and the inner mentions often matter for downstream tasks. A relation extractor that sees only the outer organisation cannot recover that the organisation is located in, or named for, a particular country. Nested mentions also expose how names are compositionally constructed, which can help with disambiguation and linking. Flat annotation guidelines force annotators to choose a single span, usually the outermost or the one that best fits a narrow [17] set of types, and the resulting "models" are blind to everything else. The research community [18] has recognised this limitation. Early work on nested NER used cascaded or layered tagging (Alex et [25] al., 2007) and discontinuous or parse-based approaches (Finkel and Manning, 2009). More recent methods include mention hypergraphs (Lu and Roth, 2015; Muis [5] and Lu, 2017; Katiyar and Cardie, 2018), layered and stacked neural taggers (Ju et al., 2018), transition-based systems (Wang et al., 2018), (6) and span-enumeration models (Sohrab and Miwa, 2018). However, (6) this body of work has been evaluated on a narrow set of resources. The most widely used are the ACE 2004 and 2005 corpora (Doddington et al., 2004; Walker [23] et al., 2006) and GENIA (Kim et al., 2003). ACE contains a small number of coarse entity types, and nesting in it is shallow and often involves pronouns or generic mentions. GENIA is restricted to the biomedical domain and has a specialised ontology. Neither provides a large, fine-grained, general-domain resource with deep nesting. Models for nested NER are therefore tested on data that does not exercise the full range of phenomena [17] they are meant to handle. Conclusions about which approaches work, and why, risk being specific to the idiosyncrasies of these corpora. Fine-grained entity typing has developed separately. Work on larger type inventories (Fleischman and Hovy, 2002, Ling and Weld, 2012; Gillick et al., 2014; Choi et al., (27) 2018) shows that richer types support more precise downstream inference. Yet [2] fine-grained resources are mostly built either by distant supervision, which introduces noise, or for typing already-identified mentions rather than detecting them. They typically do not annotate nested structure. BBN's pronoun coreference and entity type corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005) provides a hierarchical inventory of 64 types over the Wall Street Journal, but (26) it is still largely flat in its treatment of mention boundaries. As a result, no existing dataset combines three properties: broad coverage of entity types, genuinely nested annotation, and a text source that is widely studied and linguistically well understood. This paper presents NNE, a "manually" annotated dataset of fine-grained, nested named entity mentions over the full Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB; Marcus et al., 1993). Our annotation comprises 279,795 mentions of 114 entity types, with up to six layers of nesting. We build on the BBN type hierarchy and extend it to capture additional distinctions, and we annotate all mentions that fit the scheme, including those embedded within longer names and within non-name noun phrases. Choosing the PTB as the base text has several advantages. The WSJ is a standard newswire benchmark for parsing, tagging, and semantic annotation, and layers such as PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) and the CoNLL-2003 NER annotation already exist over portions of it. NNE therefore enables comparison with, and joint modelling alongside, syntactic and semantic structure. A large share of nested entity boundaries aligns with constituent boundaries, which makes it possible to study how syntax can inform nested NER and how entity structure can inform parsing. The goal of NNE is to remove a bottleneck for nested NER research. We argue that a dataset for this task should satisfy three requirements. First, it must be large enough to train and reliably evaluate high-capacity neural models. Second, it must have (11) a sufficiently rich type inventory that nesting is semantically meaningful rather than an artefact of a few coarse classes. Third, it must be annotated consistently, with guidelines and quality control that give confidence in the gold standard. We therefore describe not only the resulting data but also the annotation scheme, the process by which annotators were trained and guided, and measures of inter-annotator agreement. We also analyse the data to characterise how nesting manifests in newswire, including the distribution of types, the depth and structure of nesting, and the relationship between entity structure and the PTB's syntax. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We release NNE, to our knowledge the largest manually annotated nested NER dataset for English, with 279,795 mentions across 114 fine-grained types and up to six layers of nesting, covering the entire WSJ portion of the PTB. 2. We describe the annotation scheme and process, including type definitions, handling of ambiguous cases, and agreement statistics, so that the resource can be understood, extended, and replicated. 3. We provide a quantitative analysis of the nesting and type distributions and of how the annotation relates to the underlying syntactic structure. 4. We provide standard training, development, and test splits and evaluation of existing nested NER approaches as baselines, to indicate how much difficulty remains once data scale, type granularity, and nesting depth are increased. We hope that the public release of NNE will encourage the development of new techniques for nested and fine-grained NER and will support research on how entity structure interacts with syntax, linking, and other downstream applications. Corpus selection and preprocessing We annotated the complete Wall Street Journal (WSJ) portion of the Penn Treebank (PTB, Marcus et al., 1993), covering sections 00–24. The PTB is the most heavily annotated English newswire resource, with part-of-speech tags, constituency structure, and (through later projects) semantic role and coreference layers. Annotating it lets nested entity structure be studied alongside existing syntactic and semantic information. We kept the PTB tokenization so that mention boundaries align with the treebank. Annotators saw each sentence in its original document order and could see neighboring sentences, which let them resolve ambiguous types (for example, a (24) company name versus its product). We did not use gold parse trees to restrict candidate spans. Mentions were free to cross constituent boundaries wherever the text required. Annotation scheme Our type inventory began with the BBN Pronoun Coreference and Entity Type Corpus (Weischedel and Brunstein, 2005), which was already annotated over the same WSJ text. We extended it with ideas from the Extended Named Entity Hierarchy (Sekine et al., 2002), the ACE guidelines (Doddington et al., 2004), and the GENIA ontology (Kim et al., 2003). We then ran several rounds of pilot annotation on held-out documents, adding, merging, or splitting types whenever annotators disagreed systematically or found that frequent phenomena had no suitable label. The final scheme has 114 types organized in a three-level hierarchy. Top-level categories include person, organization, geopolitical entity, location, facility, event, product, work of art, law, language, and several numeric and temporal families (e.g., monetary values, percentages, dates, times, cardinal and ordinal numbers, and measurements). Fine-grained subtypes encode distinctions such as the kind of organization (corporation, government body, educational institution) or the kind of numeric expression. Annotators always chose the most specific applicable type, so the hierarchy can be collapsed to coarser labels when needed. Guidelines defined a mention as a contiguous token span that refers to an entity of one of the scheme's types. Names, numeric expressions, and temporal expressions were annotated, whereas pronouns and generic common-noun phrases were not. Nesting was permitted to arbitrary depth under one structural constraint. Any two mentions must be either disjoint or strictly nested, so partially overlapping spans are not allowed. Identical spans with different types were permitted only for a small set of documented cases of genuine type ambiguity, such as metonymic uses. Where a mention contained others, annotators labeled every inner mention independently. For instance, a company name contains a person name, and a date range contains two dates. Annotators were instructed to label inner mentions even when the surface form was the same as an outer mention's component, and to treat possessives, appositions, and coordinations according to explicit rules in the guidelines. For coordinated structures with shared modifiers, annotators marked each conjunct as its own mention. They did not use discontinuous spans, which keeps the annotation compatible with standard span-based and tree-structured models. Annotation procedure The annotation team consisted of trained annotators with linguistics backgrounds, who received a guideline document and supervised practice before working on the main corpus. We built a browser-based interface for efficient span selection and hierarchical type assignment. It supports keyboard shortcuts, type search over the hierarchy, and visual display of nested mentions so that annotators can verify structure at a glance. To reduce effort and improve consistency, the tool pre-populated candidate annotations from the existing BBN labels where these were compatible with our scheme, and annotators then corrected, extended, and re-typed them. BBN annotation is flat and uses a different type set, so it served only as a starting point. Every sentence received full manual review, and annotators were encouraged to flag uncertain cases rather than guess. Annotation proceeded in batches by PTB section. After each batch, a senior annotator reviewed a sample and all flagged items, and recurring problems were resolved through guideline revisions and group discussion. When a guideline changed, earlier batches were searched for affected patterns, using type and string queries over the existing (29) annotations, and corrected. In a final consistency pass, we ran automatic checks to catch structural errors and implausible labelings. These [32] checks looked for partially overlapping spans, mentions whose boundaries split a token, inner mentions of a type not licensed inside a given [7] outer type, and strings that received different labels in different places without a contextual reason. Flagged items were manually adjudicated. Quality assessment We measured inter-annotator agreement on a subset of documents that were annotated independently by multiple annotators from scratch, without [16] pre-populated labels. Because the number of mentions per sentence is unbounded and there is no natural notion of negative items, chance-corrected coefficients such as Cohen's kappa are poorly defined for this task. Following Hripcsak and Rothschild (2005), we instead treated one annotator's labels as (18) the reference and computed precision, recall, and F1 for the However, other, which is equivalent to pairwise F1 [19] agreement. A mention counted as matching only if its start, end, and type were all identical. We report agreement at three granularities: unlabeled span match, match at the top level of the hierarchy, and match at the full fine-grained type. This separates disagreements about where mentions are from disagreements about what they are. We also compared agreement at different nesting depths to see whether inner mentions are [8] harder to annotate than outermost ones, and we examined confusion between types to find systematically ambiguous distinctions. Code clones, fragments of source code that are identical or similar to one another, are pervasive in modern software systems. Empirical studies report that between 5% and 20% of the code in typical large systems is cloned (Roy and Cordy 2007; Kapser and Godfrey 2008). Developers create clones for many reasons, including copy-and-paste reuse, language limitations, and deliberate performance or stability trade-offs. Whether clones are harmful has been debated for more than a decade. Some studies associate clones with inconsistent updates, propagated defects, and increased maintenance effort (Juergens et al. 2009; Krinke 2007; Thummalapenta et al. 2010). Others find that clones are often short-lived, stable, or even beneficial in specific contexts (Kapser and Godfrey 2008, Göde and Koschke 2011; Hotta et al. 2012). The practical consequence is that clone detectors, which can report thousands of clone groups for a mature project (Kamiya et al. 2002; Jiang et al. 2007; Sajnani et al. 2016), leave developers with a triage problem. Not all clones are equally important, and a developer who has limited time must decide which ones are worth refactoring. Clone-removal refactoring, such as extracting a shared method or pulling members up into a common superclass (Fowler 1999), is the standard remedy when clones are judged harmful. Refactoring is not free, however. It requires understanding the context of each clone instance and often involves parameterizing differences, resolving dependencies, and updating tests. It can also introduce regressions or entangle components that were intentionally kept separate. Refactoring every detected clone is therefore neither feasible nor desirable. This motivates clone recommendation, the task of identifying, among all detected clones, those that developers are likely to find worth removing. Prior work has approached this task from two complementary angles. The first uses the present state of the code. Studies of this kind assess whether a clone group is a good refactoring candidate from its structural and syntactic properties, such as the cohesion of individual fragments, the coupling between a fragment and its surrounding context, the size of the clone, and the location of the clone peers within the class hierarchy or package structure (Higo et al. 2004, Tairas and Gray 2012; [20] Zibran and Roy 2012). The second uses the past of the project. These approaches mine version histories to determine how clone peers evolved, for example whether they changed together, how often they were modified, and whether they were modified inconsistently (Lozano and Wermelinger 2008; Mondal et al. 2014). Clones that repeatedly co-change are plausible candidates because the duplication imposes a recurring maintenance burden. Wang and Godfrey (2014) combined design, context, and history information in a learning-based recommender and showed that mixing present and past information improves the accuracy of recommendation over single-aspect heuristics. Despite this progress, existing approaches face three limitations. First, each tool considers only a restricted set of factors, chosen mostly on the basis of the authors' intuitions about what makes a clone worth refactoring. It remains unclear whether the factors used so far are sufficient, whether they overlap, or whether other properties of clones carry additional predictive signal. For example, features describing the [34] evolution of an individual clone (how long it has existed, how often it has been edited, who edited it) have received much less attention than co-change relations between clone peers, and syntactic differences between peers are seldom combined with spatial relations such as same-file or same-package placement. Second, much of the earlier evaluation relied on small data sets, on manually labeled ground truth, or on a single project, which makes generalization hard to assess. In particular, it is rarely examined whether a However, model learned on one project can recommend clones in another project, a cross-project setting that matters in practice because new projects lack the [18] history required for training. Third, the literature offers little systematic comparison of which categories of factors contribute most to recommendation accuracy, or of which learning algorithms are best suited to the task. Without such comparisons, tool builders cannot make informed decisions about which information is worth the cost of collecting. The existence However, of several tools [21] that use different yet individually useful [32] signals suggested to us that a more accurate recommender could be obtained by considering as many factors as possible within a single framework and letting a learning algorithm determine how they should be weighed. This leads to the central question of this paper: to what extent can combining a broad set of present and past features of clones, characterizing both individual clones and the relations among clone peers, improve the recommendation of clones for refactoring, [38] in both within-project and cross-project settings? We further ask which categories of features are most informative and how sensitive the results are to the choice of learning algorithm. To answer these questions, we present CREC (Clone Recommendation for refactoring based on the present and the past), a learning-based approach to clone recommendation. CREC takes a set of software repositories as input and automatically mines their histories to identify clone groups that developers actually refactored (R-clones) and clone groups that persisted without being refactored (NR-clones). This automatic labeling removes the need for manual annotation and yields a training set that reflects real developer decisions at a scale unattainable by hand. For each clone group, CREC extracts 34 features in five categories: the content of individual clones, the evolution behaviors of individual clones, and the spatial, syntactical, and co-change [5] relations of clone peers. A classifier trained on these features then predicts whether a new clone [25] group should be recommended for refactoring. To our knowledge, this is the largest feature set designed for clone recommendation [4] to date. We evaluated CREC on six large open-source projects. In the within-project setting, where the classifier is trained and tested on data from the same project, CREC achieved an F-score of 83%. [38] In the cross-project setting, where the classifier is trained on other projects and applied to an unseen one, it achieved an F-score of 76%. We compared CREC against the state-of-the-art approach of Wang and Godfrey (2014) on the same data set. That approach achieved F-scores of 70% and 50% in the two settings, so CREC's improvements are substantial, particularly when historical data from the target project are unavailable. We also [28] analyzed the contribution of each feature category and compared several widely used learning algorithms to understand which factors and models drive these results. This paper makes the following contributions: An automated approach to build ground truth. We describe a procedure that mines version histories to extract refactored (R-clone) and non-refactored (NR-clone) clone groups, enabling the construction of large training and evaluation sets without manual labeling. The largest feature set to date for clone recommendation. We define 34 features that integrate present and past information, covering the content and evolution of individual clones as well as the spatial, syntactical, and co-change relations among clone peers. A learning-based recommender, CREC. We show that CREC accurately recommends clones for refactoring in both within-project (83% F-score) and cross-project (76% F-score) settings, and that it significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art approach (70% and 50%, respectively) on our data set. An empirical analysis of factors and algorithms. We quantify the relative effectiveness of different feature categories and of different learning algorithms, and we derive insights to guide the design of future clone-management tools. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives background and motivating examples. Section 3 describes the design of CREC, including the extraction of R-clones and NR-clones, the feature set, and the classifier training. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Section 5 discusses threats to validity, Section 6 reviews related work, and Section 7 concludes. Research questions and overview. We designed the study around three questions. RQ1: How accurately does CREC recommend clone groups for refactoring in within-project and cross-project settings, compared with a state-of-the-art baseline? RQ2: How much does each feature category contribute? RQ3: How does the choice of learning algorithm affect performance? CREC has three stages: (1) automatic construction of a labeled data set of refactored clone groups (R-clones) and non-refactored clone groups (NR-clones) from version histories, (2) extraction of 34 features capturing the present and past of each clone group, and (3) training and applying a classifier that predicts whether a clone group deserves refactoring. Subject projects. We selected six open-source Java projects with long, well-maintained Git histories: Ant, Cassandra, jEdit, JGit, Lucene, and Tomcat. Projects were chosen using three criteria: more than 5,000 commits, at least eight years of development, and varied application domains and sizes (60 to 520 KLOC at the latest studied release). To keep analysis tractable, we sampled snapshots at release tags and at every 100th commit between releases, yielding 1,412 snapshots in total. Such sampling is common in clone-genealogy research, where the unit of analysis is the However, evolution of clones across versions rather than individual commits (Kim et al., 2005). Clone detection and genealogy extraction. For each snapshot, we detected Type-2 and Type-3 clones with NiCad (Roy & Cordy, 2008), using a minimum size of 10 lines, a maximum dissimilarity threshold of 30% after pretty-printing and identifier normalization, and blind renaming. Clone fragments were grouped into clone groups (also called clone classes), where each member (clone peer) is similar to the others in the group. We then mapped clone groups across consecutive snapshots with a location- and similarity-based mapping in the spirit of clone genealogy extractors (Kim et al., 2005, Saha et al., 2013). Two groups were mapped if at least half of their fragments could be matched, with fragment similarity above 70% after accounting for line changes recovered by git diff with rename detection. The result was a set of clone genealogies describing how each group was created, changed, and removed. Automatic labeling of R-clones and NR-clones. We detected refactorings between successive snapshots with RefactoringMiner (Tsantalis et al., 2018), which reports Extract Method, Pull Up Method, Move Method, Extract Superclass, and related operations with reported precision above 95%. A clone group was labeled R-clone if (i) its genealogy ended because at least two of its fragments disappeared or became dissimilar, (ii) a clone-removal refactoring (Extract Method, Pull Up Method/Attribute, Extract Superclass, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, or Form Template Method; Fowler, 1999) was detected involving at least two fragments of the group in the same commit interval, and (iii) the consolidated code was invoked from, or inherited by, the former clone locations. Clone groups that survived at least five consecutive snapshots, or at least one year, without any clone-removal refactoring were labeled NR-clones. Groups with ambiguous histories, such as those deleted together with their containing files, were discarded. Two authors manually validated a random sample [16] of 300 labeled groups (150 per class), reaching Cohen's kappa = 0.87 with the automatic labels. [26] However, Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and 14 labels were corrected, indicating 95.3% labeling accuracy. The final data set contained 1,028 R-clones [39] and 4,876 NR-clones. Feature extraction. CREC computes 34 features at the snapshot immediately preceding [29] the labeling event (for R-clones, the version before the refactoring, for NR-clones, the final version of the However, observation window). Features are organized into five categories, covering individual clones and clone-peer relations, and the present and the past. 1. Code features [20] (10) describe the present content of a clone group: average lines of code, number of tokens, number of peers, cyclomatic complexity, number of method calls, number of parameters and local variables, fraction of identifiers shared among peers, cohesion of the clone relative However, to its enclosing method (Tairas & Gray, 2012), and coupling to surrounding code. 2. Malaria remains one of the most important parasitic diseases worldwide. The World Health Organization estimated roughly 219 million cases and 435,000 deaths in 2017, with about 93% of cases and 94% of deaths occurring in the WHO African Region (World Health Organization, 2018). Despite the substantial gains of the early 2000s, when scaled-up vector control, artemisinin-based combination therapy and improved diagnostics reduced the global burden by around 40% Bhatt et al., 2015), progress has stalled in several high-burden countries. Malaria is also strongly heterogeneous. Transmission intensity varies over small distances and across seasons and years, shaped by climate, land use, vector ecology, human movement, socioeconomic conditions and the coverage of interventions Gething et al., 2011, Kabaria et al., 2017). This heterogeneity means that national averages obscure the foci and periods of risk that matter most for control and elimination. The concern is sharper in low and middle-income countries LMICs), where resources are limited and targeting is essential. Spatio-temporal modelling has become a central tool for characterising this heterogeneity. By describing how disease risk varies jointly over space and time, such models support mapping of burden, early warning and forecasting of epidemics, identification of hotspots and high-risk periods, and evaluation of interventions (Hay et al., 2009, Pigott et al., 2015). The field has expanded rapidly for several reasons. Georeferenced data are now far more abundant, including national household surveys with GPS coordinates such as the Demographic and Health Surveys and Malaria Indicator Surveys, health facility records from routine information systems such as DHIS2, and the parasite rate databases compiled by the Malaria Atlas Project Guerra et al., 2007; Gething et al., 2011). Satellite remote sensing now provides rainfall, temperature, vegetation indices and other environmental measures at high temporal and spatial resolution Hay et al., 2006). At the same time, computational advances have made hierarchical Bayesian geostatistical inference practical on large datasets. Markov chain Monte Carlo, and more recently the integrated nested [19] Laplace approximation (INLA) with the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach, now allow flexible models to be fitted routinely (Rue et al., 2009, Lindgren et al., 2011). The methods in use are diverse. At the area level, studies typically model counts of cases yit in district i and time t using Poisson or negative binomial likelihoods, for example yit ~ PoissonEit θit), log θit = α + xitᵀβ + ui + vi + γt + δit, where Eit is the expected count or population at risk, xit are covariates, ui and vi are spatially structured and unstructured random effects (often with a conditional autoregressive prior; Besag et al., 1991), γt is a temporal term such as a random walk or seasonal harmonic), and δit is a space-time interaction (Knorr-Held, 2000). For point-referenced survey data, a geostatistical binomial model is common, with logitp(s,t)) = x(s,t)ᵀβ + w(s,t), where w is a Gaussian process with Matérn covariance that may be separable or non-separable in space and time Diggle et al., 1998, Gething et al., 2012). Alongside these, authors have used spatial scan statistics for cluster detection (Kulldorff, 1997), generalised additive models, spatio-temporal autoregressive and distributed-lag models for climate-driven forecasting, machine-learning approaches such as random forests and boosted regression trees, and mechanistic or hybrid models combining transmission dynamics with spatial structure (Smith et al., 2012, Reiner et al., 2015). Each approach rests on different assumptions about stationarity, dependence structure, interaction between space and time, and the relation between covariates and risk. The choice of approach also interacts with the scale of analysis, ranging from microspatial studies at household or village level to continental mapping, and with the quality, completeness and denominators of the underlying data. The covariates that enter these models are equally varied. Environmental and climatic variables, including temperature, rainfall, humidity, vegetation indices, elevation and hydrology, are used most often because of their biological relevance to vector and parasite development Craig et al., 1999, [7] Mordecai et al., 2013). Many studies also include socioeconomic indicators, housing quality, urbanisation, population density, access to health care, intervention coverage (insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, treatment) and human mobility, though these tend to be less consistently available and measured, [18] and their inclusion is less standardised. Decisions about lagged effects, spatial resolution matching, collinearity, variable selection and how to handle covariates that are themselves modelled or interpolated are made inconsistently, and often without clear justification. Likewise, the practices used to validate models vary from simple in-sample fit statistics (deviance information criterion, R²) to out-of-sample cross-validation, spatial block validation and prospective forecast evaluation [15] using proper scoring rules (Roberts et al., 2017, Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). Where validation does not account for residual spatial and temporal autocorrelation, predictive performance is easily overstated. Existing reviews have addressed parts of this [35] landscape but However, not its entirety. Earlier syntheses have focused on the use of geographic information systems and remote sensing in malaria epidemiology (Hay et al., 2006, Eisele et al., 2012), on early warning systems and climate-based forecasting (Thomson et al., 2006, Zinszer et al., 2012), on mapping of parasite prevalence (Hay et al., 2009), or on specific techniques. Few have systematically compared the full set of spatio-temporal approaches, the covariates used and the validation strategies adopted across settings. Consequently, researchers and national malaria control programmes who wish to build a [1] model for a specific purpose, whether burden However, estimation, forecasting or intervention targeting, have little consolidated guidance on which methods have been applied under which data conditions, which covariates have proven informative, and how models [1] have been assessed. This [4] gap matters particularly in LMICs, where data are sparse, noisy and often reported at aggregated administrative scales, and where methodological choices can directly shape resource allocation. Because the literature is heterogeneous in aims, designs and outcomes, a scoping review is more appropriate than a conventional systematic review with meta-analysis. A scoping approach allows the extent, range and nature of evidence to be mapped, key [20] concepts and gaps to be identified, and a foundation for best-practice recommendations to be laid (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010, Tricco et al., 2018). The overarching question of this review is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches have been used to assess the burden of malaria in LMICs within the limits of malaria transmission, and what covariates and validation techniques have accompanied them? Specific objectives are to i) describe the aims and settings of spatio-temporal malaria modelling studies, including the spatial and temporal scales and the data sources used, (ii) catalogue and classify the statistical and mathematical modelling frameworks applied; (iii) summarise the However, covariates included and how they were processed, (iv) document the model validation and performance assessment procedures, and v) identify methodological gaps and derive recommendations to guide future modelling decisions. This review makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, comprehensive synthesis of spatio-temporal malaria modelling over five decades 1968–2018), including grey literature that is often missed by conventional searches. Second, it links modelling choices to data characteristics, spatial scale and purpose, enabling a more transparent approach to method selection. Third, it highlights under-used methods, weaknesses in validation and reporting, and priority areas for research, supporting more rigorous and reproducible modelling in settings where it is [36] most needed. The review follows the PRISMA-P reporting guidance Moher et al., 2015) and is registered in PROSPERO CRD42017076427). Methods and Analysis Study design and reporting framework This scoping review follows the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), as refined by Levac et al. (2010) and the Joanna Briggs Institute Peters et al., 2015). The protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement Moher et al., 2015; Shamseer et al., 2015), and was registered with PROSPERO CRD42017076427) before screening began. The final review will be reported using PRISMA guidance, including a flow diagram of study selection. A scoping design was chosen because the aim is to map the range of spatio-temporal approaches, covariates and validation practices, not to pool effect estimates. The review proceeds through five stages: 1) identifying the research question, 2) identifying relevant studies, 3) selecting studies, (4) charting the data, and (5) collating, summarising and reporting the results. Research question and eligibility criteria The review question is: what spatio-temporal modelling approaches, covariates and validation techniques have been used to assess the burden of malaria in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) within the limits of malaria transmission? Eligibility was structured using the Population–Concept–Context framework. The population comprises human malaria cases, infection prevalence, incidence or mortality, at any spatial scale from household to continental. The concept is the application of a statistical, mathematical or geostatistical model that explicitly incorporates both spatial and temporal dimensions, for example Bayesian hierarchical models, spatio-temporal geostatistical models, space–time scan statistics, generalised additive or autoregressive models with spatial structure, and mechanistic models with spatial components. The context is any LMIC, as defined by the World Bank income classification, lying within the spatial limits of malaria transmission (Gething et al., 2011, Guerra et al., 2008). Studies were included if published between January 1968 and [26] April 2018, in any language for which translation was feasible, and as primary research, [32] methodological papers, theses or technical reports. Studies were excluded if they were purely spatial or purely temporal with no joint modelling, if they were conducted in high-income or non-endemic settings, if they considered only vector distribution or entomological However, outcomes without human burden, or if they were commentaries, editorials or narrative reviews without original modelling. Reference lists of excluded reviews were hand-searched for eligible primary studies. Search strategy A comprehensive search will be conducted of PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Cochrane CENTRAL via Wiley, Academic Search Complete, MasterFILE Premier, CINAHL and MEDLINE via EBSCOhost, and Google Scholar. The search strategy was developed with an information specialist and combines controlled vocabulary e.g. MeSH) with free-text terms in three concept blocks joined by the Boolean operator AND: (i) malaria (malaria OR Plasmodium OR falciparum OR vivax), ii) spatio-temporal methods "spatio-temporal" OR "spatiotemporal" OR space-time OR "geostatistic" OR "Bayesian hierarchical OR disease mapping OR "geographic information system" OR remote sensing" OR kriging OR "CAR model OR INLA); and (iii) burden or outcome terms (prevalence OR incidence OR burden OR "transmission" OR "mortality" OR risk). Terms within each block are joined by OR. A country-level filter listing LMICs, adapted from the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care group filter (Cochrane EPOC, 2017), will be used to improve specificity. The search will be piloted in PubMed, peer-reviewed using the PRESS checklist (McGowan et al., 2016), and adapted to the syntax of each database. Because Google Scholar returns very large numbers of records ranked by relevance, the first 200 hits for each search string will be screened Haddaway et al., 2015). Grey literature will be sought through OpenGrey, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, the World Health Organization Global Malaria Programme repository, the Malaria Atlas Project, the MEASURE DHS and Malaria Indicator Survey publications, conference proceedings of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Multilateral Initiative on Malaria, and institutional repositories of African universities. Experts in malaria spatial epidemiology will be contacted to identify unpublished work. Study selection All records will be exported to EndNote, where duplicates will be removed, and then imported into Rayyan (Ouzzani [14] et al., 2016) for screening. Two reviewers will independently screen titles, then abstracts, then full texts against the eligibility criteria. Before formal screening, a calibration [5] exercise on a random sample of 50 records will be undertaken to [8] refine the criteria and ensure consistent interpretation. Inter-rater agreement at each stage will be quantified using Cohen's kappa Cohen, 1960): κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. Despite decades of diversity initiatives, legal mandates, and growing public commitment to equal opportunity, the top of the organizational pyramid remains strikingly homogeneous. Women, racial and ethnic minorities, and other nondominant group members enter many professions in substantial numbers, yet their representation declines at each successive step of the career ladder (Ely & Meyerson, 2000, Kanter, 1977, Stainback & Tomaskovic-Devey, 2012). This pattern is especially visible in what I call upward mobility career systems: organizations and professions, such as universities, law firms, corporations, and research institutes, in which careers unfold as a sequence of evaluations and promotions that progressively narrow the pool of candidates. In academia, for example, women earn roughly half of doctoral degrees in many fields but remain a minority among full professors and in senior leadership (Ceci et al., 2014, European Commission, 2021). The leaky pipeline metaphor captures the attrition but obscures its cause, because it suggests passive loss rather than the outcome of repeated decisions made by identifiable people at identifiable points in the system. The persistence of this pattern is puzzling given that these systems typically understand themselves as meritocracies. Castilla and Benard 2010) described a paradox of meritocracy: organizations that explicitly emphasize meritocratic values can show greater bias in rewards favoring dominant group members, because the belief in one's own objectivity licenses decision makers to relax vigilance. Individuals who see themselves as fair are less likely to monitor [32] their own behavior and are more susceptible to moral licensing Monin & Miller, 2001; Uhlmann & Cohen, 2007). Because merit is rarely defined in a way that is independent of who displays it, evaluation criteria are readily constructed or reweighted to fit favored candidates (Uhlmann & Cohen, 2005). Decades of experimental and field research show that stereotypes shape the evaluation of competence, the attribution of success, and the interpretation of ambiguous performance information (Heilman, 2012, Moss-Racusin et al., 2012, Eaton et al., 2020). Evaluation is especially vulnerable when criteria are ambiguous, accountability is low, and time is short, conditions that characterize the upper levels of most hierarchies (Bielby & Baron, 1986; Reskin, 2000). Within this logic, gatekeepers occupy a pivotal position. By gatekeepers I mean those who control access to valued resources and positions: members of search and promotion committees, senior managers, department chairs, board members, and the panels that allocate grants, awards, and appointments. They are frequently themselves members of the dominant group, having been successful under existing rules, and they are therefore prone to reproduce homophilous patterns of selection (Kanter, 1977; Ibarra, 1992, Rivera, 2012). Yet the great majority of diversity interventions are [16] directed elsewhere. Typical programs aim to fix the nondominant group member, through mentoring, networking, or leadership training, or to change attitudes broadly through diversity training for all employees. Reviews of the evidence show that such approaches have modest and often short-lived effects, and that mandatory training can even provoke resistance (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016, Kalev et al., 2006; Paluck et al., 2021, Bezrukova et al., 2016). Programs that target the people and procedures at decision points, by contrast, have been far less studied, although the available evidence suggests that structural arrangements such as accountability, transparency, and task forces responsible for diversity outcomes are more effective than training alone (Kalev et al., 2006, Castilla, 2015). Two further limitations characterize the literature. First, much of the evidence on bias comes from laboratory or vignette experiments in which individual evaluators judge hypothetical targets. These studies are invaluable for demonstrating mechanisms, but they say little about how bias operates in the collective, repeated, and politically embedded decision processes of real organizations, or about how to change those processes (Bohnet, 2016, Paluck & Green, 2009). Second, systemic approaches, which view inequality as an emergent property of interacting parts of an organization rather than as a collection of individual prejudices, have been advocated for some time (Cox, 1991, Ely & Meyerson, 2000, Nkomo & Hoobler, 2014; Bendl & Schmidt, 2010), yet they are rarely translated into concrete guidance for practitioners. Change agents, including diversity officers and consultants, are consequently left [9] with broad principles (change [35] the culture," "address structural barriers") but few specifications of what an intervention should contain and why it should work. At the same time, the empirical base for "what works" in systemic interventions is thin, and rigorous evaluations in naturally occurring organizational settings remain scarce (Bezrukova et al., 2016, Paluck et al., 2021). This article addresses these gaps by asking: What design specifications should systemic diversity interventions meet if they are to engage gatekeepers, improve the quality of decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems? I use the term design specifications in the sense of design science (Van Aken, 2004; Romme, 2003): general, evidence-informed prescriptions that state the properties an intervention should have to produce a desired outcome in a class of contexts, while leaving room for local adaptation. Such specifications sit between abstract theory and detailed procedural recipes. They are intended to travel across settings, so that practitioners can build interventions [6] suited to their own organizations rather than adopting packaged programs whose active ingredients are unknown. I derive the specifications in two steps. First, I [23] draw on research on the paradox of meritocracy, bias in evaluation, and group decision processes to identify the mechanisms through However, which gatekeepers reproduce inequality and the leverage points at which they might be disrupted. Second, I ground the specifications in the limited empirical evidence on systemic interventions, examining three illustrative examples from academic settings, a bias literacy program (Carnes et al., 2015, Sekaquaptewa et al., 2019), participatory modeling of organizational dynamics (Vennix, 1996, Van den Belt, 2004), and participant observation of decision making in committees. Universities offer a particularly informative context because their career systems are archetypal examples of upward mobility, their gatekeeping processes are formalized and visible, and their commitment to meritocratic ideals is especially However, strong. The contribution is threefold. First, I extend the diversity literature by shifting the unit of intervention from the disadvantaged individual or the undifferentiated workforce to the gatekeepers and the decision processes they enact, thereby linking research on bias to organizational change. Second, I offer a set of design specifications that consolidate scattered evidence into usable guidance, clarifying which features of interventions, such as However, engagement rather than compulsion, self-generated insight, and attention to the decision process, are likely to matter. Third, I pair each specification with a concrete example of a successful intervention, providing inspiration for diversity officers and consultants and a basis for future evaluation research. Together, these contributions aim to make systemic change in the composition of the top of the career pyramid a more tractable and more evidence-based endeavor. Research Approach and Design Logic This paper follows a design science approach (van Aken, 2004; Romme, 2003), which seeks prescriptive knowledge in the form of design specifications: general statements of the form to achieve outcome Y in context C, use intervention feature X, because mechanism M." Design specifications differ from descriptive hypotheses in that they are judged by their utility and by the plausibility of their underlying mechanisms, not by statistical significance alone. Because rigorous evaluations of systemic diversity interventions are scarce (Bezrukova et al., 2016; Paluck et al., 2021), I combined three sources of input in an iterative, abductive process (Dubois & Gadde, 2002). The first was a theoretical analysis of the paradox of meritocracy (Castilla & Benard, 2010) in upward mobility career systems. The second was a purposive review of intervention evidence. The third was a formal sketch of how bias in gatekeeping decisions accumulates across a career pyramid. The specifications were refined by moving back and forth among these sources until each specification was tied to an identified mechanism, to at least one empirical example, and to a plausible implementation route. Scope and Definitions Upward mobility career systems are organizations in which individuals progress through hierarchical stages, with advancement decided by gatekeepers (e.g., committee members, supervisors, reviewers, and panel chairs) who evaluate candidates against criteria of merit. Academia, professional service firms, and large public bureaucracies are canonical examples. I define a systemic diversity intervention as one that targets the decision-making processes, structures, or routines through which advancement occurs, rather than only the attitudes or skills of individuals from nondominant groups (Dobbin & Kalev, 2016; Nielsen, 2017). Nondominant group members are those whose social category (e.g., gender, race/ethnicity) is underrepresented at higher organizational levels and who are subject to negative stereotyping or reduced status in the evaluative context (Ridgeway, 2011). Identification and Selection of Intervention Evidence I searched Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar for English-language publications from 2000 to 2022. Search strings combined terms for the intervention level (systemic, institutional, structural, organizational change, intervention, training, program), the target (gatekeeper, selection committee, evaluator, decision maker, hiring, promotion, tenure), the topic (diversity, gender equality, bias, inclusion), and the setting (academia, university, higher education, science). I supplemented the database search with backward and forward citation tracking from key works (e.g., Bohnet et al., 2016, Carnes et al., 2015, Moss-Racusin et al., 2012, Nielsen, 2017, van den Brink & Benschop, 2012), and with reports from funded programs such as the U.S. National Science Foundation ADVANCE initiative (Laursen & Austin, 2020) and the European structural change projects. Studies were included if they a) described an intervention aimed at influencing how gatekeepers evaluate, select, or promote candidates, or at altering the structures or routines within which they do so, (b) occurred in a career system with hierarchical progression; and (c) reported some form of outcome evidence, ranging from experimental or quasi-experimental data to qualitative accounts of change. I excluded interventions aimed solely at individual development of nondominant group members (e.g., mentoring or networking programs without gatekeeper involvement) and one-off awareness sessions without follow-up. Initial screening of titles and abstracts yielded a small candidate pool, and full-text review reduced this to the interventions that met all criteria. Given the narrow evidence base, I did not attempt an exhaustive systematic review. I used purposive, criterion-based selection (Patton, 2015) to identify exemplary cases that maximized variation in the mechanism of change. Three interventions in academic settings were chosen because each engages gatekeepers through a different route. The first was a bias literacy program, in which gatekeepers learn about the cognitive and social processes that produce biased evaluations and practice strategies to counter them (Carnes et al., 2015, Devine et al., 2012, Sekaquaptewa et al., 2019). The second was participatory modeling, in which gatekeepers and other stakeholders jointly construct a formal or semiformal model of the career system to see how local decisions aggregate into pyramid-level representation (Vennix, 1996, Voinov et al., 2018). The third was participant observation, [11] in which a researcher-practitioner observes actual decision meetings and feeds back to gatekeepers the discursive and procedural patterns that shape evaluations (van den Brink et al., 2010, van den Brink & Benschop, 2012). Data Extraction and Analysis For each intervention I extracted the [31] target group of gatekeepers, the core activities, the theory of change, the implementation conditions, the [3] outcome measures, and the reported effects and limitations. I then coded the material using a mechanism-oriented template adapted from realist evaluation Pawson & Tilley, 1997), asking what it was about the intervention that produced [23] change, for whom, and under what conditions. Coding proceeded in three passes. First, I coded open descriptive categories (e.g., "accountability," "criteria clarification," "making bias visible," However, "ownership of the problem"). Second, I clustered these into higher-order mechanisms drawing on the literatures on stereotyping and shifting standards (Biernat, 2012), accountability in judgment (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999), and structured decision [16] making (Kahneman et al., 2021, Bohnet, 2016). Third, I translated each cluster into a design specification and checked it against disconfirming cases to identify boundary conditions. Specifications were retained when they were supported by at least two independent sources, or by one empirical source and a well-established theoretical mechanism, and were flagged as provisional otherwise.
