English Language Learners (ELLs) are among the fastest growing segments of the school-age population in the United States. They made up roughly one in ten public school students, more than five million children, in the most recent national counts (National Center for Education Statistics, 2022). The majority are enrolled in elementary grades, where foundational knowledge and attitudes toward science are formed. Yet ELLs have not attained [37] the same academic success as their English-proficient peers. Results from the National Assessment of Educational Progress consistently show large gaps between ELLs and non-ELLs in [13] science, and these gaps persist across grade levels and student cohorts. Such disparities limit ELLs' access to advanced coursework and STEM pathways and ultimately restrict their participation [2] in a society increasingly shaped by science and technology Lee, [15] 2005; Lee, Quinn, & Valdés, 2013). In response to these concerns, science educators and policy documents have urged teachers to adopt inquiry approaches to instruction. Inquiry-based teaching engages students in posing questions, planning investigations, collecting and interpreting evidence, and constructing explanations, rather than receiving information passively (National Research Council [NRC], 2000). Contemporary standards, including A Framework for K–12 Science Education and [7] the Next Generation Science Standards, place these practices at the center of science learning (NGSS Lead States, 2013; NRC, 2012). Proponents argue that inquiry is especially well suited to ELLs. Hands-on investigation provides concrete, multimodal experiences that [1] make abstract ideas comprehensible. Collaborative discourse creates authentic reasons to use language, and open-ended tasks can draw on the cultural and linguistic resources students bring to class (Rosebery, Ogonowski, DiSchino, [32] & Warren, 2010, Stoddart, Pinal, Latzke, & Canaday, 2002). From this perspective, science and language are learned together, with scientific practice serving as a context for language development Lemke, 1990, Hakuta, Santos, & Fang, 2013). The evidence that inquiry improves outcomes for students in general is substantial but not unqualified. Syntheses of the literature suggest that inquiry-based instruction can yield positive effects on science achievement, particularly when students are actively engaged in investigation and when teachers guide the process (Furtak, Seidel, Iverson, & Briggs, 2012; Minner, Levy, & Century, 2010). Meta-analytic work on discovery-based learning likewise shows benefits when students receive scaffolding, feedback, or worked [22] examples, but not when instruction is unguided Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, & Tenenbaum, 2011). The broader debate over minimally guided instruction has argued that inquiry places heavy demands on working memory and may disadvantage novice learners (Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006). Others have countered that well-scaffolded inquiry supports learners in managing complexity Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, & Chinn, 2007). These syntheses, however, draw primarily on samples of students who are proficient in the language of instruction, and they rarely disaggregate results by language status. For ELLs, the question is [29] more complicated. The same features that make inquiry attractive may also create obstacles. Inquiry lessons often depend on extended oral discussion, interpretation of ambiguous data, and the production of written explanations and arguments. These tasks require command of the academic language of science, which is distinct from the conversational fluency that students typically acquire first (Cummins, 2000; Janzen, 2008). Where language support is weak, ELLs may participate less in group work and struggle to follow investigative procedures, and as a result may gain less from inquiry than their English-proficient classmates Lee, 2005). [22] Where teachers integrate language scaffolds such as visuals, sentence frames, native-language support, and explicit vocabulary instruction, inquiry may narrow gaps (Cuevas, Lee, Hart, & Deaktor, 2005, Lee, Maerten-Rivera, Penfield, LeRoy, & Secada, 2008, Settlage, Madsen, & Rustad, 2005). Thus, whether [29] inquiry is effective for ELLs, and under what conditions, is an empirical question that theory alone cannot settle. Despite a growing body of intervention studies, systematic evidence on this question is limited. Existing reviews of science education for ELLs have been largely narrative and have emphasized conceptual frameworks, research agendas, and promising practices over quantification of effects Janzen, 2008; Lee, 2005). Individual studies vary widely in design, duration, outcome measures, and the degree of language support embedded in instruction, and many involve small samples within a single school or district. As a result, it remains unclear whether the reported benefits of inquiry are consistent across studies, whether they are comparable in magnitude to those found for non-ELLs, and which features of instruction or context account for variation. Without such evidence, calls to implement inquiry with ELLs rest on theoretical appeal and the extrapolation of findings from other populations, rather than on a cumulative empirical base. The present study addresses this gap through a meta-analytic review of research on inquiry instruction and the science achievement of ELLs in elementary [4] school. We focus on the elementary grades for two reasons. First, early schooling is when science identities and foundational concepts develop, and when language support is most readily integrated into instruction. Second, the elementary literature offers a sufficiently large set of studies with comparable outcomes for quantitative synthesis. Specifically, we ask three questions: 1) What is the overall effect of inquiry instruction, relative to direct or traditional instruction, on the science achievement of ELLs? 2) Does the effect of inquiry differ for ELLs and non-ELLs when both groups are studied under comparable conditions? 3) Which contextual, instructional, and methodological factors moderate these effects? This review makes three contributions. First, it provides the first quantitative estimate of the effectiveness of inquiry instruction for elementary ELLs, converting a scattered set of studies into a cumulative evidence base. Second, by comparing ELLs and non-ELLs, it tests whether inquiry is equally beneficial across language backgrounds or whether it may unintentionally widen existing gaps, a distinction with direct implications for equity-oriented reform. Third, by examining moderators such as language support, intervention characteristics, and study design, it [14] identifies the conditions under which inquiry is most likely However, to benefit ELLs. In doing so, the review aims to inform teachers, curriculum developers, and policymakers who are implementing inquiry-oriented standards, and to guide researchers toward the questions that remain unresolved. Method Literature Search This meta-analysis followed the reporting guidelines of the PRISMA statement Moher et al., 2009) and the procedures for research synthesis outlined by Cooper (2010). We searched ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global for reports published between January [2] 2000 and December 2019. The start date reflects the period after the publication of Inquiry and the National Science Education Standards (National Research Council, 2000), which popularized inquiry-based reform in U.S. classrooms. Search strings combined three concept clusters using Boolean operators. The first covered the population (e.g., "English language learner," English learner," limited English proficient, "emergent bilingual, bilingual, ESL, "ESOL"). The second covered the intervention (e.g., inquiry, [18] hands-on, "discovery learning, problem-based, project-based, "investigation," "5E"). The third covered the outcome (e.g., "science achievement, "science learning," "science content knowledge," "science performance). To reduce publication bias, we also hand-searched key journals e.g., Journal of Research [9] in Science Teaching, Science Education, TESOL Quarterly), examined reference lists of relevant reviews, and screened conference proceedings and technical reports. Inclusion Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) enrolled students in kindergarten through Grade 6, b) identified a sample or subsample of ELLs, whether through state classification, home-language surveys, or English proficiency assessments; c) compared an inquiry-based science intervention with a comparison condition characterized as direct, traditional, or teacher-centered instruction; (d) used an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a comparison group, including pretest–posttest control group designs, (e) reported a quantitative measure of science achievement (e.g., content knowledge tests, standardized science assessments, or performance tasks); and (f) provided data sufficient to compute an effect size. We defined inquiry instruction following the National Research Council (2000) and Minner et al. 2010) as instruction in which students engage with scientific questions, give priority to evidence, formulate explanations from evidence, connect explanations to scientific knowledge, and communicate and justify their findings. Studies of activity-based instruction that lacked these features, such as cookbook laboratory exercises with predetermined outcomes, were excluded. Studies were also excluded if ELL results were aggregated with those of other subgroups so that they could not be isolated, if outcomes were limited to attitudes or language proficiency, or if the report was a duplicate of data published elsewhere. The final sample comprised 26 articles. Screening and Coding Procedures Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, and then full texts, against the inclusion criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached. Using a structured coding protocol, the same reviewers independently coded each eligible study for a) publication characteristics (year, publication type); b) sample characteristics (grade level, ELL sample size, home language, English proficiency level), (c) intervention characteristics (inquiry level, following Schwab's [1962] distinction among structured, guided, and open inquiry, duration in weeks, teacher professional development, and the presence of explicit language supports such as sentence frames, vocabulary instruction, bilingual instruction, or home-language use); (d) design characteristics (random assignment versus quasi-experimental, unit of assignment, and attrition); and (e) outcome characteristics (researcher-developed versus standardized measures, and science domain). Interrater agreement was calculated as Cohen's kappa for categorical codes and as intraclass correlations for continuous codes. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus and, where necessary, by consulting the original reports. Study Quality Methodological quality was appraised using criteria adapted from the What Works Clearinghouse standards WWC, 2020), including baseline equivalence, differential attrition, and the reliability of outcome measures. Studies were coded as high or lower quality. Quality was examined as a moderator and used in sensitivity analyses rather than as an exclusion criterion, so that the evidence base could be characterized broadly. Effect Size Computation The standardized mean difference was the primary effect size metric. For each comparison, we computed Hedges' g, which applies a small-sample correction to Cohen's d (Hedges, 1981, Hedges & Olkin, 1985). Two types of effects were computed. The first was the main effect of inquiry versus direct instruction for ELLs, calculated from posttest means and standard deviations, or from t, F, or exact p values when descriptive statistics were unavailable (Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). For quasi-experimental designs with pretest data, we calculated the difference between groups in pre-to-post change and divided it by the pooled pretest standard deviation, following Morris 2008), to adjust for baseline nonequivalence. The second was the differential effect for studies that reported outcomes for both ELLs and non-ELLs, defined as the difference between the effect size for non-ELLs and that for ELLs within the same study, with variance equal to the sum of the two sampling variances. Positive values indicated greater benefit for non-ELLs. When studies randomized classrooms or schools but analyzed individual students, we adjusted standard errors for clustering using an assumed intraclass correlation of .20 (Hedges, 2007, Hedges & Hedberg, 2007). Statistical Analysis Many studies contributed multiple effect sizes because they reported several outcomes, multiple ELL subgroups, or several treatment conditions, which violates the assumption of independence. We therefore used robust variance estimation (RVE) with correlated-effects weights (Hedges et al., 2010), which yields valid inference without requiring knowledge of the covariance structure among effect sizes within studies. We assumed a within-study correlation of ρ = .80 and tested sensitivity to values from 0 to 1 Tanner-Smith & Tipton, 2014). Because the number of studies was modest, we applied the small-sample correction of Tipton 2015), and we report degrees of freedom for all tests. Models were estimated in R using the robumeta (Fisher & Tipton, 2015) and metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010) packages. Random-effects models were fitted because we expected true effects to vary across studies owing to differences in populations, implementations, and measures (Borenstein et al., 2009). Overall mean effects are reported with 95% confidence intervals and interpreted using Cohen's (1988) benchmarks, with the caveat that such benchmarks are less informative than contextual comparisons in education research (Kraft, 2020). Heterogeneity was assessed with the Q statistic, τ², and I² (Higgins et al., 2003). To explain heterogeneity, we conducted moderator analyses using meta-regression within the RVE framework. Categorical moderators included inquiry level, presence of language supports, research design, outcome type, grade band (K–2 versus 3–6), and publication status. Continuous moderators included intervention duration

The adaptive immune system recognizes pathogens, allergens, tumors and self-antigens through the specific interaction of antibodies, B cell receptors and T cell receptors with discrete molecular features termed epitopes. Defining which regions of an antigen are recognized, by which receptors, in which host species and in which disease context, underpins vaccine design, diagnostic development, the characterization of autoimmune and allergic disease, and increasingly the development of cancer immunotherapies (Sette and Rappuoli, 2010; Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015). Over the past three decades, experimental approaches including peptide–MHC binding assays, T cell functional assays, X-ray crystallography of antibody–antigen complexes, and high-throughput screening of peptide libraries have generated an extensive body of epitope-level knowledge. This knowledge, however, is dispersed across a very large and heterogeneous literature, where it is reported in free text, tables and figures, using inconsistent nomenclature and with varying degrees of experimental detail. The Immune Epitope Database (IEDB, iedb.org) was established in 2003 with support from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to address this fragmentation by curating published epitope data into a structured, searchable and freely accessible resource (Sette et al., 2005; Vita et al., 2010). Its initial mandate emphasized epitopes from NIAID category A–C priority pathogens and emerging infectious agents, but its scope has since broadened to encompass epitope data from all species studied, including humans, non-human primates, rodents and other model organisms, and across infectious, allergic, autoimmune and transplant-related contexts (Vita et al., 2015). Data are manually extracted by trained curators from the primary literature, using a defined ontology-based schema that captures the epitope structure, the antigen and source organism, the host, the type of assay and its outcome, the immune receptor or MHC restriction involved, and the disease or immunization context (Vita et al., 2010). Complementing the curated epitope data, the IEDB hosts a suite of analysis resources that provide prediction and [16] analysis tools for MHC class I and class II binding, proteasomal processing, B cell epitope likelihood and epitope population coverage (Dhanda et al., 2018; Bui et al., 2006), which have been benchmarked and used extensively by the community (Paul et al., 2013, Jurtz et al., 2017). Since becoming publicly accessible more than a decade ago, the IEDB has grown considerably in both size and complexity. The number of curated references, distinct epitopes and assay records has increased steadily, driven by the continued expansion of the literature, by systematic curation of entire fields such as the antigens of defined pathogens, and by the inclusion of data from large-scale studies and, more recently, from direct submission of datasets generated by research consortia (Vita et al., 2015). Beyond sheer quantity, the nature of the data has become more intricate. Contemporary studies increasingly report T cell receptor sequences, peptide–MHC complexes characterized by mass spectrometry of naturally presented ligands, epitope-specific responses measured with multimer staining and single-cell approaches, and neoantigens identified through tumor sequencing (Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015, Dash et al., 2017). Each of these [1] developments introduces new data types, relationships and contextual variables that must be represented accurately and in a manner that remains interoperable with existing records. This growth presents a clear challenge for users. The IEDB serves a diverse community of immunologists, vaccinologists, computational biologists, clinicians and regulatory scientists, whose questions range from retrieving all known epitopes for a single protein to assembling large, unbiased datasets for training machine learning methods. As the database expands, simple keyword-based or single-field queries become insufficient: users need to combine many criteria, such as epitope source, host, assay type, MHC allele, and disease state, to define precisely the subset of data relevant to their question, and they need to summarize and interpret the resulting, often very large, result sets. Feedback from the user community and analysis of usage patterns have repeatedly indicated that searching and reporting functionality, rather than data availability alone, is a principal determinant of the resource's practical utility. In addition, the increasing reuse of IEDB data in However, downstream resources and in the benchmarking of prediction algorithms places a premium on stable, well-documented and reproducible data access, including bulk downloads and programmatic interfaces (Trolle et al., 2015; Dhanda et al., 2018). A further imperative arises from the broader movement toward findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable (FAIR) data principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Epitope data are most valuable when they can be integrated with information about protein sequences, structures, pathogen taxonomy and immune receptor repertoires. This requires consistent use of community ontologies and identifiers, such as the NCBI Taxonomy, UniProt, the Protein Ontology, the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations and the Disease Ontology, as well as continued coordination with related resources, including the Immunogenetics/HLA database, the Immune Receptor Repertoire community, and the Immunology Database and Analysis Portal (Bukhari et al., 2018; Breuza et al., 2016). Maintaining semantic consistency while accommodating novel experimental paradigms remains a central curation challenge. Against this background, the principal gap addressed in this work is the need for query, reporting and data-organization tools that scale with the increasing volume and complexity of curated epitope data while remaining accessible to non-expert users. Existing interfaces, designed when the database contained substantially fewer records and fewer data types, did not fully support iterative refinement of searches, transparent presentation of result composition, or rapid generation of summaries suitable for publication or for downstream computational use. Likewise, the growing importance of certain categories of data, including T cell receptor information and epitopes relevant to allergy, autoimmunity and cancer, called for targeted improvements in how these data are curated, displayed and linked to analysis tools. In this article, we present an update on the IEDB, summarizing the current status of its data holdings and describing recent developments in curation, user interface design and analytical resources. Specifically, we report: (i) the current quantity and composition of curated data, including distribution across epitope types, host species and disease categories, (ii) redesigned search and reporting functionality that allows users to build complex, multi-parameter queries and to visualize and export summaries of the results; (iii) extensions to curation and data representation to accommodate emerging data types and to improve integration with external resources and ontologies, and (iv) updates to the associated prediction and analysis tools, together with our plans for future development. Collectively, these efforts aim to ensure that the IEDB continues to serve as a comprehensive, reliable and user-oriented resource for (28) the immunological and broader biomedical research communities. Literature identification and curation. Candidate references were identified through scheduled PubMed queries that combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for epitopes, antibodies, T cell responses, and MHC ligands, as described previously (Vita et al., 2015). Retrieved abstracts were ranked with a supervised text-classification approach trained on previously curated and rejected references (Vita et al., 2010). The ranked records were then reviewed manually by curators with training in immunology to determine whether each article contained epitope-specific experimental data. Eligible articles were curated in full, including figures, tables, and supplementary files. The standing scope covers B cell, T cell, and MHC ligand elution and binding assays in any host species and in infectious, allergic, autoimmune, and transplant contexts (Peters et al., 2005; Salimi et al., 2010). Following earlier NIAID-directed priorities, we also performed targeted curation sweeps for specified pathogens and disease categories. These included the NIAID Category A–C priority pathogens, allergens, and a defined set of autoantigens. For each article, curators recorded the epitope structure and source antigen and organism, the host and its immunization or exposure history, the assay type and readout, the effector cell or antibody characteristics, and the restricting MHC molecule where relevant. Each epitope "was" linked to its source molecule through UniProt (UniProt Consortium, 2017) or NCBI Protein records. Where a defined epitope structure was not reported, we recorded the data as a non-peptidic or discontinuous epitope using ChEBI identifiers or, for conformational B [2] cell epitopes, residue positions on a Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure (Berman et al., 2000). Peptide-MHC [31] binding measurements were captured as IC50 or KD values (nM) or as qualitative categories (positive-high, positive-intermediate, positive-low, negative). T cell and B cell assay outcomes "were" recorded as positive or negative, with the corresponding quantitative [18] measure when available. Curation quality was monitored by double-checking a random subset of each curator's records, with discrepancies resolved by consensus with senior curators. Data completeness was assessed against a standard set of required fields. [32] Ontologies and data model. Curated data were stored in a relational database whose schema is aligned with "community" ontologies. Assay types, experimental conditions, and cell types were annotated with [24] the Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (Bandrowski et al., 2016) and the Cell Ontology. Diseases were annotated with the Disease Ontology, organisms with NCBI Taxonomy, molecules with ChEBI and the Protein Ontology, and MHC molecules with the MRO ontology and IMGT/HLA nomenclature (Robinson et al., 2015). Ontology terms were imported using the OBO Foundry conventions [9] (Smith et al., 2007) and refreshed on each release cycle. When new terms were required, [31] they were requested from the relevant ontology maintainers or added to the IEDB application layer and mapped as they were adopted. This structure allows hierarchical queries; for example, a search for a parent [38] disease or taxon automatically includes all of its [16] descendants. Search interface design and implementation. Query and reporting enhancements were developed through an iterative process driven by user feedback, helpdesk requests, usage logs, and periodic usability sessions with external immunologists and bioinformaticians. The web interface was implemented on a server-side framework with a relational back end and a JavaScript front end. New functionality was prioritized by the frequency of related support requests and by whether users could otherwise reproduce the result only through manual post-processing of exported files. Each feature was tested against curated reference queries with known results before release. We confirmed that query results were identical before and after implementation changes, and we verified response times on a standard set of 50 queries of varying complexity. The release process included regression testing, a staging environment, and user acceptance testing by internal staff. Data export, integration, and reporting. Search results can be exported as comma-separated files containing the complete curated fields "for" each epitope, assay, and reference. Summary reports were generated dynamically from the query results. These include distributions of epitopes by source organism, (4) assay type, MHC restriction, and (11) host, and they provide direct links to the underlying records. Cross-references to external resources include PubMed, UniProt, GenBank, PDB, and IMGT/HLA. Three-dimensional structural data for antibody–antigen and TCR–peptide–MHC complexes were identified from the PDB by combining automated searches with manual review, and were [24] linked to the corresponding epitope records (Salimi et al., 2010). Complete [17] database downloads in XML and relational formats were generated at regular intervals and archived with version identifiers so that analyses can be reproduced. Epitope analysis tools. The IEDB Analysis Resource provides predictive and analytical tools that operate on curated data and on user-supplied sequences (Kim et al., 2012). For MHC class I binding, we offered artificial neural network, stabilized matrix method (Peters and Sette, 2005), and NetMHCpan-based methods (Nielsen et al., 2007; Jurtz et al., 2017), together with a consensus approach. For MHC class II, we provided consensus methods that combine the SMM-align, NN-align, combinatorial [28] library, and structure-based predictors (16) (Wang et al., 2008), along with NetMHCIIpan (Andreatta and Nielsen, 2016). Linear and discontinuous B cell epitope prediction relied on BepiPred and DiscoTope (Larsen et al., 2006; Kringelum et al., 2012). Tool performance was evaluated by automated benchmarking against newly curated data that were not available during method training, using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and Spearman rank correlation for quantitative measurements (Trolle et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014). Binding was classified as positive at an IC50 threshold (12) of 500 nM unless otherwise specified. The wider determinants of health, including income, housing, employment, education, social connectedness, and the physical environment, account for a substantial share of the variation in population health and in health inequalities (Dahlgren & Whitehead 1991, Marmot 2010). Primary care is the first point of contact for most people with health concerns and sees many patients whose problems are rooted in social, emotional, or practical difficulties rather than in clinical disease. General practitioners in the United Kingdom (UK) estimate that a considerable proportion of their consultations are driven, at least in part, by non-clinical needs such as loneliness, debt, housing difficulties, or unemployment (Torjesen 2016, Polley et al. 2017). These consultations are time-consuming and often end in prescribing or onward referral that does not address the underlying problem. Meanwhile, health systems face growing demand from ageing populations and rising numbers of people with long-term conditions, which has intensified interest in approaches that connect patients with sources of support outside the healthcare system (Naylor et al. 2016). Social prescribing (SP) is one such approach. It is commonly described as a mechanism for enabling health professionals in primary care to refer patients with non-clinical needs to a range of local, non-clinical services and activities, usually provided by the third sector, that is, community, voluntary, and social enterprise organisations (Friedli & Watson 2004; Brandling & House 2009; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Examples include befriending schemes, arts and exercise programmes, volunteering opportunities, gardening groups, and welfare, debt, and employment advice. In many models, referral is not made directly to the activity. Instead, patients are referred to a navigator, "link worker, or "community connector," who assesses the person's needs, helps them identify goals, and supports them in accessing appropriate community resources (Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015, Polley et al. 2017). SP is therefore not only a referral pathway. It is also an attempt to build partnerships between the health and social sectors so that the wider determinants of health can be addressed in a more coordinated way. Policy interest has grown accordingly. SP has been promoted in national strategy documents in England, Scotland, and Wales, and a rapid expansion of link worker roles has been planned within primary care networks (NHS England 2016). Despite this momentum, the evidence base for SP remains limited. Several systematic and scoping reviews have examined the effectiveness of SP and related "linking" schemes, and they consistently identify methodological weaknesses in primary studies, including the absence of control groups, small samples, high attrition, short follow-up, and inconsistent outcome measurement (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Mossabir et al. 2015; Kilgarriff-Foster & O'Cathain 2015). Some evaluations report improvements in psychological well-being, self-reported health, social connectedness, and reductions in healthcare utilisation (Dayson & Bashir 2014; Cawston 2011). However, the reliability of these findings is uncertain, and the reviews have generally concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether SP is effective or cost-effective (Bickerdike et al. 2017). A further difficulty is the heterogeneity of SP. Services differ in their aims, target populations, referral routes, the presence and role of a navigator, and the range and quality of the community activities available, which complicates the interpretation of outcomes and the transfer of lessons across settings (Husk et al. 2016, Bickerdike et al. 2017). This heterogeneity points to a second and less well-examined problem. Whether an SP service achieves its intended effects depends not only on what the intervention is but also on how it is implemented and delivered. Complex interventions that cut across organisational boundaries are shaped by contextual factors such as leadership, funding arrangements, workforce stability, inter-organisational relationships, and the readiness of the settings in which they are introduced (Greenhalgh et al. 2004; Damschroder et al. 2009). Partnerships between general practices and small third-sector organisations may be particularly vulnerable to these influences, because the partners differ in culture, governance, resources, and professional language, and because many voluntary organisations operate on short-term funding. Weak implementation can undermine an otherwise promising intervention, and null findings in effectiveness studies may reflect implementation failure rather than inherent ineffectiveness. Conversely, understanding the conditions under (25) which SP services are successfully established and sustained could help to explain variation in reported outcomes and inform the design of future services and (29) evaluations. Existing syntheses have paid limited attention to these questions. Most reviews of SP have focused on outcomes, and where implementation issues have been discussed, they have typically been treated as secondary findings or described only in relation to individual evaluations (Bickerdike et al. 2017; Kilgarriff-Foster & (7) O'Cathain 2015). A realist review protocol has set out to explore what works, for whom, [35] and in what circumstances (Husk et al. 2016), but to our knowledge no systematic review has specifically collated and synthesised evidence on the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services. This is a notable gap, given that commissioners, service managers, and providers are currently making decisions about how to establish and scale up such services with little consolidated guidance on likely challenges and enabling conditions. The present review addresses this gap. Its objective was to identify and synthesise the factors that facilitate and hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services based in general practice and involving [7] a navigator. We restricted the scope to this model for two reasons. First, the presence of a navigator who links patients to community resources is a defining feature of many contemporary SP services and represents the model most prominent in current policy. Second, restricting the scope to a more clearly specified service model allowed a more coherent synthesis than would have been possible across the full range of loosely related referral schemes. (11) We focused on implementation and delivery because these processes are modifiable by decision-makers, whereas many outcomes are not directly actionable without an understanding of the mechanisms and (14) contexts that produce them. This review makes three contributions. First, it provides the first systematic synthesis of barriers and facilitators to implementing and delivering navigator-based SP services in general practice, drawing on a broad search of published and grey literature. Second, it appraises the methodological quality of the available evidence using a tool suited to studies of diverse design, which makes transparent the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn and highlights shortcomings in the reporting of SP evaluations. Third, it [4] translates the findings into considerations that can guide commissioners, managers, and providers in planning future services, and it identifies priorities for research on the implementation of SP. Design and reporting We conducted a systematic review of the literature following the principles set out by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) for undertaking systematic reviews in health care [1] and report it in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [2]. The review (7) protocol was developed a priori and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). Because the aim was to identify and integrate evidence However, on the processes of implementing and delivering a complex service, we anticipated heterogeneous study designs and outcomes, and we therefore planned a narrative synthesis using thematic analysis rather than statistical pooling [3, 4]. Definition of the intervention For the purposes of this review, Social Prescribing (SP) was defined as a service based in or linked to general practice through which patients with predominantly non-clinical needs are referred to a navigator (also termed link worker, community navigator, or health advisor). The navigator assesses the patient’s needs and signposts or connects them to local non-clinical services and activities, [30] typically provided by the third sector (community, voluntary, and social enterprise sector). Services that did not involve a navigator, such as direct referral by a clinician to a single activity (e.g., exercise on referral or arts on prescription) without a navigation or assessment step, were excluded. Eligibility criteria Eligibility criteria were structured around the population, intervention, context, and outcomes of interest. We included studies of any design (qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods) that reported factors, experiences, or perceptions (19) (12) relating to the implementation or delivery of SP services. Relevant participants included commissioners, managers, general practitioners and other practice staff, navigators, third-sector providers, and patients. Studies were eligible if they reported barriers or facilitators, either explicitly or through data that could be interpreted as such. Because we were interested in the organisational and contextual determinants of implementation, studies were not required to report clinical effectiveness outcomes. We included peer-reviewed articles and grey literature, including evaluation and service reports, provided they contained primary data and a sufficiently described methodology. Editorials, commentaries, and opinion pieces without empirical data were excluded, as were studies not available in English. No date restrictions were applied. Search strategy Searches were undertaken in June and July 2016. We searched eleven electronic databases covering health, social care, and social science literature: MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, the Cochrane Library, the Applied Social Sciences Index and Abstracts (ASSIA), Social Science Citation Index, Social Care Online, Health Management Information Consortium (HMIC), Scopus, and the Social Policy and Practice database. The search strategy combined free-text terms and, where available, controlled vocabulary for social prescribing and related concepts (e.g., social prescrib”, community referral”, “link worker”, community navigator”, “health trainer”, “care navigation”) with terms for primary care and general practice. The strategy was developed in MEDLINE with input from an information specialist and subsequently adapted for each database. Filters for study design were deliberately not applied to maximise sensitivity. To identify unpublished and hard-to-locate material, we searched the grey literature using OpenGrey, the websites of relevant organisations (including the King’s Fund, Nesta, the Health Foundation, and the National Council for Voluntary Organisations), and Google, for which the first 100 hits for each of several search strings were screened. We also contacted experts in (17) the field and examined the reference lists of all included studies and of relevant systematic reviews. Forward citation searching of included studies was carried out using Google Scholar. Study selection Records retrieved from the databases were imported into reference management software and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer consulted when consensus could not be reached. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Inter-rater agreement at the title and abstract screening stage was assessed using Cohen’s kappa [5]. The flow of records through the review is presented in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data extraction A standardised data extraction form was piloted on two studies and refined before use. One reviewer extracted data from each included (10) study [21] and a second reviewer checked the extracted data for accuracy and completeness. The following information was collected: author, year, and country, study aims and design; However, setting and funding; description of the SP service (referral pathway, (8) navigator role, duration and intensity of contact, and partner organisations), participant characteristics and sample size; data collection and (4) analysis methods, and reported barriers and [10] facilitators to implementation and delivery. For qualitative studies, we extracted both participant quotations and authors’ interpretations from the results and discussion sections, and for quantitative studies we extracted descriptive findings related to implementation, such as referral and uptake rates, attrition, and staff turnover. Quality appraisal The methodological quality of included studies was assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), Version 2011 [6]. The MMAT was selected because it permits appraisal of (4) qualitative, quantitative (randomised, non-randomised, and descriptive), and mixed-methods designs within a single framework, which suited the diversity of study types anticipated. For each study, two reviewers independently rated the relevant criteria (four criteria per design category, plus two screening questions), and scores were expressed as the percentage of criteria met (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%) [6, 7]. For mixed-methods studies, the overall score was taken as the lowest score across the qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods components, as recommended by the tool developers. Discrepancies were resolved by discussion.

The idea that the loss of one sense is offset by the enhancement of others is deeply rooted in popular culture and has a long history in philosophy and early psychology. Blind individuals are often assumed to have a "sharper" sense of smell, touch, or hearing that helps them navigate a world designed primarily for the sighted. In the olfactory domain, such beliefs are reinforced by anecdotal reports from blind people themselves, who often say they rely on smell to recognize people, locate places, and evaluate food and objects (Wakefield, Homewood, & Taylor, 2004). Olfaction is an especially interesting case because it is a chemical sense with a comparatively weak link to the visual system in everyday behavior, yet it is closely tied to cognition, emotion, and memory Herz & Engen, 1996). If sensory loss triggers compensatory adaptations, olfaction is a plausible candidate. The theoretical basis for such expectations lies in the neuroplasticity literature. In congenitally and early blind individuals, the occipital cortex is not simply silent, it is recruited for a range of non-visual functions, including Braille reading, auditory localization, speech comprehension, and verbal memory Sadato et al., 1996; Röder "et" al., 2002; Amedi et al., 2003; Bedny, 2017). Behavioral studies often report superior performance in blind people on pitch discrimination, sound localization, and tactile acuity, although the findings are not uniform and depend on task demands and the age at which vision was lost (Collignon, Voss, Lassonde, & Lepore, 2009, Wan, Wood, Reutens, & Wilson, 2010). [34] Neuroimaging has also suggested that olfactory stimulation may engage regions beyond the classical olfactory network in blind individuals. Kupers and colleagues (2011), for example, reported activation of occipital areas during odor processing, and Araneda et al. 2016) reported structural and functional differences in olfactory-related regions in early blind participants. Such results indicate that cross-modal reorganization could, in principle, have consequences for olfactory perception. The behavioral evidence, however, is far less consistent. Olfactory function is generally considered to comprise several partly separable components (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997). Lower-level, sensory-driven abilities include the detection threshold, defined as the lowest concentration at which an odorant can be perceived, and odor discrimination, which requires distinguishing between [12] different odorants. Higher-order abilities involve cognitive and linguistic processes and include cued odor identification, in which participants choose a label from a set of alternatives, and free odor identification, in which participants name an odor without help. Performance on the latter tasks depends heavily on semantic memory, verbal ability, and attention, in addition to sensory sensitivity Cain, 1979, Larsson, 1997). A plausible possibility is that blindness could selectively affect some of these components but not others, for example by improving higher-order processing through increased attention to olfactory cues, without altering peripheral sensitivity. Empirical findings do not clearly support either a general or a selective enhancement. Several studies have found lower olfactory thresholds in blind than in sighted participants Cuevas, Plaza, Rombaux, De Volder, & Renier, 2009; Beaulieu-Lefebvre, Schneider, Kupers, & Ptito, 2011), whereas others have found no difference (Smith, Doty, Burlingame, & McKeown, 1993, Rosenbluth, Grossman, & Kaitz, 2000) or even poorer performance in blind individuals (Wakefield et al., 2004). Studies of odor discrimination show a similar pattern: some report an advantage for blind participants (Cuevas et al., 2009), and others report equivalent performance Smith et al., 1993, Sorokowska, Sorokowski, & Karwowski, 2013). The picture for identification is also mixed. Some investigations have shown superior free or cued identification in blind participants (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Cuevas et al., 2009), while others have found no group differences (Smith et al., 1993; Sorokowska et al., 2013). Heterogeneity in methods may partly explain these discrepancies. Studies differ in the psychophysical procedure used (e.g., staircase methods vs. forced-choice batteries), the odorants tested, the criteria for sample selection, and the way blindness is characterized. Moreover, many studies have small samples, which limits statistical power and increases the probability that observed effects, whether positive or null, are unreliable Button et al., 2013). Participant characteristics are a further source of uncertainty. Olfactory function declines with age and differs between women and men, with women often outperforming men on several olfactory measures Doty & Cameron, 2009; Sorokowska et al., 2017). If the age or sex composition of blind and sighted samples differs, or if these factors moderate the effects of sensory deprivation, estimates of group differences could be distorted. Most important, the timing of vision loss may be critical. Plasticity is thought to be greatest during sensitive periods of development, so early or congenitally blind individuals might show larger compensatory effects than those who lose their sight later in life (Voss, Lepore, Gougoux, & Zatorre, 2010, Collignon et al., 2009). Yet studies of olfaction have often combined [32] early and late blind participants, or have not reported onset in sufficient detail, making it difficult to determine whether the timing of blindness matters. Narrative reviews have summarized parts of this literature Sorokowska, 2016, Kupers & Ptito, 2014), and they generally conclude that evidence of superior olfaction in blindness is equivocal. Narrative approaches, however, are [7] vulnerable to selective citation and cannot quantify the magnitude or consistency of effects, nor assess whether the published record is distorted by selective reporting. Publication bias is a particular concern in this field: an intriguing and intuitively appealing finding of superior performance in blind people may be more likely to be published than a null result, which would inflate the apparent evidence for compensation (Rothstein, Sutton, & Borenstein, 2005). Meta-analytic methods allow the combination of effect sizes across studies, the examination of heterogeneity, the testing of moderators, and the application of procedures that detect and adjust for small-study effects (Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Duval & Tweedie, 2000). To our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively synthesized the evidence on olfactory abilities in blind individuals across the full range of olfactory functions. The present work therefore provides a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing blind and sighted individuals on four outcomes: odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification. Our primary question was whether blindness is associated with better olfactory performance, and whether any such effect differs between sensory-driven tasks threshold, discrimination) and higher-order tasks (identification). Because publication bias could influence these estimates, we explicitly assessed and corrected for it. In addition, we conducted exploratory moderator analyses to test whether participants' age, the proportion of women in the samples, and the onset of blindness early vs. late) explain variability in effect sizes across studies. This work contributes in three ways. First, it offers the first comprehensive quantitative estimate of olfactory performance in blindness, replacing impressionistic summaries with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Second, it examines whether the published literature supports the notion of compensatory plasticity in olfaction once bias is taken into account. Third, it identifies methodological gaps, such as small samples and inconsistent reporting, that can guide the design of future research on sensory [10] compensation. Protocol and reporting standards The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher, Liberati, Tetzlaff, & Altman, 2009) and followed recommendations for meta-analysis in the behavioral sciences Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, & Rothstein, 2009; Cooper, Hedges, & Valentine, 2009). The inclusion criteria, outcomes, and the analytic strategy for the primary analyses were specified before data extraction. The analyses [32] of moderators were exploratory. Literature search Relevant articles were identified through a computerized search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO, supplemented by Google Scholar. The search combined terms related to blindness (blind, visual impairment, visual deprivation, visually impaired, anophthalmi, early blind, late blind, congenital blind) with terms related to olfaction (olfact, smell, odor, odour, chemosens, threshold, discrimination, identification). No restrictions on publication year were imposed, and the search covered records from database inception until the date of the final search. We also screened the reference lists of all eligible articles and of relevant narrative reviews, and we searched for conference abstracts and unpublished dissertations to reduce the risk of missing unpublished data. When essential statistics were missing, corresponding authors were [16] contacted by e-mail. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they (a) compared a group of blind participants with a group of sighted controls, (b) assessed at least one of four olfactory outcomes (odor detection threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, or free odor identification), (c) used human participants, and d) reported data sufficient to calculate an effect size (means and standard deviations, t or F statistics, exact p values with sample sizes, or equivalent). Blindness was defined as congenital or acquired total blindness or severe visual impairment, as described by the original authors. Studies were excluded if they lacked a sighted control group, if participants had additional conditions However, known to affect olfaction (e.g., neurodegenerative disease, Kallmann syndrome, head trauma, or chronic rhinosinusitis), if the data were reported only for subjective ratings of odor properties (e.g., intensity, pleasantness) or for olfactory-related tasks that did not map onto the four outcomes, or if the data duplicated those of another included study. Where a sample was reported in more than one article, only the most complete report was retained. Studies in languages other than English were considered if they could be translated. Outcome definitions Odor threshold tasks estimated the lowest concentration at which an odorant (typically n-butanol or phenylethyl alcohol) could be detected, usually through a staircase, forced-choice procedure e.g., Sniffin' Sticks). Discrimination tasks required participants to identify the odd item among three odorants presented in a triangle test. Cued [11] identification required selection of the correct "label" from a list of alternatives typically four), whereas free identification required participants to name the odor without any response options. Because threshold is generally considered a sensory-driven function and identification a higher-order function dependent on semantic and mnemonic processes (Hummel, Sekinger, Wolf, Pauli, & Kobal, 1997), the four outcomes were analyzed separately. Where studies reported more than one measure within an outcome e.g., several odorants or subtests), we averaged them to obtain one effect size per study and comparison. When separate early-blind and late-blind groups were compared with the same sighted group, the shared control group was handled as described below. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third author. Data were extracted independently by two coders using a standardized form, which recorded: authors and year, country, sample size per group, mean age, proportion of women, onset of blindness early/congenital vs. late), olfactory test used, and the statistics necessary to compute effect sizes. Inter-coder agreement was high (Cohen's κ > .90 for categorical variables) and discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Studies were classified as early blind when blindness was congenital or began in early childhood (typically before the age of 5 years, or as defined by the authors), and as late blind otherwise. Effect size computation The effect size was the standardized mean difference, Hedges' g, with positive values indicating better performance in blind than in sighted participants. For threshold tasks, in "which" lower scores reflect higher sensitivity (in studies reporting concentration), the sign was reversed accordingly. For each study, d = Mblind − Msighted) / SDpooled, with SDpooled = √[((n₁ − 1)SD₁² + n₂ − 1)SD₂²) / (n₁ + n₂ − 2)], and the small-sample correction g = d × [1 − 3 / 4(n₁ + n₂) − 9)]. The sampling variance was vg = n₁ + n₂)/(n₁n₂) + g² / (2(n₁ + n₂)) multiplied by the squared correction factor. Patents are among the most systematically recorded outputs of technological activity. They disclose inventions, delimit property rights, and, through their citations, document the lineage of knowledge on which new [27] inventions build (Jaffe & Trajtenberg, 2002). For corporate managers, investors, and policymakers, this record is a primary input to decisions about research and development allocation, mergers and acquisitions, licensing, and technology forecasting. Because the volume of However, patent filings has grown to several million per year worldwide (World Intellectual Property Organization, 2022), manual inspection cannot keep pace, and However, considerable effort has gone into automated methods for scoring and ranking patent documents according to their technological or economic importance. The most established indicators of patent importance are derived from citation counts. Forward citations correlate with the private and social value of an invention (Hall, Jaffe, & Trajtenberg, 2005; Harhoff, Narin, Scherer, & Vopel, 1999), and have been refined into measures that account for technological field and cohort effects. Network-based refinements extend this idea by exploiting the structure of the entire citation graph rather than the number of direct links alone. PageRank (Brin & Page, "1998) [4]" and related eigenvector-type centralities assign higher scores to patents cited by other highly ranked patents, and they have been applied to identify key patents and pivotal technologies (Lukach, Lukach, & Kuperman, 2007; Yan & Ding, 2010). Main path analysis (Hummon & Doreian, 1989; Verspagen, 2007) and measures of disruptiveness (Funk & Owen-Smith, 2017; Wu, Wang, & Evans, 2019) offer further perspectives on how individual inventions shape the trajectory of technological development. Despite their utility, these approaches share a limitation: they are fundamentally static. A ranking score computed at a given time summarizes the accumulated influence of a patent in the past, but it says little about whether the technological domain in which the patent resides is expanding, maturing, or declining. A patent can obtain a high PageRank score because it was central to a field that has since been superseded; conversely, a patent with a modest score may sit at the origin of a rapidly emerging cluster. Because [10] citations accrue with a time lag and are strongly influenced by the life cycle of the technology (Abernathy & Utterback, 1978; Adamson & [36] others, 2012), a static score conflates historical importance with prospective value. For an investor or manager who must decide where to commit resources, the latter is typically the quantity of interest. What is needed is therefore a framework that i) partitions the citation network into coherent technology clusters and ii) forecasts the future However, citation activity of each cluster, thereby characterizing its scale and life-cycle stage. The first requirement concerns community detection. Technology clusters have commonly been identified through modularity maximization (Newman, 2006; Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte, & Lefebvre, 2008), the Infomap algorithm (Rosvall & Bergstrom, 2008), or text-based topic modeling. Modularity-based approaches, however, suffer However, from a resolution limit (Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007), do not rest on an explicit generative model, and offer no principled way to select the number of clusters or to compare competing partitions. The stochastic block model (SBM) addresses these concerns by representing the network as a probabilistic mixture of groups with block-specific connection probabilities (Holland, Laskey, & [28] Leinhardt, 1983; Karrer & Newman, 2011). In its Bayesian, nonparametric formulation, model selection can be performed through minimum description length, which avoids overfitting and infers the number of groups from the data (Peixoto, 2014). The hierarchical "or" nested SBM further organizes groups into a multilevel structure (Peixoto, 2014, 2017), which is attractive for patents because technologies are naturally organized hierarchically, from broad sectors to narrow subfields, as reflected in classification systems such as the International Patent Classification. Although SBMs have been applied extensively to social, biological, and information networks, their use for patent citation networks, and in particular the comparison of flat, degree-corrected, and nested variants on such data, remains limited. The second requirement concerns prediction. Forecasting citation dynamics has attracted growing attention, with models ranging from preferential-attachment and aging mechanisms (Wang, Song, & Barabási, 2013) to machine-learning predictors of future impact (Abrahams, Fan, Wang, Zhang, & Jiang, 2019; Yan, Tang, Liu, Shan, & Li, 2011). Most of this work targets individual documents, for which [2] citation trajectories are sparse, heavy-tailed, and noisy. Aggregating at the level of technology clusters yields smoother and more interpretable time series that reflect "the" collective evolution of a field. Recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory [19] (LSTM) networks [27] in particular (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), are well suited to learning nonlinear temporal dependencies and have shown strong performance in sequence forecasting in economics, energy, and bibliometrics Fischer & Krauss, 2018). Yet, to our knowledge, no study has coupled generative network clustering with deep sequence models to forecast the growth potential of patent clusters, and the extent to which such forecasts are accurate in magnitude and in direction has not been "established." Against this background, [28] this study "addresses" the following research questions. First, which variant of the SBM provides the most appropriate description of patent citation networks, as judged by description length and the interpretability [14] of the inferred partitions? Second, can the growth potential of the resulting technology clusters, defined as the future number of citations received, be predicted [18] by an LSTM network with accuracy sufficient to support managerial and investment decisions? We evaluate prediction quality using both the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), which measures errors in magnitude, and directional accuracy, which measures whether an increase or decrease in citation activity is correctly anticipated and is arguably more relevant for [8] strategic decisions than point accuracy. This paper makes three contributions. First, it proposes an integrated framework that moves patent evaluation from static scoring to dynamic, cluster-level assessment by combining Bayesian community detection with deep sequence learning. Second, it provides empirical evidence that the nested SBM is the most suitable [25] model for clustering patent citation networks, as it captures the multilevel organization of technologies and permits analysis at several scales. Third, it demonstrates that LSTM-based forecasts of cluster growth, although yielding high MAPE values that reflect the volatility of citation counts, attain a directional accuracy exceeding 50%, indicating a modest but practically relevant ability to anticipate whether a technology cluster will expand or contract. Together, these findings offer corporate managers and investors a quantitative means of evaluating the scale and life cycle of technologies, and they identify avenues for improving the forecasting of technological change. We constructed a patent citation network from the PatentsView database maintained by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which provides disambiguated bibliographic records and citation links for utility patents granted from 1976 onwards (Toole et al., 2021). [2] Patents granted between 1976 and 2019 were retained for one technology domain, selected through Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) subclass codes. Each patent was a node, and a directed edge was drawn from a citing patent to each earlier patent it cited. [14] Citations [25] to patents outside the sampled set were discarded. Because the stochastic block model (SBM) assumes a single connected structure, we restricted analysis to the largest weakly connected component. Self-loops and duplicate edges were removed. Citations were treated as unweighted, as multiple citations between the same pair of patents do not occur in the source data. Examiner-added and applicant-added citations were pooled, although we acknowledge that these represent different citing behaviors Alcácer and Gittelman, 2006). Community detection used the SBM, a generative model in which the probability of an edge between two nodes depends only on the groups to which they belong (Holland et al., 1983). We considered three variants. The first was the flat, non-degree-corrected SBM. The second was the degree-corrected SBM (DC-SBM), which adds node-specific propensity parameters to accommodate the heavy-tailed degree distributions typical of citation data Karrer and Newman, 2011). Online reviews have become a central resource for consumers, merchants, and platform operators, and their automatic analysis has driven a large body of work in sentiment analysis, recommendation, and text generation (Pang and Lee 2008, Liu 2012). Most of this work has concentrated on full-length reviews. Many platforms, however, also let users leave tips: short, informal remarks that capture the most salient experience of a visit or purchase, such as "great cocktails, go early for a seat." Tips are typically a single sentence of ten words or fewer. They are written quickly and are easy to read on mobile devices, so they are often the first piece of user-generated text a prospective customer sees. In a sample of Yelp and Foursquare data, tips were on average roughly one-eighth the length of reviews while still conveying a clear evaluative judgment and a specific aspect of the item (Li et al. 2019). Despite this practical value, tips have received much less attention than reviews, and the problem of generating them automatically remains largely unexplored. Generating tips is useful for two reasons. First, it lowers the effort of contributing content. A system that proposes a draft tip tailored to a user and an item can encourage participation, which in turn improves the coverage of items with few reviews. Second, a tip generator can supply concise explanations for recommendations, which improve user trust and decision efficiency Zhang and Chen 2020). Both uses require that the generated text read as if it were written by the particular user about the particular item. A generic sentence such as "good food and service" is fluent and nearly always sentiment-consistent, but it is neither informative nor personal. Prior work on review-related generation has moved toward personalization. Attribute-to-sequence models condition a recurrent decoder on user, item, and rating identifiers to produce reviews (Dong et al. 2017). Explainable recommendation methods generate justifications from aspects or features (Ni and McAuley 2018; [12] Li et al. 2017). Related studies on [4] review summarization and tip generation have used multi-task learning to share representations between rating prediction and text generation (Li et al. 2017; Wang and Ling 2016). These methods generally treat users and items as learned lookup embeddings trained end-to-end with the generation loss. That design has three limitations. First, a deterministic embedding trained for next-word prediction tends to capture the most frequent patterns and neglects the distinctive language habits that define an individual. Second, the same embedding must encode both the user's sentiment preference and the user's writing style, two properties that are only loosely related. Third, rare words that are specific to a user or an item, such as dish names, local idioms, or a reviewer's habitual phrases, are rarely reproduced, because the softmax over a large vocabulary assigns them low probability. We argue that these limitations can be addressed by modeling persona explicitly. We use the term persona to denote the latent characteristics reflected in the historical text associated with an entity. For a user, persona captures an intrinsic language style: preferred vocabulary, level of formality, verbosity, and favored aspects. For an item, persona captures its distinguishing characteristics, such as cuisine, atmosphere, and typical complaints. Persona is more stable than the content of any single review. It is also not the same as sentiment, since two users may share a rating [32] of an item yet describe it very differently. Persona-aware generation therefore requires representations that summarize the full history of tips and reviews for each user and item and that remain useful when the history is noisy and sparse. To obtain such representations, we propose a framework built on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE). A variational auto-encoder (Kingma and Welling 2014) learns a probabilistic latent space in which similar inputs map to nearby regions, and the stochasticity regularizes the representation and reduces overfitting for entities with little data. A known weakness is that the aggregate posterior can diverge from the prior, which "produces" poor samples and weakly informative codes (Bowman et al. 2016). Following the adversarial auto-encoder idea Makhzani et al. 2016), we add a discriminator that pushes the aggregate posterior toward the prior, improving the regularity of the latent space. We train separate aVAE encoders on the historical documents of users and of items, and treat the latent variables as persona embeddings. Latent embeddings are compact but lose lexical detail. We therefore add a persona memory that stores words associated with each user and item, drawn from their histories. During decoding, a Pointer Network Vinyals et al. 2015; See et al. 2017) learns when to copy a word from the memory and when to generate one from the vocabulary. This lets the model produce entity-specific terms without needing high softmax probability for them, and it complements the continuous persona embedding with direct access to the surface forms that characterize each entity. Persona also needs to interact with sentiment. The persona embeddings of a user and an item serve as latent factors in a rating prediction component, similar to matrix factorization (Koren [26] et al. 2009), which estimates the user's sentiment toward the item. The predicted sentiment, together with the persona embeddings, conditions a recurrent neural However, network decoder that generates the tip. Rating prediction thus contributes a supervised signal that aligns the persona space with evaluative preferences, while the generation objective and the memory support stylistic and lexical fidelity. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We formulate persona-aware tips generation as a new task. It requires generated tips to reflect both the language style of the user and the characteristics of the item, in addition to being fluent and sentiment-consistent. 2. We introduce an aVAE-based persona modeling approach that learns latent user and item embeddings from historical tips and reviews, and show that adversarial regularization of the latent space gives more informative persona representations than a standard VAE or deterministic embeddings. 3. We design a persona memory with a Pointer Network that retrieves user- and item-specific words during generation, and integrate it with a rating prediction component and an RNN-based decoder in a single framework that is trained jointly. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets, evaluating the framework with automatic metrics for overlap and diversity, with rating prediction error, and with human judgments, and we analyze each component through ablation studies and case studies. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on review and tip generation, personalized text generation, and latent-variable models. We then describe the framework, present the experimental setup and results, and conclude with a discussion of limitations and directions for future work. Datasets and preprocessing We evaluated the proposed framework on two public review corpora that contain both full-length reviews and short tips: the Yelp Dataset Challenge data (restaurants and services) and the Amazon Product Data for the Books category (McAuley et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2019). Each instance is a tuple of user, item, star rating (1–5), review text, and tip text. Following prior work on tips and review summarization (Li et al., 2017), we removed instances with empty tips, tips shorter than three or longer than 30 tokens, and reviews longer than 300 tokens. To [39] obtain reliable persona signals, we kept only users and items with at least five interactions. After filtering, the Yelp subset contained 213,402 instances (14,871 users, 11,206 items), and the Books subset contained 287,915 instances (18,342 users, 15,630 items). The mean tip length was 11.4 tokens on Yelp and 13.1 on Books. Text was lowercased and tokenized with the NLTK tokenizer. The vocabulary comprised the 20,000 most frequent tokens in each corpus, with other tokens mapped to an unknown symbol. Each dataset was split chronologically per user into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, so that a user's earliest interactions were used for training and persona construction. Persona information for a user or item was built exclusively from training-set reviews and tips. This prevented leakage of test-time text into the persona representations. Users and items without training history were excluded from the test sets. Framework overview The framework has four components: (i) a persona modeling component based on adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE), (ii) a persona memory with [38] a pointer-based retrieval mechanism, (iii) a rating prediction component, and (iv) a recurrent tips generator. All components were trained jointly. Persona modeling with aVAE. For each user u and item i, we concatenated the historical reviews and tips up to 500 tokens, most recent first) into a document d. Words were embedded using 300-dimensional GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) that were fine-tuned during training. A bidirectional GRU encoder (Cho et al., 2014) mapped d to the parameters of a diagonal "Gaussian" posterior q(z|d), and a latent persona vector z of dimension 64 was sampled with the reparameterization trick Kingma & Welling, 2014). A GRU decoder reconstructed the document from z. Because the Kullback–Leibler [32] (KL) term of a standard VAE often causes posterior collapse in text models (Bowman et al., 2016), we replaced it with an adversarial regularizer in the manner of adversarial auto-encoders [15] (Makhzani et al., 2016). "A" discriminator, implemented as a two-layer perceptron with 128 hidden units, was trained to distinguish samples from the prior N(0, I) from encoded posterior samples, while the encoder was trained to fool it (Goodfellow et al., 2014). The resulting aVAE objective was the sum of the reconstruction loss and the adversarial loss. Separate encoders were used for users and items, which yielded user persona embeddings zᵤ and item persona embeddings zᵢ. Persona memory and pointer retrieval. To preserve lexical features that a compact latent code may lose, we constructed a persona memory for every user and item. For each entity, we ranked the words in its history by TF–IDF weight, removed stop words, and stored the 50 highest-scoring words as memory slots. Each slot held the word's embedding. At each decoding step t, the decoder state attended over the concatenated user and item memories (Bahdanau et al., 2015). The attention distribution served as a pointer distribution over memory words (Vinyals et al., 2015). The final output distribution was a mixture of the vocabulary softmax and the pointer distribution, weighted by a learned gate pgen (See et al., 2017; Gulcehre et al., 2016). This design lets the model copy persona-specific wording, such as characteristic expressions of a user or distinctive attributes of an item. Rating prediction. The persona embeddings were [16] used as latent factors in a rating predictor in the spirit of latent factor models Koren et al., 2009). The predicted rating was r̂ = MLP([zᵤ; zᵢ; zᵤ⊙zᵢ]) + bᵤ However, + bᵢ + μ, where μ is the global mean [9] and bᵤ and bᵢ are learned biases. The hidden layer of the MLP is 64-dimensional [32] with ReLU [19] activation. The penultimate layer of this predictor yields a sentiment vector s that summarizes the expected polarity of the user toward the item. The rating loss was the mean squared [27] error against the observed rating. Tips generation. The tips generator was a single-layer GRU with 512 hidden units. Its initial state was a linear projection of [zᵤ; zᵢ, s]. At each step, the input was the concatenation of the previous word embedding and the same persona-sentiment vector, which helps keep the generated text consistent with the persona and the predicted sentiment. Generation was trained with teacher forcing and token-level cross-entropy over the mixed vocabulary and pointer distribution. The total loss was L = Lgen + λ₁Lrating + λ₂LaVAE. We set λ₁ = 0.5 and λ₂ = 0.1 based on validation performance. At inference time we used beam search [35] with width 4 and a length penalty, and forbade repeated trigrams.
