1. Introduction The past fifteen years have seen the rise of a family of data-processing systems built around the map-shuffle-reduce paradigm. Dean and Ghemawat (2004) showed that a large class of computations could be expressed as a pair of user-supplied functions, with a runtime responsible for partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance, and data movement. Open-source implementations, most prominently Hadoop (White, 2012), brought this abstraction to organizations that could not build such infrastructure themselves. Later systems such as Spark (Zaharia et al., 2012) relaxed the rigid two-stage structure and added in-memory caching. Even so, they kept the central premise that data are gathered into large, bounded collections, partitioned across a cluster, and processed in coarse passes. The approach has been successful for good reasons. It makes horizontal scaling accessible, hides distributed-systems complexity behind a small programming interface, and tolerates commodity hardware failures. The success of the paradigm has also had less technical causes. The term "Big Data" has acquired considerable value for vendors, investors, and clients, and it is often adopted as a marker of organizational modernity rather than as the result of a requirements analysis [7] (Boyd and Crawford, 2012). Surveys of production workloads suggest that the problems being solved are frequently much smaller than the infrastructure applied to them. Appuswamy et al. (2013) observed that the median job size in several large analytics deployments fits comfortably in the memory of a single server, and McSherry et al. (2015) showed that a carefully written single-threaded program can outperform a cluster of machines on common graph benchmarks. These findings do not diminish the real capabilities of map-reduce systems on truly massive and unstructured datasets. They do indicate that popularity is a poor proxy for suitability, and that the default choice of a batch-oriented cluster framework deserves scrutiny. This scrutiny matters most for a category of problems we call time-dependent and boundable. In these problems, the answer required at a given moment depends on data arriving continuously, the relevance of any datum decays or is limited to a window, and the result of a computation can be bounded, approximated, or cached without loss of practical value. Examples include monitoring and alerting, fraud scoring, recommendation freshness, sensor aggregation, and operational dashboards. For such problems, the batch model introduces structural inefficiencies. Data must be accumulated before processing, so latency is bounded below by the batch interval. The shuffle phase moves intermediate data across the network even when the result of earlier computations could be reused. Each run recomputes over a mostly unchanged history, because the model has no natural notion of persistent, incrementally updated state. Practitioners have responded with workarounds, such as shorter batch intervals, micro-batching (Zaharia et al., 2013), and the lambda architecture, which maintains parallel batch and speed layers (Marz and Warren, 2015). These patterns reduce latency but at the price of duplicated logic, operational complexity, and consistency problems between layers (Kreps, 2014). A parallel line of work has approached the problem from the stream-processing side. Early data stream management systems (Babcock et al., 2002) and later systems such as Storm, Flink, and MillWheel (Akidau et al., 2013; Carbone et al., 2015) treat data as unbounded sequences and support windowing, event-time semantics, and managed state. The dataflow model of Akidau et al. (2015) unified batch and streaming under one formalism. These contributions are significant, but they tend to retain much of the architecture of the systems they replace: a cluster runtime, a partitioned and often shuffled keyed state, and checkpointing machinery designed for very large state. For workloads in which state is [16] small or can be bounded, this machinery may be disproportionate. Moreover, the programming abstractions typically remain tied to operators over distributed collections rather than to simple, composable functions over flows. The gap we address lies between these "two" bodies of work. Batch frameworks are simple but ill-suited to time-dependent problems, while general streaming engines are expressive but heavy; and neither exploits systematically the fact that many practical computations are bounded and cacheable. What is lacking is a processing model that treats statelessness as the default, confines state to explicit, bounded, and cacheable locations, and expresses computation as flows of data through functions, thereby avoiding the global redistribution step that defines the shuffle. Such a model would also have to retain the properties that made map-reduce attractive: a small programming interface, predictable scaling, and straightforward recovery from failure. This paper therefore asks the following research question: can a partly stateless, flow-oriented function and data model replace the map-shuffle-reduce model for time-dependent, boundable "problems," delivering lower latency and lower resource consumption without sacrificing scalability or ease of programming? We break this into However, three subquestions. First, under what formal conditions on time dependence and boundedness does a computation admit a flow-oriented decomposition that needs no shuffle? Second; how should state and caching be represented so that functions remain [35] composable and recoverable? Third, how does the resulting model compare empirically with batch and streaming baselines? The paper makes the following "contributions." First, we characterize the [32] class of However, time-dependent, boundable problems and [15] argue, with reference to published workload analyses, that it covers a substantial share of practical analytics tasks currently handled by batch systems. [29] Second, we present a flow-oriented model in which computations are partly stateless functions composed along data flows, with explicitly scoped caches that replace the shuffle and the recomputation of history. Third, we show how this model supports incremental updates and failure recovery by means of replayable inputs and bounded state. Fourth, we evaluate an implementation against [11] map-reduce and streaming baselines on representative workloads, reporting latency, throughput, and resource cost. We also discuss the limits of the approach, including the problem classes for which map-reduce remains the more appropriate choice. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in more detail, Section 3 presents the model, Section 4 describes the implementation and evaluation, and Section 5 discusses implications and concludes. Overview [27] and Design Rationale We designed a flow-oriented processing model, referred to here as Fast Data Flow (FDF), [34] and compared it empirically with a conventional map-shuffle-reduce implementation. The design follows from three premises. First, many time-dependent workloads have solutions that are bounded, meaning the relevant state at time t depends only on a finite window of recent events, or cacheable, meaning that previously computed results can be reused when inputs recur (Akidau et al., 2015). Second, batch-oriented map-shuffle-reduce (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008) pays fixed costs for materializing intermediate data and redistributing keys across the network, and these costs are unnecessary when state can be kept [39] local and partial results [13] combined incrementally. Third, functions that are stateless However, with respect to the global dataset, while retaining small, bounded local state, permit pipelined execution and straightforward horizontal scaling (Carbone et al., 2015). The study was therefore structured as a controlled comparison of architectures on identical workloads, hardware, and input streams. Model Specification FDF represents a computation as a directed acyclic graph of operators. Each operator is a function f: (e, s) → (E', s'), where e is an input event, s is a bounded local state, E' is a (possibly [8] empty) set of output events, and s' is the updated state. State is limited to one of three forms: (a) a sliding or tumbling time window of fixed duration W, (b) a fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache of size C keyed by a deterministic function of the event, or (c) a constant-size accumulator for associative and commutative aggregates. Operators are partitioned by a stable hash of the event key, and events are routed directly to the owning partition, eliminating the global shuffle barrier. Partial results from partitions are merged using commutative monoid operations (Boykin et al., 2014), allowing late or out-of-order events within an allowed lateness bound L to be incorporated without recomputation. Events beyond L are diverted to a side output for optional offline reconciliation. Backpressure is propagated through bounded queues between operators, and fault tolerance is provided by periodic asynchronous snapshots of local state using a barrier-based algorithm (Chandy & Lamport, 1985; Carbone et al., 2017). Baseline Systems The baseline was an Apache Hadoop MapReduce implementation and an Apache Spark batch implementation (Zaharia et al., 2012) of each workload, with micro-batch intervals of 1, 5, and 30 seconds for the Spark Streaming variant. A Flink-based implementation of FDF operators served as the runtime for the proposed model, so that differences reflect model semantics rather than language runtimes. All implementations were written in Java 11 and used the same serialization format (Apache Avro) and identical business logic classes wherever possible. Workloads and Data Three workloads were selected to represent time-dependent problems with bounded or cacheable solutions. W1 was a sliding-window aggregation (per-key mean, 95th percentile via a t-digest sketch (Dunning & Ertl, 2019), and count) over sensor telemetry. W2 was a session and recurrence-detection task in which repeated inputs allow cache hits, modeled on clickstream enrichment. W3 was a streaming join between an event stream and a slowly changing reference table. To test the limits of applicability, we added W4, a global computation (full-corpus inverted index construction) for which bounded state is not sufficient, expected to favor map-reduce. Input data combined a public dataset and synthetic streams. Real data comprised the NYC Taxi trip records for 2019 (approximately 84 million events) and a public web clickstream sample. Synthetic generators produced events with key cardinalities of 10^3, 10^5, and 10^7, with Zipfian key skew (exponent s = 0.8 and 1.2) to emulate realistic hot keys (Breslau et al., 1999). Arrival rates ranged from 10,000 to 1,000,000 events per second. For W2, the repetition rate (the proportion of events whose result had been computed within the cache horizon) was varied from 0% to 90% in increments of 10%. Out-of-order arrival was injected by delaying a random 5% of events by up to 60 seconds. Experimental Environment Experiments ran on a cluster of 12 identical nodes (16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM, NVMe storage, 10 Gbit/s network). One node ran coordination services and the load generator; ten nodes were workers. Scaling experiments used 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 workers. JVM settings, garbage collector (G1), and operating system parameters were fixed across systems, and caches were cleared between runs. Procedures and Metrics Each configuration was run for 30 minutes after a 5-minute warm-up, and repeated 10 times with different random seeds. Primary metrics were end-to-end latency (event time to result emission; median, 95th, and 99th percentiles), sustained throughput (maximum rate with bounded queue growth); and resource efficiency (CPU-seconds and bytes shuffled per million events). Secondary metrics were result accuracy and recovery time. Accuracy was measured against an exact offline computation, using relative error for aggregates and the Jaccard similarity for set outputs. Recovery time was measured by terminating one worker at a random point and recording time until output latency returned to within 10% of its pre-failure median. For batch systems, latency was defined as the delay from event time to the completion of the job containing that event, with jobs launched at the same intervals as the micro-batches. Statistical Analysis Because latency distributions are heavy-tailed, we report medians and percentiles and avoid reliance on means. Differences between systems for each configuration were tested with the Mann–Whitney U test, with effect sizes expressed as Cliff's delta and 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap resampling with 10,000 replicates (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). Non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, [15] chronic respiratory disease and cancer, account for roughly 70% of deaths worldwide, and the burden is increasingly concentrated in low- and However, middle-income countries (World Health Organization, 2018). Primary care is widely regarded as the setting best placed to deliver [1] However, the continuous, coordinated and person-centred care that chronic conditions require, and it is central to global strategies for universal health coverage (Starfield et al., 2005; Kruk et al., 2018). [19] Consequently, a large number of interventions have [25] been developed to improve the detection, management and long-term support of people with NCDs in primary care. These include structured self-management education, decision support for clinicians, task-shifting to nurses and community health workers, audit and feedback, and multicomponent models of integrated care (Wagner et al., 2001, Coleman et al., 2009). Many of these have been evaluated in randomised controlled trials (RCTs), and systematic reviews of such trials suggest that effects are frequently [34] modest and [20] heterogeneous, with similar interventions producing markedly different results [5] in different settings (Smith et al., 2016, Tricco et al., 2012). This heterogeneity is not surprising. Interventions in primary care are typically complex: they contain several interacting components, target multiple levels (patients, providers, practices and organisations), require tailoring to local circumstances, and depend on the behaviour of many actors (Craig et al., 2008; Hawe et al., 2004). Their effects are shaped by the context in which they are delivered, including the structure and financing of the health system, workforce availability, and local social and cultural norms Pfadenhauer et al., 2017). A conventional trial that reports only whether an intervention "worked" on average cannot explain why an effect was or was not observed, whether [17] the intervention was delivered as intended, which components were responsible for any change, or how the findings might transfer to other settings. Null results are particularly difficult to interpret without this information, since they may reflect a flawed intervention theory, poor implementation, or an unsuitable context (Oakley et al., 2006). Process evaluations (PEs) have been advocated to address these limitations. The UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions defines their purpose as examining implementation (what is delivered, and how), mechanisms of impact (how delivered activities produce change), and contextual factors that shape both (Moore et al., 2015). By answering questions of for whom, how and why interventions have an impact, PEs help distinguish implementation failure from theory failure, identify unintended consequences, and provide the information needed to refine interventions and support scale-up. Earlier frameworks for describing implementation, including those of Steckler and Linnan (2002), Baranowski and Stables (2000) and Grant et al. 2013), and widely used theory-based approaches such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (Damschroder et al., 2009), normalisation process theory May and Finch, 2009) and RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 1999), have similarly [7] emphasised the need to examine reach, fidelity, dose and adaptation alongside outcomes. The MRC guidance further stresses that PEs should be underpinned by a clearly articulated intervention theory or logic [18] model, so that data collection and analysis are directed at the hypothesised causal pathway rather than being purely descriptive (Moore et al., 2015, De Silva et al., 2014). Despite this guidance, there is concern that PEs are [18] inconsistently conducted and reported. Reviews in other fields, such as school-based health promotion and public health, have found that PEs often lack explicit theoretical grounding, apply inconsistent definitions of constructs such as fidelity and context, and rely on convenience samples or purely descriptive data Oakley et al., 2006, Bonell et al., 2012, Grant et al., 2013). Where theory is absent, it is difficult to judge whether the right processes were examined, and findings from one PE are hard to compare with, or build upon, those of another. Improvements in reporting have been proposed, including the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) and the TIDieR checklist for describing interventions (Pinnock et al., 2017; Hoffmann et al., 2014), but it is unclear how far these have influenced practice in primary care. Several existing syntheses bear on this topic but leave important gaps. Systematic reviews of barriers and facilitators to implementing chronic disease interventions have mostly drawn on qualitative studies or on single conditions, for example diabetes self-management or hypertension control, and have [19] not examined how the underlying evaluations were designed (Gagliardi et al., 2011, Jeet et al., 2017). Reviews of PEs, in contrast, have concentrated on public health, school or community settings, where the organisational features of primary care, such as gatekeeping, multidisciplinary teams, continuity of care and payment systems, are less salient. To our knowledge, no review has systematically described the methods used in PEs conducted alongside RCTs of primary care interventions for NCDs, assessed the extent to which they follow recognised guidance, and synthesised their findings on implementation barriers and facilitators across conditions and health systems. This matters because primary care interventions are increasingly being adapted for and tested in diverse settings, including low-resource health systems where many of the assumptions underpinning interventions developed in high-income countries may not hold Kruk et al., 2018; Legido-Quigley et al., 2013). We therefore conducted a systematic review of PEs alongside RCTs of primary care interventions aimed at improving outcomes for people with NCDs, using the MRC guidance for process evaluation as an organising framework. We had two aims. First, to describe and appraise the methods used, including the use of intervention theory and theoretical frameworks, the choice of data collection and analytic approaches, sampling, and the integration of qualitative and quantitative data. Second, to synthesise the principal findings of these evaluations regarding barriers and facilitators to implementation, with attention to the context in which interventions were delivered. This review makes three contributions. It provides the first comprehensive overview of how PEs in primary care chronic disease research are being designed and reported, identifying strengths and weaknesses that can inform methodological practice and the application of the MRC guidance. It offers a cross-condition synthesis of recurring implementation challenges, which may be more useful to intervention developers and health system decision-makers than condition-specific accounts. Finally, it draws out implications for how future interventions should be developed, with the aim of improving the fit between interventions, local needs and health system contexts, and thereby the chance that effective interventions can be implemented and sustained at scale. Design and reporting We conducted a systematic review of process evaluations (PEs) conducted alongside randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of primary care interventions for non-communicable diseases. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO CRD42016035572) before screening began. The review is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). We used the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) guidance on process evaluation of complex interventions (Moore et al., 2015) as an organising framework for both data extraction and appraisal. This guidance specifies that a PE should describe the intervention and its causal assumptions, examine implementation (fidelity, dose, adaptations and reach), explore mechanisms of impact, and consider contextual influences on delivery and outcomes. Because we did not assess intervention effectiveness, we did not conduct a meta-analysis. Eligibility criteria Eligibility was defined using the Population, Intervention, Context and Study design elements. Studies were eligible if they reported a PE, defined as a study that assessed implementation, mechanisms of impact or context, alongside an RCT (individually or cluster randomised, including pilot and feasibility trials with a full-scale PE). The trial intervention had to be delivered in primary care or community-based primary health care settings and aim to improve outcomes for patients with non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, cancer, mental health conditions and musculoskeletal disorders. Interventions could be targeted at patients, providers, practices or the wider health system. We excluded studies of infectious diseases, those conducted solely in hospital or specialist settings, trials with no PE component, and PEs reported only as protocols without results. Studies that reported only a post hoc satisfaction survey, with no examination of implementation or context, were also excluded. The PE did not need to be published in the same paper as the trial, but it had to be clearly linked to an identified RCT. We included reports in any language for which translation was feasible, and the search was restricted to 1998 onward, reflecting the emergence of the contemporary complex intervention literature (Campbell et al., 2000). Search strategy We searched MEDLINE, SCOPUS, PsycINFO, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature CINAHL), EMBASE and Global Health from 1998 to June 2018. The strategy combined three concept blocks: (1) process evaluation terms (for example process evaluation”, “implementation”, fidelity, “mixed methods”, “qualitative”), 2) primary care terms for example primary health care”, general practice”, community health worker”, “family practice”), and (3) non-communicable disease terms, together with a trial filter to identify randomised designs. Search terms were developed with an information specialist, piloted against a set of known PEs, and adapted to the syntax and controlled vocabulary of each database. We supplemented electronic searches by hand-searching the reference lists of included studies and of relevant methodological reviews, and by checking trial registries and linked publications to identify companion papers reporting PE findings. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and de-duplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria, followed by independent full-text assessment. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with a third reviewer adjudicating where consensus could not be reached. Agreement between reviewers at the full-text stage was calculated using Cohen’s kappa: κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the proportion expected by chance. Reasons for exclusion at full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form, structured around the MRC framework and piloted on five studies, was used. Two reviewers independently extracted data and a third reviewer checked a random sample (approximately 20%) of extractions for accuracy and consistency as quality assurance. Extracted information included: bibliographic details; country and income setting World Bank classification), clinical condition; description of the intervention using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) items (Hoffmann et al., 2014), level of intervention (patient, provider, practice or system); trial design, and the timing of the PE relative to the trial concurrent, prospective or retrospective). For PE methods, we extracted whether the authors stated an explicit intervention theory or logic model, whether an existing theoretical or implementation framework was used (for example the Normalisation Process Theory, the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, RE-AIM, or the Theoretical Domains Framework); the PE research questions, the components assessed (context, recruitment and reach, fidelity, dose, adaptation, mechanisms of impact, and unintended consequences), data collection methods (interviews, focus groups, observation, surveys, document review, routine data and audio-recorded consultations), sampling strategy and sample size; the respondents included; analytic approach; and whether qualitative and quantitative data were triangulated or integrated. We also recorded whether the PE findings were used to interpret trial outcomes. For findings, [7] we extracted all reported barriers and facilitators to implementation, together with the authors’ interpretations and illustrative data, where available. These were extracted from the results and discussion sections, including participant quotations. Quality and reporting appraisal Rather than excluding studies on quality grounds, we appraised [19] the methodological characteristics of PEs against the MRC guidance to describe the field and to identify strengths and weaknesses. Criteria included clarity of intervention theory, a priori specification of PE questions, appropriateness of sampling, use of multiple data sources, transparent analysis, and consideration of context. Qualitative components were additionally assessed with reference to the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme CASP) qualitative checklist, with the aim of contextualising the weight placed on individual findings rather than determining inclusion. Appraisal was carried out independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Data synthesis We conducted [17] a two-part synthesis. First, the methodological data were summarised descriptively using frequencies and proportions, stratified by country income group, intervention level and whether a theoretical framework had been used. Lactococcus lactis is the principal component of the mesophilic starter cultures used worldwide in the manufacture of cheese and other fermented dairy products. Starter bacteria are responsible for the rapid conversion of lactose into lactic acid, which controls spoilage and pathogenic microbiota, drives curd formation and syneresis, and contributes to the development of texture and flavor (Smid and Kleerebezem 2014). Besides acidification, L. lactis contributes to flavor through proteolytic and peptidolytic activities, amino acid catabolism, and the production of diacetyl, acetoin and other volatile compounds derived from citrate and pyruvate metabolism Smit et al. 2005; Cocaign-Bousquet et al. 2002). The success of a dairy fermentation therefore depends on the viability and metabolic activity of the starter, and strains must withstand a sequence of stresses, first during starter production, concentration and storage (freezing, freeze-drying, cold storage), and later during cheese manufacture heat, osmotic, acid and oxidative stress) van de Guchte et al. 2002, Papadimitriou et al. 2016). Oxidative stress is one of the least appreciated but most pervasive of these challenges. Although L. lactis is aerotolerant, it lacks a complete respiratory chain unless exogenous heme is supplied, and it possesses a limited set of defenses against reactive oxygen species (ROS) Duwat et al. 2001). In the presence of oxygen, flavoprotein oxidases such as NADH oxidase, together with pyruvate oxidase and other enzymes, generate hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, which damage DNA, proteins and membrane lipids and cause growth arrest and loss of viability (Rochat et al. 2006). Milk is aerated during handling, and oxygen is introduced during pumping, stirring and vat filling, while the large-scale propagation of starters is frequently carried out under non-anaerobic conditions. Oxygen also influences the metabolic fate of pyruvate, diverting flux from lactate towards acetate, acetoin and diacetyl, with implications for flavor (Lan et al. 2006). Strains with improved oxygen tolerance are thus of practical interest, as they could display more consistent performance in industrial environments and might provide an additional route to modulate aroma formation. Cultivation under respiratory conditions, i.e. in the presence of heme and oxygen, improves biomass yield and robustness (Duwat et al. 2001, Pedersen et al. 2012), but it requires specific process modifications and is not applicable to all dairy applications. Strain improvement in food microorganisms is constrained by regulation and consumer perception, and genetically modified organisms are not widely accepted in the dairy sector. Consequently, non-recombinant approaches such as spontaneous mutant selection and adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) are attractive alternatives (Bachmann et al. 2012). ALE exploits the capacity of bacteria to acquire beneficial mutations under sustained selective pressure, and it has been used to improve industrially relevant traits in lactic acid bacteria, including acid and thermal tolerance, osmotolerance, growth in specific substrates, and bacteriophage resistance (Derkx et al. 2014; Zhu et al. 2020). A [16] particularly interesting feature of this approach is that selection under one stress frequently results in cross-protection against other stresses, as a result of the overlap in cellular responses and of global regulatory changes (Mols and Abee 2011). Selecting for a trait that depends on a global physiological response, such as the integrity and remodeling of the cell envelope, could therefore be a way to obtain strains with generally more robust phenotypes. The cell envelope is the first barrier against environmental insults, and its stress response is well characterized in L. lactis. Envelope-targeting agents trigger the CesSR and other two-component systems, which induce a regulon that includes genes involved in cell wall biosynthesis, modification of the envelope and protein quality control Martínez et al. 2007; Roces et al. 2012). Lcn972 is a non-lantibiotic bacteriocin produced by L. lactis IPLA972 that inhibits cell wall biosynthesis in sensitive lactococci by binding to lipid II, the cell wall precursor, at the septum, thereby impairing septum formation and cell division Martínez et al. 1996; Martínez et al. 2008; Roces et al. 2009). Its [33] [39] narrow spectrum, restricted to L. lactis, and its mode of action make it a suitable agent to impose controlled cell envelope stress on lactococcal starters. Previous work has shown that the response to Lcn972 involves the CesSR system, the overexpression of the stress-inducible protein encoded by the lcn972 resistance-associated locus, and the activation of genes of unknown function, and that spontaneous resistant mutants carry mutations affecting sugar metabolism, in particular the phosphotransferase system component ptnD, as well as other envelope-related genes (Roces et al. 2012; Kramer et al. 2008; Tymoszewska et al. 2017). Notably, resistance to Lcn972 in mutants of the laboratory strain L. lactis IPLA947 or its derivatives has been linked to [16] altered growth, cell wall properties and metabolic regulation, which in turn may influence how cells handle other stresses (Roces et al. 2012). Whether resistance to cell wall-active bacteriocins can be harnessed to improve technological robustness of an industrial starter has not been explored. The strain L. [34] lactis IPLA947 is a well-characterized, phage-resistant dairy starter used in the manufacture of artisanal and industrial cheeses, with good acidifying properties and a genome that has been sequenced and annotated (Rodríguez-Alonso et al. 2009, Flórez et al. 2016). Given its industrial relevance, it is an appropriate model on which to test whether cell envelope stress-driven adaptive evolution may generate variants with enhanced technological traits. Importantly, any improvement in stress tolerance must not come at the expense of the core functions of the starter, namely rapid acidification, a stable lactose-to-lactate conversion and an adequate contribution to flavor. Trade-offs between stress resistance and growth, which are well described for mutants affected in global regulators or in carbon catabolite control (Ferenci 2016), can render stress-tolerant variants useless for dairy applications. In this work, we applied adaptive evolution under cell envelope stress by consecutive exposure of L. lactis IPLA947 to increasing doses of Lcn972, and we screened the resulting derivatives for cross-protection against oxidative stress. We hypothesized that resistance to this envelope-active bacteriocin [28] would select for variants with modified envelope physiology and/or metabolic regulation that [19] would confer a more robust phenotype in the presence of oxygen. We characterized [2] the selected mutant, L. lactis R5, regarding its survival after hydrogen peroxide challenge, its growth in aerobic and respiratory conditions, and its tolerance to the stresses encountered during starter production and storage, namely cold storage and freeze-drying. We then evaluated its performance as a dairy starter in aerated milk cultures, its acidification kinetics, its lactose consumption and organic acid production, and the profile [30] of volatile compounds in experimental cheese curds. Our results show that Lcn972 resistance can be used to obtain a stable, oxygen-tolerant derivative that retains the technological properties of the parental strain and displays an "enhanced" capacity to produce acetoin, supporting the use of cell envelope "stress" as a driver of intra-strain diversification in industrial lactococci. Presence-absence data, in which a binary matrix records which species occur at which sites, are among the most common data types in community ecology and biogeography. A recurrent question is whether such a matrix exhibits structure that would not be expected by chance. Examples include nestedness, where the species found at species-poor sites tend to form subsets of those found at richer sites Patterson and Atmar 1986, Almeida-Neto et al. 2008), checkerboard patterns suggestive of competitive exclusion (Diamond 1975; Stone and Roberts 1990); and co-occurrence more generally Gotelli 2000). Because the matrix summaries used to quantify these patterns, such as the NODF or temperature metrics, have no natural scale, their values are almost always interpreted relative to a null distribution obtained by randomizing the data. The credibility of the resulting conclusions thus depends on [30] how well the null model represents the "no pattern" hypothesis. Null models for presence-absence matrices differ mainly in which features of the observed data they preserve. Unconstrained models treat all cells as exchangeable and are well known to produce inflated type I error rates, because the observed matrix has heterogeneous species prevalences and site richnesses that by themselves induce nestedness-like structure Gotelli and Graves 1996; Wright et al. 1998). The dominant response has been to preserve the row and column sums of the observed matrix, giving the so-called fixed-fixed model (Connor and Simberloff 1979; Gotelli 2000). Fixed-fixed randomization has become something of a default: it is implemented in widely used software (e.g., Oksanen et al. 2022), is recommended in several methodological comparisons because it keeps type I error low in simulation studies (Gotelli 2000; Ulrich and Gotelli 2007), and has been applied in hundreds of studies of nestedness and co-occurrence. Computationally, sampling uniformly from the set of binary matrices with given margins is not trivial, and a considerable literature has developed on the Curveball, swap, and sequential importance sampling algorithms and on their mixing properties (Snijders 1991, Miklós and Podani 2004; Strona et al. 2014; Carstens 2015, Verhelst 2008; Chen et al. 2005). Less attention has been paid to the statistical meaning of conditioning on both margins. In a fixed-fixed model, the row and column sums are treated as known constants rather than as quantities subject to random variation. This is a strong assumption. Species richness at a site and prevalence of a species are themselves outcomes of the ecological and sampling processes that one wishes to study, and nestedness is directly related to the distribution of the margins: a perfectly nested matrix is fully determined by its margins. Consequently, for many empirical matrices the set of matrices sharing the observed margins is small, and in extreme cases it may be a single matrix, so that no randomization is possible at all (Fulkerson and Ryser 1962, Gale 1957). Even when that set is not trivially small, it can be tightly clustered in terms of the test statistic, so that the observed matrix is either typical by construction or, if it deviates, appears extreme relative to an artificially narrow reference distribution. We refer to this phenomenon as limited randomizability. Related concerns have been voiced in the ecological literature, where it has been noted that fixed-fixed models may remove part of the very signal of interest and so show reduced power (Ulrich and Gotelli 2007; Gotelli and Ulrich 2012), but the converse risk, that conclusions of significance become overly optimistic, has received little systematic study. A natural alternative is to relax the However, margin constraints and let row and column sums vary around their observed values, thereby preserving them only in expectation. Several such models exist. The fixed-equiprobable and equiprobable-equiprobable models use only a subset of margin information [34] Gotelli 2000), and proportional models sample cells with probabilities that depend on observed margins. Many of these are ad hoc, and it is not obvious in which statistical sense they reproduce the margins or what probabilistic model of the data they represent. In contrast, the psychometric and ecological literatures offer principled parametric models in which each cell is an independent Bernoulli variable whose probability depends on a row effect and a column effect. The Rasch model Rasch 1960) is the canonical example, a logistic model with one parameter per site and one per species. It has been used to describe species-site data (ter Braak et al. 2003, Ulrich et al. 2009), and is closely related to the maximum-entropy distribution on binary matrices with margins fixed in expectation, the exponential random graph or β-model familiar from network analysis (Chatterjee et al. 2011). The Rasch model offers sound statistical properties, including well-understood estimation by conditional or marginal maximum likelihood (Andersen 1970), diagnostics for goodness of fit, and the fact that fixed-fixed randomization is exactly the conditional distribution of the Rasch model given its sufficient statistics, the margins. This last property places fixed-fixed models and Rasch models in a common framework and suggests that their differences can be understood as the difference between conditioning on, and averaging over, the margins. Despite these connections, to our knowledge, the practical consequences of choosing between strictly constrained and relaxed null models have not been systematically compared on empirical presence-absence data with attention to the reliability of the resulting significance statements. Existing comparisons have focused largely on type I error and power in synthetic matrices generated from specific mechanisms, rather than on the behavior of the null models themselves when applied to real data sets whose margins differ greatly in how much freedom they leave. This paper addresses that gap. Our research questions are: (i) how severely do the margin constraints of fixed-fixed models limit the randomizability of real presence-absence matrices, (ii) can Rasch models serve as a statistically principled alternative with relaxed constraints for assessing nestedness and related statistics; and (iii) how do significance measures obtained from the two families of models compare in practice? The contributions are as follows. First, we analyze the properties of fixed-fixed models, showing "how" the size and structure of the set of matrices with given margins constrain the null distribution, and we quantify limited randomizability on a collection of empirical data sets. Second, we present Rasch models as a null model for presence-absence data, describe their estimation and sampling, and discuss their [13] relationship to fixed-fixed models. Third, we compare the models empirically and find, surprisingly, that fixed-fixed models yield unreasonably optimistic measures of statistical significance, with extremely small p-values for observed structure that appears unremarkable under relaxed models. This result gives practical insight into the consequences of limited randomizability and cautions against treating fixed-fixed models as a uniformly conservative default. Row sums are ri = Σj xij and column sums are cj = Σi xij. Rows and columns with sum 0 or m (respectively n) carry no information under the models below and were removed before [39] analysis. Arabic is spoken by more than 400 million people and is the liturgical language of nearly two billion Muslims, and it has one of the longest continuous written records of any living language (Versteegh, 2014). Its earliest extended attestations, the Qur'anic text and pre-Islamic poetry, date to the sixth and seventh centuries CE. Since then it has been used for scripture, law, philosophy, science, historiography, belles-lettres, and, in the modern period, journalism and digital communication. Over this span the language has been shaped by conquest and migration, by contact with Persian, Turkish, Aramaic, and European languages, by the codification efforts of medieval grammarians, and by nineteenth- and twentieth-century modernization (Owens, 2006; Holes, 2004). Despite this record, the history of written Arabic is still described mostly in broad qualitative terms. The standard account distinguishes Classical Arabic, the codified literary language of the early Islamic centuries, from Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), the written and formal register that emerged with the Nahḍa (the Arabic cultural revival) and the rise of the modern press (Badawi, 1973; Versteegh, 2014). Intermediate stages are often invoked, including Post-Classical or Middle Arabic, but their boundaries and linguistic content are contested (Lentin, 2008, Owens, 2006). The picture is complicated by diglossia, the coexistence of a prestigious written standard with unwritten colloquial varieties (Ferguson, 1959). Because many writers deviated from the standard, either unintentionally or by choice, texts mix registers in ways that resist simple classification. Most evidence for these accounts comes from close reading of selected manuscripts, authors, or genres. Such analyses are valuable, but they are small in scale and may not generalize across the full range of the written record. They also depend on the analyst's prior assumptions about where period boundaries lie. Computational methods could test such claims at scale. Diachronic corpora and statistical methods have transformed the study of English, German, French, and other languages. Examples include large-scale analyses of lexical change in digitized books (Michel et al., 2011), distributional models of semantic shift (Hamilton et al., 2016; Kutuzov et al., 2018), and data-driven approaches to periodization (Gries & Hilpert, 2008; Tahmasebi et al., 2021). The Arabic NLP community has built a substantial infrastructure of its own, including morphological analyzers and disambiguators (Habash, 2010, Pasha et al., 2014), open toolkits (Obeid et al., 2020), pretrained language models (Antoun et al., 2020, Inoue et al., 2021), and dialectal resources (Bouamor et al., 2018). Corpora such as Arabic Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011), ArTenTen (Arts et al., 2014), and the King Saud University Corpus of Classical Arabic (Alrabiah et al., 2013) have supported much of this work. However, this effort has concentrated almost entirely on contemporary written Arabic, namely news and web text in MSA, and on the spoken dialects (Zaghouani, 2017). Where historical text has been used, it has usually been treated as a single "Classical" block, often to evaluate the transfer of tools built for MSA (Belinkov et al., 2016). To our knowledge, no existing resource or study treats the Arabic written record as a continuous diachronic object spanning the full 1400 years of its history. The raw material for such a study exists. Large-scale digitization by library projects, volunteer initiatives, and OCR pipelines has produced collections of premodern Arabic texts, such as the OpenITI corpus (Nigst et al., 2020) and the Shamela digital library, as well as contemporary archives. These collections were assembled for retrieval and philological use rather than linguistic analysis, and they [30] pose several problems for a quantitative history of the language. Their metadata are inconsistent, and dates of authorship [16] are often approximate or uncertain. Texts contain OCR and transcription errors, editorial apparatus, and modern commentary interleaved with the historical text. Perhaps most importantly, Arabic scholarly culture relied heavily on quotation, paraphrase, compilation, and commentary, so a large share of the text in any collection is reused from earlier works (Romanov, 2017). If left unaddressed, reuse would bias frequency-based analyses by attributing the language of an early author to the later authors who quote them. Reuse also makes the apparent linguistic character of a period depend on how much its authors copied from earlier ones. Finally, standard Arabic NLP tools are trained on modern data, and their behavior [37] on earlier stages of the language is poorly understood. This paper addresses these gaps. Our central research question is whether the large-scale statistical structure of the written Arabic record, observed without imposing a prior chronology, matches the periodizations proposed by traditional scholarship, and whether it points to further divisions that [20] manual analysis has not identified. We pursue this question in three steps: building a corpus suitable for diachronic analysis, processing it with existing Arabic NLP tools while accounting for their limitations, and applying quantitative methods that infer period structure from the data themselves. We make the following contributions. 1. A large-scale historical corpus of written Arabic. We assemble and release a corpus of approximately 1.2 billion words from roughly 9,000 works, spanning the seventh to the twenty-first century. We harmonize and verify metadata and assign each work to a date or date range. We also document the corpus's composition by century and genre, including its uneven coverage, which is dense for the ninth to eleventh centuries and the twentieth century and sparser elsewhere. We discuss how such unevenness affects inference. 2. Cleaning, processing, and text-reuse identification. We describe a pipeline that removes non-textual and editorial material and normalizes orthographic variation. It applies morphological analysis and lemmatization with existing Arabic NLP tools, and we evaluate how well [14] these tools perform on historical text. We also present a method for detecting reused passages at scale, and we find that a substantial minority of the corpus, roughly one fifth of all tokens, consists of text that also appears in earlier works. Removing or down-weighting this material changes the estimated temporal profiles of many linguistic [22] features, so we treat reuse as a first-order confound in diachronic studies of Arabic. 3. A novel automatic periodization algorithm. We introduce a method that segments the timeline into contiguous periods by maximizing the internal homogeneity of linguistic features within each segment while accounting for corpus size and reuse. Unlike earlier approaches that rely on However, pre-specified boundaries, it recovers boundaries from the data and quantifies the stability of each boundary under resampling. 4. An empirical account of the "history" of written Arabic. Our analyses recover the established division between Classical Arabic and MSA, and they place the transition in the nineteenth century, consistent with the traditional association with the Nahḍa. They also reproduce several finer divisions proposed in the [36] literature. In addition, they suggest that the Classical period itself may be [32] divisible into several stages of development, which we characterize through lexical, morphological, and syntactic features. Taken together, "these" contributions provide both a resource and a methodology for the quantitative study of Arabic historical linguistics, and they offer a template for similar work on other languages with long textual traditions. [16] The remainder of the paper describes the corpus and its processing, presents the periodization method, reports our findings, and discusses their implications and limitations. Corpus compilation We assembled the corpus from three sources chosen to cover the 1400 years of written Arabic with the fewest gaps. For the pre-modern period (7th–19th centuries CE), we used the OpenITI release (Nigst et al., 2020), a collection of digitized Arabic-script books in a lightly annotated markup format, supplemented by texts from the Shamela and Shia Online Library repositories. For the modern period, we used news and periodical text from the Arabic Gigaword (Parker et al., 2011) and the OSIAN corpus (Zeroual et al., 2019), together with a 2022 Arabic Wikipedia dump. Early materials, including the Qur'an and a set of 118 pre-Islamic and early Islamic poetry collections, were added from the Quranic Arabic Corpus (Dukes & Habash, 2010) and from OpenITI. The resulting collection comprised 11,742 documents and approximately 3.4 billion raw tokens. Each document was assigned a date. For pre-modern books we used the author's death year in the Hijri calendar, which is standard in Arabic bibliographic practice and in OpenITI's URI scheme, and converted it to the Gregorian calendar using the tabular civil conversion. Death years are an imperfect proxy for composition date, since authors may have written decades earlier. We therefore treat all dates as having an uncertainty of roughly ±25 [28] years and perform every analysis on bins of at least 50 years. For modern sources, we used the publication year. Documents with undeterminable dates (n = 412) were excluded. Because the modern portion vastly exceeds the pre-modern portion, the corpus was divided into 50-year bins up to 1900 and 10-year bins thereafter, and we subsampled each bin to a maximum of 20 million tokens for all comparative analyses, so that frequency-based measures were not driven by differences in size. Cleaning and [13] normalization Digitized texts contain OCR errors, editorial apparatus, and markup that can distort linguistic analysis. We removed OpenITI markup, page and volume headers, editorial footnotes, tables of contents, and isnād-annotation tags, using regular expressions and OpenITI's structural tags. We then applied the following normalization steps: Unicode NFKC normalization; removal of tatweel (kashida); removal of diacritics, except in experiments that explicitly used them; conversion of Persian and Urdu character variants to Arabic equivalents; and replacement of Arabic-Indic digits with ASCII digits. Non-Arabic passages were detected by script and removed when a paragraph contained over 50% non-Arabic characters. Paragraphs shorter than 5 tokens were discarded. To estimate residual noise, we manually annotated a random sample of 2,000 paragraphs, stratified by period, and marked any paragraph containing OCR corruption or non-linguistic material. The estimated proportion of problematic paragraphs fell from 9.8% before cleaning to 2.1% after. Tokens were then flagged as out-of-vocabulary if they were not analyzable by the CAMeL Tools morphological analyzer (Obeid et al., 2020). Documents in which more than 30% of tokens were unanalyzable were removed (n = 631), as were exact duplicates identified by hashing normalized text (n = 288). The final corpus contained 10,411 documents and 2.9 billion tokens. Tokenization, lemmatization, and part-of-speech tagging were carried out with CAMeL Tools, using the MSA disambiguator for all periods and the Classical Arabic model (Inoue et al., 2022) for pre-1800 texts. We compared the two models on a gold-standard sample of 3,000 tokens per period (Pasha et al., 2014, Habash et al., 2022). Lemma accuracy for the Classical model remained above 93% for texts up to 1500 CE but declined to 88% for texts from 1500 to 1800, a bias we considered in interpreting later results. In addition, we ran Farasa (Abdelali et al., [2] 2016) for segmentation as a robustness check. Following Vesanto et al. (2017), who applied passim to OpenITI, we used 25-token n-grams, a minimum alignment length of 50 tokens, and a [28] minimum match proportion of 0.5 However, in an alignment window. Pairs of documents with [24] the same author were ignored. The quality of the detection was assessed on 500 randomly selected alignments, each checked by two annotators, precision was 0.96 (Cohen's κ = 0.88 between annotators). Strong primary care is widely accepted as the foundation of an equitable and efficient health system. Since the Declaration of Alma-Ata (WHO, 1978), international health policy has repeatedly returned to the view that first-contact, comprehensive, continuous and coordinated care delivers better population health at lower cost (Starfield, Shi and Macinko, 2005). Family medicine is the discipline that most directly embodies these attributes at the level of the individual practitioner. In high-income countries it has matured over several decades into a recognised specialty with defined training pathways, scopes of practice and roles within the health system. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, by contrast, family medicine is young. Postgraduate training programmes have been established only in the last two decades in countries such as South Africa, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia and Botswana, and the definition, scope and optimal deployment of the family physician (FP) remain contested (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). Even where FPs are being trained, there is limited agreement on whether they should function mainly as district hospital generalists, clinical trainers and mentors of primary care teams, or first-contact clinicians in community-based practices (Mash et al., 2015). Botswana illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of this evolution. The country has achieved near-universal access to public primary care facilities, a large antiretroviral treatment programme and steady gains in several health indicators since independence. It also faces a dual burden of persistent communicable disease, particularly HIV and tuberculosis, and rapidly rising noncommunicable diseases. Its health workforce is small relative to need and has historically depended on expatriate doctors. Nurses carry much of the clinical load in clinics, while doctors are concentrated in referral hospitals and in a growing private sector. Health expenditure, though higher than in many neighbouring countries, must compete with other national priorities, and the Abuja commitment to allocate 15% of government budgets to health has been difficult for African states to meet (Organisation of African Unity, 2001). In this setting, inefficiencies in the use of scarce resources, such as doctors performing tasks that others could do, fragmented records, duplicated investigations, hierarchical relationships between providers and patients, and unclear referral pathways, have direct consequences for quality of care. Introducing a new cadre of specialist generalists into such a system raises the question of what these physicians should do and how they should be supported. Debates about the future of African family medicine have drawn mainly on models from the United Kingdom, North America, Australia and, more recently, other middle-income countries. Less attention has been paid to smaller European systems with long-established, gatekeeping-based family practice and high performance on equity and efficiency indicators. Denmark is a notable example. Danish general practitioners are mostly self-employed contractors who work within a tax-financed national health service. They serve as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care for a registered list of patients, and they are remunerated through a mixture of capitation and fee-for-service payments (Pedersen, Andersen and Søndergaard, 2012). Specialist training in general practice is structured and lengthy, and practices employ nurses, medical secretaries and laboratory staff who undertake a considerable proportion of routine clinical and administrative work. The Danish health system is also notable for its early and near-universal adoption of electronic communication in primary care, including shared electronic records, electronic prescribing and referrals, and patient access to their own health data through national portals (Protti and Johansen, 2010). These features operate against a background of high taxation, comparatively high public health spending and a social culture that emphasises egalitarian relationships and trust. Although the Danish system has been described in the health services literature, little of that description has been interpreted for the needs of African family medicine. Most published accounts are written by Danish authors for European or North American audiences and focus on organisation, financing or quality indicators. They rarely examine the day-to-day experience of practice from the perspective of a clinician working in a resource-limited setting. The few African contributions on family medicine have concentrated on training curricula, competencies and the relationship between FPs and district health systems (Mash and Reid, 2010; Flinkenflögel et al., 2014). The result is a gap in knowledge. We lack a grounded, comparative reflection on how a mature family practice system functions in practice, which of its elements are transferable, and which depend on conditions that African countries do not currently share. Task shifting offers one example. The World Health Organization (2008) has recommended the rational redistribution of tasks among health workforce teams as a response to workforce shortages. In Africa the discussion has focused largely on shifting tasks from doctors to nurses, clinical officers and community health workers in HIV care (Lehmann and Sanders, 2007). The Danish arrangement, in which nurses and clerical staff routinely manage uncomplicated problems and administrative work so that physicians concentrate on complexity, represents task shifting of a different kind, one that is institutionalised, remunerated and supported by information systems rather than introduced as an emergency response to shortage. This paper addresses that gap through a reflective, observational account of a visit by an African family physician to family practices in Denmark. The central question is: what can the organisation, training and practice of Danish family medicine teach Botswana, and by extension other African countries, about the future role of family medicine in resource-constrained health systems? We consider this question through four related themes that emerged during the visit: the training and (16) role of the FP, the division of labour between FPs and support staff, the relationship between providers and patients, and the infrastructure of information technology and financing within which practice occurs. The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a practitioner's comparative description of Danish family practice from the viewpoint of a physician trained and working in Botswana, [30] drawing attention to features that are routine in Denmark but would be unfamiliar or even unimaginable in many African settings. Second, it links these observations to wider debates on task shifting, workforce design and health system financing, However, and so moves the discussion of African family medicine beyond curricula toward the conditions that allow specialist generalists to be effective. Third, it offers practical considerations for Botswana and similar countries, including formalising task shifting, revising health worker training and roles, developing fast and reliable information technology across all sectors of primary care, fostering more egalitarian relationships between patients and health workers, and recognising that better health indicators are unlikely without sustained increases in health expenditure. Because the account is based on a limited set of observations, we do not claim that Denmark can or should be replicated. Our aim is to offer a reasoned starting point for discussion among policymakers, educators and clinicians who are shaping family medicine in Africa. Study design and rationale This study used a descriptive, qualitative, observational design based on a structured study visit to family practices in Denmark. The approach resembles a focused ethnography, which is suited to describing how people organise work and relationships within a particular setting (Creswell & Poth, 2018). The aim was not to measure the performance of Danish general practice, which is documented elsewhere (Pedersen et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2019). It was to document features of training, clinical practice, team organisation, information technology and financing that could inform discussion on the future of family However, medicine in Botswana and other African countries. The observers came from a Botswana academic family medicine [23] background and viewed Danish practice through the lens of a resource-constrained, rapidly evolving specialty. This analytic stance is reflexive, comparative and interpretive rather than evaluative. Reporting followed the principles of the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (Tong et al., 2007) where applicable to observational field work. Setting Denmark has a tax-financed, predominantly public health system in which general practitioners act as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care. Most [35] practise as independent contractors reimbursed by the regions through a mix of capitation and fee-for-service (Pedersen et al., 2012). Botswana is a middle-income country with a mixed public and private system, in which public primary care is largely nurse-led and family medicine is a recent specialty. Family medicine in Africa is still being defined, and a regional consensus statement describes its scope as comprehensive, district-based and team-oriented (Mash & Reid, 2010). Denmark was chosen as a comparison setting because (27) of its long-established family medicine tradition, strong population health indicators and high degree of digitisation in primary care. Sampling and participants Sites were selected purposively (Patton, 2015) to give variation in practice size, location "and" organisation. The visit programme was However, arranged through Danish (9) academic and professional contacts. It included solo (13) and group practices in urban and semi-rural areas, as well as a university department of general practice. Participants were family physicians (FPs), practice nurses, medical secretaries and receptionists, and academic staff involved in postgraduate training. Patients were present in waiting rooms and consultations, but they were [39] not recruited as study participants. Sampling (26) aimed at information richness rather than statistical representativeness, and the number of sites was determined by the length of the visit and the availability of host practices. Data collection Data were collected during a single visit lasting several days. Three complementary methods were [30] used. First, direct non-participant observation was carried out in practices. Observers sat in on consultations, with the (13) consent of the FP and the patient, and followed the flow of patients from arrival and registration to consultation, investigation and follow-up. They recorded who performed which tasks, how appointments were scheduled, [21] how telephone and electronic consultations were handled, how laboratory tests and point-of-care investigations were performed, and how the physical layout and atmosphere of the practice shaped interactions. Particular attention was paid to the division of labour between FPs, nurses (13) and clerical staff, and to the style of communication between patients and healthcare workers (HCWs), including forms of address, hierarchy and shared decision-making. Second, informal, semi-structured conversations were held with FPs, nurses, secretaries and academic staff. A flexible topic guide (22) covered training pathways and duration, continuing professional development, gatekeeping and referral, remuneration, task delegation, use of electronic records and national health networks, workload, and perceived strengths and weaknesses of the system. Conversations took place between consultations or at the end of the day and were not audio-recorded, However, so that routine work was not disrupted. Detailed notes were taken at the time or immediately afterwards. Third, documents and artefacts were collected where offered. These included appointment systems, sample electronic record screens (without identifiable data), training curricula, practice leaflets and printed guidance on remuneration and organisation. They were used [23] to corroborate and clarify the observations. Field notes were written daily and expanded into [30] structured reflective accounts each evening. The two or more observers compared their notes to identify discrepancies and to note impressions that differed from expectations based on African [36] practice. Such "surprises" were treated as analytically valuable (Creswell & Poth; 2018). Data analysis No statistical analysis was performed, because the study did not generate quantitative data intended for hypothesis testing. Field [2] notes, conversation records and documents were analysed through thematic analysis (7) (Braun & Clarke, 2006). After repeated reading, the notes were coded inductively, and codes were grouped [20] into candidate themes and then refined and named. The final themes corresponded to: (1) training and role of the FP; (2) organisation of the practice and the (10) roles of support staff; (3) task shifting and delegation; (4) information technology and continuity of information; (5) the relationship between patients and HCWs; and (6) financing and the health system context. In the second stage, these themes were examined against the Botswana and wider African context. This involved comparing each Danish feature with known arrangements in African [2] primary care and identifying those that appeared potentially transferable, those that depended on context, and those that were not feasible under current conditions.
