Graphs have become a primary representation for data in domains such as social networks, the web, bioinformatics, and knowledge bases. Their sizes have grown accordingly: the web graph contains tens of billions of pages, and social networks such as Facebook and Twitter contain billions of vertices and hundreds of billions of edges Ugander et al., 2011; Kwak et al., 2010). Querying such graphs, whether through subgraph pattern matching, reachability, path queries, or keyword search, is a core requirement for analysis and decision making. Much of the work on graph querying, however, assumes that the graph, or at least its index, fits in main memory (Cordella et al., 2004; Gallagher, 2006). When this assumption fails, in-memory algorithms either thrash through virtual memory or cannot run at all. Buying larger machines is costly and only postpones the problem, since graph growth routinely outpaces memory growth. Several families of solutions exist. Disk-based graph stores and indexes (Angles and Gutierrez, 2008; Wang et al., 2008) reduce memory demands but typically require index structures whose construction and maintenance are expensive on very large graphs, and whose performance degrades when access patterns are not local. Distributed graph systems such as Pregel Malewicz et al., 2010), GraphLab (Low et al., 2012), and Trinity Shao et al., 2013) spread a graph across the memory of a cluster, and Map/Reduce-based approaches (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) have been used for graph processing and subgraph matching (Lin and Schatz, 2010; Sun et al., 2012). These approaches generally presuppose a cluster large enough to hold the graph and are oriented toward whole-graph analytics (e.g., PageRank, connected components) rather than ad hoc queries that return a user-specified number of answers. Such resources are not always available, and many users need to query large graphs on a single commodity machine or a small, fixed set of machines. In this paper we pursue [25] a divide-and-conquer strategy. The graph is partitioned into pieces, each small enough to fit in memory, and queries are evaluated over the partitions. Because scalability is then bounded by the size of a partition rather than the size of the graph, a graph However, of any size can be queried with a fixed amount of memory. The strategy is simple to state but raises nontrivial problems. First, a query answer may span several partitions, so a partition-local evaluation is incomplete: matches crossing partition boundaries must be found by combining partial results from different partitions. Second, an answer may require the same partition more than once, for example when a path leaves a partition and later re-enters it, or when different query components map into the same partition at different stages. Third, answers must be neither lost nor duplicated, which requires careful bookkeeping of intermediate results without retaining so much state that the benefit of partitioning is lost. Finally, because loading a partition from disk dominates the cost, the response time depends strongly on how many partitions are loaded and in what order, which in turn depends on how the graph was partitioned and on the characteristics of the query. We consider three ways to evaluate a query given a set of partitions: (i) One Partition At a Time (OPAT), in which a single partition is resident in memory at any time and partial results are carried between loads; ii) a traditional multi-processor approach, in which several processors, each with its own memory, process different partitions concurrently and exchange intermediate results; and iii) a Map/Reduce approach, in which partitions are processed in map tasks and partial answers are combined in reduce tasks. OPAT provides scalability through independent processing of partitions and is the main focus of this paper. The latter two address response time in addition to scalability, and we present and analyze them to place OPAT in context. The research questions addressed are the following. (1) What is the minimal information that must be maintained across partition loads so that a query over a partitioned graph yields exactly the same answers as over the unpartitioned graph, including answers that span several partitions or revisit a partition? (2) How do partitioning schemes, such as those based on balanced edge-cut minimization (Karypis and Kumar, 1998), hash or range assignment, and locality-preserving methods, influence the number of partition loads and the volume of intermediate results for different query types? (3) Given a query and a set of partitions, can quantitative partition and query metrics be used to select a loading order that reduces response time, particularly when only a specified number of answers is required rather than the complete answer set? 4) How do the three evaluation approaches compare in scalability and response time under [22] varying resource constraints? Our work differs from earlier work on partitioned or distributed graph querying in several respects. Many systems partition a graph for load balancing and assume that all partitions are concurrently available (Malewicz et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2011). Work on distributed subgraph matching often relies on replicating boundary neighborhoods or on precomputed indexes to avoid cross-partition joins (Fan et al., 2010), which increases storage and preprocessing and may not bound the memory used. Out-of-core graph systems such as GraphChi (Kyrola et al., 2012) and X-Stream (Roy et al., 2013) process a graph in sequentially loaded pieces but target iterative analytics in which every vertex or edge is visited in each pass; they do not address queries that can terminate early or that have selective structure. In contrast, we treat query answering as the central problem, establish correctness conditions for cross-partition and repeated-partition answers, and exploit query selectivity and partition characteristics to determine how many partitions need to be loaded and in which sequence. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We present an OPAT query evaluation framework for partitioned graphs that identifies the necessary minimal bookkeeping, and we prove that it computes complete and duplicate-free answers, including those that span multiple partitions or require the same partition more than once. 2. We analyze the interaction between partitioning schemes and query processing, and we correlate query properties (e.g., structure, size, selectivity, and the number of answers requested) with partition characteristics to estimate the number of loads and the resources needed. 3. We define a set of quantitative metrics over partitions and intermediate results and use them to formulate heuristics for ordering partition loads, aimed at reducing response time both for all answers and for a specified number of answers. 4. We extend an existing graph querying system to evaluate queries on partitioned graphs and report experiments on large synthetic and real-world graphs, using several partitioning schemes and a variety of query types, to evaluate the heuristics. 5. We develop and analyze the multi-processor and Map/Reduce approaches, and we contrast all three approaches with respect to scalability, response time, and resource requirements, providing guidance on when each is appropriate. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the query model and the partitioned-graph evaluation framework, including the correctness argument. Section 3 presents partitioning analysis, metrics, and heuristics. Section 4 describes the multi-processor and Map/Reduce approaches. Section 5 reports the experimental evaluation; and Section 6 discusses the findings and concludes. Problem setting and overall design We model a graph as a directed, labeled multigraph G = (V, E, λ), where λ assigns labels to vertices and edges. A query Q is a connected pattern of k edges with optional label and value predicates. It is evaluated under subgraph-isomorphism semantics (Ullmann, 1976) with a result limit r, [9] where r is either all answers or a user-specified number. G is divided into n partitions {P₁,…,Pₙ}. Each vertex belongs to exactly one partition, and "edges" whose endpoints lie in different partitions are cut edges. Each partition is stored as a self-contained unit that holds its internal edges, its outgoing cut edges, and [2] a catalogue of its boundary vertices. A partition is sized so that it, together with the intermediate results it produces, fits in the [25] memory budget M. Query evaluation therefore needs no more than M, regardless of |G|. We study three evaluation strategies: (i) One Partition At a Time OPAT), (ii) a traditional multiprocessor approach with shared or message-passing [17] workers, and (iii) a Map/Reduce formulation (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004). OPAT is the primary experimental subject. The other two are specified and analyzed with a cost model, and their behavior is compared to OPAT on the same workloads. OPAT evaluation and minimal bookkeeping OPAT loads one partition at a time into memory and evaluates Q against it with the in-memory engine. A partial match is a binding of a connected subset of Q's edges to graph edges. When a partial match reaches a boundary vertex v whose continuation edge lies in another partition Pj, it is suspended. Two answers can [38] then be lost or duplicated. The first is an answer that spans partitions, which is lost if the suspension is not recorded. The second [29] is an answer that needs the same partition more than once, which is lost if a partition is considered finished after one visit. To prevent both, we keep a minimal record for each suspended partial match m: B(m) = ⟨σ(m), e(m), π(m)⟩, where σ is the vertex-to-query-node binding, e is the next query edge to be matched together with the boundary vertex that [6] must be expanded, and π is the set of (partition, query-edge) expansions that m has already consumed. "Storing" π, and not only a set of visited partitions, is [20] what allows a partition to be reloaded for a different query edge without repeating work. Final answers, together with the suspended partial matches, are written to disk [34] between loads. Each partition Pi also carries a "pending" queue of the [35] suspended matches that need it. Processing proceeds as follows. (1) Choose the next partition by the ordering heuristic below. (2) Load it, together with its pending queue. (3) Extend the pending partial matches, and start new matches of Q from its internal edges. (4) Emit completed answers, and re-queue any match that again reaches a boundary into another partition. (5) Stop when r answers have been found or when all pending queues are empty. Only partitions with non-empty pending queues, [28] or those not yet used to [32] seed matches, are candidates at step 1. Correctness is argued as soundness and completeness. Soundness holds because every emitted answer is a binding that satisfies all Q edges and predicates against edges that physically exist in G. Completeness follows by induction on the number of query edges matched. Any answer is a sequence of edge matches; whenever the sequence crosses from Pa to Pb, the cut edge is held in Pa's boundary catalogue and a record Bm) is appended to Pb's queue. Hence the answer is eventually extended, however many times partitions are revisited. Duplicate suppression follows from π, because the pair (σ; e) uniquely identifies the expansion and is consumed once. We verified both properties empirically by comparing the OPAT result sets with those of the unpartitioned in-memory engine on all graphs that fit in memory (set equality, 100% agreement required). Partitioning schemes We compare four schemes of increasing structural awareness: a) hash partitioning of vertex identifiers, (b) random balanced assignment, (c) a streaming heuristic, Linear Deterministic Greedy (Stanton and Kliot, 2012), and d) multilevel k-way partitioning with METIS (Karypis and Kumar, 1998), which minimizes edge cut under a balance constraint. The imbalance tolerance is 1.05 for all schemes, and n ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. For each partitioning we compute the edge-cut ratio, the number of boundary vertices |Bi|, and the size skew maxi|Pi| / meani|Pi|. Dental hygiene is a distinct health profession whose scope of practice has expanded considerably over the past several decades. Dental hygienists now provide preventive, educational, and therapeutic services across diverse settings, including private [17] practices, schools, long-term care facilities, and [12] public health programs, and in a growing number of [13] jurisdictions they practice with greater autonomy or under direct access arrangements (Gurenlian, 2007). This expansion has been accompanied by sustained (17) efforts to build a discipline-specific body of knowledge. Professional organizations (8) and accrediting bodies increasingly call for evidence-based practice, a research agenda grounded in the profession's own theoretical frameworks, and the preparation of graduates who can locate, appraise, and apply scientific evidence (Fried et al., 2016). These aims [10] depend on a literature that is both sizable and accessible, and on information professionals who understand how that literature is organized, where it is published, and how [34] it is indexed. Bibliometric mapping offers a systematic way to characterize the literature of a field. The Medical Library Association's "Nursing and Allied Health Literature Mapping Project" has, since the 1990s, applied a standardized method to many health professions. The method collects references cited in a [27] sample of core journals, classifies [33] them by format and age, and ranks the cited journals according to Bradford's "Law" of Scattering (Bradford, 1934; Allen, 1994). Bradford's Law holds that the [25] journals contributing to a subject can be divided into zones, each yielding roughly equal numbers of relevant citations, with a small nucleus of core titles producing as many citations as a much larger number of peripheral titles. Mapping studies thereby identify the journals that are most important to a discipline, indicate how widely its literature is dispersed across other fields, and assess how well major bibliographic databases index the titles that practitioners and researchers actually cite. For librarians, such findings inform collection development decisions, license negotiations, database selection, and instruction on searching strategies. For researchers, they indicate where relevant evidence (18) is likely to be found and where it may be missed. Haaland (1999) published the first mapping study of dental hygiene literature in this tradition. Analyzing citations from a sample of dental hygiene (16) journals, the study identified a small core [6] of titles, demonstrated that the literature relied heavily on journal articles, with books as the next most frequent format, and documented a substantial reliance on literature from dentistry and other health-related fields. Haaland's findings (6) were consistent with the profile of a However, relatively young, applied discipline: a literature concentrated in a few profession-specific journals, supplemented (16) by sources from dentistry, medicine, and education. The study has served (28) since as a (20) reference point for librarians supporting dental hygiene programs and for those evaluating database [4] coverage of the field. Since 1999, however, the conditions under which dental hygiene literature is produced, indexed, and consumed have changed profoundly. First, the transition from print to electronic publishing has altered the formats researchers cite and the speed with which they can obtain them. Online journal platforms, open access publishing, institutional (24) repositories, and freely accessible websites of professional and governmental organizations have broadened the range of sources available to authors (Tenopir et al., 2009). Studies (17) in other health professions have documented the corresponding rise of Internet sources (11) in reference lists and, in several cases, a decline in citations to books and other monographic literature (Ugaz et al., 2010; Shipman et (28) al., 2013). Second, the volume of health sciences literature has grown dramatically, and the number of indexed journals has expanded accordingly. Databases that once offered limited coverage of allied health fields have enlarged their holdings; CINAHL, for example, has broadened its scope of allied health titles and now exists in a "Complete" edition that includes full-text content, whereas MEDLINE and EMBASE have also expanded the number of dental and related journals they index. Third, dental hygiene itself has developed its own research infrastructure, including the establishment of doctoral and master's programs, the creation of new peer-reviewed journals, and more explicit research priorities set by professional associations (Gurenlian et al., 2016). Whether these developments have changed the structure of the discipline's literature, such as the number of core journals, the reliance on literature from other fields, or the age of cited material, has not been systematically examined since Haaland's original study. This gap matters for several reasons. Collection development decisions made on the basis of two-decade-old data may overlook emerging titles or overvalue formats that have declined in importance. Without current estimates of database coverage, librarians cannot advise students and clinicians reliably on which resources best capture the dental hygiene literature, nor can they judge whether supplementary searching However, in additional databases is warranted. In addition, because evidence-based practice depends on comprehensive retrieval, uneven indexing of the literature can bias systematic reviews and clinical guidelines. Finally, longitudinal comparisons of mapping studies are uncommon in the health sciences, and replication of an earlier study (19) with the same methodology provides rare evidence of how a discipline's literature evolves over time. The present study therefore updates Haaland's (1999) analysis. We address three research questions. First, how have the formats and ages of sources cited in dental hygiene journals changed between the original study and the present sample, in particular with respect to journal articles, books, government publications, and Internet sources? Second, which journals constitute the core of the dental hygiene literature when ranked according to Bradford's Law of Scattering, and how does their disciplinary focus compare with that of the earlier core? Third, to what extent are the cited journals indexed in CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, and how does this coverage inform database selection? This study makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides a current map of the dental hygiene literature based on cited references from a three-year sample of core journals, and it quantifies change relative to 1999 in the number of cited titles, the size of the core zone, format distribution, and citation age. Methodologically, it extends the standard mapping protocol by adding an Internet source category, reflecting the changed citation landscape, and by pairing the Bradford (19) analysis with a multi-database coverage survey. Practically, it supplies librarians, educators, and researchers with evidence to guide collection building, user education, and search strategy design, and it offers a baseline against which future developments in dental hygiene scholarship can be measured. Study design and conceptual framework This study followed the protocol established by the Medical Library Association's Mapping the Literature of Nursing and Allied Health project, which uses citation analysis to identify the journals most frequently cited in a discipline's literature (Allen 1991, Haaland 1999). The design replicates and extends Haaland's (1999) original dental hygiene mapping study to permit direct comparison across approximately two decades. The analytic framework rests on Bradford's Law of Scattering, which holds that journals contributing to a subject can be divided into a core zone and successive peripheral zones, each yielding approximately one-third of the relevant citations while requiring progressively more journals (Bradford 1934). Citation analysis was selected as the primary approach because cited references reflect the sources on which authors actually rely, and thus provide a more direct indicator of use than subscription or circulation data (Haaland 1999). Selection of source journals The source journals were those identified as core dental hygiene titles in the original study and in current subject listings: the Journal of Dental Hygiene, the International Journal of Dental Hygiene, the Journal of Clinical Periodontology-independent hygiene titles recognized by the American Dental Hygienists' Association, and Canadian Journal of Dental Hygiene, with eligibility confirmed against the National Library of Medicine catalog and CINAHL subject headings. Journals were included if they (1) were published in English, (2) were peer reviewed, (3) addressed dental hygiene practice, education, or research as a primary focus, and (4) published research or review articles during 2015–2017. Newsletters and trade publications consisting solely of news items were excluded. Selecting a three-year window balanced representativeness against feasibility and reduced the influence of anomalous issues or themed supplements on the citation distribution. Sampling and data collection All articles published in the selected journals from January 2015 through December 2017 were screened for eligibility. Original research articles, systematic and narrative reviews, case reports, and position papers containing reference lists were retained. Editorials, letters, book reviews, abstracts of conference proceedings, and items without bibliographies were excluded. For each eligible article, the complete reference list was extracted from the publisher's website, PubMed Central, or the full-text PDF when necessary. Reference lists were transferred to a spreadsheet, with each row representing a single citation. Recorded fields included source journal, source article identifier, publication year of the source article, cited item title, cited journal or publisher, cited publication year, and cited format. Citations were collected in 2018. To minimize (11) transcription error, a second reviewer independently verified a random 10% sample of articles against the original reference lists; discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, where systematic errors were found, the affected batch was rechecked in full. Categorization of cited formats Each citation was assigned to one of five mutually exclusive format categories: journal articles, books (including monographs, chapters, and edited volumes), government publications, Internet sources, and other. Haaland's (1999) scheme employed categories for journals, books, government documents, and miscellaneous items; an "Internet sources" category was added here because web-based material was virtually absent from the earlier sample but had become a common citation target. Internet sources were defined as web pages, online reports, and online resources lacking a traditional publication frame, such as organizational websites, clinical guidelines hosted solely online, and data repositories. Where an item had both a print and an online version (for example, a journal article accessed electronically or a government report available as a PDF), it was categorized according to its original publication type rather than its mode of access. Items that could not be reliably classified, such as personal communications, theses, conference presentations, and software, were assigned to "other." Two reviewers independently coded a pilot set of 200 citations; interrater agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa, and disagreements were resolved through discussion before coding of the full dataset. Analysis by format and publication age Citation counts and proportions were calculated for each format and compared descriptively with Haaland's (1999) published values. Age of cited material was computed as the difference between the publication year of the citing article and the publication year of the cited item. Citations were grouped into age categories of 0–5, 6–10, 11–15, 16–20, and more than 20 years, and the cumulative proportion of citations aged 10 years or younger was used as a summary indicator of currency of the literature, consistent with the earlier study. Citations lacking an identifiable year were retained in format counts but excluded from age analyses. Because proportions from the two studies derive from different samples, differences were interpreted descriptively; where appropriate, 95% confidence intervals for proportions were calculated using the Wilson method, and chi-square tests of independence were used to compare the distribution of formats between [16] 1999 and the present sample, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05. Bradford analysis of journal citations Citations to journal articles were aggregated by cited journal title. Journal titles were normalized by resolving abbreviations, title changes, and variant spellings against the NLM Catalog and ISSN Portal; titles that had merged or split were counted separately (1) if they were indexed separately. Journals were ranked in descending order of citation frequency, and ties were ordered alphabetically. The ranked list was then divided into three zones, each containing as close as possible to one-third of the total journal citations (Bradford 1934; [39] Allen 1991). Zone 1 was designated the core, Zone 2 the first peripheral group, and Zone 3 the remaining titles. Because titles cannot be divided, the boundary placed each journal wholly in the [33] zone nearest the one-third cutoff. Ovarian cancer is the eighth most common [33] cancer in [24] women worldwide and one of the most lethal gynaecological malignancies, with an estimated 295,000 new cases and 185,000 deaths annually (Bray et al., 2018). Because early disease is typically asymptomatic and no effective population screening exists, approximately three-quarters of women are diagnosed at an advanced stage (Torre et al., 2018; Reid et al., 2017). The standard of care combines cytoreductive surgery with platinum- and taxane-based chemotherapy. Although most women achieve an initial clinical response, the majority of those with advanced disease relapse, and five-year survival remains below 50% (Torre et al., 2018). Ovarian cancer is increasingly conceptualised as a chronic, relapsing condition, in which patients alternate [34] between periods of intensive [38] treatment, surveillance and uncertainty about recurrence. This trajectory, together with the physical burden of surgery, treatment toxicity, symptoms such as ascites and bowel obstruction, and threats to fertility and body image, places women with ovarian cancer at substantial risk of psychological morbidity. Depression and anxiety are the most common psychiatric complications in oncology. A meta-analysis of interview-based studies estimated the prevalence of major depression at around 14% in oncological settings and 16% in palliative-care settings, with anxiety and adjustment disorders contributing a further substantial burden (Mitchell et al., 2011). Psychological distress in cancer has consequences extending well beyond subjective suffering. It is associated with poorer adherence to treatment, reduced quality [28] of life, greater healthcare utilisation, impaired functioning and increased suicide risk (Pitman et al., [21] 2018; Fann et al., 2008). Meta-analytic evidence also links depression to higher cancer-specific and all-cause mortality (Satin et al., 2009). In ovarian cancer specifically, experimental and [11] clinical work has suggested that behavioural and neuroendocrine pathways, including adrenergic signalling, may influence tumour progression, providing a biological rationale for the clinical relevance of affective symptoms in this disease (Lutgendorf et al., 2008, 2012). Whatever (2) the causal mechanisms, the detection and management of depression and anxiety are widely recognised as integral to comprehensive cancer care. Despite this, psychological distress in cancer remains underrecognised and undertreated. Clinicians tend to attribute [7] low mood, fatigue, sleep disturbance and loss of appetite to the disease or its treatment rather than to a treatable affective disorder, and consultations are frequently dominated by oncological and physical concerns (Mitchell et al., 2011; Pitman et al., 2018). In gynaecological oncology, where patients are often managed within time-limited clinic appointments and with limited access to psycho-oncology services, there is a particular risk that distress goes unidentified. Appropriately targeting screening and intervention requires robust data on how common these conditions are, and at which points in the illness trajectory the risk is greatest. The existing literature on depression and anxiety in ovarian cancer is, however, fragmented and inconsistent. Reported prevalence estimates range widely, from under 10% to more than 40% for depressive symptoms and similarly for anxiety, and several factors contribute to this heterogeneity. Studies vary in their sampling frames and sample sizes, in disease stage and treatment modality, and in the instruments used to define caseness, which include self-report screening [31] questionnaires such as the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, the Beck Depression Inventory and the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, as well as structured diagnostic interviews (Norton et al., 2004, Hipkins et al., 2004). Perhaps most importantly, the timing of assessment relative to treatment differs between studies. Women assessed shortly after diagnosis, when they face the shock of a life-threatening illness and the prospect of major surgery, may experience a different psychological profile from those undergoing chemotherapy, with its cumulative toxicity, alopecia and fatigue, or those in remission who must contend with fear of recurrence and the late effects of treatment. Yet previous reviews of psychological outcomes in gynaecological or ovarian cancer have generally pooled findings across the care pathway, or have focused on quality of life and broader constructs of distress rather than on clinically meaningful depression and anxiety. As a result, it remains unclear whether prevalence differs systematically across the stages of treatment, and how it compares with that in the general female population, in which the 12-month prevalence of major depression and of anxiety disorders is estimated at roughly 6% to 8% and 10% to 15%, respectively (Kessler et al., 2005, Baxter et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2013). This gap has practical as well as scientific importance. If depression and anxiety peak at particular junctures, for example around diagnosis, during chemotherapy or after treatment completion, then screening schedules, referral pathways and supportive interventions could be timed and resourced accordingly. Conversely, if prevalence is uniformly elevated across the illness course, continuous surveillance of psychological well-being should be embedded within routine follow-up. Contemporary survivorship frameworks and the growing emphasis on patient-reported outcomes in oncology make such evidence timely. Moreover, quantitative synthesis can quantify the extent to which observed prevalence exceeds population norms, and so can inform health-service planning and the design of future trials of psychological and pharmacological interventions in this population. The present study therefore aimed to systematically review and meta-analyse the published literature on the prevalence of depression and anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, stratified by stage of treatment. Specifically, we sought to estimate pooled prevalence rates of depression and anxiety separately [33] before treatment, during active treatment and after treatment completion, and to compare these with prevalence in the healthy female population. We hypothesised that the prevalence of both conditions would be elevated relative to the general population at every stage, and that it would vary with the phase of the treatment pathway. This work makes several contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first meta-analytic estimates of depression and anxiety prevalence in ovarian cancer that are explicitly differentiated by treatment stage, rather than aggregated across heterogeneous clinical contexts. Second, by applying systematic search procedures and explicit inclusion criteria to primary research, and by pooling data from several thousand patients, it offers more precise estimates than any individual study can provide, together with an appraisal of the sources of between-study variability. Third, it benchmarks these estimates against population-level data, thereby clarifying the magnitude of excess psychological morbidity in this patient group. Finally, by identifying where evidence is sparse or methodologically limited, the review highlights priorities for future research and informs ongoing efforts to ensure that psychological distress in ovarian cancer is recognised and adequately treated. Protocol and reporting standards This [21] systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines (Stroup et al., 2000). The review protocol was developed a priori by all authors, and any deviations from it were resolved by consensus. Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible if they (1) were full-length, peer-reviewed journal articles published in English; (2) enrolled adult women (≥18 years) with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of ovarian cancer, including fallopian tube and primary peritoneal carcinomas where these were analysed together with ovarian cancer; (3) assessed depression, anxiety, or both using a validated self-report instrument or a structured or semi-structured clinical interview, and (4) reported, or allowed calculation of, the number of patients meeting a defined threshold for depression or anxiety, together with the total sample size. Cohort, cross-sectional, and baseline data from randomised or non-randomised trials were considered. Studies were excluded if they (1) reported only continuous symptom scores without a clinically defined cut-off; (2) enrolled mixed gynaecological or mixed cancer populations without presenting ovarian cancer data separately; (3) were case reports, qualitative studies, reviews, conference abstracts, or dissertations; or (4) recruited participants exclusively on the basis of pre-existing psychiatric diagnoses or selected them for psychological distress. Where multiple publications described the same cohort, the report with the largest sample or the most complete data was retained to avoid double counting. Search strategy We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to the date of the final search. The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms relating to ovarian neoplasms (e.g., ovarian cancer”, ovarian carcinoma”, “ovarian neoplasm”), depression (e.g., “depress”, depressive disorder”, mood disorder”), and anxiety (e.g., “anxi”, “anxiety disorder”, “psychological distress”), and was adapted to the syntax of each database. No restrictions were placed on publication date. The reference lists of all included articles and of relevant previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies, and forward citation tracking was performed for key papers. Study selection All records were imported into reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant records were then retrieved and assessed independently by the same reviewers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or, where necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified using Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960). Data extraction Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardised, piloted form. Extracted variables included first author, year of publication, country, study design, sample size, mean or median age, cancer stage and histology where available, the instrument used to assess depression and anxiety, the cut-off score applied, and the number of patients above threshold. Treatment stage at the time of assessment was recorded and classified into three categories: pretreatment (after diagnosis but before the commencement of surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy), on-treatment (during active primary or recurrent treatment, including adjuvant and palliative chemotherapy), and post-treatment (following completion of primary treatment, including survivorship and surveillance periods). Where a study reported data at multiple time points, each time point was extracted and assigned to the relevant category; however, to preserve independence, a single study contributed no more than one estimate to any given treatment-stage pooled analysis. In such cases, the time point closest to the midpoint of the stage was selected. Where data were unclear or missing, corresponding authors were contacted by email. Assessment of risk of bias Methodological quality was appraised independently by two reviewers using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data (Munn et al., 2015). This instrument evaluates the appropriateness of the sampling frame and sampling method, adequacy of sample size, description of participants and setting, coverage of the sample in data analysis, validity and reliability of the measurement of the condition, appropriateness of statistical analysis, and adequacy of the response rate. Each item was rated as yes, no, unclear, or not applicable, and studies were classified as being at low (≥7 of 9 items satisfied), moderate (5–6 items), or high (≤4 items) risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Quality ratings were used to inform sensitivity analyses rather than as grounds for exclusion. Outcomes The primary outcomes were the pooled prevalence of depression and the pooled prevalence of anxiety in women with ovarian cancer, each stratified by treatment [20] stage (pretreatment, on-treatment, and post-treatment). Prevalence was defined as the proportion of participants scoring at or above the validated cut-off of the instrument used in the primary study, or meeting diagnostic criteria on clinical interview. Because instruments differ in their operating characteristics, the instrument type was recorded and examined as a potential source of heterogeneity. Statistical analysis Prevalence estimates and their standard errors were computed for each study from the number of cases and sample size. As proportions close to 0 or 1 violate the assumption of normality and yield variance instability, the study-level proportions were stabilised using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine [30] transformation (Freeman & Tukey, 1950) prior to pooling, and pooled estimates were back-transformed for presentation as percentages with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Given the anticipated clinical and methodological diversity among studies, a random-effects model with the DerSimonian–Laird estimator was used for all primary analyses (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). Separate meta-analyses were conducted for depression and anxiety at each treatment stage. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and quantified using the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and 75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al., 2003). Panic disorder is a common and burdensome anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, persistent concern about further attacks or their consequences, and often maladaptive behavioral changes such as avoidance of situations associated with feared bodily sensations (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Population-based surveys estimate lifetime prevalence at roughly 2% to 5% and 12-month prevalence at around 2% to 3%, depending on the diagnostic criteria and region (Kessler et al., 2005; Wittchen et al., 2011). Panic disorder typically begins in early adulthood and, if untreated, tends to follow a chronic or relapsing course. It is associated with marked functional impairment, reduced quality of life, high rates of comorbid depression and agoraphobia, and substantial healthcare utilization, particularly in primary and emergency care settings (Roy-Byrne et al., 2006; Wittchen et al., 2011). Effective and widely accessible treatment is therefore a public health priority. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best-established psychological treatment for panic disorder. Its core components include psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring of catastrophic misinterpretations of bodily sensations, interoceptive exposure, and in vivo exposure to avoided situations. Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) consistently report large effects of CBT relative to waitlist and other inactive controls, as well as durable gains at follow-up (Mitte, 2005; Otte, 2011). A network meta-analysis of psychological therapies for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia likewise found CBT-based approaches, especially those including exposure, to be superior to many comparators (Pompoli et al., 2016). Clinical guidelines in several countries accordingly recommend CBT as a first-line treatment, alongside pharmacotherapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Despite this evidence, most people with panic disorder never receive adequate care. Epidemiological data from the World Mental Health Surveys show that only a minority of individuals [12] with anxiety disorders receive minimally adequate treatment, with the shortfall most pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (Kohn et al., 2004; Alonso et al., 2018). Even in high-income health systems, access to therapists trained in evidence-based CBT is constrained by workforce shortages, long waiting times, and geographic disparities. At the individual level, stigma, cost, time constraints, limited mental health literacy, and reluctance to engage in face-to-face exposure exercises further hinder help-seeking (Andrade et al., 2014; Collins et al., 2004). Closing this treatment gap requires delivery models that are scalable and flexible while retaining the active ingredients of CBT. Internet-delivered psychological treatments have been proposed as one such model. These interventions deliver structured therapeutic content, typically in modular form, via web-based platforms or, more recently, mobile applications, and often combine text, audio, video, and interactive exercises with homework assignments and self-monitoring. They can be accessed at any time and place, may reduce therapist time per patient, and may lower the threshold for seeking help because of their anonymity and convenience (Andersson & Titov, 2014). Meta-analytic evidence indicates that Internet-delivered CBT can produce clinically meaningful improvements across anxiety disorders and, in some trials, outcomes comparable to those of face-to-face treatment (Andrews et al., 2010; Olthuis et al., 2016). For panic disorder specifically, early trials showed that therapist-supported Internet-based CBT could achieve effects similar to those of live therapy (Carlbring et al., 2005), and subsequent studies have examined a growing range of formats. Several features distinguish current internet-delivered treatments and may influence both their effectiveness and their feasibility in routine care. First, the degree and type of human support vary substantially, from regular individualized therapist feedback, to minimal or on-demand contact, to fully self-guided programs with no personal contact. Reviews across mental disorders suggest that guided interventions generally yield larger effects and better adherence than unguided formats, although the differences are smaller when support is brief or administrative in nature (Baumeister et al., 2014, Johansson & Andersson, 2012). Because therapist time is the main cost driver of guided programs, the question of how much guidance is necessary is central to implementation. Second, treatment approaches differ in scope. Disorder-specific programs target the maintaining mechanisms of panic disorder directly, whereas transdiagnostic programs address common processes across anxiety and mood disorders and may therefore suit patients with comorbidity or diagnostic uncertainty, as well as services seeking to offer a single flexible program (Newby et al., 2015). Third, theoretical orientation is no longer confined to CBT, as alternative frameworks such as psychodynamic or acceptance-based approaches are being adapted for online delivery. Efficacy under trial conditions does not guarantee real-world benefit. The potential of internet-delivered treatments depends equally on their acceptability to users and providers, commonly operationalized through attrition, adherence to treatment modules, and treatment satisfaction. Dropout and nonusage are persistent problems in digital health, a phenomenon described [24] as the law of attrition (Eysenbach, 2005). Attrition and adherence rates vary [38] widely across trials and are influenced by program design, support, and participant characteristics (Christensen et al., 2009; Kelders et al., 2012). Moreover, uptake outside research settings is limited by skepticism among both the public and health professionals, concerns about the therapeutic relationship, data [13] security, and suitability for severe or complex presentations (Apolinário-Hagen et al., 2018, Andersson & [6] Titov, 2014). Because clinicians often act as gatekeepers who recommend, prescribe, or integrate digital programs into stepped-care pathways, they need a clear and current overview of which formats work, for whom, and with what level of user engagement. The existing evidence syntheses [20] only partly meet this need. Many reviews pool findings across anxiety disorders or across mental disorders in general, which [24] can obscure differences between diagnostic groups (Andrews et al., 2010, Olthuis et al., 2016). Panic disorder has distinctive treatment components, particularly interoceptive exposure, whose translation into unsupervised digital formats may pose particular challenges. In addition, the field has developed rapidly: newer trials have tested self-guided and transdiagnostic programs, compared different support intensities, and examined alternatives to CBT. These developments have not been summarized with a dual focus [21] on clinical effectiveness and However, acceptability indicators specific to panic disorder. Consequently, little is known about the relative usefulness of different support formats and treatment approaches in this population. To address this gap, the present narrative review synthesizes recent RCT evidence on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. We pursued two overarching questions. First, how efficacious are internet-delivered treatments for panic disorder compared with control conditions, [29] and do outcomes differ according to the format of support (e.g., guided versus self-guided) or the treatment approach (e.g., disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic)? Second, how acceptable are these interventions, as reflected in attrition, adherence, and participant satisfaction? We restricted the review to trials published within the past five years to capture the current generation of programs and to reflect technological and methodological developments in the field. This review contributes in three ways. It provides a panic disorder-specific update on the efficacy of internet-delivered treatments, complementing broader anxiety-focused syntheses. It systematically contrasts support formats and treatment approaches that are directly relevant to decisions about implementation in [7] routine and stepped care. Finally, it integrates efficacy data with indicators of acceptability, thereby identifying where the evidence is strong, where it is limited, and which research priorities, [26] such as improving uptake and identifying moderators of outcome, should guide future trials. Design We conducted a narrative review of recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on internet-delivered psychological treatments for adults with panic disorder. A narrative synthesis was chosen over a quantitative meta-analysis because the interventions, support formats, comparison conditions, and outcome measures were expected to be too heterogeneous to pool meaningfully (Popay et al., 2006). The literature search and reporting followed the structure of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009) where applicable to a narrative format. The review was not prospectively registered. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) were RCTs published in English-language peer-reviewed journals between 10 December 2012 and 12 December 2017; (b) included adult participants (≥18 years) [9] with a primary diagnosis of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia, established according to DSM-IV, DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), or ICD-10 criteria, ideally by a structured or semi-structured clinical interview; (c) evaluated a psychological treatment delivered predominantly via the internet (e.g., web-based or browser-based programs, including those accessed on mobile [4] devices), irrespective of whether therapist guidance was provided, and (d) reported at least one symptom-related outcome for panic disorder, such as panic frequency or severity, agoraphobic avoidance, or general anxiety symptoms. No restrictions were placed on the theoretical orientation of [7] the intervention, the type of support (self-guided, minimally guided, or therapist-guided), or the comparison condition. Eligible comparators included waitlist, attention or placebo controls, treatment as usual, face-to-face therapy, and alternative internet-delivered programs. Transdiagnostic or disorder-specific programs were both considered, provided that outcome data were reported for participants with panic disorder or the trial sample was defined by this diagnosis. We excluded study protocols, uncontrolled or non-randomized trials, secondary or follow-up analyses that did not report new data on efficacy or acceptability, conference abstracts, dissertations, and studies conducted exclusively with children or adolescents. Interventions that used the internet only as an adjunct to face-to-face treatment (e.g., therapist-delivered sessions supplemented by online homework) or delivered only by telephone or videoconference without a structured online program were also excluded. Trials of pharmacological or purely psychoeducational information websites without a therapeutic component were not considered. Information Sources and Search Strategy A systematic search was performed in PubMed/Medline and PSYNDEX, which together cover biomedical and German- and English-language psychological literature. The search covered the period from 10 December 2012 to 12 December 2017, thereby reflecting the most recent five years of research in this rapidly developing field. The search string combined terms for the condition “panic disorder” OR “panic attack” OR agoraphobia), the mode of delivery (“internet” OR “online” OR web-based OR “computer” OR digital OR “e-health” OR mobile), and the study design (randomized controlled trial” OR randomised OR RCT OR controlled trial”). Controlled vocabulary (Medical Subject Headings in PubMed/Medline) was combined with free-text terms in titles and abstracts, and the strategy was adapted to the syntax of each database. In addition, we conducted a hand search by screening the reference lists of included articles and of recent reviews and meta-analyses on internet-delivered treatments for anxiety disorders (e.g., Andersson et [22] al., 2014; Olthuis et al., 2016) to identify trials not captured by the database search. Study Selection Records were exported to a reference [20] management program, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and the full texts of potentially relevant articles were subsequently retrieved and assessed in detail. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were documented. Disagreements or uncertainties regarding eligibility were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached. Where multiple publications reported on the same trial, the primary outcome paper was used as the main source and complemented with information from related publications. Data Extraction Data were extracted using a standardized form. For each study, we recorded the authors, year of publication, country, sample size, and participant characteristics (mean age, proportion of women, diagnostic procedure, and comorbidity criteria). Intervention characteristics included the theoretical approach (e.g., Cognitive Behavioral Therapy [CBT] versus other approaches), the specificity of the content (disorder-specific versus transdiagnostic), program duration in weeks, number of modules, and the type and amount of human support (self-guided, minimal guidance, or therapist guidance, and whether support was provided via email, telephone, or a messaging platform). We also extracted information on the comparison condition, the primary and secondary outcome measures, the timing of assessments (post-treatment and follow-up), and the analytic approach (intention-to-treat versus completer analyses). Outcomes Efficacy was defined as the superiority of an internet-delivered intervention over a control condition, or differences between active treatment formats, on measures of panic symptoms. These included, for example, the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al., 1997), the Body Sensations Questionnaire, the Agoraphobic Cognitions Questionnaire, and the Mobility Inventory (Chambless et al., 1984, 1985), as well as broader anxiety and depression measures when reported.
