Concern about the growing distance between people and the natural world has become a central theme in environmental scholarship, education, and public health. Louv's (2005) popular account of "nature-deficit disorder" gave wide currency to the idea that urbanized, screen-saturated societies are producing generations estranged from the outdoors, and a large empirical literature has since documented the psychological, physical, and civic benefits of contact with nature. Exposure to green space is associated with reduced stress, improved attention, and better mental health (Kaplan 1995; [3] Ulrich et al. 1991; Bratman et al. 2019), while childhood experiences outdoors are linked to environmental concern and pro-environmental behavior in adulthood Wells and Lekies 2006; Chawla 2020). Scholars have developed numerous constructs to capture these relationships, including connectedness to nature Mayer and Frantz 2004), nature relatedness (Nisbet, Zelenski, and Murphy 2009), and biophilia (Wilson 1984, Kellert and Wilson 1993). Collectively, this work has sought to explain how and why people come to feel part of, or apart from, the natural world. Most of this research, however, relies on structured scales that ask respondents to agree or disagree with researcher-defined statements. Such instruments are valuable for measuring the strength of a connection, but they reveal little about the content of people's thoughts when they contemplate nature. A respondent who scores low on connectedness may be bored by nature, afraid of it, indifferent to it, or simply unaccustomed to it, one who scores high may [28] be thinking of tranquil forests, of [35] recreation, or of ecological interdependence. Because the meanings attached to nature are socially constructed and historically contingent (Cronon 1995, Williams 1980), the [22] associations that come to mind are likely to vary with the social positions and experiences of those who hold them. Few scholars have therefore asked the simple, prior question of what people tend to ponder when they think of nature, and fewer still have examined how those thoughts differ [15] across social groups. This gap matters because the "positive" framing that dominates the literature may obscure a more ambivalent reality. Nature has long evoked fear as well as reverence. Tuan (1979) documented the landscapes of fear that shape human settlement and imagination, and Ulrich (1993) and [10] Öhman and Mineka (2001) argued that humans are predisposed to learn fear of certain natural stimuli [30] such as snakes, heights, and darkness. Wilderness, in the American imagination, has been simultaneously sublime and menacing, a site of both spiritual renewal and mortal danger (Nash 2001; Cronon 1995). Environmental psychologists have likewise noted that fear of crime, getting lost, or encountering dangerous animals can deter outdoor recreation (Jorgensen and Anthopoulou 2007, Bixler and Floyd 1997). [33] Bixler and Floyd (1997), for example, found that disgust, fear, and discomfort with wildland settings were associated with a preference for indoor activities among adolescents. These fears are not merely individual quirks but may be patterned by social experience. Research on race and the outdoors suggests that this patterning is substantial. Historical exclusion, segregation, and racial violence in rural and wild places have shaped the relationships many Black, Indigenous, Latino, and Asian American communities have with [20] parks and wilderness (Finney 2014; Taylor 2016, Mock 2018). Studies of outdoor recreation have traced differential participation to a combination of marginality, discrimination, cultural preferences, and unequal access Floyd 1999, Washburne 1978, Flores, Falco, and Morales 2018). Lynching and the legacy of plantation landscapes, for example, complicate any assumption that rural nature is a universally safe or restorative space (Finney 2014, Kimmerer 2013 offers a contrasting Indigenous perspective emphasizing reciprocity rather than fear). At the same time, scholars caution against essentializing. Minority communities have deep traditions of farming, fishing, gardening, and environmental stewardship (Taylor 2016, Mohai, Pellow, and Roberts 2009), and survey evidence frequently shows that racial and ethnic minorities express equal or greater environmental concern than whites (Pearson, Schuldt, and Romero-Canyas 2016). Characterizing minorities as uniformly fearful or disconnected would thus be both empirically and ethically problematic. Race, moreover, is only one of several dimensions along which thoughts about nature may vary. Gender has been associated with differences in fear of crime and of natural hazards in outdoor settings (Pain 2001, Valentine 1989), and with differing environmental attitudes more generally (Zelezny, Chua, and Aldrich 2000). Social class and parental education shape access to leisure time, travel, camps, and parks (Stodolska and Shinew 2010), and first-generation college students may bring distinctive experiences and constraints to higher education Stephens et al. 2012). Age and life stage influence both exposure and attitude. Academic interest or major is another plausible influence: students in environmental or natural science fields receive sustained exposure to ecological concepts, fieldwork, and hazard knowledge that could alter what they associate with nature (Hungerford and Volk 1990). Yet these factors are seldom analyzed together, and when they are not, apparent racial differences may reflect confounding with class, gender, or educational background. An intersectional and multivariate approach is needed to separate these influences (Crenshaw 1991; Finney 2014). College and university students constitute a useful population for such an inquiry. They are at a formative stage in which environmental identities and career orientations are consolidating, and they are the future leaders, professionals, and voters whose decisions will shape environmental policy. Campuses are also increasingly diverse in race, class, and generational status, allowing comparisons across groups that share a common institutional context. Moreover, educators who aim to foster environmental literacy and outdoor engagement need to understand the associations students bring with them, including fear, danger, and loathing, if programs are to be welcoming and effective Chawla 2020; Rickinson et al. 2004). This study therefore addresses two research questions. First, how do college and university students think about nature, and in particular, how often do they bring to mind concepts of fear, danger, disconnection, and loathing, such as predators, natural hazards, human-made hazards, getting lost, and loathsome or hateful places? Second, which social and academic factors, including race and ethnicity, gender, age, social class, parental education, first-generation status, and academic interest, are most significant in shaping those thoughts? Using open-ended responses from 287 American students, coded into thematic categories and analyzed through descriptive and multivariate techniques, the paper offers three contributions. It shifts attention from the strength of human–nature connection to the content of students' thoughts about nature. It highlights the negative and ambivalent associations that tend to be overshadowed in the literature. And it demonstrates that although race matters, it operates alongside academic interest, gender, age, and family educational background, cautioning against simplistic narratives of minority disconnection from nature. Research Design and Data Collection The study used a cross-sectional survey design with a mixed approach to analysis. Open-ended responses were systematically coded into categories (Krippendorff, 2019), and the resulting binary indicators were then analyzed with descriptive and multivariate statistics (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018). This approach suited the research question. Closed-ended instruments such as the Connectedness to Nature Scale (Mayer & Frantz, 2004) or the New Ecological Paradigm (Dunlap et al., 2000) measure attitudes toward researcher-defined constructs. Our aim was to learn what students spontaneously think about when they contemplate nature, so respondents had to be free to name their own ideas. Data were collected from undergraduate students at two public universities in the United States during one academic term. Instructors in a range of general education and discipline-specific courses distributed an anonymous online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform, following tailored-design principles for web surveys Dillman et al., 2014). Courses were chosen deliberately to reach students with different academic interests, including environmental science, biology, sociology, business, education, and the humanities. Participation was voluntary, and some instructors offered a small amount of extra credit, with an alternative assignment of equal effort available. The institutional review board at the lead author's university approved the protocol and classified it as exempt. Informed consent was obtained electronically before respondents could begin the survey. A total of 301 students opened the survey. Fourteen were excluded because they did not complete the open-ended prompt or the demographic items, leaving an analytic sample of 287 (95.3% of those who started). Because the sample is non-probability and drawn from a limited number of courses, the findings are not generalizable to all American students. We treat the analysis as exploratory and focus on the direction, magnitude, and consistency of associations rather than population estimates. Instrument and Measures The questionnaire contained an open-ended prompt followed by demographic and background items. The prompt read: "When you think of nature, what thoughts, ideas, images, or feelings come to mind? Please list or describe as many as you wish." It was deliberately neutral. It did not mention fear, danger, or any other valence, so that such themes would emerge only if respondents introduced them (Kellert, 1996). Responses ranged from single words to multi-sentence paragraphs. Dependent variables. Responses were coded for eight concepts that prior scholarship links to negative or ambivalent relationships with nature: 1) disconnection from or lack of contact with nature; (2) predators or dangerous animals, 3) getting lost, (4) loathsome or hateful places (e.g., statements that nature is disgusting, dirty, boring, or hated); (5) fear, 6) danger, (7) natural hazards (e.g., storms, wildfires, floods, venomous insects); and (8) human-made hazards (e.g., pollution, toxic exposure, development, climate disruption). These categories build [22] on research on fear and avoidance of natural settings Bixler & Floyd, 1997; Ulrich, 1993), on racialized experiences of outdoor spaces (Finney, 2014, Flores et al., 2018, Mott, 2018), and on the notion of "nature-deficit" (Louv, 2005). Each concept was coded 1 if the respondent mentioned it at least once and 0 otherwise. We analyzed presence rather than frequency of mention because the responses were brief and counts would have conflated verbosity with salience. Independent variables. Race/ethnicity was collapsed into a binary variable (white = 1, racial/ethnic minority = 0) because cell sizes for individual groups were too small for stable estimation. Gender was coded as woman = 1 and man = 0. Seven respondents who identified as non-binary or declined to answer were retained in descriptive tables but excluded from multivariate models for lack of power. We discuss this limitation below. Age was measured in years. Class standing (first-year through senior) was entered as an ordinal variable treated as continuous after sensitivity tests with dummy coding produced substantively identical results. Parental education was the highest level attained by either parent (ordinal, 1 = less than high school to 6 = graduate degree). First-generation status was coded 1 if neither parent had completed a four-year degree. Because parental education and first-generation status are conceptually and empirically related, they were never entered in the same model. Academic interest was operationalized as whether a student's major or intended major was in a natural resource, environmental, or life science field 1) or another field 0). Using major as a proxy for interest follows prior work on how [32] disciplinary socialization shapes environmental orientations (Hand & Van Liere, 1984). Coding Procedure and Reliability Coding followed a hybrid deductive–inductive strategy (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006). A preliminary codebook was derived from the literature, and two coders then independently read a random 20% subsample (n = 57) and proposed additional categories and clarified decision rules. Definitions and exemplar quotations were revised in two rounds. Both coders then independently coded the full dataset, blind to respondent demographics. Intercoder agreement was assessed with Cohen's kappa: [2] κ = (p₀ − pₑ) / 1 − pₑ), where p₀ However, is observed agreement and pₑ is agreement expected by chance. [22] Kappa values for the eight categories ranged from 0.78 to 0.91, which Landis and Koch (1977) classify as substantial to almost perfect. Disagreements were resolved by discussion until consensus was reached, and the consensus codes were used in all analyses. Statistical Analysis Analysis proceeded in three stages. First, we calculated frequencies and percentages for each concept for the full sample and by race/ethnicity, gender, and academic interest. Bivariate associations between the binary outcomes and categorical predictors were tested with Pearson's chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when any expected cell count was below five.

Spoken language identification (SLD) is the task of determining the language of a speech utterance without prior knowledge of its content or speaker. It is a front-end component of many multilingual speech processing systems, including automatic speech recognition, spoken-document retrieval, speech translation; and [30] call-center routing (Zissman, 1996; Li et al., 2013). A growing application area is the intelligent vehicle, where voice interfaces must serve drivers and passengers who speak different languages and who expect the system [19] [38] to respond to short commands without manual language selection (Deng and Huang, 2004). In this setting, utterances are often brief, typically one to three seconds; the acoustic environment is noisy, and computational resources are limited. These conditions make accurate, low-latency SLD both practically valuable and technically demanding. Early SLD systems relied on phonotactic information. Parallel phone recognition followed by language modeling PPRLM) decodes speech into phone sequences with one or "more" phone recognizers and scores the sequences with language-specific n-gram [18] models (Zissman, 1996). Although effective for long utterances, these systems require phonetically transcribed data and degrade sharply when little speech is available, because short utterances yield too few phone tokens for reliable statistics. Acoustic approaches, in contrast, model the spectral distribution of each language directly. Gaussian mixture models trained on shifted delta cepstral (SDC) features (Torres-Carrasquillo et al., 2002) and total variability i-vector modeling (Dehak et al., 2011) became the dominant paradigm in the 2000s and early 2010s, and i-vectors combined with discriminative back-ends achieved strong results in the NIST language recognition evaluations (Martínez et al., 2011). However, i-vector estimation is itself unreliable for short segments, since the posterior of the latent variable has high variance when few frames are observed (Kanagasundaram et al., 2011). Deep neural networks (DNNs) have substantially changed the field. Lopez-Moreno et al. (2014) showed that a DNN taking SDC-like inputs and trained directly for language classification outperformed i-vector baselines, particularly on short test segments. Subsequent studies used DNN-derived posteriors or bottleneck activations as replacements for, or complements to, conventional cepstral features in the i-vector pipeline (Richardson et al., 2015; Ferrer et al., 2014). Bottleneck features are taken from a narrow hidden layer of a network trained on an auxiliary classification task, and they compress phonetically discriminative information into a low-dimensional representation (Grézl et al., 2009). Because the auxiliary task, typically senone or phone classification, can be trained with abundant transcribed speech from a single resource-rich language, However, bottleneck extraction is a form of transfer learning that carries linguistic [2] knowledge into settings where language-labeled data are scarce. Recurrent architectures have also been applied to SLD. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) model temporal dependencies and can produce an utterance-level decision in an end-to-end fashion, and they have been reported to be particularly effective for short utterances (Gonzalez-Dominguez et al.; 2014). Further end-to-end systems based on However, convolutional and attention mechanisms have since been proposed (Lozano-Diez et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2018). Despite this progress, several issues remain unresolved. First, the performance of nearly all SLD systems still declines markedly as the test duration shrinks from 10 s or 30 s to 3 s or [2] 1 s. The AP16 and AP17 Oriental Language Recognition [5] (OLR) challenges, which focus on closely related and acoustically confusable Asian languages, illustrate this clearly: error rates on 1 s utterances are several times those on 3 s or longer utterances (Wang et al.; 2018). Second, most work on improving short-utterance performance has concentrated on the model side, for example through improved embeddings, variance compensation, or data augmentation of the training set. Comparatively little attention has been paid to manipulating the test utterance itself so as to provide the classifier with more diverse evidence from the same limited signal. Third, although bottleneck features trained on phonetic targets are widely used with i-vector back-ends, their combination with LSTM-based end-to-end classifiers has received less systematic study, particularly when the phonetic training language (here Mandarin) is itself one of the target languages or is closely related to them. Speech rate offers a possible route to addressing the second issue. Speaking rate varies naturally across speakers, languages, and situations, and it alters the temporal structure of phonetic realizations while leaving much of the spectral identity intact. Time-scale modification (TSM) algorithms alter the duration of a signal without changing its pitch. The phase vocoder, which operates in the short-time Fourier domain and adjusts the synthesis hop size while maintaining phase coherence, is a well-established TSM technique (Flanagan and Golden, 1966; Laroche and Dolson, 1999). We hypothesize that presenting a classifier with the original utterance together with slowed and accelerated versions of it effectively lengthens the observed sequence and exposes the network to several plausible temporal realizations of the same content, thereby reducing the uncertainty of the decision for very short inputs. Related uses of speed perturbation have been shown to benefit training of acoustic models (Ko et al., 2015), but the application of TSM and splicing at test time for SLD [38] has not, to our knowledge, been examined. The research question addressed here [30] is therefore twofold: whether LSTM networks fed with deep bottleneck features learned from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classifier provide an effective end-to-end SLD solution for short utterances, and whether phase-vocoder-based TSM of the test utterance, combined with splicing of the original, slowed, and accelerated versions, can further reduce errors when only one to three seconds of speech are available. The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we propose an end-to-end SLD framework in which an LSTM classifier is trained on bottleneck features extracted from a DNN trained for Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification, thereby transferring phonetic knowledge into the language identification task while keeping the model compact enough for in-vehicle deployment. Second, we introduce a test-time augmentation strategy that applies phase-vocoder TSM to produce speech-rate-reduced and speech-rate-increased versions of an utterance and splices them with the original to extend its effective length. Third, we evaluate the approach on the AP17-OLR database and show that it improves identification performance relative to baseline systems, with the largest gains for 1 s and 3 s test durations, which are the conditions most relevant to intelligent-vehicle interaction. The remainder of this paper describes the proposed system, the experimental configuration, and the results, and then discusses the findings and their implications. Database and experimental design Experiments were run on the AP17-OLR database released for the Oriental Language Recognition challenge (Tang et al., 2017), an extension of AP16-OLR (Wang et al., 2016). It contains telephone-quality and close-talking recordings of ten languages: Mandarin, Cantonese, "Indonesian," Japanese, Russian, Korean, Vietnamese, Kazakh, Tibetan and Uyghur. All audio was resampled to 16 kHz with 16-bit quantization. The training partition provides roughly 10 h of speech per language from multiple speakers of both genders. The test partition was evaluated at nominal durations of 1 s, 3 s and a longer full-length condition. The 1 s and 3 s conditions were the main focus because they best represent the short-utterance constraint of in-vehicle voice interfaces. A held-out 10% of the training utterances, stratified by language and speaker, served as a development set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. No test data were used in However, model fitting or tuning. The study used [14] a controlled; ablation-style design with three factors: (i) the input representation conventional filterbank features versus deep bottleneck features, DBF), ii) the back-end classifier frame-level DNN [26] versus LSTM), and (iii) the test-time utterance extension strategy (original utterance only versus splicing with time-scale-modified versions). Each factor was varied while the others were held fixed, so the contribution of each component could be isolated. Bottleneck feature extraction by transfer learning DBFs were obtained by transfer learning from a Mandarin acoustic-phonetic classification task. A feed-forward DNN was trained to classify each frame into context-dependent tied-state (senone) targets derived from a Mandarin corpus with forced alignments (Bu et al., 2017). Alignments came from a GMM-HMM system built with Kaldi (Povey et al., 2011). The input was 40-dimensional log Mel-filterbank coefficients with cepstral mean normalization, computed over 25 ms windows with a 10 ms shift. Frames were spliced with a context of ±5 to give a 440-dimensional input vector. The network had five hidden layers of 1024 sigmoid units, with a 64-unit linear bottleneck layer placed before the final hidden layer, following Grézl et al. [36] (2007). It was initialized by layer-wise pre-training and then fine-tuned with stochastic gradient "descent" to minimize cross-entropy. The learning rate was halved when the development-set frame accuracy improved by [11] less than 0.5% absolute. After training; the layers above the bottleneck were discarded. The 64-dimensional bottleneck activations of each frame [5] were used as the language-independent but phonetically informed representation for all ten OLR languages. The mapping was frozen during LSTM training, so no language labels influenced the DBF extractor. LSTM-based language identification The back-end was an end-to-end sequence classifier based on the LSTM architecture Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), following its application to LID by Gonzalez-Dominguez et al. (2014). The DBF sequence of an utterance [19] was fed to two stacked [16] unidirectional "LSTM" layers of 512 cells each. A fully connected layer with a 10-way softmax followed. Unidirectional recurrence was chosen to allow low-latency operation in embedded settings. Training used truncated backpropagation through time over segments of 100 frames, and the label was applied to every frame. At test time the utterance-level posterior was the mean of "the" frame-level log posteriors over the last 80% of frames, which discards the initial [10] frames before the recurrent state has accumulated sufficient context. To match the target conditions, training utterances were randomly cropped to 1–5 s segments in each epoch. Optimization used Adam (Kingma & [29] Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of 1×10⁻³, a mini-batch of 64 segments, gradient-norm clipping at 5, and dropout of 0.3 on non-recurrent connections Srivastava et al., 2014). Training stopped when development-set cross-entropy had not improved for five consecutive epochs, and the best checkpoint was retained. Two baselines used the same data and tuning protocol: an LSTM on 40-dimensional filterbank features, and a frame-averaging DNN on DBF. Phase-vocoder time-scale modification and utterance splicing To lengthen short test utterances without needing additional speech, each test signal was modified in speaking rate by a phase-vocoder-based time-scale modification (TSM) algorithm (Flanagan & Golden, 1966). We used the identity phase-locking variant; which reduces phasiness artifacts (Laroche & Dolson, 1999). The short-time Fourier transform used a 32 ms Hann window with 75% overlap at the analysis stage. The synthesis hop was scaled by the TSM factor α, defined as the ratio of output to input duration. Two factors were used, α = 1.25 slower speech) and α = 0.80 (faster speech). These values were selected on the development set from the candidate set {0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.1, 1.25, 1.4}, because they changed rate noticeably while keeping spectral envelopes and pitch intelligible. Because the vocoder preserves pitch and formant structure, the modified signals preserve language-specific spectral cues while changing the temporal realization of phonemes. For each test utterance, three versions (original, slowed, accelerated) were passed through the same DBF extractor. The three DBF sequences were concatenated in time to give a single sequence about 1.0 + 1.25 + 0.8 = 3.05 times the original duration. A single LSTM forward pass over the spliced sequence yielded the decision. The splicing order was fixed as original, slowed, accelerated, and a development-set check with all six permutations showed no meaningful differences. The LSTM was not retrained on spliced data, which allowed us to test whether the extension strategy acts purely as a test-time enhancement. Evaluation metrics and statistical analysis Performance was reported with the average cost Cavg and the identification accuracy. Cavg was computed following the NIST LRE 2009 definition, which averages miss and false-alarm costs over all target–non-target language pairs with equal priors (Ptarget = 0.5) and unit costs (Brümmer & van Leeuwen, 2006). Relational tables are the dominant format for structured data on the web, in enterprise databases, and in open data portals. Understanding what the columns of [29] a table represent is a prerequisite for many data management tasks. Knowing that a column contains person names, birth places, or monetary amounts, rather than merely strings or numbers, enables data cleaning and validation, schema matching and data integration, data discovery in large lakes, and semantic search over tables (Cafarella et al., 2008; Fernandez et al., 2018, Hulsebos et al., 2019). Such semantic types go beyond the atomic types (integer, string, date) used by database systems, and they correspond to concepts in knowledge bases such as DBpedia and Freebase, [10] or to the properties of schema.org (Bizer et [34] al., 2009; Guha et al., 2016). In practice, however, the semantic [25] types of columns are rarely available. Column headers are frequently missing, ambiguous, abbreviated, or inconsistent across sources, and manual annotation does not scale to the millions of tables that must be processed in modern pipelines. Automatic semantic type detection has therefore received sustained attention. Existing approaches fall broadly into four families. Dictionary and regular-expression approaches, as implemented in commercial data preparation tools, match [24] column values against curated lists [8] or patterns (Trifacta, 2019; Microsoft, 2019). These are precise for types with regular surface forms, such as email addresses or postal codes, but they cope poorly with dirty or incomplete values and they support only a small, manually maintained set of [28] types. Knowledge-base matching approaches link cell values to entities and infer a column type from the linked entities' classes Limaye et al., 2010, Venetis et al., 2011, Mulwad et al., [35] 2013, Ritze et al., 2015). These approaches depend on the coverage of the knowledge base and on the quality of entity linking, and they work less well for numeric columns and for long-tail or domain-specific values. Probabilistic and graphical-model approaches jointly infer types, entities, and relations in a table, but they typically require expensive [18] inference and large knowledge resources (Limaye et al., 2010; Mulwad et al., 2013). Finally, machine learning approaches treat type detection as a classification problem over columns. Early work used hand-crafted features of column values with traditional classifiers (Pham et al., 2016, Ramnandan et al., 2015). More recently, Sherlock (Hulsebos et al., 2019) trained a multi-layer neural network on over six hundred thousand columns from the VizNet corpus (Hu et al., 2019), using character-level, word-embedding, and global statistical features of the values in each column to predict one of 78 DBpedia-derived semantic types. Related deep learning models for tables, such as those used for column type annotation with learned embeddings (Chen et al., 2019, Zhang, 2018), also show that learned representations can outperform rule-based baselines. Despite this progress, the existing approaches share a limitation that we consider fundamental: they predict the type of each column in isolation. A column is treated as an unordered bag of values, and the other columns of the same table are ignored. Yet values alone are often insufficient to determine a type. A column of short strings such as "Florence", Warsaw, and "Lyon" could be a city, a [31] birth place, or a location of a company; a column of numbers between 1 and 100 could be an age, a rank, a weight, or a percentage. Human annotators resolve such ambiguity effortlessly by looking at the rest of the table. If neighboring columns contain player names, teams, and positions, the ambiguous string column is more likely to be a birth place than a company location, whereas the same values beside company names and revenues suggest the opposite. The semantic types in a table are thus not independent: they co-occur in systematic patterns reflecting the table's subject, and they exhibit dependencies among adjacent or related columns. Single-column models cannot exploit these regularities, and as a result they confuse types with similar value distributions, perform poorly on the many types for which values are uninformative, and degrade when columns are noisy. Incorporating table context raises several challenges. First, context must be represented in a way that generalizes across tables of different widths and compositions, without presupposing the identity of the other columns' types, [3] which are themselves unknown at prediction time. Second, the model must capture two kinds of context: a global, table-level notion of subject or theme, and a local notion of how the type of one column constrains the types of others. Third, the approach should remain scalable and trainable on a realistic corpus of web tables in which type frequencies are highly skewed, so that rare types are not sacrificed to improve aggregate accuracy. [36] Finally, evaluation must go beyond support-weighted metrics, which are dominated by frequent types, and also consider macro-averaged measures that reflect performance across the whole type inventory. This paper asks whether, and to what extent, the semantic types of columns can be detected more accurately by jointly modeling column values and the table context in which the column appears. We further ask which kinds of context are useful, how much each contributes, and for which types the gains are concentrated. To answer these questions we introduce Sato, a hybrid model for contextual semantic type detection. Sato builds on a single-column deep learning predictor with value-based features and augments it with two complementary sources of context. To capture table-level semantics, Sato derives a table intent vector with a topic model (Blei et al., 2003) trained on the values of entire tables, treating each table as a document, and supplies this vector as additional input to the column-wise predictor. To capture dependencies among the types of columns within a table, Sato [3] employs structured prediction in the form of a linear-chain conditional random field (Lafferty et al., 2001) that sits on top of the column-wise scores and decodes a jointly [5] consistent type assignment for all columns. The combination allows the model [35] to use value evidence, However, global table theme, and inter-column type co-occurrence in a single framework while remaining efficient at inference time. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We evaluate Sato on a large-scale corpus of web tables with 78 semantic types, showing support-weighted and macro-average F1 scores of 0.925 and 0.735, respectively, which exceed the state-of-the-art by a significant margin, with the largest gains for types that are ambiguous from values alone and for types with few training examples. 4. We provide an extensive analysis of overall and per-type performance, with ablations that isolate the contribution of each modeling component and each feature category, and we discuss the cases in which context [17] helps, and those in which it does not. The proliferation of network-based services in the home has changed what residential networks are expected to deliver. A typical smart home now carries high-definition video streaming, cloud gaming, video conferencing, voice assistants, security cameras, and dozens of low-power Internet of Things (IoT) devices, all sharing one broadband access link (Sivaraman et al., 2015). These applications place very different demands on the network. Interactive voice and gaming traffic is sensitive to delay and jitter, streaming video needs sustained throughput, and sensor telemetry tolerates delay but requires reliability. Best-effort forwarding cannot satisfy all of these demands at once, and a single congested gateway can degrade the quality of experience (QoE) of the whole household (Dainotti et al., 2012). Network operators therefore need to measure and manage network quality of service (QoS) per application, not only per link or per subscriber. Software-defined networking (SDN) gives operators new tools for this. By separating the control plane from the data plane, SDN allows centralized, programmable allocation of resources in the core and aggregation networks (Kreutz et al., 2015). Operators can steer flows, reserve bandwidth, and adjust queue disciplines in response to measured conditions. However, core-network control alone cannot guarantee end-to-end QoS. Much of the delay variation, packet loss, and contention occurs at the last hop, where the home gateway multiplexes traffic from many devices over a constrained access link. Without knowing which application generated a given packet, the operator cannot attribute degradation to a particular service, cannot verify that service-level agreements are met, and cannot apply differentiated treatment where it matters most. The smart home gateway is therefore a natural vantage point for application-aware measurement and control from the operator side. Obtaining application awareness at the gateway is difficult because most traffic is now encrypted. Over 90% of web traffic uses TLS, and QUIC, VPN tunnels, and DNS-over-HTTPS further reduce the information visible on the wire (Rescorla, 2018). Port-based classification has long been unreliable because applications share well-known ports or use dynamic ones, and deep packet inspection DPI) is ineffective on encrypted payloads while also raising legal and ethical concerns about user privacy (Moore & Papagiannaki, 2005; Finsterbusch et al., 2014). Consequently, research has moved toward statistical and machine-learning methods that use only side-channel features such as packet sizes, inter-arrival times, directions, and flow durations (Nguyen & Armitage, 2008). Early work used classical classifiers such as naïve Bayes, support vector machines, and decision trees on hand-crafted flow statistics (Williams et al., 2006; Moore & Zuev, 2005). More recent studies apply deep learning, including convolutional and recurrent networks, to raw or lightly processed traffic, reporting high accuracy for encrypted traffic characterization and application identification (Wang et al., 2017; Lotfollahi et al., 2020; Aceto et al., 2019). Related work has also shown that IoT devices can be identified from their traffic signatures (Sivanathan et al., 2019) and that encrypted video services leak identifiable patterns (Dubin et al., 2017). Despite this progress, three gaps limit the applicability of existing approaches to operator-side management in smart home gateways. First, most studies treat classification as a single flat problem, assigning each flow to one of many fine-grained applications. This ignores the fact that the operator's QoS decisions depend mainly on the traffic's service requirements, such as real-time interactive, streaming, bulk transfer, or background, and not on application identity. A flat classifier with many classes is also more costly and often less accurate than needed for such decisions. Second, accuracy and latency are rarely considered together. Many high-accuracy models need However, complete flows or long observation windows, which delays the decision until a flow is nearly finished and is of little use for real-time QoS control. Conversely, lightweight early-classification methods "typically" sacrifice the granularity needed for tasks such as statistical reporting or billing. Third, the classification objective is seldom linked to the operator's needs. QoS measurement, usage statistics, and billing between network and service "providers" all require trustworthy application-level information, yet it must be obtained without decrypting traffic or compromising user privacy and network security. These gaps motivate our central research [25] question: how can a network operator classify encrypted traffic at the smart home gateway so as to support both real-time, QoS-driven resource management and accurate fine-grained application accounting, without inspecting payloads? We hypothesize that the two requirements are best [3] handled by separate classifiers operating at different levels of abstraction and on different time scales, rather than by one monolithic model. To test this hypothesis, we propose a two-level hierarchical encrypted packet classification scheme. The service level groups applications that share the same network QoS requirements and uses a fast deep-learning classifier designed for real-time operation with high accuracy on a small number of classes. Its output can drive SDN-based traffic prioritization and end-to-end QoS measurement directly. The application level distinguishes fine-grained applications within and across service classes using a non-real-time classifier that can exploit richer flow-level information to maximize accuracy. Its output [18] supports statistical data collection, billing to service providers, and longer-term analytics. Both levels rely only on metadata observable from encrypted traffic, so user privacy is preserved and no keys or payload However, access are required. The contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We formulate encrypted traffic classification for smart home gateways as a hierarchical problem whose service level and application level are tied to distinct operator objectives, real-time QoS management and fine-grained accounting, respectively, and we describe how the scheme fits into an SDN-managed network architecture. 2. We design a fast deep-learning classifier for the service level that achieves real-time classification from limited per-flow information while maintaining high accuracy. 3. We develop a non-real-time application-level classifier that attains high accuracy for fine-grained applications, and we show how it complements the service-level classifier. 4. We evaluate both classifiers experimentally, comparing accuracy, classification latency, and computational efficiency against representative baselines, and we discuss the trade-offs that justify the hierarchical design. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system architecture, the data, and the design of the two classifiers. Section 3 presents the evaluation results. Section [4] 4 discusses implications, limitations, and directions for future work. Overview of the hierarchical framework The proposed classifier runs at the smart home gateway and uses only metadata observable in encrypted traffic, so payloads are never inspected. Classification has two levels. The service level maps each flow to one of K However, classes that share network QoS requirements (e.g., real-time conferencing, streaming video, interactive/IoT control, bulk transfer, and background traffic). It must [14] decide within a "short" observation window so that the gateway can mark or queue packets in real time. The [24] application level assigns the flow to a fine-grained application (e.g.; a specific video-conferencing or streaming service). It is run on completed or long-observed flows, offline or near-line, for billing, statistics, and QoS auditing. The two levels are decoupled. The service-level decision is not conditioned on the application label, which avoids error propagation, but the application-level classifier can use the service-level output as a prior to restrict its candidate set. Data collection and labeling Two data sources were used. The first was the public ISCX VPN–nonVPN dataset (Draper-Gil et al., 2016), which contains labeled encrypted and tunneled traffic from common applications and is widely used as a benchmark for encrypted traffic classification (Wang et al., 2017; Lotfollahi et al., 2020). The second was traffic captured in a smart home testbed built for this study. It comprised a residential-grade gateway running Open vSwitch on a Linux single-board computer, with a mix of smartphones, laptops, a smart television, IP cameras, voice assistants, and smart plugs. Traces were captured at the LAN-facing interface with tcpdump over several weeks, under both Wi-Fi and wired access and at different times of day, to capture variation in congestion and background load. Ground-truth application labels were obtained by running one application at a time in controlled sessions, and by host-side process-to-socket attribution for concurrent sessions (in the manner of Taylor et al., 2016). Each application label was then mapped to one of the K service classes according to published QoS requirements for delay, jitter, loss, and throughput (ITU-T G.1010; 3GPP TS 23.203). Two annotators independently checked the mapping. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Preprocessing and flow definition Packets were grouped into bidirectional flows by the 5-tuple (source and destination IP, source and destination port, transport protocol), with a 120 s inactivity timeout for flow termination. Non-informative traffic such as DNS, mDNS, and DHCP was removed, as was any flow with fewer than 10 packets. To avoid label leakage, IP addresses, ports, and TLS handshake fields such as SNI were masked and not used as inputs. Retransmitted and zero-payload ACK packets were retained, because they carry information on transport behavior. For the service-level classifier, each flow was represented by its first N = 30 packets (N was selected in the experiments described below), as a matrix X ∈ ℝ^{N×3}. Each row contains the signed packet size (positive for uplink, negative for downlink), the inter-arrival time, and the transport-layer window size. Shorter flows were zero-padded. Packet sizes were scaled by the MTU, and inter-arrival times were log-transformed and standardized: x̃t = (log(1 + Δtt) − μ) / σ, where μ and σ were estimated on the training set only. For "the" application-level classifier, each flow was summarized by 96 statistical features computed over the full flow. These included the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, skewness, and kurtosis of packet length and inter-arrival time per direction, flow duration, byte and packet counts, uplink/downlink ratios, burst length and burst interval statistics, and the number of active/idle periods (Draper-Gil et al., 2016; Moore & Zuev, 2005). Features were ranked by mutual information with the label, and those with pairwise correlation above 0.95 were pruned. Service-level classifier The service-level model is a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network, chosen for low inference latency on gateway-class hardware. It has three convolutional blocks (kernel size 3, with 32, 64, and 64 channels), each followed by batch normalization, ReLU activation, and max-pooling. Global average pooling and a 64-unit fully connected layer with dropout (p = 0.3) follow, and a softmax layer outputs the class probabilities: p(k | X) = exp(zk) / Σj exp(zj). Parameters θ were learned by minimizing class-weighted cross-entropy, L(θ) = −(1/B) Σ{i=1}^{B} Σ{k=1}^{K} wk y{ik} log p(k | Xi; θ) + λ‖θ‖², where wk is inversely proportional to class frequency, which counters class imbalance, and λ is the weight decay. Training used Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of [28] 10⁻³, batch size 128, and early stopping on validation loss with a patience of 10 epochs. The window length N was varied over {5, 10, 20, 30, 50} to characterize the [14] trade-off between classification delay and accuracy. To satisfy the real-time constraint, the model was exported to ONNX and benchmarked on the testbed gateway CPU, without a GPU. Application-level classifier The application-level classifier is a gradient-boosted "decision" tree ensemble (XGBoost; Chen [28] & Guestrin, 2016) operating on the statistical features. Gradient boosting minimizes the regularized [8] objective 𝓛 = Σi l(yi, ŷi) + Σm Ω(fm), Ω(f) = γT + ½λ‖w‖², where T is the number of leaves and w the leaf [10] weights. Random forest (Breiman, 2001), k-nearest neighbors, and a support vector machine with RBF kernel were trained as baselines, as was a CNN–LSTM on raw packet sequences, which represents recent deep learning approaches (Lopez-Martin et al., 2017). Hyperparameters (tree depth, learning rate, number of estimators, subsample ratio, γ, λ) were tuned by Bayesian optimization with 50 trials on the validation folds. Experimental design and evaluation protocol Data were split at the session level, not the flow level, into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test sets. This prevents near-duplicate flows from the same session appearing on both sides of a split. Stratified five-fold cross-validation, repeated three times with different seeds, was used for model selection and [25] for [20] estimating variability. Two additional tests assessed generalization. Microsurgical free tissue transfer has become a cornerstone of reconstructive surgery. It is used to restore form and function after tumor resection, trauma, burns, and chronic wounds, and in the head and neck, breast, and extremities. With experienced teams and refined techniques, reported success rates now exceed 95% in many high-volume centers (Khouri et al., 1998; Pohlenz et al., 2012). Even so, vascular compromise at the anastomosis remains the leading cause of flap loss. Arterial inflow obstruction or venous outflow obstruction, usually due to thrombosis, kinking, compression, or vasospasm, occurs in roughly 5% to 25% of cases, depending on the series and the type of flap (Chen et al., 2007; Kroll et al., 1996). Most of these events occur within the first 48 to 72 hours after surgery (Kroll et al., 1996). The prognosis of a compromised flap depends strongly on how quickly the problem is recognized. Muscle and other metabolically active tissues tolerate warm ischemia poorly, and the no-reflow phenomenon limits reperfusion after prolonged ischemia (Wang et al., 2015). Salvage rates are high when re-exploration takes place within a few hours of vascular compromise. They fall sharply when the diagnosis is delayed, reaching about 30% or lower for flaps explored late (Yii et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2007). Reliable early detection is therefore as important to flap survival as the original operation. Many monitoring methods have been proposed. Clinical observation of skin color, capillary refill, temperature, turgor, and bleeding on pinprick is still the most widely used approach and the standard against which other techniques are compared (Smit et al., 2010). It costs little and needs no equipment. However, it is subjective and depends on the experience of the examiner. Intermittent assessment can miss events that develop between rounds, and nighttime examination under poor lighting is unreliable. Clinical signs also tend to appear late, when ischemia is already established. Buried flaps and those without a skin paddle, such as free jejunum or muscle flaps used in pharyngeal and intraoral reconstruction, cannot be assessed by skin appearance at all. Several adjunctive technologies have been developed to address these limitations. Handheld Doppler ultrasonography detects flow in the pedicle or in perforators, but it is operator dependent and intermittent, and it can give false reassurance when the signal comes from adjacent vessels (Smit et al., 2010). Implantable Doppler probes allow continuous monitoring of anastomotic flow but need a second invasive procedure to place and remove, may dislodge, and have been reported to produce false-positive results (Rozen et al., 2008). Laser Doppler flowmetry and photoplethysmography give continuous measures of microcirculatory perfusion. They are sensitive to motion, probe position, and ambient light, and they provide relative rather than absolute values (Hölzle et al., 2006). Tissue oxygen tension, pH, and temperature probes, microdialysis, and fluorescence angiography with indocyanine green offer physiological information. Their drawbacks include invasiveness, cost, the need for specialized personnel, and the lack of true continuous bedside measurement (Udesen et al., 2000; Smit et al., 2010). No single technique has become a universal standard, and the search for a monitor that is noninvasive, continuous, objective, and simple to use is still active. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is an optical technique that may meet these requirements. Biological tissue is relatively transparent to light in the near-infrared range of about 700 to 900 nm. In this range oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin have distinct absorption spectra, so measuring light attenuation at several wavelengths allows the relative concentrations of each chromophore to be estimated. From these, a regional tissue oxygen saturation can be calculated (Jöbsis, 1977). Because the signal comes mainly from small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, and venules), NIRS reflects the balance between oxygen delivery and consumption in the microvascular bed. It does not require pulsatile flow. NIRS has been used for years to monitor cerebral oxygenation during cardiac and carotid surgery and in neonatal intensive care, and in muscle physiology and the evaluation of peripheral vascular disease (Murkin and Arango, 2009). Its use in reconstructive surgery has been explored more recently. Early clinical studies in breast reconstruction and in head and neck and extremity flaps suggested that falling tissue oxygen saturation accompanies both arterial and venous compromise "and" may precede visible clinical changes (Keller, 2009; Repez et al., 2008; Steele et al., 2011). Different devices, probe designs, and algorithms have been used, however, and published experience is still heterogeneous. Many reports concentrate on breast flaps or on small series. Descriptions of the temporal relationship between the fall in regional oxygen saturation and the onset of visible color change are limited. This relationship determines whether the technique has practical value for earlier intervention and salvage. Information on how NIRS performs across the varied flap types and recipient sites seen in routine practice is also limited, particularly for the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy (INVOS) system, which uses a disposable adhesive sensor with a continuous bedside display. The gap this study addresses can be stated briefly. Flap surveillance still relies largely on subjective clinical examination, and the available adjuncts are invasive, intermittent, or technically demanding. NIRS is promising, but evidence is needed on whether continuous, noninvasive measurement of regional oxygen saturation can reliably detect arterial and venous insufficiency in a mixed series of free flaps, and whether it does so before clinical signs appear. We therefore asked whether postoperative monitoring of regional oxygen saturation with the INVOS system can detect vascular compromise in free flaps early enough to allow successful salvage. We prospectively monitored 57 patients undergoing free tissue transfer. We recorded regional oxygen saturation continuously after surgery and compared the trends with clinical findings and with the outcomes of re-exploration. This study makes three contributions. First, it describes the use of the INVOS system as a continuous, noninvasive flap monitor in a consecutive clinical series. Second, it documents the temporal behavior of regional oxygen saturation in cases of arterial and venous insufficiency, particularly its decline before pallor or congestion became visible. Third, it reports that all patients in whom insufficiency was detected were salvaged by re-exploration, which supports NIRS as a practical addition to postoperative flap monitoring. Study Design and Patients We conducted a prospective, single-center observational study of consecutive patients who underwent microsurgical free tissue transfer in our department of plastic and reconstructive surgery. A total of 57 patients were enrolled. Eligible patients were adults who had free flap reconstruction with a cutaneous or musculocutaneous component large enough to accommodate the optical sensor. Reconstructive indications included head and neck cancer defects, breast reconstruction, and traumatic or oncologic defects of the extremities. We excluded patients with flaps that had no skin paddle (e.g., buried flaps), patients with severe skin pigmentation disorders or extensive scarring at the planned sensor site, and patients who could not be monitored for at least 72 hours. The institutional review board approved the protocol. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Recorded demographic and clinical variables were age, sex, comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking history), flap type, recipient site, ischemia time, and anastomotic details. Surgical Procedure and Standard Postoperative Care Experienced microsurgeons performed all operations under general anesthesia. Anastomoses were done under an operating microscope with 9-0 or 10-0 monofilament nylon. Arterial anastomoses were end-to-end or end-to-side according to recipient vessel conditions. Venous anastomoses were done by hand-sewn technique or with a coupling device. Venous outflow was reconstructed with one or two veins depending on flap type. Intraoperative vessel patency was confirmed by the milking test However, and by inspecting flap bleeding after reperfusion. We did not use routine postoperative anticoagulation beyond a standard protocol of low-dose aspirin and adequate hydration, with unfractionated heparin given only at the surgeon's discretion in high-risk cases. After surgery, patients were nursed in a warm room (about 25–28 °C) [31] with the flap kept free of external pressure and with controlled head and limb positioning. Standard clinical monitoring was performed in parallel [6] with the investigational device. [6] It consisted of hourly assessment of flap color, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, and bleeding on pinprick for the first 24 hours, then every 2–4 hours until postoperative day 3, and every 8 hours thereafter. These However, clinical criteria have long been the reference standard for detecting vascular compromise (Disa et al., 2001; Smit et al., 2010). The nursing staff and clinicians who made clinical decisions applied the same criteria as for any patient. The clinical team also knew the oximetry readings, so decisions about re-exploration were made on the (17) combined clinical and device data. [29] Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Monitoring Regional tissue oxygen saturation (rSO2) was measured with the In-Vivo Optical Spectroscopy [7] (INVOS) oximeter (Somanetics, Troy, MI). The device uses the principle of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), which exploits the relative transparency of biological tissue to light at 700–1000 nm and the differing absorption spectra of oxygenated and (10) deoxygenated hemoglobin (Jöbsis, 1977). The oximeter uses two wavelengths (approximately 730 and 810 nm) generated by a light-emitting diode in a disposable adhesive sensor. Two silicon photodiode detectors placed at different distances from the emitter (shallow and deep) record the returning [30] light. Subtracting the shallow signal from the deep signal reduces the contribution of superficial tissue, so that the reported value reflects mainly a mixed arteriolar, capillary, and venular compartment in the (12) underlying tissue (Irwin et "al.," 1995; Stranc et al., 1998). The result is displayed continuously as a percentage (rSO2), and the device updates it every few seconds. Because the measurement is not pulsatile, it can be used in flaps with low or absent pulse pressure. Sensors were applied in the operating room immediately after completion of the anastomoses and reperfusion, once the flap was stable and bleeding had been controlled. The sensor was placed on the skin paddle, away from the pedicle and from the flap [14] edges and suture lines, and avoiding visible superficial [16] veins. Placement was chosen to minimize interference from ambient light. The sensor was covered with an opaque dressing and fixed with minimal pressure so that it would not compress the flap. A second sensor was placed on normal skin at a comparable site near the flap as an internal reference for systemic changes in oxygenation. The position of the probe was marked so that it could be replaced at the same site if it detached. Baseline rSO2 was defined as the mean value over the first 30 minutes of stable recording after reperfusion. 1. Introduction Local features are among the most widely used building blocks of computer vision. A local feature consists of a detected image location, which may be a point or a region with an associated scale and orientation or affine shape, and a descriptor that summarises the appearance of its neighbourhood in a form suitable for comparison. Establishing correspondences between such features across images underpins a broad range of applications, including panorama stitching Brown and Lowe 2007), structure-from-motion SfM) and multi-view stereo (Snavely et al. 2006, Agarwal et al. 2011, Schönberger and Frahm 2016), visual localisation (Sattler et al. 2018), simultaneous localisation and mapping, and image retrieval. The central idea has been stable for decades. Distinctive, repeatable, and locally invariant structures are extracted independently in each image and then matched, typically by nearest-neighbour search in descriptor space followed by geometric verification with robust estimators such as RANSAC Fischler and Bolles 1981). The first generation of local features was entirely handcrafted. Corner detectors (Harris and Stephens 1988) and their scale-covariant extensions provided the foundations for the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) Lowe 2004), which combines a difference-of-Gaussians detector with a 128-dimensional gradient-orientation histogram descriptor. [19] SIFT proved so effective that, more than two decades after its introduction, it remains the default reference in many pipelines. Subsequent work pursued two goals: efficiency and invariance. SURF (Bay et al. 2008) approximated Gaussian derivatives with box filters and integral images. Binary descriptors such as BRIEF Calonder et al. 2010), ORB Rublee et al. 2011), BRISK (Leutenegger et al. 2011), and FREAK (Alahi et al. 2012) replaced floating-point vectors with bit strings compared via Hamming distance, together with fast corner detectors such as FAST [27] (Rosten and Drummond 2006). These changes reduced descriptor size and matching cost by one to two orders of magnitude. Parallel efforts, notably the affine-covariant region detectors systematically compared by Mikolajczyk et al. (2005), addressed viewpoint changes that exceed the capacity of similarity-invariant detectors. Since the early 2010s, machine learning has progressively replaced hand-design. Initially, learning was used to optimise individual components of an otherwise handcrafted pipeline. Examples include learned descriptor pooling regions and dimensionality reduction (Brown et al. 2011) and learned binary codes. Detectors were also trained to be repeatable under strong illumination changes Verdie et al. 2015). With the advent of deep convolutional networks (Krizhevsky et al. 2012), patch descriptors were learned end-to-end with siamese and triplet architectures (Han et al. 2015, Simo-Serra et al. 2015, Balntas et al. 2016). Hard-negative mining and descriptor-space regularisation then produced compact and highly discriminative descriptors such as L2-Net Tian et al. 2017) and HardNet (Mishchuk et al. 2017). More recently, networks have been trained to perform detection and description jointly, as in LIFT (Yi et al. 2016), LF-Net (Ono et al. 2018), SuperPoint (DeTone et al. 2018), D2-Net (Dusmanu et al. 2019), and R2D2 Revaud et al. 2019). Learned matchers that reason jointly over sets of features, such as SuperGlue (Sarlin et al. 2020), have further blurred the boundary between the feature and the matching stage. This rapid development has produced a large and heterogeneous literature. Methods differ in what they learn (detector, descriptor, orientation estimator, or matcher), in the supervision they require (patch labels, pose and depth from SfM, or self-supervised homographic adaptation), and in the data on which they are trained and evaluated. As a result, it is often unclear to a newcomer, and sometimes to experts, why [5] a particular design decision was made, which limitations of earlier approaches it addresses, and which of the many claimed improvements transfer to practical settings. Existing surveys either predate the deep-learning era (Mikolajczyk and Schmid 2005; Tuytelaars and Mikolajczyk 2008) or focus on one component, most commonly patch descriptors. They therefore rarely trace how the principles of handcrafted design, such as invariance by construction, normalisation, and robust pooling, reappear in learned models as data augmentation, architectural priors, and loss functions. The evaluation of local features raises a second and related difficulty. Early benchmarks measured detector repeatability and descriptor precision–recall on small sets of planar scenes with known homographies (Mikolajczyk et al. 2005, Mikolajczyk and Schmid 2005). Large-scale patch-level benchmarks later enabled deep descriptors to be trained and compared, with HPatches (Balntas et al. 2017) a prominent example. However, improvements measured However, on patch verification, retrieval, and matching tasks have not always carried over to downstream applications. Schönberger et al. (2017) showed that, within a full SfM pipeline, [9] learned descriptors that clearly outperformed SIFT on patch-level metrics did not consistently yield more complete or more accurate reconstructions. They also found that carefully tuned handcrafted variants remained highly competitive. Similar observations have been made for visual localisation (Sattler et al. 2018) and for wide-baseline stereo in the Image Matching Challenge Jin [34] et al. 2021). In that benchmark, performance depended strongly on the interplay between the feature type, the number of keypoints, the matcher, and the robust geometric estimator. These findings indicate that no single metric captures the quality of a local feature, and that the requirements of a task must guide both method choice and evaluation protocol. Our perspective is [30] motivated by 3D reconstruction, where the precise localisation of features is critical. In SfM and related geometric pipelines, correspondences are not merely used to decide whether two images show the same scene, they provide the measurements entering triangulation and bundle adjustment. Keypoint localisation errors of even However, a fraction [20] of a pixel therefore [31] propagate directly into pose and structure estimates. This requirement places particular emphasis on properties that are underemphasised in classification-style benchmarks, namely sub-pixel accuracy, repeatability [17] under viewpoint and illumination change, the spatial distribution of features, [37] and the rate of outliers after matching. Many modern learned detectors operate on downsampled feature maps or optimise a coarse notion of matchability, which can compromise localisation precision relative to scale-space detectors. Understanding where and why this happens requires returning to the design principles of the handcrafted methods. This paper makes three contributions. First, we provide a largely chronological overview of local features, moving from handcrafted detectors and descriptors, through methods that employ classical machine learning, to deep-learning-based approaches. For each family we explain the motivation behind its design, the challenges of feature [13] extraction it addresses, and the limitations that prompted subsequent developments. Second, we review the principal benchmarks and evaluation studies of local features, discussing the tasks they measure, the datasets and metrics they use, and the extent to which their conclusions hold for geometry-oriented applications. Third, we collect pointers to the most relevant literature and publicly available implementations, so that readers can reproduce, compare, and build upon the methods discussed. Taken together, we argue that understanding the handcrafted foundations is a prerequisite for using modern learned features effectively. It clarifies which invariances must be built into a model or learned from data, and it helps identify where learning provides genuine benefits for 3D reconstruction and where established methods remain difficult to surpass. Review design and scope. We conducted a structured narrative review of local feature detection and description, structured around the requirements of image-based 3D reconstruction, where sub-pixel localization accuracy and geometric consistency matter more than recognition-level invariance. The review followed the transparency principles of systematic reviews (Page et al., 2021) while retaining a chronological narrative organization, because the conceptual dependencies between methods for example, how learned descriptors inherit design choices from SIFT-like gradient histograms) are central to our argument. We distinguish three families: (i) handcrafted methods, whose detectors and descriptors are fully specified by analytical operators Harris and Stephens, 1988, Lowe, 2004; Bay et al., 2008, Rublee et al., 2011), (ii) classical machine-learning methods, in which parameters, pooling regions or binary tests are optimized from data without end-to-end representation learning (Winder and Brown, 2007; Brown et al., 2011; Calonder et al., 2010); and iii) deep-learning methods, in which a convolutional network produces keypoints, descriptors, or both Yi et al., 2016, DeTone et al., 2018, Mishchuk et al., 2017; Dusmanu et al., 2019; Revaud et al., 2019). Literature identification and selection. Candidate publications were retrieved from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library and arXiv, together with the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, BMVC, and TPAMI/IJCV from 1988 to 2022. Search strings combined local feature", "keypoint", "interest point", "patch descriptor, "feature matching" and "structure from motion with learned, "binary", or "convolutional". Backward and forward citation chaining was applied to seminal papers and benchmark studies. Inclusion criteria were: (a) a method that either detects keypoints or regions, or computes a descriptor from a local image support; (b) a quantitative evaluation on at least one public dataset, and c) sufficient detail for the algorithm to be reproduced, or publicly available code. Papers addressing only global image descriptors, learned matchers operating without a local-feature stage, or semantic keypoints (such as human pose) were excluded, although detector-free and graph-based matching approaches (Sarlin et al., 2020) are mentioned where they clarify the role of the descriptor. Where several versions of a method existed, we used the peer-reviewed version and noted the official implementation. For each included method we extracted a fixed set of attributes: detector type (corner, blob, learned score map), scale and affine handling, descriptor dimensionality and data type (floating point or binary), training data and supervision, and reported computational cost. Benchmarks and datasets considered. We reviewed evaluation protocols according to the task they measure. Patch-level benchmarks include the Brown et al. 2011) dataset Liberty, Notre Dame, Yosemite), which provides matching and non-matching 64 × 64 pixel patch pairs derived from multi-view stereo ground truth, and HPatches (Balntas et al., 2017), which contains 116 scenes (57 with illumination changes and 59 with viewpoint changes), each with six images and known homographies, and defines verification, matching and retrieval tasks. Image-level detector benchmarks include the Oxford affine-covariant regions dataset (Mikolajczyk et al., 2005), the Webcam dataset used for TILDE Verdie et al., 2015) and the HPatches sequences, in which keypoints are evaluated through the known homography. Task-level 3D benchmarks include the DTU multi-view data (Aanæs et al., 2016), the Strecha et al. benchmark, the structure-from-motion comparison of Schönberger et al. (2017), and the Image Matching Challenge Jin et al., 2021), which evaluates relative pose and reconstruction quality on large-scale Internet photo collections. We deliberately weighted the latter group, because patch-level scores have been shown to correlate only moderately with downstream reconstruction accuracy Schönberger et al., 2017). Evaluation measures. To compare [16] results across papers, we mapped every reported measure to a small set of standard definitions. Detector repeatability is the fraction of keypoints in a reference image that has a counterpart in the second image [14] after projection with the ground-truth transformation, with overlap error of regions below 40% (Mikolajczyk et al., 2005) or, for point detectors, a localization error below ε pixels (typically ε = 3 in HPatches-based protocols). Localization error is the mean distance in pixels between corresponding keypoints after projection. Matching score is the ratio of correct nearest-neighbour matches to the number of detected features in the shared field of view. For patch descriptors, the false-positive rate at 95% true-positive recall FPR95) is used on the Brown dataset; mean average precision mAP) is used for the verification, matching and retrieval tasks in HPatches. For geometric tasks, we report homography accuracy at a threshold of 1, 3 or 5 pixels on the mean corner error, the relative pose error as the angular error of rotation and translation direction, and the mean average accuracy (mAA) of pose over angular thresholds up to 10° (Jin et al., 2021). For reconstruction, we use the number of registered images, the number of triangulated 3D points, the mean track length, and [30] the mean reprojection error in pixels, as produced by incremental pipelines such as COLMAP (Schönberger and Frahm, 2016). Where papers report efficiency, we recorded descriptor [10] size in bytes, extraction time per image, and hardware. Standardization of reported results.
