Self-driving vehicles are moving from research prototypes to commercial deployment, and with this transition comes a stringent requirement: the perception stack must protect vulnerable road users. Pedestrians account for a substantial share of road [23] fatalities worldwide, roughly one in five according to the World Health Organization's global status reports, and automated systems will be judged by whether they can reliably avoid them. Two scenarios are especially [36] demanding. In imminent-crash situations, the vehicle may have to choose between striking an inanimate object and striking a pedestrian, and must therefore recognize people with high recall and low latency so that it can steer or brake toward the less harmful outcome. At road intersections, pedestrians cross from multiple directions, often partially occluded by other vehicles or street furniture, and the vehicle must stop reliably and promptly. In both cases, a missed detection is far more costly than a false alarm, which [17] makes the log-average miss rate, rather than raw average precision, the metric of primary interest in this domain Dollár et al., 2012). Pedestrian detection has progressed through several generations of methods. Early detectors relied on hand-crafted features such as histograms of oriented gradients combined with linear support vector machines (Dalal and Triggs, 2005), later extended with deformable part models Felzenszwalb et al., 2010) and integral channel features (Dollár et al., 2009). The Caltech Pedestrian Benchmark (Dollár et al., 2012) established a common evaluation protocol and showed that these approaches still missed a large fraction of small, occluded, or low-contrast pedestrians. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) changed this [16] picture. Region-based detectors such as R-CNN (Girshick et al., 2014), Fast [10] R-CNN (Girshick, 2015), and Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) greatly improved accuracy, and pedestrian-specific adaptations followed, including CompACT-deep Cai et al., 2015), the region proposal network with boosted forests (Zhang et al., 2016), and approaches that exploit semantic segmentation or multi-scale feature pyramids (Brazil et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2016). Among these, the Fused Deep Neural Network F-DNN) of Du et al. (2017) currently reports the lowest miss rate on the Caltech benchmark. F-DNN generates candidate boxes with a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector SSD), classifies them using an ensemble of several deep classifiers (such as ResNet and GoogLeNet variants), and fuses their outputs, with a soft-rejection mechanism that further reduces false positives, and an optional semantic-segmentation refinement stage. The accuracy of F-DNN is obtained at considerable computational cost. Running multiple deep classifiers on a large number of candidate regions, and subsequently performing fusion and segmentation, yields processing rates far below those needed for a vehicle traveling at speed. At 50 km/h a car covers nearly 14 meters each second; a perception pipeline operating at only a few frames per second leaves "large" blind intervals, and the added latency lengthens the effective stopping distance. Real-time operation, typically understood as at least 25–30 frames per second on full-resolution video with bounded and predictable latency; is therefore [4] a hard requirement and not merely a convenience (Lin et al., 2018). Furthermore, the on-board computing platform operates under tight power, thermal, and cost budgets, which excludes the use of multiple high-end server-class GPUs. Single-stage detectors offer a more favorable However, accuracy–speed trade-off. SSD Liu et al., 2016) [38] and YOLO (Redmon et al., [28] 2016) predict class scores and box offsets directly from feature maps in a single forward pass, eliminating the separate proposal and per-region classification stages. SSD in particular predicts from multiple feature maps of different [31] resolutions with default boxes of several aspect ratios, which makes it reasonably robust to scale variation. However, SSD was designed and tuned for general-purpose, multi-class benchmarks such as PASCAL VOC and MS COCO. [20] Pedestrians are a specific case: they have a characteristic, narrow range of aspect ratios approximately 0.41 width-to-height), they frequently appear at small scales, and they are often occluded. Default-box configurations, matching thresholds, hard-negative-mining ratios, and data-augmentation strategies chosen for generic objects are unlikely to be optimal for this setting, and the potential gain from tailoring them has not been thoroughly [14] explored. A second line of work addresses the computation itself. Hardware acceleration of CNN inference has been studied on GPUs, ASICs, and FPGAs. GPUs provide high throughput but at high power consumption and with variable latency. ASICs such as the TPU (Jouppi et al., 2017) and Eyeriss (Chen et al., 2016) are efficient but inflexible and expensive to develop. FPGAs occupy an attractive middle ground: they allow custom datapaths, reduced-precision arithmetic, and deep pipelining, offering deterministic latency and strong performance per watt Zhang et al., 2015; Qiu et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017). Most published FPGA accelerators, however, target image classification [2] networks such as AlexNet and VGG; and comparatively few address full object-detection pipelines with their multi-scale prediction heads, default-box decoding, and non-maximum suppression. The Altera (Intel) Arria 10 family, with its hardened floating-point DSP blocks, large on-chip "memory," and support for OpenCL-based design flows (Aydonat et al., 2017), is a promising yet underexplored target for such workloads. This leaves a clear gap. The most accurate pedestrian detector, F-DNN, is too slow for real-time deployment, while faster detectors have not been systematically adapted to pedestrians nor mapped to an efficient, automotive-suitable hardware platform. The research question we address is [27] therefore: can a pedestrian-optimized SSD, accelerated on an FPGA, approach the accuracy of F-DNN while meeting real-time throughput and latency requirements within an embedded power budget? [39] To answer this question, this paper makes two contributions. First, we train SSD for pedestrian detection and systematically tune its hyperparameters, including default-box scales and aspect ratios, matching thresholds, negative-to-positive sampling ratios, input resolution, and augmentation, to improve miss rate on the Caltech benchmark. Preliminary results show that the tuned SSD is within 3% of the miss rate of F-DNN while running four times faster in software. Second, we propose a new FPGA design for accelerating the tuned model on the Altera Arria 10 platform, exploiting parallelism across convolution channels and feature-map tiles, on-chip data However, reuse, and pipelined execution of the detection heads. We expect this design to yield a further speedup that substantially outweighs the small loss in accuracy; enabling real-time pedestrian detection in self-driving vehicles. The remainder of this paper describes the SSD adaptation and training procedure, details the accelerator architecture, presents accuracy and performance results, and discusses implications and limitations. Overview [29] The proposed system has two parts: (i) a Single Shot Multi-Box Detector (SSD; Liu et al., 2016) whose training procedure and hyperparameters were tuned for pedestrian detection, and (ii) an FPGA accelerator for the trained network, targeting the Altera (Intel) [19] Arria 10 platform. The software and hardware parts were developed in sequence. The tuned network defines the computational workload; and the accelerator is designed around its layer shapes, numerical precision, and memory footprint. The F-DNN of Du et al. (2017) is the accuracy and latency reference throughout. Dataset and Evaluation [12] Protocol Training and evaluation used the Caltech Pedestrian Detection Benchmark "Dollár" et al.; 2012), which contains about 10 hours of 640×480 video at 30 Hz recorded from a vehicle in urban traffic. Following the standard protocol, sets 00–05 were used for training and sets 06–10 for testing. Training frames were sampled every third frame (the commonly used "10x" setting) to reduce redundancy between consecutive frames. The annotations in Zhang et al. 2016) were used for training because they correct many labeling errors in the original ground truth. Test results are reported on the original annotations for comparability with published results. Evaluation follows the Caltech "Reasonable" setting: pedestrians at least 50 pixels tall and at least 65% visible. Detections are matched to ground truth at an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5, and the performance metric is the log-average miss rate (MR), computed from the miss rate against false positives per image (FPPI) curve: MR = exp (1/9) Σ{i=1}^{9} ln( mr(fi) ) ), where the fi are nine FPPI values evenly spaced in log space over [10⁻², 10⁰] and mr(fi) is the miss rate at the largest FPPI not exceeding fi. Lower is better. A validation split was held out from the training sets (set 05) for hyperparameter selection, and the test sets were used only for final reporting. SSD Architecture and Adaptation The baseline was SSD300 with a VGG-16 backbone pretrained on ImageNet Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). The fully connected layers were converted to convolutions, and extra feature layers were appended to give six detection scales. At each location of each feature map, the network predicts class confidences and four box offsets relative to a set of default boxes. The training objective is the weighted sum of a localization loss and a confidence loss: L(x, c, l, g) = (1/N) [ Lconf(x, c) + α Lloc(x, l, g) ], where N is the number of matched default boxes, Lconf is the softmax loss, Lloc is a smooth-L1 loss between the predicted box l and the ground-truth box g, and α weights the two terms. Because pedestrians are a single class with a narrow aspect-ratio distribution, the model was reduced to two classes (pedestrian and background). Default-box aspect ratios were restricted to {1:2.4, 1:2} around the typical pedestrian ratio of about 0.41 (width/height) found in Caltech, replacing the generic {1, 2, 3, 1/2, 1/3} set. Minimum and maximum default-box scales were re-estimated from the distribution of annotated pedestrian heights so that small pedestrians are covered by the finest feature maps. Input images were upsampled to 640×480 prior to feature extraction, since the small pedestrians that dominate the benchmark are otherwise lost after repeated downsampling. Training and Hyperparameter Tuning Training used stochastic gradient descent with momentum 0.9 and weight decay 5×10⁻⁴. Data augmentation followed Liu et al. (2016): photometric distortion, random expansion, random cropping constrained by minimum IoU with ground-truth boxes, and horizontal flipping. Hard negative mining kept the ratio of negatives to positives at 3:1. The hyperparameters tuned were the base learning rate, learning-rate schedule, batch size, matching IoU threshold for default boxes, negative-to-positive mining ratio, the localization weight α, default-box scales and aspect ratios, and input resolution. A staged search was used rather than a full grid. First, the learning rate (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, log-spaced) and batch size (8, 16, 32) were scanned with other parameters at their default values. Then, with these fixed, the matching threshold 0.4–0.6), mining ratio 2:1–5:1), and α (0.5–2) were varied one at a time. Finally, the default-box configuration and input resolution were tuned jointly because they interact strongly. Each configuration was trained for a shortened schedule and scored by log-average MR on the validation set; the best configurations were then retrained for the full schedule. Non-maximum suppression used an IoU threshold of 0.45, which was also tuned on validation data. Training was performed using the Caffe framework on a single GPU. Accuracy and Speed Comparison The final SSD was compared with F-DNN Du et al., 2017), which fuses several detectors and refines their outputs with a bank of classification networks, using published F-DNN miss rates and, for speed, inference runs on the same GPU and image size. Latency was measured as the mean per-frame time over the test sequences after warm-up, excluding image I/O, and throughput is reported in frames per second (fps). The speedup is the ratio of F-DNN to SSD per-frame time. Because training is stochastic, the final SSD configuration was trained with five random seeds, and the mean and standard deviation of MR are reported. The difference from F-DNN is expressed in absolute percentage points of MR. FPGA Accelerator Design Workload analysis. Per-layer multiply-accumulate (MAC) counts, parameter sizes, and activation sizes of the tuned SSD were computed analytically. For a convolutional layer with Cin input channels, Cout output channels, K×K kernels, and an H×W output map, the MAC count is MACs = H · W · Cout · Cin · K². These values determine the compute-to-memory ratio of each layer and thereby identify which layers are compute-bound or bandwidth-bound. Architecture. Biomedical research and healthcare increasingly depend on the reuse of data collected from patients and research participants. Electronic health records, biobanks, consumer devices, and high-throughput sequencing now produce information at a scale and granularity that [2] was unimaginable two decades ago. Combining such data across organizations promises more powerful studies of disease, faster recruitment for clinical trials, and a learning health system in which care and discovery inform one another. Funders, journals, and policy makers have responded with expectations that data be shared and made findable, accessible, [12] interoperable, and reusable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Examples include the National Institutes of Health Genomic Data Sharing Policy (NIH 2014) and the growing use of repositories and data discovery indexes (Ohno-Machado et al. 2017). [39] The same data are often sensitive. Clinical records reveal diagnoses, treatments, and behaviors, and genomic data disclose information about biological relatives and persist over a lifetime. A long line of research has shown that removing explicit identifiers does not reliably protect privacy. Demographic combinations can single out individuals in "de-identified" releases (Sweeney 2002), and patients can be linked to hospital discharge records and other secondary sources (Malin and Sweeney 2004; El Emam et al. 2011). Genomic data have proven especially vulnerable. Aggregate allele frequencies can reveal whether a person participated in a study (Homer et al. 2008), surnames can be inferred from Y-chromosome markers and public genealogy databases (Gymrek et al. 2013), and even yes/no "beacon" services can leak membership in a dataset through repeated queries (Shringarpure and Bustamante 2015). These findings have [35] eroded the assumption that a dataset can be labeled anonymous or "public" without ongoing assessment of risk. The tension between access and privacy is therefore both technical and social. Overly permissive sharing can expose participants to discrimination, stigma, or loss of trust, and the resulting public concern can jeopardize the research enterprise. Overly restrictive practices impede reproducibility, delay discovery, and waste the contributions of participants who volunteered their data in the expectation that it would be used. Legal and ethical [38] frameworks have tried to manage this tension, including the HIPAA Privacy Rule in the United States and the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union (European Parliament and Council 2016). These frameworks emphasize consent; purpose limitation, de-identification, and governance. Yet they were largely [28] designed for settings in which data were collected for a specific purpose and held by a [16] single organization. They fit less easily with contemporary research, in which data are repurposed, linked across institutions, and analyzed by parties the original participants never met. Consent models are also evolving, from study-specific agreements to broad and dynamic approaches that give participants more continuing involvement (Kaye et al. 2015; Grady et al. 2015). How such models should operate in emerging environments, such as mobile health studies and large precision medicine cohorts, remains an open question. A second set of challenges concerns infrastructure. Data are distributed across hospitals, consortia, and repositories with different policies, formats, and risk tolerances. Researchers need ways to discover whether suitable data exist before they can request access. Federated query tools such as i2b2 and SHRINE let investigators estimate cohort sizes across institutions without centralizing patient-level records (Weber et [19] al. 2009; Murphy et al. 2010). Even aggregate counts can leak information, however, especially for small or distinctive populations. This has motivated work on cryptographic protocols, such as homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation, as well as statistical protections such as differential privacy (Dwork and Roth 2014). These techniques promise formal guarantees, but their costs in computation, communication, and loss of data utility are still being characterized for clinical and genomic applications. A third challenge is that privacy risk is not static. It depends on the data type, the auxiliary information [20] available to an adversary, the incentives to attack, and the countermeasures in place. Recent work has therefore moved from asking whether a dataset is "safe" to modeling how risk varies with context and how data holders can make principled tradeoffs. Quantitative risk assessment, decision-theoretic and game theoretic models of data recipients and adversaries, and calibrated release of summary statistics are examples (Wan et al. 2017). Such approaches treat privacy (26) protection as an optimization problem, balancing the utility of shared information against the likelihood and cost of misuse, rather than as a binary property. Despite this progress, the literature is fragmented. Consent, data discovery, risk measurement, secure computation, and data publication are often studied by different communities and described in different vocabularies, which makes it difficult for informaticians and data stewards to see how advances fit together across the data lifecycle. Each year brings a large volume of publications, and it is not obvious which contributions are most significant for practice or for shaping future research. This paper addresses that gap by surveying notable contributions from 2017 on biomedical data sharing, with an emphasis on data access and privacy. The guiding question is: what advances published in 2017 most meaningfully expand the ability to share and use biomedical data while managing the privacy risks to the individuals who provide it? To answer it, we searched PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library. We selected candidate papers, had international experts review them against six predefined criteria, and had the editorial board of the However, IMIA Yearbook make the final selection of best papers. The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a structured, reproducible account of how the leading 2017 literature on data sharing and privacy was identified and evaluated. Second, it synthesizes five selected papers along the lifecycle of biomedical data: consenting strategies for emerging environments, software for searching and retrieving datasets across organizations, measurement of privacy risks for newer data types such as genomic data, cryptographic techniques for cohort discovery over clinical data, and game theoretic strategies for publishing summary information from genome-phenome studies. Third, it draws cross-cutting lessons, chiefly that no single solution to privacy fits all biomedical data and settings, but that emerging technologies create opportunities to enable data use while reducing risk. We hope this perspective helps researchers, data stewards, and policy makers choose among approaches and identify where further work is needed. Study design We conducted a structured, multi-stage review of the 2017 literature on biomedical data sharing, with a focus on the tension between data access and privacy. The process followed the selection procedure used (17) for the section papers of the International Medical Informatics Association (IMIA) Yearbook. It moves from a broad bibliographic search, to a curated set of candidate papers, to expert review, and finally to editorial selection of the best papers. The goal was to identify and summarize notable contributions, not to estimate pooled effects, so we did not conduct a formal systematic review or meta-analysis. We organized the work around the lifecycle of biomedical data, from collection and consent, through discovery, retrieval, and analysis, to dissemination of derived or summary information. We chose this framing because privacy and access concerns arise at different points in the lifecycle and call for different technical and policy responses (Sweeney, 2002; Dwork, 2006). Data sources and search strategy We searched five bibliographic resources to cover both the biomedical and the computational literatures in which data sharing and privacy research appears: PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and the AAAI Digital Library. PubMed/Medline and Web of Science capture clinical, biomedical, and informatics journals. The remaining three capture computer science, security, cryptography, and artificial intelligence venues, where many methodological advances in privacy-enhancing technology are first published (Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008). The search was limited to papers published in calendar year 2017, including articles that appeared electronically in 2017 ahead of print. We restricted the search to English-language, peer-reviewed publications. Queries combined controlled vocabulary with free-text terms for two concept groups. The first group addressed data sharing and access: data sharing, data access, information dissemination, data release, open data, data repositories, cohort discovery, data integration, and consent. The second addressed privacy and confidentiality: privacy, confidentiality, de-identification, anonymization, re-identification, data security, encryption, differential privacy, and genomic privacy. Within PubMed, we used Medical Subject Headings (e.g., Confidentiality, "Computer Security," Information Dissemination," Informed Consent") alongside title and abstract keywords. Because the other databases lack comparable indexing, we adapted the queries to each platform's syntax and searched titles, abstracts, and author keywords. Terms within a concept group were joined with OR, and the two groups were joined with AND. We also added queries on data types that have drawn attention in recent privacy research, including genomic, phenotypic, electronic health record, and mobile or sensor-derived data. The topics of the Yearbook section guided query refinement, and the queries were adjusted iteratively until further modification no longer yielded relevant results. Records were exported to a reference manager and de-duplicated by title, author, and digital object identifier. Step 1: Selection of candidate best papers Two section editors independently screened the titles and abstracts of the de-duplicated records. We excluded papers that did not substantially address biomedical or health-related data, or that mentioned privacy only in passing (e.g., as a motivation in the introduction). We also excluded editorials, commentaries without original analysis, and purely narrative opinion pieces, although such pieces informed our understanding of the policy context. Papers that passed this screening were read in full or in substantial part and tagged by lifecycle stage (consent and collection, storage and retrieval, analysis and querying, publication and release), by data type, and by contribution type (new method or system, empirical measurement of risk, policy or ethical analysis, or evaluation of an existing approach). The editors then nominated candidate best papers. Nomination emphasized originality, the potential to influence practice or subsequent research, and diversity of perspective across the lifecycle and across technical, empirical, and ethical or legal work. Disagreements about inclusion were settled by discussion until consensus was reached. In keeping with Yearbook procedure, the candidate set was kept deliberately small enough for in-depth review while still spanning the major themes of the screened literature. Step 2: Expert review of candidate papers Each candidate paper was sent to a team of international reviewers with expertise in biomedical informatics, privacy and security, ethics, or related fields. Reviewers included the section editors and external experts who were not authors of, and had no declared conflicts of interest with, the papers they evaluated. Each candidate was assessed by multiple independent reviewers, in line with the Yearbook's standard of several reviews per candidate. Reviewers rated each paper against six predefined criteria: (i) relevance to the section topic of data (17) sharing, access, and privacy; (ii) originality and novelty of the contribution; (iii) scientific rigor and soundness of the methodology; (iv) significance and potential impact on research or practice; (v) validity and clarity of the results, including whether claims were supported by the evidence or experiments; and (vi) quality of presentation and organization. Scientific findings in health and medicine are disseminated first and foremost through peer-reviewed publication. Yet the audience for such articles is narrow: specialist readers with access to journals and the training to interpret technical prose. For most members of the public, knowledge of new health research is mediated by the mass media. Surveys consistently show that television, newspapers, and online news outlets are among the principal sources from which lay audiences learn about science and medicine 1,2]. News coverage of health research can shape public understanding, influence health behaviors, inform policy debate, and affect clinical practice, including patients' demands for particular tests and treatments [3–5]. Media coverage is also associated with downstream scholarly impact; articles covered by the press tend to be cited more frequently than comparable articles that are not [6,7]. Which health science findings reach the public is therefore a consequential question, both for science communication and for population health. The path from journal article to news story is not direct. A substantial body (19) of research in communication studies describes the role of "information subsidies," materials produced by interested parties, such as press releases, that reduce the costs journalists incur in gathering and verifying information [8,9]. In health science, these subsidies are typically prepared by journal editorial offices or university and institutional press offices, who identify findings deemed likely to interest reporters and package them for distribution through channels such as EurekAlert!. Journalists, themselves operating under time pressure and with shrinking specialist science desks, rely heavily on these materials; studies have found that a large fraction of health news stories draw directly on press releases, sometimes reproducing their language and their exaggerations [10–12]. The pipeline is thus characterized by at least two successive selection steps. First, journal editors or press officers decide which published articles merit a press release. Second, journalists and news editors decide which articles, whether or not accompanied by a press release, merit a story. Each step filters the large volume of published research, and each presumably reflects judgments about what is "newsworthy." The concept of newsworthiness has a long history in journalism scholarship. Foundational work on news values identified features such as timeliness, proximity, prominence, consequence, conflict, and human interest as determinants of which events are selected for coverage [13,14]. Subsequent research has adapted these ideas to science reporting, suggesting that journalists favor findings that are novel, that bear on common or personally relevant health conditions, that carry clear implications for individuals, or that can be narrated in a compelling way [15,16]. Empirical studies of health news selection have examined features such as study design, journal prestige, sample size, and the presence of industry funding, and have reported, for instance, that observational studies and findings with striking or surprising results are overrepresented in coverage relative to their prevalence in the literature, while randomized trials and null results are comparatively neglected [17–19]. Such work has been invaluable, but it has generally relied on manual coding of modest numbers of articles, on predefined hypotheses about which attributes matter, and on metadata rather than the substantive content of the research itself. Manual (20) annotation is laborious, which limits sample sizes; hypothesis-driven designs can only confirm or refute features the investigators thought to examine; and metadata such as journal or study type say little about the topics, populations, exposures, and outcomes that make a paper attractive to the press. Meanwhile, advances in natural language processing and statistical machine learning make it feasible to analyze text at scale and to discover associations without specifying (1) them in advance. Text-based However, models have been used to predict the citation impact of papers; the popularity of online news items, and the (10) virality of social media content [20–22], and topic models in particular offer a means (23) of summarizing large corpora in terms of latent themes that (22) can be related to outcomes of interest [23,24]. However, these approaches have (26) seldom been applied to the specific question of which health science articles are selected for press release issuance and mainstream media (9) coverage. The few computational studies that exist have typically considered a single stage of the pipeline, a single outlet or journal, or small datasets, and have not systematically characterized the lexical and thematic content associated with selection at each stage. As a result, we lack a data-driven account of how the content of health research relates to its perceived newsworthiness, and of whether the factors that lead editors to issue press releases coincide with those that lead journalists to write stories. This study addresses that gap. We ask two questions. First, which attributes of published health science articles, as reflected in their abstracts, correlate with the issuance of a press release by the journal or publisher? Second, which attributes correlate with coverage in mainstream (5) news media? To answer these questions, we assembled four novel datasets: two for press release issuance and two for media coverage. Each links the text of published article abstracts to a binary indicator of whether the article received the relevant form of attention, (12) and the corpora range from hundreds to tens of thousands of articles or article–story pairs. Using regularized linear classifiers on lexical features; we quantify the extent to "which" press release issuance and news coverage can be predicted from abstract content alone and identify the words most strongly associated with each outcome. We then apply a supervised topic modeling approach to uncover latent themes predictive of selection; providing a more interpretable, higher-level view of the kinds of research that attract attention. This work makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first large-scale, data-driven characterization of content associated with both stages of the science-to-news pipeline, built on newly constructed corpora that we (6) describe in detail to facilitate further research. Second, it demonstrates empirically that both press release issuance and media coverage are predictable, to a degree that varies across datasets, from the text of the corresponding article, and thereby provides evidence that the content of research systematically informs perceived newsworthiness. Third, it surfaces specific words and topics that distinguish selected (27) from unselected research, generating hypotheses about editorial and journalistic preferences, such as an apparent affinity for epidemiological studies of common behaviors; that can be tested in subsequent work. Beyond describing current practice, such findings may help researchers, institutions, and journals understand the filters through which health science passes and consider whether those filters serve the public interest. Study design and data sources. We conducted a retrospective, observational analysis of published health science articles, framing the selection of articles for press releases and for mainstream news coverage as two supervised binary classification problems. For each problem we assembled two independent corpora, giving four datasets in total. The unit of analysis was the article abstract. Abstracts are the textual summary (16) most (12) likely to be read by press officers and journalists; and they are consistently available through (26) bibliographic databases [1,2]. Article metadata and (3) abstracts were obtained from PubMed and its application programming interface. Only articles with an English-language abstract of (24) at least 50 words were retained. Because the study However, used only (20) publicly available, published material and contained no human participant data, it was exempt from institutional review. Press release datasets. The first press release corpus comprised 3024 articles from journals whose publishers routinely issue releases through (29) the EurekAlert! service. We labeled an article positive if a (29) press release explicitly citing its DOI or title appeared on the service within 30 days of publication. Negative articles were drawn from the same journals and the same publication periods but had no linked release. The second corpus comprised 10,760 articles. It was assembled from a broader set of journals (28) and applied the same labeling rule. In both corpora we matched positives and negatives by journal and publication year to limit confounding by venue-specific press policies. Matching also limits confounding by temporal trends in release volume [3]. Duplicate records; errata, editorials, and commentaries were excluded, so the analysis covered primary research and review articles only. Media coverage datasets. The first media corpus contained 422 article pairs. The second contained 28,910 article pairs. Each pair consisted of one article that received coverage and one article that did not. Coverage was defined (26) as at least (23) one mention of the article in a mainstream news However, outlet. Mentions were identified from altmetric news-tracking records linking news stories to article identifiers [4]. The set of qualifying outlets was restricted to general-interest national and regional newspapers, broadcasters, and their online editions. Blogs, aggregators, and (25) press release redistribution sites were excluded. Each covered article was paired with an uncovered article from the same journal published within the same calendar month. This design holds constant the venue and timing of publication; so the (14) models must rely on content differences. When several uncovered candidates existed, one was selected uniformly at random. The first media corpus was smaller because it required manual verification of the news links. Two reviewers independently checked each link, and disagreements (19) were resolved by discussion. Text preprocessing. Abstracts were lowercased and tokenized. Punctuation, numerals, and standard English (13) stop However, words were removed, and the remaining tokens were (18) lemmatized. Structural section labels (for example, “background” and “conclusions”) were also removed so that classifiers could not exploit formatting conventions. We discarded terms appearing in fewer than five abstracts or in more than 50% of abstracts. Vocabulary was built from the training data only within each cross-validation fold, to avoid information leakage. Abstracts were then represented in two ways. The (1) first was a bag-of-words representation with term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting, using unigrams and bigrams 5]. The second was a latent topic representation, described below. Word-level predictive models. To identify words correlated with press release issuance or news coverage, we trained L1-regularized (lasso) logistic regression classifiers 6] and, for comparison, linear support vector machines [7]. L1 regularization yields sparse (7) solutions and so aids interpretation, because only a limited set of informative terms receive nonzero coefficients. Regularization strength was selected by (12) nested cross-validation. For the pair-based media datasets, we modeled each pair as the difference between the feature vectors of the covered and uncovered article, labeling the orientation of the difference at random. This is equivalent to a conditional logistic formulation, and it ensures that the classifier learns within-pair differences rather than between-pair baselines [8]. Words were ranked by regression coefficient, and we report coefficients stable across folds. Models were implemented in Python using scikit-learn [9]. Topic modeling. To uncover latent (8) thematic structure associated with perceived newsworthiness, we fit latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [10] to the abstracts of each corpus. LDA models each abstract as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words. Inference used online variational Bayes 11]. We evaluated candidate topic counts (K = 20, 50, 100, and 200) using held-out perplexity and topic coherence (Cv) [12], and we selected the value that balanced the (7) two criteria. Each abstract was then represented by its inferred K-dimensional topic proportion vector. This vector served as input to the same classifiers described above. In a complementary analysis, we fit supervised LDA [13], which jointly estimates topics and a regression on the outcome label, to encourage topics that are discriminative with respect to press release or coverage status. Topics were labeled by two authors, who each reviewed the 20 highest-probability words and the 10 most representative abstracts. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. To rank topics by predictive value, we used the regression coefficients of the topic-based classifier, with topic proportions standardized before fitting. Model evaluation. The primary performance metric was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), which is insensitive to class imbalance and has a probabilistic interpretation as the likelihood that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one [14]. Tobacco use remains the leading cause of preventable death worldwide, responsible for more than eight million deaths each year, of which roughly 1.2 million occur among non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke World Health Organization [WHO], 2021). Although the burden of tobacco-related disease falls mainly on adults, the epidemic is sustained by initiation in adolescence and early adulthood. Most adult users begin before the age of 25, and nicotine dependence can develop within weeks of first use, well before young people have the capacity to assess long-term risks (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2012; DiFranza et al., 2007). The adolescent brain is particularly vulnerable to nicotine, with exposure linked to altered development of prefrontal circuits, impaired attention and cognition, and greater susceptibility to other substance use (Yuan et al., 2015, Counotte et al., 2011). [14] Tobacco use among youth is therefore best understood not only as a risk behavior but as the primary pipeline through which the tobacco industry replaces the customers lost to disease and cessation. The Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS), coordinated by WHO and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has provided school-based, nationally comparable estimates of tobacco use among students aged 13–15 years in more than 140 countries since 1999. These data show substantial heterogeneity. Current use of any tobacco product among adolescents exceeds 20% in several countries in Europe, the Western Pacific, and parts of the Americas, while in South-East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa smokeless tobacco accounts for a large share of use, often exceeding cigarette smoking (Veeranki et al., 2015, Xi et al., 2016). Gender gaps are narrowing in many settings, and the rapid spread of electronic nicotine delivery systems has reversed declines in nicotine use in high-income countries, with e-cigarette use among adolescents now exceeding cigarette use in several of them (Cullen et al., 2019, Gentzke et al., 2022). Youth tobacco use is thus changing in form, geography, and social distribution, and policies designed for conventional adult cigarette smoking may not be adequate. The international policy response has been organized largely around the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC), adopted in 2003 and now ratified by more than 180 Parties, and the MPOWER package of measures derived from it: monitoring tobacco use and prevention policies, protecting people from tobacco smoke, offering help to quit, warning about the dangers of tobacco, enforcing bans on advertising, promotion and sponsorship, and raising taxes (WHO, 2008). Evidence from adult populations supports the effectiveness of these measures, and price increases in particular are considered the single most effective instrument, with youth typically more price-sensitive than adults (Chaloupka et al., 2012, International Agency for Research on Cancer, 2011). Other measures with youth-relevant evidence include comprehensive advertising bans, graphic health warnings and plain packaging, smoke-free legislation, minimum-age-of-sale laws with retailer enforcement, school-based and mass-media prevention programs, and, more recently, "Tobacco 21 laws and flavor restrictions (Hammond, 2011, Brown et al., 2014; Friedman et al., 2021, Kowitt et al., 2017). However, FCTC articles refer to minors mainly in the contexts of sales and access (Article 16), and most provisions are framed for the whole population. Evidence on whether, and through what mechanisms, population-level measures reach adolescents and young adults is uneven, and the evidence for youth-specific interventions is mixed. Systematic reviews of school-based programs, for example, show modest and often short-lived effects, with the strongest results for those using social-influence and life-skills approaches (Thomas et al., 2015), while the evidence on youth access laws is limited by weak enforcement and by the availability of social sources of tobacco (DiFranza, 2012). Several gaps in the literature motivate the present review. First, existing policy assessments, including the WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic and the Tobacco Control Scale in Europe, classify countries by the presence and strength of policies but rarely disaggregate by age or examine whether a policy is designed for, or reaches, young people (Joossens & Raw, 2012, WHO, 2023). Second, the term "youth" is used inconsistently, ranging from 10 to 24 years in different United Nations and national definitions, which complicates synthesis and cross-country comparison. Third, the literature is dominated by studies from high-income countries and by cigarette smoking, whereas the greatest growth in tobacco industry activity is in low- and middle-income countries, and smokeless tobacco, waterpipe, and novel products are often neglected in policy design and evaluation Siddiqi et al., 2020, Sinha et al., 2015). Fourth, little attention has been paid to how young people engage with policies physically, physiologically, and psychologically: how they perceive warnings, respond to price signals, circumvent age restrictions through illicit or cross-border trade and social sourcing, and use peers as both risk factors and resources for cessation. Finally, existing reviews generally examine a single instrument, such as taxation, packaging, or school programs, rather than describing the overall landscape of policies, their documented impacts, and the national and international obstacles to implementation, including industry interference under Article 5.3 and the tension between public health goals and [26] trade [15] and economic interests (Smith et al., 2013, Gilmore et al., 2015). Given these gaps, a broad, structured synthesis is warranted. Because the field is heterogeneous in policy type, study design, outcomes, and population definitions, a conventional meta-analysis of effects is neither feasible nor the most useful first step. We [33] therefore conducted an explorative systematic policy review, a design suited to mapping what policies exist, how they have been studied, what impacts have been reported, and where the evidence is thin (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005; Munn et al., 2018). [3] Such a review can integrate peer-reviewed studies with surveillance data such as GYTS and with policy documents and grey literature, which are essential for capturing policies that have been adopted but not formally evaluated. The study addresses three research [31] questions. First, what is the current situation of youth tobacco use, as documented in GYTS and related sources, and what tobacco control However, policies have been adopted that affect young people across [14] countries and continents? Second, what impacts, intended and unintended, have been reported for these policies, both at the national level and in terms of youth engagement? Third, what national and international challenges, such as illicit trade and smuggling, smokeless [9] tobacco, novel products, industry influence, and weak enforcement, constrain the control of tobacco use among youth, and what creative, youth-focused strategies might address them? This review makes four contributions. It provides an age-sensitive classification [8] of tobacco control policies, distinguishing population-wide measures from those that explicitly target young people. It brings together situational, national, and global evidence in a single framework, anchored in the MPOWER strategies. It identifies neglected areas, notably smokeless tobacco and youth participation, that require research and policy attention. Finally, it argues that tobacco control for youth should be positioned as a social, public health, and quality-of-life priority rather than primarily as a matter of business and trade, and it outlines directions for more youth-centered policy and research. Study design and reporting framework We conducted an explorative systematic policy review that combined a structured literature search with a descriptive analysis of survey surveillance data. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 statement for the identification, screening, and reporting of records (Page et al., 2021). Because the topic spans peer-reviewed evaluations, government documents, and international instruments, we also used the scoping-review principles of Arksey and O'Malley (2005) and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (Tricco et al., 2018). These principles allowed us to map the breadth of evidence rather than to answer a single narrowly defined effectiveness question. The protocol was not registered, which is consistent with the explorative aim. The review questions were: (i) what is the current situation of tobacco use among youth, ii) which tobacco control policies target or reach youth at the national level, (iii) what impacts have been reported, and iv) what national and international challenges remain. Definition of youth and policy classification No single age definition is used across the tobacco control literature. The United Nations defines youth as 15–24 years, WHO defines adolescence as 10–19 years, and the Global Youth Tobacco Survey (GYTS) samples students aged 13–15 years Warren et al., 2008). We therefore applied a flexible operational definition of 10–24 years and recorded the exact age range reported in each source. This flexibility was a deliberate trade-off, and we return to it as a limitation. Policies were classified using the WHO MPOWER framework: Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies, Protect people from tobacco smoke, Offer help to quit; Warn [23] about the dangers of tobacco; Enforce bans on advertising, promotion, and sponsorship; and Raise taxes (WHO, 2008). MPOWER operationalizes the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC, WHO, 2003). Policies that did not map onto a single MPOWER domain were coded under two additional categories created inductively. These were youth-specific measures (minimum legal sales age, restrictions on youth access, school-based and peer-based programmes) and measures addressing illicit trade, including youth involvement in smuggling. Data sources and search strategy We searched PubMed, the Health Inter-Network Access to Research Initiative (HINARI), Scopus, and the Cochrane Library. We also searched [9] Google and Google Scholar to capture grey literature, including government reports, WHO and CDC technical documents, and non-governmental organization evaluations. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (MeSH where available) with free text [6] and Boolean operators. A representative PubMed string was: ("tobacco control" OR smoking reduction" OR tobacco policy" OR FCTC OR "MPOWER") AND (youth OR adolescent OR young people" OR student) [6] AND (prevalence OR tax OR plain packaging OR "warning label" OR advertis OR "smoke-free" OR minimum age" OR incentive OR "peer-based" OR smuggling OR "smokeless tobacco). Strings were adapted to the syntax of each database. For Google and Google Scholar, we screened the first 200 results per query, ranked by relevance (Haddaway et al., 2015). Additional records were identified by backward citation tracking of key reviews and by hand-searching the WHO FCTC, WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic, and CDC GYTS repositories. The search covered publications from January 2003, the year the WHO FCTC was adopted, to the date of the final search. Only English-language records were considered. The search strategy was shaped by five considerations: timeline (post-FCTC), specificity and popularity of the policies (those most often implemented or cited), reliability of the source, significance (relevance to youth and to national or global policy), and applicability potential transferability across settings). To achieve geographic breadth, we purposively sought records from each WHO region and continent and from countries at different income levels, using World Bank income classifications. Exhaustive coverage of all countries was not feasible. Eligibility criteria We included records that (a) described, evaluated, or critiqued a tobacco control [37] policy, programme, or legislation that targeted youth or whose effects on youth were reported, (b) reported youth tobacco prevalence or determinants of use, or c) discussed national or international challenges to controlling youth tobacco use. Eligible designs included observational studies, quasi-experimental and experimental evaluations, systematic and narrative reviews, economic analyses, qualitative studies, and official policy documents. We excluded records that a) addressed only adult populations, (b) were opinion pieces without policy content, [28] (c) focused solely on clinical cessation pharmacotherapy, or (d) were duplicate publications. Studies of smokeless tobacco and emerging products were eligible, although we anticipated they would be underrepresented. Screening and selection All records were imported into reference-management software and de-duplicated. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then full texts, against the eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by a third reviewer. Inter-rater agreement at the full-text stage was quantified with Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960): κ = po − pe) / 1 − pe), where po is the observed proportion of agreement and pe is the agreement expected by chance. We interpreted κ using the benchmarks of Landis and Koch (1977), with values above 0.60 indicating substantial agreement. A total of 122 studies and documents met the inclusion criteria and entered the synthesis. Data extraction A standardized extraction form was piloted on ten records and then refined. 1 (18) Introduction Marine mass casualty events, such as capsizing passenger vessels, hurricane flooding, and mass migrant crossings, present rescuers (7) with large numbers of victims dispersed over wide areas of open water, often under severe time pressure. Survival in cold or rough water is measured in minutes to hours, and the first responders who (17) arrive are frequently limited by the number of available boats, crews, and rescue swimmers. Unmanned systems have been proposed and used to extend the reach of human responders in such events (Murphy, 2014). Early field deployments, including the cooperative use of unmanned surface and micro aerial vehicles after Hurricane Wilma, showed that the two platform types are complementary: surface vehicles can physically reach victims and carry flotation, whereas aerial vehicles provide a rapid, elevated view "of" the scene (Murphy et al., 2008). More recently, rescue unmanned surface vehicles [32] (USVs) capable of delivering flotation devices to people in the water have been developed to reduce risk to rescue personnel and to increase the number of victims who can be reached simultaneously. A persistent obstacle to the practical use of rescue USVs is how they are controlled. Teleoperating a low-profile craft from shore or from a ship is However, difficult; because the operator's view from the water surface is restricted by waves, spray, and the horizon. Distance, glare, and limited visibility also make it hard for the operator to judge the craft's position and heading relative to victims and hazards. Dedicating one skilled operator to each USV (19) also works against the goal of conserving scarce manpower. An unmanned aerial system (UAS) flying above the USV offers a promising alternative. From altitude, a UAS can observe the USV and its surroundings, and if it can estimate the USV's pose However, in real time, it can support or automate navigation by (21) providing position and heading feedback. In this arrangement a single operator [17] could supervise several USVs; and the UAS would also act as a communication and sensing relay. Making this vision work requires a reliable method for the UAS to estimate the pose of the USV from its onboard camera. Visual pose estimation is a mature topic in computer vision and robotics, but the conditions of this application make it unusually demanding. First, the estimate must be a full pose, that is, both position and orientation, because heading is essential for guiding a vehicle toward a victim. Second, the system must operate outdoors, where illumination, (27) sun glare, water reflections, and wave texture vary continuously and cannot be controlled. Third, because the UAS must keep a large area in view and cannot always hover directly overhead, the camera views the [34] USV from oblique angles of up to 85° from nadir, at distances up to 180 m. At such (29) ranges the (29) USV occupies only a small number of "pixels" and is strongly affected by perspective distortion. Fourth, the estimate must be produced in real time; here defined as at least 5 Hz, to support closed-loop navigation on embedded hardware. Finally, both the observer and the target move: the UAS may travel at up to 22 m s⁻¹ and the USV at up to 10 m s⁻¹, which precludes assumptions of a static background or camera. Existing literature addresses parts of (25) this "problem" but; to our knowledge, not the whole. We reviewed 58 studies on visual pose estimation and tracking of vehicles and other objects from aerial or comparable platforms. Fiducial marker systems such as AprilTag and ArUco provide accurate six-degree-of-freedom pose, but they require "the" marker to be sufficiently large [17] in the image and thus fail at the distances and oblique angles considered here. Model-based approaches that solve the perspective-n-point problem (Lepetit et al., 2009) depend on reliably detected, known keypoints that are not available when the target spans only a few dozen pixels. Classical trackers based on color histograms, such as mean shift and CamShift (Bradski, 1998), and on color indexing (Swain However, & Ballard, 1991) are fast and tolerate motion, but they are generally used to recover image position and coarse orientation, not full pose. Deep learning detectors such as YOLO (Redmon (16) et al., 2016) can localize objects with high accuracy, yet they usually output axis-aligned bounding boxes rather than orientation, depend on large annotated datasets that are scarce for rescue USVs at (12) oblique aerial views, and may not reach 5 Hz on a small UAS payload. Many of the remaining studies assumed a stationary camera, near-nadir views, short distances, controlled indoor conditions, or a slowly moving target. None of the 58 reviewed studies satisfied all of the requirements stated above simultaneously. This gap motivates the central research question of the present article: [10] can the full pose of a rescue USV be estimated in real [3] time from a moving (15) UAS; in an outdoor environment, at long range and oblique viewing angles, using computationally light visual cues? We hypothesize that the combination of the [24] USV's distinctive hue, which is robust to scale change and does not require resolving fine structure, and its characteristic shape, which carries information on heading, is sufficient to provide position and orientation estimates of useful accuracy. We further ask [21] how different ways of exploiting hue (14) compare in terms of accuracy and the amount of manual configuration they require. Specifically; we compare simple color thresholding with histogram-based segmentation, a distinction that has practical consequences because "every" additional tunable parameter increases the burden on the operator in the field (Otsu; 1979, illustrates the long-standing interest in reducing such parameters). This article makes four contributions. First, it formalizes the requirements (10) for UAS-based visual pose estimation [32] of a rescue USV in marine mass casualty events and shows, through a review of 58 studies, that (26) no existing approach meets them all. Second, it presents two algorithms for visual position estimation that use the object's hue, one based on [29] thresholding and the other on histogramming, both [20] designed to run at 5 Hz or faster. Third, it presents four techniques for estimating orientation from the object's shape, which operate on the segmented region and do not need a detailed appearance model. [11] Fourth, it reports four physical experiments conducted outdoors under varied environmental conditions and physical settings. These experiments validate (14) feasibility and quantitatively compare the two position algorithms, and the associated orientation estimates, using position error in pixels and orientation error in radians; with statistical tests of the differences. The experiments also expose the limitations of [10] the approach: orientation error remains substantial; manual tuning is required before each trial, and neither algorithm recovers from large illumination changes. We discuss these limitations and outline two remedies, inverse perspective warping to reduce distortion and machine learning to (18) remove tuning and increase robustness. The study [37] was designed to test whether the pose of a rescue USV can be estimated from a UAS-mounted camera under the operational constraints of marine mass casualty events. These constraints are oblique viewing angles up to 85° from nadir, distances up to 180 m, a processing rate of at least 5 Hz, UAS speeds up to 22 m s⁻¹, and USV speeds up to 10 m s⁻¹. Two position estimation algorithms, thresholding and histogramming, were implemented and compared in four physical experiments. Both rely on the hue of the object. Orientation was then derived from the object's shape, as described below. Both algorithms operate on frames from a monocular RGB camera on the UAS. Each frame was converted from RGB to the hue-saturation-value (HSV) color space, which separates chromatic content from illumination intensity and is therefore more tolerant of changing lighting (29) than RGB (Smith, 1978). The USV was assumed to have a dominant, distinctive hue, such as the orange or red typical of rescue craft. The target hue was specified by the operator before each trial from a sample image of the USV acquired under the prevailing conditions. The thresholding algorithm classifies a pixel as belonging to the USV if its hue, saturation, and value each fall within an operator-defined interval, which yields six parameters. The resulting binary mask was cleaned with morphological opening and closing to suppress speckle noise and fill small gaps (Gonzalez & Woods, 2018). The largest connected component was retained as the USV candidate, and its centroid, computed from image moments (Hu, 1962), was taken as the position estimate in pixel coordinates. The histogramming algorithm replaces (26) fixed intervals with a probabilistic model of the hue distribution. A normalized hue histogram was computed from a region of interest manually delineated around the USV in the sample image. Following the histogram back-projection principle (Swain & Ballard, 1991), each pixel in later frames was assigned the histogram value of its hue bin, giving a likelihood map for the USV. This map was smoothed and thresholded with a single cutoff. The same morphological cleaning, largest-component selection, and centroid computation as in the thresholding algorithm were then applied. To reduce computation and false positives, the search was restricted to a window around the previous estimate, in the spirit of mean-shift and CamShift tracking (Bradski, 1998). The window was enlarged in proportion to the previous USV size and recent displacement so that it could accommodate rapid UAS and USV motion. Because the histogram encodes the observed hue distribution, the algorithm required fewer operator-set parameters than thresholding, namely the number of bins and the likelihood cutoff. Orientation was estimated from the shape of the segmented region, which is elongated along the USV's longitudinal axis. Four techniques were implemented. The first computed the principal axis from the second-order central moments of the binary region (Hu, 1962). The second fitted an ellipse to the region contour by least squares (Fitzgibbon et al., 1999) and took the major-axis direction. The third fitted a minimum-area rotated bounding rectangle to the contour and took the direction of its longer side (Freeman & Shapira, 1975). The fourth fitted a straight line to the contour [11] points by least-squares regression and took its direction (Bradski & Kaehler, 2008). All four techniques yield an axis, which leaves a 180° ambiguity. This was resolved by assuming continuity with the previous estimate and, at initialization, by an operator-specified heading. Orientation was expressed as the in-image angle in radians in the interval [−π/2, π/2] and was not corrected for perspective distortion. The algorithms were implemented in Python with the OpenCV library (Bradski; 2000) and ran on an onboard-equivalent computer at a minimum of 5 Hz. Four physical experiments were conducted to evaluate feasibility and to compare the algorithms. Trials differed in location, time of day, background (water, shoreline, vegetation), illumination, USV type, camera altitude and distance, and viewing angle. This was done to examine the variation in environmental conditions and physical settings expected in operational use. In each trial the camera was carried by a UAS flown manually or on a programmed path and recorded video of the USV while the USV moved under manual control. Distances, viewing angles, and speeds ranged up to the stated requirements, although not every trial covered the full range. Both algorithms processed exactly the same recorded frames so that differences in error could be attributed to the algorithm rather than to the data. Parameters for each algorithm were tuned manually on a sample frame at the start of each trial, and no retuning was done during a trial. This reflects the operational need for unattended tracking and allowed the robustness of the tuning to be assessed. Ground truth was obtained by manual annotation of the USV in image coordinates. 1 Introduction Density estimation is a fundamental building block of statistical learning and data mining. Estimates of the probability density function underlie exploratory analysis and visualisation of static data (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015). They also underpin probabilistic classification through class-conditional densities (Hastie et al., 2009), and they support the detection of outliers, novelties, and distributional changes Chandola et al., 2009). Established approaches include kernel density estimators (Rosenblatt, 1956; Parzen, 1962), finite mixture models McLachlan & Peel, 2000), and, more generally, expansions in a set of basis functions with data-dependent weights. Nearly all of these methods assume that the observations are independent draws from a single, fixed distribution. This assumption is increasingly at odds with practice. Embedded systems, sensor networks, and the ongoing digitisation of business processes and public health monitoring produce observations that arrive continuously and whose generating distribution evolves over time (Gama et al., 2014; Krempl et al., 2014). In consumer credit scoring, the composition of applicants changes with macroeconomic conditions and lending policies (Thomas et al., 2017). In environmental health, pollutant concentrations and exposure profiles shift with regulation, climate, and land use. In such settings the density is better described as a function of both the data space and time, p(x | t), than as a single static object. Research on streaming [24] density estimation has mainly addressed how to keep an estimate current. Sliding windows, exponential forgetting, and resource-aware compression schemes allow kernel and mixture estimators to track a distribution under bounded memory and in a single pass (Aggarwal et al., 2003; Heinz & Seeger, 2008; Kristan et al., 2011). The concept drift literature likewise focuses on detecting change and adapting models once it has occurred (Widmer & Kubat, 1996; Gama et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2019). These approaches are fundamentally reactive. They yield an estimate of the density at, or shortly before, the most recent observation, and they implicitly assume that the recent past is a good proxy for "the" near future. If the distribution drifts steadily, this proxy is systematically biased. An estimator trained on a window ending at time t describes the distribution at roughly the window's centre, so it lags behind the current state by an amount that grows with the window length and the drift speed. This limitation matters whenever the density is required at a time point outside the training window. Examples include forecasting the risk profile of next quarter's loan applicants when labels or observations are delayed, anticipating exposure distributions for planning purposes, and supplying classifiers or change detectors with a reference distribution for a period in which no data have yet been observed. We call this task temporal density extrapolation: given samples observed at time points in a training window, estimate the density at a later time point. To our knowledge, this task has received little attention. Related work on predicting future distributions exists, but it differs from our setting in important respects. Lampert 2015) extrapolates a time-varying distribution through its embedding in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which yields a predicted mean embedding rather than a normalised density that can be queried directly. Kumagai and Iwata (2016) and related work on learning future classifiers forecast decision functions or parameters of a prescribed model family, [19] so their results depend on a specific parametric form. In the stream classification setting, approaches such as APT (Krempl, 2011) and COMPOSE (Dyer et al., 2014) exploit assumed drift regularities, but they typically rely on cluster structure or on a particular, simple drift model. A general, [15] nonparametric, and computationally light approach to extrapolating densities has so far been missing. [24] Several characteristics make the problem difficult. [16] First, the extrapolated object must itself be a valid density, that is, [16] non-negative and integrating to one. Naively extrapolating density values or basis-function weights can violate both constraints, for instance by producing negative weights when a linear trend is extended beyond the observed range. Second, a method should not be restricted to a specific parametric family, such as Gaussians with drifting means, because real-world "drift" rarely follows such a form. Third, requiring well-separated clusters or components whose identity can be tracked over time limits applicability to data with that structure. Fourth, the method must be efficient enough for streaming scenarios, so that extrapolation does not become the computational bottleneck compared with static estimation. In this paper we address the following research question: how [23] can the density of a gradually and monotonically evolving distribution be extrapolated to future time points without assuming [6] a parametric distribution or a cluster structure, while guaranteeing valid densities and incurring only modest computational overhead? We propose Temporal Density Extrapolation (TDX), which answers this question [4] using a dynamic basis approach. TDX represents the density as an expansion in a fixed set of basis functions, with However, nonnegative weights that sum to one. These weights are therefore compositional data in the sense of Aitchison (1986), and they live on a simplex rather than in unconstrained Euclidean space. TDX estimates the weights in consecutive time slices of the training window and maps them to real-valued coordinates through the isometric log-ratio ilr) transformation (Egozcue et al., 2003). In this space, the temporal evolution of each coordinate is modelled by a regression function, which is then extrapolated to the requested time point. The extrapolated coordinates are back-transformed to the simplex, which ensures that the [12] resulting weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and hence that the extrapolated density is valid by construction. Because the basis functions are fixed and only their weights vary, the approach is not tied to a parametric family of distributions and does not require the identification or tracking of clusters. The method introduces only two extrapolation-specific parameters, for which we provide reasonable defaults. The contributions of this paper are as follows. 1. We formalise temporal density extrapolation as a distinct learning task, separate from stationary density estimation and from reactive density tracking, and we delineate it from related work on drift adaptation and future classifier prediction. 2. We introduce TDX, a method that combines basis-function density estimation with ilr-transformed compositional weights "and" regression-based extrapolation. It guarantees valid densities, requires neither parametric assumptions nor cluster structure, and has only two additional parameters. 3. We evaluate TDX on synthetic streams with controlled drift patterns and on real-world data from credit scoring and environmental health. We compare it with static estimators and with existing approaches that adapt to drift. The results show that TDX captures monotonic drift more accurately than the competing methods. 4. We analyse its computational cost and show that the run time never exceeds 1.5 times that of the corresponding static density estimator, which makes the method suitable for streaming use. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. We first review the relevant background on density estimation and compositional data analysis. We then present the TDX method, report the experimental evaluation, and discuss the results and limitations, including the restriction to gradual monotonic drift. Problem formulation. Let a data stream be a sequence of observations xi ∈ ℝ^d with time stamps ti, drawn from a time-varying density p(x, t). [35] Given observations within a training window [t0, tT], the task of temporal density extrapolation is to estimate p(x, t) for a time point t > tT, [33] for which no data are available. We restrict attention to gradual, monotonous drift, in which the change of the density over time However, follows a consistent direction rather than oscillating or switching abruptly. This setting covers many practically relevant processes, such as demographic shifts or slowly increasing environmental exposure, and it is distinct from the concept-drift literature, which focuses on detecting and adapting to [13] change after it has occurred (Gama et al., 2014). Basis expansion. The density is represented as a finite mixture of K fixed basis functions, p(x, t) = Σk wk(t) φkx), with wk(t) ≥ 0 and Σk wkt) = 1, where each φk is a normalised density. We use isotropic Gaussian kernels, φk(x) = N(x, ck, σ²I), as is common in kernel and radial-basis-function density estimation [10] Silverman, 1986; Scott, 1992). The centres ck are placed by k-means clustering on the training data (K = 50 by default), which concentrates resolution where data are dense without assuming that the data themselves form clusters. The bandwidth σ is selected on the pooled training sample by maximising a five-fold cross-validated log-likelihood. Because the basis is fixed across time, all temporal [24] change is carried by the weight vector w(t). The model is therefore not tied to a specific parametric family, and the number of free quantities does not grow with the number of observations. Estimation of time-resolved weights. The training window is partitioned into M consecutive, equally wide segments (M = 10 by default) with midpoints τ1, …, τM. For each segment m, the weight vector ŵm is estimated by maximum likelihood on the observations in that segment. The basis is held fixed, so the log-likelihood is concave in w, and the weights are found with the expectation–maximisation updates for mixture proportions (Dempster et al., 1977). To avoid zero entries, which would make the subsequent log-ratio transformation undefined, a small additive pseudo-count ε "=" 10⁻³ of the total mass) is applied before renormalisation (Martín-Fernández et al., 2003). Segment-wise estimation yields a sequence of M points on the simplex S^K, which is the compositional time series to be extrapolated. Isometric log-ratio transformation. Mixture weights are compositional data: they are non-negative, sum to one, and "carry" only relative information. Applying ordinary regression directly to them can produce extrapolated values outside the simplex, and Euclidean distances on the simplex are misleading (Aitchison, 1986). We therefore map each ŵm to ℝ^(K−1) using the isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformation Egozcue et al., 2003), [1] zm = ilr(ŵm) = Ψᵀ log ŵm, where the log is applied element-wise and Ψ is a K×(K−1) matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of the hyperplane orthogonal to the vector of ones. In contrast to the additive log-ratio, the ilr is an isometry between the Aitchison geometry of the simplex and Euclidean space, so that standard multivariate regression can be applied without distorting distances. The inverse transformation, w = softmaxΨz), guarantees valid weights for any real-valued z. Extrapolation of weights. Each of the [25] K−1 ilr coordinates is modelled as a function of time by a regularised linear regression, zj(t) = αj + βj t + εj, fitted to the M segment midpoints by ridge regression with penalty λ on the slope (Hoerl & Kennard, 1970). Linear trends in ilr space correspond to exponential-ratio change in the weights, which is a natural form for gradual monotonous drift. The two extrapolation-specific parameters of the method are the number of segments M and the regularisation strength λ. Defaults were set to M = 10 and λ = 1 after preliminary experiments on separate synthetic streams that were not used for the evaluation reported below. For a requested time point t, the coordinates ẑ(t) are predicted, back-transformed to ŵt) = ilr⁻¹(ẑ(t)), and the density estimate is p̂x, t) = Σk ŵk(t) φk(x). Evaluating the estimate has the same cost as for a static mixture, and the additional training cost consists only of the M weight estimations and K−1 low-dimensional regressions. Data. Evaluation used synthetic and real-world streams. Synthetic streams (n = 20,000 observations each, time stamps uniform on [0, 1]) were generated from Gaussian mixtures in d ∈ {1, 2, 5} dimensions with three drift patterns: (i) linear translation of component means, (ii) monotone change of mixing proportions, and (iii) a combination of both with a gradual increase in variance. For each pattern, 30 random replicates were generated with different seeds. The first 70% of the time axis served for training and the remaining 30% as the extrapolation horizon. Because the true density is known, accuracy could be measured against ground truth. Two real-world data sets were used.
