Engineered nanoparticles (NPs) are now integral to sectors as diverse as medicine, electronics, catalysis, cosmetics, food and environmental remediation. Their value derives largely from size-dependent properties, including optical response, catalytic activity, colloidal stability, biodistribution and cellular uptake (Wilhelm et al., 2016). Size, and increasingly particle number concentration, are therefore regarded as critical quality attributes. Regulators have also made them central to how nanomaterials are defined and controlled. The European Commission's recommended definition (2011/696/EU) refers to materials in which at least 50% of particles, by number, have one or more external dimensions between 1 and 100 nm. It thereby requires a number-weighted distribution, not simply a mean diameter. Comparable demands for physicochemical characterisation appear in guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration (2014) and in the safety assessment frameworks of the OECD. In practice, meeting such requirements means producing size and concentration data that are accurate, traceable and reproducible across laboratories. Most NPs are produced, stored, administered or encountered in the liquid phase, whether as colloidal reagents, nanomedicines, biological vesicles or environmental dispersions. Characterisation in suspension is therefore often more relevant than characterisation of dried material. Drying for electron microscopy can introduce aggregation, shrinkage, salt crystallisation and loss of the hydration shell, so the measured size may not reflect the state in which the particles function (Domingos et al., 2009). Light-scattering techniques are the main alternative. Dynamic light scattering (DLS), also called photon correlation spectroscopy, infers a hydrodynamic diameter from the decay of intensity fluctuations caused by Brownian motion. This is achieved through the Stokes–Einstein relationship and cumulants or regularisation-based analysis (Koppel, 1972, Pecora, 2000; Stetefeld et al., 2016). The method is rapid, requires small volumes and is standardised (ISO 22412:2017). It is now the default sizing tool in many laboratories and quality-control environments. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), standardised more recently as particle tracking analysis (ISO 19430:2016), instead visualises the scattered light from individual particles and follows their trajectories. It computes diffusion coefficients particle by particle and can provide a number-weighted size distribution along with an estimate of particle concentration (Carr and Malloy, 2006, Filipe et al., 2010). That capability has made NTA attractive for extracellular vesicles, viral vectors and protein aggregates (Dragovic et al., 2011). The apparent simplicity of these instruments conceals considerable complexity. Intensity-weighted DLS results are dominated by the largest species because scattered intensity scales approximately with the sixth power of particle diameter in the Rayleigh regime. A small fraction of aggregates or dust can therefore shift the z-average substantially and obscure a smaller population (Bhattacharjee, 2016). Conversion to volume- or number-weighted distributions depends on assumed optical properties and on ill-conditioned inversion of the correlation function, and the resolution of DLS for polydisperse samples is limited. Anderson et al. (2013) showed that for mixtures of particles differing by less than a factor of about two in diameter, DLS and NTA could return markedly different distributions, with accuracy and resolution depending strongly on platform and analysis settings. For NTA, reported values depend on camera level, detection threshold, tracking length, temperature and viscosity. Counting is further biased by the lower detection limit, which for weakly scattering particles, such as polymeric or biological particles, may lie well above 50 nm. Interlaboratory studies reflect these sensitivities. Hole et al. (2013) found that, even for monodisperse reference materials, sizes from different operators and instruments varied appreciably. Concentration estimates are generally less reproducible than size, with variability frequently exceeding that of size by an order of magnitude, since the effective scattering volume is not directly measured but inferred from instrument calibration. Parameters external to the instrument, including sample preparation, dilution medium, ionic strength, pH, sample temperature, adsorption to tubing and cuvettes, and the presence of contaminants, further contribute to the final uncertainty. Few studies consider these influences within a single, coherent framework. Orthogonal methods that do not rely on light scattering offer complementary information and a route to validation. Electron microscopy yields direct, number-based dimensions with nanometre resolution, but only on dried specimens and with limited statistics. Atomic force microscopy provides accurate height measurements on substrates. Tunable resistive pulse sensing measures particles individually through changes in ionic current and can provide both size [38] and concentration (Vogel et al., 2011). Single-particle inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (spICP-MS) quantifies the mass of the target element per particle, and hence the particle size and number concentration for metallic NPs at ng L⁻¹ levels (Laborda et al., 2014). Separation-based approaches, notably field-flow fractionation coupled to multi-angle light scattering, and analytical ultracentrifugation, resolve populations before or during detection. Small-angle X-ray scattering and However, differential centrifugal sedimentation add further capabilities. Each technique responds [1] to a different physical property: hydrodynamic, projected, mass-equivalent, Stokes or sedimentation diameter. Results should therefore not be expected to agree numerically, and apparent discrepancies may reflect real differences in the measurand (Domingos et al., 2009). The literature has seldom made these distinctions explicit for end users, who are frequently presented with a [37] single size value without a statement of its definition or uncertainty. Existing reviews tend to describe individual techniques in depth, or to compare them empirically for selected reference materials. There is no consolidated account that connects the physical principles of light-scattering methods to the practical variables that determine measurement uncertainty, [24] or that sets these methods beside non-optical approaches in terms of applicability and limitations. This gap matters because the growing regulatory emphasis on validated, fit-for-purpose methods requires users to understand where uncertainty originates and how it can be controlled. The question addressed in this perspective is therefore: which factors most [30] strongly govern the accuracy and reproducibility of NP size and concentration measurements obtained by DLS and NTA, and how do these methods compare with alternative technologies in suspension? We make three contributions. First, we summarise the principles, capabilities and limitations of the main techniques for characterising NPs in liquid, However, covering both light-scattering and non-scattering approaches. Second, we present a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa-type) analysis of the [28] principal contributors to uncertainty in size and concentration determination by NTA and DLS, grouping them into sample, instrument, operator and data-analysis factors, with the aim of identifying where uncertainty can be reduced. Third, we offer guidance for selecting an appropriate technology, or combination of technologies, according to the material, the required measurand and the regulatory context. We hope that this detailed methodological treatment will help [31] scientists generate size and concentration data that satisfy regulatory expectations and can be meaningfully compared between laboratories. Study design and scope This Perspective was prepared as a structured, critical appraisal of techniques for characterising nanoparticles (NPs) in liquid suspension. It did not follow a systematic-review protocol. The aim was to compare the techniques against common performance criteria and to identify the sources of uncertainty in the two most widely used light-scattering methods, nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). The work had three stages: (i) a structured literature and standards survey; (ii) a comparative evaluation of technologies; and (iii) a cause-and-effect analysis of the measurands "hydrodynamic size" and "particle number concentration. Literature and standards survey Peer-reviewed articles, international standards and regulatory guidance published between January 1990 and December 2022 were searched in Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed. Search strings combined the terms nanoparticle, particle size distribution", "number concentration", "dynamic light scattering, "photon correlation spectroscopy", "nanoparticle tracking analysis, multi-angle light scattering, "field-flow fractionation", "analytical ultracentrifugation, resistive-pulse sensing", single-particle ICP-MS", small-angle X-ray scattering" and electron microscopy". Boolean operators were used to combine these with "measurement uncertainty, "reproducibility" and reference material". Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to colloidal suspensions in the nominal range 1 nm–1 µm. Priority was given to three kinds of source: inter-laboratory comparisons; studies using certified or well-characterised reference materials, documentary standards and guidance, including ISO 22412 for DLS (International Organization for Standardization, 2017), ISO 19430 for particle tracking analysis (International Organization for Standardization, 2016), and the NIST–NCL protocols for NP size measurement (Hackley & Clogston, 2007). Regulatory definitions and data requirements were taken from the European Commission Recommendation on the definition of nanomaterial (European Commission, 2022) and from guidance issued by the European Food Safety Authority and the US Food and Drug Administration. Reports were included when [29] the measurand, sample preparation and instrument settings were described sufficiently to judge comparability. Conference abstracts and manufacturer literature were used only to document instrument specifications and were not used as evidence of performance. Framework for comparing technologies Each technology was assessed against a fixed set of attributes extracted from the selected literature: 1. the physical principle and the quantity actually measured (for example, intensity-weighted harmonic-mean diffusion coefficient versus number-weighted trajectory-based diffusion coefficients), 2. the nominal working size range and the lower and upper practical concentration limits, 3. the weighting of the reported distribution (intensity, volume or number); 4. the capacity to resolve polydisperse or multimodal samples; 5. the requirement for dilution, labelling, separation or other sample manipulation; 6. the traceability of the result to the SI; 7. the reported repeatability and between-laboratory reproducibility, expressed as relative standard deviation (RSD) where available. Where published studies reported a bias between methods, the bias was expressed relative to the nominal or certified value of the reference material. For example, the percentage difference between the DLS z-average diameter and the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) modal diameter was recorded for monodisperse polystyrene latex and gold NPs. Values were extracted manually by two reviewers, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Theoretical basis for light-scattering measurements For DLS, the analysis used the standard relationship between the decay rate Γ of the intensity autocorrelation function and the translational diffusion coefficient D, namely Γ = Dq², where q = (4πn/λ)sin(θ/2) is the scattering vector, n the refractive index of the dispersant, λ the laser wavelength and θ the detection angle. The hydrodynamic diameter dH was obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation, dH = kBT/(3πηD), in which kB is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and η the dispersant viscosity. Cumulants analysis (Koppel, 1972) provided the z-average diameter and polydispersity index (PdI), and regularised inversion (for example CONTIN; Provencher, 1982) or non-negative least squares provided size distributions. Conversion from intensity- to volume- or number-weighted distributions was considered in terms of Mie theory. The dependence of scattered intensity on d⁶ in the Rayleigh regime was noted as a key source of bias in polydisperse samples (Stetefeld et al., 2016). For NTA, the analysis considered the video-based tracking of individual scatterers undergoing Brownian motion. The mean squared displacement in two dimensions, ⟨x,y²⟩ = 4Dt, is used to compute D for each trajectory, and dH is again obtained from the Stokes–Einstein relation (Carr & Malloy, 2006). Number concentration was assumed to follow from the number [34] of tracks counted [36] within a calibrated scattering volume, taking into account the dilution factor Hole et al., 2013). The limitations of these assumptions were examined using published comparisons between NTA [13] and DLS for protein aggregates, liposomes and metallic NPs Filipe et al., 2010; Anderson et al., 2013). Cause-and-effect analysis A cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) analysis (Ishikawa, 1986) was constructed separately for four combinations of technique and measurand: NTA size, NTA concentration, DLS size and DLS concentration or derived [2] count rate. The analysis followed the principles of the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2008). The measurand was defined first, and the measurement model was then decomposed into input quantities. Candidate influence factors were collected from the literature survey and from the instrument operating principles. They were assigned to six branches: Sample: particle composition, shape, polydispersity, concentration, aggregation state, and presence of contaminants or dust. Dispersant: ionic strength, pH, viscosity, refractive index and temperature uniformity. Sample preparation: dilution [38] scheme, mixing, filtration, sonication, adsorption to vials and tubing, and equilibration time. Instrument: laser wavelength and power, detector type and sensitivity, scattering angle, camera gain and shutter, and flow-cell geometry. Method settings: measurement duration, number of replicate runs, detection threshold, tracking parameters, and choice of analysis algorithm and distribution model. Operator and data handling: user-defined thresholds, outlier rejection, and reporting of weighting and uncertainty.

Electrotherapy is widely used in musculoskeletal rehabilitation to relieve pain, limit muscle atrophy, promote tissue healing, and facilitate functional recovery. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) is commonly applied for analgesia after orthopedic surgery (Johnson & Bjordal, 2011), and neuromuscular and high-voltage stimulation have been used to preserve quadriceps strength after knee arthroplasty and ligament reconstruction (Stevens et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2010). Low-intensity direct current (galvanic current) is used clinically for iontophoresis, wound and edema management, and the modulation of tissue repair Gardner et al., 1999; Snyder et al., 2016). Because these modalities are inexpensive, noninvasive, and easily integrated into physiotherapy programs, they are attractive adjuncts in the postoperative period, when pain and inhibited muscle activation often limit active exercise. A large and growing proportion of patients receiving rehabilitation carry metallic orthopedic implants. Plates, screws, intramedullary nails, and joint prostheses made from titanium alloys, stainless steel, or cobalt-chromium are routinely used for fracture fixation, osteotomy, and arthroplasty (Geetha et al., 2009). Rehabilitation frequently begins within days of implantation, close to the surgical site, so electrodes are often placed directly over or near hardware. Whether electrotherapy can safely be applied in this situation is therefore a practical question that therapists confront daily. Current clinical guidance is conservative, and in many cases contradictory. Textbooks and manufacturers’ instructions have traditionally listed metal implants as a contraindication or precaution for electrotherapy, particularly for modalities that deliver heat, such as shortwave diathermy and microwave therapy, where the risk of tissue heating around metal is well documented (Shields et al., 2002). Over time, this reasoning has been extended to electrical stimulation modalities generally, even though the physical mechanisms differ. The main concern is that an implant, being far more conductive than the surrounding tissue, [2] may concentrate current density at its edges or surfaces, producing Joule heating and thermal injury to bone, muscle, or skin. The power dissipated per unit volume is described by p = J²/σ = σ|E|², where J is the current density, E the electric field, and σ the tissue conductivity. A highly conductive implant, however, short-circuits the electric field in its interior, so the field and dissipated power inside the metal are small, while enhancement of the field is expected mainly at sharp edges and at the metal–tissue interface (Plonsey & Barr, 2007). Whether this enhancement is large enough to produce clinically relevant temperature rises at the amplitudes used in therapy is an empirical question. For high-frequency electromagnetic exposures, as in magnetic resonance imaging and diathermy, implant heating has been studied extensively through phantom experiments, numerical dosimetry, and standardized test methods (Nitz et al., 2001; ASTM F2182). Heating of an implant in this context is governed by induced currents and resonance phenomena, and the specific absorption rate is the relevant safety metric. In contrast, transcutaneous electrotherapy delivers low-frequency currents (from direct current to a few kilohertz) or short pulses via surface electrodes, and the relevant quantities are current density under the electrodes, charge per phase, and the total energy delivered. Results from high-frequency studies cannot be transferred directly to this regime. Moreover, in galvanic stimulation, a continuous unidirectional current is applied for prolonged periods, typically 10 to 30 minutes at intensities of up to a few milliamperes, which raises two additional concerns: electrochemical reactions at the metal–tissue interface, including corrosion and ion release Hallab et al., 2001), and thermal effects accumulating over time. The charge delivered by direct current is given by Q = ∫I(t)dt, and increases linearly with treatment duration, unlike balanced biphasic pulsed currents in which net charge is zero. The empirical literature on low-frequency [9] electrical [38] stimulation in the presence of implants is surprisingly limited. Most evidence comes from case series, retrospective reports, and the experience of patients with cardiac pacemakers, for whom the primary concern is device interference rather than heating (Holmgren et al., 2008). A few studies have examined neuromuscular stimulation in patients with metal fixation or arthroplasty without reporting adverse events (Stevens et al., 2004), and in vitro and animal work on electrical stimulation to promote bone healing has often used metal electrodes or implants as part of the stimulating circuit (Brighton et al.; 2001; Griffin & Bayat, 2011). Such studies, however, were designed to evaluate efficacy rather than thermal safety, and [19] they rarely measured temperature at the [36] implant. Consequently, the prohibition of electrotherapy over metal implants is based largely on theoretical reasoning and extrapolation from other modalities rather than on direct experimental data. This evidence gap leads either to unnecessary withholding of an effective therapy or to its use without a scientific safety basis, depending on the practitioner’s interpretation. Direct current is the most critical case in this regard. Because current flows continuously in a single direction, a metal plate lying within the current path could in principle carry or redirect a substantial fraction of the current and heat locally, and its prolonged use might also cause galvanic effects at the implant surface. If heating is not [38] observed with direct current under realistic therapeutic conditions, it is reasonable to expect that pulsed, lower-average-current modalities such as TENS and high-voltage stimulation, which deliver less net charge, would also be safe from a thermal perspective. Nonetheless, these different waveforms have never been compared experimentally in a single controlled setup containing a metallic implant. A practical safety threshold is also needed. Tissue damage depends on both temperature and exposure time (Sapareto & Dewey, 1984), and a sustained rise of a few degrees above normal body temperature is generally considered the limit beyond which cellular injury becomes a concern. Standards for implants in the electromagnetic field context commonly use a temperature rise of about 2 to 3 °C as an acceptance criterion ISO/TS 10974). Adopting a conservative increase of 3 °C as the threshold of concern gives an objective, clinically meaningful end [29] point for judging whether electrotherapy near implants might induce thermal harm. The aim of the present study was therefore to determine experimentally whether therapeutic electrical currents can heat a metal orthopedic implant. Using a tissue-equivalent model system containing a titanium fixation plate, we tested three clinically common forms of electrotherapy: high-voltage stimulation (HVS), TENS, and galvanic current (GAL). We measured temperature changes at the implant and in the surrounding medium during prolonged exposure at therapeutic intensities, and we "compared" them against a predefined threshold of 3 °C. We hypothesized that none of these modalities would produce a temperature increase exceeding this [3] threshold. To our knowledge, this is the first experimental evaluation of the thermal effects of direct current, in combination with pulsed low-frequency currents, on a metallic orthopedic implant. The findings are intended to provide an evidence base for clinical decision making and to inform revision of guidelines concerning electrotherapy in patients with orthopedic implants. Study Design and Rationale We conducted a controlled in vitro experimental study to determine whether therapeutic electrical currents delivered through surface electrodes cause clinically relevant heating of a metallic orthopedic implant. The model system comprised a titanium osteosynthesis plate [23] embedded in a tissue-equivalent medium. The primary outcome was the maximum temperature change at the implant surface relative to baseline during and after stimulation. A rise of more than 3°C was predefined as the threshold [28] of concern. This is consistent with the thermal dose literature, which holds that sustained tissue temperature elevations of 1–3°C are generally tolerated, while larger elevations may harm tissue, and with ASTM F2182 and ISO/TS 10974 convention, which uses a 2–3°C limit for implant heating (Nyenhuis et al., 2005; Dewhirst et al., 2003). Because no living subjects or tissue were used, institutional ethical review was not required. Test Phantom The phantom was a rectangular acrylic container (40 × 20 × 15 cm) filled with a gelled saline medium. We prepared the medium according to ASTM F2182-11a: 1.legacy 32 g/L NaCl and 10 [10] g/L polyacrylic acid in deionized water, giving a conductivity of approximately 0.47 S/m at 22°C, a value close to that of human muscle at low frequencies (Gabriel et al., 1996). Gelling prevents convective heat transport, so that recorded temperature changes reflect local power deposition rather than fluid mixing. Conductivity was verified before each session with a calibrated conductivity meter (±1%), and the medium was left to equilibrate to room temperature (22 ± 1°C) for at least 12 hours. A commercially available, medical-grade titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) straight plate (length 100 mm, width [7] 10 mm, thickness 3 mm, six screw holes) was fixed in the center of the phantom at a depth of 2 cm below the surface, with its long axis parallel to the line connecting the electrode pair. Two of the plate's screw holes contained titanium screws to reproduce a "typical" fixation configuration. In a second configuration the plate was positioned directly beneath one electrode to represent a worst-case geometry with maximal current density. A control run without a plate was performed for each stimulation condition to separate implant-related heating from heating of the medium or electrodes. Electrotherapy Conditions [1] Three stimulation modalities were tested using [30] clinical devices commonly found in physiotherapy practice. High-volt stimulation (HVS) used twin-peak [37] monophasic pulses (pulse duration 100 µs, pair interval 50 µs, peak voltage up to 150 V) at a frequency of 100 Hz. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation TENS) used a symmetrical biphasic rectangular waveform (pulse width 200 µs, frequency 80 Hz), a conventional-mode protocol for analgesia. Galvanic current (GAL) used continuous direct current at an intensity of 0.1 mA/cm² electrode area, the upper limit generally recommended to limit electrochemical skin effects (Watson, 2008). Each modality was delivered at two intensities: a "therapeutic" level and a "maximum" level. The therapeutic level was defined as the intensity producing a strong but comfortable sensation in a pilot of five healthy volunteers (not [3] part of the experimental data) and was translated into the device settings (mean current for GAL, peak current for HVS and TENS). The maximum [1] level was the highest output the device could deliver into the phantom load without alarm or compliance cutoff. Delivered current and voltage were monitored using a digital oscilloscope (100 "MHz)" across a 10 Ω series shunt resistor, and root-mean-square (RMS) current was calculated as Irms = sqrt( (1/T) ∫₀ᵀ i(t)² dt ). Since Joule heating in a conductive medium scales with the square of current density (SAR = σE²/ρ, with σ the conductivity, E the electric field, and ρ the density), we also estimated the specific absorption rate to enable comparison with the temperature data. Under the assumption of negligible heat loss over a short interval, the initial temperature rise rate follows ΔT/Δt ≈ SAR/c, where c is the specific heat capacity of the medium (approximately 4,000 J·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹ for a water-based gel; Hasgall et al., 2018). Electrodes were self-adhesive carbon-rubber pads (5 × 5 cm for HVS and TENS; 5 × 10 cm for GAL), coupled with conductive gel and positioned on the phantom surface 8 cm apart, flanking the implant. For GAL, polarity was assigned so that, in separate runs, the anode and then the cathode lay directly over the plate. Electrodes were replaced between sessions to avoid electrode degradation. Temperature Measurement Temperature was recorded with fiber-optic probes (fluoroptic, accuracy ±0.2°C, sampling rate 1 Hz), chosen because they are immune to electromagnetic interference and do not distort the electrical field (Wickersheim and Sun, 1987). Four probes were used: two placed in direct contact with the plate (at the end nearest the anode and at the end nearest the cathode); one in contact with the screw head, and one reference probe in the medium 10 cm from the plate and electrodes to account for ambient drift. A fifth probe was placed under an electrode to document electrode-site heating. Probe positions were fixed with a template and verified after each session. Introduction Continuous deployment (CD) [13] is a software engineering practice in which code changes are automatically built, tested, and "released" to end users through an automated deployment pipeline (Humble and [15] Farley, 2010). Organizations adopt CD to shorten release cycles, [34] obtain faster customer feedback, and reduce the manual effort of releasing software. Industry surveys associate frequent, automated deployment with better organizational performance and faster recovery from failures (Forsgren et al., 2018). A central enabler of CD is infrastructure as code [9] (IaC), the practice of provisioning and configuring computing infrastructure through machine-readable scripts rather than manual procedures (Humble and Farley, 2010; Rahman et al., 2019a). Tools such as Puppet, Chef, and Ansible let practitioners specify the desired state of servers, services, and dependencies in source code. That code can then be version-controlled, reviewed, tested, and executed repeatedly and consistently across environments. Treating infrastructure as software also exposes it to the defects that affect any other software artifact. A defect in an IaC script can propagate to every machine on which the script is executed, and so can compromise the reliability "of" the whole deployment pipeline. Misconfigured infrastructure has been implicated in widely reported service disruptions, including a 2017 outage of Amazon's Simple Storage Service that followed an erroneous operational command and affected a large number of dependent websites and services (Amazon Web Services, 2017). Prior empirical work shows that such defects are However, not rare. Jiang and Adams (2015) observed that infrastructure code in open source projects co-evolves with, and is often as change-prone as, production code. Rahman and Williams (2018) found that defect-related commits constitute a substantial share of the commits to IaC scripts in several open source repositories. Defective IaC scripts can cause frequent deployment failures and consume considerable developer effort, which undermines the benefits that motivate CD in the first place. Researchers and practitioners have begun to study the quality of IaC along several lines. A systematic mapping study found that research on IaC remains sparse relative to its adoption in industry, and that few studies have examined the relationship between source code characteristics and script quality (Rahman et al., 2019a). Sharma et al. (2016) catalogued configuration smells in Puppet code and showed that they can be detected with static analysis, and Schwarz et al. (2018) extended this line of work to Chef. Hanappi et al. (2016) and Hummer et al. (2013) proposed approaches for testing the idempotence and convergence of configuration scripts. These studies are valuable, but they mostly rely on smells [13] and rules defined a priori by researchers or tool builders. They do not establish which properties of IaC source code are actually associated with [31] defects observed in practice. Without empirical evidence of [35] this kind; practitioners lack data-driven guidance on where to focus code review and testing, and researchers lack a principled basis for building automated defect prediction models for IaC. In the broader software engineering literature, source code properties have long been used to characterize and predict defects. Size, complexity, and change metrics are known to correlate with defect proneness in general-purpose languages (Nagappan et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2012; "Menzies" et al., 2007). IaC languages, however, differ markedly from general-purpose languages. They are declarative or hybrid in nature, they describe resources and their relationships rather than algorithms, and they are dominated by configuration values, file paths, and invocations of external modules. Properties that matter in conventional code, such as inheritance depth or loop structure, may therefore carry little signal in IaC scripts, whereas properties specific to configuration, such as how values are specified or how dependencies are included, may carry considerable signal. [35] It is thus unclear whether findings from conventional defect prediction transfer to IaC, and which IaC-specific properties are worth measuring. We hypothesize that certain properties of IaC source code, for example the number of lines of code and the use of hard-coded strings as configuration values; are correlated with defective scripts. The objective of this paper is to help practitioners increase the quality of IaC scripts through an empirical study that identifies source code properties of defective IaC scripts. To this end, we pursue three research questions: RQ1: What source code properties characterize defective infrastructure as code scripts? RQ2: Do practitioners agree with the identified source code properties? RQ3: How accurately can we predict defective infrastructure as code [26] scripts using the identified source code properties? To answer RQ1, we apply qualitative analysis to defect-related commits mined from open source repositories. We derive candidate properties from the code changes that fixed defects, and then quantify the relationship between each property and script defectiveness using statistical tests and effect sizes. To answer RQ2, we survey practitioners to assess their level of agreement with each identified property, which provides a check on whether the empirical findings match practitioner experience. To answer RQ3, we construct defect prediction models from the identified properties and evaluate them on 2,439 Puppet scripts drawn from four datasets collected from open source organizations, namely Mirantis, Mozilla, Openstack, and Wikimedia. We follow established practice in defect prediction by comparing several learners and reporting precision and recall, the measures that matter most to practitioners who must decide how much inspection effort to allocate (Hall et al., 2012; Menzies et al., 2007). Our analysis identifies 10 source code properties that correlate with defective IaC [13] However, scripts. Of these, lines of code and hard-coded string show the strongest correlation with defective scripts. Hard-coded string denotes the property of specifying a configuration value as a hard-coded string. In the practitioner survey, the majority of respondents agreed with two properties: include, the property of executing external modules or scripts, and hard-coded string. Prediction models built on the identified properties achieve a precision of 0.70 to 0.78 and a recall of 0.54 to 0.67, which suggests that these properties carry practical predictive signal for IaC defects. This paper makes the following contributions: A list of 10 source code properties of IaC scripts that correlate with defects, derived from defect-related commits in open source repositories. A quantitative assessment of the strength of the relationship between each property and script defectiveness, which shows that lines of code and hard-coded string are the most strongly associated. An assessment of practitioner agreement with the identified properties, based on a survey that contrasts empirical evidence with practitioner perception. Defect prediction models for IaC scripts that use the identified properties, together with an evaluation of their precision and recall on 2,439 scripts from four datasets. The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. We first provide background on IaC and review related work. We then describe our methodology, report results for each research question, and discuss implications for practitioners and researchers, followed by threats to validity and conclusions. We conducted a three-phase empirical study. First, we applied qualitative analysis to defect-related commits to derive source code properties of defective infrastructure as code (IaC) scripts. Second, we quantified the association of each property with defective scripts and surveyed practitioners on their agreement with the properties. Third, we built defect prediction models from the properties to evaluate their practical utility. We focus on Puppet, a declarative configuration management language widely used in continuous deployment (Jiang and Adams, 2015; Sharma et al., 2016). The research questions were: (RQ1) Which source code properties characterize defective IaC scripts? (RQ2) Do practitioners agree that these properties are associated with defective scripts? (RQ3) How well can the properties predict defective scripts? Datasets. We mined repositories from four organizations that use Puppet in production: Mirantis, Mozilla, OpenStack, and Wikimedia. We selected repositories using three criteria (Munaiah et al., 2017). First, at least 11% of the files in a repository had to be Puppet scripts, which excludes repositories where IaC is incidental. Second, the repository had to be under active development with at least two commits per month. Third, the repository had to contain enough history to support defect mining. We cloned each repository and extracted the full commit history with the PyDriller library. The resulting datasets comprised 299 scripts Mirantis), 322 (Mozilla), 1,383 OpenStack), and 435 (Wikimedia), for 2,439 scripts in total. We treated each dataset separately in all analyses to limit the influence of organization-specific conventions, and we pooled data only where noted. Identifying defect-related commits. Following Rahman and Williams (2018), we classified a commit as defect-related if its message described the correction of a defect in a Puppet script. We first applied a keyword filter on commit messages (e.g., fix, bug, error, fail, crash, incorrect) and retained only commits that modified at least one Puppet script. Keyword matching alone yields false positives (Herzig et al., 2013), so two raters manually inspected every retained message, together with the associated diff where the message was ambiguous. [38] Commits that described feature additions, refactoring, or documentation changes were excluded. We measured inter-rater agreement with Cohen's κ (Cohen, 1960) on the initial independent labels and resolved disagreements by discussion. A script was labeled defective if it was modified by at least one defect-related commit, and neutral otherwise. Qualitative analysis (RQ1). To identify source code properties, we applied open coding (Strauss and Corbin, 1998) to the code changes in the defect-related commits. The first author examined the lines removed or modified by each defect-fixing commit and recorded the code elements implicated in the defect, for example a hard-coded string assigned to a configuration attribute, a dependency declared through include, or a conditional statement. We grouped related codes into candidate properties through iterative comparison, and each property was given a name and an operational definition. A second rater independently applied the definitions to a random sample of 200 defect-related commits, and we computed Cohen's κ to evaluate the reliability of the resulting scheme. Disagreements prompted refinement of the definitions until the raters reached consensus. This process yielded a set of properties that we could compute automatically from script source code. Measurement and statistical analysis (RQ1). For each script, we computed the count of each property with a parser built on the Puppet language grammar, normalizing nothing except where noted so that counts reflected raw code characteristics. Lines of code (LOC) was included as a baseline property because size is a well-established correlate of defects (Zhang, 2009). To quantify the relationship between each property and defective scripts, we compared the property's distribution in defective and neutral scripts within each dataset. Because property counts were non-normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk tests, p < 0.05), we used the non-parametric Mann–Whitney U test (Mann and Whitney, 1947) at α = 0.05; applying the Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple comparisons across properties. We quantified effect sizes with Cliff's δ (Cliff, 1993), and we interpreted magnitudes using the conventional thresholds of negligible [11] (|δ| < 0.147), small (< 0.33), medium (< 0.474), and large (≥ 0.474) (Romano et al., 2006). We However, additionally computed the median property value for defective and neutral scripts, and we ranked properties by their effect size. Together these [1] analyses show which properties are most [8] strongly correlated with defective scripts. Practitioner survey (RQ2). To assess whether the properties reflect practitioner experience, we conducted a web-based survey. For each property, the questionnaire gave its name, definition, and a short code example from a real Puppet script, then asked respondents to rate their agreement with the statement that scripts containing the property are more likely to be defective. Responses used a five-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932) from [23] strongly disagree to strongly agree. We also collected respondents' years of "IaC" experience and primary role, and we included an optional free-text field for comments. We distributed the survey by email to practitioners who had contributed commits to the studied repositories and to other open-source Puppet projects, and through public developer forums and mailing lists. Before deployment we piloted the instrument with three practitioners, whose feedback led to clearer wording and the removal of ambiguous examples. Participation was voluntary and anonymous. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood; affecting roughly one in 1,000 children and encompassing a heterogeneous group of conditions defined by arthritis of unknown cause that begins before age 16 and persists for at least six weeks [1, 2]. Over the past two decades, the treatment of JIA has changed substantially. Early and more aggressive use of conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, particularly methotrexate, together with the introduction of biologic agents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and T-cell costimulation, has increased the proportion of children who achieve low disease activity or clinical remission [3, 4]. Despite these advances, a considerable number of youth continue to report poor health-related quality of life (HRQOL), including limitations in physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, even when clinical measures indicate that disease is well controlled [5–7]. Pain, fatigue, and psychosocial difficulties persist in many patients whose joint counts and laboratory markers are unremarkable [8, 9]. This discrepancy suggests that the standard clinical indicators used to guide care capture only part of what matters to patients and families, and that other factors contribute to the lived experience of JIA. HRQOL is a multidimensional construct reflecting an individual's perception of how health and illness affect physical, psychological, and social wellbeing [10]. In pediatric rheumatology, HRQOL has been measured with generic instruments such as the Pediatric Quality of However, Life Inventory (PedsQL), as well as with disease-specific tools and the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) [11–13]. Studies using these instruments have shown that HRQOL in JIA is lower than in healthy peers, and that disease activity; functional disability, and pain are correlated with HRQOL [5, 14]. However, associations between clinician-assessed disease activity and HRQOL are typically modest, and most of the variance in HRQOL remains unexplained [6, 15]. Identifying the additional determinants of HRQOL; especially those that are modifiable, is therefore a priority for improving outcomes. One set of potentially modifiable determinants relates to the burden of treatment. Children with JIA frequently take medications for years, often in combination, and these regimens involve injections, infusions, laboratory monitoring, and the risk of adverse effects. Methotrexate, the most widely used first-line systemic therapy, is effective but is commonly associated with gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and abdominal pain, as well as with anticipatory and associative symptoms in which children experience nausea or distress before or at the thought of taking the drug [16, 17]. Methotrexate intolerance has been reported in a substantial minority of [2] patients, can lead to reduced adherence, (29) dose changes, or discontinuation; and has been associated with poorer HRQOL and greater distress [34] for both children and parents [17, 18]. Other medications, including glucocorticoids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and biologic agents, carry their own risks of side effects, and fear of such effects can shape treatment decisions and adherence [19]. Although clinicians recognize that treatment can be burdensome, the contribution of treatment experiences to HRQOL has rarely been quantified alongside the contribution of disease burden, so it is unclear whether adverse treatment experiences affect wellbeing independently of disease symptoms. A second domain of patient experience that is incompletely captured in routine care is the day-to-day symptom burden of disease. Morning stiffness, However, a classic feature of inflammatory arthritis and a component of some disease activity assessments, is not consistently However, recorded in clinical encounters, and its relationship to HRQOL in contemporary JIA cohorts is not well characterized [20]. Pain interference, which reflects the extent to which pain disrupts activities, social participation, and mood rather than pain intensity alone, has emerged as an important patient-reported outcome, and PROMIS provides a validated pediatric measure of it [13, 21]. Pain interference may remain elevated in children with inactive disease, and may therefore represent an important and under-recognized source of reduced HRQOL [8, 22]. Together, (15) morning stiffness and pain interference offer a patient-centered "view" of disease burden that complements physician-reported disease activity. Patient-centered outcomes research has increasingly emphasized collecting information directly from patients and families to understand which experiences matter most and how they relate to outcomes [23]. Multisite disease registries offer a platform for "such" work because they enroll large and diverse samples and already contain detailed clinical data; including diagnosis, disease activity, and medication history. The Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry is a North American observational registry of children with rheumatic diseases, including JIA, that has enrolled thousands of patients across dozens of centers [24]. The registry's clinical data have supported research on treatment patterns and safety, but it has not routinely included patient- or parent-reported measures of HRQOL and of experiences of disease and treatment. Integrating such measures would allow researchers to link patients' perspectives to clinical characteristics at scale and to identify targets for intervention that clinical data alone cannot reveal. The aim of this study was to add patient-reported outcomes to the CARRA Registry and to use them to quantify HRQOL and experiences of disease and treatment burden among youth with JIA. Parents served as proxy reporters of their child's HRQOL, pain interference, morning stiffness, history of serious medication side effects, and, for those taking methotrexate, methotrexate intolerance. We asked three questions. First, what is the distribution of HRQOL and of these disease and treatment experiences in a multisite registry (5) sample? Second, how is each experience associated with HRQOL? Third, do associations between treatment burden and HRQOL persist after accounting for disease burden, disease activity, and patient characteristics? We hypothesized that both disease and treatment burden would be independently associated with lower HRQOL. This study makes several contributions. It demonstrates the feasibility of augmenting an established multicenter registry with patient-reported measures; creating a model that other registries may adopt. It provides estimates of the prevalence of morning stiffness, serious medication side effects, and methotrexate intolerance in a registry cohort with long disease duration. Most importantly; it evaluates the independent contributions of disease and treatment burden to HRQOL, testing the proposition that adverse treatment experiences undermine wellbeing beyond the effects of disease symptoms and activity. The findings may help clinicians and researchers identify routinely assessable, modifiable targets for improving the quality of life of youth with JIA. Study Design and Setting We conducted a cross-sectional, observational study nested within the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry, a multisite, prospective registry of children with pediatric rheumatic diseases enrolled at North American pediatric rheumatology centers (Beukelman et al., 2017). The registry collects clinician-reported demographic, diagnostic, disease activity, and medication data at enrollment and at regular follow-up visits. For this study, we added a patient-centered data collection component in which parents completed a survey about their child's health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and experiences of disease and treatment. Participating sites obtained approval from their local institutional review boards "or" from the central IRB used by the registry, and parents provided informed consent (and children provided assent where required by local policy). Participants and Recruitment Eligible patients were enrolled "in" the CARRA Registry, had a physician diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) according to International League of Associations for Rheumatology criteria (Petty et al., 2004), were between 2 and 18 years of age, and had a parent or legal guardian who could read and respond in English. Because the survey was completed by parent proxy, youth who were too young or unable to self-report were not excluded on that basis. Participating sites identified eligible patients from the registry and invited their parents to complete the survey either during a clinic visit or remotely by mail or secure electronic link. Parents completed the survey once. Registry data from the visit nearest to survey completion were linked to survey responses using a unique study identifier. We restricted the analytic sample to patients with complete data on the primary HRQOL outcome and key covariates. Measures Health-related quality of life. HRQOL was measured with the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0 Generic Core Scales, parent-proxy report (Varni et al., 2001). The PedsQL contains 23 items spanning physical, emotional, social, and school functioning, with a recall period of the previous month. Items are rated on a five-point scale, reverse-scored and linearly transformed to a 0–100 scale, with higher scores indicating better HRQOL. We used the Total Scale Score as the primary outcome and also examined physical and psychosocial summary scores. Age-appropriate parent-proxy forms were used for children aged 2–4, 5–7, 8–12, and 13–18 years. Pain interference. Pain interference was assessed with the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pediatric Pain Interference parent-proxy short form (Varni et al., 2010; Cella et al., 2010). Raw scores were converted to T-scores standardized to a reference population with a mean of 50 and standard deviation of 10, with higher scores reflecting greater interference of pain with daily activities. Morning stiffness. Parents reported the typical duration of their child's morning stiffness on a usual day. Because prolonged stiffness is a recognized marker of active inflammatory arthritis and is incorporated in disease activity assessment (Consolaro et al., 2009), we dichotomized duration as more than 15 minutes versus 15 minutes or less. Medication side effects. Parents were asked whether their child had ever experienced side effects from arthritis medications and, if so, to describe their nature and severity. Responses were reviewed and classified using predefined criteria; a serious side effect was one that led to medication discontinuation or dose change, required medical evaluation or treatment, or substantially disrupted the child's daily functioning. We created a binary indicator of one or more serious medication side effects. Methotrexate intolerance. For children currently or previously treated with methotrexate, parents completed the Methotrexate Intolerance Severity Score (MISS), which assesses abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and restlessness or irritability, each in anticipatory, associative, and behavioral domains (Bulatović et al., 2011). Scores range from 0 to 25, and a score of 6 or higher indicates clinically relevant methotrexate intolerance. Analyses of methotrexate intolerance were restricted to methotrexate users. Clinical and demographic characteristics. From the registry, we obtained patient age, sex, race and ethnicity, disease duration, JIA category, and treating site. Disease activity was captured using the clinical Juvenile Arthritis Disease Activity Score based on 10 joints (cJADAS-10), which combines physician global assessment, parent global assessment of wellbeing, and active joint count (McErlane et al., 2013). Current medication use, including methotrexate and biologic agents, was abstracted from registry records. Statistical Analysis We summarized participant characteristics and study measures using means and standard deviations for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. Distributions of PedsQL, pain interference, and disease activity scores were inspected for normality and outliers. Our primary aim was to estimate the associations between measures of disease burden (pain interference and morning stiffness) and treatment burden (serious side effects and methotrexate intolerance) and HRQOL. Because patients were clustered within participating "sites," we used generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable working correlation structure and robust standard errors (Liang & Zeger, 1986). The outcome was the PedsQL Total Scale Score, modeled with an identity link and Gaussian distribution. We fit models in a sequential manner. First, unadjusted models estimated the association between each burden measure and HRQOL individually. Second, models were adjusted for [15] patient demographics (age, sex, and race/ethnicity) and disease duration, with clustering by site. Third, we added disease burden measures (pain interference and morning stiffness) to models of treatment burden to determine whether treatment-related associations persisted independent of disease symptoms. Finally, we additionally adjusted for disease activity (cJADAS-10) and current medication use to evaluate whether associations were attenuated by clinical characteristics. Because the methotrexate intolerance analysis included only methotrexate users, it was conducted in that subsample with parallel model-building. We compared coefficients across successive models to assess attenuation. Collinearity among covariates was assessed using variance inflation factors. Regression coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals and p-values. Given the multiple related exposures, we considered p-values below 0.01 to indicate statistical significance in primary analyses to limit the risk of type I error. Many real-world recognition problems cannot be posed as standard multi-class classification, because only one class is well characterized during training. Examples include fault detection in industrial systems, intrusion detection, medical screening, and the verification of a person's identity. In these settings the class of interest is abundant or well defined, while the remaining data are rare, heterogeneous, or impossible to enumerate in advance Chandola et al., 2009; Pimentel et al., 2014). One-class classification OCC) addresses this scenario by learning a decision rule from examples of a single class and then deciding whether a new sample belongs to it Khan & Madden, 2014; Perera et al., 2021). The best-known OCC methods are the One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM), which separates the data from the origin in a kernel-induced feature space Schölkopf et [33] al., 2001), and Support Vector Data Description (SVDD), which finds the minimum-volume hypersphere enclosing the target data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Both can be extended [22] to non-linear boundaries through kernels and are widely used baselines. More recently, deep variants such as Deep SVDD have coupled representation learning with a compact description of the target class (Ruff et al., 2018). The performance of any one-class method depends heavily on the feature space in which the data are described. Because no negative samples are available to guide the choice of features, the data representation is often high-dimensional, redundant, or noisy, and the compactness assumption underlying SVDD may then be poorly satisfied. Dimensionality reduction is therefore commonly applied as a separate pre-processing step. Classical techniques such as Principal Component Analysis are unsupervised and optimize criteria like reconstruction error or variance. These criteria are not tied to the objective of the subsequent one-class classifier. Subspace Support Vector Data Description S-SVDD) addressed this mismatch by jointly learning a linear or non-linear projection and the SVDD description, so that [39] the target data become compact in a subspace optimized for the one-class objective (Sohrab et al., 2018). Related graph-embedded formulations similarly use the geometry of the target class to regularize the learned representation (Iosifidis et al., 2015). However, these approaches assume that every sample is represented by a single feature vector from a single source. This assumption is increasingly at odds with how data are acquired. Objects, events, and subjects are now routinely observed through multiple modalities: different sensors, imaging devices, or feature extractors that capture complementary aspects of the same underlying phenomenon Baltrušaitis et al., 2019). Examples include visual and thermal imagery, audio and video streams, and multi-sensor measurements in industrial monitoring. Multimodal and multi-view learning exploits the consensus and complementarity among such sources and has been shown to improve robustness and accuracy compared with learning from a single source (Xu et al., 2013; Ramachandram & Taylor, 2017). Classical subspace methods such as Canonical Correlation Analysis CCA) Hotelling, 1936; Hardoon et al., 2004) and its kernel and deep extensions (Andrew et al., 2013) learn projections that maximize cross-modal correlation, and deep multimodal architectures learn shared representations (Ngiam et al., 2011). These techniques, however, are designed to model statistical dependence between modalities and do not take into account the objective of a downstream one-class classifier. Their projections are not optimized to make the class of interest compact, nor do they exploit the fact that training information is available only for that class. In the OCC literature, the multimodal setting is typically handled in one of two ways, both of which are limiting. The first is to train a separate one-class model on each modality and combine the resulting decision scores (late fusion). This ignores relations among modalities during representation learning and can be adversely affected by weak or noisy modalities. The second is to concatenate the features of all modalities into a single vector (early fusion) and apply a standard one-class method. This increases dimensionality, typically leaves modality-specific scale and noise characteristics unaddressed, and makes the description susceptible to the curse of dimensionality when training samples are limited. Neither strategy learns modality-specific mappings into a common space that is designed from the outset for describing the target class. Consequently, there is a clear gap: no existing approach jointly learns, for each modality, a transformation into a shared low-dimensional space and a single compact description of the target class using data from all modalities, while relying exclusively on target-class samples. The question motivating this work is therefore the following: can multimodal one-class learning be improved by learning modality-specific projections to a common subspace in which a single hypersphere, trained only on target data from all modalities, provides a tighter and more discriminative description than that obtainable from any single modality or from naive fusion? Answering this requires dealing with several challenges. The projections must be learned in conjunction with the data description, since otherwise the subspace is not adapted to the one-class criterion. The formulation must also admit regularization strategies that prevent degenerate solutions, such as collapsing all data onto a point, and that encourage consistency across modalities. Finally, it should handle both linear relations and the non-linear structure commonly encountered in real data. In this paper we introduce Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MS-SVDD), a method that extends the S-SVDD framework to data from multiple modalities. MS-SVDD iteratively optimizes two components: a set of modality-specific transformations that map each original feature space into a common subspace, and a joint SVDD description of the projected data from all modalities. The transformations are learned using information from the class of interest only, so the method remains a genuine one-class approach and requires no negative or outlier examples at training time. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1. We formulate the problem of learning a shared one-class-optimized subspace from multiple modalities and propose MS-SVDD, which jointly learns modality-specific projections and a single compact description of the target class. 2. We propose several regularization strategies for the method. These control the geometry of the learned subspace and the relationships among the projected modalities, which allows the formulation to be adapted to different degrees of cross-modal agreement. 3. We provide both linear and non-linear (kernel-based) formulations, together with an iterative optimization procedure, so that the method can be applied to data with simple as well as complex structure. 4. We conduct an extensive experimental evaluation on five multimodal datasets, comparing MS-SVDD with one-class methods trained on a single modality and on fused data from all modalities. The proposed method outperforms all competing approaches on four of the five datasets, which indicates that learning a task-specific common subspace is more effective than either individual-modality models or direct fusion. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background on SVDD and S-SVDD. Section 3 presents the proposed MS-SVDD method, its regularization strategies, and its linear and [14] non-linear formulations. Section 4 describes the datasets and experimental protocol and reports the results, and Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. Problem formulation and notation Let 𝒳 "=" {X¹,…,X^M} denote data from M modalities, where X^m ∈ ℝ^{Dm×N} contains the N training samples of the target class represented in the m-th modality, with Dm the modality-specific [36] dimensionality. Only target-class samples are used during training, in line with the one-class classification (OCC) setting (Tax & Duin, 2004). Samples are assumed to be paired across modalities. Each modality is z-score normalized using training statistics before projection. Support Vector Data Description (SVDD) seeks the smallest hypersphere; with centre a and radius R, enclosing most training data (Tax & Duin, 2004). Subspace SVDD (Sohrab et al., 2018) jointly learns a projection Q ∈ ℝ^{d×D} and the hypersphere in the projected space. We extend this idea to the multimodal case by defining a modality-specific projection Qm ∈ ℝ^{d×Dm} that maps every modality into a common d-dimensional "subspace," where one shared hypersphere a, R) describes data from all modalities. The multimodal objective is min{R,a,ξ,{Qm}} R² + C Σm Σi ξi^m + λ/2) Ω({Qm}), subject to ‖Qm xi^m − a‖² ≤ R² + ξi^m and ξi^m ≥ 0 for i = 1,…,N and m = 1,…,M. Here C > 0 controls the trade-off between the volume of the hypersphere and the training errors, and Ω is a regularization term weighted by λ ≥ 0. Optimization procedure The problem is non-convex jointly in {Qm} and the hypersphere parameters, so we use an alternating scheme. With the projections fixed, the problem reduces to a standard SVDD on the pooled projected samples {Qm xi^m}, and its Lagrangian dual is a quadratic program, which we solve with a sequential minimal optimization solver (Chang & [24] Lin, 2011). The dual variables αi^m satisfy 0 ≤ αi^m ≤ C and Σ{m,i} αi^m = 1, and the centre is a = Σ{m,i} αi^m Qm xi^m. The step size η was set to 10⁻³ and the Adam update rule (Kingma & Ba, 2015) was [5] used for stability. The two steps alternate until the relative change "of" the objective falls below 10⁻⁵ or 100 iterations are reached. Each Qm was initialized by one of three schemes: PCA of the corresponding modality (Jolliffe, 2002), a random Gaussian matrix with entries drawn from [2] 𝒩(0, 1/Dm), or the canonical correlation analysis CCA) directions between pairs of modalities (Hotelling, 1936). The default was PCA initialization; the other two were examined in an ablation. Because shared radius and centre are [26] used, a test sample is scored in modality m by its distance ‖Qm x^m − a‖², and is accepted as a target if "this" distance does not exceed R². (i) Norm regularization: Ω₁ = Σm ‖Qm‖²F, which limits the scale of the projections and prevents the trivial solution in which all data collapse to a point. ii) Variance regularization: Ω₂ = Σm tr(Qm Sm Qmᵀ), where Sm is the scatter matrix of modality m. (iii) Cross-modal alignment: Ω₃ = Σ{m<l} Σi ‖Qm xi^m − Ql xi^l‖²; which encourages paired samples from different modalities to coincide in the shared subspace, similarly to the correlation-maximization principle of CCA but without requiring non-target data.
