Population ageing and the fiscal pressures it places on pension systems have made the extension of working lives a central objective of social policy across Europe. Many countries have raised statutory pension ages, restricted access to early retirement schemes, and introduced incentives to remain in employment (OECD 2015, European Commission 2012). The European Union's Europe 2020 strategy explicitly targets higher employment among older workers, and several governments are now debating or legislating retirement ages of 67 or beyond. Employment rates among those aged 55 to 64 have indeed risen in most European countries over the past two decades (Eurostat 2014). Yet beyond the age of 65, paid work remains a minority activity, and its prevalence varies strongly across countries, from a few percent in France or Belgium to considerably higher shares in Sweden, Switzerland, or Estonia (Hofäcker and Naumann 2015; Scherger et al. 2012). The scientific literature on late careers has so far concentrated predominantly on the opposite end of the spectrum: those who leave the labour market early. A large body of work examines the determinants of early or premature exit, including poor health, physically and psychologically demanding jobs, low job control, and unfavourable pension incentives (Blekesaune and Solem 2005, Siegrist et al. 2007; Van den Berg et al. 2010; de Wind et al. 2014). Stressful psychosocial work environments, conceptualised, for example, through the demand-control model Karasek and Theorell 1990) and the model of effort-reward imbalance (Siegrist 1996), have been shown to predict both poor health and the intention or decision to retire early (Siegrist et al. 2006; Wahrendorf et al. 2013). From this perspective, early exit is often interpreted as a response to adverse working conditions and deteriorating health, a "push" factor, while financial incentives and attractive leisure opportunities constitute "pull" factors (Shultz et al. 1998; Radl 2013). By comparison, relatively little is known about people who continue working after reaching the age at which most of their peers have retired. Existing studies suggest that working beyond conventional retirement ages is selective. Older workers who continue are, on average, healthier, more highly educated, and more likely to be self-employed than those who retire (Dingemans and Henkens 2014; Kanabar 2015, Principi et al. 2014). Motives for continued work are heterogeneous: some individuals work because they enjoy their job, value social contacts, or wish to remain active, whereas others work out of financial necessity because of low pension entitlements Platts et al. 2016; Vickerstaff 2010). This distinction matters, because the policy discourse on "active ageing" often implicitly assumes that longer working lives are voluntary and beneficial, whereas the empirical reality may comprise both privileged and vulnerable groups Alcover et al. 2014, Lain 2012). Whether extended working lives are accompanied by favourable or unfavourable job characteristics is therefore an important empirical question. Several gaps remain in the existing evidence. First, most studies of late-life employment focus on the transition ages between 50 and 65 and thus rarely describe people who work at ages 65 to 80, a group that is small but growing and of particular relevance for debates on raising pension ages further. Second, studies of older workers often consider a limited set of characteristics, such as demographic and health status, and pay less attention to detailed employment conditions, including employment status (employee, self-employed with or without employees), occupational position, and weekly working hours. Third, while there is considerable evidence on the psychosocial work environment as a predictor of early exit, we know little about how exposure to stressful work, such as low control or effort-reward imbalance, differs between those working beyond 65 and those who are retired. Because retired persons, by definition, no longer work, a meaningful comparison requires information on their conditions in the last job before retirement. Such a comparison can indicate whether those who continue to work come from systematically better or worse job circumstances than those who have left, which is crucial for judging whether policies that postpone retirement would burden particular groups. Fourth, much research is limited to single countries, which complicates generalisation given the institutional diversity of European pension, labour market, and welfare systems (Ebbinghaus 2006). Comparative, harmonised data covering a wide age range and diverse institutional settings are required. The present study addresses these gaps using data from the fourth wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE, Börsch-Supan et al. 2013), collected between 2009 and 2011. SHARE is a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of people aged 50 and over, offering harmonised information on health, socio-economic circumstances, and employment. Importantly, wave 4 includes measures of psychosocial working conditions for current workers and, retrospectively, for the last job of retired respondents, as well as indicators of physical and mental health. This allows us to compare current workers and retirees aged 65 to 80 across 16 European countries within a single analytical framework. We pursue three research questions. First, which sociodemographic characteristics (age, gender, education, partnership and financial situation) are associated with working beyond age 65? Second, how do employment conditions, namely employment status, occupational position, and working hours, and stressful psychosocial working conditions (low control and effort-reward imbalance) differ between those working at ages 65 to 80 and the retired in their last job? Third, how are these working conditions and health (physical and mental) related to the likelihood of being in paid work in this age group, once country context and potential confounders are taken into account? We expect that people working beyond 65 are more often self-employed, hold advantaged occupational positions, report more favourable psychosocial working conditions, and are in better health than their retired counterparts. This expectation follows from selection arguments: those with greater autonomy, rewards, and resources have both more opportunities and more incentives to remain employed, while those exposed to strain or ill health are more likely to withdraw (Wahrendorf et al. 2013; Dingemans and Henkens 2014). The study contributes to the literature in three ways. It shifts attention from early exit to prolonged participation and describes in detail who works at ages 65 to 80 in Europe. It brings together a broad set of employment characteristics and established measures of psychosocial work stress, and it compares current workers with retirees using information on their previous jobs. Finally, it uses multilevel random intercept) models to take cross-national variation into account. Together, these contributions provide evidence on the social selectivity of extended working lives and thus inform debates on the consequences of rising pension ages for different social groups. Data and study population We used data from wave 4 of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), a multidisciplinary, cross-national panel study of community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older and their partners (Börsch-Supan et al. 2013). Wave 4 fieldwork [36] was conducted between 2009 and 2011, and release 1.1.1 was used. Samples in each participating country were drawn as probability samples, mostly from population registers or multi-stage area sampling, and interviews were conducted face-to-face using computer-assisted personal interviewing. Methodological details, including sampling design and response rates, are described elsewhere (Börsch-Supan and Jürges 2005; Malter and Börsch-Supan 2013). Wave 4 included 58,000 respondents in 16 countries: Sweden, Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Spain, Estonia, Slovenia, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Poland and Portugal. Because information on the last job before retirement was collected in the life history interview (SHARELIFE) in wave 3 and in the baseline interview for refreshment samples, we linked wave 4 information with these sources where required. We restricted the analytic sample to [13] men and women aged 65 to 80 years who were either in paid work or retired at the time of interview. This age band was chosen because 65 corresponds to the statutory pension [4] age, or a close approximation, in most of the countries studied during the observation period, and because employment becomes very rare after age 80. Respondents were classified as working if they reported "employed or self-employed including working for family business)" as their current main labour force status, and as retired if they reported being retired. Respondents who described themselves as homemakers, unemployed, permanently sick or disabled, or other were excluded, as were retired persons who had never been in paid employment and thus could not report on any previous working conditions. After these exclusions and removal of cases with missing information on key variables, the [1] final sample comprised 17,625 individuals N working = 1,647 and N retired = 15,978). Measures The outcome variable was labour market participation, coded 1 for current paid work and 0 for retirement. Employment conditions were measured for the current job among workers and for the last [19] job before retirement among retirees. Employment status distinguished employees, self-employed persons with employees, and self-employed persons without employees (own-account workers). Occupational position was based on the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-88) and grouped into high (managers, professionals, technicians and associate professionals), intermediate (clerks, service and sales workers, skilled agricultural and craft workers) and low (plant and machine operators, elementary occupations) categories cf. Ganzeboom and Treiman 1996). Weekly working hours were categorised as part-time (fewer than 35 hours), full-time 35–44 hours) and long hours 45 hours or more), following [22] conventions in the literature on extended working hours (Virtanen et al. 2011). Psychosocial working conditions were assessed using two established stress models. Low control at work was derived from the demand–control model Karasek and Theorell 1990) and was measured with two items in SHARE: I have very little freedom to decide how to do my work" and "I have an opportunity to develop new skills", the latter reverse coded. Items were rated on a four-point scale from strongly agree to strongly disagree, and were summed and dichotomised at the country-pooled lowest tertile of control, with the lowest tertile defined as low control. Effort–reward imbalance (ERI) was derived from the model by Siegrist (1996) and calculated using the short SHARE version (Siegrist et al. 2004, 2014). Effort was assessed with two items (constant time pressure, physically demanding work), and reward with five items (recognition, adequate salary, promotion prospects, job security, and support). The ERI ratio was calculated as ERI = (e / r) × c, where e is the sum score of the effort items, r the sum score of the reward items, and c a correction factor (here, 5/2) accounting for the unequal number of items in the numerator and denominator. Values above 1 indicate that high effort is not matched by adequate reward, and respondents were classified as [29] experiencing effort–reward imbalance if ERI > 1. For retirees, the same items referred retrospectively to the last job before retirement; the potential for recall bias is addressed in the Discussion. Health was captured by physical and mental health indicators. Physical [15] health was measured by a) self-rated health (dichotomised as fair or poor versus good, very good or excellent), (b) presence of at least one limitation in activities of daily living (ADL) or instrumental activities of daily living IADL), and (c) the number of chronic diseases 0, 1, 2 or more). Mental health was assessed with the EURO-D scale, a 12-item depression symptom scale validated across European countries Prince et al. 1999). A score of 4 or above indicates clinically relevant depressive symptoms Prince et al. 1999). Covariates included age (in years, entered as a continuous term), sex, educational attainment (ISCED-97, grouped as low [levels 0–2], medium [3–4] and high [5–6]), partnership status (living with a partner versus not), and household net wealth quintile within country as an indicator of financial resources. Wealth was used instead of income because of the high proportion of missing income values and because it better represents resources in later life Hurd and Rohwedder 2010). Country was used as the clustering unit. Statistical analysis We first described the sample by labour market status, stratified by sex, using proportions for categorical variables and means with standard deviations for continuous variables. Public health interventions are typically complex. They comprise multiple interacting components, target several levels of influence from individuals to communities and systems, and are [9] delivered in settings where context shapes both implementation and outcome (Craig et al., 2008). Evaluating such interventions is challenging. Experimental designs may show whether an intervention "worked" on average, but they often reveal little about why, for whom, or under what conditions. Funders, policy makers and practitioners increasingly ask for evaluations that explain the mechanisms by which change occurs, so that effective interventions can be adapted, scaled up or transferred to new settings (Moore et al., 2015). This has led to growing interest in approaches that make the assumptions underlying an intervention explicit and open to testing. Theory-based evaluation is one such family of approaches. Its central premise is that an intervention can be understood as a set of hypotheses about how activities will lead to outcomes, and that evaluation should examine whether the hypothesised steps occur as expected (Weiss, 1995; Chen, 1990). Within this tradition, "theory of change" (ToC) has become one of the most widely used terms. Emerging from the evaluation of community initiatives in the United States in the 1990s, ToC was proposed as a way to address the difficulty of evaluating comprehensive programmes whose goals were broad and whose pathways to impact were poorly specified (Weiss, 1995; Connell and Kubisch, 1998). In its most common form, ToC describes how and why a desired change is expected to happen in a particular context, usually by identifying long-term goals and working backwards to the preconditions, intermediate outcomes and activities required to reach them, together with the assumptions linking each step (Connell and Kubisch, 1998; Vogel, 2012). The product is often a diagram or narrative, developed through participatory processes involving stakeholders, that serves as a shared representation of the intervention logic. The appeal of ToC is considerable. International development agencies, philanthropic foundations and government departments now frequently request or require a ToC in funding applications, programme planning and monitoring frameworks (Vogel, 2012, Stein and Valters, 2012). Proponents argue that ToC encourages clearer thinking about the problem and the intended solution, promotes dialogue among stakeholders, exposes unrealistic or untested assumptions, and provides a framework for selecting indicators and interpreting evaluation findings (Anderson, 2005; De Silva et al., 2014). In public health, where interventions are often delivered across health, social and environmental sectors and rely on behaviour change by multiple actors, these attributes seem particularly valuable. ToC has been applied to areas as diverse as HIV prevention, maternal and child health, mental health, tobacco control and health systems strengthening. Despite this popularity, ToC is used inconsistently and its definition is contested. The term is applied to logic models, logframes, results chains, conceptual frameworks, impact pathways and more elaborate causal maps, often interchangeably (Rogers, 2008; Breuer et al., 2016). Some authors treat ToC as a planning tool to be used at the outset of intervention design; others use it retrospectively to reconstruct the logic of an existing programme; still others treat it as an evaluation framework against which data are collected and findings interpreted. ToC may be drawn from social science theory, from empirical evidence, from the tacit knowledge of programme staff, or from combinations of these, and the extent to which it is actually informed by formal theory varies widely (Davidoff et al., 2015). Several commentators have noted that the term is sometimes invoked superficially, with a diagram produced to satisfy a funder but with little influence on how the intervention is designed, implemented or evaluated (Stein and Valters, 2012; Vogel, 2012). Without transparent accounts of how a ToC was developed and used, it is difficult to judge its quality, to learn from others' experience, or to assess whether the claimed benefits are realised. Existing guidance on ToC is largely found in practitioner manuals and grey literature produced by evaluation organisations and funders, and it is not always consistent about recommended steps. Meanwhile, the academic literature contains a growing number of reports that mention ToC, but no systematic account of how it has been applied in public health. Reviews of theory use in health interventions have tended to focus on behaviour change theories and their relationship to effectiveness (Michie and Prestwich, 2010, Davis et al., 2015), rather than on ToC as a distinct approach to intervention development and evaluation. Related work on [2] intervention development frameworks and on the reporting of complex interventions highlights the importance of explicit programme theory, but does not tell us how often or how well ToC specifically has been used (Craig et al., 2008; Hoffmann et al., 2014). Consequently, little is known about who is using ToC, in which settings and for what purposes, how ToCs are developed and who is involved, whether they inform intervention design as well as evaluation, and how reporting could be improved. This gap matters for several reasons. First, if ToC is to be recommended as good practice, we need evidence on how However, it is actually done and what is reported about its contribution. Second, poor reporting limits replication and prevents the accumulation of methodological learning, a problem well recognised in the wider literature on intervention reporting (Hoffmann et al., 2014). Third, researchers and programme planners who wish to use ToC currently have few worked examples that describe the process in enough detail to be adapted. This paper therefore presents a systematic review of the use of ToC in the design and evaluation of public health interventions. Our research questions were: (1) How has ToC been developed in public health interventions, including the methods used, the stakeholders involved and the evidence or theory drawn upon? (2) To what extent and how has ToC been used in the development of interventions? (3) To what extent and how has ToC been used in their evaluation? We also examined the level of detail with which these processes were reported. The review makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic overview of the extent and nature of ToC use in public health across settings, topics and study designs. It identifies weaknesses in current reporting practice that limit the field's capacity to appraise and learn from ToC. Finally, it proposes a checklist for reporting ToC development and use, intended to promote transparency and to be refined by authors and users of the approach. Review design and protocol We conducted a systematic review of published and unpublished literature reporting the use of theory of change (ToC) in the development or evaluation of public health interventions. The review followed the general principles of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the guidance of the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination on undertaking systematic reviews [2]. Because the aim was descriptive (to characterise how ToC has been developed and applied rather than to estimate intervention effects), we did not assess effectiveness outcomes or conduct a meta-analysis. A protocol specifying the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy and extraction items was However, agreed by the review team before searching began. Definitions For the purposes of the review, a ToC was understood as a description or illustration, usually developed through a participatory or consultative process, of how and why a desired change is expected (10) to happen in a particular context [3, 4]. ToC approaches typically involve identifying long-term goals, working backwards to specify the preconditions or intermediate outcomes required to achieve them, and articulating the assumptions underlying the causal pathways and the activities that will trigger them [3]. We included only (17) papers that explicitly used the term "theory of change". Papers using related terms alone (for example logic model, logical framework, results chain or programme theory) were excluded unless they also described their work as a ToC. Public health interventions were defined broadly as organised activities aimed at preventing disease, promoting health or improving health systems and the social determinants of health at the population or community level, in any country setting. Eligibility criteria We included papers of any date, language and study design that reported the use of ToC in the development of a public health intervention, in its evaluation, or both. This encompassed intervention development reports, protocols, process evaluations, outcome and impact evaluations, qualitative studies, and descriptive or reflective papers. We excluded papers that mentioned ToC only in passing without describing its application to a specific intervention or programme, papers that were purely methodological discussions of ToC with no reference "to" a public health intervention, and interventions outside the health domain (for example education or governance programmes with no health outcome). Where the same intervention was reported in several documents, each was screened, and those meeting the criteria were included and linked during extraction. Search strategy We searched electronic bibliographic databases of peer-reviewed literature, including Scopus, PubMed and PsycINFO, using the search term "theory of change" combined with terms relating to health, public health and health interventions. No date or language restrictions were applied. To identify grey literature, we searched specialist grey literature databases and the [32] Google search engine, screening results until relevance dropped substantially. We (23) additionally searched the websites of major development funders and agencies that commonly commission or require ToC, and we examined the reference lists of included papers and of key ToC guidance documents [3, 5] for further eligible sources. Searches were last updated in 2015, and non-English papers were to be translated or reviewed by speakers of the relevant language. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles (20) and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Records judged potentially relevant by either reviewer proceeded to full-text assessment. [35] Full texts were then double screened by two independent reviewers, with reasons for exclusion recorded. Disagreements at either stage were resolved by discussion and, where necessary, by consultation [16] with (28) a third reviewer. Before formal screening, reviewers piloted the criteria on a sample of records to ensure consistent interpretation. Data extraction A [21] standardised data extraction form was developed in a spreadsheet, piloted on a subset of included papers and refined. Data were extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second reviewer. Extracted information comprised: publication characteristics (year, type of document, geographic setting, income classification of (3) the country); intervention characteristics (health topic, target population, level of delivery), the purpose for which ToC was used; and details (7) of how the ToC was developed. For ToC development we recorded who was involved (for example programme implementers, funders, beneficiaries, researchers, policy-makers), the methods used (workshops, interviews, document review, literature review, or combinations), whether existing evidence or theory informed However, the ToC, whether the process was participatory, whether [37] a ToC diagram or narrative was produced, whether assumptions were made explicit, and whether the ToC was revised over time. For use in intervention design, we recorded whether the ToC informed the selection of intervention components, targeting, or implementation However, planning. For use in evaluation, we recorded whether the ToC guided evaluation questions, the selection of [39] indicators and data collection tools, the analysis, process evaluation, or the interpretation of findings, and whether the ToC was tested or refined using evaluation data. We also recorded any reported benefits and challenges of using ToC, and the level of detail provided about the ToC process and outputs. Papers could be coded under more than one use category. Quality and reporting appraisal Because the review (12) focused on reporting and application of the ToC approach rather than on the strength of effect estimates, we did not apply a formal risk-of-bias tool. Instead, we assessed the completeness of reporting of the [3] ToC process by noting which of the elements above were described. These observations, together with the reporting gaps identified, informed the development of a proposed checklist for reporting ToC use. The checklist items were drawn from the extraction categories and from existing ToC [36] guidance [3, 5], and were discussed and refined by the review team through consensus. Modern software systems operate in environments that are rarely fully known at design time. Resource availability fluctuates, workloads vary, and network conditions and user behavior change in ways that are hard to predict. Self-adaptation addresses this problem by [24] equipping a system with a feedback loop that monitors the system and its environment, analyzes the collected data, and adapts the system when the adaptation goals are at risk (Cheng et al., 2009; de Lemos et al., 2013). The best-known reference model for such a loop is MAPE-K, in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan, and Execute components share a Knowledge base (Kephart & Chess, 2003). Self-adaptation is now a key concern in domains as varied as cloud computing, cyber-physical systems, and the Internet of Things (IoT), where manual reconfiguration is too slow, too costly, or simply impossible (Weyns, 2019). Because self-adaptive systems frequently operate in safety-, mission-, or business-critical settings, stakeholders need assurances that the system satisfies its adaptation goals despite uncertainty (Weyns et al., 2012, Calinescu et al., 2012). Traditional design-time verification cannot provide these assurances alone, since many sources of uncertainty only resolve during operation. This has led to a research stream on the use of formal methods at runtime, often called models@run.time combined with runtime verification and quantitative analysis (Bencomo et al., 2019; Calinescu et al., 2011). Representative approaches use probabilistic model checking to predict, before adaptation, the quality properties of candidate adaptation options with respect to the adaptation goals (Calinescu & Kwiatkowska, 2009; Epifani et al., 2009; Filieri et al., 2011; Camara et al., 2016). Runtime models are updated with monitored data, and the verification results guide the selection of the best option. Related work on control-theoretic adaptation (Filieri et al., 2015) and on search-based and learning-based planning (Quin et al., 2019, Jamshidi et al., 2019) pursues similar goals with different guarantees. Despite this progress, we identify three limitations in existing formal approaches that affect their practical applicability. First, existing approaches focus on guaranteeing properties of the managed system or its adaptation decisions, but they largely ignore the correctness of the feedback loop itself. The feedback loop is software, and it can contain faults: wrong sequencing of the MAPE activities, deadlocks between components, violated timing constraints, or incorrect handling of the knowledge. Formal guarantees about adaptation options are of limited value if the loop that applies them does not behave as intended. In most approaches the feedback loop is implemented in conventional code, while formal models are used only as auxiliary artifacts to support analysis. Consequently, a gap remains between the verified model and the code that actually runs, and the guarantees established at design time cannot be assumed to hold during execution (Weyns et al., 2012; Gerasimou et al., 2018). Second, most approaches rely on exhaustive verification at runtime to select adaptation options. Every time adaptation is triggered, the system verifies each candidate configuration against the adaptation goals with techniques such as probabilistic model checking. The state-space explosion that makes verification expensive at design time becomes more acute at runtime, where time and computational resources are limited. For systems with large adaptation spaces, such as IoT networks with many configurable nodes and parameters, verifying all options is often infeasible within the available time window (Weyns et al., 2022). Proposed remedies, such as incremental or compositional verification (Filieri et al., 2011; Gerasimou et al., 2015) and machine-learning-based reduction of the adaptation space (Quin et al., 2019; Weyns et al., 2022), reduce this cost but either remain tied to specific model "structures" or introduce their own sources of uncertainty. Efficient verification remains [12] a barrier to practical use. Third, [14] existing approaches provide limited or no support for changing adaptation goals at runtime. Goals reflect stakeholder requirements, and these evolve: new quality concerns emerge, thresholds are revised, and priorities shift. Yet in most approaches the goals are hard-wired into the feedback loop or into the formal properties that are verified, so changing them requires stopping the system, modifying [37] code, and redeploying (Bencomo et al., 2019; Vogel & Giese, 2014). This undermines the very flexibility that self-adaptation is meant to provide, particularly for long-lived systems that must evolve in operation. These limitations motivate the following research question: How can we engineer self-adaptive systems so that the correctness of the feedback loop behavior is ensured, adaptation goals [2] are achieved efficiently at runtime, and adaptation goals can be changed during operation? To answer this question, we present ActivFORMS (Active FORmal Models for Self-adaptation), a formally founded, model-based approach. The central idea is [31] to make [32] formal models of the feedback loop active: instead of serving as documentation or verification input, the models are directly executed by a virtual machine at runtime, so that the behavior that was verified at design time is the behavior that runs. ActivFORMS covers four stages of the life cycle of a feedback loop. At design time, the feedback loop and its adaptation goals are specified as formal models, and the correctness of the loop is verified against its requirements. At deployment, the verified models are loaded into an execution engine that interprets them and interacts with the managed system through well-defined probes and effectors. At runtime, the loop uses the executable models for adaptation However, and applies efficient analysis, rather than exhaustive verification, to select options that satisfy the goals. During evolution, the models, and in particular the adaptation goals, can be updated while the system is running, and the changes can be verified before they are applied, without redeploying the system. We also present ActivFORMS-ta, a tool-supported instance of the approach. It uses timed automata (Alur & Dill, 1994) as the formalism, UPPAAL (Behrmann et al., 2004) for design-time verification of the loop, and statistical model checking (Legay et al., 2010; David et al., 2015) at runtime to evaluate adaptation "options." Statistical model checking trades the exhaustiveness of numerical analysis for a quantifiable statistical confidence, reducing the resources needed to evaluate options and making quantitative analysis feasible within the time available for adaptation. We validate ActivFORMS using DeltaIoT, an IoT application for building security monitoring deployed at the Campus Group T of KU Leuven (Iftikhar et al., 2017), and evaluate its use with realistic network conditions and goals. The contributions of this work are fourfold. (1) A end-to-end, model-based approach that spans design, deployment, runtime adaptation, and evolution of feedback loops and that supports guarantees about the loop's behavior. (2) A runtime analysis strategy based on statistical techniques that achieves the adaptation goals efficiently and avoids exhaustive verification. (3) A mechanism for changing adaptation goals at runtime, supported by verification of the changes. (4) ActivFORMS-ta, [29] a tool-supported instance, together with an empirical validation on a deployed IoT system showing correctness of the loop behavior, efficient achievement of the goals, and runtime goal [19] changes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we introduce the running example and background, present the approach and its instantiation, report the evaluation, and discuss related However, work, limitations, and [5] conclusions. Research design and [12] questions We evaluated ActivFORMS through a design-science study that combined the engineering of the approach with an empirical evaluation on a deployed Internet-of-Things (IoT) system. The evaluation addressed three questions. RQ1: does the approach ensure correctness of the feedback loop's behavior? RQ2: does it achieve the adaptation goals efficiently compared with exhaustive runtime verification? RQ3: does it support changing adaptation goals at runtime without redeploying the system? The ActivFORMS approach ActivFORMS follows the MAPE-K reference model (Kephart and Chess 2003), However, in which Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute components share a Knowledge repository. Unlike approaches that treat formal models as design-time artifacts, However, ActivFORMS represents the feedback loop itself as a set of formal models that are executed at runtime by a virtual However, machine, so the verified models are the running loop (Weyns and Iftikhar 2016). The approach covers four life-cycle stages. At design time, engineers model the managed system, its environment, and the MAPE behavior as networks of timed automata (Alur and Dill 1994). In the deployment stage, the verified models are loaded into the virtual machine, which runs on top of the managed system's effectors and probes. At runtime, [35] the loop adapts the system and may [8] use the knowledge models to reason about adaptation options. In the evolution stage, goals and models are updated at runtime through a goal-management interface, which can also adjust the behavior of the loop. ActivFORMS-ta instantiation ActivFORMS-ta is implemented with UPPAAL (Behrmann et al. 2004). The feedback loop is "a" network of timed automata whose templates correspond to the Monitor, Analyze, Plan and Execute activities and whose channels synchronize them with the knowledge repository. We verified correctness of the loop at design time using UPPAAL's exhaustive model checker against TCTL properties, covering deadlock freedom, the absence of lost or unprocessed monitoring data, termination of each adaptation cycle within the period, and ordering constraints on the MAPE stages. A typical property has the form A□ ¬deadlock, or A□ (planning → x ≤ Tplan), where x is a clock and Tplan is the time budget for planning. Models were verified before deployment and re-verified after each evolution step that modified the loop's structure. At runtime, the Analyzer and Planner use statistical However, model checking (SMC) (Legay et al. 2010, David et al. 2015) on a parameterized model of the managed system. To reduce the [19] number of options that must be verified, adaptation selection proceeds in two steps. First, a quick evaluation of every option is made with a "small" number of simulation runs. Second, a larger number of runs is spent on the most [20] promising candidates. For a property whose probability p is estimated from N independent runs, we select N using the Chernoff–Hoeffding bound (Hoeffding However, 1963): N = ⌈ ln(2/α) / (2ε²) ⌉, which guarantees P(|p̂ − p| > ε) ≤ α. We used ε = 0.05 and α = 0.05 for the refined stage, and a fixed small sample for the screening stage. Quantitative qualities, such as energy consumption, were estimated as expected values over the same runs, with 95% confidence intervals (Student's t). Goals and utility Adaptation goals were expressed as threshold goals on a quality qi, gi: qi ⊲ θi with ⊲ ∈ {≤, ≥}, and optimization goals, gj: min/max qj. Among options that satisfy all threshold [38] goals, the planner selects c = argmin{c ∈ Csat} E[qenergy(c)], where Csat is the set of options whose estimated quality satisfies the thresholds. If Csat is empty, the planner selects the option that minimizes the weighted violation of the thresholds. Goals are stored in the knowledge repository as data, so that goal changes only update parameters θi) or goal definitions without modifying the loop's models. Case study: DeltaIoT We validated the approach on DeltaIoT, an IoT network for building security monitoring deployed at the KU Leuven campus (Iftikhar et al. 2017). The network consists of 15 battery-powered LoRa motes with passive infrared, door, and motion sensors, which forward packets through multi-hop links to a gateway. Time is divided into communication cycles of 10 minutes. Uncertainties include interference on the links, which varies the signal-to-noise ratio, and fluctuating packet generation due to occupancy of the building. The adaptation options are the transmission power setting of each link (0–15) and the distribution of packets over the links of motes that have two parents. After applying "the" constraints of the network topology, this gives an adaptation space of several thousand configurations per cycle. The quality properties are packet loss (PL), energy consumption (EC), and latency, with the initial goals G1: PL ≤ 10%, G2: latency ≤ 5% of the cycle, and G3: minimize EC. Experiments were run on the DeltaIoT simulator, which replays measured traces from the deployed network and thereby preserves realistic interference and load patterns (Iftikhar et al. 2017). Selected runs were also executed on the physical deployment to confirm the findings. Each experiment spanned 96 cycles (16 hours of operation), and each configuration was repeated 30 times

1. Introduction The automotive industry is undergoing a profound transformation in which software has become the dominant source of innovation, complexity, and, increasingly, risk. Modern premium vehicles contain on the order of one hundred electronic control units ECUs) and well over one hundred million lines of code, and functions once realized mechanically or hydraulically, such as braking, steering, and power distribution, are now implemented through software-intensive mechatronic systems (Broy, 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007). The shift toward electrification, advanced driver assistance, and automated driving amplifies this trend. Consequently, a large share of engineering work in the sector involves specifying, designing, implementing, and verifying embedded software that interacts directly with physical hardware and, in many cases, with human safety. Safety-critical functions cannot be developed in an ad hoc manner. The industry is governed by a layered framework of standards and process models. ISO 26262 defines functional safety lifecycle activities and requirements for road vehicles (ISO, 2018), while Automotive SPICE ASPICE) provides a process assessment model, derived from ISO/IEC 33000 and 15504, that is used by original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to evaluate the capability of their suppliers (VDA QMC, 2023). ASPICE organizes development along the V-model, linking each left-hand specification activity (system requirements, architectural [28] design, detailed design) to a corresponding right-hand verification activity (unit verification, integration testing, system testing). Bidirectional traceability between requirements, design elements, test cases, and test results is a defining feature of this process and a prerequisite for demonstrating that safety goals have been satisfied. Among the verification techniques used at the upper levels of the V-model, Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) simulation has become indispensable. In HiL testing, the real ECU is connected to a real-time simulation of the plant and its environment through electrical interfaces and bus communication, allowing the controller to be exercised under nominal, boundary, and fault conditions that would be dangerous, costly, or practically impossible to reproduce in a vehicle Bacic, 2005, Isermann et al., 1999). Because HiL permits automated, repeatable, and early testing of the integrated hardware-software system, it supports both the verification evidence demanded by ISO 26262 and the regression-testing cadence required by agile and continuous-integration practices that are now penetrating automotive development (Ebert & Favaro, 2017). Working effectively in such an environment demands a blend of competencies: the ability to derive testable requirements, to design test cases using systematic methods such as equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, to understand communication protocols such as CAN and LIN, to script automated tests, to interpret diagnostics, and to document all of this in a form that is auditable. Despite the centrality of these practices, there is a noticeable discrepancy between what industry expects from new graduates and what university programs typically provide. Electrical engineering and mechatronics curricula traditionally emphasize circuit theory, control engineering, signal processing, and embedded programming, usually through isolated laboratory exercises in which a small program is written, run on a development board, and judged correct by informal observation. Students rarely encounter formal requirements engineering, structured test specification, traceability management, or the concept of process capability levels. Prior studies of software engineering education have repeatedly noted that graduates enter industry insufficiently prepared in testing, requirements, and process-related topics (Garousi et al., 2020; Radermacher & Walia, 2013), and that the problem is aggravated in embedded and safety-critical domains where domain-specific standards add further layers of knowledge Armbrust et al., 2009). Industry therefore frequently invests months of onboarding to bring novice developers to productivity, absorbing a cost that tighter coupling between curricula and practice could reduce. The literature offers partial remedies. Several authors describe automotive software engineering courses, project-based learning with small-scale vehicle platforms, or HiL laboratories built for teaching control systems (Gietelink et al., 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007). Others analyze competence profiles for the automotive software engineer, usually at a high level, for example by listing technology fields such as model-based development, AUTOSAR, or functional safety (Ebert & Favaro, 2017). However, these contributions tend to concentrate either on pedagogical technique or on broad skill taxonomies. What is largely missing is a concrete, practitioner-level description of what a novice actually does when working through the upper part of the V-model on a safety-critical device with HiL, accompanied by representative examples of the artifacts that must be produced, such as requirements statements, test case specifications, and test reports, and an explicit mapping from these activities to the knowledge and skills that a curriculum should supply. Without such a description, academic staff who wish to adapt courses must infer industrial needs from generic standards documents that are lengthy, abstract, and not written for educators. This paper addresses that gap. Its guiding research question is: which knowledge and skills must a graduate of an MSc program in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics possess in order to contribute [30] effectively, as a novice developer, to the software design and HiL-based testing of a safety-critical automotive device within an ASPICE-compliant process? A secondary question follows from it: how can the activities and artifacts of the relevant process phases be presented so that they are directly usable in curriculum design? The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides a concise, application-oriented overview of the development process following Automotive SPICE, concentrating on the tip of the V-model, that is, the phases closest to the system level and to HiL integration and qualification testing, rather than on the full lifecycle. Second, for each phase it supplies typical examples of written documentation, including requirements, test cases, and related artifacts, which illustrate the expected level of precision, wording, and traceability and which are rarely accessible to students. Third, drawing on this material, it derives a structured set of knowledge and skill requirements, spanning technical, methodological, and professional dimensions, which can serve as input for adapting existing curricula to the needs created by contemporary industrial development and testing processes. The remainder of the paper is organized to move from process description [8] to competence requirements and finally to implications for teaching. This study uses a qualitative, process-oriented design to identify the knowledge and skills a novice engineer needs to design and test a safety-critical automotive device using Hardware-in-the-Loop HiL) simulation. It does not test hypotheses or collect experimental measurements. Instead, it derives competence requirements by analysing the industrial development process and mapping each activity in it to the learning outcomes expected of an MSc graduate in Electrical Engineering or Mechatronics. The approach follows the logic of competence-based curriculum design, in which requirements are traced from the professional work context to educational objectives (Crawley et al., 2007). It had four stages: definition of the process scope, analysis of work products, derivation and classification of competences, and consolidation against external references. The first stage fixed the reference process. Automotive SPICE VDA QMC, 2017), which is based on ISO/IEC 33020 process measurement principles, was used as the normative framework because it is "the" assessment model most commonly demanded by original equipment manufacturers when selecting suppliers (Hanser et al., 2018). The analysis was restricted to the lower, implementation-near part of the V-model, which the paper calls its "tip." This covers software requirements analysis SWE.1), software architectural and detailed design (SWE.2, SWE.3), software unit construction and verification (SWE.4), software integration and integration testing SWE.5), and software qualification testing (SWE.6), together with the supporting processes for configuration, problem and change management, and quality assurance. System-level processes (SYS.2–SYS.5) were considered only at their interfaces with software. The tip of the V-model is where a graduate is most likely to be placed on first employment, and it is where HiL testing is typically applied. Functional safety aspects were "taken" from ISO 26262 (ISO, 2018), mainly Part 6 on product development at the software [37] level, to the extent that they influence design and test activities. The ASIL concept and its effect on the rigour of verification methods were included, [3] but safety management and hazard analysis were not examined in depth. The second stage analysed work products. For each Automotive SPICE base practice in the selected processes, the expected output work products were identified: software requirements specification, architecture and interface descriptions, detailed design, unit test specification and reports, integration and qualification test specifications, traceability records, and review minutes. For each work product, representative documentation excerpts were prepared and later presented in the paper as typical examples. These cover a verifiable requirement statement, a requirement-based test case with preconditions, stimuli and expected results, and a bidirectional traceability entry. The excerpts were written to be consistent [8] with common practice in the field and with the guidance on well-formed requirements and test documentation in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and 29119 ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018; 2013). They are illustrative and abstracted. They are not reproductions of any proprietary project documentation, so as to protect confidentiality and keep the examples generic. The HiL environment However, was treated as a distinct object of analysis. The method considered the typical configuration of a HiL test bench: a real-time simulation of the plant and vehicle environment, signal [27] conditioning and electrical failure insertion, load emulation, and communication interfaces to [38] the electronic control unit (ECU) under test, such as CAN, LIN, and diagnostic access via UDS Isermann et al., 1999, Bacic, 2005). The test activities this environment supports were then enumerated: requirement-based functional testing, fault injection and robustness testing, diagnostic and communication testing, and regression testing with automated execution. The knowledge and skills needed to carry out each activity were derived by task analysis. For example, writing a test case that checks a debounced signal requires understanding of timing, sampling, and signal tolerances, whereas interpreting a failed test requires distinguishing a defect in the ECU software from an error in the test specification, the plant model, or the bench configuration. The third stage derived and classified the competences. Each task identified in the preceding stages was expressed as a statement of required knowledge (concepts, standards, and [29] technologies) or skill (applied capabilities such as writing, analysing, scripting, and debugging). The statements were grouped into categories: process and standards literacy; requirements engineering; software design for embedded real-time systems, including C programming under coding guidelines such as MISRA C (MISRA, 2013) and architectural concepts from AUTOSAR; verification and test methodology, including equivalence class partitioning, boundary value analysis, and structural coverage criteria Myers et al., 2011); automotive communication and diagnostics; However, measurement, instrumentation, and test automation; and professional competences such as teamwork, review practice, and technical writing. Each statement was assigned a cognitive level using the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) to indicate the depth of mastery expected at entry level, from remembering and understanding for standards terminology to applying and analysing for test design and fault diagnosis. This level assignment supports the later discussion of what [35] can realistically be achieved within a university course and what is "better" left to on-the-job training. The fourth stage consolidated the derived list against external sources to reduce the subjectivity of a single-perspective analysis. The list [4] was compared with published accounts of automotive software engineering challenges and [7] skill needs (Broy, 2006; Pretschner et al., 2007) and with the typical content of Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics programmes, in order to However, identify gaps. The comparison was qualitative and based on module descriptions rather than a formal survey of institutions. The analysis also draws on the authors' professional experience in developing and testing ECU software on HiL benches, including onboarding and mentoring novice engineers. This experience guided the selection of tasks and the judgement of their relative importance. This is a recognised limitation: the findings reflect a particular segment of the industry, namely safety-critical ECU software developed under Automotive SPICE, and may transfer less readily to other domains such as infotainment or purely model-based development workflows. No statistical analysis was performed, because "the" study did not collect quantitative data from participants or experiments. The credibility of the results [33] rests on transparent derivation, in which every stated competence can be traced to a process [6] activity, work product, or standard clause. It also rests on triangulation between normative documents, the literature, and practitioner experience (Wohlin et al., 2012).

Research competence is increasingly regarded as a core attribute of the physician. Evidence-based practice, critical appraisal of rapidly changing knowledge, and the capacity to contribute to scientific advancement all depend on graduates who can engage with research as users, participants, and producers (Frank et al., 2010; Ten Cate, 2007). In response, medical schools worldwide have introduced undergraduate research programmes, ranging from short elective projects to extended scholarly concentrations and mandatory research theses (Laidlaw et al., 2014; Ommering et al., 2018). Such programmes are also seen as a means of countering the decline of physician-scientists and of sustaining a pipeline of clinicians who can bridge laboratory, clinical, and educational inquiry (Ley & Rosenberg, 2005). The educational rationale for undergraduate research extends beyond training future researchers. Following Boyer's (1998) influential report on the research university, undergraduate research has been promoted as a high-impact practice that places students in the role of inquirers rather than recipients of established knowledge Kuh, 2008). Healey and Jenkins (2009) described a continuum of research-teaching linkages in which students may be an audience for research, apply research findings, learn through research methods, or participate as producers. Learning through inquiry is thought to foster critical thinking, independence, communication, and teamwork Hunter et al., 2007, Lopatto, 2004). In medical education, studies report gains in research skills, confidence, and positive attitudes toward research following participation, and in some cases associations with later research engagement and academic careers (Amgad et al., 2015, Chang et al., 2015, Ommering et al., 2018). Much of this literature, however, is outcome-oriented. Evaluations generally rely on self-reported gains in skills, satisfaction, or publication counts, usually collected through surveys at a single time point or in pre-post designs with predetermined items (Amgad et al., 2015, Lopatto, 2004). These approaches capture whether students feel more competent, but say little about how their understanding of research itself changes, nor how that understanding shapes the way they learn. Yet research on student learning has long indicated that conceptions of knowledge and learning are crucial in determining educational outcomes. Marton and Säljö (1976) distinguished deep from surface approaches to learning, the former involving an intention to understand and relate ideas, the latter focusing on reproduction. Subsequent work showed that approaches to learning are not stable traits but emerge from the interaction between students' prior experience, perceptions of the learning context, and conceptions of what learning and knowledge entail (Biggs & Tang, 2011; Entwistle & Ramsden, 1983; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). Students who view knowledge as a set of facts to be received tend to adopt surface approaches, whereas those who see knowledge as constructed and contestable are more likely to pursue deeper strategies (Säljö, 1979; Perry, 1970). This perspective suggests an important, but underexplored, possibility: that participation in research may influence students' epistemological beliefs, and thereby their approaches to learning, rather than merely adding discrete skills. Research is fundamentally a knowledge-construction practice; engaging in it could prompt students to reconsider how knowledge is produced, validated, and used. Studies in other disciplines indicate that students' conceptions of research vary qualitatively, from seeing research as the accumulation of information or the product of experts, to seeing it as a process of inquiry and meaning-making in which they themselves can take part (Brew, 2001, Meyer et al., 2007). Brew's (2001) phenomenographic study of academics identified domino, trading, layer, and journey conceptions of research, illustrating that how research is understood is neither uniform nor trivial. Whether, and how, such conceptions shift among medical students during undergraduate research is poorly documented. Medical curricula are often content-heavy and examination-driven, conditions known However, to encourage surface learning (Newble & Entwistle, 1986; Reid et al., 2007), so any experience capable of promoting deeper engagement is of considerable educational interest. A further gap concerns the social conditions of undergraduate research. Many [17] [33] programmes require students to work in small groups, partly for practical reasons of [29] supervision and resources and partly to cultivate collaboration. Collaborative inquiry can enhance learning through shared sense-making and reflection (Dillenbourg, 1999; Vygotsky, 1978), but group work also generates tensions concerning unequal contribution, communication styles, and differing expectations (Hall & Buzwell, 2013). Medical students arrive with prior experiences of schooling and assessment that may be competitive and individualistic, which could shape how they negotiate group research. Few studies have examined the difficulties students encounter in group research projects, or how these difficulties relate to prior learning experiences and to students' evolving understandings of research. Without this knowledge, curriculum [16] designers risk implementing undergraduate research in ways that overlook the interpersonal and conceptual challenges that determine whether the experience becomes transformative or merely burdensome. Methodologically, the questions of interest call for approaches that foreground students' own experiences. Phenomenography, developed [3] in the Gothenburg tradition, aims to describe the qualitatively different ways in [23] which people experience, understand, or conceptualise [14] a phenomenon (Marton, 1981, Marton & Booth, 1997). It treats variation in understanding as the object of study and organises findings into categories of description that are logically related and hierarchically inclusive. This makes it particularly suited to investigating changes in students' perceptions of research and learning, because change can be described as a movement between categories, for example However, from a focus on [5] research outcomes to a focus on research processes. Longitudinal, qualitative designs that gather students' reflections before and [21] after an experience also make it possible to link shifts in understanding to specific features of the learning environment, something that cross-sectional surveys cannot [1] easily achieve (Åkerlind, 2005). Against this background, the present study investigates third-year medical students' experiences of a group-based undergraduate research course. It is guided by two research questions: (1) How do students' perceptions of research and of learning change through participation in undergraduate research? and (2) What factors affect the process of students' engagement in research projects? The study makes three contributions. First, it offers an However, in-depth, student-centred account of qualitative change in medical students' conceptions of research, moving beyond skill and satisfaction measures. Second, it explores the proposition that recognising the linkage between research and learning represents an epistemological shift that supports deep approaches to learning, thus connecting the undergraduate research literature with established learning theory. Third, it identifies the personal, relational, and experiential factors that hinder or facilitate collaborative research, providing practical insights for designing and supporting undergraduate research in medical education. Research Design and Methodological Orientation This study used a qualitative design grounded in phenomenography, an approach that aims to describe the qualitatively [19] different ways in which people experience, conceptualize, and understand a phenomenon Marton, 1981, Marton & Booth, 1997). Phenomenography was chosen because the study sought to capture variation in how students understood "research" and "learning" before and after undergraduate research, rather than to test the effect of an intervention. The focus was on the second-order perspective, that is, the participants' own accounts of their experience, rather than on an objective description of the course. The unit of analysis was the conception, and the outcome space was a set of logically related categories of description (Åkerlind, 2005). The study is reported in accordance with the COREQ and SRQR guidelines (Tong et al., 2007, O'Brien et al., 2014). Context and the Undergraduate Research Course The study was conducted in a six-year undergraduate medical program at a university in Japan, where a compulsory research course is embedded in the third year. Over approximately eight weeks, students work in small groups of three to five in a basic science, clinical, or social medicine laboratory. Under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, each group identifies a research question, reviews the literature, designs and conducts a small investigation, analyzes data, and presents its findings in a poster session and a written report. The course is explicitly intended to develop inquiry skills and self-directed learning, consistent with models of student research as active, collaborative knowledge construction (Healey & Jenkins, 2009). Because the projects were group-based and the However, supervisors varied in their style of guidance, the course provided a naturally varied setting for examining differing experiences. Participants and Sampling All 118 third-year students enrolled in the course were invited by e-mail and in a classroom announcement to take part. Participation was voluntary and unrelated to course assessment. Fourteen students (eight men and six women) volunteered and completed both interviews. We used purposeful maximum-variation sampling among volunteers, considering sex, prior research exposure (e.g., previous laboratory experience or a prior degree), and assigned research field, in order to maximize the variation in experience that phenomenography seeks to describe Patton, 2015). The sample size is consistent with recommendations that phenomenographic studies include roughly 10 to 20 participants to capture the range of conceptions without redundancy (Trigwell, 2000, Sandbergh, 1997). Sampling adequacy was judged by information power, with the last two interviews yielding no new categories of description (Malterud et al., 2016). Data Collection Data were collected through semi-structured individual interviews at two time points: before the course (pre-course) and within two weeks after its completion (end-of-course). Interviews were conducted face to face in a private room by the first author, who was not involved in grading, and were conducted in Japanese. Each lasted 30 to 60 minutes and was audio-recorded with consent. The pre-course interview guide explored (a) what students understood by "research" and what they thought researchers do, (b) previous experiences of research and learning, (c) expectations of and concerns about the course, and (d) how they usually approached learning. Following phenomenographic practice, we used open questions and follow-ups such as "What do you mean by that?" and "Can you give an example? to elicit the meaning behind statements and to encourage reflection (Bowden, 2005). The end-of-course interview guide was developed in [28] an iterative manner. A preliminary thematic analysis of the pre-course interviews (Braun & Clarke, 2006), together with researcher–participant observations recorded during the course, informed the questions. The first author attended group meetings and poster preparation sessions as a non-participating observer and wrote field notes on group dynamics, division of labor, and student–supervisor interactions. These observations were used only to shape interview prompts and were not analyzed as a separate dataset. The end-of-course interviews revisited the pre-course topics so that changes could be explored (for example, "How would you now describe research?" and "How, if at all, has your way of learning changed?) and added questions on collaboration, difficulties encountered, and the role of the supervisor and peers. Both guides were pilot tested with two fourth-year students who were not part of the study, leading to minor wording changes. Modern statistical analysis increasingly involves data that are naturally infinite dimensional. Functional data analysis treats curves and surfaces as the basic unit of observation (Ramsay and Silverman, 2005, Hsing and Eubank, 2015). Shape analysis works with objects on manifolds. Nonparametric statistics produces estimators that are themselves functions, such as densities, regression surfaces, and covariance operators. Many of these data are sensitive. Examples include physiological trajectories from wearable devices, genomic profiles, mobility traces, and neuroimaging scans. Releasing even summaries of them can reveal information about the individuals who contributed. Differential Privacy DP) (Dwork et al., 2006) provides a rigorous framework for quantifying and limiting this risk, and it has become the standard for privacy-preserving data release in both academia and industry (Dwork and Roth, 2014). Its application to infinite-dimensional summaries, however, is far less developed than its application to finite-dimensional vectors. The most common approach to DP is to add noise calibrated to the sensitivity of a statistic. In However, finite dimensions, the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms accomplish this with well-understood trade-offs between privacy and accuracy Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork et al., 2014). Extending them to function spaces requires care. Hall et al. 2013) showed that for functional data, privacy can be obtained by adding a scaled Gaussian process to the target function. Calibration then depends on the sensitivity measured in the Cameron–Martin space of the process. Mirshani et al. 2019) generalized this to arbitrary separable Hilbert spaces, and Awan and Slavković (2021) studied related mechanisms. These results rely on a fundamental dichotomy. Two Gaussian measures with different means are either equivalent or mutually singular (Feldman, 1958; Hájek, 1958), so privacy is possible only when the sensitivity lies in the Cameron–Martin space. This restricts which statistics can be privatized by additive noise. Moreover, additive mechanisms are not suited to outputs subject to geometric constraints, such as unit-norm eigenfunctions, positive semidefinite operators, or points on a manifold. Noise added to such objects typically leaves the constraint set and requires ad hoc projection. The exponential mechanism McSherry and Talwar, 2007) is a natural alternative. Instead of perturbing a statistic, it samples an output from a distribution whose density, relative to a base measure, is proportional to the exponential of a utility function scaled by the privacy budget and the utility's sensitivity. It guarantees ε-DP under minimal assumptions and automatically respects the output space, since the base measure can be supported on the constraint set. The mechanism is closely related to posterior sampling and Gibbs distributions Wang et al., 2015; Minami et al., 2016; Dimitrakakis et al., 2017). It has been used for private PCA Chaudhuri et al., 2013, Kapralov and Talwar, 2013), for convex empirical risk minimization Kifer et al., 2012), and for private median and quantile estimation Smith, 2011). Most existing theory, however, concerns finite-dimensional or discrete output spaces. Three questions are open for infinite-dimensional outputs. First, how should the mechanism be defined when no uniform or Lebesgue measure exists? Second, what is the sampling distribution of the privatized output, and can it be used for downstream inference? Third, how much accuracy is lost to privacy relative to the intrinsic statistical error, asymptotically? The last question matters because the conventional wisdom is that privacy is "free" in large samples. For many mechanisms, the noise required for privacy shrinks at rate n⁻¹, faster than the n^{-1/2} sampling error. Privacy then has an asymptotically negligible effect on efficiency Smith, 2011; Wasserman and Zhou, 2010). The behavior of the exponential mechanism in this regard is less transparent, particularly when the utility is a general M-estimation criterion and the output space is infinite dimensional. In this paper we address these gaps. Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the exponential mechanism over a separable Hilbert space with respect to [39] an explicitly chosen base measure, such as a Gaussian process. We show that the base measure is a genuine design choice. It determines the support of the output, its regularity, and the geometry in which accuracy is measured. We give conditions under which the resulting mechanism is well defined, namely integrability of the exponentiated utility with respect to the base measure, and we verify that it satisfies ε-DP. We also discuss how Gaussian-process base measures interact with the Cameron–Martin structure that governs additive mechanisms. Second, we establish a Central Limit Theorem for the exponential mechanism under broad conditions. When the utility is the [28] (scaled) empirical objective of an M-estimator with a sufficiently smooth population counterpart, we show that the privatized output, after centering at the population target and scaling by √n, converges weakly to a well-characterized Gaussian limit. The limit is the convolution of the estimator's asymptotic distribution with an independent Gaussian term induced by the mechanism. The result holds in finite dimensions and in Hilbert spaces. It gives a tractable description of the distribution of privatized outputs and is a first step toward valid inference from them. Third, and in tension with the prevailing view, we show that this privacy-induced Gaussian term is of the same order as the statistical error. The exponential mechanism therefore inflates the asymptotic variance by a constant factor that [11] depends on ε, rather than by a vanishing amount. The mechanism is still consistent and converges at the √n rate, but its asymptotic efficiency relative to the non-private estimator is strictly below one for any fixed ε. We characterize the inflation explicitly. We describe the result as an "apparent" negative one for two reasons. It reflects the mechanism's generality and strong pure-DP guarantee, and it identifies precisely how the constant depends on ε, the sensitivity, and the curvature of the utility. This clarifies where gains from alternative mechanisms or relaxed privacy notions can be expected. Fourth, we apply the framework to functional principal component analysis (FPCA), a central tool for dimension reduction and exploratory analysis of [36] functional data. We develop an ε-DP mechanism for estimating leading eigenfunctions of a covariance operator in [2] a separable Hilbert space. The mechanism samples from a distribution on the "unit" sphere with a density, relative to a Gaussian-process-derived base measure, proportional to the exponential [18] of the [24] scaled Rayleigh quotient. This extends the finite-dimensional Bingham-type mechanism of Chaudhuri et al. (2013) to the functional setting. It does not require discretizing the curves, and it returns elements that satisfy the unit-norm constraint exactly. We derive a sampling procedure and verify the privacy and asymptotic results for this case. Finally, we evaluate the method in simulations and on two real datasets. The simulations vary sample size, privacy budget, and eigengap, and we compare accuracy with additive Gaussian-process mechanisms Hall et al., 2013, Mirshani et al., 2019). They confirm the asymptotic variance inflation predicted by our theory. The applications illustrate the practical utility of private FPCA on sensitive functional data.
