Deep neural networks now inform decisions in settings where errors are costly, including autonomous driving (Bojarski et al., 2016), medical diagnosis Esteva et al., 2017), and the prioritization of candidate compounds in drug development Preuer et al., 2018). In these settings a point prediction is rarely sufficient. A practitioner also needs to know how much confidence to place in it, whether the input lies within the regime the model was trained on, and whether the model's uncertainty is large enough to justify deferring to an expert or running another experiment. Standard networks trained by maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation provide no such information, and their softmax outputs are often poorly calibrated and overconfident, particularly under distribution shift Guo et al., 2017; Ovadia et al., 2019). Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has therefore become a central requirement for the responsible deployment of deep learning. The Bayesian framework offers a principled route to UQ. Placing a prior over network weights and computing the posterior given the training data yields a predictive distribution, p(y | x, D) = ∫ p(y | x, w) pw | D) dw, which captures epistemic uncertainty arising "from" limited data Neal, 1996; MacKay, 1992). For modern networks with millions of parameters, however, the posterior is intractable, and exact methods such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo scale poorly. A range of approximations has been developed, including variational inference [4] (Graves, 2011, Blundell et al., 2015), stochastic-gradient MCMC (Welling & Teh, 2011), Laplace approximations (Ritter et al., 2018), and deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). Among these, Monte Carlo dropout, or permanent dropout, has been especially popular because of its simplicity (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016). Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) is ordinarily used as a regularizer during training and switched off at test time. Gal and Ghahramani showed that if dropout is left active during inference, then T stochastic forward passes with independently sampled masks yield draws from an approximate posterior, corresponding to a variational distribution over weights. The predictive mean [20] and variance can then be estimated as E[y] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x; ŵₜ), Var[y] ≈ (1/T) Σₜ f(x; ŵₜ)ᵀ f(x; ŵₜ) − E[y]ᵀ E[y] + τ⁻¹I, where ŵₜ denotes the weights under the t-th dropout mask and τ is a precision term capturing observation noise. The method requires no change to the architecture or training procedure of an existing dropout network, which has made it attractive [31] in applications ranging from medical image segmentation (Kendall & Gal, 2017) to molecular property prediction. This convenience comes at a cost that is easily overlooked. Permanent dropout moves the computational burden from training to inference: each prediction requires T forward passes, with T typically [29] in the tens to hundreds for stable estimates of predictive variance and tail quantiles. The energy cost of inference is already a dominant share of the lifecycle footprint of deployed models (Patterson et al., 2021), and multiplying it by T can be prohibitive for high-throughput screening pipelines, for real-time systems, and especially for edge platforms with strict power budgets, such as wearable medical devices, vehicles, and embedded sensors. Practitioners are consequently forced to trade uncertainty fidelity against latency and energy, often [19] by reducing T to the point where the uncertainty estimates become noisy. Neuromorphic computing offers a potential remedy. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse, event-driven binary spikes "rather" However, than dense real-valued activations, and when run on dedicated hardware such as Intel's Loihi (Davies et al., 2018), IBM's TrueNorth Merolla et al., 2014), or SpiNNaker (Furber et al., 2014), they can perform inference at orders of magnitude lower energy than conventional processors, since computation occurs only when spikes arrive (Roy et al., 2019). Historically, the obstacle to adopting SNNs has been the difficulty of training them directly, owing to the non-differentiability of spike generation (Neftci et al., 2019). An alternative has emerged in the form of ANN-to-SNN conversion, in which a conventional network is trained with standard backpropagation and its parameters are then mapped onto spiking neurons whose firing rates approximate the original activation functions Cao et al., 2015, Diehl et al., 2015, Rueckauer et al., 2017). Recent work has refined these techniques to the point of near-lossless conversion for deep architectures (Hunsberger & Eliasmith, 2016; Deng & Gu, 2021; Bu et al., 2022), and software frameworks such as Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) make such conversions accessible and deployable across neuromorphic backends via NengoDL and related tools. Despite this progress, the neuromorphic literature has focused almost exclusively on point-prediction accuracy, typically on image classification benchmarks. Whether converted SNNs can faithfully reproduce the full predictive distribution of a stochastic network, and thus support Bayesian-style UQ, has received comparatively little attention. The few existing efforts on probabilistic spiking computation have either exploited the intrinsic stochasticity of spiking neurons for sampling Buesing et al., 2011, Neftci et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2019) or trained Bayesian SNNs through bespoke procedures, requiring specialized training and sacrificing the convenience of conversion. No work, to our knowledge, has asked whether permanent dropout, with its unusually simple requirement of random masking at inference, can be carried over to a converted SNN so that the energy advantages of neuromorphic hardware offset the multiplicative cost of repeated sampling. The question is non-trivial: spiking approximations introduce their own quantization and temporal noise, which could inflate, distort, or mask the dropout-induced variability on which the UQ depends. In this paper we investigate the following research question: can a dropout network be converted to a spiking network such that, when dropout is kept active during inference, the resulting predictive distribution is statistically indistinguishable from that of the original classical network? Answering this would establish that approximate Bayesian inference via permanent dropout can be moved onto neuromorphic platforms without retraining or architectural redesign. We study this question in a domain where UQ is essential: predicting the response to combination drug therapies in cancer treatment. Combination therapy datasets are high-dimensional [3] and expensive to generate, experimental coverage of the combinatorial space is sparse, and clinical or experimental follow-up based on overconfident predictions is costly (Preuer et al., 2018; Menden et al., 2019). Calibrated uncertainty is therefore directly actionable, guiding which combinations merit validation. Our contributions are as follows. First, [19] we propose a pipeline that trains a standard dropout network, converts it to a spiking network in Nengo, and applies stochastic masking at inference to generate Monte Carlo predictive samples on spiking hardware-compatible models. Second, we compare the classical and spiking predictive distributions using measures of both pointwise agreement and distributional similarity, including means, variances, and calibration. Third, we show on a cancer combination therapy dataset that the spiking approximation yields a predictive distribution practically indistinguishable from the classical one. Finally, we discuss the implications for energy-efficient UQ at scale and on edge devices, and identify the conditions under which the approach is expected to hold. Data We used a publicly available combination-therapy screen of the kind "commonly" used for synergy prediction, drawn from the NCI-ALMANAC collection (Holbeck et al., 2017) and accessed through the DrugComb portal (Zagidullin et al., 2019). Each record is a pair of anticancer compounds, tested at fixed concentrations on one cell line from the NCI-60 panel, together with a continuous synergy score. We used the ComboScore as the regression target. Each drug was encoded by a 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprint of radius 2 (Rogers and Hahn, 2010). Fingerprints were combined symmetrically by summing the two drug vectors, so that the representation did not depend on drug order. Cell lines were represented by baseline expression of [37] the 1,000 most variable genes, standardized "and" reduced to 100 principal components. The input vector was therefore the [27] summed drug fingerprint, the cell-line components, and the [16] log concentrations of both drugs. We split the data at the level of drug pairs, not individual measurements, to avoid leakage between replicates and dose levels: 70% for training, 10% for validation, and 20% for testing. Targets were standardized with training-set statistics. Because uncertainty quantification matters most under distribution shift, we also built a second test set, in which all combinations containing a [7] randomly held-out 10% of compounds were removed from training. Results are reported for both the in-distribution and the shifted test sets. The entire partitioning procedure was repeated for five random [37] seeds. Classical network and permanent dropout The reference model was a fully connected feed-forward network with three hidden layers of 256 units. It used ReLU activations and no biases on the hidden layers, which simplifies conversion to spiking form (Rueckauer et al., 2017). Dropout with probability p = 0.2 followed each hidden layer. Training minimized mean squared error with L2 weight decay, using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015). Learning rate and weight decay were tuned on the validation set, and early stopping was applied. At inference we kept dropout active, following the Monte Carlo dropout interpretation of Gal and Ghahramani (2016). For an input x, T stochastic forward passes with independent Bernoulli masks produce outputs ŷt = f(x; W, mt), where mt ~ Bernoulli(1−p). The predictive mean and variance are approximated as μx) ≈ (1/T) Σt ŷt, σ²(x) ≈ 1/T) Σt (ŷt − μ)² + τ⁻¹, where τ⁻¹ is the observation-noise term. We estimated τ⁻¹ on the validation set by maximizing the Gaussian [9] log-likelihood. Unless stated otherwise, T = 100. We assessed the convergence of [37] the predictive moments by varying T from 5 to 500. Conversion to a spiking network The trained network was converted to a spiking network without retraining the weights, following the rate-based conversion framework of Diehl et al. (2015) and Rueckauer et al. (2017). Hidden ReLU units were replaced by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with membrane dynamics τm "dv/dt" = −v + J(t), with a spike emitted and the membrane reset when v reaches its threshold. Here J is the input current and τm the membrane time constant. For constant input J > 1, the steady-state firing rate is rJ) = [τref − τm ln(1 − 1/J)]⁻¹, where τref is the refractory period. We used τm = 20 ms and τref = 2 ms. The ReLU slope was matched to the LIF response curve through a gain scaling. Gains were normalized layer by layer using the 99.9th percentile of activations on the training data, to keep firing rates within the dynamic range of the neurons and to limit saturation (Rueckauer et al., 2017). For comparison, we also fine-tuned a variant of the network in which the LIF rate curve was smoothed soft LIF) in the forward pass during training Hunsberger and Eliasmith, 2015). Synaptic connections used exponential low-pass filters with τs = 5 ms to smooth spike trains. We implemented the network in Nengo (Bekolay et al., 2014) and used NengoDL (Rasmussen, 2019) for weight transfer and for batched simulation. The simulation time step was 1 ms. Each test input was presented as a constant current for a window of Tpres = 100 ms, and the network state was reset between presentations. The output was read as the filtered decoded value averaged over the last 30 ms of the window, which discards the initial transient. Permanent dropout in the spiking network Dropout was implemented by multiplying the spike output of each hidden layer by a binary mask. This is equivalent to silencing the corresponding presynaptic neurons. The mask m^(l) was sampled at the start of a presentation window and held fixed throughout it, with scaling 1/(1−p) applied to the outgoing weights. Holding the mask fixed ensures that each window realizes a single sampled subnetwork, as in the classical case. Masks were resampled for each of the T repeated presentations of the same input. The spiking predictive distribution was then computed using the same moment estimators as above. This design yields two sources of variability: the dropout masks, which are the intended Bayesian approximation, and spike-timing noise, which is an artifact of the substrate. To separate them, we ran a control with masks fixed and only spiking noise active, and used it to estimate the spiking noise variance σ²spk.

Spontaneous spoken dialogue is rarely fluent. Speakers pause, hesitate, restart and repair their own utterances as they plan and produce speech, and in conversational corpora such phenomena are frequent: roughly 5–6% of words in the Switchboard corpus are part of a disfluency (Shriberg, 1994; Godfrey et al., 1992). Disfluencies are not merely noise. Following Shriberg (1994) and Levelt (1983), a typical self-repair can be analysed as having a reparandum (the material to be abandoned or corrected), an optional interregnum (e.g. an editing term such as uh or "I mean), and a repair (the material that replaces the reparandum). Listeners process this structure effortlessly and often use it to infer the speaker's intended meaning and their cognitive state Brennan and Schober, 2001). A dialogue system that cannot do the same will misinterpret users, fail to track what they actually want, and respond in ways that feel unnatural. Disfluency processing in dialogue systems faces two requirements that are not always addressed together. The first is incrementality. Human conversation is highly interactive: participants complete each other's utterances, interrupt, backchannel, and begin responding before the other has finished Schlangen and Skantze, 2011). To exhibit such behaviour, a system must interpret input word by word and must decide, as each word arrives, whether it belongs to a reparandum, an interregnum or a repair. Many successful disfluency detectors operate on complete utterances, using bidirectional context, parsing-based features, or reranking over entire sentences (Johnson and Charniak, 2004, Qian and Liu, 2013, Honnibal and Johnson, 2014). These approaches are useful for cleaning transcripts, but they cannot support the low-latency processing needed in live interaction. Incremental approaches (Hough and Purver, 2014; Hough and Schlangen, 2015) have been proposed, but their accuracy on standard benchmarks has lagged behind that of non-incremental ones, and the more recent neural sequence-tagging methods that achieve strong results typically rely on bidirectional encoders or on features that are not available online (Zayats et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016). The second requirement concerns data efficiency and robustness. From a developer's perspective, it is highly desirable to build a dialogue system from clean examples of the target task, since collecting and annotating large amounts of disfluent, domain-specific speech is expensive. Disfluencies, however, are diverse: the same intended content can be realised with an unbounded variety of hesitations, restarts and substitutions. A model trained on one domain's disfluent data may not transfer to another, and a model trained only on fluent data will typically break when faced with repairs (Eshghi et al., 2017; Shalyminov et al., 2017). Ideally, a disfluency detection component would be domain-general. It would be trained once on a general-purpose resource and then be used in new domains, passing on fluent-equivalent input or structural annotations to downstream components trained only on clean data. The extent to which this is realistic, and which types [11] of disfluency are amenable to such domain-general treatment, is poorly understood, since most work evaluates disfluency detectors only in-domain on Switchboard. This paper addresses these two requirements jointly. We ask: can a simple, strictly word-by-word incremental neural model detect disfluency structure accurately enough to compete with existing incremental systems, and does what it learns from a large general corpus of human conversation transfer to a different domain without any additional training? To answer the first part, we train and evaluate on the Switchboard Dialogue Acts (SWDA) corpus (Stolcke et al., 2000), which provides disfluency annotations over transcribed telephone conversations. To answer the second, we test the same trained model on bAbI+ (Shalyminov et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI goal-oriented dialogue task (Bordes et al., 2017) in which clean dialogues are systematically augmented with disfluencies generated by controlled templates. Because bAbI+ gives us control over the distribution and types of hesitations, restarts and self-corrections, as well as exact gold-standard annotations, it permits a fine-grained analysis of generalisation that is impossible with naturally occurring data alone. Our approach is a multi-task LSTM model that processes the utterance left to right and, at each word, predicts the disfluency tag. Training with multiple related objectives is known to improve representations and generalisation in sequence labelling (Caruana, 1997; Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016; Rei, 2017). Here, the auxiliary task is to predict the next word, a language-modelling objective that encourages [14] the shared recurrent layer to capture local lexical and syntactic regularities, including the repetitions and mismatches that signal a repair (Hough and Schlangen, 2017). Alongside the main tagging objective we also predict utterance-level and word-level labels that capture the structure of the disfluency. The resulting architecture is considerably simpler than previous neural incremental systems, requires no hand-crafted features or external parsers, and can be attached to any incremental consumer of text, such as an incremental semantic parser Eshghi et al., 2011), or used on its own to produce a continuously updated "cleaned" version of the utterance. The paper makes the following contributions. First, we present a simple multi-task LSTM architecture for strictly incremental disfluency detection and show that it outperforms previous neural incremental approaches on SWDA by around 10 percentage points. Second, we show through experiments on bAbI+, without any retraining or adaptation, that the model transfers to a domain with very different vocabulary and dialogue structure, supporting the claim that disfluency detection can be treated as a domain-general capability. Third, exploiting the controlled nature of bAbI+, we analyse performance by disfluency type, identifying which phenomena for example, hesitations versus self-corrections of different kinds) are readily handled in a domain-general way and which remain challenging. This However, analysis sheds light on where future work, whether in modelling or in data collection, should concentrate. Data We used [8] two datasets. The first [21] is the Switchboard Dialogue Acts However, corpus (SWDA; [17] Stolcke et al., 2000), a subset of the Switchboard telephone conversations Godfrey et al., 1992) annotated with disfluency structure following Meteer et However, al. 1995). [3] We used the standard split of Zayats et al. (2016) and Hough and Schlangen (2017): the training portion comprises the conversations with identifiers beginning sw2–sw3, the held-out set sw4[5-9], and the test set sw4[0-1]. Transcripts were lower-cased, and punctuation and partial-word markers were removed. Each token was labelled with a tag from the disfluency scheme described below, and pre-processing followed Hough and Schlangen (2017) so that results are comparable with earlier incremental work. The [23] second dataset is bAbI+ (Shalyt et al., 2017; Eshghi et al., 2017), an extension of the bAbI Dialog Task 1 (Bordes et al., 2017) restaurant-booking dialogues. bAbI+ adds disfluencies to the otherwise clean utterances through template-based transformation. These are of three types: hesitations (e.g. "we will be uh eight), restarts or false starts (e.g. "can you make a restaurant uh sorry a reservation), and corrections of previously mentioned content (e.g. "with Italian uh sorry Spanish food"). The insertion probabilities are controlled, so the distribution of disfluency types is known, and gold annotations are available for every token. The bAbI+ data was used for evaluation only. At no point was the model [3] trained or tuned on it, so its performance measures zero-shot, domain-general transfer from SWDA. Disfluency Annotation Scheme We adopted the standard reparandum–interregnum–repair structure (Shriberg, 1994; Meteer et al., 1995). The reparandum is the material to be repaired or abandoned. The interregnum contains editing terms such as "uh" or "I mean". The repair is the material that replaces the reparandum. Following Hough and Schlangen (2017), we converted the bracketed annotation into word-level tags: <e/> for edit terms (interregnum and filled pauses), <rmn/> for a reparandum word, where n gives the number of tokens back in the utterance at which the reparandum begins, <rpn/> for a repair word, and <f/> for fluent words. This encoding is strictly incremental, as each tag can be assigned with only left context, and it lets the system recover the extent of the reparandum rather than merely detect that one exists. Repairs are further distinguished as substitution (<rpSub/>), repetition (<rpRep/>) or deletion (<rpDel/>), following Hough and Schlangen (2017). Model Architecture The model is a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) sequence tagger that processes an utterance [16] one word at a time, so each tag prediction depends only on the words seen so far. Words are mapped to 50-dimensional embeddings, and the vocabulary is restricted to the training data, with singletons replaced by an unknown token. Part-of-speech (POS) tags were produced for SWDA using the tags available in the corpus; the embedding of the POS tag is concatenated with the word embedding as input in the POS-enriched conditions. A single LSTM layer with 50 hidden units feeds a softmax output layer. Multi-Task Design The core design element is multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997, Søgaard & Goldberg, 2016). Two output layers share the same LSTM representation. The primary task is the disfluency tagging described above. The auxiliary task is prediction of the next word in the sequence, that is, incremental language modelling. A related auxiliary task is prediction of the utterance's POS tag sequence, which we evaluated in separate ablations. The auxiliary tasks provide a training signal that does not depend on disfluency annotation and encourages the shared layer to represent syntactic and lexical context. The total loss is a weighted sum of the cross-entropy losses of the tasks, L = Ltag + λLaux, with λ selected on the held-out set from {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}. We also trained a single-task baseline with the same architecture but no auxiliary output. Training Procedure Models were implemented in Keras with a TensorFlow backend and trained with the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with a batch size of 32. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) of 0.2 was applied to the embedding and LSTM outputs, and early stopping was based on tagging loss on the held-out set, with a patience of 5 epochs. Hyperparameters were selected on the held-out set only. Because LSTM training is stochastic, each configuration was trained with ten random initialisations, and we report the mean and standard deviation across runs. Evaluation Evaluation on SWDA used three families of measures. First, token-level F1 was computed for the reparandum tags (<rm>) and for edit terms (<e>), following common practice in disfluency detection (Ferguson et al., 2015; Zayats et al., 2016). Second, because the system is meant to be incremental, we evaluated However, it as it processes the utterance. We report the time-to-detection, the number of words after the onset of a reparandum or edit at which the correct tag is first output, and edit overhead, the proportion of unnecessary tag revisions made as the utterance unfolds (Hough & Schlangen, 2017, Zwarts et al., 2010). Third, we report the utterance-level exact match of the predicted tag [15] sequence against gold. For bAbI+, the trained SWDA model was applied without any retraining or fine-tuning, and word embeddings for out-of-vocabulary tokens were mapped to the unknown token. POS tags were not available in this dataset, so for this experiment we used the model variants that take only words as input. We report F1 for each tag type, split by disfluency category (hesitation, restart, correction) to see which phenomena transfer across domains. As a complementary measure, we compute the proportion of utterances whose "cleaned" output, after removing tokens tagged as reparandum or edit, exactly matches the original clean bAbI utterance. This measures the practical goal that a downstream interpreter, trained only on fluent dialogues, receives the intended input. Named entity recognition (NER) is a foundational step in biomedical text mining. Identifying mentions of genes, proteins, cell lines, chemicals, diseases, and organisms in the literature underlies downstream tasks such as relation extraction, database curation, and literature-based discovery (Krallinger et al., 2017, Huang and Lu, 2015). The volume of biomedical publications, which now exceeds one million new PubMed entries per year, makes manual annotation infeasible at scale, and accurate automated NER has therefore been a central focus of community evaluations including BioCreative, BioNLP, and JNLPBA Kim et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2008; Arighi et al., 2017). NER is conventionally cast as a sequence labeling problem. A document is segmented into sentences and tokens, and each token receives a label, typically in a BIO or BIOES scheme, indicating whether it begins, continues, or lies outside an entity (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Feature-based models such as conditional random fields (Lafferty et al., 2001) dominated early biomedical systems, for example BANNER (Leaman and Gonzalez, 2008) and ABNER (Settles, 2005). More recently, neural architectures have replaced hand-engineered features. Bidirectional LSTMs with CRF output layers, combined with word and character embeddings, became the standard approach (Huang et al., 2015; Lample et al., 2016, Ma and Hovy, 2016), and have been successfully adapted to biomedical corpora (Habibi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Crichton et al., 2017). Pretrained contextual representations such as ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), and domain-specific variants including BioBERT Lee et al., 2020), SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019), and PubMedBERT (Gu et al., 2021) have further raised performance on benchmark datasets. Despite this progress, nearly all of these systems share a hidden dependency: they assume that the input has already been split into tokens, and that the boundaries of entities coincide with the boundaries of those tokens. In general-domain newswire text, this assumption is largely benign, since entity names are usually separated from adjacent text by whitespace or punctuation. In biomedical text, it frequently fails. Entity mentions are often embedded within hyphenated compounds, slash-separated expressions, or alphanumeric strings, such as "IL-2-dependent," p53/MDM2, GFP-tagged, TNF-alpha–induced, or Ras-GAP. In these cases the entity occupies only part of what a conventional tokenizer treats as a single word. Annotation guidelines for corpora such as GENETAG Tanabe et al., 2005) and BioCreative Bio-ID (Arighi et al., 2017) explicitly permit sub-word entity spans, and the JNLPBA corpus Kim et al., 2004) contains many mentions whose boundaries fall inside whitespace-delimited strings. A model that predicts labels only at the word level cannot, by construction, recover such spans exactly, and under strict-match evaluation each of these errors counts as both a false positive and a false negative. The standard remedy is to rely on specialized tokenization. Biomedical tokenizers apply hand-crafted rules or learned heuristics to split text at hyphens, slashes, digit–letter transitions, and case changes, so that entity boundaries are more likely to coincide with token boundaries (He and Kayaalp, 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007, Neumann et al., 2019). Such tokenizers can improve NER performance, but they carry their own costs. They require domain expertise to design and maintain, they are tuned to a particular corpus or entity class, and they introduce a pipeline dependency in which tokenization errors propagate irrecoverably to the tagger. Over-segmentation fragments entities and inflates sequence lengths, while under-segmentation leaves boundary mismatches unresolved. Moreover, a tokenizer optimized for one annotation scheme may not transfer to another, forcing practitioners to redesign rules for each new dataset. Subword [28] representations offer a natural way to relax the dependence on word-level tokenization. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), originally a data compression technique (Gage, 1994), was adapted for neural machine translation to handle rare and unseen words by decomposing them into frequent character sequences (Sennrich et al., 2016). Related approaches include WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016) and the unigram language model (Kudo, 2018), as well as SentencePiece, which operates on raw text without pre-tokenization (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). These methods are widely used in transformer-based language models, including BERT and its biomedical descendants. However, in NER they are typically used only to build input representations, labels are still assigned at the level of whole words, usually by taking the prediction of the first subword piece Devlin et al., 2019). The subword units thus improve the handling of out-of-vocabulary terms but [23] do not allow the model to predict entity boundaries within a word. Character-level models (Kim et al., 2016; Gillick et al., 2016) can in principle label at arbitrary positions, but they produce long sequences, lack a learned inventory of meaningful units such as morphemes and common biomedical affixes (for example, -ase, "anti-," [30] or "-mab"), and are often harder to train and scale. This leaves an unaddressed gap. [36] Existing biomedical NER methods either operate at the word level and depend on carefully engineered tokenization to align with entity boundaries, or use subword units merely as inputs while still predicting at the word level. What is missing is an approach in [30] which the units of prediction themselves are learned, subword-sized, and independent of domain-specific tokenization rules, so that entity spans can start and end wherever the data indicate. We therefore ask the following research question: can a model that assigns entity labels directly to BPE units, learned from raw text, recover biomedical entity spans, including those that fall within words, with accuracy competitive with systems that depend on specialized tokenizers? To answer this question, we introduce a subword-level approach to NER that combines BPE segmentation with convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Text is segmented using a BPE vocabulary learned from the training data, with minimal pre-processing. Convolutional [13] layers capture local orthographic and morphological patterns within and across adjacent units, and recurrent layers model longer-range context across [21] the sentence. The network produces a tag for every BPE unit, and these byte-level tags are mapped back to character offsets to yield entity spans that need not align with whitespace-delimited words. Our contributions are as follows. First, we propose a tokenization-agnostic NER architecture that predicts labels at the BPE level, allowing entity boundaries to fall inside words without hand-written splitting rules. Second, we evaluate the approach on three widely used biomedical benchmarks, the BioCreative VI Bio-ID, [2] JNLPBA, and GENETAG corpora, which differ in entity types, annotation conventions, and degree of boundary misalignment. Third, we show that the method achieves competitive performance relative to established systems while eliminating the need for specialized biomedical tokenization expertise. Finally, we analyze the cases in which entity boundaries do not coincide with word boundaries, quantifying how much a conventional word-level approach loses and how much a subword-level approach recovers. Together, these results suggest that moving the unit of prediction from words to learned subword units is a simple and effective way to make biomedical NER more robust and easier to deploy across corpora. Datasets We evaluated on three widely used biomedical NER benchmarks that differ in domain, entity inventory, and annotation conventions. The BioCreative VI Bio-ID corpus (Arighi et al., 2017; Islamaj Doğan et al., 2019) consists of figure legends from open-access articles annotated for multiple entity classes, including genes and proteins, small molecules, cell types and lines, tissues, and organisms. These annotations are normalized to database identifiers, but only the mention spans and coarse types were used here. The JNLPBA shared-task dataset (Kim et al., 2004) derives from the GENIA corpus (Kim et al., 2003) and contains MEDLINE abstracts annotated with five types: protein, DNA, RNA, cell line, and cell type. The GENETAG corpus Tanabe et al., 2005), as used in BioCreative II Gene Mention (Smith et al., 2008), contains 20,000 MEDLINE sentences annotated for a single gene/protein class, with alternative acceptable boundaries [6] provided for some mentions. We used the official training and test partitions for each dataset. For GENETAG we used the BioCreative II partition of 15,000 training [9] and 5,000 test sentences. A random 10% of each training set, drawn at [12] the document level where document identifiers were available, was held out as a development set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The test sets were used only for [4] final evaluation. Annotations were converted to character offsets relative to the raw text of each sentence, so that all downstream processing and scoring operated on characters rather than on any dataset-specific tokenization. Subword segmentation Rather than applying a rule-based biomedical tokenizer, we segmented raw text with byte-pair encoding (BPE; Sennrich et al., 2016), following the compression algorithm of Gage 1994). Text was split only at whitespace, and a boundary symbol marked the start of each whitespace-delimited chunk. Punctuation, hyphens, slashes, digits, and parentheses were therefore left for the learned merges to handle. BPE began from a character inventory and iteratively merged the most frequent adjacent symbol pair until a target vocabulary size V was reached. Merges were learned on the training split of each dataset, without the development or test text. For comparison, we also trained a SentencePiece BPE model Kudo & Richardson, 2018) on the same text, and we found its segmentations to be comparable. We treated V ∈ {500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, 8,000} as [26] a hyperparameter. Every BPE unit retained its character start and end offsets in the original string, so a sentence became a sequence of units u₁,…,uₙ with offsets (sᵢ, eᵢ). Because merges are frequency driven, common morphemes such as -ase, kappa, or "IL-" often form single units, and entity boundaries that fall inside whitespace-delimited chunks (e.g., "IL-2R-mediated") can be represented whenever a unit boundary coincides with them. Tag scheme and span reconstruction Gold character-level spans were projected onto the BPE units using a BIO scheme with entity types. A unit was labeled B-t if it started an entity of type t, I-t if it lay inside one, and O otherwise. Predicted spans were converted back to character offsets by taking the start offset of the first unit and the end offset of the last unit of each [38] decoded entity. Spans therefore never depended on a word-level tokenizer in either direction. A gold boundary that falls strictly inside a BPE unit cannot be reproduced by this scheme. To quantify the resulting ceiling, we computed an oracle recall for each dataset and each V. This is the fraction of gold entities whose start and end offsets both coincide with unit [6] boundaries. We report this quantity as a diagnostic and as a criterion for choosing V, alongside development F1. For comparison, we computed the same oracle recall [32] for word-level tokenizations from a whitespace tokenizer and from a rule-based biomedical tokenizer (the scispaCy tokenizer; Neumann et al., 2019). Model architecture Each unit uᵢ was mapped to an embedding eᵢ ∈ ℝ^d, with d = 128, initialized randomly (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) and learned jointly with the network. Local subword context was captured by a one-dimensional convolution over the embedding sequence. For a window of half-width k, cᵢ = ReLU Wc [eᵢ₋ₖ ; … , eᵢ , … , eᵢ₊ₖ] + bc ), where [ , ] denotes concatenation and sequences were zero-padded at the boundaries. We used parallel filters with widths 1, 3, and 5, each with 128 channels, and concatenated their outputs. A linear layer and a softmax gave the distribution over tags yᵢ, p(yᵢ | u₁:ₙ) = softmax(Wo hᵢ + bo), and the training objective was the token-level negative log-likelihood 𝓛 = −(1/N) Σ{sentences} Σᵢ log p(yᵢ\ | u₁:ₙ), with N the total number of units. The proliferation of GPS-enabled mobile devices has [19] driven the rapid growth of Location-based Social Networks (LBSNs) such as Foursquare, Gowalla, and Yelp, where users share their physical presence at Points-of-Interest (POIs) through check-ins, tips, and reviews (Bao et al., 2015). The resulting records of human mobility support a wide range of services, including urban planning, location-targeted advertising, and personalized travel assistance. Among these, POI recommendation, which suggests unvisited venues that match a user's preferences, has become a central task. It helps users explore [39] their surroundings and helps businesses reach potential customers (Ye et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017). As the numbers of users and venues grow into the millions, effective POI recommender systems are needed to counter information overload. Early POI recommenders were largely adapted from general-purpose collaborative filtering. Matrix factorization (MF) approaches learn latent user and POI representations whose inner product approximates observed preferences Koren et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2008). Because check-in data record only [35] positive, implicit feedback, such methods typically treat unobserved entries as weighted negatives or optimize pairwise ranking objectives Rendle et al.; 2009). Researchers soon recognized that POIs differ [10] from items such as movies or books because they are anchored in geographic space. Existing work has therefore augmented collaborative filtering with spatial information, for example by fitting power-law or kernel density models of check-in distances (Ye et al., 2011; Zhang & Chow, 2013), by embedding activity areas into latent factors Lian et al., 2014), or by combining social, temporal, and categorical signals with geographical influence (Cheng et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015). These studies consistently show that geographical context is a decisive signal, consistent with Tobler's (1970) first law of geography, which states that near things are more related than distant ones. Despite this progress, two challenges remain. The first is modeling non-linear user–POI interactions from implicit feedback. MF and its geographical extensions assume that preference is a linear function of latent factors, which limits their capacity to capture the complex, heterogeneous motivations behind check-in behavior. Deep learning offers a remedy. Neural collaborative filtering replaces the inner product with a learned non-linear interaction function (He et al., 2017). Autoencoder-based models such as AutoRec Sedhain et al., 2015), the [12] collaborative denoising autoencoder (Wu et al., 2016), and variational autoencoders for collaborative filtering (Liang et al., 2018) reconstruct a user's interaction vector through non-linear mappings and achieve strong top-N performance. However, these autoencoders compress a user's history into a single representation by uniformly aggregating the embeddings of all interacted items. In the POI setting this is problematic because a user's check-ins are highly diverse. A single user may frequent a workplace cafeteria, a gym, and a handful of tourist sites, each reflecting a different intention and with different significance for predicting future behavior. Treating all of these POIs equally ignores such differences in preference degree and can dilute informative signals with incidental visits. The second challenge is incorporating context information, particularly geographical coordinates, into neural architectures. [24] Most neural recommenders operate on identifiers alone, and the few that exploit location typically feed coordinates or discretized grid cells as additional input features (Yang [9] et al., 2017). This design discards the continuous nature [12] of geographic distance and does not express the underlying behavioral principle that a user who visits a POI is likely to visit its nearby and similar neighbors. Moreover; the data are extremely sparse. Typical LBSN check-in matrices have densities well below 1%, so propagating a user's preference to spatially adjacent venues is a natural way to mitigate sparsity and improve generalization. The question is how to inject such neighborhood effects into a non-linear model in a principled, end-to-end trainable manner rather than as a post-hoc re-ranking step. These observations motivate the central research question of this paper: can a non-linear autoencoder framework i) adaptively weigh the multiple facets of a user's check-in history and (ii) explicitly encode geographical neighborhood influence, so as to produce more accurate POI recommendations from sparse implicit feedback? Attention mechanisms provide a promising route to the first goal. They were introduced to align and weigh elements of a sequence in neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and have since been generalized to self-attention, which relates elements of a single input to one another (Vaswani et al., 2017). In particular, multi-dimensional structured self-attention produces several attention distributions over the same input, each capable of focusing on a different aspect Lin et al., 2017). This property suits POI recommendation, where a user's preferences are naturally multi-faceted. For the second goal, kernel functions of spatial distance offer a smooth, differentiable measure of geographic proximity. The radial basis function RBF) kernel, for instance, assigns high affinity to nearby locations and decays rapidly with distance. Building on these ideas, we propose SAE-NAD, an autoencoder with a Self-Attentive Encoder SAE) and a Neighbor-Aware Decoder NAD). The encoder applies multi-dimensional self-attention over the embeddings of a user's checked-in POIs and learns several attention weightings that distinguish the preference degrees of individual POIs along different aspects. These weightings are aggregated into a compact user representation. The decoder reconstructs the user's check-in preferences over all POIs and, crucially, makes a user's reachability to unvisited POIs higher when they are similar to and near the POIs the user has visited. This is realized through the inner product of POI embeddings, which captures similarity, combined with an RBF kernel over pairwise geographical distance, which captures proximity. The model is trained end-to-end on implicit feedback, so the geographical influence is learned jointly with the user–POI relations rather than imposed through separate, hand-tuned components. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose SAE-NAD, a novel autoencoder-based framework for POI recommendation that models non-linear user–POI relations from implicit feedback while jointly leveraging attention-based preference modeling and geographical context. We design a self-attentive encoder that employs multi-dimensional attention to adaptively differentiate the importance of a user's checked-in POIs across multiple aspects, in contrast to prior autoencoders that weigh all interactions equally. We devise a neighbor-aware decoder that integrates POI embedding similarity with an RBF kernel of geographical distance, thereby raising users' reachability on the similar and nearby neighbors of their checked-in POIs in a differentiable manner. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world LBSN datasets, comparing against a range of state-of-the-art baselines under multiple ranking metrics. The results demonstrate that SAE-NAD consistently outperforms the competing methods, and ablation analyses confirm that both the self-attentive encoder and the neighbor-aware decoder contribute to the gains. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related [9] work on POI recommendation and autoencoder-based collaborative filtering. Section 3 formulates the problem and presents the SAE-NAD model in detail. Section 4 describes the experimental setup and reports results, and Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. Datasets and preprocessing. We evaluated the proposed SAE-NAD model on three public LBSN check-in datasets: Gowalla (Cho et al., 2011), Foursquare Yang et al., 2016), and Yelp Liu et al., 2017). Each check-in record contains a user identifier, a POI identifier, a timestamp, and the POI's geographical coordinates [31] latitude and longitude). Following common practice in POI recommendation Ma et al., 2018; Li et al., 2015), we removed users with fewer than 15 check-ins and POIs visited by fewer than 10 users, which mitigates extreme sparsity and yields stable estimates. After filtering, Gowalla contained 18,737 users, 32,510 POIs, and 1,278,274 check-ins (density 0.21%). Foursquare contained 24,941 users, [7] 28,593 POIs, and 1,196,248 check-ins (0.17%). Yelp contained 30,887 users, 18,995 POIs, and 860,888 check-ins (0.15%). Candidate sets for ranking comprised all POIs absent from a user's training and validation records. Model architecture. SAE-NAD is an autoencoder that maps xu to a latent representation (encoder) and reconstructs a dense score vector over all POIs decoder). The encoder is a self-attentive encoder SAE). Each POI j has an input embedding ej ∈ ℝ^d. Let Eu ∈ ℝ^{nu×d} stack the embeddings of the nu POIs visited by user u. Rather than average these embeddings or weight them equally, we adopt the multi-dimensional structured self-attention of Lin et al. (2017) to capture several aspects of preference: Au = softmax(W₂ tanh(W₁ Euᵀ)), where W₁ ∈ ℝ^{t×d} and W₂ ∈ ℝ^{r×t} are learnable parameters, t is the attention hidden size, r is the number of attention aspects (attention "hops"), and the softmax is taken over the user's visited POIs, so that each row of Au ∈ ℝ^{r×nu} sums to one. A standard autoencoder decoder would compute ŷuj = σ(wjᵀzu + bj) and ignore geography. To incorporate geographical context, we add a neighbor term that raises the reachability of POIs that are both similar to, and near, the user's visited POIs. Loss of an upper limb is a life-altering event that affects a person's ability to work, care for themselves, maintain relationships, and participate in leisure activities. The hand and arm are central to manipulation, tactile exploration, and non-verbal communication, so their absence produces disability well beyond the physical deficit. Population estimates suggest that more than a million people in the United States live with limb loss, and the figure is projected to more than double by mid-century as vascular disease and diabetes [11] become more prevalent (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Lower-limb amputation is mostly dysvascular in origin. Upper-limb loss, (10) by contrast, is mainly traumatic and tends to occur in younger, working-age people, including those injured in industrial accidents, road traffic collisions, and armed conflict (Dillingham et al., 2002; Atkins et al., 1996). Because these individuals face decades of life with limb loss, the quality of their care has large functional, psychological, and socioeconomic consequences. Prosthetic fitting is the best-known intervention for upper-limb amputation. Available devices range from passive cosmetic restorations and body-powered hooks to myoelectric hands and, more recently, multi-articulating and pattern-recognition-controlled systems. Techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation have increased the number of intuitive control signals available to people with high-level amputations (Kuiken et al., 2009). Even so, technological sophistication has not translated reliably into sustained use. Surveys and reviews across 25 years of literature report substantial rates of prosthesis rejection and abandonment, which are often attributed to discomfort, weight, poor functional return, and insufficient training (Biddiss & Chau, 2007, Davidson, 2002). Satisfaction depends on factors beyond the device, (17) including the timing of fitting, the quality of follow-up services, (19) and how well the user is prepared to operate the prosthesis in daily life (Pezzin et al., 2004; McFarland et al., 2010). Comparative (18) evidence on myoelectric and body-powered (20) devices also shows that neither is uniformly superior, which suggests that the user's training and context matter at least as much as the component technology (Carey et al., 2015). This situation points to However, rehabilitation as a critical but under-examined part [38] of the care pathway. Prosthetic rehabilitation is the structured, multidisciplinary process that begins at or before amputation and continues after definitive fitting. It typically includes pre-prosthetic care such as wound healing, edema control, desensitization, and maintenance of range of motion and strength. It then moves to training in muscle control and signal acquisition, followed by donning and doffing, controlled operation of the terminal device, and bimanual functional activities. Throughout, it addresses phantom sensation and pain, and However, the psychosocial adjustment needed to reintegrate into work and community roles (Smurr et al., 2008; Resnik et al., 2012). As prosthetic technology grows more complex, these needs become greater. Advanced devices place heavier cognitive and motor demands (25) on users, and clinicians have noted that the evidence base for training approaches has not kept pace with engineering developments (Resnik et al., 2012). Several rehabilitation strategies have been proposed or tested. They include general conditioning programs, graded motor tasks, phantom limb exercises, mirror therapy, myoelectric training However, with biofeedback, neuromuscular [36] reeducation, and virtual reality or augmented reality environments in which users practice control before or alongside physical device (17) use. Mirror therapy and related visual-feedback methods have been investigated mainly for phantom limb pain (Ramachandran & Rogers-Ramachandran, 1996; Chan et al., 2007), and recent work suggests that virtual and augmented reality combined with myoelectric pattern recognition can both improve control and relieve pain (Ortiz-Catalan et al., 2016; Powell & Thakor, 2013). (1) (12) These approaches draw on different theoretical bases, including motor learning, cortical reorganization, and task-specific practice, and they are applied in many settings and at different times after amputation. The resulting literature is varied. Most studies are small case series or single-center studies with heterogeneous outcome measures, and descriptions of the content, intensity, and sequencing of training are often incomplete. This fragmentation limits both clinical practice and research. Clinicians who plan rehabilitation for a new upper-limb amputee lack a consolidated summary of which components have been tried, how they are delivered, and what outcomes they are associated with. Health systems that must decide how much to invest in therapy services, as opposed to devices alone, have little synthesized evidence on the added value of rehabilitation. Previous reviews have mostly examined prosthesis design, control strategies, or user acceptance and abandonment (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Carey et al., 2015). Others have focused on phantom limb pain interventions or on lower-limb amputation. To our knowledge, few have [36] systematically examined the content of rehabilitation programs specifically for people with upper-extremity amputations or considered what this body of work implies about the importance of rehabilitation to successful prosthetic use. The present review addresses this gap. Its central question is: what rehabilitation protocols have been described for people with upper-extremity amputation who receive or are being prepared for a prosthesis, and what do they indicate about the value of structured rehabilitation for functional outcomes? Following the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009), we searched the literature systematically, applied explicit inclusion criteria, extracted data on intervention components, and assessed methodological quality. The review makes three contributions. First, it identifies and catalogs the components of upper-limb prosthetic rehabilitation reported in the literature, including general exercise, motor tasks, phantom exercises, muscle training, edema control, functional activities, signal strengthening, prosthetic education, neuromuscular reeducation, and virtual image and virtual reality exercises. This gives clinicians a consolidated reference. Second, it appraises the methodological quality of the available studies, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of the evidence and indicating where more rigorous trials are needed. Third, it argues that rehabilitation should be regarded as an integral part of prosthetic provision rather than an optional adjunct, with implications for service planning, clinical guidelines, and future research on upper-limb loss. Design and Reporting Framework This systematic review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement 2009 (Moher et al., 2009). The review question was framed using the PICO structure: the population comprised individuals of any age with an acquired or congenital upper extremity amputation or limb deficiency, the intervention was any prosthetic rehabilitation program, including pre-prosthetic and prosthetic training, the comparator was an alternative rehabilitation approach, standard care, or no comparator in the case of single-group designs; and the outcomes were functional performance, prosthesis use, muscle control, pain, and related patient-reported measures. Because the aim was to describe and appraise the content and importance of rehabilitation protocols rather than to estimate a pooled treatment effect, a narrative synthesis was planned in advance. A formal protocol was not registered. Data Sources and Search Strategy A systematic literature search was performed to identify studies concerning prosthetic rehabilitation of the upper extremity. The electronic databases searched were PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, PEDro, and Google Scholar. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords linked with Boolean operators. Terms for the population included "upper extremity," "upper limb, "arm," hand, amputee, and amputation, terms for the intervention included rehabilitation, "prosthesis," "prosthetic training," "myoelectric," occupational therapy, (26) "physical therapy," [30] and virtual reality." An example of the PubMed strategy was: ("upper extremity" OR upper limb) [5] AND (amputation OR amputee) AND (rehabilitation OR prosthetic training" OR prosthesis). Search syntax was adapted to the indexing rules of each database. The reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies. No restriction was placed on year of publication up to the date [12] of the final search, (5) and only articles published in English were considered. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they (a) involved participants with upper extremity amputation or limb loss at any level, from partial hand to shoulder disarticulation; (b) examined a rehabilitation intervention directly connected with prosthetic fitting or use, whether delivered before, during, or after prosthesis provision; (c) reported at least one functional, physical, or patient-reported outcome; [11] and (d) were original research published in a peer-reviewed journal. Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized trials, cohort studies, (15) [31] case series, and case reports were eligible. [38] Studies were excluded if they concerned lower extremity amputation exclusively, addressed only surgical or purely However, technological aspects of prosthesis design without a rehabilitation component, were narrative (16) reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, or animal and laboratory studies, or if the full text was unavailable. Study Selection All records retrieved were exported to reference management software, and duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility However, criteria. Full texts of potentially relevant records were then obtained and assessed independently by [1] the same reviewers. Disagreements at either stage were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted (6) when consensus could not be reached. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram that recorded the number of records identified, screened, excluded with reasons, and included. The initial search identified 620 records, of which nine studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were retained for data extraction. Data Extraction A standardized extraction form was developed and piloted on two studies before full use. Two reviewers independently extracted data, and discrepancies were reconciled by consensus. Assessment of Methodological Quality The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers. Because [15] the included studies were However, expected to vary in design, the instrument was selected according to study type. Randomized and controlled trials were appraised with the PEDro scale, which scores eleven items related to eligibility, randomization, allocation concealment, baseline comparability, blinding, follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis, between-group comparisons, and point and variability measures (Maher et al., 2003). Risk of bias judgments were (19) considered [24] when interpreting results, but quality scores were not used as a basis for excluding studies, since the number of eligible studies was small. Inter-rater agreement was examined during the process, and disagreements were resolved by discussion. Instead, a structured narrative synthesis was undertaken. Study characteristics and results were tabulated, and findings were grouped according to the type of rehabilitation component and the outcome domain addressed. Descriptive statistics, including frequencies and percentages, were used [32] to summarize the number of studies by design, quality category, and protocol component. Universities are among the most important producers of health research and health technologies. In the United Kingdom (UK), higher education institutions conduct a large share of publicly funded biomedical research and contribute to the discovery of many new medicines, diagnostics, and vaccines [1,2]. Their choices about what research to pursue, how to manage the resulting intellectual property, and how to disseminate findings therefore shape not only the scientific frontier but also who ultimately benefits from it. Because universities are publicly funded, charitable in purpose, and committed to the public good, they bear a particular responsibility to ensure that the benefits of their research reach the people with the greatest need, including those in low-income settings. That need is poorly matched by the current distribution of research effort. The 10/90 gap, the observation that only about 10% of global health research spending addresses conditions responsible for 90% of the global disease burden, has been described for more than two decades [3,4]. Neglected diseases (NDs), including neglected tropical diseases, malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS, disproportionately affect the poorest populations, yet attract little commercial investment because affected patients cannot generate sufficient market returns [5,6]. Analyses of pharmaceutical development pipelines have repeatedly found that a very small proportion of new chemical entities are directed at these diseases [7,8]. Public and philanthropic funders and product development partnerships have partly filled this gap 9], and the G-FINDER survey documents annual global investment in neglected disease research and development 10]. Even so, the proportion of research addressing the health problems of low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) remains modest relative to burden. Universities, as recipients of public and charitable funding, are central to whether this imbalance is corrected or perpetuated, yet little is known about how much of their research addresses these needs or how concentrated such activity is across institutions. Equitable health outcomes depend on more than the direction of research; they also depend on access to its outputs. Two mechanisms are especially relevant to universities. The first is the licensing of intellectual property. Medical discoveries made in universities are frequently patented and licensed exclusively to a single company, which can then set prices without competition [11,12]. Exclusive licensing may be justified when it is necessary to attract the investment required for development, but it can produce high prices and restrict supply in settings where patients and health systems cannot pay [13]. Well-known examples, such as the antiretroviral stavudine developed at Yale University and licensed to Bristol-Myers Squibb, illustrate how university licensing decisions can affect access to essential medicines in low-income countries, and how student and public pressure may bring about change 14]. In response, advocacy groups and university alumni and student organizations have promoted "global access or "equitable access" licensing, in which licensees commit to affordability, non-exclusive licensing for use in low-resource settings, or humanitarian carve-outs 15,16]. The Statement of Principles and Strategies for the Equitable Dissemination of Medical Technologies, endorsed by a number of North American and European institutions, and the Nine Points to Consider in Licensing University Technology, set out expectations for socially responsible licensing [17,18]. Universities Allied for Essential Medicines (UAEM) has further advocated for such policies and has produced a university report card in the United States and Canada [19]. However, the extent to which UK universities have adopted comparable policies, and how their licensing practices operate in practice, has not been systematically described. The second mechanism is the publication of research findings. Subscription-based publishing makes much of the scientific literature inaccessible to researchers, clinicians, and policy-makers in resource-poor settings, where library budgets are limited, even with initiatives such as HINARI that provide reduced-cost or free access to selected institutions [20,21]. Open access (OA) publishing, whether through publication in OA journals ("gold" route) or deposit of manuscripts in repositories ("green" route), aims to remove these barriers [22]. The permissive licence under which an article is published also matters: Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licensing allows unrestricted reuse, including text and data mining, translation, and redistribution, which are valuable for research and for health programmes in LLMICs [23]. In the UK, funder mandates from Research Councils UK, the Wellcome Trust, and other charities, together with the Finch Report and the Higher Education Funding Council for England's OA requirement for the post-2014 Research Excellence Framework, have substantially changed the publishing environment [24–26]. Universities are the institutions (5) that must implement these mandates through policies, repositories, and article-processing-charge funds, and their approaches have varied 27]. Whether the resulting proportion of health research that is freely available, and available under truly open licences, is high across institutions is not well documented. Taken together, these three domains (research priorities, intellectual property management, and publication practices) represent the principal levers through which universities can contribute to global health equity. Previous work has examined each in isolation, typically at the level of funders, countries, or individual technologies, or in institutions in North America [19,28]. To our knowledge, no However, study has brought them together in a single assessment of UK universities, despite (3) the UK's prominent role as a funder and producer of global health research [29]. Without such a landscape, universities cannot benchmark themselves, funders cannot target support, and students, staff, and the public cannot hold institutions to account. We therefore sought to describe the current state of global health equity policies and practices in a sample of 25 UK universities. Our research questions were: (1) What proportion of each university's health research funding from major UK funders is directed to neglected diseases and to health in low- and lower-middle-income countries; and how is this funding distributed across institutions? (2) What policies and practices govern the licensing of university-owned health technologies, and do they promote global access? (3) What are universities' open-access publishing policies, and what proportion of their health research articles is freely available and licensed under CC-BY? This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first institution-level quantification of UK university health research funding for neglected diseases and LLMIC health, enabling comparison with the global burden of disease. Second, it documents the presence and content However, of equitable licensing and open-access policies, together with observed practice. Third, it identifies where gaps lie and suggests practical steps through which universities can better align their research, licensing, and publishing with the needs of the world's poorest populations. Text classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with applications in news categorization, sentiment analysis, spam filtering, and information retrieval. Supervised classifiers perform well when abundant labeled data are available and when training and test documents are drawn from the same distribution. In practice, both conditions are often violated. Labeling documents is expensive and time-consuming, and a classifier trained on one collection, such as product reviews or one set of news categories, frequently degrades when applied to another collection whose vocabulary, style, and topical composition differ Blitzer et al., 2007; Pan and Yang, 2010). Cross-domain text classification addresses this difficulty by leveraging labeled data from a source domain, together with unlabeled or sparsely labeled data from a target domain, to build an effective target-domain classifier. The central obstacle is distribution shift: the feature distributions of the source and target domains differ, so a model [17] fitted to the source generalizes poorly to the target (Ben-David et al., 2010). A prominent line of work therefore tries to reduce the discrepancy between the two feature distributions. Structural correspondence learning identifies pivot features shared across domains and learns a projection that relates domain-specific features to them (Blitzer et al., 2006). Transfer component analysis and related methods find a latent subspace in which the distance between domain distributions, measured for example by maximum mean discrepancy, is minimized (Pan et al., 2011). Co-clustering approaches link domain-specific words through shared words (Dai et al., 2007), and deep models align hidden representations through marginalized denoising or adversarial training (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012; Ganin et al., 2016). Probabilistic topic models have also been adapted to this setting, in which latent topics play the role of a shared semantic space between domains Zhuang et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013). Despite their differences, [33] most of these methods share one assumption: that domain differences can be eliminated by an exact alignment. Features are matched one-to-one, as when a word in the source is paired with a word in the target, or the two domains are forced through a common projection matrix or a shared topic–word distribution. Exact alignment is attractive because it is simple and has clear theoretical motivations. However, it also imposes a strong constraint on what the model can learn. When the semantic distributions of the domains are very different, as when the same category is expressed through largely different vocabularies or when a domain contains topics absent from the other, forcing a precise correspondence compels the model to compromise. Topics learned under such constraints may mix domain-specific semantics, blur category boundaries, and ultimately reduce classification accuracy in the target domain. In other words, the stricter the alignment, the less capacity the model has to represent the genuine differences between domains. We argue that alignment should instead be performed at a coarser, more flexible level. Semantic content in a domain is naturally organized into groups, such as sets of related topics that together describe a broader theme (for example, a group of topics about computer hardware and software, or about sports). Two domains may describe the same theme using different specific words and different fine-grained topics, yet the themes themselves correspond. Aligning the domains at the level of such semantic groups requires only that each group be shared, leaving the particular topics and words within a group free to vary by domain. We call this mechanism group alignment. It preserves the transfer benefits of shared semantics while allowing domain-specific semantics within groups, relaxing the restriction imposed by exact alignment. Group alignment alone does not guarantee that the learned groups are meaningful or that the topics within them are discriminative. Unsupervised topic models are driven by word co-occurrence, and their topics need not correspond to the categories relevant to classification. Supervised variants, including supervised LDA and Labeled LDA, tie topics to document labels and can substantially improve discrimination Blei and McAuliffe, 2007, Ramage et al., 2009). In the cross-domain setting, labels are available only in the source domain, which suggests a partial supervision: labels guide the learning of semantic groups and of the topics within them in the source domain, whereas the target domain is modeled without labels but is connected to the source via the group structure. This helps the model learn better groups and better within-group semantics, and the resulting representation is both transferable and class-informative. Based on these ideas, we propose Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), a probabilistic topic model that embeds group alignment and partial supervision in a single generative framework. Source-domain labels define semantic groups, each of which is associated with a set of topics that are shared by both domains at the group level. Topics within a group may have domain-specific word distributions, so that the same group is realized differently in the source and the target. Documents in the target domain draw their topics from the same groups without requiring label information. Inference yields topic-based document representations that can be fed to a standard classifier. Our study addresses the following research questions. First, does aligning semantics at the group level yield better target-domain classification than exact alignment, especially when domain semantics diverge? Second, does partial supervision in the source domain improve the quality of the learned groups and of the semantics within them? Third, are the resulting topics interpretable and consistent with the underlying categories? The contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We identify the restrictive nature of exact alignment in cross-domain text classification and propose group alignment, which aligns domains at the level of semantic groups while permitting domain-specific semantics within each group. 2. We introduce a partial supervision scheme in the source domain that helps the model learn more coherent semantic groups and more discriminative within-group topics. 3. We integrate both mechanisms in CDL-LDA, a cross-domain topic model, and derive an inference procedure for it. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on the standard 20Newsgroups and Reuters datasets, including quantitative evaluations of classification accuracy and perplexity and qualitative topic detection analyses, demonstrating the effectiveness of group alignment and partial supervision. Because the background group carries no class information, the predicted label was ĉ = argmax{c} P(Gc | d), considering only class groups. As a second variant, we used the K-dimensional vector θd as features for a linear SVM trained on source documents, to test the quality of the learned representation independent of the group-based decision rule.
