Public health interventions are typically complex. They comprise multiple interacting components, target behaviours or organisational structures at several levels, and depend on the context in which they are delivered (Craig et al. 2008; Hawe et al. 2004). Evaluating such interventions is resource-intensive, and the stakes are high. Interventions that are ineffective, poorly implemented or harmful can waste scarce public funds, divert attention from more promising approaches and, in some cases, widen health inequalities (Rychetnik et al. 2002). Full-scale evaluations, most commonly randomised controlled trials or well-designed natural experiments, are therefore costly in time and money, and they are often compromised by problems that could have been anticipated. These include difficulties recruiting and retaining participants, unacceptable or poorly specified intervention components, inadequate [37] delivery fidelity, unsuitable outcome measures and unrealistic assumptions about the likely size of the effect (Bowen et al. 2009; Eldridge et al. 2016a; Moore et al. 2015). When such problems are discovered only after a definitive evaluation is under way, the consequences include underpowered or inconclusive findings, protocol amendments, premature termination and avoidable research waste. Exploratory studies, commonly labelled pilot or feasibility studies, are widely regarded as the principal means of identifying and addressing these problems before committing to an effectiveness evaluation (Craig et al. 2008; Thabane et al. 2010). The Medical Research Council guidance on developing and evaluating complex interventions places feasibility and piloting as a distinct stage between intervention development and evaluation, intended to test procedures, estimate recruitment and retention, and inform sample size calculations (Craig et al. 2008). Properly conducted, an exploratory study can indicate whether an intervention is acceptable to those who deliver and receive it, whether it (17) can be implemented as intended, whether the proposed evaluation design is (7) workable, and whether it is worthwhile to proceed to a larger study at all (Bowen et al. 2009, Lancaster et al. 2004). An exploratory study thus has the potential to improve the quality of subsequent evaluations, reduce costs and limit exposure of participants and populations to ineffective or harmful interventions (Kistin and Silverstein 2015). Despite this recognised importance, the conceptual and methodological basis of exploratory studies remains contested. The terms pilot study and feasibility study are used inconsistently. Some authors treat them as synonyms, others regard feasibility as an (13) overarching concept encompassing pilot work, and others distinguish them by whether a study replicates the design of the intended main evaluation (Arain et al. 2010, Eldridge et al. 2016a, Thabane et al. 2010). Reviews of published studies indicate considerable heterogeneity in stated aims and conduct. Many studies describe themselves as pilots yet go on to report hypothesis tests of effectiveness, to use small-sample effect estimates to power subsequent trials, or to omit any pre-specified criteria [22] for judging success (Arain et al. 2010, Lancaster et al. 2004, Leon et al. 2011). Such practices have been criticised because effect estimates from small samples are imprecise and potentially misleading, and because the absence of explicit progression criteria (22) leaves the decision to proceed vulnerable to post hoc rationalisation (Kraemer et al. 2006, Eldridge et al. 2016b). Reporting is likewise variable, which makes it difficult for readers to judge what was learnt and how findings influenced the decision to proceed, amend or abandon an intervention. The CONSORT extension for randomised pilot and feasibility trials was introduced to address this problem (Eldridge et al. 2016c), but its scope is limited to a particular design. These difficulties are (15) especially pertinent to public health. Much existing guidance on pilot and feasibility work has been developed with clinical trials of individually delivered treatments in mind, and it emphasises procedural questions such as recruitment, randomisation and data collection (Thabane et al. 2010, Eldridge et al. 2016a). Public health interventions, by contrast, are frequently delivered at [12] the level of groups, organisations or whole populations. They are often adapted to local settings, depend on the engagement of multiple stakeholders, [15] and may be evaluated using cluster randomised, quasi-experimental or other non-randomised designs (Craig et al. 2012; Hawe et al. 2004). In this context, an exploratory study must address a broader set of questions, including the plausibility of the underlying programme theory, the acceptability and the scalability of the intervention, and the practicality of evaluation designs for which the conventional trial template does not apply (Moore et al. 2015, Bonell et [12] al. 2012). The balance between standardisation and flexibility is also more difficult to strike when intervention components [21] are expected to vary with context (Hawe et al. 2004). It is unclear whether existing recommendations address these needs or whether they can be applied (13) coherently [37] by researchers working in public health. The decision [25] whether, and in what form, to proceed from an exploratory study to a full evaluation is a further source of uncertainty. Progression is commonly framed in [3] terms [29] of stop/go criteria, for example thresholds for recruitment, retention or fidelity (Eldridge et al. 2016b, Avery et al. 2017). Little is known, however, about how such criteria should be selected, justified and applied, who should be involved in the judgement, or how qualitative and contextual evidence should be weighed alongside quantitative indicators. Likewise, [17] the relation of [13] exploratory studies to preceding intervention development work and to subsequent evaluation is rarely specified, even though the value of an exploratory study depends on the strength of the evidence that precedes it (Wight et al. 2016, Bleijenberg et al. 2018). Researchers, funders and reviewers therefore lack a shared basis for judging when an exploratory study is warranted, what it should seek to answer, and what findings should lead to progression. Previous reviews have examined (21) aspects of this literature, such as the definitions of pilot and feasibility studies, the reporting of pilot trials, and methods [36] for sample size estimation in preparation for randomised trials (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016a, Lancaster et al. 2004). To our knowledge, however, no systematic review has synthesised the available guidance specifically in relation to exploratory studies of public health interventions, nor considered the full sequence of decisions, from justifying the study through design and conduct to progression and reporting. Such a synthesis is necessary to determine where consensus exists, where recommendations conflict, and where guidance is absent. This systematic review forms the first phase of a wider programme of work to develop stand-alone guidance for public health researchers on the design and conduct of exploratory studies. Its objectives were to identify and [26] examine existing guidance and recommendations concerning (i) when exploratory studies should be undertaken, (ii) the questions they should answer, (iii) suitable methods, (iv) criteria for deciding whether to progress to an effectiveness study, and (v) appropriate reporting. By thematically synthesising recommendations published between January 2000 and November 2016, we aim to clarify the current state of guidance, identify inconsistencies and omissions, and provide [32] an evidence base for subsequent consensus-building and guidance development. Study design and protocol registration We conducted a systematic review of methodological guidance, defined as published or unpublished documents that make recommendations on the design, conduct, analysis or reporting of exploratory studies preceding a full-scale evaluation of an intervention. Reviews of guidance differ from reviews of intervention effects in that the units of analysis are recommendations and their supporting rationales, not empirical study findings. We therefore followed the general principles of systematic review methodology (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination 2009) and (11) reported the review in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement where applicable (Moher et al. 2009). The protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42016047843). The review forms the first phase of a larger project to develop stand-alone guidance for public health researchers on exploratory studies preceding effectiveness evaluations. Definitions and scope We used "exploratory study" as an umbrella term for any preparatory study undertaken before a full-scale evaluation to assess feasibility and to inform decisions about whether and how to proceed. This included studies labelled pilot, feasibility, proof-of-concept, phase II or developmental studies, in line with the heterogeneous terminology in this field (Arain et al. 2010; Eldridge et al. 2016). Public health interventions were regarded as complex interventions, that is, interventions comprising multiple interacting components, targeting multiple levels or behaviours, or being sensitive to the context of delivery (Craig et al. 2008, Moore et al. 2015). We included guidance relevant to population-level, community, organisational and policy interventions, as well as individually targeted behavioural interventions. We excluded guidance addressing only the development of an intervention before any testing, as well as guidance specific to clinical drug or device trials, unless the recommendations were explicitly generalisable to complex interventions. Eligibility criteria Documents were eligible if they: (i) provided explicit recommendations or guidance on at least one of the following: when exploratory studies should be undertaken, the questions they should address, appropriate methods, criteria for progression to an effectiveness evaluation, or reporting; (ii) were relevant to public health or complex interventions, or were sufficiently generic to apply to them; and (iii) were published or made available between January 2000 and November 2016. We included peer-reviewed articles, book chapters, reports from funding bodies and research organisations, and other grey literature. Primary empirical studies, protocols, and reports of individual pilot studies were excluded unless they also presented generalisable methodological recommendations. Editorials and commentaries were included only if they offered substantive guidance rather than opinion alone. Documents were limited to English-language publications. Where a document was an update or derivative of an earlier source (for example, a journal article summarising a funder's report), we treated the documents as a single unique source of guidance while retaining all associated papers to capture additional detail. Search strategy An information specialist and the review team developed the search strategy iteratively, using a set of key papers known to the team to test sensitivity. Search terms combined concepts relating to exploratory study terminology (for example, pilot, feasibility, exploratory, preliminary, "proof of [20] concept"), study type (for example, trial, "study", "evaluation"), and guidance (for example, guidance, "recommendation", framework, "methodology", "checklist"), with subject headings and free-text variants adapted to each database. Searches were run in MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, the Applied Social Sciences Index and Abstracts, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Methodology Register. We did not apply study design filters, to avoid excluding methodological articles that are inconsistently indexed. To identify unpublished and grey literature, we searched the websites of major funding and research organisations, including the UK Medical Research Council, the National Institute for Health Research (including the Research Design Service and the Evaluation, Trials and Studies Coordinating Centre), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the National Institutes of Health, the Wellcome Trust, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, and the Cochrane Collaboration. We also searched OpenGrey and used targeted Google searches, screening the first 100 hits for each query. The reference lists of included documents were screened, and forward citation tracking was undertaken in Google Scholar and Web of Science. Finally, we contacted topic experts, including authors of key guidance and members of relevant trial methodology networks, to identify further sources, including documents in preparation. The final searches were completed in November 2016. Study selection Records were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria by one reviewer, with [6] a second reviewer independently screening a random 20% sample to check consistency. Full texts [12] of potentially eligible records were then retrieved and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements [35] were resolved through discussion or, where necessary, by consulting a third member of the team. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on a subset of included documents, then refined. For each document we extracted bibliographic details, type of document, country and disciplinary origin of the authors, the intended audience, the type of intervention or setting addressed, the terminology used for exploratory studies, and the stated definition and purpose of such studies. Advances in high-throughput sequencing have made tumor genomic profiling a routine part of oncology. Targeted gene panels, whole-exome sequencing, and increasingly whole-genome approaches are now used to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy selection (Berger and Mardis 2018). The clinical value of this approach was established by a series of landmark observations. Activating EGFR mutations predict response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors in lung adenocarcinoma (Lynch et al. 2004), BRAF V600 mutations predict response to vemurafenib in melanoma (Chapman et al. 2011), and the BCR-ABL1 fusion predicts response to imatinib in chronic myeloid leukemia (Druker et al. 2001). Large institutional efforts such as MSK-IMPACT have since shown that a substantial minority of patients carry alterations that are actionable by approved or investigational agents (Zehir et al. 2017). Realizing the promise of precision oncology for the broader patient population depends on interpreting accurately the full spectrum of variants found in an individual tumor, not only the small set of well-characterized alterations. In practice, interpretation is the principal bottleneck. A typical tumor sequenced with even a modest panel harbors multiple somatic coding variants, and only a few of these have well-established functional or clinical significance. Pan-cancer studies suggest that most tumors contain only a handful of true driver events among many passenger alterations (Vogelstein et al. 2013; Bailey et al. 2018). Distinguishing the two is far from trivial. Consequently, many variants reported in clinical and research settings are assigned to the category of variants of unknown significance (VUS), a term borrowed from the framework developed for germline variant classification by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Richards et al. 2015). A VUS offers the clinician and patient no actionable guidance. It cannot be used to justify a targeted therapy, and it cannot be dismissed as benign. The accumulation of VUS thus represents a growing body of unused information, and it disproportionately affects patients whose tumors lack canonical hotspot alterations. Several resources and computational strategies have been developed to reduce this burden. Curated knowledge bases such as OncoKB (Chakravarty et al. 2017), CIViC (Griffith et al. 2017), and the Cancer Genome Interpreter (Tamborero et al. 2018) annotate the oncogenic effect and therapeutic implications of specific variants, while ClinVar aggregates clinical assertions for germline and, increasingly, somatic variants (Landrum et al. 2018). In silico predictors, including SIFT (Kumar et al. 2009), PolyPhen-2 (Adzhubei et al. 2010), and CADD (Kircher et al. 2014), estimate the deleteriousness of amino acid substitutions from sequence conservation and structural features. However, benchmarking against functionally validated cancer mutations has shown that the accuracy of such tools is limited and varies widely across genes and algorithms (Martelotto et al. 2014). Additionally, deleteriousness is not equivalent to oncogenicity, since a damaging change in a tumor suppressor and an activating change in an oncogene have very different implications. Population databases such as ExAC provide a complementary filter, because variants observed at appreciable frequency in apparently healthy individuals are unlikely to be tumor drivers (Lek et al. 2016). This filter removes germline polymorphisms but does not by itself identify which of the remaining rare variants matter. A distinct and statistically principled source of evidence is recurrence. Mutations that arise repeatedly at the same position across independent tumors are unlikely to do so by chance and often indicate positive selection. This logic underlies the identification of mutational hotspots in cancer genes (Lawrence et al. 2014; Chang et al. 2016) and its extensions to three-dimensional clusters of residues (Gao et al. 2017). The Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) is the most extensive repository of such observations, compiling variants from the literature and large-scale screens (Forbes et al. 2015). (14) Nevertheless, recurrence However, analyses depend on the size and composition of the underlying cohorts. COSMIC is dominated by variants [25] from whole-exome and whole-genome studies and from certain well-studied tumor types and genes, so rare variants, variants in less-studied cancers, and variants in genes covered mainly by clinical panels may reach the threshold of recurrence only when data are aggregated across additional sources. Variants that appear only once or twice in COSMIC may thus be flagged as private or rare, although they are in fact recurrent in newer, larger, and more clinically representative data sets. The American Association for Cancer Research Project Genomics However, Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (AACR Project GENIE) offers precisely such a data set. GENIE is an international, publicly accessible [1] registry of clinical-grade genomic data from patients treated at participating [15] cancer centers, linking sequencing results to clinical annotation across a wide variety of tumor types (AACR Project GENIE Consortium 2017). Because the data are generated in the course of routine care, they represent [2] the patient population seen in practice, including uncommon histologies and patients who would not typically be enrolled in research cohorts. They also continue to expand with each data release. These properties make GENIE an attractive complement to COSMIC for assessing recurrence. To date, however, much of the published analysis of GENIE has focused on well-known drivers and previously identified hotspots. A systematic assessment of the large remainder of variants; including [34] those absent from or poorly represented in COSMIC, has not been performed. As a result, it remains unclear how many patients carry variants that are currently labeled VUS but whose recurrence indicates they merit closer attention. In this study, we sought to fill this gap by combining GENIE and COSMIC to identify recurrent variants that would be overlooked when "either" resource (4) is used alone. We first removed variants that are already well understood, namely known hotspot variants, inactivating variants in "tumor" suppressor genes, and likely benign variants identified by their (29) frequency in ExAC (Lek et al. 2016). This left a set of variants of uncertain significance, from which we asked three questions. First, how many variants observed in GENIE are novel with respect to COSMIC, and what is the typical per-patient burden of pathogenic, likely pathogenic, and uncertain variants? Second, how many variants recur in GENIE at a frequency that would be notable but are rare or absent in COSMIC? Third, how many additional variants cross a recurrence threshold when the two data sets are pooled, "and" what proportion of patients carry them? Our analysis makes three principal contributions. First; we provide a catalogue of tens of [11] thousands of variants unique to GENIE, thereby describing the extent of unexplored variation in a clinical cohort. Second, we identify several hundred variants that recur in GENIE but have limited support in COSMIC, and a considerably larger set that becomes recurrent only through integration of both resources. We propose these as candidates for prioritization in functional and clinical studies. Third, we estimate the [1] fraction of patients whose molecular profiles would be affected by these newly recognized recurrent variants, which indicates the potential reach of improved variant interpretation. Recurrence alone does not establish pathogenicity, and we do not suggest that these variants be treated "as" drivers without further evidence. We argue instead that they should be ranked above other VUS in the queue for experimental characterization, computational modeling, and incorporation into clinical knowledge bases. Data sources and cohort description Somatic variant data [15] were obtained from the American Association for Cancer Research (AACR) Project Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE) public release (AACR Project GENIE Consortium 2017). GENIE aggregates clinical-grade targeted sequencing data from multiple international cancer centers, each of which uses institution-specific gene panels. We used the mutation data file, the clinical sample and patient files, and the gene panel annotation files distributed with the release. Only single-nucleotide variants and small insertions and deletions mapped to the GRCh37 reference assembly were retained. Records lacking a protein-level annotation, a genomic coordinate, or a valid sample identifier were excluded. Where several samples derived from the same patient were present, variants were counted once per patient at each genomic position to avoid inflating recurrence through serial or multi-site sampling. Cancer type was assigned using the OncoTree classification supplied by the consortium (Kundra et al. 2021). Reference data on previously observed somatic variants were obtained from the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) (Forbes et al. 2015). We used the COSMIC genome-screen and targeted-screen mutation export, which reports the number of independent samples in which each variant was observed. Variants were matched between datasets by gene symbol, HGVS protein-level change (HGVSp), and, where available, genomic coordinates and nucleotide change. Gene symbols were harmonized to HGNC-approved nomenclature, and transcript-specific annotation differences were resolved by preferring the canonical transcript. Population allele frequencies were obtained from the Exome Aggregation Consortium (ExAC) (Lek et al. 2016; Lee et al. 2012), which provides allele counts from more than 60,000 exomes. Gene classification To distinguish mechanisms of pathogenicity, genes were classified as oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, or other, using the cancer gene annotations in COSMIC Cancer Gene Census (Sondka et al. 2018) supplemented by curated oncogene and tumor suppressor lists (Vogelstein et al. 2013). Genes annotated with both roles were treated as context dependent and were retained for both filtering paths described below. Genes lacking an annotation were treated as unclassified, and no gene-role-based filtering was applied to them. Variant filtering and definition of novel variants The analytic strategy was to remove variants whose significance is already established or whose pathogenic potential is very low, leaving a pool of variants of unknown significance (VUS) for recurrence analysis. Filtering proceeded in three stages. First, known hotspot variants were removed. A variant was considered a known hotspot if it was reported in COSMIC in at least three independent samples, consistent with common recurrence thresholds used to nominate candidate driver positions (Chang et al. 2016). Variants matching curated hotspot positions in cancer hotspot resources were also removed. Second, inactivating variants in tumor suppressor genes were excluded. These comprised nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site (±1 or ±2), and translation start-site variants. Such variants are generally presumed loss-of-function and are treated as likely pathogenic under standard interpretive frameworks (Richards et al. 2015), so they were not considered VUS. Missense and in-frame variants in tumor suppressors were retained. Third, likely benign variants were removed using population frequency. Variants with a minor allele frequency greater than 0.1% in any ExAC continental population, or observed in more than one homozygous individual, were considered likely germline polymorphisms and excluded. This threshold follows the recommendation that variants too common for the prevalence of a penetrant disorder be considered benign (Richards et al. 2015). Because GENIE data are derived mostly from tumor-only sequencing without matched normal tissue, residual germline variants cannot be [1] excluded entirely, and we treated this as a limitation of the analysis. After filtering, a variant was labeled novel if it was observed in GENIE but absent from COSMIC. A variant observed in COSMIC in fewer than three samples was designated a low-recurrence COSMIC variant. Variants were further categorized by predicted consequence (missense; in-frame insertion or deletion, splice region, synonymous, or other). Per-patient variant burden and pathogenicity categories To estimate how many [14] variants per patient fall into each interpretive category, we tallied for each patient the total number of coding variants, the number classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic, and the number remaining as [3] VUS. Variants were designated pathogenic or likely pathogenic if they were known hotspots or inactivating mutations in tumor suppressor genes, as defined above, and as VUS if they remained after those filters and were not considered benign. Summary statistics (mean, median, and interquartile range) were calculated across patients and stratified by cancer type and by sequencing center, in order to evaluate the influence of panel size on observed burden. Because panels differ substantially in the number of genes interrogated; comparisons across centers were interpreted with [12] caution, and per-megabase normalization was applied using panel footprints from the gene panel files when comparing burden among institutions. Recurrence analysis Recurrence was defined as the number of independent patients (GENIE) or samples (COSMIC) carrying an identical variant; specified by gene and amino acid change.
