Ambient air pollution is among the leading environmental risk factors for premature death and disease worldwide. The World Health Organization estimates that outdoor air pollution contributes to several million premature deaths each year, mainly through cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease and lung cancer (World Health Organization, 2016, Cohen et al., 2017). Short-term exposure to elevated concentrations of particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone and nitrogen dioxide is associated with increased hospital admissions, exacerbations of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and cardiovascular events (Brook et al., 2010, Atkinson et al., 2014). Although the largest gains in population health are likely to come from structural reductions in emissions, such reductions are slow and, in many settings, incomplete. Pollution episodes will therefore continue to occur, and individuals at risk will need to take steps to protect themselves in the meantime. To support such protective action, many countries and cities have introduced air quality warning systems. These typically translate monitored or modelled pollutant concentrations into an index or banding scheme, such as the US Air Quality Index, the UK Daily Air Quality Index or the Air Quality Health Index used in Canada and Hong Kong. The index is communicated through media, websites, mobile applications, text messages or public displays, and is usually accompanied by tiered health advice. The advice commonly encourages sensitive groups, and at higher levels the general population, to reduce or reschedule strenuous outdoor activity, avoid busy roads, and, for people with respiratory or cardiac conditions, to follow their treatment plans and keep reliever medication to hand (Environmental Protection Agency, 2014, Defra, 2013). The logic of these systems is a simple one: if people know when air quality is poor and understand what to do, they will change their behaviour, [18] reduce their exposure and thereby avoid some of the associated harm. The effectiveness of this chain depends on every link holding. People must be aware of the warning, understand it, believe that it is relevant to them, and be willing and able to act on the advice. There is reason to doubt that this always happens. Studies of health risk communication more broadly have shown that awareness of a hazard does not necessarily translate into behaviour change, and that perceptions of risk, trust in information sources and confidence in one’s ability to act all mediate responses (Witte and Allen, 2000; Ferrer and Klein, 2015). In the context of [20] air pollution, the hazard is often invisible, its effects are probabilistic and delayed, and the recommended actions may conflict with work, caregiving, commuting or exercise routines. Furthermore, the benefits of short-term avoidance are uncertain at the individual level, and some recommended behaviours, such as reducing physical activity, could have negative health consequences if applied indiscriminately (Giles and Koehle, 2014). Evidence on whether air quality warnings change behaviour is nevertheless scattered. Economists have examined averting behaviour in response to smog alerts, using attendance at outdoor venues, transport use or purchases of protective products as proxies, and have reported mixed results (Neidell, 2009, Zivin and Neidell, 2009). Public health researchers have conducted surveys and panel studies of awareness, intended behaviour and self-reported behaviour among general populations and among people with asthma or cardiovascular disease, in North America, Europe and Asia (e.g. McDermott et al., 2006, Wen et al., 2009). These studies vary considerably in their populations, in the warning systems studied, in the behaviours considered and in how adherence was measured. Some assess only a single behaviour, such as staying indoors; others consider a broad repertoire, including mask wearing, closing windows, changing travel mode or using medication. Studies also differ in whether they ask about behaviour on a specific poor-air-quality day or in general, which affects estimates of adherence. As a consequence, it remains unclear how many people follow the advice that accompanies air quality warnings, and which behaviours are most and least likely to be adopted. A second, related gap concerns who adheres and why. Several studies have examined demographic characteristics, such as age, sex, education, income and the presence of a health condition, as correlates of protective behaviour, but findings seem inconsistent. Others have explored psychosocial factors, including knowledge, risk perception, symptom attribution, self-efficacy, social influences and practical barriers. These are rarely organised within a coherent theoretical structure, which makes it hard to see which determinants are most promising targets for intervention. Behaviour change frameworks offer a way to do this. The COM-B model proposes that behaviour (B) [38] arises from the interaction of capability (C), opportunity (O) and motivation (M), and underpins the Behaviour Change Wheel, which links these sources of behaviour to intervention functions and policy options (Michie, van Stralen and West, 2011). Capability includes physical and psychological capacities such as knowledge and understanding, opportunity covers physical and social factors external to the individual, including time, resources and the influence of others; and motivation includes reflective processes such as beliefs, intentions and perceived threat, as well as automatic processes such as habits and emotional responses. Applying this framework to the air quality literature may help show whether non-adherence is mainly a problem of understanding, of circumstances or [3] of motivation, and thus what kinds of advice and delivery would be [32] likely to improve uptake. Existing reviews have addressed adjacent questions but not this one directly. Some have synthesised evidence on the health effects of air pollution or on the effectiveness of personal-level interventions such as face masks and air filters for reducing exposure or improving health outcomes (Laumbach, Meng and Kipen, 2015, Barn et [3] al., 2008). Others have considered risk perception of air pollution or the design of air quality indices (Bickerstaff and Walker, 2001; Kelly and Fussell, 2015). However, to our knowledge no previous systematic review has examined the extent to which people adhere to the health advice that accompanies air quality warning systems, nor has it systematically identified the demographic and psychosocial factors that predict adherence or non-adherence. Without such a synthesis, public health agencies lack an evidence base for designing advice that people will actually follow. We therefore conducted a systematic review with two aims. The first was to establish to what extent air quality warning systems influence protective behaviours in the general public, by estimating intended and actual adherence to the accompanying health advice. The second was to identify the demographic and psychosocial factors associated with adherence and non-adherence, including self-reported reasons for following or not following the advice, and to interpret these within the COM-B framework. To keep the focus on the warning systems themselves, we included only studies in which participants used, or were aware of, such systems, and excluded studies that examined protective behaviours prompted solely by subjective perceptions of poor air quality. This review makes three contributions. It provides the first systematic summary of adherence rates to health advice linked to air quality alerts, distinguishing advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activity from broader protective behaviours. It clarifies whether demographic characteristics are useful in identifying people who are less likely to adhere. Finally, it identifies modifiable psychosocial facilitators and [37] barriers and maps them onto a behavioural framework, providing a basis for the design and evaluation of more effective air quality [16] communication. Protocol and reporting This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). Because the literature was expected to be heterogeneous in [35] design, populations, warning systems and [4] outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was planned [1] in advance, [17] following guidance from the Economic and Social Research Council on narrative synthesis in systematic reviews (Popay et al., 2006). Findings were interpreted using the COM-B model of behaviour (Capability, Opportunity, Motivation – Behaviour), which forms part of the Behaviour Change Wheel (Michie, van Stralen and West, 2011). However, Under this model, behaviour (B) is a function of interacting components, which can be summarised as B = f(C, O, M), where capability comprises physical and psychological capacity, opportunity comprises physical and social environmental factors, and motivation comprises reflective and automatic processes. Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible if they assessed intended or actual adherence to health advice accompanying an air [18] quality warning system, where such advice encouraged people to reduce their exposure to air pollution (for example by reducing or rescheduling outdoor activity, [34] avoiding busy roads, staying indoors, or using preventative medication). Studies were also eligible if they examined predictors of adherence (demographic or psychosocial) or self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. Participants had to be members of the general public, including those with pre-existing conditions such as asthma, who were either using or aware of a warning system. Studies had to report [2] original data and to be published in English in a peer-reviewed journal, qualitative, cross-sectional, cohort and experimental designs were all considered. Studies were excluded if they examined only protective behaviours arising from subjective perception of poor air quality (for example, noticing haze or smell) without reference to a warning system, since such behaviour cannot be attributed to the influence of the warning. Studies were also excluded if participants were not aware of or using the warning system, if they assessed only the effects of policy interventions on pollution levels (for example traffic restrictions) rather than individual behaviour, if they were focused on occupational exposure, or if they were reviews, commentaries or conference abstracts without full data. Studies of indoor air pollution and of wildfire smoke, volcanic ash or dust [29] events were considered eligible only where a formal warning or advisory system and accompanying advice were evaluated. Search strategy In August 2016 we searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus and the Cochrane Library from inception. The search strategy combined three concept blocks using Boolean operators: (1) air quality terms (e.g. “air pollution”, air [31] quality”, smog, ozone, particulate matter”); (2) warning terms (e.g. warning, alert, forecast, “advisory”, index, health advice”, health message”); and (3) behavioural terms (e.g. “adherence”, compliance, behavio, avoidance, protective, “response”, “risk perception”). Search terms were adapted to the controlled vocabulary of each database. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched, and forward [5] citation tracking was carried out in Google Scholar. Grey literature was not systematically searched, but we screened the first 100 results of Google Scholar queries using the main search terms. Study selection Records [15] were exported to reference management software and duplicates removed. One reviewer screened all titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria; a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subsample, and agreement was assessed using Cohen’s kappa (κ = (po − pe)/(1 − pe), where po is observed agreement and pe is agreement expected by chance). Full texts of potentially relevant articles were obtained and assessed independently by two reviewers. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or, where necessary, by consultation with a third author. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage were recorded. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on three studies. Extracted information included: country and setting, study design, sampling method and sample size; participant characteristics (age, sex, health status, ethnicity, socioeconomic indicators), type of warning system (for example air quality index, forecast, smog alert), the pollutants covered and the dissemination channels; the content of the accompanying health advice; whether adherence was intended or actual; how adherence was measured (self-report questionnaire, diary, interview, or objective measure), adherence rates, demographic and psychosocial predictors tested, with effect estimates (odds ratios, regression coefficients, correlation coefficients, p values) where available, and self-reported reasons for adherence or non-adherence. One reviewer extracted data and a second checked all entries for accuracy. Where studies reported adherence to several behaviours, we separated adherence to the advice to reduce or reschedule outdoor activities from adherence to a wider range of protective behaviours (such as avoiding busy roads, closing windows, or taking preventative medication), because the former is the most commonly recommended and most comparable behaviour. Where adherence was reported for subgroups only, the rates were extracted by subgroup and the overall rate was calculated as a weighted proportion

Speech is produced by a coordinated sequence of movements of the articulators, including the lips, jaw, tongue, velum, and larynx. These movements continuously reshape the vocal tract, the airway extending from the glottis to the lips. By modulating airflow and creating different resonant cavities, the time-varying vocal tract shape determines the acoustic properties of the speech signal (Fant, 1970, Stevens, 1998). Vocal tract configurations therefore carry rich information about the underlying speech production mechanism, and understanding the mapping between vocal tract geometry and acoustics remains a central problem in speech science, with implications for phonetics, speech technology, clinical assessment, [31] and the study of language variation Narayanan et al., 2014, Lingala et al., 2016). Progress on this problem has depended on instrumentation for observing articulation. Electromagnetic articulography, ultrasound, X-ray microbeam, and video of the face each provide partial views, capturing flesh-point trajectories, the tongue surface, or the external lips (Whalen et al., 2005; Stone, 2005). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is attractive because it is non-invasive, involves no ionizing radiation, and provides a view of the entire vocal tract, including regions such as the pharynx and velum that are hard to reach by other modalities. Advances in fast acquisition and reconstruction have made real-time MRI (rtMRI) of speech practical, with frame rates sufficient to capture dynamic articulation in the midsagittal plane during natural, continuous speech (Narayanan et al., 2004; Bresch et al., 2008; Lingala et al., 2016). Large "rtMRI" corpora, such as "the" USC-TIMIT database and related multi-speaker collections, now allow quantitative study of articulation across many speakers (Narayanan et al., 2014). Most computational work on rtMRI speech data has relied on hand-designed or semi-automatic representations of the vocal tract. These include air–tissue boundary segmentation, cross-distance functions along the vocal tract midline, and region-of-interest time series that capture constriction formation at the lips, tongue tip, tongue body, and velum (Kim et al., 2014, Bresch & Narayanan, 2009; Proctor et al., 2010). Such representations are interpretable and have supported insights into coarticulation, compensatory articulation, and the composition of articulatory gestures Browman & Goldstein, 1992). However, they require segmentation or parameterization pipelines that may be sensitive to image quality and speaker anatomy, and they may discard information that is not captured by the chosen parameters. A complementary strategy is to learn representations directly from the image sequences, letting the data determine which spatial and temporal features are informative about the speech sounds being produced. Deep learning [29] provides tools for this strategy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn hierarchical visual features and have achieved strong results in image recognition (Krizhevsky et al., 2012, Simonyan However, & Zisserman, 2015, He et al., 2016). For video, the challenge is to also model temporal dynamics. Approaches include 3D convolutions (Ji et al., 2013, Tran et al., 2015), two-stream [21] networks combining appearance and motion Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), and architectures that couple per-frame CNN features with recurrent networks such as long short-term memory LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) are a prominent [36] example of the last family: a CNN extracts deep visual features from [21] each frame, and a recurrent layer integrates them over time, making the model deep in both space and time [24] (Donahue et al., 2015). Such models [19] have been successful in action recognition, video description, and other sequence-learning tasks, and have also been applied to visual speech recognition from lip images (Assael et al., 2016; Chung et al., 2017). Applying them to rtMRI of the full vocal tract is a natural extension, but one that has received comparatively little systematic attention. There is a gap in the existing literature. Studies of automatic recognition from articulatory data have mostly used point-tracking measurements or lip-region video, or have used articulatory features as auxiliary inputs to acoustic recognizers (King et al., 2007; Hueber et al., 2010). Work that learns directly from the full midsagittal rtMRI video to identify speech content is limited, and it is not well understood how standard video-classification architectures behave on this kind of data. Vocal tract videos differ from the natural-scene videos for which these architectures were designed. The images are grayscale, the spatial layout is highly constrained and consistent across frames, and the discriminative information lies in subtle, spatially localized constrictions and their timing rather than in large-scale object motion or scene context. Moreover, the sequences of interest, such as vowel-consonant-vowel VCV) utterances, are short and the relevant dynamics are brief and coarticulated, so assumptions about the value of long temporal context or of pretrained appearance features may not carry over. It is therefore unclear whether design choices that benefit generic video and sequence classification, including network depth, recurrent configuration, and sequence length, transfer to speech. This paper takes a step towards automatic mapping of vocal tract shape geometry to speech acoustics by addressing a closely related question: can speech content be identified directly from the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in rtMRI, using video action recognition techniques? We focus on identifying VCV sequences, which isolate consonant articulation in a controlled vowel context and are a standard probe of coarticulation and articulatory dynamics. We ask how LRCN-style models perform on this task, how their performance depends on parameter settings such as the CNN and recurrent components, and whether the behavior observed differs from that known for generic video or sequence classification. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we formulate speech identification from rtMRI as a video classification problem and apply LRCN models that combine deep CNN feature extraction with recurrent sequence modeling to 2D rtMRI of VCV utterances from 17 speakers. Second, we conduct a comparative evaluation of this class of models under various parameter settings and for several classification tasks, providing an empirical characterization of what matters for this data. Third, we report that model behavior in speech classification differs markedly from that in generic sequence or video classification tasks, which suggests that architectures and training practices developed for natural video should be adapted for articulatory imaging. Together, these findings inform the design of data-driven models linking vocal tract dynamics and speech, and they provide a baseline for future work on acoustic mapping from articulation. Data We used a database of two-dimensional real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rtMRI) of the midsagittal vocal tract acquired from 17 native speakers of American English during the production of vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences. Image acquisition followed the established protocol for rtMRI of speech production (Narayanan et al., 2004; Narayanan et al., 2014). Participants lay supine in a scanner. A fast spiral gradient-echo sequence with a flexible receiver coil placed around the head and neck was used to image a single midsagittal slice that covered the lips, tongue, velum, larynx, and pharyngeal wall. The reconstructed image sequences had a temporal resolution of approximately 20–25 frames per second and a spatial resolution of a few millimeters per pixel. Reconstructed frames were stored as grayscale video. Audio was recorded simultaneously through a noise-cancelling optical microphone and denoised (Bresch et al., 2006), so the acoustic signal could be used to segment utterances. Audio was used only for segmentation and was not an input to any classifier. Each speaker produced a set of VCV tokens with a symmetric vowel context, in which the same vowel precedes and follows the consonant. The inventory crossed a set of English consonants spanning stops, nasals, fricatives, and approximants with the corner vowels /a/, /i/, and /u/. Each token was repeated several times in a carrier-free, isolated manner. Individual tokens were cut from the continuous recording using the acoustic signal. Each clip began shortly before the onset of the first vowel and ended shortly after the offset of the second vowel, and we manually checked the boundaries. Tokens with visible motion artifacts, incomplete articulations, or acquisition failures were discarded. Each remaining clip was labeled with its VCV identity, and by derivation with its consonant and with its vowel context. Preprocessing Frames were cropped to a fixed region of interest around the vocal tract, resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bilinear interpolation, and replicated across three channels so that ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks could be used directly (Deng et al., 2009). Intensities were normalized per speaker, by subtracting that speaker's mean and dividing by that speaker's standard deviation. This reduces inter-speaker differences in coil sensitivity and overall brightness. Because the number of frames varied across tokens with speaking rate, every clip was converted to a fixed length of T frames. Clips longer than T were uniformly subsampled, and shorter clips were padded by repeating the last frame. We treated T as a design parameter (see below). No horizontal flipping was applied, since the sagittal view has a fixed anatomical orientation. Training-time augmentation consisted of small random translations and rotations (±5°), small brightness and contrast jitter, and mild temporal jitter of the sampled frame indices, applied identically to all frames of a clip. Model architecture The main model was a Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN, Donahue et al., 2015). A convolutional network processes each frame independently and yields a fixed-length feature vector. The sequence of feature vectors is passed to a recurrent network, whose outputs are mapped to class probabilities. We used VGG-16 (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015) as the main visual feature extractor and took the activations of its penultimate fully connected layer. ResNet-style backbones (He et al., 2016) and a small CNN trained from scratch were used as alternatives. The temporal component was a long short-term memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), which we compared with a gated recurrent unit variant Cho et al., 2014). The final hidden state, or alternatively the mean of the outputs across time steps, was fed to a softmax layer. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) was applied before the recurrent and output layers. To place the LRCN results in context, we trained three reference models on the same splits: (i) a frame-wise CNN whose per-frame predictions were averaged over the clip, which ignores temporal order, (ii) a late-fusion CNN that concatenates features over time (Karpathy et al., 2014); and (iii) a 3D convolutional network that learns joint spatiotemporal filters (Tran et al., 2015). Comparing these tests whether explicit sequence modeling helps beyond what is captured by static vocal tract shape. Experimental design We defined three classification tasks. In the VCV identification task, the model predicted the full VCV label, so the consonant and the vowel context had to be inferred together. In the consonant classification task, clips from all vowel contexts were pooled and labeled only by the consonant, which required invariance to the surrounding vowel. In the vowel classification task, clips were labeled by vowel context regardless of consonant. For each task we varied several parameters, one at a time around a default configuration. The parameters were: (a) clip length T, from short clips of about 10 frames to longer clips of about 30 frames; (b) the number of LSTM units (64, 128, 256) and layers (1 or 2), (c) the CNN backbone; (d) initialization, either ImageNet-pretrained weights with the convolutional layers frozen, pretrained weights fine-tuned end to end, or random initialization; and (e) unidirectional versus bidirectional recurrence. We also ran a comparison with the label set restricted to consonants grouped by manner [13] of articulation, to examine whether errors concentrate within articulatory classes. Training and evaluation protocol To estimate generalization to unseen speakers, we used speaker-independent evaluation. The 17 speakers were partitioned into folds for cross-validation, so that all tokens from a speaker were in the test [38] set of exactly one fold. In each fold, a subset of the remaining speakers (about 10%) was held out as a validation set for early stopping and hyperparameter selection, and no test speaker data influenced model selection. For comparison we "also" ran a speaker-dependent condition in which tokens from every speaker were split across training and test sets by repetition, to quantify the gap caused by inter-speaker variability in vocal tract anatomy. Networks were trained by minimizing categorical cross-entropy with the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015). The initial learning

Phylogeography is the study of the processes that govern the geographic distribution of genealogical lineages (Avise et al., 1987). For rapidly evolving organisms such as RNA viruses, in which evolutionary and epidemiological timescales overlap, phylogeographic analysis allows researchers to reconstruct how pathogens emerge, disperse and diversify across space and time (Holmes, 2004; Grenfell et al., 2004). Bayesian phylogeographic frameworks that treat location as a discrete trait evolving along a phylogeny (Lemey et al., 2009) have been used to trace the origins and spread of influenza A viruses (Bedford et al., 2015), rabies virus (Biek et al., 2007), HIV-1 (Faria et al., 2014), Ebola virus (Dudas et al., 2017) and SARS-CoV-2 (Worobey et al., 2020), among others. These analyses inform infectious disease surveillance, the targeting of control measures, the selection of vaccine [9] strains and the assessment of zoonotic risk. Their reliability, however, depends critically on the quality of the geographic information associated with each sampled sequence. The principal source of viral sequences for (25) such studies is GenBank and the other members However, of the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (Sayers et al., 2022). Each GenBank record contains structured metadata, including fields such as /country, /isolationsource and /geolocname, that may describe where the infected host was sampled. In practice, these fields are of limited use for many phylogeographic applications. Submitters often omit them, provide only country-level information, or enter free-text values that vary widely in format and granularity (Scotch et al., 2011; Tahsin et al., 2016). Country-level resolution is frequently inadequate: modelling the transmission of a virus within a country, between [29] neighbouring provinces or between a city and its rural hinterland requires locations at the level of states, counties, cities or even individual farms. Moreover, a record's country may reflect the [3] location of the sequencing laboratory rather than the origin [9] of the host, and for viruses sampled from migratory animals or from travellers, the place of infection may differ from the place of sampling. Several studies have shown that the choice of location granularity and the accuracy of the assigned locations can substantially alter inferred migration networks and [38] root-location estimates (Scotch et al., 2011; Dudas et al., 2017). When the metadata are insufficient, researchers turn to the publications linked to GenBank records, which typically describe the sampling campaign in more detail in the abstract, methods or supplementary material. Retrieving this information requires locating the article, reading it, identifying the sentences that describe the sampling sites, and mapping the resulting [27] place names to records. For studies involving hundreds or thousands of sequences drawn from many articles, this manual curation is slow, error-prone and difficult to reproduce. Automating the extraction of geographic locations from text therefore offers a practical route to enriching viral sequence metadata and to making phylogeographic studies more precise and scalable. The computational task of [33] recognising place names in text is known as toponym recognition, and it is the first step in the broader problem of geographic information retrieval, which also includes toponym resolution, the grounding [32] of names to coordinates or gazetteer entries (Leidner and Lieberman, 2011; Gritta et al., 2018). Toponym recognition is conventionally treated [38] as a form of named entity recognition (NER) and addressed with sequence labelling models such as conditional random fields (CRFs; [3] Lafferty et al., 2001; Finkel et al., 2005) and, more recently, with neural architectures and pretrained language models (Lample et al., 2016; Devlin et al., 2019). Although general-purpose NER systems perform well on newswire, their performance degrades on biomedical text, where geographic names are intermingled with names of strains, genes, hosts and institutions that share surface forms with places (for instance, Victoria, "Hong Kong or Texas in strain names such as A/Hong Kong/1/68). Strain names in particular create a serious ambiguity: a place name embedded in an isolate identifier does not necessarily denote a sampling location of interest, yet it may be the only mention of that place in the article. Biomedical resources for location extraction are also scarce. Existing efforts have focused on annotating place names in the context of disease outbreaks, news reports or social media (Lieberman et al., 2010; Weissenbacher et al., 2015, 2019), and annotated corpora specific to virus-related articles are limited. Weissenbacher et al. (2015) demonstrated that supervised toponym recognition for the phylogeography of viruses is feasible but depends on annotated data and carefully designed features, and that performance remains well below that achieved on general text. The scarcity of annotated [39] data is the central obstacle. Manual annotation of geographic mentions requires domain expertise, is costly, and must be repeated whenever the target domain or entity type changes. Distant supervision offers an alternative: rather than relying on hand-labelled examples, training labels are generated automatically by aligning an existing knowledge base with unlabelled text (Mintz et al., 2009). In our setting, the geographic metadata already present in GenBank records, together with gazetteers such as GeoNames (Wick and Vatant, 2012), can in principle supply weak labels for place names in the linked articles. Such labels are inherently noisy, however. Metadata values may be incomplete, may not appear verbatim in the text, or may match unrelated strings, and gazetteer matching generates many false positives owing to ambiguity between place names and common words, personal names and abbreviations. Distant supervision has been applied successfully to relation extraction and biomedical NER (Mintz et al., 2009; Fries et al., 2017), but strategies for reducing label noise in the specific context of toponyms in virology articles have not been systematically explored. Thus, two gaps remain. First, there is no established method for extracting from the literature the fine-grained geographic locations required for virus phylogeography that is designed around the peculiarities of virus-related articles, such as strain nomenclature, sampling descriptions and host-related terminology. Second, it is unclear whether weak supervision derived from existing database records can approximate the accuracy of fully supervised models, thereby removing the annotation bottleneck. We therefore ask two questions: (i) to what extent can a supervised sequence labelling model with features tailored to virology articles detect geographic location mentions, and (ii) can a distant supervision approach with explicit noise-reduction strategies achieve comparable performance without manually labelled training data? To address these questions, we make the following contributions. First, we present a supervised CRF-based sequence labelling approach that incorporates innovative features capturing the lexical, syntactic and document-level context of place names in virus-related articles, including features that help to distinguish sampling locations from places embedded in strain names or other entities. Second, we introduce a distant supervision approach that derives training labels from GenBank metadata and gazetteer entries, and we propose novel noise-reduction methods that filter ambiguous and spurious matches before model training. Third, we evaluate both approaches against a manually annotated gold standard of articles linked to virus-related GenBank records, and we compare their performance with baseline systems. Our supervised approach attains an F-score of 0.81, and the distant supervision approach attains an F-score of 0.66 without using manual annotations for training. Finally, we analyse the sources of error and the contribution of individual features and noise-reduction steps, providing guidance for (19) building location-extraction tools for phylogeographic research and for other domains where annotated data are scarce. Data collection and corpus construction We built the corpus from GenBank nucleotide records (Benson et al., 2013) for viruses, retrieved through the NCBI Entrez Programming Utilities. Records were eligible if they (i) belonged to the taxonomic division Viruses, (ii) cited at least one published article through a PubMed identifier, and (iii) had an article available in full text in the PubMed Central Open Access subset. Full text was necessary because sampling locations are often reported in Methods sections and supplementary tables rather than in abstracts. For each eligible article we extracted the title, abstract, section headings, body text, and table captions from the JATS XML, and discarded reference lists and author affiliations. Affiliations were excluded because they name institutional rather than sampling locations. Text was split into sentences and tokenized with the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit (Manning et al., 2014). Tokens were tagged for part of speech and lemmatized with the same toolkit. From the eligible set we drew a random sample of 600 articles, stratified by virus family so that no family contributed more than 20% of the sample. This prevented highly sequenced groups such as influenza viruses and retroviruses from dominating the data. The sample was divided into a manually annotated gold-standard set (n = 150) and a development set (n = 50) used for feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. The remaining 400 articles formed the pool from which distant-supervision training data were generated. The three subsets contained no overlapping articles. Gold-standard annotation Annotators marked every mention of a geographic location that referred to the place of origin of an infected host or of a viral isolate. This included countries, administrative regions, cities, villages, and named natural features such as lakes when they described a sampling site. We did not annotate locations that appeared only as part of a laboratory or institution name, locations used as adjectives in strain nomenclature without a sampling interpretation (e.g., “Sydney-like”), or locations mentioned only in the context of prior literature. This follows the distinction between toponym recognition and the more general task of geoparsing (Leidner and Lieberman, 2011). Two trained annotators independently labeled the 150 articles using the BRAT annotation tool after a calibration round on 20 separate articles. Disagreements were resolved by consensus with a third annotator, a virologist. Inter-annotator agreement was computed on the span level as the pairwise F-score between annotators and on the token level as Cohen’s kappa (Cohen, 1960). We encoded the final annotations in the IOB2 scheme (Tjong Kim Sang and Veenstra, 1999). Supervised sequence labeling We treated detection of sampling locations as a sequence labeling problem and trained a linear-chain conditional random field (CRF; Lafferty et al., 2001), implemented in CRFsuite (Okazaki, 2007). Parameters were estimated by L-BFGS optimization with elastic-net regularization. The L1 and L2 coefficients were tuned on the development set over the grid {0, 0.01, 0.1, 1}. The baseline feature set was standard for named entity recognition (Finkel et al., 2005). It comprised the lowercase token, lemma, prefixes and suffixes of up to four characters, word shape, capitalization, part-of-speech tag, and the same attributes for tokens within a ±3 window. We added membership features derived from a gazetteer built from GeoNames, which was restricted to populated places, administrative divisions, and countries and [15] was augmented with common alternative names. Gazetteer matching used longest-match lookup, and we encoded the feature type (country, However, region, or city) and a binary flag indicating whether the match was also a common English word. We added four feature groups designed for the virological domain. First, document-structure features encoded the section type of the sentence (e.g., Methods, Results, Discussion) and whether it fell in a table caption, because sampling locations are concentrated in particular sections. [16] Second, sampling-context features flagged trigger words within a ten-token window (“isolated,” collected, sampled, “obtained from,” “patients from,” “outbreak in”), identified from the development set by a log-likelihood ratio comparison of tokens surrounding annotated and non-annotated gazetteer matches. Third, strain-name features indicated whether a candidate token appeared inside a strain designation following a virus nomenclature [14] pattern such as A/Hong Kong/1/68. A regular expression recognized these patterns, and locations inside them were treated as sampling locations. Fourth, document-level consistency features captured the number of times a candidate string occurred [39] in the article and whether the string appeared in the article’s GenBank record (the country or isolate-name field), which gave the model a document-specific prior. For the continuous-valued count we used logarithmic binning. Feature ablation was performed on the development set by removing each group in turn. Distant supervision To avoid the cost of manual annotation, we also generated training labels automatically, following [2] the distant-supervision paradigm (Mintz et al., 2009). For each article in the 400-article pool we collected the location strings in the metadata of its linked GenBank records (the country, geolocname, and isolate fields). We normalized

The dissemination of scientific knowledge has long depended on a small number of channels: the printed journal, the scientific meeting, and, more recently, the journal website and indexing databases. Over the past decade, social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have been added to this list, and many medical journals [23] now maintain [25] active accounts with large followings. The assumption underlying this investment is intuitive. (4) Posting a brief message and a link to a new article should expose the work to readers who might not otherwise encounter it, and greater exposure should translate into more page views, downloads, and ultimately citations. Editors, publishers, and professional societies have embraced this logic, and social media activity is now a standard element of the publication process for many journals, including those in cardiovascular medicine (Bonow & Fuster, 2013; Ladeiras-Lopes et al., 2020). The evidence supporting this assumption is largely observational. Several studies have reported that articles mentioned on Twitter or other social platforms accumulate more views, downloads, and citations than articles that are not mentioned (Eysenbach, 2011; Shuai et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2016). Such findings have fueled the development of alternative metrics, which aggregate online attention to research outputs and are increasingly displayed alongside traditional bibliometric indicators (Priem et al., 2010). Yet associations of this kind are highly susceptible to confounding. Articles that attract social media attention may differ systematically from those that do not: they may address topics of broad public interest, originate from well-known investigators or institutions with large online followings, or be more novel or clinically important. In addition, readers who encounter an article through social media may already be inclined to read it. Observational comparisons therefore cannot separate the causal effect of social media promotion from the characteristics of the articles and authors selected for promotion (Haustein et al., 2014). Randomization offers a direct way to address this limitation. A previous randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation allocated original research articles to social media exposure or to no exposure and compared 30-day page views between the groups (Fox et al., 2016). Social media exposure in that trial consisted of posts on the journal's Facebook and Twitter accounts. The investigators found no significant difference in page views [24] between the arms, a result that contrasted with the favorable associations seen in observational work. A trial in a different setting reported similar findings for the effect of social media promotion on article-level readership, which suggests that the null result was not unique to a single journal (Adams et al., 2019). Nonetheless, the Circulation trial left an important question unresolved. Because a single post from a journal account may reach [14] only a modest portion of potential readers, the lack of effect might have reflected an intervention that was too weak to produce a measurable change, rather than a true absence of benefit from social media exposure at any level of intensity. This distinction matters for both scientific and practical reasons. If a light-touch approach fails because the dose is inadequate, then journals could reasonably expect that a more concerted effort would succeed, and the resources devoted to expanding followings and repeating posts would be justified. If, in contrast, a more intensive strategy also fails to change readership, then the case for social media as a driver of article traffic becomes considerably weaker, and journals might need to reconsider the expectations they place on these platforms or the goals they (10) pursue through them. The importance of a dose-response perspective is well recognized in the evaluation of behavioral and communication [32] interventions, where a negative trial of a low-intensity program is generally not considered sufficient to rule out the value of a more substantial one (Craig et al., 2008). Social media campaigns in health are heterogeneous in reach, frequency, and engagement, and the effect of exposure is likely to depend on the size and engagement of the audience, the frequency with which content is delivered, and the extent to which the content is amplified by algorithmic or paid mechanisms (Chou et al., 2009; Moorhead et al., 2013). Several features of platform behavior make intensity a particularly plausible determinant of effect. On Twitter, the lifespan of an individual post is short, and a message may be seen by only a fraction of followers in the narrow window during which it is visible. On Facebook, organic reach to followers is limited, and paid promotion, or boosting, can substantially extend the audience of a post. Repeating messages at different times of day can increase the likelihood of being seen, and retweets by the journal account can extend visibility further. A larger follower base provides a larger potential audience for each of these actions. An intensified intervention that combines audience growth, repeated posting, and paid amplification would therefore represent a considerably stronger test of whether social media can alter readership of original research. We therefore conducted a second randomized controlled trial at Circulation to determine whether a more intensive social media strategy increases 30-day page views of original research articles. Building on the design of the earlier trial, we randomized accepted manuscripts to social media exposure or to no exposure (control). To increase intensity, we expanded the journal's follower base through advertising and organic growth, presented However, each exposed article in three separate posts, boosted (6) posts on Facebook, and retweeted posts on Twitter. We prespecified an interim analysis with stopping rules for futility, and we examined whether the effect of the intervention differed by manuscript type, geographic location of the corresponding author, timing of publication, and the presence of an accompanying editorial. This study makes three contributions. First, it provides randomized evidence on the effect of a substantially intensified social media intervention, thereby addressing the principal limitation of the earlier trial. Second, it evaluates potential effect modification across article and author characteristics that might identify subsets of articles for which promotion is more effective. Third, it offers practical guidance for journals deciding how to allocate effort and resources to social media, and it contributes to a broader understanding of the distinction between online attention and the actual readership of scientific work. Study Design and Setting This was a prospective, parallel-group, single-center randomized controlled trial conducted at Circulation, a weekly peer-reviewed cardiovascular journal of the American Heart Association. The trial was designed as a follow-up to an earlier randomized evaluation of social media exposure at the same journal, which found no increase in 30-day page views with a standard-intensity strategy (Fox et al., 2016). The unit of randomization was the individual original research manuscript. Randomization began with articles published in January 2015. Because the study involved no human participants and used only publicly available, aggregate journal web metrics, it was considered exempt from formal institutional review. The trial followed the CONSORT recommendations for reporting randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010). Eligibility and Randomization Eligible articles were original research manuscripts accepted for publication in Circulation and [22] scheduled for release in the weekly print and online issues. Other content types, such as editorials, letters, and case reports, were not randomized, although the presence of an accompanying editorial for (19) a randomized article was recorded. Manuscripts were allocated in a 1:1 ratio to social media exposure (intervention) or no social media exposure (control). Allocation was performed by a statistician not involved in the social media activity, using a "computer-generated" random sequence. Randomization was stratified by article type (e.g., basic science, clinical, population science) to promote balance across arms. Because the intervention was delivered by journal staff, blinding of those staff was not possible. Page view data were extracted objectively from the journal's web analytics, so outcome measurement was not subject to observer bias. Authors were not told of the (6) randomization assignments. Intervention Articles assigned to the intervention arm received social media exposure through the journal's official Facebook and Twitter accounts. To increase intensity relative to the earlier trial; we used several strategies. First, we expanded the follower base of both accounts before and during the trial through paid advertising campaigns and organic growth; such as regular posting of engaging content, cross-promotion across American Heart Association channels, and interaction with followers. Follower counts were recorded at the start and end of the study period to document growth. Second, each (6) intervention article was promoted in triplicate, meaning that three distinct posts were published on each platform at different times and on different days [38] after publication, with varied wording and images to reduce redundancy and capture different audiences across time [7] zones. Third, on Facebook, posts were boosted using paid promotion to extend reach beyond existing followers. Fourth, on Twitter, the journal's posts were retweeted from the journal account (22) at later times to extend visibility. Each post included a short descriptive message, a link to the article on the journal website, and, where applicable, a (19) graphical element such as the visual abstract or a key figure. Posts were designed by the journal's social media editors [9] using a standardized template to limit variation in content between articles. Control articles received no promotion from the journal's Facebook or Twitter accounts. Control articles were still subject to all other standard journal dissemination mechanisms, including the table of contents e-mail alerts, press releases for selected articles, and the journal's (20) website and (8) print edition. Authors, "readers," and outside organizations were not prevented from independently sharing any article on social media, and such activity was not controlled; (24) we assumed that it would be distributed evenly [4] across arms because of randomization. Outcomes The primary outcome was the number of page views of the article during the first 30 days after publication, defined as the sum of full-text HTML and abstract views recorded by (13) the journal's website analytics. Page (10) views were counted from the day of online publication. Secondary descriptive measures included the number of followers of each (15) account, the reach and engagement of social media posts, and page views at other time points when available. Baseline covariates recorded for each manuscript included article type, geographic location of the corresponding author (grouped [4] by region), the presence of an accompanying editorial, and the date of publication, categorized by trimester to [22] account for potential temporal trends in readership and follower growth. Sample Size and Stopping Rules The target enrollment was based on the number of original research articles expected to be published in Circulation across the calendar year, anticipating roughly 300 manuscripts. Given the (19) practical limit on the available sample, the study was designed to detect a moderate difference in 30-day page views between arms. We prespecified an interim analysis once 50% of the anticipated manuscripts had been randomized and had completed 30 days of follow-up. At this interim analysis, groups were to be compared on the primary outcome, and the trial would be stopped (2) for futility if there was no evidence of a treatment effect, defined by conditional power calculations under the observed trend (9) (Lachin, 2005). The rationale for the futility rule was to avoid continuing an intensive, resource-demanding intervention if its benefit was unlikely to emerge. Stopping for efficacy was not planned, because the focus was on whether increased [12] intensity would produce a benefit that the previous trial failed to demonstrate. Statistical Analysis All analyses followed "the" intention-to-treat principle; with articles analyzed according to their randomized assignment. Baseline characteristics were summarized by arm using counts and percentages for categorical variables and medians with interquartile ranges for continuous variables. Balance between arms on article type, corresponding author location, and editorial status was However, assessed using chi-square or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. Because page view counts are right-skewed, the primary outcome was summarized using medians and interquartile ranges; and arms were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. As a sensitivity analysis, (28) we log-transformed page views and compared arms with linear (7) regression, reporting the ratio of geometric means with 95% confidence intervals. We additionally (23) fit models adjusted for the stratification factor and baseline covariates

Empirical software engineering relies on observable artifacts such as source code, version histories, and defect reports to derive claims about how software is built and maintained. Such claims are rarely confined to the data from which they were drawn. A technique that performs well on a set of open-source projects is commonly presented as a general solution, and a result observed in one period is implicitly assumed to hold in the next. This assumption is seldom tested, even though software projects change continuously through new features, shifting teams, refactoring, and evolving development practices. The question this article asks is whether a researcher's conclusions will still hold a year from now for the same software projects. There are reasons to doubt that they will. Menzies and Shepperd (2012) argued that many findings in software analytics are unstable, and that "conclusion instability is a central obstacle to building a cumulative body of knowledge. Subsequent work has shown that conclusions often vary across data sets, learners, and experimental configurations (Menzies et al. 2013; Shepperd et al. 2014; Tantithamthavorn et al. 2016). Findings that appear robust on one collection of projects may weaken or reverse on another. Most of this work examines variation across space, that is, across projects, data sets, or methods. Far less attention has been paid to variation across time, even though software evolves and any practical use of a prediction model is necessarily temporal. Defect prediction is a particularly informative setting in which to study this problem. It has been an active research area for more than two decades, with the goal of identifying files, modules, or changes likely to contain defects so that limited quality-assurance effort can be directed effectively (Zimmermann et al. 2009; Hall et al. 2012). A large body of work proposes new learners, features, and transfer strategies, and reports improvements over prior approaches. Cross-project defect prediction CPDP), in which a model trained on one or more source projects predicts defects in a different target project, has received particular attention because it addresses the common situation where a project lacks sufficient historical data to train its own model (Turhan et al. 2009; Zimmermann et al. 2009, Nam et al. 2013). Comparative studies have identified approaches that appear to outperform others (Herbold et al. 2018; Hosseini et al. 2019), and such rankings are routinely taken as guidance for both researchers and practitioners. However, the way defect prediction models are usually evaluated can obscure temporal instability. Standard protocols, including k-fold cross-validation and random train/test splits, ignore the chronological order of the data. They allow models to be trained on instances from the future of the instances being predicted, a form of information leakage that no practitioner could replicate in deployment (Tan et al. 2015, Jimenez et al. 2019). In addition, defect labels are often derived with delay, since a defect may be discovered long after the code that introduced it. Evaluations that disregard this lag can overstate performance. Even when time is respected, evaluations typically report a single aggregate figure computed over a whole history. A single number hides how performance fluctuates between releases or periods, so a method that looks superior on average may be superior only in some intervals. Aggregation therefore masks exactly the temporal behavior on which a practitioner's decision to adopt a model depends. This gap matters for several reasons. First, a defect predictor is deployed on future releases, so the relevant evidence is its performance on data that postdate its training. Second, if the ranking of techniques changes from one release to the next, a study that selects the "best" approach from one evaluation window cannot support a claim that this approach will remain best. Third, the metrics used to quantify performance may themselves behave differently over time. Defect-prone ratios shift between [28] releases, and metrics such as F-Score are sensitive to class imbalance, whereas the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is more robust to it (Yao and Shepperd 2020, Chicco and Jurman 2020). Reporting only one [3] metric may thus provide an incomplete view of stability. In this article, we empirically investigate the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction models. We adopt However, a time-aware evaluation approach in which models are trained only on data available in [2] the past and are evaluated only on data from the future. Instead of one aggregate result, we examine performance as a function of the evaluation period, and we compare how conclusions drawn in one period compare with those drawn in subsequent periods. We measure performance with three complementary indicators: F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve AUC), and MCC. We then ask whether the relative performance of CPDP approaches, and the conclusions one would draw about them, remain consistent as the evaluation window moves forward in time. Our study is guided by the following research questions: RQ1: How does the performance of cross-project defect prediction models vary across time periods? We quantify the variability of F-Score, AUC, and MCC when the same models are evaluated on successive periods of the [34] same projects. RQ2: Are conclusions about the relative performance of defect prediction approaches stable over time? We examine whether the ranking of approaches, and the statistical significance of differences between them, persist across evaluation periods or change from one period to the next. RQ3: How sensitive is conclusion stability to the choice of performance metric? We compare the three metrics to determine whether instability is an artifact of a particular measure or a more general phenomenon. This work makes the following contributions. First, we present, to our knowledge, one of the first systematic investigations of time-based conclusion stability in cross-project defect prediction, shifting the focus from [8] stability across data sets to stability across time for the same projects. Second, we provide a time-aware evaluation procedure in which training uses only past data and testing uses only [10] future data, avoiding the leakage inherent in conventional cross-validation and allowing performance to be tracked period by period. Third, we show empirically that the performance of defect predictors, in terms of F-Score, AUC, and MCC, varies depending on the period evaluated, and that conclusions drawn in one period are frequently not reproduced in [16] another. Fourth, we show that the next release of a product, particularly one that differs substantially from its predecessor, can drastically alter prediction performance. Finally, we offer practical guidance: in the absence of evidence of conclusion stability, researchers should restrict claims about defect prediction performance to the contexts in which they were evaluated, [15] and should report results over multiple time periods rather than as a single aggregate. We also make our evaluation scripts and data available to support replication and extension. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on defect prediction, cross-project transfer, and conclusion stability. Section 3 describes the data, the prediction approaches, and our time-aware evaluation design. Section 4 presents results for each research question. Section 5 discusses implications and threats to validity, and Section 6 concludes. We examine the time-based conclusion stability of cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) through three research questions. RQ1: How much does the performance of CPDP models, measured by F-Score, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve AUC), and the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), vary across successive evaluation periods? RQ2: Do comparative conclusions, [24] such as "learner A outperforms learner B", remain consistent across periods? RQ3: Is the magnitude of change between consecutive releases associated with the change in predictive performance? Complex systems in nature, society, and technology are composed of many interacting units whose collective behavior cannot be understood from the units in isolation. Network science has provided the dominant language for describing such systems, with nodes representing units and links representing interactions among them However, [Newman 2003, Boccaletti et al. 2006]. For a long time, however, the standard formulation assumed a single type of interaction, so that a system could be represented by a single graph. This assumption is increasingly recognized as too restrictive. Individuals in a society interact through face-to-face contact, online social platforms, and professional ties, a transportation system comprises airline, rail, and road connections among the same set of cities, a cell relies on genetic, protein, and metabolic interactions among overlapping sets of molecular components. In each of these cases a common set of nodes participates in several distinct layers of connectivity, and its role may differ substantially from layer to layer. The multilayer or multiplex framework was developed to capture this structure [Kivelä et al. 2014; Boccaletti et al. 2014; De Domenico et al. 2013], and it has revealed phenomena with no counterpart in isolated networks, including abrupt, cascading failures in interdependent systems [Buldyrev et al. 2010], altered percolation and robustness properties [Gao et al. 2012], modified synchronization and controllability, and rich interplay between coupled spreading processes such as an epidemic and the diffusion of awareness about it [Granell et al. 2013, Wang et al. 2019]. Almost all of these advances presuppose that the multiplex topology is known. In practice, the connection structure of real systems is often only partially observable or entirely hidden, whereas time series of the nodal states are comparatively easy to record. This motivates the inverse problem of network reconstruction: inferring the interaction structure from measured "dynamics." For single-layer networks, a substantial literature now exists. Approaches include driving-response and perturbation schemes [Timme 2007], methods based on correlation and information-theoretic measures [Bullmore and Sporns 2009; Schreiber 2000], and compressive sensing, which exploits the sparsity of real networks to recover topology from short data records [Wang et al. 2011; Han et al. 2015; Shen et al. 2014]. Compressive sensing has been applied to evolutionary games, epidemic spreading, and oscillator networks, and variants have been developed for hidden nodes and for identifying network structure from binary-state dynamics Su et al. 2014; Shen et al. 2016]. Related statistical "strategies," including maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, have been proposed for diffusion and cascade networks [Gomez-Rodriguez et al. 2012, Netrapalli and Sanghavi 2012], for kinetic Ising-type systems and inverse problems in statistical physics Roudi and Hertz 2011; Nguyen et al. 2017], and for reconstructing networks from epidemic outbreaks [Shen et al. 2014; Hoffmann et al. 2019]. Such work has shown that, with appropriate dynamical models and sparsity-aware algorithms, accurate reconstruction can be achieved from limited data. Extending these ideas to multiplex networks is far from straightforward, and the problem remains largely open. The first difficulty is that the observed data are a superposition of effects from several layers. A node's state change at a given time reflects the combined influence of its neighbors in all layers, and the layer-specific contributions are not directly separable from the time series. A single-layer method applied to "such" data would "either" produce an aggregated network in which layer identity is lost, or yield spurious links through mixing of the layers. The second difficulty is dimensionality: the number of unknown parameters grows with the number of layers, so that the inference problem becomes harder precisely when each layer is only weakly constrained by the data. The third is that the layers can host dynamical processes of different kinds, with different transmission mechanisms and rates, so that a reconstruction framework must be able to attribute observed transitions to the appropriate process. Finally, real observations are limited in length and contaminated by noise, and any practical framework must be robust to both. Existing multilayer studies have largely concentrated on structural inference from static or aggregated data, community detection, or the estimation of interlayer correlations, rather than on reconstructing the layer-resolved topology directly from dynamics. The present work addresses this gap. The question we pose is the following: given only binary time series of the states of a set of shared nodes, subject to the coupled action of distinct dynamical processes propagating on different layers, can the full layer-resolved connectivity be recovered, and under what structural and dynamical conditions is the recovery accurate and robust? We focus on duplex networks, the simplest multiplex systems, which host two different types of spreading dynamics, as a prototypical setting that retains the essential However, difficulties described above while remaining analytically and numerically tractable. Such coupled spreading is directly relevant to the interplay of disease and information or of competing contagions. We develop a mean-field based maximum likelihood estimation framework for this purpose. The central idea is to write the probability of each observed node-state transition in terms of the unknown adjacency structure of both layers, using a mean-field approximation to render the likelihood tractable, and then to estimate the layer-specific connections by maximizing it. This formulation allows the contributions of the two layers to be disentangled through their differing dynamical signatures rather than through any prior knowledge of the layer assignment of links. Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the multiplex reconstruction problem for coupled spreading dynamics and provide a principled, likelihood-based solution that separates layer-specific structure from superposed binary observations. Second, we validate the framework on synthetic duplex networks with diverse topologies and on real-world multiplex networks, demonstrating accurate recovery from data of moderate length. Third, we carry out a systematic analysis of how reconstruction accuracy depends on structural parameters such as network size, mean degree, and interlayer correlation, on dynamical parameters such as spreading rates; and on the amount of data and the level of observational noise, thereby clarifying the regimes in which reconstruction is reliable. Together these results extend data-driven network inference from single-layer to multiplex systems and provide a foundation for uncovering the hidden architecture of complex systems with multiple interaction types. The large-scale collection of personal data by online services, healthcare providers, retailers, and social platforms has made it possible to release or share databases that describe individual behavior in fine detail. Such releases are routinely justified by the claim that identifiers have been removed or replaced by pseudonyms. A growing body of evidence "shows" that this form of anonymization offers weak protection. Sweeney (2002) showed that a small number of quasi-identifiers, such as ZIP code, birth [5] date, and sex, can single out most individuals in a population, which motivated [33] formal notions such as k-anonymity. Narayanan and Shmatikov 2008) later demonstrated that an anonymized [19] release of movie ratings could be linked to public profiles on a separate platform using only a handful of approximate observations per user. They subsequently applied the same principle to social-network graphs Narayanan & Shmatikov, [28] 2009). These studies show that privacy leakage is [23] [34] often not a property of a single dataset. It arises from the statistical dependence between the released data and auxiliary information available to an adversary. Differential privacy (Dwork, 2006, Dwork & Roth, 2014) provides guarantees that are robust to such side information, but it is not what is deployed in many practical data-sharing settings. A principled understanding of when de-anonymization is feasible therefore remains essential for assessing the risk of sharing data. Two broad lines of work address this question. The first is algorithmic and empirical: it designs heuristics that exploit similarity between records or neighborhoods in graphs and evaluates them on real data Narayanan & Shmatikov, 2008, 2009; Ji et al., 2016). The second is information-theoretic: it asks, under a probabilistic model for the data, how much correlation is necessary and sufficient to [36] align two databases. In graph settings, this approach has produced sharp thresholds for matching correlated Erdős–Rényi graphs (Pedarsani & Grossglauser, 2011; Cullina & Kiyavash, 2016; Korula & Lattanzi, 2014). For "databases" with feature vectors, Cullina, Mittal, and Kiyavash (2018) characterized the fundamental limits of alignment under a permutation model, and Dai et al. 2019) obtained analogous results for jointly Gaussian features. These results suggest that the mutual information between corresponding records is the natural quantity that governs matching, and that matching becomes possible once the number of attributes per record is large enough relative to the logarithm of the number of records. Existing analyses, however, typically rely on specific distributional assumptions, such as Gaussian features, Bernoulli or Erdős–Rényi structure, However, or independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) entries. These assumptions are convenient but often unrealistic. Real attributes such as time-stamped ratings, location traces, or sequential medical measurements are heterogeneous and temporally correlated, so models must permit richer dependence. This [30] paper addresses that gap. We study the matching of two high-dimensional databases in which each row corresponds to a user "and" each column corresponds to an attribute. One database is released with its rows permuted by an unknown permutation, and the other serves as the adversary's auxiliary information. The relation between corresponding entries is described by an arbitrary joint distribution, and the dependence across the [25] attributes of a given user is allowed to be non-i.i.d. Our central question [13] is: under what conditions on the joint distribution and on the relative sizes of the database dimensions can an adversary recover the unknown permutation with vanishing probability of error, and when is this provably impossible? Answering this question for general distributions, rather than for isolated families, would yield a unified criterion for the privacy risk of correlated releases. Our approach rests on concentration of measure (Ledoux, 2001; Boucheron et al., 2013). When the number of attributes grows, empirical statistics of a pair of rows concentrate sharply around their expectations. This is the mechanism behind the asymptotic equipartition property and the notion of typicality used in the proofs of channel coding theorems Cover & Thomas, 2006). We exploit it as follows. A pair of rows drawn from the same user is, with high probability, jointly typical with respect to the underlying distribution, whereas a pair of rows from different users is jointly typical only with exponentially small probability. This asymmetry suggests a matching scheme that declares a pair of rows to be a match when they are jointly typical, and then selects the permutation consistent with these declarations. A union bound over the competing permutations, combined with laws of large numbers for the relevant empirical averages, yields explicit conditions under which the scheme succeeds. This typicality-based strategy was introduced for pairs of correlated graphs by Shirani et al. (2019). Here we develop it for databases with general entry distributions. The contributions of this work are as follows. 1. A general matching scheme and achievability result. We propose a typicality-based matching scheme for databases whose entries follow an arbitrary joint distribution. We show that if the number of users grows at most exponentially in the number of attributes, with a growth rate strictly below a limiting information quantity of the source, then the scheme recovers the permutation with probability tending to one. For i.i.d. entries, this quantity is the mutual information between a pair of corresponding entries. 2. A matching converse. We prove that the achievability condition is tight. We identify a class of joint distributions for which, when the database growth rate exceeds the same information quantity, the probability of correct matching vanishes for any matching scheme. Together with the achievability result, this yields a sharp phase transition between the regimes where de-anonymization is feasible and infeasible. 3. Evaluation under specific models. We evaluate the conditions for i.i.d. databases, recovering known thresholds as special cases and thereby validating the general framework. We then treat Markovian database models, in which entries within a row are temporally correlated. The relevant threshold is an information rate expressed through the stationary distribution and transition kernel of the underlying chain. The analysis shows how memory in the data changes the number of attributes needed for reliable matching relative to an i.i.d. model with the same marginals. 4. A proof technique that extends beyond the cases treated. The analysis uses only typicality and laws of large numbers. It does not depend on closed-form likelihood computations or on specific parametric families, so it applies whenever the relevant empirical averages concentrate. We indicate how this opens the way to other dependence structures. The remainder of the paper is [35] organized as follows. Section 2 formalizes the database model and the notion of matching reliability. Section 3 presents the matching scheme and the achievability theorem. Section 4 proves the converse.
