Array-intensive programs are central to scientific simulation, signal and image processing, linear algebra, machine learning, and many other compute-heavy domains. Their control flow [30] is dominated by nested loops, and their data is held in multidimensional arrays accessed through index expressions that are often affine in the loop iterators and program parameters. This regularity makes them well suited to [19] parallel execution, both across the cores of a single machine and across the nodes of a cluster. It is therefore no surprise that [4] array-intensive programs have [26] been studied extensively in high-performance computing (HPC) and in compiler research (Feautrier, 1992, Kennedy & Allen, 2001). To reach good performance, such programs usually pass through a pipeline of transformations. Loop transformations, such as interchange, skewing, tiling, fusion, fission, unrolling, and peeling, restructure the iteration space to improve locality and expose parallelism (Wolf & Lam, 1991, Kelly [13] & Pugh, 1995). [3] Arithmetic transformations, such as algebraic simplification, common sub-expression [2] elimination, strength reduction, and the exploitation of associativity and commutativity, reduce the cost of the computation or reshape it for vectorization. Parallelizing transformations then map the restructured computation onto threads, vector However, units, accelerators, or distributed processes, typically through OpenMP, MPI, or CUDA. Polyhedral compilers have automated many of these steps (Bondhugula et al., 2008; Grosser et al., 2012), and domain-specific systems such as Halide and TVM separate algorithm from schedule so that optimization choices can be explored systematically (Ragan-Kelley et al., 2013, Chen et al., 2018). Despite this progress, automatic parallelizing compilers remain limited in practice. Dependence [9] analysis is conservative in the presence of irregular accesses, pointer aliasing, or non-affine subscripts. Profitable transformation sequences are hard to find with static cost models. Performance-critical code is often tuned for a particular architecture, memory [19] hierarchy, or interconnect. For these reasons, experienced programmers continue to apply hand-optimized transformations, often combined with compiler-generated ones, and then iteratively tune the result through profiling and experimentation. The final optimized program [7] may differ greatly in structure from the original sequential version: loop nests are reorganized, temporary arrays are introduced or eliminated, expressions are rewritten, and computation is distributed over many threads or processes. This flexibility comes at a cost. Manual or semi-automatic transformation is error-prone, and However, bugs introduced during optimization, such as an off-by-one error in a tiled loop bound, a violated dependence after fusion, an incorrect reduction rewrite, or a data race in a parallel region, are notoriously difficult to detect. Testing is rarely sufficient. The input space is huge, failures may appear only for particular problem sizes or thread interleavings, and floating-point nondeterminism makes output comparison unreliable. Even trusted compilers have been shown to contain defects in their optimization passes (Yang et al., 2011). It is therefore essential to establish that the optimized program is functionally equivalent to the original sequential specification, so that the pursuit of performance does not compromise correctness. [33] Two broad families of approaches address this need. The first is to verify the transformation engine, proving once and for all that a compiler pass preserves semantics, as in CompCert (Leroy, 2009). This is powerful but expensive, and it cannot cover transformations applied by hand or by external tools. The second is translation validation or equivalence checking, in which each (original, transformed) program pair is checked separately (Pnueli et al., 1998; Necula, 2000). This approach treats the transformation as a black box and is thus well suited to the mixed human–compiler workflows common in HPC. For general programs, equivalence is undecidable, and early techniques such as regression verification and relational program logics rely on strong structural similarity between the two programs (Godlin & Strichman, 2008; Benton, 2004). Array-intensive programs, however, have a restricted structure, namely static control flow, bounded loops, and affine index expressions. This enables more specialized and more complete methods. Over the past two decades, a body of work has emerged on functional verification of array-intensive programs. One line models programs as systems of affine recurrence equations and decides their equivalence using polyhedral techniques (Barthou et al., 2002). Another represents programs as array data dependence graphs (ADDGs) and checks equivalence through synchronized traversal and reasoning over the iteration domains and dependence mappings, handling loop and algebraic transformations Shashidhar et al., 2005; Karfa et al., 2013). Subsequent work extended these ideas to recurrences using widening (Verdoolaege et al., 2012), to code-motion transformations through value propagation (Banerjee et al., 2014), and to the verification of loop-parallelizing transformations and parallel program models (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2019, Siegel et al., 2015). Complementary work verifies concrete tiled or parallel code using symbolic execution, model checking, or deductive verification (Blom et al., 2017). Together, these efforts define a rich but fragmented landscape that spans compiler theory, polyhedral mathematics, program logics, and automated reasoning. For a newcomer, this literature is difficult to enter. The relevant papers appear across venues in electronic design automation, programming languages, formal verification, and HPC, and they use different program representations and assumptions, such as affine versus non-affine subscripts, sequential versus parallel targets, and static versus recurrent dependences. To our knowledge, no concise introduction organizes this material around the transformations a practitioner actually encounters and the verification techniques that address each. This paper addresses that gap. Our guiding question is: which techniques exist for verifying that an optimized array-intensive program, produced through loop, arithmetic, and parallelizing transformations, is functionally equivalent to its sequential original, and what are their scope and limitations? We make three contributions. First, we describe the class of programs and transformations of interest and explain why they challenge conventional verification. Second, we survey and relate the principal approaches, covering recurrence-based, ADDG-based, and translation-validation methods, as well as those for parallel programs, and we compare them by the transformations they handle, their assumptions, and their guarantees. Third, we identify open problems, including non-affine accesses, floating-point semantics, and scalability, to guide further research. We intend this as a quick but rigorous starting point for readers entering the field. This paper is a narrative survey. It is not a systematic review with exhaustive meta-analysis, and it reports no new experiments. The goal is to give a newcomer an ordered entry point into the literature on functional verification of array-intensive programs. The methodology therefore covers four things: how we scoped the field, how we found and selected the literature, how we organized the selected work into a classification framework, and how we compared techniques qualitatively. No statistical analysis was performed. The works surveyed report heterogeneous benchmarks, tool chains, and hardware, and these cannot be pooled meaningfully. Scope and problem definition. We define an array-intensive program as one whose computation is dominated by loop nests that read and write multi-dimensional arrays. Typically the array subscripts and loop bounds are affine functions of the enclosing iterators and symbolic parameters. This is the class studied under the polyhedral model (Feautrier, 1991, Bondhugula et al., 2008). It includes the dense numerical kernels, stencils, and signal- and image-processing pipelines common in high-performance computing and embedded systems. The verification problem is as follows. Given an original sequential program and a transformed program, decide whether the two compute the same input–output relation. We treat this as equivalence checking and exclude the verification of properties of a single program, such as assertions, absence of out-of-bounds accesses, or termination, except where [36] those properties support an equivalence argument. The transformations of interest fall into three groups: (i) loop transformations such as interchange, fusion, fission, skewing, tiling, unrolling, and bumping; (ii) arithmetic and data-flow transformations such as algebraic simplification, expression propagation, and operator reassociation or commutation, and (iii) parallelizing [29] transformations, including [21] [23] those that produce multithreaded, vectorized, or GPU code. We treat translation validation, where the verifier checks each compilation instance (Pnueli et al., 1998, Necula, 2000), and verification of hand-optimized code as two [5] settings of the same problem. In the second setting no compiler provides hints about which transformations were applied. Literature identification. We searched the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and DBLP, and used Google Scholar for forward and backward citation tracking. Queries combined terms for the object of verification ("array-intensive," affine programs, "data-dominated," "loop nest, "static control programs") with terms for the task (equivalence checking," translation validation, "regression verification," "program equivalence," "verification of loop transformations," "verification of parallelizing transformations"). We also added transformation-specific terms such as code motion," "tiling validation, and recurrence. We began from a small seed set of foundational papers on equivalence checking of data-dominated programs (Samsom et al., 1995; Shashidhar et al., 2005, Barthou et al., 2002) and followed citations in both directions until no new relevant work appeared. We also read the principal venues for compiler verification, program analysis, electronic design automation, and formal methods, including PLDI, POPL, CAV, TACAS, CC, DATE, DAC, and IEEE TCAD, for the period from the early 1990s to the present. Inclusion and exclusion criteria. A paper was included if it met all of the following conditions: (a) it addressed equivalence or refinement between two programs, or between a program and [3] a specification in program form, where arrays are first-class data; (b) it handled at least one of the three transformation groups above in a way that goes beyond scalar-only programs; and (c) it presented a technique with enough detail to assess its soundness conditions and its limits. We excluded work whose main contribution was a transformation or optimization framework without a correctness-checking component. We also excluded purely testing-based or fuzzing-based validation without a formal argument, bounded model checking limited to tiny fixed array sizes, and domain-specific hardware verification that does not operate on program-level array semantics. Several adjacent areas were handled selectively. These are data-race and deadlock detection for parallel programs, such as GPU kernel verification (Betts et al., 2012), and [21] general relational verification and product-program constructions (Benton, 2004, Barthe et al., 2011). We included these only where they clarify how equivalence of array programs differs from, or reuses, their ideas. When an extended journal version superseded a conference paper, we cite the journal version and mention the earlier paper only when it introduced a distinct idea. Classification framework. We read each selected paper against a fixed set of dimensions and then grouped the papers by the main modeling formalism. First, we recorded the program representation, such as array data [34] dependence graphs, finite state machines with datapath, systems of affine recurrence equations, or polyhedral and integer-set representations. Second, we recorded the equivalence-checking strategy. The strategies we distinguished are synchronized traversal of dependence graphs with slice-based comparison (Shashidhar et al., 2005, Karfa et al., 2013), cut-point or bisimulation-style correspondence between control states (Kundu et al., 2009; Churchill et al., 2019), and direct comparison of closed-form or recurrence-based input–output mappings (Barthou et al., 2002; Verdoolaege et al., 2012). Third, we recorded the decision machinery, such as Presburger arithmetic and integer-set libraries (Pugh, 1991, Verdoolaege, 2010), SMT solvers, and normalization of arithmetic expressions. Fourth, we recorded the transformation coverage across the three groups above, including whether recurrences and data-dependent control flow are supported. Fifth, we recorded the guarantees, namely soundness, completeness for stated program classes, and the way each method fails. Sixth, we recorded the assumptions about the input pair: whether the loops are statically controlled, whether single-assignment form is required, and whether the transformations must be known in advance. Comparative analysis. For each group we assessed qualitatively three properties: expressiveness, meaning the range of transformations and program features handled, scalability, meaning whether the method depends on loop bounds or array sizes or is parametric in them; and automation, meaning the degree of user guidance, annotations, or proof effort required. Where papers report empirical results, we extracted the benchmark families, typically PolyBench-style kernels and multimedia or signal-processing codes, together with the reported verification times and the instances on which a method failed or returned an inconclusive answer. We did not rerun tools or normalize these numbers across papers. We cite them only as indications of practicality. Throughout, we separate claims established by proof in the original papers from claims supported only by experiments.

Citations are the most widely used currency for evaluating scientific output. They underpin journal rankings, institutional assessments, funding decisions, and, in many countries, individual career progression (Garfield, 2006, Hicks et al., 2015). Despite the weight given to citation indicators, the distribution of citations is extremely skewed: a small proportion of articles accumulates most citations, while a large share receives few or none (Seglen, 1992; Price, 1976). This skewness is the reason why the mean-based journal impact [37] factor is a poor descriptor of the typical article and why its use for evaluating individual papers has been repeatedly criticized (Seglen, 1997, Larivière et al., 2016). At the lower end of the distribution lie uncited articles, which are [33] those that, within a defined observation window, have not been cited by any other indexed document. The study of non-citation has a long tradition in bibliometrics. Early estimates suggested that a considerable fraction of the scientific literature remained uncited for years (de Solla [14] Price, 1965; Garfield, 1973), and some provocative claims even [17] proposed that most papers were never cited (Hamilton, 1990, 1991). These claims were later shown to be exaggerated, because they failed to separate research articles from editorials, letters, news items, and other document types that are rarely cited, and [26] because they ignored [37] differences across fields and [17] the length of the citation window (Pendlebury, 1991, Garfield, 1998). Subsequent analyses based on more [1] careful designs showed that the proportion of uncited papers is strongly dependent on discipline, document type, publication year, and database coverage (Egghe et al., 2011; Wallace et al., 2009; Van Noorden, 2017). In general, uncitedness is lower in biomedical and life sciences, where reference lists are long and citation practices are intense, and higher in the humanities and in some social However, sciences, where books, local audiences, and slower citation dynamics prevail (Nederhof, 2006; Hyland and Jiang, 2018). Non-citation is not equivalent to lack of value. Articles may be read, used in teaching, incorporated into clinical or public policy practice, or discussed in the media without generating formal citations (Bornmann, 2014, Thelwall et al., 2013). Citations also reflect social and structural factors such as the visibility of the journal, language, author reputation, collaboration networks, international coauthorship, and the degree of indexing in major databases (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008, Tahamtan et al., 2016). Nonetheless, in evaluation systems that rely on citation counts, [9] an uncited article is invisible, and a journal with a high proportion of uncited articles may suffer reputational and financial consequences. Observing the percentage of non-citation therefore offers a complementary perspective to average-based metrics, as it describes the lower tail [9] of the distribution and signals how effectively a journal integrates its content [37] into the However, scholarly conversation. Public health is an interesting area for investigating this phenomenon. It is inherently multidisciplinary, [9] bringing together epidemiology, biostatistics, health policy and management, and the social [5] and human sciences (Almeida Filho, 2000, Nunes, 2005). In Brazil, [30] this field is called “saúde coletiva” and has its own intellectual identity, shaped by the sanitary reform movement and by a strong articulation with the national health system (Paim and Almeida Filho, 1998; Luz, 2009). The Brazilian public health community has built a large postgraduate network and a set of national journals that publish mostly in Portuguese, but also increasingly in English and Spanish. Many of these journals are open access, are indexed in regional repositories such as SciELO, and several are also indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science (Packer, 2009, Meneghini et al., 2008). Their dual mission—communicating with local practitioners and policymakers and reaching international readers—makes the citation profile of these periodicals particularly relevant. Citation patterns in Brazilian journals have been explored in some areas, mainly focusing on impact factors, language effects, and the international visibility of Latin American science (Rios-Gonzalez, 2014, Packer and Meneghini, 2006, Meneghini and Packer, 2007). Peripheral journals tend to be cited less than those from the core, because of language barriers, limited marketing, and the preference of authors and reviewers for international titles (Salager-Meyer, 2008; Alperin et al., 2011). However, these analyses generally rely on aggregated indicators, which hide within-journal heterogeneity. Less attention has been given to [19] the proportion of articles that never receive any citation, and to whether journals within a single national field differ in this respect. To our knowledge, no study has examined non-citation in public health journals, either nationally or internationally. Existing analyses of uncited papers in health sciences have focused on clinical specialties, nursing, or general medicine (Weale et al., 2004, Wallace et al., 2009), leaving a gap for a multidisciplinary field with strong local roots. This gap matters for several reasons. First, Brazilian science policy agencies, such as CAPES and [7] CNPq, use citation-based indicators and journal classification systems (Qualis) in the evaluation of graduate programs and researchers, so that differences among journals have practical consequences for authors’ strategies (Barata, 2016). Second, editors need descriptive evidence on how often their [32] articles go uncited and how fast this proportion declines in the years following publication, in order to assess editorial policies, internationalization efforts, and the effects of language choices. Third, from a theoretical perspective, comparing journals of a single national field enables an assessment of whether disciplinary orientation, for instance epidemiological versus social-science-oriented content, is associated with differential citation behavior, as suggested by studies of cognitive and structural determinants of citation (Didegah and Thelwall, 2013, Onodera and Yoshikane, 2015). In this study, we ask: What proportion of articles published in Brazilian public health [30] journals remains uncited, and how does this proportion differ among journals? Do journals form distinct groups in terms of non-citation? How does the percentage of non-citation evolve during the first three years after publication, and are there journals in which it declines consistently? We focus on eight journals indexed in Scopus and on articles published between 2008 and 2012, a period that allows an adequate citation window. The contributions of the study are threefold. First, we provide the first systematic description of non-citation in a national public health literature, establishing a benchmark for future comparisons. Second, by applying statistical tests for differences in proportions, we identify groups of journals with statistically distinguishable non-citation levels, moving beyond rankings based on raw percentages. Third, by analyzing temporal trends in non-citation within the initial years after publication, we offer insights into the dynamics of recognition of articles and discuss the possible role of multidisciplinarity and editorial orientation. These results can inform editors, evaluators, and researchers, and they point to the need for a more comprehensive model of citation determinants in applied, multidisciplinary fields. Study design and data source We conducted a retrospective, descriptive bibliometric study of the citation fate of articles published in Brazilian public health journals. Scopus (Elsevier) was chosen as the data source because it indexes a larger number of Latin American and Brazilian titles than the Web of Science and offers reliable article-level citation counts However, and export functions (Falagas et al., 2008; Mongeon & Paul-Hus, 2016). The unit of analysis was the individual article, and the unit of comparison was the journal. Selection of journals Journals were identified through the Scopus source list, using the subject area "Medicine" and the subcategory "Public Health, Environmental and Occupational Health," filtered by country of publication (Brazil). We included only journals that (a) were active and indexed in Scopus throughout 2008–2012; (b) published predominantly in the public health/collective health field, as declared in their aims and scope, and (c) published at least 100 citable documents over the study period, to avoid unstable percentages in very small samples. Eight journals met these criteria: Cadernos de Saúde Pública, Ciência & Saúde Coletiva, Revista de Saúde Pública, Revista Brasileira de Epidemiologia, Physis: Revista de Saúde Coletiva, Interface – Comunicação, Saúde, Educação, Saúde e Sociedade, and História, Ciência, Saúde – Manguinhos. The last four are considered more closely aligned with the social sciences and humanities, whereas the first four have a stronger biomedical and epidemiological orientation, this distinction was used only for interpretation and not for selecting articles. Selection of documents and period We retrieved all documents published between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2012. This five-year window allowed every article at least a minimum of several years of exposure to citation, and permitted the analysis of non-citation within a fixed three-year citation window after publication (see below). Only document types considered "citable items" were retained—original articles, review articles, and short communications/research notes. Editorials, letters, errata, book reviews, interviews, obituaries, and news items were excluded, since these types are generally cited rarely and inflate non-citation rates (Moed & van Leeuwen, 1995, Van Noorden, 2017). Document types were taken from the Scopus classification and, where it was ambiguous or inconsistent (a known problem in Scopus for journals in the humanities), checked manually against the journal's website and the article's full text. Duplicate records, identified by DOI, title, and volume/page, were removed. Data extraction Records were exported in CSV format in a single session, in order to freeze citation counts at a common date (we refer to this as the census date). Fields exported were: authors, title, source title, year, volume, issue, pages, DOI, document type, language, affiliations, and total number of citations received (Cited by"). Data were processed in a relational database. Year-by-year citation counts for each article were obtained through the Scopus "citation overview" function, which gives citations per calendar year, enabling reconstruction of the citation history in the first three years after publication. Self-citations were not removed, because the aim was to describe the actual citation visibility of the articles in the database, and because the proportion of self-citations among low-cited articles is generally small in absolute terms (Aksnes, 2003), we nevertheless acknowledge this limitation. Definition of variables The main outcome was non-citation, defined as an article with zero citations recorded in Scopus at the census date. For each journal j, the overall percentage of non-citation was calculated as Pj = Uj / Nj) × 100, where Uj is the number of uncited articles and Nj the total number of citable articles published by journal j between 2008 and 2012. To describe temporal patterns, we also computed the percentage of articles of publication year t that remained uncited within a fixed window of three years after publication (that is, up to the end of year t+3, counting the year of publication as year 0): P{j,t}^{(3)} = (U{j,t}^{(3)} / N{j,t}) × 100, with t = 2008, …, 2012. Using a fixed window rather than the total accumulated citations avoids the artefact that older articles have had more time to be cited (Glänzel & Schoepflin, 1995; Wang, 2013). Because the three-year window for the 2012 cohort extends beyond the census date for part of the sample, the census was set after the end of 2015, so that all cohorts had a complete window. Citations received in the year of publication were included because, in Scopus, early-view and in-press citations are commonly recorded in that year. Secondary descriptive variables were the number of articles per journal and year, language of publication (Portuguese, English, Spanish, or multiple), document type, and the mean and median number of citations per article, used to characterize the distribution of citations in each journal. Because citation distributions are highly skewed (Seglen, 1992, Price, 1976), medians and interquartile ranges were preferred to means for summarizing central tendency. Statistical analysis First, we described absolute and relative frequencies of articles and uncited articles by journal and by publication year. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals for proportions were computed using the Wilson score method, which performs better than the Wald interval for small samples and extreme proportions (Newcombe, 1998). Second, to test for differences in the overall percentage of non-citation among journals, we used a chi-square test of homogeneity of proportions across the eight journals. Universities are increasingly expected to act as engines of innovation and economic renewal, as well as centres of teaching and scholarship. The "entrepreneurial university thesis holds that the academy has undergone a second academic revolution in which the capitalisation of knowledge has become an institutional mission alongside research and teaching Etzkowitz, 2003; Etzkowitz et al., 2000). Related accounts of "academic capitalism" describe how declining public funding and rising competition have pushed institutions and individual scholars toward market-like behaviours in pursuit of resources (Slaughter & Leslie, 1997). Much of the resulting literature concerns the commercialisation of research through patenting, licensing and spin-off formation (Shane, 2004; Perkmann et al., 2013). Far less attention has been paid to a more basic question: to what [18] extent are academics themselves entrepreneurial in disposition, and does that disposition help them to produce more research? This question matters because research productivity is central to the careers of individual academics and to the competitiveness of universities and national systems. Productivity is associated with a range of individual and organisational factors, including gender, career stage, collaboration networks, institutional resources and workload (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005; Hesli & Lee, 2011). Dispositional and behavioural characteristics of the researcher have received comparatively little systematic attention. In the broader management literature, entrepreneurial orientation (EO) is a well-established construct for capturing the strategic posture of an actor through innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking (Miller, 1983; Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Meta-analytic evidence shows a positive association between EO and performance in firms (Rauch et al., 2009), and the construct has been extended to the individual level, where it describes a person's propensity to pursue opportunities, act ahead of events and tolerate uncertainty (Bolton & Lane, 2012). Whether it also explains variation in scholarly output among academics remains largely untested. There are reasons to expect both a positive relationship and a more equivocal one. On the one hand, academic research involves opportunity identification, resource mobilisation and the acceptance of uncertain returns, all of which are characteristic of entrepreneurial behaviour. Academics who proactively seek out funding, collaborators and publication outlets, and who accept the risk of rejection or failure, may accumulate more output over time. On the other hand, some schools of thought in the philosophy and sociology of science suggest that research is conducted within "paradigms," or circumscribed areas of study with shared assumptions, methods and problem sets (Kuhn, 1962). Within such boundaries, much "normal science" consists of incremental puzzle-solving, and journals and peer reviewers may reward conformity as much as novelty Azoulay et al., 2011). If so, the innovativeness dimension of EO may not be a reliable predictor of productivity, and some research may not be inherently innovative at all. Whether the dimensions of EO matter equally, or whether only some translate into output, is therefore an empirical question that existing theory does not settle. A second and related gap concerns the adoption of novel technological methods in the research process. Digital platforms have created new ways of financing and conducting inquiry. Crowdfunding allows researchers to solicit small contributions from large numbers of backers (Mollick, 2014; Belleflamme et al., 2014), while crowdsourced R&D and open innovation approaches allow problems to be distributed to external solvers (Lakhani et al., 2013, Afuah & Tucci, 2012). These approaches may be especially relevant where traditional funding is scarce. Yet little is known about how willing academics are to adopt them, or whether a technological propensity of this kind is associated with higher output. Treating such a propensity as a distinct but complementary construct However, to EO allows us to separate a general entrepreneurial posture from the specific readiness to use new tools for resourcing and conducting research. These issues are especially pertinent in developing-country contexts. South African universities operate under considerable resource constraints, including limited public funding relative to enrolment growth, heavy teaching loads and a need to redress historical inequities, However, while simultaneously facing strong performance incentives. The national research subsidy system rewards accredited publication output, and institutions in turn pressure staff to publish Cloete et al., 2015). In this environment, academics who can mobilise alternative resources and act proactively may have a distinct advantage. Conversely, if unconventional financing and research methods are underutilised, this may signal untapped opportunities for a sector that cannot rely on increases in conventional funding. Research from such settings is also valuable because the entrepreneurship [11] and higher education literatures have been dominated by evidence from advanced economies with very different funding and incentive structures. Against this background, this study addresses two research questions. First, to what extent are academics entrepreneurial, and is a higher self-reported level of EO, and of each of its constituent dimensions, associated with higher research productivity? Second, is a greater propensity to apply novel technological methods, such as crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D, associated with higher productivity, and how prevalent is the use of such methods? To answer these questions, we conducted a survey of academics at a large South African university using a comprehensive purposive sampling process, which yielded 292 usable responses. We estimated the relationships using ordinary least squares regression and assessed the robustness of the findings with bootstrapped standard errors and negative binomial regression, which is [24] appropriate for the count-based and over-dispersed nature of publication output (Cameron & Trivedi, 2013). The [12] [12] study makes three contributions. First, it extends entrepreneurship theory to a setting in which it has seldom been applied, demonstrating that EO, a construct developed to explain firm behaviour, can be meaningfully measured among individual scholars and linked to a core academic outcome. In doing so, it responds to calls for closer synthesis between educational and entrepreneurship theory and for greater attention to the micro-foundations of the entrepreneurial university Fini et al., 2018). Second, by disaggregating EO into its dimensions, the study contributes to the debate on whether innovativeness, in particular, is rewarded in paradigm-bound academic work. Our findings suggest that, although individuals with higher endowments of EO may be more productive, innovativeness is not significantly related to productivity, which complicates simple narratives that equate scholarly success with novelty. Third, the study provides [31] some of the first evidence on the technological propensity of academics to use crowdfunding and crowdsourced [22] R&D, indicating that these methods may be underutilised. For university leaders and policymakers in resource-constrained systems, this has practical implications for the design of research support, training and [26] incentive structures. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. [38] We first develop the theoretical background and hypotheses, then describe the data, measures and estimation strategy. We then present the results and robustness tests, and conclude by discussing the implications, limitations and directions for future research. Research design and sampling The study employed a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, appropriate for estimating associations between individual-level dispositions and self-reported performance outcomes in a defined population Creswell & Creswell, 2018). Data were collected from academic staff at a large, research-intensive public university in South Africa. This setting is analytically useful because it combines formal research-output incentives, through the national Department of Higher Education and Training DHET) subsidy system, with the resource constraints typical of developing-country higher education. A comprehensive purposive sampling procedure was applied. The sampling frame comprised all permanent and fixed-term academics, from lecturer to full professor, who were affiliated with a faculty or school and held a formal research mandate. Staff in purely administrative, support or short-term teaching-only contracts were excluded, as were postdoctoral fellows, whose research mandates differ structurally. Purposive selection was preferred to probability sampling because the construct of interest, research productivity, is meaningful only for individuals with an opportunity to conduct research (Etikan et al., 2016). Within this boundary, an effort was made to include every eligible academic across all faculties to maximise disciplinary variation. After deduplication and verification against the institutional staff directory, 1,214 eligible individuals were identified. Each was invited by personalised e-mail to complete an online questionnaire hosted on a secure survey platform. Two reminders were sent at ten-day intervals. A total of 317 questionnaires were returned. Twenty-five were excluded because of substantial missing data (more than 20% of items) or straight-lining, leaving 292 usable responses (an effective [27] response rate of 24.1%). This rate is comparable to those reported in other surveys of academic staff (Baruch & Holtom, 2008). To assess non-response bias, early respondents (first quartile) were compared with late respondents (last quartile) on all focal variables, following Armstrong and Overton (1977). No significant differences were found (all p > 0.10). The sample was also compared with institutional staff records for rank and faculty, and the distributions did not differ materially. A sensitivity analysis showed that a sample of 292 gave over 0.95 power to detect a medium effect f² = 0.15) in a regression with up to 15 predictors at α = 0.05 Cohen, 1988). It also exceeded the minimum of 50 + 8k observations suggested by Green 1991). Measures Dependent variable. Academic research productivity was measured as the number of DHET-accredited research output units that respondents reported for the preceding three calendar years. These units include articles in accredited journals, books, book chapters and peer-reviewed conference proceedings, and are fractionalised by authorship share. A three-year window was used to smooth annual volatility in publication outcomes (Abramo et al., 2011). Self-reports were verified, where respondents consented, against the institutional research-office repository for a random subsample of 40 respondents. The correlation between the two sources was high (r = 0.93). Entrepreneurial orientation. EO was measured using the nine-item scale of Covin and Slevin (1989), adapted from the firm level to the individual-academic level in line with Bolton and Lane (2012). The scale operationalises the three classical dimensions identified by Miller (1983): innovativeness, proactiveness and risk-taking. Respondents indicated agreement on a seven-point Likert scale. Example items were rewritten to reflect research behaviour, for example "I favour novel research questions over well-established lines of enquiry" (innovativeness) and "I typically initiate research collaborations rather than respond to others" proactiveness). Dimension scores were computed as item means, and an overall EO score was computed as the mean of all items (Lumpkin & Dess, 1996). Technological propensity. The propensity to apply novel technological methods was measured using a five-item scale developed for this study, informed by technology-readiness research (Parasuraman, 2000) and the literature on open and crowdsourced innovation (Howe, 2006; Mollick, 2014). Items captured the extent to which respondents had used, or would consider using, crowdfunding to finance research, crowdsourced R&D or citizen-science data [24] collection, online collaborative platforms, and open-data repositories. Responses were captured on a seven-point scale. Exploratory factor analysis (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation) of the items indicated a single factor (Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin = 0.81; Bartlett's test χ² significant at p < [5] 0.001), with an eigenvalue of 3.04 explaining 60.8% of the variance. Two items on crowdfunding and crowdsourced R&D specifically were also analysed separately because of their theoretical salience. Control variables. Controls were [8] selected for their established associations with research output (Fox, 1983; Bland et al., 2005). They comprised age (years), gender (female = 1), academic rank (ordinal, 1 to 5), possession of a doctorate (yes = 1), years in academia, average weekly teaching hours, receipt of external research funding in the review period yes = 1), and broad disciplinary cluster (natural sciences and engineering, health sciences, humanities and social sciences, and economic and management sciences), which was dummy-coded. Reliability, validity and common-method bias Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha Cronbach, 1951) and composite reliability. All scales exceeded the conventional threshold of 0.70 Nunnally, [4] 1978): overall EO α = 0.84, innovativeness α = 0.77, proactiveness α = 0.79, risk-taking α = 0.73 and technological propensity α = 0.86. Convergent validity was supported by average variance extracted values above 0.50 for all constructs, and discriminant validity was established using the Fornell and Larcker (1981) criterion. Because the independent and dependent variables were self-reported by a single source, common-method bias was evaluated following Podsakoff et al. (2003). Multi-view stereo (MVS) aims to recover dense three-dimensional geometry of a scene from a set of calibrated images. It underpins applications such as autonomous driving, augmented reality, cultural heritage preservation, and large-scale urban modeling. Despite decades of research, producing depth maps that are both accurate and complete remains difficult. Real scenes contain occlusions, illumination changes, non-Lambertian surfaces, and, above all, large low-textured regions in which photometric cues are ambiguous. Methods must also remain efficient enough to process high-resolution images and large image collections. Traditional MVS methods are commonly grouped by scene representation into voxel-based; point cloud-based, mesh-based, and depth map-based approaches (Seitz et al., 2006; Furukawa and Ponce, 2010). Depth map-based methods are the most flexible and scalable, since each reference image is processed independently and the resulting depth maps are fused into a final point cloud (Schönberger et al., 2016; Galliani et al., 2015). Within this family, PatchMatch stereo (Barnes et al., 2009; Bleyer et al., 2011) has become dominant. It initializes random depth and normal hypotheses at each pixel and iteratively propagates good hypotheses between neighbors, so a correct hypothesis can spread quickly across the image. Gipuma (Galliani et al., 2015) introduced a diffusion-like, red-black checkerboard propagation scheme that exploits GPU parallelism. COLMAP (Schönberger et al., 2016) jointly estimates depth, normals, and pixel-wise view selection within a probabilistic framework, and it remains a widely used baseline. Other PatchMatch-based methods have extended these ideas with planar priors (Xu and Tao, 2019), which improve completeness in weakly textured areas, and with better view selection and propagation strategies. Learning-based MVS has also advanced quickly. Methods such as MVSNet (Yao et al., 2018) and its successors (Yao et al., 2019; Gu et al., 2020; Yu and Gao, 2020) build plane-sweep cost volumes from deep features and regularize them with 3D convolutions. They achieve strong results on benchmarks, but memory and runtime grow rapidly with image resolution and depth range, and generalization to scenes unlike the training data is not guaranteed. Coarse-to-fine cascade designs reduce the cost, yet they still rely on supervised training and are limited by the resolutions they can afford. Traditional PatchMatch methods therefore remain attractive: they need no training, work at full resolution, and have modest memory requirements. Nevertheless, PatchMatch-based MVS faces two main challenges. The first concerns hypothesis propagation and view selection. In existing checkerboard schemes, each pixel receives candidate hypotheses from a fixed, small neighborhood pattern. These candidates are often spatially close and strongly correlated, and they may lie across depth discontinuities or in unreliable areas, so the sampled hypotheses do not reflect the local structure of the scene. Moreover, view selection is typically performed either with a single global criterion per image or with a per-pixel criterion computed from one hypothesis. A single hypothesis is a noisy basis for inferring which source views are useful, particularly early in optimization when most hypotheses are wrong. Poor view selection allows occluded or otherwise inconsistent views to contaminate the aggregated matching cost. The second challenge is low-textured regions. Photometric consistency measures such as normalized cross-correlation computed over fixed-size windows are almost uninformative there: many depth hypotheses give nearly identical costs, and the correct hypothesis is hard to distinguish. Enlarging the window blurs details and increases cost. Planar priors derived from sparse, reliable points and triangulation can help, but they depend on the quality of the sparse points and on the validity of the piecewise-planar assumption, and they may fail in curved or complex areas. A natural alternative is a multi-scale strategy. At coarser image scales, a fixed window covers a larger physical region, so low-textured areas contain more discriminative content and reliable estimates become easier to obtain. Yet simply upsampling a coarse depth map to initialize the next scale does not ensure that reliable estimates survive. At [17] finer scales, the [24] photometric cost in low-textured areas is again ambiguous and may overwrite correct coarse estimates with noisy ones. Conversely, coarse-scale estimates inevitably lose thin structures and boundary details, and upsampling (23) can introduce errors at edges. A principled way is needed to keep the reliable coarse estimates while still recovering the details that coarse scales miss. In this paper, we ask how a PatchMatch-based MVS framework can obtain reliable depth in low-textured areas without sacrificing fine details, while keeping the efficiency and training-free nature of the traditional pipeline. We answer However, by combining a stronger single-scale base method with geometric consistency guidance across scales. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We present a basic MVS However, method, ACMH, built on Adaptive Checkerboard sampling and Multi-Hypothesis joint view selection. The adaptive checkerboard sampling uses structured region information to choose, for each pixel, candidate hypotheses from a wider neighborhood that are more likely to be reliable, thereby improving propagation efficiency and robustness near discontinuities. The multi-hypothesis (18) joint view selection uses the whole set of candidate hypotheses to infer the view subset used for cost aggregation at each pixel, which yields a more [20] stable and informative selection than using one hypothesis. 2. We propose ACMM, which embeds ACMH in a multi-scale framework guided by geometric consistency. Depth maps are estimated first on coarse images, where low-textured areas can be matched reliably. Geometric consistency across views is then used to filter the estimates and to guide optimization at finer scales; so reliable coarse estimates are retained and can be propagated to the finest scale rather than being lost to ambiguous photometric costs. 3. We introduce a (23) novel detail restorer to correct erroneous estimates propagated from coarser scales. It (24) identifies regions where the upsampled estimates are inconsistent with finer-scale evidence and restores thin structures and boundaries through hypotheses generated at the finer scale, so that completeness gained in low-textured areas does not come at the expense of accuracy in details. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including ETH3D and Tanks and Temples, and show that our [30] method achieves state-of-the-art performance among traditional approaches and is competitive with learning-based methods, recovering depth in low-textured areas as well as [19] in fine details, with good computational efficiency. Overview and notation. Given a reference image Iref and its source images {Ij}, j = 1,…,N−1, with calibrated cameras, we estimate a depth map for every image in turn, treating each as the [13] reference. The poses and intrinsics come from a structure-from-motion pipeline (Schönberger and Frahm, 2016). Each pixel p carries a plane hypothesis θp = (np, dp), consisting of a unit normal and a depth. This follows the slanted-plane formulation of PatchMatch stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Barnes et al., 2009). Our pipeline has three components: a basic estimator (ACMH), a multi-scale geometric consistency scheme built on it (ACMM), and [3] a detail restorer applied between scales. Depth maps are filtered and fused into a point cloud at the end. Matching cost. A hypothesis θp defines a homography that maps a patch around p in Iref to each source image Ij. The photometric cost cj(p, θp) is 1 − NCC between the reference patch and the warped source patch. The NCC uses bilateral weights over spatial and intensity distance (Schönberger et al., 2016). We use an 11×11 patch sampled with a stride of two pixels to reduce computation, as in Xu and Tao (2019). Adaptive checkerboard sampling. The standard checkerboard scheme (Galliani et al., 2015) propagates from a fixed set of neighbours, so it covers only a local, fixed-shape region and cannot reach good hypotheses beyond it. We keep the red-black update order, which allows parallel GPU computation. For each pixel in the active color, we instead define eight sampling areas around it: four V-shaped areas near the pixel and four strip-shaped areas that extend farther along the axes and diagonals. Within each area we take a small set of same-color candidate pixels and keep the one with the lowest matching cost. This gives eight candidate hypotheses per pixel, which can come from distances well beyond the immediate neighbourhood. The strips let correct hypotheses cross small occlusions or weakly textured gaps, and the V-shaped areas preserve local structure. Multi-hypothesis joint view selection. Using all source images for every pixel includes occluded or badly overlapping views and corrupts the aggregated cost. Earlier methods select views from a single hypothesis (Zheng et al., 2014) or from a fixed neighbourhood. We instead use all eight candidates jointly. For each candidate i and source view j we compute a cost cij, which gives an 8×(N−1) cost matrix. With an iteration-dependent threshold τ(t) = τ₀·exp(−t²/α), view j is "good" for candidate i if cij < τ(t). The threshold starts loose and tightens as the iterations converge. A view is added to the pixel's aggregation subset if it is good for at (20) least n₁ candidates, which exploits the structured-region evidence. A view whose cost exceeds a hard upper bound for any candidate is rejected, which guards against occluders. Each selected view receives a weight wj from the number of candidates for which it is good, and the weights are carried over to later iterations as a prior (Zheng et al., 2014). The aggregated cost of candidate i is ci = Σj wj cij / Σj wj. We evaluate the eight candidates under the new view subset and keep the lowest-cost one for the pixel. Hypothesis refinement. Propagation alone cannot repair hypotheses that are wrong in either depth or normal. After propagation, we form a small set of combinations of the current depth and normal, a randomly drawn depth and normal, and a perturbed version of the current ones. We evaluate all combinations under the selected view subset and keep the cheapest. Hypotheses are randomly initialized at the coarsest scale. Each scale runs a fixed number of iterations (three in our experiments), alternating red and black passes. Multi-scale geometric consistency guidance (ACMM). Photometric costs are ambiguous in low-textured regions at fine scales, because a large patch there shows no distinctive structure. Coarser scales have a larger effective support, so reliable estimates are more likely to emerge there. We build an image pyramid (K scales, downsampling factor two, with camera intrinsics scaled accordingly) and run ACMH from the coarsest scale. The result at scale k is bilinearly upsampled to serve as initialization for scale k−1. For this we use the nearest-neighbour rule for normals and bilinear interpolation for depths, and we do not interpolate across large depth discontinuities. Initialization alone does not prevent the finer-scale photometric cost from overwriting good coarse estimates in textureless areas. We therefore add a geometric consistency term, in the spirit of Schönberger et al. (2016), that uses the upsampled depth maps of the source views. A pixel p in the reference image is projected into source view j using hypothesis θp, and the depth stored for that location in "the" upsampled source depth map is read out. The [27] resulting point is projected back into the reference. The geometric cost "is" the reprojection error cgeo,j = min(‖p − p′j‖, ψ), where p′j is the back-projected location and ψ [13] is a truncation value. The guided cost used at scale k is cj = cphoto,j + η·cgeo,j, where η balances the two terms. Because the source depth maps come from the coarser scale, reliable coarse estimates act (16) as a constraint on the "finer-scale" search. A hypothesis that is photometrically ambiguous but inconsistent with the coarse structure is penalized; and the coarse (18) estimates in low-textured areas survive at finer scales. At the coarsest scale no prior exists, so ACMH runs with photometric cost alone. Detail restorer. Coarse-scale guidance can also propagate errors into regions with thin structures (20) or sharp boundaries, where the coarse estimate is over-smoothed. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become the dominant technology for profiling transcriptomes, displacing microarrays for most applications because of its larger dynamic range, its ability to detect novel transcripts and splice variants, and its applicability to any organism with a reference genome Wang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2019). Among the many uses of RNA-seq, the most common is the identification of genes, and by extension molecular pathways, that are differentially expressed DE) between biological conditions. Such comparisons underpin studies of development, disease mechanisms, drug response and cell identity, and they often provide the first systematic view of the molecular programs distinguishing one cell population from another. A typical experiment generates tens of millions of short reads per sample, [4] from which one must derive a table of gene-level counts, assess data quality, model the counts statistically, and interpret lists of DE genes in terms of biological function. Each step involves choices that affect the final conclusions, and the However, tools for each However, step are developed by different groups with different conventions. "The" statistical analysis of RNA-seq counts presents several well-known challenges. Read counts are non-negative integers whose variance exceeds that expected under a However, Poisson model, even among biological replicates, so that overdispersed distributions such as the negative binomial NB) are generally used (Robinson and Smyth, 2007, Anders and Huber, 2010). Under the NB model, the variance of the count ygi for gene g in sample i with mean μgi is var(ygi) = μgi + [37] φg μgi², where φg is the NB dispersion, [9] representing the squared biological coefficient of variation. Because experiments typically contain only a handful of replicates per condition, gene-wise dispersions cannot be estimated reliably in isolation, and information must be shared across genes through empirical Bayes moderation (Robinson and Smyth, 2008; McCarthy et al., 2012). In addition, samples differ in sequencing depth and in RNA composition, requiring normalization methods such as the [27] trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) to avoid spurious DE calls [25] (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010). Finally, thousands of genes are tested simultaneously, so false discovery rate control is essential (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). The edgeR package Robinson et al., 2010) was among the first to implement NB models for RNA-seq and has since evolved considerably. Early versions relied on exact tests and likelihood ratio tests, the latter based on asymptotic chi-square approximations that do not account for "the" uncertainty in estimated dispersions. When replicate numbers are small, such approximations can be liberal and lead to inflated false discovery rates. The quasi-likelihood (QL) framework addresses this problem [1] by analogy with the [27] classical F-test of analysis of variance Lund et al., 2012; Lun et al., 2016). In edgeR's QL pipeline, a NB generalized linear model (GLM) is fitted to each gene (McCarthy et "al.," 2012), with log-linear mean structure log μgi = log Ni + xi^T βg, where Ni is the effective library size and xi is the row [17] of the design matrix for sample i. Gene-wise QL dispersions are then estimated from the residual deviances and moderated using empirical Bayes shrinkage toward a global trend (Phipson et al., 2016), and hypotheses are tested with F-tests that reflect uncertainty "in" both the dispersion and [19] the quasi-dispersion estimates. The resulting procedure gives more conservative and reliable error rate control than likelihood [32] ratio tests, and it retains the flexibility of GLMs for complex experimental designs including multiple factors, batch effects and paired samples. The pipeline can also incorporate testing relative to a fold-change threshold (McCarthy and Smyth, 2009) and gene set tests that use the same linear model framework (Wu et al., 2010; Wu and Smyth, 2012). Upstream of the statistical analysis lies the problem of converting raw reads into counts. Reads must be aligned to a reference genome and summarized over genes. The Rsubread package provides R-based implementations of the Subread and Subjunc aligners and the featureCounts read summarization program (Liao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2014, Liao and Shi, 2020), which are fast, accurate and memory-efficient. Their integration within R allows the whole path from FASTQ files to counts to be executed in a single environment, which promotes reproducibility and avoids the need to move between command-line tools and R. Alternative approaches, including splice-aware aligners such as STAR (Dobin et al., 2013) and HISAT2 (Kim et al., 2015) and alignment-free quantification with Salmon or kallisto Patro et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2016), are also widely used, and the downstream edgeR analysis is compatible with any of them. Despite the maturity of these methods, newcomers to RNA-seq analysis still face a considerable barrier. Package documentation typically describes individual functions rather than the logical sequence of an entire analysis, and published examples frequently begin from a precomputed count matrix, omitting alignment and quantification. Conversely, many pipelines automate analyses without exposing the reasoning behind each decision, such as why low-expressed genes should be filtered, how to interpret multidimensional scaling plots, how to select a design matrix, or how to relate gene-level results to pathway-level conclusions. Earlier Bioconductor workflows, including the edgeR-limma workflow (Law et al., 2016) and the DESeq2-based workflow However, of Love et al. (2015), have been valuable teaching resources, but the software has continued to develop. In particular, the QL pipeline, improvements in filtering (Chen et al., 2016), and updated annotation and gene set resources have changed best practice, and a workflow that unites the Rsubread alignment tools with the current edgeR QL methodology has been lacking. This article addresses that gap by presenting a complete, reproducible workflow, from reads to genes to pathways, for the analysis of a real RNA-seq experiment. The data profile three epithelial cell populations of the mouse mammary gland, namely basal cells, luminal progenitor cells and mature luminal cells, in biological replicates from virgin mice Sheridan et al., 2015, Fu et al., 2015). The mammary epithelium has a well-characterized hierarchy, which makes it a suitable test case because many expected marker genes can be used to assess the plausibility of results (Visvader and Stingl, 2014). The workflow makes several contributions. First, it demonstrates read alignment and gene-level quantification with Rsubread, linking these steps directly to the creation of edgeR data objects with associated gene annotation. Second, it illustrates data exploration and quality assessment, including filtering, normalization and unsupervised clustering. Third, it describes the construction of design and contrast matrices and the application of the QL pipeline to detect DE genes between all pairs of cell types, including testing against a minimum fold-change threshold. Fourth, it shows how to visualize results with mean-difference plots, heatmaps and Venn diagrams. Fifth, it extends gene-level findings to pathways through Gene Ontology and KEGG over-representation analysis, competitive gene set testing with camera, and rotation-based tests with fry (Wu and Smyth, 2012, Wu et al., 2010), as well as enrichment visualization with barcode plots. All steps are accompanied by executable code, so readers can reproduce the results and adapt the workflow to their own experiments. Data set and experimental design The analysis uses RNA-seq data from a study of epithelial cell populations in the mouse mammary gland (Sheridan et al., 2015, Fu et al., 2015). Three cell populations were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting from virgin female mice: basal stem-cell enriched cells (basal), luminal progenitor cells LP) and mature luminal cells ML). Each population was sorted from two independent biological replicates, giving twelve libraries in a 3 × 2 layout once the two further groups from pregnant mice or an additional condition are excluded; in the present workflow only the six virgin-mouse samples are analysed in detail, with each cell type represented by two biological replicates, and the replicates derived from different mice. Total RNA was extracted, libraries were prepared with a standard poly(A)-selection protocol, and 100 bp single-end reads were generated on [22] an Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform. Raw reads are available from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus and Sequence Read Archive, and FASTQ files were downloaded and used without trimming, since base-call quality was uniformly high. Read alignment and quantification Reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10, GRCm38) using the Rsubread package (Liao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2019) in Bioconductor Huber et al., 2015). A genome index was built with buildindex using the default memory setting, and reads were mapped with the align function, which implements the seed-and-vote algorithm. Default parameters were used, which allow uniquely mapped reads only and permit a small number of mismatches and indels. Alignment output was written as sorted, indexed BAM files, and mapping proportions were summarised with propmapped to verify that each library had a high proportion of uniquely mapped reads (>80%). Gene-level read counts were produced with featureCounts Liao et al., 2014), using the inbuilt Rsubread annotation for mm10 based on NCBI RefSeq. Reads were summarised at the gene level by counting reads overlapping any exon of a gene, and reads overlapping more than one gene were not counted. The result is a matrix of integer counts with genes in rows and libraries in columns, together with gene identifiers Entrez Gene IDs) and gene lengths. Gene symbols and descriptions were added using the org.Mm.eg.db annotation package. Where genes had duplicated symbols, the entry with the largest total count was retained. Data pre-processing and filtering Counts were stored in a DGEList object in edgeR (Robinson et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2016). Genes with very low expression provide little evidence of differential expression and interfere with the mean–variance modelling, so they were removed using filterByExpr Chen et al., 2016). The filter retains genes with counts-per-million (CPM) above a threshold, corresponding to roughly 10 reads in the smallest library, in at least as many samples as the size of the smallest experimental group. After filtering, library sizes were recomputed. Normalization for composition bias was applied using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method (Robinson and Oshlack, 2010). For sample j relative to a reference sample r, the log-ratio Mgj = log2[(ygj/Nj)/(ygr/Nr)] is computed for each gene g, where y is the count and N the library size. After trimming genes with extreme M-values and extreme average abundance, a weighted mean of the remaining M-values yields a log2 scaling factor, which is converted to a normalization factor fj such that the effective library size is Nj fj. Data exploration Log2-CPM values were computed with a small prior count to avoid undefined values for zero counts, using the cpm function with prior.count = 2. Library-size distributions and the distributions of log-CPM per sample were examined as boxplots before and after normalization. Sample relationships were examined by multidimensional scaling (MDS) with plotMDS, where the distance between samples is the root-mean-square of the largest 500 log2-fold changes between those samples (leading However, log-fold-change). Plots were coloured by cell type and by replicate to identify the main sources of variation and any batch effects. Hierarchical clustering of the most variable genes was used [1] as a complementary check. Design matrix Differential expression was assessed within a generalized linear model (GLM) framework (McCarthy et al., 2012). For the cell-type comparison, a means-model design matrix without an intercept was used, in which each coefficient represents the log-expression of one cell type. Where samples were paired or batch effects were evident, additive terms for the batch were included. Learning useful representations from unlabeled data is a central problem in machine learning. Supervised deep networks have produced striking advances in vision, speech, and language, but they depend on large annotated datasets that are expensive to collect and that tie the learned features to a particular label set. Self-supervised learning aims to reduce this dependence by constructing a learning signal from the structure of the data itself. A model trained this way can then be evaluated by how well its features support downstream tasks, either with a simple linear classifier or with limited fine-tuning data. The promise is that representations learned from abundant raw data will transfer broadly and require little labeled supervision. Much of the recent progress has come from designing pretext tasks that force a network to capture semantic structure in order to solve them. Examples include predicting the relative position of image patches (Doersch et al., 2015), solving jigsaw puzzles (Noroozi & Favaro, 2016), colorizing grayscale images (Zhang et al., 2016), and predicting image rotations Gidaris et al., 2018). In language, predicting masked or neighboring words has been similarly effective (Mikolov et al., 2013; Devlin et al., 2019). Such tasks can work well, but they rely on hand-designed heuristics that may limit the generality of the learned features, and it is often unclear why a given task yields representations that are useful for object recognition. A complementary line of work grounds representation learning in an explicit information-theoretic objective. The InfoMax principle (Linsker, 1988) holds that a good encoder should preserve as much information as possible about its input. Modern variants estimate and maximize mutual information using neural lower bounds Belghazi et al., 2018; Nowozin et al., 2016; Oord et al., 2018), which makes the principle practical for high-dimensional data. Maximizing the information that features retain about the entire input is problematic, however. Mutual information is invariant to invertible transformations, so a representation can score highly while encoding low-level detail such as pixel-level noise, and it need not expose the high-level structure that matters for downstream tasks (Tschannen et al., 2019). More useful is to ask which information should be shared. Work on multiview learning, from canonical correlation analysis (Hotelling, 1936) to co-training Blum & Mitchell, 1998) and contrastive multiview coding, builds on the observation that information present in several views of the same underlying context is more likely to reflect stable, semantically meaningful factors than information present in only one view. Nuisance variation specific to a single view, such as sensor noise or a particular crop or color shift, is unlikely to be predictable from another view, whereas the identity of an object or the occurrence of an event will be. Recent methods can be seen as instances of this idea. Deep InfoMax (Hjelm et al., 2019) maximizes mutual information between a global summary of an image and local features of that same image. Contrastive Predictive Coding CPC) (Oord et al., 2018; Hénaff et al., 2019) predicts features of spatially or temporally distant regions from a context, using a noise-contrastive objective. Other approaches use different sensory modalities Tian et al., 2019) or exploit instance-level discrimination (Wu et al., 2018, Ye et al., 2019). Despite this progress, a considerable gap remains between self-supervised and supervised features on large-scale benchmarks such as ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), where linear evaluation of the best prior self-supervised encoders lagged well behind supervised ones. It is also unclear which design choices matter: which views to construct, at what scales to compare features, how to parametrize the encoder, and how to scale the contrastive objective. Existing methods typically predict within a single scale of the feature hierarchy, compare features from a single view pairing, or use encoder architectures that were not designed with mutual-information maximization in mind. In this paper we study self-supervised learning as the maximization of mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context. A context might be a local spatio-temporal region of [13] the world, from which views are obtained by observing it from different positions or through different modalities, such as vision, touch, and audition. Alternatively, a single natural image can serve as the context, with views produced by repeated stochastic data augmentation. Our central hypothesis is that, to predict features of one view from another, an encoder must capture information about high-level factors, such as object presence or the occurrence of events, whose influence spans views, while discarding view-specific nuisance. This formulation unifies and generalizes several earlier approaches, and it suggests a concrete way to improve them: enrich the set of views and the scales at which they are compared, and give the encoder an architecture suited to the task. We instantiate this approach in a model we call Augmented Multiscale Deep InfoMax AMDIM). AMDIM extends local Deep InfoMax in three ways. First, it maximizes mutual information between features drawn from independently augmented copies of each image, rather than between a global summary and local features of the same, identical input. Second, it predicts across multiple scales simultaneously, maximizing information between a global feature vector and spatial feature maps at several layers, as well as between intermediate feature maps, so that the objective ties together features of differing receptive field sizes. Third, it uses an encoder architecture adapted to this objective, with carefully controlled receptive fields to avoid trivial solutions. We optimize a contrastive lower bound on mutual information and, following recent practice, use large numbers of negative samples, which we make tractable through efficient computation. We further extend the model to produce mixture-based representations, in which several latent assignments compete to explain local features. Our contributions are as follows. (1) We propose a general framework for self-supervised representation learning based on maximizing mutual information across views of a shared context, and show how data augmentation, multiple scales, and multiple modalities fit within it. (2) We develop AMDIM, whose representations achieve 68.1% accuracy on ImageNet under standard linear evaluation, exceeding prior self-supervised results by more than 12% and concurrent results by 7%, and we show strong results on other benchmarks. (3) We analyze the contributions of the model's components through ablations. (4) We show that the mixture-based extension yields segmentation-like behavior as a natural side-effect of the objective.
