Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is among the most pressing threats to global public health, food security and economic development. By compromising the effectiveness of drugs used to treat infections in people, animals and plants, it undermines modern medicine, including surgery, chemotherapy, organ transplantation and neonatal care (World Health Organization [WHO], 2015). The most comprehensive estimate to date, from the Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance project, attributed about 1.27 million deaths directly to bacterial AMR in 2019. A further 3.68 million deaths were associated with it, making AMR a leading cause of death worldwide, ahead of HIV/AIDS and malaria (Murray et al., 2022). The burden was unevenly distributed. Age-standardised mortality attributable to resistance was highest in western sub-Saharan Africa, at approximately 27 deaths per 100,000 population (Murray et al., 2022). Earlier projections warned that, without effective intervention, drug-resistant infections could cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050 and cumulative economic losses of up to US$100 trillion (O'Neill, 2016). Although these projections are uncertain, particularly for regions with sparse data, they underline the urgency of the problem for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The drivers of AMR in sub-Saharan Africa are multiple and interlinked. Poverty, weak health systems, limited diagnostic capacity, inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, and poor infection prevention and control all promote the emergence and spread of resistant organisms Ndihokubwayo et al., 2013, Essack et al., 2017). Antibiotics are often dispensed without prescription, sold in informal markets, or used empirically in the absence of microbiological confirmation, which encourages inappropriate use and the circulation of substandard or falsified products (Okeke et al., 2005; Ayukekbong et al., 2017). The pressure is not confined to human medicine. Global demand for animal protein has intensified antimicrobial use in livestock production for therapy, prophylaxis and growth promotion, and consumption in food animals is projected to rise substantially in LMICs (Van Boeckel et al., 2015, 2019). Resistant bacteria and resistance genes can pass between humans, animals and the environment through food chains, direct contact, wastewater, manure and contaminated water sources Robinson et al., 2016). Hospital effluents, municipal sewage and agricultural runoff may act as reservoirs and mixing vessels for resistance determinants, especially where waste management is inadequate. Because resistance emerges and circulates across these interfaces, an assessment confined to clinical isolates gives only a partial view of its epidemiology. This recognition underpins the One Health approach, which integrates human, animal and environmental health in the design and implementation of policies, programmes and research (Robinson et al., 2016). The Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015 identified One Health surveillance and the strengthening of the evidence base as strategic objectives, and called on Member States to develop multisectoral national action plans (WHO, 2015). The WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) has since sought to standardise the collection, analysis and sharing of data. Participation and data completeness remain markedly lower in Africa than in other regions (WHO, 2022). Many countries lack the laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, quality assurance and information systems needed for routine surveillance Leopold et al., 2014, Ndihokubwayo et al., 2013). A systematic review of antibiotic resistance in sub-Saharan Africa concluded that the available data were fragmented, geographically uneven and heterogeneous in methods, which limits their usefulness for policy (Tadesse et al., 2017). Cameroon illustrates these challenges. It is a Central African country of roughly 27 million inhabitants, divided into ten administrative regions, with a bilingual English and French) scientific and administrative landscape. It carries a high burden of infectious disease, including diarrhoeal illness, respiratory infections, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS and malaria, and these conditions drive heavy reliance on antibiotics. Livestock production, including poultry, pig and However, cattle farming, is expanding to meet urban demand, and in many settings veterinary oversight of antimicrobial use is limited. Antibiotics are widely available from informal vendors, and surface water contamination and inadequate sanitation are common in urban and peri-urban areas. These conditions favour the selection and dissemination of resistant bacteria across sectors. Cameroon has made commitments to the global agenda, including the development of a national action plan against AMR within a multisectoral framework. Implementing it requires a reliable baseline of the prevalence and patterns of resistance among clinically and epidemiologically important pathogens, and no national laboratory-based surveillance system currently provides one. Although numerous studies of AMR have been undertaken in Cameroon, they are scattered across journals, institutional reports and theses. They are published in English or French, and they differ in setting, population, sampling strategy, laboratory methods, breakpoints and reporting conventions. Most [14] are single-centre, hospital-based investigations of a limited number of pathogens, which makes them difficult to compare or aggregate. Studies of animal and environmental reservoirs are comparatively few However, and are rarely interpreted alongside human data. As a result, policymakers, clinicians and programme managers [11] lack a consolidated, quantitative picture of the resistance burden, of which pathogen–antibiotic combinations are most affected, and of where the principal evidence gaps lie. Previous reviews of However, AMR in Africa have mostly addressed the continent or sub-region as a whole, or have focused on a single sector, syndrome [16] or organism, and have not provided a country-level synthesis across the human, animal and environmental domains Tadesse et al., 2017; Essack et al., 2017). Such a synthesis is necessary to inform empirical treatment guidelines, to prioritise targets for stewardship and infection control, and to design a surveillance system fit for the national context. We therefore conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the published However, and grey literature on AMR in Cameroon through a One Health lens. The central question was: what is the current prevalence of resistance, [7] and of multidrug resistance MDR), among bacterial pathogens isolated from humans, animals and the environment in Cameroon, and how are the evidence and its limitations distributed across regions, sectors, organisms and antibiotics? Specifically, we aimed to (i) characterise the geographic and sectoral distribution of available studies; (ii) identify the bacterial species and antibiotics most commonly investigated; iii) estimate pooled prevalence of resistance for pathogen–antibiotic pairs and of MDR using random-effects models; and (iv) identify methodological and reporting gaps that constrain the use of existing data for surveillance and clinical decision-making. This study makes three main contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first integrated quantitative synthesis of AMR in Cameroon spanning human, animal and environmental sources, and so offers a baseline against which future surveillance data can be compared. Second, by pooling [16] estimates for specific pathogen–antibiotic pairs, it provides evidence that can support the revision of empirical treatment guidelines and the prioritisation of antibiotics and organisms for national monitoring. Third, by documenting heterogeneity in diagnostic methods, breakpoints and reporting, it identifies concrete priorities for standardisation and data sharing, which are prerequisites for effective, coordinated and sustainable laboratory-based AMR surveillance in Cameroon and comparable settings. Study design and reporting standards We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of published and unpublished studies reporting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacteria isolated from humans, animals [19] and the environment in Cameroon. The review was designed and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al., 2021). A One Health framework was applied throughout, in line with the tripartite definition of the interconnected health of people, animals and ecosystems (World Health Organization [WHO], Food and Agriculture Organization [FAO] and World Organisation for Animal Health [OIE], 2019). Studies were therefore classified a priori into three compartments: human (clinical and community samples), animal (livestock, poultry, aquaculture and companion animals, including animal-derived foods) and environment water, soil, hospital surfaces and effluents). The protocol was prepared before the searches began and followed the structure recommended for reviews of prevalence data Munn et al., 2015). Search strategy PubMed, Google Scholar and African Journals Online (AJOL) were searched for articles published in English or French. The search combined Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms in three concept blocks using Boolean operators: (i) resistance antimicrobial resistance, antibiotic resistance", drug resistance, microbial", multidrug resistance, "susceptibility", ESBL); (ii) setting "Cameroon", "Cameroun", and the names of the ten administrative regions); and (iii) host or source ("human", patient, "animal", livestock, poultry, "environment", water, "hospital"). French equivalents were used for searches targeting French-language records. Because Google Scholar returns results ranked by relevance and in very large numbers, only the first 200 records of each search string were screened (Haddaway et al., 2015). Reference lists of included articles and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify additional records. Grey literature, including theses, dissertations, conference abstracts and institutional reports, was identified through web searches and by directly contacting corresponding authors and national laboratories, who were asked to share unpublished or free-text data. The last search was run in the final week of the search period, and all records were exported to a reference manager for removal of duplicates. Eligibility criteria Studies were eligible if they i) were conducted in Cameroon; (ii) reported original phenotypic or genotypic data on antimicrobial susceptibility of bacterial isolates recovered from humans, animals or the environment, (iii) specified the bacterial species and the antibiotics tested; (iv) reported the number of isolates tested and the number resistant (or percentages from which these could be derived); and v) used a recognised susceptibility testing method, namely disk diffusion, broth microdilution, agar dilution, gradient diffusion, or automated systems, interpreted according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute CLSI) or the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST) breakpoints, or equivalent guidance such as the Comité de l'Antibiogramme de la Société Française de Microbiologie (CA-SFM). Studies were excluded if they were reviews, editorials, case reports with fewer than ten isolates, in vitro evaluations of plant extracts or novel compounds, studies on mycobacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites, studies in which data from Cameroon could not be disaggregated from those of other countries, or studies in which the denominator of tested isolates was not identifiable. When the same dataset was published more than once, the most complete report was retained. Study selection Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria, and potentially relevant articles were retrieved in full text. Two reviewers independently assessed the full texts, and disagreements were resolved by discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The selection process was documented in a PRISMA flow diagram showing the numbers of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was piloted on five articles and then applied to all included studies. The following variables were extracted: first author, year [3] of publication, year(s) of sampling, region of Cameroon, setting (hospital, community, farm, market, water body), One Health compartment, sample type, population characteristics, sample size, bacterial species, number of isolates tested, antibiotics tested with the number of resistant isolates, susceptibility testing method and interpretive standard, and the reported resistance mechanisms (for example extended-spectrum β-lactamase [ESBL] or methicillin resistance). Antibiotics were grouped by class following the WHO Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification and the WHO AWaRe categories (WHO, 2021). Intermediate results were classified as non-susceptible and pooled with resistant isolates only where the original authors did not report the categories separately. Data were extracted independently by two reviewers and cross-checked, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Authors were contacted to clarify missing or ambiguous information. Definition of outcomes The primary outcome was the proportion of isolates resistant to a given antibiotic for each pathogen–antibiotic pair. The secondary outcome was the prevalence of multidrug resistance (MDR), defined as acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more antimicrobial classes (Magiorakos et al., 2012). Where studies did not report MDR directly but provided isolate-level resistance profiles, MDR was derived using this definition. Studies in which MDR was defined differently by the authors were retained only if the definition was compatible with the above criterion. Intrinsic resistance was excluded from the numerator and denominator where it could be identified. The Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta is among the most densely populated and most dynamic landscapes on Earth. Its fertile alluvial soils, abundant freshwater, and productive coastal waters have enabled Bangladesh to sustain more than 165 million people on roughly 148,000 km², a density exceeding 1,100 persons per square kilometre (Nicholls et al., 2018). The same geography exposes the population to recurrent natural hazards. Monsoon floods inundate between one fifth and two thirds of the country in a given year (Brammer, 2004). Riverbank erosion permanently removes land and homesteads along the large braided rivers (Mutton & Haque, 2004). Drought affects the north-western regions during the dry season, and tropical cyclones and storm surges repeatedly strike the southern coast. The human cost of these events has been enormous: the 1970 Bhola cyclone killed an estimated 300,000 people and the 1991 cyclone about 138,000, while Cyclone Sidr in 2007 killed roughly 3,400 (Paul, 2009; Alam & Collins, 2010). Cumulative effects of sea-level rise, salinity intrusion, changing precipitation patterns, and more intense cyclones are expected to amplify these pressures (Dasgupta et al., 2014, IPCC, 2022). Bangladesh therefore regularly appears among the countries most vulnerable to climate change (Eckstein et al., 2021). Bangladesh is also widely recognised for reducing disaster mortality. Investments in early warning systems, cyclone shelters, embankments, and community-based preparedness have sharply lowered death tolls from cyclones and floods over the past five decades (Paul, 2009; Haque et al., 2012). This record has encouraged a view of Bangladesh as a global model of adaptation. Yet declining mortality does not mean that livelihoods are secure. Households may survive an event but lose land, crops, livestock, housing, and productive assets, and these losses can push them into long-term indebtedness, food insecurity, or displacement (Adger, 1999; Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013). Disaster statistics and macro-scale vulnerability indices capture such trajectories poorly. They show how many people were affected, but not how individuals and households weigh risks, mobilise resources, and decide what to do before, during, and after an event. Livelihood approaches offer a useful lens on these questions. Building on the sustainable livelihoods framework (Chambers & Conway, 1992; Scoones, 1998), recent work conceptualises livelihood resilience as the capacity of people to sustain and improve their well-being despite environmental, economic, and political disturbances (Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience in this sense is not simply a return to the pre-disturbance state. It involves buffering capacity, the ability to adjust and learn, and, where necessary, [9] transformation of livelihood systems (Béné et al., 2012, Folke, 2016). It is also embedded in social relations: access to assets, networks, markets, and institutions is unevenly distributed by class, gender, caste, religion, and location, and so is the ability to cope with stress (Adger, 2006; Ribot, 2014). A people-centred perspective accordingly treats the strategies of households as the central object of analysis, while taking seriously the structural constraints and opportunities within which they act. A large literature documents how rural households in Bangladesh respond to environmental stress. Farmers adjust crop calendars, adopt flood- and salt-tolerant varieties, and shift from rice to shrimp or other aquaculture in saline zones (Ayers & Huq, 2009; Dasgupta et al., 2014). Households diversify their incomes through petty trade, wage labour, or fishing, and increasingly send family members to cities or abroad (Black et al., 2011, Mallick & Vogt, 2014). Migration may be a successful adaptive strategy, but it may equally be a last resort that exposes migrants to precarious urban conditions (Penning-Rowsell et al., 2013; Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Some people, moreover, do not move or adapt at all, because they lack the resources, because they are attached to place, or because moving would mean abandoning assets they cannot carry with them (Adams, 2016, Ayeb-Karlsson et al., 2016). Adaptation is therefore neither automatic nor uniformly beneficial. Planned interventions and autonomous household strategies can generate maladaptation, in which actions intended [4] to reduce vulnerability instead increase it for the same or other groups, for instance through embankments that cause waterlogging or shrimp farming that salinises land and reduces food security (Barnett & O'Neill, 2010, Paprocki & Cons, 2014). Despite this body of knowledge, three gaps remain. First, most studies analyse a single hazard or a single region, so little is known about how people in different environmental settings of the delta experience and respond to floods, erosion, drought, and cyclones. Second, much of the evidence is derived from cross-sectional surveys or short interviews that capture current coping practices but not the sequence of [22] decisions through which resilience is built or eroded over a lifetime. Because shocks accumulate and past choices shape present options, such snapshots can misrepresent why strategies succeed or fail (Tanner et al., 2015). Third, evacuation research has emphasised warning dissemination, shelter capacity, and distance, but has paid less attention to the livelihood considerations that lead people [6] to stay put. Reports that residents delay or refuse evacuation because of fear of looting or of losing livestock and belongings (Alam & Collins, 2010, Paul, 2009) suggest [27] that decisions in the face of hazard are strongly shaped by livelihood risk, not only by perceptions of physical danger. This article addresses these gaps using material from the Gibika project, which studies livelihood resilience in seven sites representing the main environmental settings of Bangladesh, including coastal, riverine, and drought-prone areas. We apply a new methodology, the personal Livelihood History interview, which reconstructs the chronology of a person's livelihood activities, the shocks and stresses encountered, the decisions taken, and their outcomes. Drawing on 28 such interviews, we ask three questions. How do floods, riverbank erosion, drought, and cyclones affect the livelihoods of people in the study sites? Which strategies do people use to build resilience, and why do some of these fail? And how do livelihood considerations shape decisions during cyclone threats, including the decision not to evacuate? The article makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides comparative, longitudinal accounts of how people experience multiple hazards across contrasting environments of the delta. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of Livelihood Histories for tracing decision making in risk-prone settings and for identifying the turning points at which strategies succeed or fail. Conceptually [32] and [23] for policy, it shows that adaptation and disaster risk reduction must be built on the lived experience of people currently However, facing environmental stress, including the (5) trade-offs between protecting life and protecting livelihoods. In the sections that follow, we describe the study sites and methodology, present the findings by hazard and strategy, and discuss their implications for adaptation planning. Study design and conceptual framing This article draws on [11] the Gibika project, a multi-sited research programme However, on livelihood resilience in Bangladesh ("gibika" means livelihood in Bengali). The project adopts a people-centred, actor-oriented approach in which livelihood resilience is understood as the capacity of households to maintain and improve their wellbeing through exposure to environmental stress, shocks, and disturbances (Chambers and Conway, 1992, Scoones, 1998; Tanner et al., 2015). Resilience is therefore treated as [31] an outcome of decisions made under constraint, not as a fixed attribute of households or places. To capture these decisions, we used a qualitative, retrospective design based on personal Livelihood History interviews. This design was chosen because the processes of interest, namely incremental adaptation, delayed responses to slow-onset hazards, and decisions during acute events, unfold over years and are poorly captured by cross-sectional surveys (Adger, 2000, Tompkins and Adger, 2004). Individual life-course approaches also allow the identification of turning points at which strategies succeed or fail (Elliott et al., 2005). Study sites Seven study sites were purposively selected to span the principal hydro-climatic hazard regimes of the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta and its margins. Selection used four criteria: (i) dominant exposure to at least one of cyclones and storm surge, riverine and flash flooding, riverbank erosion, or drought, (ii) variation in livelihood base (rice and other crop farming, aquaculture, fishing, daily labour, small business); (iii) variation in institutional context, including embankment coverage, cyclone shelter provision, and NGO presence; and (iv) logistical feasibility and security for repeated fieldwork. Three sites lie in the south-west and south-central coastal zone and are exposed to cyclones, tidal flooding, and salinity intrusion. Two sites lie along major rivers in the north and centre of the country and are affected by seasonal flooding and riverbank erosion. One site is in the north-west, where rainfall variability and groundwater dependence produce recurrent drought, and one is in the north-eastern haor wetland basin, where early monsoon flash floods threaten the single annual rice crop. Site-level information on hazard history and demographic profile was compiled from national statistics, previous studies, and key informant discussions during an initial scoping visit. Sampling and participants Within each site, four participants were selected, yielding 28 interviews (N = 28). We used purposive, maximum-variation sampling (Patton, 2015) to ensure diversity in gender, age, primary occupation, landholding, and hazard experience. Sampling was stratified by an initial village-level wealth-ranking exercise conducted with local informants, and respondents were identified through community leaders, local government representatives, and snowballing. Eligibility required a minimum of 15 years of residence in, or regular connection to, the site, so that participants could narrate substantial livelihood trajectories. Where respondents had left the site, for example through migration after displacement, they were interviewed where they currently lived if they remained reachable. Of the 28 participants, 14 were women and 14 were men, ages ranged from 24 to 71 years (median 46). Primary occupations at the time of interview included smallholder and tenant farming (n = 10), fishing and aquaculture (n = 6), wage labour (n = 6), petty trade and small enterprise (n = 4), and household-based work (n = 2). Because the study sought analytic depth and variation across contexts, not statistical representativeness, the sample was sized following guidance that thematic saturation in relatively homogeneous qualitative samples is commonly reached within 12 interviews (Guest et al., 2006). Across the seven contrasting sites, we judged that four interviews each, supplemented by contextual data, provided adequate information power (Malterud et al., 2016). The Livelihood History interview The Livelihood History interview is a semi-structured, life-course instrument developed within the project to elicit how people make livelihood decisions in risk-prone environments. Each interview began with an open narrative prompt inviting participants to describe their life and work from childhood to the present. This was followed by a timeline exercise in which the interviewer and respondent jointly marked livelihood activities, residential moves, household composition changes, and hazard events on a visual calendar, using locally recognised events (for example, named cyclones and major floods) as temporal anchors to improve recall (Bernard, 2011). A third phase probed each identified turning point using a standard set of questions on the stress or shock involved, the options considered, the resources However, and networks mobilised, the decision taken and by whom, and the subsequent outcome. A final section examined perceptions of risk, [19] trust in warnings and public services, and expectations for the future. For respondents in cyclone-exposed sites, additional questions addressed experiences of warnings, evacuation, However, and shelter use. The guide was developed in English, translated into Bangla, and piloted with four respondents [27] outside the main [24] sample, leading to revisions of question wording and the timeline procedure. Data collection procedures Fieldwork was carried out by a team of Bangladeshi and international researchers, with interviews conducted in Bangla by trained interviewers of the same gender as the respondent wherever culturally appropriate. Interviews took place at times and locations chosen by participants, usually at home, and lasted between 60 and 150 minutes (mean ≈ 95 minutes). Obesity remains one of the most persistent and costly public health problems in the [5] United States. Nationally, roughly four in ten adults have obesity, and prevalence has risen steadily since the late 1970s (Hales et al., 2020, Fryar et al., 2018). Excess weight is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, several cancers, and premature mortality, and it contributes substantially to medical expenditures and lost productivity (Kopelman, 2000; Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012; Ward et al., 2021). Because the determinants of weight status operate at multiple levels, from individual behavior to the food, transportation, and economic environments in which people live, effective responses increasingly rely on place-based strategies such as zoning, transportation investment, food retail policy, and community programming (Swinburn et al., 2011; Story et al., 2008). Targeting and evaluating these strategies requires reliable information on where excess weight is concentrated and how it changes over time. Existing surveillance systems provide only limited geographic resolution. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) measures height and weight directly and is the national standard, but its sample is designed to support national and some subgroup estimates, not estimates for states or small areas. The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) offers state and, in some cases, county or metropolitan-area estimates, yet it relies on self-reported height and weight, which are known to produce underestimates of body mass index (BMI) and prevalence of obesity, with error that varies by sex, age, and body size (Gillum and Sempos, 2005, Connor Gorber et al., 2007). Response rates for telephone-based surveys have also fallen over time, raising concerns about nonresponse bias (Pierannunzi et al., 2013). Model-based approaches such as multilevel regression and poststratification, used in the CDC PLACES project, can produce census tract estimates from BRFSS data (Zhang et al., 2014, Wang et al., 2018). However, such estimates borrow strength from area-level covariates and are shrunk toward predicted values, so they may understate true variation among neighborhoods and can partly build in the very associations researchers wish to study. Because the estimated outcome is partly a function of the predictors, using these estimates to examine correlates of obesity is potentially circular. Several alternative data sources have been explored to fill this gap. Electronic health records can provide measured heights and weights for large populations and have been used to construct neighborhood and county-level obesity maps (Schwartz et al., 2017, Tomayko et al., 2021). Their coverage, however, is restricted to patients of participating health systems, who are not representative of the general population and who may differ systematically in weight and health care use. School-based body measurement programs yield population-level data for children (Ogden et al., 2018), but no comparable program [4] exists for adults. Researchers have also used commercial data, social media, and wearable devices, which carry their own selection and validity concerns (Althoff et al., 2017). A source that covers most adults in a jurisdiction, includes a recorded address, and is already collected and maintained by a government agency would therefore be valuable. State-issued driver licenses and identification cards meet many of these criteria. In the United States, the great majority of adults hold either a driver license or a state identification card, and the application process records height, weight, date of birth, sex, and residential address. These [20] records are held by state motor vehicle agencies and are routinely updated at renewal. Weight on a license is typically self-reported and may be rounded or outdated, and prior work comparing license data with measured values suggests systematic underreporting, particularly among women and older adults (Ezzati et al., 2006, Hodge et al., 2020). Even so, the same biases affect nearly all areas, and the sheer volume of records makes it possible to produce stable estimates for small geographic units [9] without the sampling error that limits surveys. Earlier work using license data from Massachusetts found that aggregated BMI estimates were strongly correlated with obesity prevalence from independent sources and varied meaningfully across municipalities (Ezzati et al., 2006; Hodge et al., 2020). Despite this promise, applications remain rare, and few studies have used identification card data to evaluate the neighborhood characteristics associated with weight status across an entire state, including rural areas, where obesity prevalence is often highest and survey coverage is weakest [30] (Befort et [10] al., 2012; Trivedi et al., 2015). The neighborhood correlates of weight status are well documented in other data but not uniformly so. Area-level socioeconomic disadvantage, including low income, low educational attainment, and low housing values, has been consistently associated with higher BMI and obesity prevalence in the United States and other high-income countries (Wang and Beydoun, 2007; Black and Macinko, 2008, Singh et al., 2010). Racial and ethnic composition is also associated with weight status, reflecting structural inequities in housing, food access, and exposure to environmental stressors (Williams and Collins, 2001; Bell et al., 2019). Features of the built environment, such as supermarket access, the density of fast food outlets, and automobile dependence, have been linked to weight, though findings are mixed and often sensitive to how neighborhoods are defined and how confounding by socioeconomic status is handled (Cobb et al., 2015, Frank et al., 2004; Lovasi et al., 2009). Rural residence adds a further dimension, as rural adults tend to have "higher" BMI than urban adults, with differences in food environments, physical activity opportunities, and travel distances all "proposed" as contributing factors (Befort et al., 2012). Few studies have been [37] able to examine these domains jointly, at the census tract "level," using a measure of BMI that is not itself modeled from the covariates under study. This study addresses these gaps by using approximately three million Oregon state-issued identification card records to estimate average adult BMI for every census tract in the state. We ask three questions. First, can identification card data [11] be processed into age-adjusted, tract-level BMI estimates that are stable and plausible? Second, how much of "the" variation in [11] tract-level BMI is explained by population characteristics, food access, commuting behavior, and geography, and which of these factors are independently associated with [19] BMI? Third, are the observed associations consistent with the established literature on socioeconomic and environmental disparities in weight status, which would support the validity of identification card data for surveillance? We make three contributions. First, we demonstrate a replicable approach for deriving small-area BMI estimates from administrative records that are already held by state agencies, which could be adopted by public health departments at low marginal cost. Second, because the estimates are computed directly from records rather than modeled from area characteristics, they allow unbiased examination of the neighborhood factors associated with weight status in urban, suburban, and rural settings. Third, by assessing the associations of home values, education, race, ethnicity, car commuting, and rural-urban commuting area classification with BMI, we provide evidence on the validity of this data source and identify potentially modifiable environmental targets for obesity prevention in Oregon and similar states. Data sources and study population We obtained de-identified records from the Oregon Driver and Motor Vehicle Services Division (DMV) for all active driver licenses, instruction permits, and state-issued identification cards held by Oregon residents aged 18 years or older at the time of extraction. The extract contained approximately three million records. Each record included the cardholder's self-reported height and weight as recorded at the most recent issuance or renewal, date of birth, sex, and residential address. Names, license numbers, and other direct identifiers were removed by DMV staff before transfer, and addresses were geocoded by the research team within a secure environment and then discarded after assignment to 2010 census tracts. The study used only existing administrative data and was determined to be exempt from review by the institutional review board. We excluded records with missing or implausible anthropometric values (height <122 cm or >213 cm; weight <32 kg or >227 kg; resulting BMI <15 or >60 kg/m²), following conventions used in other survey-based BMI analyses (Flegal et al., 2012). We also excluded records that could not be geocoded to an Oregon census tract (for example, post office boxes without a physical address match). Of 3.02 million eligible records, 2.88 million (95%) were retained for analysis. Tracts with fewer than 100 valid records were suppressed to protect confidentiality and to avoid unstable estimates. Body mass index and age adjustment BMI was calculated for each cardholder as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Because identification card data rely on self-reported measures, and because self-reported weight tends to be underestimated and height overestimated (Connor Gorber et al., 2007), absolute BMI values are expected to be biased downward. Our primary interest was in the relative distribution of BMI across tracts, which is less sensitive to a systematic reporting bias than are absolute prevalence estimates, though we acknowledge that reporting error may differ across population subgroups. Age composition varies substantially among census tracts and is strongly related to BMI. We therefore computed age-adjusted mean BMI for each tract by direct standardization. Cardholders were grouped into six age strata (18–24, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and ≥65 years). The age-adjusted mean for tract j was BMIadj,j = Σk wk · (Σi BMIijk / njk), where k indexes age strata, njk is the number of valid records in stratum k of tract j, and wk is the proportion of the statewide adult population in stratum k, taken from the 2010 decennial census (the standard population). Tracts with no records in one or more age strata were handled by collapsing adjacent strata. The standard error of each tract estimate was computed from the stratum-specific variances using the usual formula for a weighted sum of independent means (Klein & Schoenborn, 2001). Because a license or identification card is not held by all adults, we compared the number of cardholders in each tract with the 2010–2014 American Community Survey (ACS) adult population to estimate coverage. Statewide coverage exceeded 90% of adults, and tract-level coverage was lower in some dense urban tracts (where non-driving is more common) and in tracts with large student or institutional populations. Tract-level explanatory variables We selected explanatory variables on the basis of prior literature on the social and environmental determinants of obesity (Black & Macinko, 2008, Drewnowski, 2009) and grouped them into four domains. Population characteristics. From the 2010–2014 ACS five-year estimates we obtained median home value, the percentage of adults aged 25 years or older with a bachelor's degree or higher, median household income, percentage of residents living below the federal poverty level, percentage of residents identifying as non-Hispanic white, Black, Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Hispanic or Latino (any race), and median age. Median home value was used as a proxy for neighborhood wealth, since it captures accumulated assets and is available for nearly all tracts, and was log-transformed to reduce right skew. Food access. We used the [15] U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Access Research Atlas to identify tracts designated as low income and low access (LILA), and the percentage of residents living more [3] than one-half mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from the nearest supermarket (Ver Ploeg et al., 2015). We additionally computed the density of fast-food and convenience-store establishments per square kilometer from a commercial business listing, using North American Industry Classification System codes 722513 and 445120. Commuting behavior. From the ACS journey-to-work tables we [39] obtained the percentage of workers aged 16 years or older who commuted by However, car (drove alone or carpooled), by public transit, by bicycle, and on foot, along with mean travel time to work. Geography. We classified [17] each tract using the 2010 rural-urban commuting area (RUCA) codes developed by the USDA Economic Research Service and the WWAMI Rural Health Research Center. We collapsed the 10 primary codes into four categories: metropolitan core (codes 1–3), large rural town 4–6), small rural town (7–9), [33] and isolated rural (code 10), with metropolitan as the reference. We also defined region (Portland metropolitan area, Willamette Valley, Southern Oregon, Central Oregon, Eastern Oregon, and the Coast) for sensitivity analyses.

Introduction Traumatic hand and upper extremity injuries are among the most common reasons patients seek emergency care. Epidemiologic analyses of national emergency department (ED) data suggest that hand and wrist injuries account for roughly 20% of all ED visits, with lacerations, fractures, crush injuries, and amputations making up a large share of these presentations [1,2]. Although many of these injuries are minor, a substantial proportion require timely specialized evaluation and often operative management. Open fractures, tendon lacerations, vascular compromise, high-pressure injection injuries, compartment syndrome, and flexor sheath infections all benefit from early expert intervention. Delay can lead to infection, permanent stiffness, loss of grip strength, chronic pain, and prolonged work disability [3]. Because the hand is central to (16) occupation, self-care, and social participation, these outcomes carry high personal and societal costs. Hand injuries disproportionately affect working-age adults, so the economic burden [31] through lost productivity and compensation claims is considerable [2,3]. Despite this burden, access to emergency hand care has been described as inadequate. Under the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA), hospitals with EDs must provide a medical screening examination and stabilization, and they must maintain an on-call (21) roster of specialists to meet the needs of their [32] patients [4]. In practice, however, compliance with this requirement is difficult for many [13] institutions. Over the past two decades, studies of ED on-call coverage have documented a decline in specialists willing to take emergency call, particularly in surgical and procedural subspecialties [5,6]. Physicians cite uncompensated care, medicolegal exposure, disruption to elective practice and personal life, and inadequate reimbursement among their reasons for (12) withdrawing from (17) call panels [5,6]. Hospitals have responded by paying call stipends, employing specialists, or transferring patients to other facilities. These strategies are unevenly available and are often shaped by local market conditions rather than (5) by patient need. Hand surgery is especially vulnerable to these pressures. Hand surgeons are a relatively small workforce drawn from orthopedic, (16) plastic; and general surgery backgrounds, and many practice in outpatient or ambulatory settings in which elective procedures such as carpal tunnel release, trigger finger release, and arthroplasty are more predictable and better reimbursed than unscheduled trauma [7]. Because most elective hand surgery is performed outside the hospital or in same-day facilities, a surgeon may maintain a busy elective practice at a hospital while declining to participate in (19) its emergency call schedule. When (23) no hand specialist is available; patients may be evaluated by general orthopedic, plastic, or emergency physicians with varying hand-specific training, or they may be transferred to another institution, sometimes [18] over considerable distances. Transfers increase cost, delay definitive treatment, [19] strain receiving centers, and fragment continuity (11) of care [8]. Several recent regional surveys have reported a mismatch between the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery. These studies, conducted in different states and using similar telephone-based methods, found that a larger share of hospitals offered elective hand services than offered around-the-clock emergency hand coverage [7,9,10]. They also identified geographic and institutional variation in coverage, and some suggested that patients in underserved areas had the most limited options. Taken together, these reports raise the possibility that the discrepancy reflects a structural feature of the health care system rather than local anomalies. Even so, the evidence remains scattered. Most studies describe a single state or region, use different definitions of coverage, and rarely evaluate whether coverage is related to community characteristics such as proximity to a trauma center or the socioeconomic status of the surrounding population. These contextual factors are plausibly important. Level I trauma centers concentrate surgical resources, and nearby community hospitals may rely on them (12) as referral destinations. This may reduce the incentive; or the capacity, of neighboring hospitals to [6] maintain their own hand call panels. Alternatively, hospitals (11) in counties without a trauma center may have to maintain broader local coverage because transfer (20) options are [18] limited. Likewise, hospitals serving economically disadvantaged However, communities typically have a higher proportion of uninsured and Medicaid patients, which may deter specialists from taking call because of poor reimbursement [5,11]. Prior work on trauma center access has shown that vulnerable populations often face geographic and financial barriers to specialized care [12]. Whether these patterns extend to emergency hand surgery has not been well characterized. New Jersey provides a useful setting in (11) which to examine these questions. It is the most densely populated state in the nation; with a dense network of community hospitals, (26) several level I (10) and II trauma centers; and marked variation in income and urbanization across municipalities. Its proximity to major metropolitan areas in New York However, and Pennsylvania might be expected to buffer patients against limited local coverage; yet it could also encourage a reliance on referral that undermines local (12) emergency capability. (28) To our knowledge; the availability of emergency versus elective hand surgery coverage across (15) New Jersey hospitals has However, not been systematically evaluated. The purpose of this study was therefore to assess the availability of elective and emergency hand surgery coverage among non-university hospitals in New Jersey and to determine whether a disproportionate availability of emergency relative to elective services exists. However, We further sought to examine whether emergency hand coverage varied according to the presence of a level I trauma center within the hospital's county and according (15) to the poverty level of the hospital's city. Finally, we place our findings in the context of previously (14) published state-level surveys to evaluate whether a national trend toward limited emergency hand care is emerging. This study makes three contributions. First, it provides the first state-wide description of the gap (1) between elective and (6) emergency hand coverage in New Jersey, using a standardized survey of hospitals. Second, it identifies geographic and socioeconomic correlates of coverage that may point to modifiable drivers of access; such as call compensation, regionalization, and (15) referral patterns. Third, by comparing our results with those from other states, it assesses whether the discrepancy is a national phenomenon. If it is, the findings (1) argue for policy and system-level responses, including regional hand trauma networks, structured triage and transfer protocols, and alternative models of emergency hand care, rather than reliance on individual hospital call arrangements. Study Design and Setting We conducted (28) a cross-sectional telephone survey of acute-care hospitals in the state of New (13) Jersey in August (8) 2014. The aim was to compare the availability (10) of elective hand surgery (1) with that of emergency hand coverage. The design followed standard recommendations for (6) structured telephone surveys of organizations; which stress a brief fixed-script instrument; a defined respondent population, and repeated contact attempts to limit nonresponse (Dillman et al., (4) 2014). The survey collected only [26] institutional-level information about service availability. It involved no patient However, data and no individually identifiable information about respondents. We therefore regarded the study as non-human-subjects research and exempt from full institutional review board review. Participation was voluntary, and respondents were told the purpose of the call at the outset. Hospital Identification (16) and Eligibility We compiled the sampling frame from the New Jersey Department of Health's public licensure listing of acute-care general hospitals. We cross-checked it against the state hospital association directory to remove closed; merged, or renamed facilities. Hospitals with an emergency department were eligible, because the study concerned the availability of emergency hand coverage and elective services. We excluded university-affiliated hospitals. These institutions generally have residency-based, in-house subspecialty coverage, and including them would have inflated estimates of availability for (7) the community-hospital setting where access concerns are greatest. We also excluded specialty hospitals without an emergency department, such as rehabilitation, psychiatric, and pediatric-only facilities. After applying these criteria, 58 hospitals remained, and all were contacted. We did not draw a sample, so the study was a census of eligible institutions. Survey Instrument and Data Collection The instrument consisted of two questions, chosen to reflect how a transferring clinician or patient would assess access to hand care. The first was Does your hospital provide elective hand surgery?" and had a yes/no response. The second was "Is there a hand specialist/surgeon on call always, sometimes, or never? We defined "hand specialist" as any surgeon, whether plastic, orthopedic, or general, who provides hand surgery services at the hospital. This matches the multidisciplinary nature of hand surgery training in the United States. "Always" meant the hospital provided immediate hand coverage 24 hours per day, 7 days per week, and we labeled this "24/7 coverage" in the analysis. Sometimes indicated limited coverage, such as weekday-only, scheduled-day, or variable call. "Never" indicated no hand call coverage. A single trained caller placed all calls during regular business hours. The caller first reached the hospital operator and asked to be connected to the emergency department, the operating room scheduling office, or the medical staff office. These were the departments most likely to know the call schedule and elective service lines. The caller used an identical script for every call to reduce interviewer variability. The caller recorded the response, the title of the respondent, and the date of the call. When the first respondent was unsure, the caller asked to be referred to someone with knowledge of the call roster, such as a charge nurse, a staff coordinator, or a medical staff office employee. We counted a hospital as a respondent only if both questions were answered. If a hospital did not answer, the caller made at least two further attempts on different days and at different times. Hospitals that declined, could not identify a knowledgeable respondent, or remained unreachable after repeated attempts were classified as nonresponders. We did not verify responses against written call schedules. Consistent with the intent of a "mystery caller approach, we accepted the information that a patient or referring provider would receive as the effective measure of availability. Hospital and Community Characteristics To explore whether geography and community socioeconomic context were associated with coverage, we collected two sets of hospital-level covariates from public sources. The first was proximity to a level I trauma center. We obtained trauma designations from the New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Emergency Medical Services, and assigned each hospital to a county. Hospitals were then classified as located either in the same county as at least one level I trauma center or in a county with no level I trauma center. This county-level definition reflects the catchment within which a hospital might reasonably transfer patients to a trauma center, and it allowed us to test whether nearby tertiary resources were associated with less local coverage. The second set of covariates was the socioeconomic profile of the city in which each hospital is located. We extracted the percentage of residents living below the federal poverty line for each city from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey five-year estimates. Cities were dichotomized at the median poverty rate among the cities in the responding sample into higher-poverty and lower-poverty groups. A median split was chosen because the sample was too small for stable multi-category comparisons, and because the study aimed to detect broad disparities in access rather than to model a dose-response relationship. Outcome Definitions The primary outcome was the proportion of hospitals reporting 24/7 hand coverage. The comparison measure was the proportion reporting elective hand surgery. The discrepancy between the two proportions served as the principal indicator of disproportionate availability. Secondary outcomes were the proportion of hospitals with 24/7 emergency hand coverage stratified by trauma center presence in the county and by city poverty level. For analysis, we collapsed "sometimes" and never into less than 24/7 coverage" when comparing groups, because both mean a patient with an acute hand injury cannot be assured of immediate specialist evaluation. This is the central concern under federal on-call obligations (Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, 1986) and in the epidemiology of hand trauma, which accounts for a substantial share of emergency department visits (Ootes et al., 2012).
