The rapid growth of social media and online discussion platforms has transformed how people communicate, but it has also created an environment in which abusive content can spread quickly and at scale. Offensive language, hate speech, sexist and racist remarks, and personal attacks are now common in comment sections, microblogging services, and collaborative platforms Waseem and Hovy, 2016, Wulczyn et al., 2017). Exposure to such content has been linked to psychological harm for targets, to the withdrawal of users from public discussion, and to the degradation of the communities in which it occurs (Duggan, 2017). Platform operators and policy makers are consequently under pressure to moderate content. Manual moderation, however, is slow, expensive, and emotionally taxing for the people who perform it, and it cannot keep pace with the volume of content generated every day. This has motivated a substantial body of work on the automatic detection of abusive language Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017, Nobata et al., 2016). Early approaches treated abuse detection as a supervised text classification problem and relied on hand-engineered features, including bag-of-words and n-gram representations, part-of-speech tags, syntactic dependencies, and lexicons of offensive terms (Yin et al., 2009, Warner and Hirschberg, 2012; Davidson et al., 2017). Although such systems are reasonably effective on well-behaved text, they are brittle and require considerable feature engineering. More recently, neural network models have become However, dominant. Convolutional and recurrent architectures that [1] operate on learned word embeddings, often initialised from vectors pre-trained on large corpora, have been shown to outperform feature-based classifiers on several benchmarks Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017; Gambäck and Sikdar, 2017). Among these, recurrent neural networks with gated units, such as the LSTM Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), and in particular models that combine them with attention or with additional user-level information (Pavlopoulos et al., 2017, Founta et al., 2019), currently define the state of the art on datasets drawn from Twitter and from Wikipedia talk pages. Despite this progress, a fundamental difficulty remains that is specific to the abusive-language setting: users frequently obfuscate their words. Because many platforms deploy keyword filters and automated classifiers, authors of abusive messages have an incentive to alter offensive terms in ways that preserve readability for humans but defeat automatic matching. Typical strategies include replacing letters with visually similar digits or symbols (e.g., a$$hole, "n1gger"), inserting or repeating characters (iiidiot, "stuuupid"), inserting punctuation or whitespace within a word f u c k", "id.iot"), deliberately misspelling words (fck, "biatch"), and concatenating words goaway). Obfuscation also arises without any evasive intent, as a consequence of informal writing conventions, typing errors, and the creative orthography typical of social media Eisenstein, 2013). Whatever the motive, the effect is the same: the surface form of the token falls outside the vocabulary the model has seen during training. Word-level neural models handle such tokens poorly. A standard pipeline fixes a vocabulary of the most frequent training words and maps every other token to a single shared out-of-vocabulary (OOV) symbol, whose embedding is learned, if at all, from the few training instances in which it occurs. This design has an important consequence for abuse detection. Because one embedding must stand in for every unseen word, the model cannot distinguish an obfuscated slur from a rare proper noun, a misspelled but harmless word, or a genuinely novel term. All of these are collapsed into the same representation, and any evidence carried by the form of the word, such as its resemblance to a known offensive term, is discarded. The problem is not merely one of coverage. In abuse detection the unseen word is often the most informative token in the message, and replacing it with a generic However, placeholder removes precisely the signal that the author sought to hide from simple filters but not from a human reader. Pre-trained embeddings mitigate the problem only partially, since obfuscated variants are by their nature sparse and idiosyncratic, and are rarely represented in the corpora from which general-purpose embeddings are trained. Prior work in other areas of natural language processing suggests a remedy: build word representations from their characters. Character-level and subword models have been shown to improve language modelling, part-of-speech tagging, and machine translation, especially for morphologically rich languages and noisy text (Ling et al., 2015, Kim et al., 2016; Plank et al., 2016, Bojanowski et al., 2017; Sennrich et al., 2016). Such models can in principle produce representations for arbitrary strings and exploit regularities between a word and its variants. In abuse detection, however, the use of these ideas has so far been limited. Some studies employ character n-gram features within linear classifiers Nobata et al., 2016, Mehdad and Tetreault, 2016), and a few apply character-level networks to entire comments (Park and Fung, 2017). These approaches either discard word boundaries, and with them the word-level structure on which the strongest recurrent models depend, or they treat the character information as an additional input [5] channel rather than as a principled means of handling unseen words. To our knowledge, the best-performing recurrent classifiers for abuse detection still fall back on a single OOV embedding and thus do not address the obfuscation problem explicitly. This paper addresses that gap. Our central research question is whether a recurrent abuse detection model that composes embeddings for unseen words from their characters can recover the information lost by the generic OOV representation, and thereby improve detection performance, particularly in the presence of obfuscated or rare vocabulary. Related questions concern which composition function is most suitable for this purpose, and whether any benefit is consistent across domains that differ in style, annotation scheme, and the degree to which obfuscation occurs. We make the following contributions. First, we propose a neural architecture for abuse detection in which in-vocabulary words retain their ordinary word embeddings, while words not found in the vocabulary receive embeddings computed by a character-based composition function. We investigate several such functions, including recurrent and convolutional encoders over character sequences, so that the model can distinguish unseen words from one another according to their orthography rather than mapping them to a single shared vector. Second, we evaluate the approach on However, two datasets from different domains, namely Twitter data annotated for racist and sexist abuse (Waseem and Hovy, 2016) and comments from Wikipedia talk pages annotated for personal attacks (Wulczyn et al., 2017), and show that it significantly improves over the current state of the art on both. Third, we provide an analysis of the model's behaviour showing where the gains originate, including how it treats obfuscated However, and rare tokens relative to a baseline using a single OOV embedding. Finally, we discuss the implications for the robustness of automated moderation systems to adversarial manipulation by users. Task formulation We treat abuse detection as supervised text classification. Given a post x = (w1, …, wn) of n tokens, the model predicts a label y from a dataset-specific label set Y. We compare [19] a word-level recurrent baseline, which maps all unseen words to a single OOV vector, with models that compose a representation for each unseen word from its characters. The comparison is controlled: all models share the [4] same recurrent classifier, differing only in how word representations are built. Datasets We used two public corpora from different domains. The first is the Twitter corpus of Waseem and Hovy (2016), which contains roughly 16,900 tweets annotated as racism, sexism, or neither. Because of tweet deletions, we could only retrieve a subset of the original collection. The class distribution is skewed, with the majority of tweets labelled neither. As is standard for this dataset (Badjatiya et al., 2017; Park and Fung, 2017), we report results from 10-fold cross-validation. In each fold, 10% of the training portion was held out for early stopping and hyperparameter selection. The second is the Wikipedia talk page corpus of Wulczyn et al. (2017), containing approximately 115,000 comments labelled by crowd workers as personal attacks or not. Attacks are a minority class, at around 12% of comments. We used the provided train, development, and test partitions, so results are directly comparable with earlier work. Both corpora were preprocessed in the same way. We lower-cased text, replaced URLs and user mentions with placeholder tokens, and tokenized with a Twitter-aware tokenizer. We deliberately did not apply spelling normalization or de-obfuscation, since the aim is for the model to cope with noisy tokens itself. For each dataset, the vocabulary V consisted of words in the training partition that also have a pretrained embedding. All other words, including misspellings, character substitutions (e.g., b!tch, fk), and concatenations, are treated as out-of-vocabulary (OOV). We quantified the OOV rate on the validation and test partitions to confirm the extent of the problem. Baseline architecture Words in V are represented by pretrained embeddings e(w) ∈ ℝ^d (d = 300), initialized from GloVe vectors (Pennington et al., 2014) and fine-tuned during training. In the baseline, every OOV word is mapped to one shared trainable vector eUNK: e(w) = E[w] if w ∈ [2] V, eUNK otherwise. The embedded sequence is encoded by a unidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), whose gates are defined as it = σWi [h{t−1}, xt] + bi), ft = σ(Wf [h{t−1}; xt] + bf), ot = σ(Wo [h{t−1}, xt] + bo), ct = ft ⊙ c{t−1} + it ⊙ tanh(Wc [h{t−1}; xt] + bc), ht = ot ⊙ tanh(ct), [24] where xt is the input vector at step t. The final hidden state hn (hidden size 128) is passed through dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) and a softmax layer: py | x) = softmax(Wy hn + by). Character-based composition models To compose representations for unseen words, each OOV word w is decomposed into its character sequence c1, …, cm). Each character is mapped to a trainable embedding of dimension 50, initialized randomly. The character sequence is then passed through a composition function fcomp to produce a word vector ecomp(w) ∈ ℝ^d. We explored two such functions. Character LSTM Char-LSTM). Following Ling et al. (2015), a bidirectional LSTM reads the characters. The word vector is a linear projection of the concatenated final forward and backward states: ecomp(w) = Wc [→hm , ←h1] + bc. Character CNN Char-CNN). Following Kim et al. (2016), we apply filters of widths k ∈ {2, 3, 4} (100 filters per width) over the character embedding matrix C ∈ ℝ^{m×50}. Each filter produces a feature map z = ReLU(Wk C + bk), and max-over-time pooling gives a fixed-size vector. The pooled outputs are concatenated and projected to ℝ^d. The two functions differ in inductive bias. The Char-LSTM models long-range order within a token, whereas the Char-CNN captures local character n-gram patterns, which are often informative for obfuscation by substitution or insertion (e.g., idi0t, "sluuuut"). We evaluated two ways of using the composed vectors. In the OOV-only variant, composition is applied only to words outside V, and known words keep their pretrained embeddings: e(w) = E[w] if w ∈ V, fcomp(w) otherwise. In the all-words variant, a word's embedding is combined with its composed representation through a learned gate: g = σ(Wg [E[w]; fcomp(w)] + bg), e(w) = g ⊙ E[w] + (1 − g) ⊙ fcomp(w), with E[w] replaced by eUNK for OOV words. The gate lets the model weight orthographic evidence against distributional evidence per dimension. All composition parameters are trained jointly with the classifier by backpropagation, so the character encoder learns from the abuse detection objective directly. To make the composition function useful for unseen words at test time, we randomly replaced in-vocabulary training words with the OOV path at a rate of 10%, so the composition networks receive training signal for words whose pretrained embeddings are available. Comparison systems We compared our models with three published systems. The first is the LSTM with random embeddings followed by a gradient-boosted decision tree classifier Badjatiya et al., 2017), which has been the strongest reported system on the Waseem and Hovy data. The second is the hybrid word- and character-CNN of Park and Fung 2017). The third is a logistic regression classifier

Non-communicable diseases NCDs), principally cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory disease, are [32] the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for roughly two-thirds of global mortality (World Health Organization, 2011). Their economic burden is substantial. Bloom and colleagues (2011) projected cumulative global output losses of approximately US$30 trillion between 2011 and 2030. The costs also include health-care expenditure, lost productivity and reduced quality of life for individuals and families. A considerable proportion of this burden is attributable to modifiable risk factors, and poor diet is among the most important (Lim et al., 2012). Dietary patterns characterised by high intakes of energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, saturated fat and sodium, together with low intakes of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, are consistently associated with obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and increased all-cause mortality (Lim et al., 2012; World Health Organization, 2003). Modelling studies suggest that population-level dietary change could deliver sizeable health gains at relatively low cost (Cecchini et al., 2010). The combined economic and social costs of NCDs therefore provide a compelling rationale for strategies that target dietary behaviour. Overall dietary patterns are built from many individual, repeated decisions about what to eat. These discrete food choices, such as selecting fruit rather than a confectionery snack, ordering a sugar-sweetened beverage, or trimming visible fat from meat, are the proximal behaviours that interventions must ultimately change. Discrete food choices are also more amenable to precise definition and measurement than global dietary patterns, and they are the level [16] at which many policy instruments, such as menu labelling, price signals and school food standards, operate. Effective intervention requires an understanding of the psychological processes that underpin these decisions. Interventions that are explicitly grounded in theory are widely recommended because theory specifies the mechanisms through which behaviour is expected to change and allows these mechanisms to be tested (Craig et al., 2008; Michie & Prestwich, 2010). Theoretical models thus provide the conceptual order that allows programme designers and policy makers to identify the elements that drive behaviour and to select appropriate intervention techniques. Among social cognition models, the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB, Ajzen, 1991) is one of the most frequently applied in health research. The TPB, an extension of the [27] Theory of Reasoned Action (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975), proposes that the proximal determinant of behaviour is [39] intention, which reflects the motivation to perform the behaviour. Intention is in turn determined by three [37] constructs: attitude (the overall evaluation of performing the behaviour), subjective norm perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behaviour) and perceived behavioural control (PBC; perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behaviour). Because many behaviours are not fully under volitional control, PBC is additionally proposed to exert a direct effect on behaviour to the extent that it reflects actual control (Ajzen, 1991). The model's parsimony, its clear operational definitions and its generalisability across behaviours have made it attractive to researchers and practitioners alike. Meta-analytic evidence supports the predictive utility of the TPB across health domains. Armitage and Conner (2001), in a review [22] of 185 independent studies, found that the TPB accounted for 39% of the variance in intention and 27% of the variance in behaviour. Subsequent syntheses have reported similar [17] findings for physical activity (Hagger et al., 2002), and for a range of health behaviours using prospective designs (McEachan et al., 2011). Reviews of the intention–behaviour relationship indicate that intentions explain approximately 28% of the variance in behaviour (Sheeran, 2002), although experimental evidence suggests that even medium-to-large changes in intention produce only small-to-medium changes in behaviour (Webb & Sheeran, 2006). The TPB [27] has also been subject to substantial criticism. Critics have questioned whether it omits important determinants such as habit, affect and automatic processes, whether its constructs are sufficiently distinct, and whether it has generated interventions that effectively change behaviour Sniehotta et al., 2014). These concerns are especially pertinent for food choice, which is often habitual, cue-driven and shaped by hedonic and environmental factors that lie outside conscious deliberation. The TPB has nevertheless been widely used to study eating behaviour, and the primary literature now spans a diverse array of food choices. These include increasing consumption of fruit and vegetables, choosing low-fat or whole-grain foods, limiting sweets, snacks and fast food, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages. Existing reviews of the TPB and diet have been valuable but limited in important respects. Some have examined dietary behaviour as a single undifferentiated category, or combined food choice with other health behaviours such as physical activity and substance use (Armitage & Conner, 2001; McEachan et al., 2011). Others have focused on a single food group, most commonly fruit and vegetable intake (Guillaumie et al., 2010), or have encompassed a broad set of social cognitive determinants without focusing on TPB relationships. Aggregating across heterogeneous food behaviours may mask meaningful differences in the strength of TPB associations. Conceptually, there are good reasons to expect such differences. Choosing to consume a health-promoting food (an approach behaviour) may be governed by different processes than refraining from a health-compromising but palatable food an avoidance behaviour), the latter requiring self-regulation against strong hedonic temptations and ready availability. Perceived control may matter more for behaviours that involve resisting temptation than for those that are simply performed. Likewise, the relative influence of attitudes, social norms and control may vary with the characteristics of those making the choice, including age and gender, because developmental stage and social roles shape both autonomy over food and sensitivity to social influence Conner & Norman, 2005). Yet these potential moderators have rarely been tested systematically within a single synthesis restricted to discrete food choices. A second limitation concerns the evidential basis of earlier reviews. Rapid growth in the number of TPB food choice studies in recent years means that earlier syntheses omit a considerable body of evidence, and few have systematically sought unpublished work, which may reduce the risk of publication bias. Without a current, comprehensive and behaviourally specific synthesis, researchers lack the quantitative information needed to judge when the TPB is an appropriate framework for understanding dietary decisions, and to prioritise the constructs that interventions should target. The primary aim of the present systematic review and meta-analysis was therefore to quantify the associations between TPB variables and discrete food choice behaviours. Specifically, we estimated pooled effect sizes for the relationships of attitude, subjective norm and PBC with intention; of intention and PBC with behaviour; and, where data permitted, the inter-correlations among predictors. A secondary aim was to examine the extent and sources of heterogeneity in these associations. Using meta-regression, we tested whether effect sizes were moderated by the type of food choice behaviour health-promoting versus health-compromising foods, and approach versus avoidance behaviours) and by participant characteristics (age and gender). This review makes three contributions. First, it provides up-to-date, precise estimates of TPB relationships specific to food choice, drawing on both published and unpublished studies. Second, by testing behavioural and demographic moderators, it moves beyond the question of whether the TPB predicts food choice to consider when and for whom it does so, thereby informing the selection of theory in relation to the nature of the target behaviour. Third, it identifies the constructs most strongly associated with intention and behaviour, offering an empirical basis for prioritising intervention targets while recognising the limits of the model in explaining dietary behaviour. Search strategy and eligibility criteria The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Electronic searches were run in PsycINFO, MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses from database inception to the search date. Search strings combined terms for the theory (e.g., "theory of planned behavio, theory of reasoned action", [24] "perceived behavio control, "subjective norm", attitude, intention) with terms for food choice (e.g., food choice", "diet", "fruit", "vegetable", [1] snack, [12] "fat", "sugar", soft drink, fast food, "eating"). Terms [1] were adapted to the indexing vocabulary of each database. The reference lists of included studies and of earlier reviews of the TPB and health behaviour Armitage & Conner, 2001, McEachan et al., 2011) were hand-searched. Authors were contacted when the data needed for effect size calculation were not reported. Studies were eligible if they (a) were published in English as a peer-reviewed journal article or as an unpublished doctoral or master's dissertation, b) used the TPB (Ajzen, 1991) as the primary theoretical framework, (c) measured at least one TPB construct (attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control [PBC], or intention) and a measure of a discrete food choice behaviour; and d) reported a bivariate association between constructs, or sufficient information to compute one. Discrete food choice behaviours were defined as the selection, purchase, or consumption of a specific food or food group (e.g., fruit, fast food), as opposed to composite dietary patterns, weight management, or general healthy eating" indices. Studies were excluded if they focused on clinical populations requiring prescribed diets, on eating disorders, or on breastfeeding or infant feeding practices, or if they reported only multivariate or structural equation modelling results without zero-order correlations. Where several publications reported on the same [27] [28] sample, the report with the most complete data was retained. Study selection and data extraction Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer, and a second reviewer independently screened a random 20% subset; disagreements were resolved by discussion. Full texts of potentially relevant records were assessed independently by two reviewers against the eligibility criteria. Data were extracted using a standardised form, piloted [7] on five studies, covering bibliographic details, country, sample size, mean age, percentage female, study design, time lag between measures, TPB constructs assessed, type of behavioural measure (self-report versus objective), and the correlations among constructs. Extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by a second, discrepancies [18] were resolved by consensus. Coding of moderator variables Three moderators were specified a priori. First, type of food choice behaviour was coded as (a) consumption of health-promoting foods (e.g., fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, low-fat options), b) consumption of health-compromising foods e.g., fast food, sugar-sweetened beverages, high-fat snacks), or (c) avoidance or limitation of health-compromising foods. This classification distinguished approach behaviours from avoidance behaviours, which are thought to differ in their volitional demands (Conner & Armitage, 2002). Second, participant age was coded as the sample mean age, and categorically as children/adolescents <18 years), young adults 18–25 years), and adults (>25 years) where the continuous value was not reported. Third, gender composition was coded as the percentage of female participants in the sample. Samples with no gender information were excluded from the gender analyses. Coding was completed independently by two reviewers (κ = 0.91 for behaviour type), with disagreements resolved by discussion. Methodological quality Study quality was appraised using an adapted checklist drawing on [39] criteria used in earlier TPB meta-analyses (Cooke & French, 2008; McEachan et al., 2011). Items addressed the use of a prospective design, the use of validated or elicitation-based TPB measures, the correspondence between attitudinal and behavioural measures with respect to target, action, context, and time (Ajzen & Fishbein, 1977), the reporting of reliability coefficients, the reporting of attrition, and the use of an objective behavioural measure. Each item was scored 0 or 1, and total scores were examined descriptively and used in sensitivity analyses. Effect size computation The effect size of interest was the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient r) for each bivariate association [31] in the TPB: attitude–intention, subjective norm–intention, PBC–intention, intention–behaviour, and PBC–behaviour. Where studies reported more than one correlation for the same relationship (e.g., multiple foods or multiple items), correlations were averaged within the study after Fisher's z transformation to avoid inflating the weight of any single sample (Borenstein et al., 2009). Where studies reported effect sizes for independent subgroups (e.g., males and females), each subgroup was treated as a separate sample for moderator analyses and combined for overall analyses. Scene understanding has long been a central goal of computer vision, and its definition has expanded considerably over the past decade. Early work concentrated on recognizing objects and labeling pixels, whereas more recent efforts ask systems to produce rich, structured accounts of what an image contains. Dense captioning (Johnson et al., 2016), scene graph generation (Xu et al., 2017), and visual question answering (VQA) (Antol et al., 2015) all require models to relate visual evidence to language, and they have substantially broadened what we expect a vision system to do. Datasets such as VQA, CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017), and GQA Hudson and Manning, 2019) probe increasingly sophisticated skills, including counting, attribute comparison, spatial reasoning, and multi-step compositional inference. In principle, question answering is an open-ended format: any aspect of a scene that can be phrased as a question can be posed to a model. In practice, however, the prevailing formulations are overwhelmingly about the present. Given an image, the question asks what is there, how many, what color, or what is to the left of what. Even tasks that involve video or commonsense, such as video question answering (Tapaswi et al., 2016) or visual commonsense reasoning (Zellers et al., 2019), mostly ask about events that were observed or about plausible explanations of what is already visible. The future state of a scene, [39] and especially its dependence on an action that has not yet occurred, remains largely unexplored. Yet this is precisely the kind of reasoning that intelligent agents need. A robot deciding whether to push a cup, a person judging whether stacking one more box will topple a tower, or an assistant asked to predict the outcome of a plan all must reason about counterfactual, action-conditioned futures. Humans do this routinely and with apparent ease, drawing on an intuitive understanding of physics (Battaglia et al., 2013) that lets them mentally simulate how objects will move and collide. In this paper, we study this capability by introducing a task that we call visual what-if question answering. The system is given an observation of the current scene, in the form of an image, and a question that contains a hypothetical action, such as "What happens to the red cube if the green sphere is pushed to the left?" The answer must describe some aspect of the scene after the action has taken place, for instance which objects end up in contact, which object ends up in a particular position, or whether an object remains in place. The task thus extends VQA along a new axis: instead of describing the scene as it is, the model must predict the scene as it would become, conditioned on an intervention. This problem is difficult for several reasons. First, the answer is not directly observable in the input; it has to be inferred through a model of how the world evolves. Second, the [4] outcome depends on object-object interactions, in which an action on one object propagates through collisions to others, so that small differences in geometry, position, or motion can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. Third, the question is expressed in natural language, so the system must ground the described action in the visual scene, translate it into a physical intervention, and finally map the resulting future state back into a linguistic answer. One natural approach would be to train a monolithic end-to-end network that maps the image and question directly to an answer. Such models have been successful on many VQA benchmarks, but they must acquire the dynamics of the physical world implicitly from question-answer pairs, which is a weak and indirect [14] supervisory signal. Related work on learned intuitive physics; including interaction networks Battaglia et al.; 2016), visual predictive models (Lerer et al., 2016; Mottaghi et al., 2016), and neural physics simulators (Chang et al., 2017), shows that data-driven prediction is possible, but also that generalization to novel configurations, numbers of objects, and long horizons is limited. Conversely; physics engines already encode rigid-body dynamics accurately and generalize by construction, but they operate on explicit symbolic scene descriptions rather than on pixels and language. Motivated by this complementarity, we propose a hybrid model that integrates a physics engine into a question answering architecture. The model first perceives the scene and recovers an object-level representation including object identities, attributes, and positions. It then parses the question to identify the hypothetical action and its target, instantiates this action in a reconstructed simulated scene, and uses the physics engine to roll the [24] scene forward and anticipate the consequences of object-object interactions. The predicted future scene state is then used, in place of the observed one, to answer the question. In this way, the parts of the problem that are well understood, namely rigid-body dynamics, are handled by an explicit simulator, while learning is reserved for the parts that are hard to specify by hand, namely perception and language understanding. Our contributions are as follows. First, we formulate the problem of answering visual what-if questions, in which answers concern future scene states conditioned on hypothetical actions, and thereby extend the scope of scene understanding from describing the present to anticipating the [2] consequences of actions. Second, we present a hybrid architecture that couples a physics engine with a question answering pipeline, enabling explicit simulation of object-object interactions caused by an action. Third; we provide first results on this new problem and compare against fully data-driven end-to-end baselines, showing that our approach outperforms them. We hope that this work encourages further research on action-conditioned, predictive scene understanding and on combining learned and simulated components for reasoning about how the world will change. Task Formulation We define the visual what-if question answering task as follows. Given an image I of a [14] scene containing a set of rigid objects, and a question q that describes a hypothetical action a applied to one object e.g., "What happens to the red cube if the blue sphere is pushed to the left?), the system must produce an answer y from a fixed answer vocabulary. Answers refer to the state of the scene after the action has unfolded, and concern properties such [3] as whether an object is displaced, which objects are in contact, or which objects fall off the support surface. The task therefore requires the model to reason about the current scene, to parse the action, and to anticipate the physical consequences of object-object interactions. Dataset We built a synthetic dataset using the Blender rendering pipeline coupled with the Bullet physics engine (Coumans and Bai, 2016), following the general design principles of CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017). Each scene contains between three and six objects placed on a planar surface, [7] drawn from three shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder), two sizes, two materials, and eight colors. Object positions and orientations are sampled randomly with rejection of initial interpenetrations, and scenes are simulated until at rest to guarantee a stable initial state. [36] Images are rendered at 480×320 resolution from a fixed camera with small random jitter in position and lighting. For each scene we sample actions from a set of four primitives: push in one of four cardinal directions on the ground plane, with a randomly sampled force magnitude; applied to [22] a randomly chosen object. The action is simulated for a fixed duration of five seconds, and the resulting final state is stored together with the full trajectory. Questions are generated from templates with functional programs, analogous [35] to CLEVR, but evaluated on the simulated future state rather than the initial state. Question families comprise (i) movement queries (does object X move?), (ii) counting queries (how many objects are displaced/fall off?), (iii) relational queries (what is to the left of X after the action?), and (iv) collision queries [17] (does X collide with Y?). Answer distributions are balanced per template by rejection sampling to limit language priors. In total the dataset contains 12,000 scenes, 48,000 scene-action pairs, and 240,000 questions, split 70/10/20 into training, validation, and test sets with no scene overlap. Because the [24] physical state of each object is known in simulation; we additionally store ground-truth object attributes, 3D positions, and orientations as auxiliary supervision. Model Our model is a hybrid with three components: a perception module, a physics-based simulation module, and a question answering module. Perception. A Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) trained on the training images detects objects and predicts masks and categorical attributes [20] (shape, size, material, color). A separate regression head, operating on ROI-pooled features, estimates the object's [4] 3D position on the ground plane. Using the known camera parameters we back-project the mask centroid and refine the estimate with the regression output. Object scale is derived from the predicted size class. This produces a structured scene representation S0 = {(ci, pi, si)}, where ci denotes attributes, pi position, and si size. Question parsing. An LSTM sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), following Johnson et al. 2017), translates the question into a functional program. The action is parsed into [22] a tuple consisting of the target object (described by attributes and relations), the direction, and the force class. Program generation is trained with 5,000 annotated question-program pairs using cross-entropy, followed by fine-tuning with the answer-level reward as in REINFORCE (Williams, 1992). Physics simulation. The parsed action is grounded to a specific detected object, and the scene S0 is instantiated in the Bullet engine with objects represented by primitive collision shapes of the predicted type and size. Material is mapped to friction and restitution coefficients. As these quantities are not directly observable, we calibrate them on the validation set by grid search minimizing the position error between simulated and ground-truth outcomes. The simulation is run for the same duration as in data generation, yielding the predicted future state S1. To account for [20] perception uncertainty, we run N = 10 simulations with positions perturbed by Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is estimated from validation residuals, and aggregate the answers by majority vote. Answering. The program is executed symbolically on S1 by a deterministic executor in the manner of neuro-symbolic approaches (Yi et al., 2018), producing the final answer. Thus the only learned components are perception and parsing; the dynamics are provided by the physics engine. Baselines We compare against fully data-driven, end-to-end models. (1) A language-only baseline (LSTM) that answers using the question alone, which quantifies dataset bias. (2) CNN+LSTM, which concatenates image features from a ResNet-101 (He et al., 2016) with the question embedding. (3) CNN+LSTM+SA, which adds stacked attention Yang et al., 2016). (4) FiLM (Perez et al., 2018), which conditions convolutional features on the question. For all baselines, the action is part of the question text. We additionally evaluate an oracle variant of our model that receives ground-truth scene states, to separate perception errors from errors due to simulation mismatch, and an ablation that substitutes a learned dynamics network (an interaction network; Battaglia et al., 2016) for the physics engine, trained on the stored trajectories. Training Procedures Baselines are trained with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) at a learning rate of 1e-4, batch size 64, for up to 30 epochs with early stopping on validation accuracy. Image encoders are initialized from ImageNet pretraining and fine-tuned. Mask R-CNN is trained for 40 epochs with standard augmentation excluding flips, which would change the semantics of directional actions. Hyperparameters of baselines are tuned on the validation set. All neural models are trained with five random seeds. Evaluation and Statistical Analysis The primary metric is answer accuracy on the held-out test set, reported overall and per question family. For counting questions we additionally report mean absolute error. We report means and standard deviations across the five seeds for learned components; the deterministic simulator contributes variance only through the stochastic perturbations, which we also average over five runs. Differences between our model and the strongest baseline are assessed with a paired bootstrap test over test questions (10,000 resamples) and McNemar's test on per-question correctness, with a significance threshold of p < 0.01 after Bonferroni correction

Anaemia remains one of the [12] most prevalent nutritional and haematological disorders worldwide, and children in low- and middle-income countries carry a disproportionate share of the burden. The World Health Organization estimated that roughly one quarter of the global population, and approximately 40% of preschool children, were anaemic in 2011, with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (WHO, 2015). Although anaemia is aetiologically heterogeneous, iron deficiency is considered its single most important cause, and has been estimated to account for around half of all cases (Kassebaum, (5) 2016; Stevens et al., 2013). Clinically, anaemia presents with fatigue; lethargy, reduced exercise tolerance and increased physiological strain on the cardiovascular system, as the body compensates for diminished oxygen-carrying capacity. In children, however, the consequences may extend beyond haematological symptoms, because iron is also required for neuronal energy metabolism, myelination, neurotransmitter synthesis and dendritic development (Beard & Connor, 2003; Lozoff & Georgieff, 2006). Biological plausibility for an association [37] between iron status and neurodevelopment is substantial. Iron-dependent enzymes participate in dopaminergic, serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, which underpin attention, motor control and memory. Animal models and neuroimaging studies suggest that iron deficiency during sensitive periods of [28] brain growth produces changes in hippocampal structure and basal ganglia function that may persist after haematological correction (Lozoff, 2011; Lukowski et al., 2010). In humans, infants with iron deficiency anaemia have repeatedly been shown to exhibit poorer cognitive, motor and socio-emotional outcomes, and some of these deficits have been reported to persist into adolescence despite iron repletion (Lozoff et al., 2000; Lozoff, Jimenez, & Smith, 2006). Evidence for school-aged children "is" less consistent but nonetheless suggestive. Cross-sectional work from the United States linked iron deficiency, with However, or without anaemia, to lower mathematics scores (Halterman et al., 2001), [24] and trials in Indonesia and India reported improved attention, concentration or school [11] participation following iron supplementation (Sungthong et al., 2004; Bobonis, Miguel, & Puri-Sharma, 2006). A meta-analysis of randomised trials concluded [23] that iron supplementation improved global cognitive scores and attention in school-aged children, particularly among those who were anaemic at baseline (Low et al., 2013). Earlier reviews, however, emphasised methodological limitations, including small samples, short follow-up, heterogeneous outcome (17) measures and inadequate control of confounding (Grantham-McGregor & Ani, 2001). Confounding is a particular concern in settings where iron deficiency coexists with other adversities. Poverty, food insecurity, poor sanitation, limited caregiver education and chronic infection frequently cluster in the same households and independently impair child development (Walker et al., 2007). Soil-transmitted helminth infections are an important example. [15] Hookworm causes chronic intestinal blood loss, while Ascaris and Trichuris may impair nutrient absorption and appetite, so that helminth burden contributes to anaemia and may also directly influence growth and cognition (Stoltzfus et al., 1997; Bethony et al., 2006). Disentangling the contribution of iron [11] status (17) from that of infection and socioeconomic disadvantage therefore requires (14) concurrent [15] assessment of haematological, parasitological, anthropometric and contextual variables, an approach seldom adopted in school-based studies from the region. In South Africa, the policy context has [25] been shaped by national food fortification, introduced in 2003 with the mandatory addition of iron and other micronutrients to maize meal and wheat flour, alongside school feeding through the National School Nutrition [36] Programme. Nationally representative surveys have since indicated that anaemia remains a public health concern in young children, although prevalence estimates differ by survey year, age band and the cut-offs applied (Labadarios et al., 2011; Shisana et al., 2013). Importantly, national figures can mask marked within-country heterogeneity. Rural and peri-urban communities (5) in provinces such as KwaZulu-Natal combine high rates of poverty, household food insecurity, a heavy burden of HIV and tuberculosis, and endemic helminth transmission (Appleton et al., 2008). These conditions create a plausible setting for elevated rates of iron deficiency [36] [20] and iron deficiency anaemia, yet locally derived estimates for (9) primary school-aged children are scarce. Most South African studies of iron status have focused on infants, pregnant women or adolescent girls, leaving the early school years, when formal learning begins and cognitive demands escalate, comparatively under-investigated. This evidence gap matters for several reasons. First, children from disadvantaged communities frequently fail to attain their (27) age-appropriate educational potential, and grade repetition (9) and early school leaving remain persistent problems in South Africa, with consequences for lifelong health and economic productivity. Second, iron deficiency is potentially modifiable through low-cost interventions, including dietary diversification, targeted supplementation and deworming, so that even modest effects on learning could be of considerable public health importance. Third, assessment of whether anaemia and iron deficiency are associated with developmental and educational outcomes (5) in (14) this age group [24] is essential for determining whether school health programmes should include haematological screening or iron-focused interventions. [1] In the absence of context-specific data, South African policy must extrapolate from studies conducted in settings that differ in diet, infectious disease ecology and educational systems. A further limitation of the existing literature is that anaemia and iron deficiency are often conflated. Haemoglobin concentration is a late and non-specific indicator of iron depletion, whereas ferritin, transferrin saturation and soluble transferrin receptor provide information on iron stores and iron-restricted erythropoiesis, albeit with the complication that ferritin behaves as an acute-phase reactant [25] and rises with (4) inflammation. However, Studies relying on haemoglobin alone may therefore misclassify children and attenuate or obscure true associations. Likewise, studies examining a single outcome, such as an intelligence quotient score, may overlook domain-specific effects on fine motor coordination, memory, attention or [6] "behaviour," which may be more sensitive to iron status and more directly relevant to classroom functioning (Lozoff, 2007). Against this background, the present study investigated anaemia (2) and iron status in children aged 6 to 8 years attending school in a peri-urban, disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Its first objective was to estimate the point prevalence of anaemia, iron deficiency, iron deficiency anaemia and helminth infection. Its second objective was to examine whether anaemia and iron status were associated with psychomotor development, including cognitive performance, fine motor skills, memory, attention and behaviour. Its third was to determine whether these haematological variables, together with helminth infection, predicted school performance as reported by teachers, caregivers and the children themselves. We conceptualised anaemia and iron deficiency as mediating variables through which environmental and nutritional exposures influence growth, development and educational outcomes, and we combined clinical, biochemical and educational data to capture this pathway. This study makes three contributions. It provides current, locally grounded prevalence estimates for a population under-represented in national surveys. It integrates iron biomarkers, parasitological screening and (28) multi-informant educational assessment within a single design, thereby allowing the relative roles of anaemia, iron deficiency and helminth infection to be considered concurrently. Finally, it documents the practical and methodological challenges of conducting health and education research in rural South African schools, including consent procedures, sampling, laboratory logistics and the statistical constraints of low outcome prevalence, with the aim of informing the design of adequately powered future studies. Study design and setting We conducted a cross-sectional, "school-based" study in a peri-urban, socioeconomically disadvantaged community in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. The area is characterised by high unemployment, reliance on social grants, and limited access to piped water and sanitation, which together create conditions conducive to both nutritional anaemia and soil-transmitted helminth transmission (Labadarios et al., 2005; Hotez et al., 2006). The study was guided by a conceptual framework in which anaemia and iron deficiency were treated as hypothesised mediating variables through which socioeconomic disadvantage, nutritional status and parasitic infection influence physical growth, psychomotor development and school performance (Lozoff et al., 2006; Walker et al., 2007). The study is reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies (von Elm et al., 2007). Participants and sampling Eligible participants were children aged 6 to 8 years enrolled in the participating no-fee public primary schools and living within the catchment community. Children were excluded if they had a known haemoglobinopathy, chronic systemic illness, or neurodevelopmental disorder diagnosed before enrolment, or if they had received iron supplementation or anthelminthic treatment in the preceding four weeks. Schools were purposively selected on the basis of accessibility and quintile ranking, and children were then recruited from Grade 1 and Grade 2 class lists. Information sheets and consent forms in isiZulu and English were sent home via the schools. The target sample size was calculated for estimating prevalence with a specified precision, using the formula n = Z²p(1 − p)/d². Assuming an anaemia prevalence of 20%, a 95% confidence level and an absolute precision of 6%, the minimum sample was 171 children. This was inflated to allow for non-response and incomplete [11] data. A total of 184 children were enrolled and constituted the analytic sample. We note that the sample was powered for prevalence estimation rather than for detecting associations between exposure and the less common developmental and educational outcomes, and the analyses of associations should be regarded as exploratory. Data collection procedures Three domains of data were collected: clinical, biochemical, and school performance. Data collection took place at the schools during school hours in private rooms allocated for the purpose. Fieldworkers, comprising a paediatrician, registered nurses and a trained psychometrist fluent in isiZulu, underwent standardisation training before fieldwork. Instruments not available in isiZulu were translated and back-translated by independent bilingual speakers, and the translations were piloted on a [2] small group of children outside the study sample. Clinical data. Caregivers were interviewed by trained fieldworkers using a structured questionnaire covering household demographics, caregiver education, household income and assets, food security, water and sanitation facilities, breastfeeding history, birth history, and the child’s past medical history. A socioeconomic index was derived from household assets and services. Each child underwent a standardised physical examination. Weight was measured to the nearest 0.1 kg using a calibrated electronic scale, and height to the nearest 0.1 cm using a portable stadiometer, with children wearing light clothing and no shoes. Height-for-age and body-mass-index-for-age z-scores were computed against the WHO growth reference for school-aged children (de Onis et al., 2007), and stunting and thinness were defined as z-scores below −2. Clinical pallor was recorded but was not used for case definition. Biochemical data. Haemoglobin concentration was measured at the point of care from a capillary sample using a HemoCue Hb 201+ photometer (HemoCue AB, Ängelholm, Sweden), which has acceptable agreement with reference laboratory methods (Neufeld et al., 2019). Anaemia was defined according to WHO criteria as a haemoglobin concentration below 11.5 g/dL for children aged 5 to 11 years (WHO, 2011a), with mild, moderate and severe categories defined as 11.0–11.4, 8.0–10.9 and below 8.0 g/dL respectively. A venous blood sample was drawn by a registered nurse, stored on ice, and transported to an accredited laboratory within four hours. Serum ferritin, serum iron, transferrin and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured by automated immunoassay and colorimetric methods, and transferrin saturation was calculated. Iron deficiency was defined as a serum ferritin concentration below 15 µg/L (WHO, 2011b) or transferrin saturation below 16%. Because ferritin is an acute-phase protein, children with CRP above 5 mg/L were considered to have inflammation, and in these children ferritin below 70 µg/L was interpreted as indicating iron deficiency in line with recommended approaches (Thurnham et al., 2010; WHO, 2020). Iron deficiency anaemia was defined as the co-occurrence of anaemia and iron deficiency. Stool specimens were collected in labelled containers and examined within 24 hours using the Kato-Katz thick-smear technique (Katz et al., 1972) for Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura and hookworm. A child was classified as helminth-infected if ova of any species were detected. All children with anaemia, iron deficiency or helminth infection were referred to the local clinic for treatment according to national guidelines, and children with infection received albendazole. Psychomotor and cognitive assessment. Cognitive ability was assessed using Raven’s Coloured Progressive Matrices, a non-verbal test of reasoning that minimises linguistic and cultural bias (Raven et al., 1998). Raw scores were converted to age-referenced standard scores, and scores more than one standard deviation below the mean were classified

Infliximab, a chimeric IgG1 monoclonal antibody against tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), was one of the first biologic agents to change the treatment of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. Randomised trials established its efficacy in Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Targan et al., 1997; Maini et al., 1999; Rutgeerts et al., 2005). It is now also used for ankylosing spondylitis (AS), psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and plaque psoriasis. These agents have improved disease control and reduced the need for surgery and hospitalisation. Their cost, however, places a considerable burden on health systems and has limited access in many settings. As patents and exclusivity periods on reference biologics expire, biosimilar versions have been developed to broaden access and generate savings. CT-P13 was the first biosimilar monoclonal antibody approved by the European Medicines Agency, in 2013, and was followed by additional infliximab biosimilars in Europe and the United States. Biosimilars are not generic drugs. Small-molecule generics are chemically identical to their reference products. Biologics are large, structurally complex proteins produced in living cell systems, and their characteristics depend on the cell line and manufacturing process. Even a reference product shows some batch-to-batch variability, for example in glycosylation, so a biosimilar can be highly similar to its reference but cannot be an exact copy (Kurki et al., 2017). Regulatory approval therefore rests on a stepwise comparability exercise. It combines extensive analytical and functional characterisation with non-clinical and pharmacokinetic studies, and usually at least one adequately powered comparative clinical trial. The aim of this exercise is to show no clinically meaningful differences in quality, safety or efficacy. The pivotal infliximab studies, PLANETAS in AS and PLANETRA in RA, demonstrated pharmacokinetic equivalence and comparable efficacy and safety over the study period (Park et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2013). These trials mainly addressed initiation of therapy or continued dosing of one product, and they were not designed to answer what happens when a patient moves between products. Switching has become common in practice. Many patients have been stable on reference infliximab for years, and payers, hospitals and national tender systems increasingly move them to a biosimilar for economic reasons. This kind of non-medical switching raises questions that approval studies of biosimilars in treatment-naïve or newly started patients do not fully address. Infliximab is immunogenic, and anti-drug antibodies can accelerate clearance, reduce clinical response and cause infusion reactions (Baert et al., 2003). Because small structural differences could in principle alter immunogenic epitopes, concern has been raised that exposing a patient alternately to two similar but non-identical molecules might provoke new antibody formation or loss of response. Evidence that antibodies to reference infliximab cross-react with CT-P13 in vitro suggests the products share dominant epitopes (Ben-Horin et al., 2016). Such in vitro data do not show what happens in patients over time, and they do not settle whether multiple transitions carry additional risk. Perception-related effects must also be considered. Open-label switching can cause patients to report subjective worsening or discontinue treatment because of negative expectations, a nocebo effect that makes interpretation of uncontrolled switching data difficult. Regulatory frameworks treat switching and interchangeability differently. The European Medicines Agency evaluates biosimilarity but has historically left decisions on substitution and switching to individual Member States and clinicians. In the United States, the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act created a separate "interchangeable" designation. It allows pharmacy-level substitution without prescriber intervention under state law, and it requires that a product be expected to produce the same clinical result as the reference in any patient and, if administered more than once, that the risk of alternating or switching not exceed the risk of (24) continuing the reference product. Consistent with this, the US Food and Drug Administration guidance on demonstrating interchangeability recommends that sponsors normally conduct a switching study with multiple alternations between reference and proposed product. It also recommends a sufficiently [3] sensitive population and pharmacokinetic endpoints, with comparison against patients who remain on the reference product (16) (US FDA, 2019). The guidance thus sets [32] a high evidentiary standard, involving repeated switches and a control group, that most of the existing clinical literature on infliximab was not designed to meet. Professional societies in gastroenterology and rheumatology have acknowledged that evidence on switching is incomplete, and they have generally accepted a single, physician-managed switch from reference infliximab to a biosimilar while advising caution about multiple or non-medically driven switches (Danese et al., 2017). The NOR-SWITCH trial, a randomised, double-blind, non-inferiority study, found that switching from reference infliximab to CT-P13 was not inferior to continued reference treatment in terms of disease worsening across several diagnoses, although it was not powered to show equivalence within individual diseases (Jørgensen et al., 2017). Since then, many randomised trials, extension studies, registry analyses and single-centre cohorts have reported outcomes after switching in CD, UC, RA, AS, PsA and psoriasis. Most are observational, uncontrolled, short in follow-up (16) and heterogeneous in design, switching conditions, outcome definitions and concomitant therapy. Much of the information is also available only in congress abstracts, which makes the literature difficult to assemble and appraise. Clinicians, formulary committees and regulators therefore lack a consolidated view of how far the evidence supports the safety and efficacy of switching, and how closely it matches the conditions in which interchangeability is defined. This systematic review addresses that gap. Its question is whether switching patients between reference infliximab and its biosimilars, in either direction, (11) is associated with changes in efficacy, safety, immunogenicity or drug exposure in patients with inflammatory disorders. We searched the published literature and relevant congress abstracts for studies However, that reported switching data across all approved indications of infliximab. We describe the study designs and populations, the number and type of switches and the follow-up, (24) and we compare the findings with the evidence standard (16) described [26] in regulatory guidance. The review makes three contributions. First, it brings together journal and congress data across gastroenterology, rheumatology and dermatology, which have typically been considered separately. Second, it distinguishes randomised, controlled evidence from uncontrolled observational findings and so shows how much of the reassurance comes from each source. Third, it identifies limitations in the current evidence, particularly the scarcity of data on [24] multiple or [28] alternating switches, and highlights the populations and scenarios in which further research is [28] needed to establish interchangeability. Study design and reporting We conducted a systematic review of published evidence on switching between reference infliximab (Remicade, originator) and its biosimilars (CT-P13 and SB2, including the products marketed under various trade names) in patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases. The review was planned and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement.[1] The review question was framed with reference to the [32] US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) draft guidance on interchangeability. [24] This guidance states (15) that, to support a designation of interchangeability, a sponsor should show that the biosimilar produces the same clinical result as the reference product in any given patient, and that the risk of alternating or switching between the two products is not greater than the risk of continuing the reference product.[2] We therefore extracted data that bore on the safety, efficacy, immunogenicity and pharmacokinetics of switching, and recorded the number and direction of switches in each study. Eligibility criteria We considered studies of patients of any age with Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis or plaque psoriasis. These are the principal indications for infliximab, and the review covered the indications for which both the reference product and biosimilars are approved. Eligible studies reported outcomes in patients who were switched from reference infliximab to a biosimilar. Studies that also included switches from a biosimilar back to the reference product, or between biosimilars, were eligible if the outcomes of the switch were reported. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including open-label extension phases of RCTs with a switching component, as well as non-randomised interventional studies, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, registry analyses, case series and (22) pharmacokinetic studies. Case reports, narrative reviews, editorials, commentaries, in vitro studies and studies of patients who started biosimilar treatment without switching were excluded. We also excluded studies that did not report switching outcomes separately from outcomes in biologic-naive patients, as well as studies of non-infliximab biologics. We did not restrict studies by sample size, follow-up duration or country. Only English-language full-text articles and abstracts were considered. Information sources and search strategy Published journal articles were identified by searching MEDLINE (via PubMed). The strategy combined controlled vocabulary and free-text terms for infliximab and its biosimilar products (for example, infliximab, CT-P13, SB2, "Remsima", Inflectra, "Flixabi", biosimilar) with terms for switching and related concepts ("switch", switching, "transition", "interchang", substitut, non-medical switch, conversion). We did not apply a limit on publication date at the lower bound, although biosimilar infliximab had been available only since the early 2010s. Reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant review articles were hand-searched to identify additional eligible reports. Because much of the available switching evidence was expected to appear first, or only, in congress presentations, we also searched for abstracts. EMBASE was searched using equivalent terms, restricted to conference abstracts. We manually searched the abstract archives and proceedings of relevant congresses for the most recent years in which biosimilar switching data were available. These included meetings of the European Crohn's and Colitis Organisation, Digestive Disease Week, United European Gastroenterology Week, the American College of Gastroenterology, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR), the American College of Rheumatology and the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology. Where an abstract was later published in full, we treated the full article as the primary source and used the abstract only to supplement information that was not otherwise reported. Abstracts that duplicated one another, or that reported interim data (9) from a study already included, were merged to avoid double counting of patients. Study selection All records were exported to reference management software and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts were screened against the eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially relevant journal articles, and the full abstracts of congress records, were then assessed. For each excluded full-text record, the primary reason for exclusion was documented. Disagreements about eligibility were resolved by discussion and, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. The numbers of records identified, screened, assessed for eligibility and included were tabulated and summarised in a PRISMA flow diagram. Data extraction A standardised extraction form was developed and piloted on a subset of studies. For each included study we extracted the following: first author, year and type of publication (journal article or abstract); study design (RCT, open-label extension, prospective or retrospective observational study, registry); country or countries; disease population; number of patients switched; the nature of the switch (reference to biosimilar, biosimilar to reference, or multiple switches); the presence and type of a control group (such as patients continuing on reference product); [31] duration of follow-up; and whether the switch was mandated by protocol, driven by non-medical policy or made by clinician and patient choice. Efficacy outcomes were extracted as reported, using disease-specific measures. These included clinical remission and response, Harvey–Bradshaw Index, Crohn's Disease Activity Index, partial Mayo score, Disease Activity Score in 28 joints, Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index, Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, C-reactive protein, faecal calprotectin, and rates of drug persistence or discontinuation. Safety outcomes comprised adverse events, serious (3) adverse events, infusion reactions, infections and discontinuations due to adverse events. Immunogenicity outcomes comprised the incidence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising (29) antibodies, with the assay used. Pharmacokinetic outcomes included (10) trough serum infliximab concentrations before and after switching. Where available we also recorded the definitions of the outcomes and the time points of [22] assessment. Assessment of study quality Because the (8) review was expected to include mostly uncontrolled observational data, we described the strength of the evidence (10) in terms of design features rather than excluding studies on quality grounds.
