Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are now deployed in a wide range of settings, including voice search, dictation, and conversational assistants on mobile and embedded devices. In these settings, what a user is likely to say depends strongly on the context in which she speaks. A request such as "call Jason" is only recognizable if the system has some knowledge of the contacts stored on the user's phone, and "play Anomalisa" is only plausible if that title is a candidate in the user's media library or a recent query. The same acoustic signal can therefore warrant different transcriptions in However, different contexts. This is especially true for rare words, proper names, and other terms that are scarce or absent in the text used to [35] train the recognizer's language model. Such terms are often the most important words in an utterance because they carry the entities on which downstream actions depend. Errors [24] on them are disproportionately costly (Aleksic et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015). In conventional ASR systems, contextual information is typically represented as a set of words or word n-grams (phrases) that are relevant to the current user, device state, or dialogue turn. These phrases are incorporated by dynamically biasing the language model during decoding. A common approach compiles the phrases into a weighted finite-state transducer (WFST), or an equivalent n-gram model, which is combined on the fly with the static language model, boosting hypotheses that match the contextual entries (Aleksic et al., 2015, Hall et al., 2015). Pronunciations of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) context terms can be obtained from a grapheme-to-phoneme system or a learned pronunciation model (Bruguier et al., 2016). This design is effective because the acoustic model, pronunciation lexicon, and language model are separate components, and the language model can be modified at inference time without retraining anything else. The cost is that the modules are trained independently, with different objectives, and are only loosely coordinated at test time through hand-tuned interpolation weights and boosting factors. Recent work has moved toward sequence-to-sequence models that [20] fold the acoustic, pronunciation, and language modeling components into a single neural network trained end [38] to end (E2E). Examples include connectionist temporal classification (CTC, Graves et al., 2006), the recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T; Graves, 2012), and attention-based encoder–decoder models such as [3] Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS; Chan et al., 2016; Chorowski et al., 2015). When trained on sufficient data, E2E models have matched or exceeded the accuracy of strong conventional systems on large-vocabulary tasks (Chiu et al., 2018; Prabhavalkar et al., 2017). They also have a much smaller footprint, because they do not require a separate [12] lexicon, decision tree, or large decoding graph. This makes them attractive for on-device recognition (He et al., 2019). The same integration, however, makes contextualization harder. An E2E model has no explicit language model or lexicon that can be modified at inference [25] time. Its implicit language model is learned from the transcribed audio–text pairs alone, which are far fewer than the text-only corpora available However, to conventional systems. Rare words and OOV terms that never appear in training are therefore difficult for E2E models to recognize without external help. The most common remedy is to import the conventional technique directly. An external language model, or an n-gram model built from the context phrases, is trained independently and combined with the E2E model's output scores during beam search, usually by log-linear interpolation known as shallow fusion (Gülçehre et al., 2015; Kannan et al., 2018, Toshniwal et al., 2018). This approach is simple and keeps the base model unchanged, but it inherits the weaknesses of modular design. The E2E model is not trained to exploit the contextual information, and the external model has no access to the acoustic evidence or to the model's internal state. The fusion weight is a single global hyperparameter that must trade off accuracy on contextual phrases against regressions on utterances where the context is irrelevant. Moreover, shallow fusion with word-level or phrase-level n-grams must operate on the sub-word units (such as graphemes or word pieces) emitted by the E2E decoder. This requires the context to be composed with the model's output space and makes biasing sensitive to the beam search and to early pruning of However, correct but initially low-scoring hypotheses. This leaves a gap. We lack an E2E recognizer that treats contextual information as an input that the network itself learns to use, rather than as an external score added after the fact. Such a model would be trained so that its acoustic and language modeling behavior is conditioned on arbitrary, variable-sized sets of phrases supplied at inference time, including phrases containing words never seen in training. Doing so raises several questions. Can a single network learn when and how to use context, so that it improves recognition of contextual phrases without degrading performance when the context is irrelevant or empty? Can the representation of the context be learned jointly with the recognizer, so that no pronunciation dictionary or separate biasing model is needed? And does such joint optimization yield better accuracy than the standard practice of independently trained components combined during decoding? In this paper we address these questions with Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS), an all-neural E2E contextual ASR system. CLAS extends the LAS architecture with a context encoder that embeds each context phrase, represented as a sequence of sub-word units, into a fixed-dimensional vector. An additional attention mechanism lets the decoder attend over these phrase embeddings at every output step, alongside its attention over the acoustic encoding. Because the embeddings are computed from the phrases' sub-word spellings, any phrase can be embedded at inference time, including phrases with OOV words. The context encoder, the attention modules, and the standard LAS components are optimized jointly with a single cross-entropy objective. To make the model learn to use context, we simulate contextual information during training by sampling phrases from the reference transcripts and adding distractors, so the model must determine from the audio which phrases are relevant. We also introduce a mechanism that lets the model ignore the context entirely when it does not help. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we present CLAS, a unified E2E architecture that incorporates arbitrary lists of context n-grams without a separate language model, lexicon, or pronunciation model. Second, we describe a training procedure that exposes the model to randomly sampled contextual phrases and distractors, enabling it to generalize to new phrases, including OOV terms, at test time. Third, we compare CLAS with a strong baseline that applies on-the-fly shallow-fusion biasing to an independently trained LAS model, following the established practice for conventional and E2E systems. We evaluate both on several tasks covering different types of context, such as contact names, media requests, and location queries. Across these tasks, CLAS consistently outperforms the shallow-fusion baseline, reducing word [28] error rate (WER) by as much as 68% relative. These results indicate that jointly optimizing the recognizer together with the representation of its context is more effective than combining separately trained components at inference time. Model architecture. We build on the Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) framework (Chan et al., 2016), an attention-based encoder-decoder that models the posterior of a wordpiece sequence y = (y1, …, yT) given acoustic features x as P(y|x) = ∏t P(yt | y<t, x). The input features are 80-dimensional log-Mel filterbank energies computed over 25 ms windows every 10 ms. Three consecutive frames are stacked and sub-sampled to a 30 ms frame rate. The encoder is a stack of unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layers (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) that maps the features to a sequence of hidden states h = (h1, …, hK). At each output step t, the decoder state dt is computed by a multi-layer LSTM from the previous embedded wordpiece and the previous attention context. Attention weights over the encoder states are obtained with an additive scoring function (Bahdanau et al., 2015), ut^k = v^T tanh(Wh hk + Wd dt), normalized by a softmax over k. The acoustic context vector ct is the attention-weighted sum of h. The decoder state and ct are concatenated and passed through a softmax layer over a vocabulary of 4,096 wordpieces (Schuster and Nakajima, 2012), which allows arbitrary words, including those unseen in training, to be composed from sub-word units. The proposed Contextual LAS (CLAS) extends this model with a bias-encoder and a second attention module. At inference time, CLAS receives a list of N context phrases P = {p1, …, pN}, such as contact names, song titles or application names. Each phrase is tokenized into wordpieces and embedded, and the embedded sequence is passed through a single-layer LSTM. The final hidden state of this LSTM serves as a fixed-dimensional embedding bi of phrase pi. We also include a learned no-bias embedding b0, which lets the model decline to use any phrase when the context is irrelevant to the utterance (for example, when no relevant phrase is present in P). At each step the decoder attends over {b0, b1, …, bN} with a second additive attention, ut^i = vb^T tanh(Wb bi + Ws dt), which yields a context vector ct^b. The decoder then conditions on the concatenation [dt; ct; ct^b], so that P(yt | y<t, x, P) is computed with explicit access to the context. Because the phrase embeddings are produced by a sub-word-level encoder, phrases containing out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words can [10] be embedded without modification. All components (the audio encoder, the decoder, both attention modules and the bias-encoder) are trained jointly by maximizing the log-likelihood of the reference transcripts. Training data and bias-phrase simulation. Models were trained on approximately 35 million anonymized, hand-transcribed English utterances (about 27,500 hours) from voice-search and dictation traffic. To improve robustness, we used multi-style training in which clean utterances were corrupted with simulated room reverberation and additive background noise (Kim et al., 2017), with signal-to-noise ratios between 0 and 30 dB. Training transcripts do not come with natural context lists, so we simulated them. For each training utterance, we sampled a random number of n-grams (n between 1 and 4) from the reference transcript, with a fixed per-utterance probability of selecting any bias phrases at all. This ensures that the model sees utterances both with and without relevant context. To teach the model to discriminate between relevant and irrelevant phrases, we padded each list with distractor n-grams sampled from the transcripts of other utterances in the same mini-batch, up [8] to a fixed list size per example. The number of phrases per utterance was varied during training so that the model would generalize across a range of list sizes at test time. "Because" the reference n-grams are drawn from natural speech, the model learns the general relationship between the biasing list and the audio, rather than memorizing specific phrases. This design is what allows phrases not observed during training to be exploited at inference. Baseline. The baseline was a LAS model with [32] the same acoustic encoder and decoder configuration as CLAS but without the bias-encoder, trained on the identical data and with the same optimization [9] settings. Contextualization was performed at decoding time using shallow fusion (Gülçehre et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2018) with [39] an on-the-fly contextual language model, following the biasing approach used in conventional ASR (Aleksic et al., 2015, Hall et al., 2015). The context n-grams were compiled into a weighted finite-state transducer (FST) acceptor over words, composed with a speller FST that maps wordpiece sequences to words. During beam search, the hypothesis score was the sum of the LAS log-probability and λ times the contextual LM log-probability, with However, λ tuned on a held-out development set for each task. Because the speller transducer operates on wordpieces, this baseline can also produce phrases with OOV words. Since the contextual LM is built only from the n-grams in P, it contributes no information about the acoustics and cannot be optimized jointly with LAS, which is the fundamental difference from CLAS. Psychological therapy now occupies a central place in the organization of public mental healthcare in the United Kingdom. Much of this prominence stems from a single initiative: the Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme, launched in England in 2008 and rebranded in 2023 as NHS Talking Therapies. IAPT was designed to expand the provision of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence NICE)-recommended interventions, notably cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), for people diagnosed with depression and anxiety disorders (Clark, 2011). By the late 2010s, well over a million people were being referred to IAPT services each year, and the programme had been identified as a cornerstone of national mental health policy (NHS England, 2016, 2019). For many citizens, therapy is therefore no longer a marginal, privately purchased or specialist offering. It is a routinely available, publicly funded, and statistically monitored component of everyday healthcare. This development is striking given the longer history of psychological expertise in Britain. Psychological disciplines have long shaped how selves, distress, and conduct are understood and governed (Rose, 1985, 1996), and the 'therapeutic' has been identified as a pervasive cultural register through which suffering is framed (Illouz, 2008). Yet, for much of the twentieth century, the delivery of talking therapies within the National Health Service (NHS) was patchy, locally variable, and often subordinate to pharmacological and custodial approaches. That a psychological intervention could become infrastructural to a national health system, with explicit targets for access and outcome, thus warrants sustained analytic attention. It raises the question of how psychological therapy came to be configured as a public good and a legitimate object of national investment, and with what consequences for the knowledge and practices of mental healthcare itself. Existing scholarship has examined IAPT from several vantage points. Evaluative literatures, produced largely by the programme's architects and affiliated clinicians, document reported outcomes: recovery rates approaching the 50% target, and an expansion in access towards a goal of reaching 25% of the estimated population with common mental disorders (Clark et al., 2018; NHS England, 2019). Critical commentators in psychology, psychotherapy studies, and sociology have, in contrast, questioned the programme's evidence base and cost-effectiveness claims (Griffiths and Steen, 2013), its narrow therapeutic repertoire and apparent privileging of CBT (Pilgrim, 2011; House and Loewenthal, 2008), and the effects of performance measurement on clinical work and practitioner subjectivity (Rizq, 2012; Scott, 2018). These contributions are valuable. However, they tend either to take IAPT's founding rationale as given or to treat it as an instance of broader neoliberal or managerial trends, rather than examining empirically how the initiative's rationale was assembled, justified, and stabilized over time. Less attention has been paid to the specific configurations of expertise, evidence, and accountability through which IAPT became thinkable and, subsequently, durable. The case also speaks to wider debates in the sociology of health and illness regarding the trajectory of biomedicine. Concepts such as medicalization and biomedicalization have been used to describe the expanding jurisdiction of medical authority and its reconstitution through technoscientific practices (Conrad, 2007, Clarke et al., 2003). In mental health specifically, scholars have charted the ascendancy of neuroscientific and biological framings, as well as their uneven uptake and contestation (Rose and Abi-Rached, 2013; Pickersgill, 2013). Against this background, the rise of a psychologically oriented intervention might be read as a partial debiomedicalization: a movement away from drug-based, brain-centred models towards talk, cognition, and behaviour. Yet such a reading risks assuming linear, directional change in health systems. If psychological therapy has been re-legitimized, we must ask on what terms, and whether the resources used to do so are in fact characteristically [31] biomedical. This article addresses these concerns through an analysis of how IAPT was developed, accounted for, and sustained as a national response to mental ill-health. Drawing on policy documents, economic reports, clinical guidelines, and published evaluations, I trace the problematization (in the sense developed by Foucault and elaborated by Rabinow and Rose) of [37] common mental disorders as a challenge simultaneously clinical, economic, and political. The analysis attends in particular to the role of economic expertise, exemplified by the influential case for expanded therapy articulated by Layard and colleagues (Layard, 2006; Layard et al., 2007). Here, the costs of unemployment, sickness absence, and welfare dependency associated with depression and anxiety were rendered commensurable with the costs of therapy, such that treatment could be presented as self-financing. Such calculative forms of reasoning have been shown to be performative, shaping the very realities they purport to describe (Callon, 1998; Miller and Rose, 1990). I argue that, in the case of IAPT, they were joined to particular accounts of pathology and mechanisms of therapeutic change, and to forms of evidence, most notably the randomized controlled trial (RCT) and its attendant hierarchy of knowledge, that are more familiar within biomedical settings (Timmermans and Berg, 2003). The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides an empirically grounded account of the emergence of IAPT that foregrounds the co-production of economic argument, psychological knowledge, and policy rationale, thereby extending analyses of audit and accountability in public services (Power, 1997; Strathern, 2000; Porter, 1995) into the domain of psychological therapy. Second, it demonstrates that the revival of psychological framings of distress has proceeded through, rather than against, biomedical epistemic and administrative forms. This complicates narratives of linear biomedicalization or debiomedicalization and instead suggests more entangled, mutually conditioning dynamics. Third, I introduce the concept of contextification to describe a process by which IAPT has shifted from being primarily a content of mental healthcare (a set of interventions delivered within services) to a context for it: an organizing presence in relation to which other services, pathways, and professional identities are increasingly designed, justified, and evaluated. Understanding this transformation matters for anyone concerned with how mental health provision is currently being reshaped. By documenting these developments, the paper contributes to re-centring questions about the place and role of psychology within contemporary healthcare, a topic that has been overshadowed in social science by the prominence of psychiatry and neuroscience. In what follows, I first outline the conceptual resources on which the analysis draws, before describing the materials and methods employed. I then examine in turn [26] the problematization of common mental disorders, the formation [37] of IAPT's evidential and economic justification, and the mechanisms through which the programme has been sustained and extended. I conclude by considering the implications of contextification for the future of psychological therapy and for theorizing change in health systems. Research design and analytic approach This study adopts a problematization-oriented, mixed-methods documentary design to examine how IAPT was formulated, justified, and stabilized as a national response to mental ill-health. The analytic orientation draws on Foucauldian studies of governmentality (Rose, 1999; Miller and Rose, 2008) and on the What's the problem represented to be?" approach to policy analysis (Bacchi, 2009), which treats policies as proposals that constitute the problems they [15] claim to address. Following sociological work on biomedicalization (Clarke et al., 2003) and on the sociology [25] of expertise, I was particularly attentive to how psychological, economic, and biomedical forms of knowledge were combined and to the evidentiary practices [25] used to link them. The design had three components: (1) a qualitative analysis of policy and expert documents, (2) a supplementary set of semi-structured interviews, and (3) a quantitative descriptive analysis of publicly available IAPT activity and outcome data. Their purposes were respectively to reconstruct the problematization, to examine how it was understood and sustained by those involved in it, and to assess how far its institutional prominence was reflected in service-level trends. Components were integrated sequentially. Documentary analysis informed the interview schedule, and the quantitative analysis was used to contextualize and test claims that emerged in the qualitative material (Fetters et al., 2013). Documentary corpus Documents were identified through a purposive, iterative strategy designed to capture the period between the first public articulation of the programme's rationale and its integration into wider system planning (2004–2021). I began with canonical texts, notably the Depression Report Layard et al., 2006) and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence [32] guidance on depression and anxiety, and then followed citation and reference trails forward and backward ("snowball" [36] sampling; Bowen, 2009). Further [24] material was retrieved from the UK Government Web Archive, Department of Health and NHS England repositories, Hansard, the National Audit Office, the Health Select Committee, and the websites of professional bodies and charities. Search terms included "Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, IAPT, "talking therapies," "cognitive behavioural therapy," "Increasing Access," and "Layard." Documents were included if they (a) set out the rationale, design, evaluation, or expansion of IAPT or (b) positioned other mental health services in relation to it. Duplicates, press releases without substantive content, and purely operational guidance (e.g. rota or commissioning templates) were excluded. This produced a corpus of 214 documents: 61 [36] national policy and strategy documents, 38 commissioning and service specifications, 29 evaluation and audit reports, 34 peer-reviewed articles and commentaries by programme architects and critics, [12] 27 parliamentary records, and 25 professional-body and third-sector publications. Following Prior's (2003) emphasis on documents as active agents in organizational fields rather than neutral containers of information, I paid close attention to document genre, authorship, intended audience, and intertextual relations (what each text cited, and how it was cited [10] by subsequent texts). Because publicly available documents [18] necessarily reflect curated and strategic representations, I treated them as evidence of how the programme was publicly accounted for, not as transparent records of internal deliberation (Scott, 1990). Interviews To complement the documentary record, I conducted 19 semi-structured interviews between March 2019 and [8] February 2020 with individuals purposively sampled for their involvement in IAPT's development, delivery, or critique: national policy officials and advisers (n = [5] 5), clinical and academic leads (n = 6), service managers and commissioners (n = [20] 5), and representatives of professional or service-user organizations (n = 3). Participants were approached by email and through snowball referral. Interviews lasted [22] 42–94 minutes mean = 63), were conducted in person or by video call, and were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The schedule covered participants' accounts of the programme's origins, the role of evidence and economic argument in its [36] justification, perceived changes in the relationship between IAPT and other services, and the principal points of contention. Because several participants held prominent roles, I report findings in ways that prevent identification, referring to broad role categories only and removing identifying details. Interview material was used primarily to interpret and triangulate the documentary analysis, not as an independent evidentiary base, and its limited scale does not support claims of representativeness. Qualitative analysis Documents and transcripts were imported into NVivo 12 and analyzed through a combination of theory-informed and inductive coding. An initial round of open coding on a 20% stratified sample of documents generated a provisional framework, which was refined through discussion with two colleagues who independently coded a further 10% of the corpus. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and the framework was revised accordingly. Inter-coder agreement on the final framework, assessed on a further 10% subsample, was acceptable (Cohen's κ = 0.78). The remaining material was then coded by me. Codes were organized around four analytic domains: representations of the problem (how mental ill-health and its costs were defined), representations of the solution (how therapy, and CBT in particular, was characterized), evidentiary practices (the types of evidence invoked, such as randomized controlled trials, health-economic modelling, and routine outcome data), and relational positioning how IAPT was situated relative to other services, professions, and policy agendas). I then traced these domains chronologically, in line with the temporal focus of the study, and compared across document genres to identify points of stabilization, translation, and contestation. Reflexive thematic analysis principles (Braun and Clarke, 2006) guided the move from codes to themes, and I kept an analytic memo log to document interpretive decisions. Negative cases, such as documents critical of or ambivalent about the programme's framing, were deliberately sought and retained to avoid a purely confirmatory reading. Ad-hoc information retrieval (IR) has long been characterized by a diversity of ranking methods whose relative merits vary across queries. Probabilistic and language-modeling approaches such as BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (Zhai and Lafferty, 2004) remain strong, efficient baselines. Pretrained transformers, most prominently BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), have since reshaped the field. Applied as re-rankers (Nogueira and Cho, 2019; Dai and Callan, 2019), they yield large average gains on benchmarks such as MS MARCO. Average gains conceal substantial per-query variance, however. Neural re-rankers can underperform simple lexical baselines on individual queries, and sometimes on entire collections when evaluated outside their training distribution (Yang et al., 2019; Lin, 2019, Thakur et al., 2021). A practitioner who wants robust effectiveness therefore faces a question that mean performance does not answer: for this particular query, which method should be trusted? This question is an instance of the algorithm selection problem (Rice, 1976), in which a meta-level model uses instance features to choose, or combine, algorithms from a portfolio (Kotthoff, 2014). In IR, related ideas appear in several forms. Rank fusion and data fusion combine the outputs of multiple systems with query-independent rules such as CombSUM or reciprocal rank fusion (Fox and Shaw, 1994, Cormack et al., 2009). Selective query expansion, retrieval-model selection, and ranker selection instead make query-dependent decisions, typically using "query" performance prediction (QPP) signals such as clarity, collection statistics, or score distributions (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002, Balasubramanian and Allan, 2010; Peng et al., 2010, Hauff et al., 2008). More recently, selection between sparse and dense retrieval has been framed as a trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency (Arabzadeh et al., 2021). These approaches share a limitation. Their features generally describe how confident a system is, or how difficult a query is, but not why one family of methods should be preferred over another for a given information need. Consequently, they provide little insight into the conditions under which, for example, a neural model's semantic matching is preferable to exact lexical matching. A complementary line of work offers a vocabulary for such conditions. Axiomatic IR formalizes desirable properties of retrieval functions as constraints, including term frequency, document length normalization, term discrimination, and semantic matching constraints (Fang et al., 2004; Fang and Zhai, 2005, Fang et al., 2011). Originally used to analyze and derive classical models, axioms have been extended to diagnose neural rankers (Rennings et al., 2019, Câmara and Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022) and to regularize or re-rank their outputs (Hagen et al., 2016; Rosset et al., 2019, Völske et al., 2021). These studies consistently show that neural models and traditional models satisfy axioms to different degrees. BERT-based rankers, for instance, appear to respect some term-frequency and document-length heuristics only weakly while capturing semantic relationships that lexical models cannot. If the methods differ systematically in their axiomatic behavior, then properties of the query and its candidate documents that determine whether an axiom is applicable, such as the variation in term frequency or length among top-ranked documents, may signal which method is more reliable for that query. To our knowledge, this hypothesis has not been tested systematically. We therefore examine whether axiom-related properties of a query and its top-ranked documents can inform per-query selection between two retrieval methods. Rather than making a hard binary choice, we consider the more general problem of predicting how to combine the methods' relevance scores. Formally, given a query and a pair of retrieval methods, we train a [4] meta-learner that outputs a query-specific interpolation of the two scores into a single relevance score. Hard selection is the special case in which the weight is at an extreme. This soft formulation is more robust to prediction errors, because a mistaken but moderate weight degrades [39] the ranking less than a wrong categorical choice. It also lets the learner exploit complementary evidence when both methods contribute useful signals. The meta-learner's inputs are features that quantify axiomatic properties of the query and the documents retrieved at the top of the ranking, so that its predictions are grounded in [4] interpretable, theoretically motivated quantities rather than opaque QPP scores. Our investigation is guided by the following research questions: RQ1: Can a meta-learner that uses axiomatic features predict query-specific score combinations that improve effectiveness over each of the individual retrieval methods? RQ2: Which axiomatic features contribute most to the meta-learner's predictions, and do they agree with what is known about the axiomatic differences between lexical and neural methods? RQ3: For which queries does the meta-learner deviate most from a uniform [3] combination, and does this behavior reflect query characteristics that are plausible given the methods' respective strengths? To answer these questions, we evaluate on the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track (Collins-Thompson et al., [27] 2013, 2014), a long-standing benchmark with diverse, sometimes ambiguous and underspecified queries over a web-scale corpus. Such queries make the choice of retrieval method nontrivial. We consider pairs formed from a lexical baseline and neural re-rankers and assess the meta-learner using cross-validation with query-level splits, reporting standard effectiveness metrics with paired significance testing. We then analyze feature importance and per-query weights to characterize what the model has learned. This paper makes the following contributions: 1. A formulation of retrieval method selection as score-combination prediction. We cast pairwise method selection as predicting a query-dependent interpolation [37] weight, unifying selection and fusion within one supervised framework. 2. Axiomatic features for meta-learning. Motivated by the observed axiomatic differences between neural and traditional models, we introduce a set of query- and ranking-level features that quantify how strongly axiom-relevant conditions hold among the top-ranked documents. To our knowledge, this is the first use of such features as inputs to a method-selection model rather than as diagnostics or ranking constraints. 3. An empirical evaluation on TREC Web Track data. We show that the meta-learner often significantly improves over the individual methods, and we characterize the settings in which it does and does not. 4. Feature and query-weight analyses. Through ablations, feature importance estimates, and inspection of individual queries and their predicted weights, we provide evidence on which axiomatic properties guide the meta-learner's behavior and how this relates to the complementary strengths of the methods. Beyond the immediate performance gains, our results speak to a broader question in neural IR: whether the well-documented axiomatic gaps between neural and classical rankers can be turned from a diagnostic observation into an operational signal. The remainder of this paper first reviews related work on axiomatic IR, rank fusion, and algorithm selection. We then describe the meta-learner and the axiomatic features, present the experimental setup and results, and conclude with an analysis of feature importance and query-level behavior. Task formulation and data. We study algorithm selection for ad-hoc retrieval in a pairwise setting. Given a query q, a candidate set Dq of documents, and two retrieval methods A and B that assign relevance scores sA(q,d) and sB(q,d), the meta-learner predicts a query-specific interpolation weight αq ∈ [0,1]. The final score is s(q,d) = αq·ŝA(q,d) + (1 − αq)·ŝB(q,d). Here ŝ denotes min–max normalisation of a method's scores over the top 100 documents for q. This formulation includes selecting a single method as the special cases αq ∈ {0,1}, while allowing soft combinations when neither method is clearly preferable. We used the ad-hoc tasks of the TREC Web Track from 2009 to 2014 (Clarke et al., 2009; Collins-Thompson et al., 2013, 2014). This yields 300 topics, 50 per year. The 2009–2012 topics were judged on ClueWeb09 Category B (about 50 million pages) and the 2013–2014 topics on ClueWeb12-B13 (about 52 million pages). We used the short topic title as the query. Graded judgments were used as released, with non-relevant and spam-labelled documents given a grade of zero. Documents in the ClueWeb09 collection with a Waterloo spam score below 70 were removed before retrieval (Cormack et al., 2011). Effectiveness is reported as nDCG@20, the official primary measure of the track (Järvelin & Kekäläinen, 2002), with ERR@20 as a secondary measure. Because judgments are shallow, unjudged documents were treated as non-relevant. Retrieval methods. First-stage candidates were obtained with BM25 (k1 = 0.9, b = 0.4; Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009), implemented in Anserini (Yang et al., 2017). The top 100 documents per query were retained as Dq, and all methods rank this same set. We considered one pair of methods from each of two families. The first family comprises two lexical models, BM25 and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing (μ = 2000; Zhai & Lafferty, 2004). The second comprises a lexical and a neural method. The neural methods were a BERT-base cross-encoder (Nogueira & Cho, 2019) and a kernel-based interaction model (K-NRM, Xiong et al., 2017). Both were trained on MS MARCO passage data (Bajaj et al., 2016) and applied to the [34] first 512 word pieces of each document. Pairs are denoted by their constituent methods, for example BM25–BERT. Neural models were not fine-tuned on Web Track data, so differences between pairs reflect pre-existing properties of the methods rather than collection-specific adaptation. Axiomatic features. Our features are motivated by findings that neural rankers differ from classical models in their adherence to retrieval constraints (Rosset et al., 2019, Câmara & Hauff, 2020; MacAvaney et al., 2022). We implemented diagnostic versions of the following axioms from Fang et al. (2004, 2011): TFC1, TFC2, TDC, LNC1, LNC2, TF-LNC, M-TDC, and the proximity-oriented constraint of Tao and Zhai (2007). Each axiom specifies a precondition on a document pair (di, dj) for the query, for example that the documents have equal length and differ in the frequency of a query term (TFC1). It also specifies the ranking the axiom requires, for example that the document with higher term frequency is scored higher. "For" each query we considered all pairs among the top k = 20 documents under the first-stage ranking, giving at most 190 pairs. For each axiom a, we computed two quantities. The first is applicability, the fraction of pairs satisfying the precondition. Following Fang et al., we used a tolerance of 10% for length and frequency equality, since exact equality is rare in web documents. Applicability depends only on the query and the documents and is independent of the methods. The second is agreement for each method m, the fraction of applicable pairs whose order under sm matches the order prescribed by a. Pairs with equal scores were counted as half agreements. Agreement is set to the neutral value 0.5 when [35] no pairs are applicable. Because the meta-learner must decide [5] between two methods, we use the difference in agreement between them as a feature, together with applicability. This yields two features per axiom, and the difference feature is informative only when applicability is high. We added query-level descriptors that the literature associates with method suitability. These were query length, mean and maximum inverse document frequency of the query terms, the normalised query clarity score (Cronen-Townsend et al., 2002), and the mean and standard deviation of document length in Dq. We also included the normalised score gap between the first and tenth documents for each method, and Kendall's τ between the two top-20 rankings. The full set comprises 27 features, standardised to zero mean and unit variance using training-fold statistics only. Target construction and meta-learner. For each training query and method However, pair, we evaluated nDCG@20 for α ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 1}. The target is the mean of the α values attaining the maximum nDCG@20. Queries on which the range of nDCG@20 [3] across α is below 0.01 are uninformative for selection and were excluded from training, though not from testing. For these queries, any α produces essentially the same ranking. The meta-learner is a gradient-boosted regression tree ensemble (LightGBM; Ke et al., 2017) minimising squared error on α. We also tested a linear ridge regression to assess whether non-linear interactions among features were necessary. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. Prevalence now exceeds 0.3% in North America, Europe, and Oceania, and incidence is rising rapidly in newly industrialized regions of Asia, South America, and the Middle East (Ng et al., 2017, Kaplan, 2015). Pediatric-onset disease is of particular concern. Pediatric incidence has risen in most regions with reliable surveillance data Benchimol et al., 2011), and children typically present with more extensive disease, growth impairment, and a longer lifetime exposure to inflammation and its therapies. Although advances in biologic therapy have improved outcomes, a substantial proportion of patients do not achieve sustained remission, and the cumulative burden of surgery, hospitalization, and treatment-related adverse events remains high. Identifying modifiable causal factors is therefore a central objective of IBD research. The pathophysiology of IBD is not fully understood, but it is widely accepted to arise from an inappropriate mucosal immune response to intestinal microbes in genetically susceptible hosts, shaped by environmental exposures (Ananthakrishnan, 2015). Genome-wide association studies have identified more than 160 susceptibility loci, many implicating epithelial barrier function, innate microbial sensing, autophagy, and cytokine signaling (Jostins et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015). However, these variants explain only a minority of disease heritability, estimated at approximately 14% for CD and 7.5% for UC (Jostins et al., 2012). The geographic and temporal patterns of IBD, together with its rise in migrants who move to high-incidence regions, point to environmental determinants. Diet is among the most plausible of these, as it directly shapes the intestinal luminal milieu, the composition and metabolic activity of the microbiota, and the integrity of the mucus layer and epithelium Hou et al., 2011). Among dietary changes associated with industrialization, the growing share of energy derived from ultra-processed foods has attracted attention (Monteiro et al., 2019). In the Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology cohort, individuals consuming five or more servings of ultra-processed food daily had an 82% higher risk of incident IBD than those consuming fewer than one serving daily (hazard ratio [HR] 1.82; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.33–2.49) (Narula et al., 2021). Similar associations with CD, but not clearly with UC, were observed in large North American cohorts of health professionals (Lo et al., 2022). The ultra-processed category is heterogeneous, covering refined sugars, saturated fats, low fiber content, and a wide range of industrial additives, so these epidemiological associations cannot identify the causal components. Mechanistic evidence is required to determine whether specific constituents, rather than overall dietary pattern, contribute to intestinal inflammation. Emulsifiers, thickeners, and stabilizers are attractive candidates. They are added in large quantities to improve texture, shelf life, and appearance, and they are consumed daily by many people for decades. Two of the most widely used are carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC). Carrageenan is a family of sulfated galactans extracted from red seaweed and used as a gelling and stabilizing agent E407) in dairy products, plant-based milks, infant and enteral formulas, processed meats, and desserts. CMC (E466) is a chemically modified, anionic cellulose derivative that serves as a thickener and emulsifier in baked goods, ice cream, sauces, and low-fat products. Both are classified as safe for human consumption by regulatory agencies, and their European re-evaluation in 2018 concluded that exposure at authorized levels was not of concern, though uncertainties were acknowledged regarding the low-molecular-weight fraction of carrageenan and the limited data on additive-specific effects in vulnerable populations EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food, 2018). These conclusions rest largely on toxicological assessments that do not capture subtle effects on the microbiota, mucosal barrier, or immune signaling, nor effects in a genetically or immunologically predisposed host. The experimental literature on these compounds spans more than five decades. Marcus and Watt (1969) first reported that degraded carrageenan administered in drinking water produced colonic ulceration in guinea pigs and other laboratory animals, and degraded carrageenan has since become a standard method of inducing experimental colitis (Tobacman, 2001). It has been argued that undegraded, food-grade carrageenan differs fundamentally from this low-molecular-weight form (Weiner, 2014), yet in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that food-grade preparations can activate innate immune pathways, including Toll-like receptor 4 and BCL10-dependent nuclear factor-κB signaling, and can induce interleukin-8 expression in human colonic epithelial cells (Bhattacharyya et al., 2008, Bhattacharyya et al., 2010). Similarly, CMC has been shown to promote bacterial overgrowth and inflammation in susceptible mice (Swidsinski et al., 2009) and, in the work of Chassaing and colleagues (2015), to reduce microbial diversity, encroach on the mucus layer, and promote low-grade inflammation and metabolic syndrome in wild-type animals, as well as more severe colitis in genetically predisposed models. Subsequent ex vivo work with human microbiota communities indicated that CMC and other emulsifiers can alter bacterial composition and increase proinflammatory potential (Chassaing et al., 2017), and a small controlled-feeding study in healthy volunteers reported adverse changes in microbiota and metabolome after CMC ingestion (Chassaing et al., 2022). Together, these observations suggest that the additives may act through convergent mechanisms: perturbing microbial ecology, weakening epithelial and mucus barrier function, and amplifying innate immune activation. These findings also bear directly on clinical nutrition. Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) with a polymeric formula is recommended as first-line induction therapy for pediatric CD, achieving remission rates comparable to or higher than corticosteroids with superior mucosal healing and growth outcomes (Ruemmele et al., 2014; Narula et al., 2018). The mechanisms underlying the efficacy of EEN are unclear, and it has been proposed that the exclusion of dietary components, rather than the nutritional composition of the formula alone, may contribute. Dietary strategies such as the Crohn's disease exclusion diet explicitly eliminate emulsifiers and processed foods and have shown efficacy in inducing remission in children (Levine et al., 2019). Relapse after EEN is common upon return to a habitual diet, raising the possibility that reintroduction of specific additives contributes to recurrent inflammation. Moreover, ironically, some commercially available enteral formulas contain carrageenan or CMC, highlighting the lack of consensus on their safety in patients with active disease. Despite the volume of experimental data, the evidence is fragmented. Studies differ in molecular weight and source of carrageenan, dose, duration, route of administration, and animal strain. The relevance of high-dose rodent models to human dietary exposure is contested, and direct interventional trials of these additives in people with IBD are ethically and practically constrained. No recent review has integrated animal, cellular, microbiome, and early human evidence, or considered it in the context of dietary therapy for CD. In this review, we therefore critically appraise the literature on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation. We first summarize their chemistry, patterns of consumption, and regulatory status. We then examine evidence from animal models regarding histopathology, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, antimicrobial defenses, and cytokine responses, before evaluating data from human epithelial cell and microbiota studies. Finally, we consider the implications for EEN and other nutritional strategies for inducing and maintaining remission. Our contributions are threefold: a synthesis of mechanistic evidence across experimental systems; an assessment of the strength and limits of translation to human disease, including the "likelihood" that these additives act as modifiers or amplifiers rather than sole causes of IBD, and identification of priorities for research to determine whether additive restriction could improve prevention and relapse reduction in susceptible individuals. Study design and reporting framework We conducted a structured narrative review of preclinical and human mechanistic evidence on the effects of the food additives carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) on intestinal inflammation. A narrative design was chosen over a quantitative meta-analysis because the available literature is heterogeneous in model systems, additive formulations, doses, exposure durations, and outcome measures. The review was planned and reported in line with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) criteria (Baethge et al., 2019). The search, screening, and selection processes were documented according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement to maximize transparency and reproducibility (Page et al., 2021). The review was not prospectively registered. Because it used only [2] published data, institutional review board approval was not required. Review questions Four questions guided the review. First, However, do carrageenan and [24] CMC induce histopathological or clinical features of intestinal inflammation in animal models? Second, through which mechanisms might they act, including alteration of the gut microbiota, disruption of the epithelial barrier and mucus layer, impairment of antimicrobial [32] defenses, and activation of pro-inflammatory signaling? Third, do [39] studies of human cells, human-derived microbial communities, or human dietary exposure support these findings? Fourth, what are the implications for dietary strategies in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), particularly exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) [20] with polymeric formulas and the prevention of relapse after EEN? Information sources and search strategy We searched MEDLINE via PubMed), Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [1] from database inception to [month, year]. We also searched Scopus and Google Scholar to capture additional records. The search combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH and Emtree terms) and free-text keywords in three concept blocks. The first covered the additives: carrageenan, carrageenin, Irish moss, E407, carboxymethylcellulose, carboxymethyl cellulose, cellulose gum, sodium CMC, E466, polysorbate, and food additive. The second covered the outcomes: inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, colitis, intestinal inflammation, enteritis, ileitis, intestinal permeability, and epithelial [4] barrier. The third covered the mechanisms and models: microbiota, microbiome, dysbiosis, mucus, cytokine, Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, Bcl10, Caco-2, organoid, in vitro, mouse, rat, guinea pig, rabbit, and human. Boolean operators combined the blocks, and syntax was adapted to each database. We also searched for dietary [2] context with terms such as enteral nutrition, polymeric formula, ultra-processed food, Western diet, and pediatric. We hand-searched the reference [26] lists However, of included articles and relevant reviews, and used forward citation tracking of seminal studies, including the early work on degraded carrageenan and experimental colitis and subsequent reports on dietary emulsifiers and CMC (Chassaing et al., However, 2015; Swidsinski et al., 2009; Tobacman, 2001), to identify additional eligible publications. Eligibility criteria We included [28] peer-reviewed, English-language original studies that met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vivo animal studies in which carrageenan or CMC was administered orally, in drinking water, or in feed, with intestinal inflammation, histology, barrier function, or microbiota assessed; (ii) in vitro or ex vivo studies using human or animal intestinal epithelial cells, immune cells, organoids, or "intestinal" tissue exposed to either additive; (iii) studies of human fecal or mucosal microbiota, including ex vivo or in vitro fermentation and continuous-culture models, exposed to [36] either additive; and (iv) human studies, whether observational, dietary, or interventional, reporting exposure to either additive and a gastrointestinal or inflammatory outcome. Studies in which carrageenan was injected into subcutaneous tissue, the paw, [10] or the pleural cavity as a generic inflammatory stimulus were excluded because they "do" not model intestinal exposure. The Internet of Things (IoT) has moved in little more than a decade from a laboratory concept to a general-purpose architectural paradigm. In it, uniquely identifiable physical objects sense, compute, and communicate with minimal human intervention (Atzori, Iera, & Morabito, 2010, Gubbi, Buyya, Marusic, & Palaniswami, 2013). Industry estimates project more than 25 billion connected endpoints by 2025, spanning manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, energy, and urban infrastructure. Healthcare is among the domains where the paradigm promises the most. Populations are ageing, with the number of people aged 65 years or older expected to reach roughly 1.5 billion by 2050 (United Nations, 2019). Chronic conditions impose a growing burden, and cardiovascular diseases alone account for an estimated 17.9 million deaths annually (World Health Organization, 2021). These pressures strain episodic, clinic-centred care models and strengthen the case for continuous, remote, and personalised monitoring. Health informatics is a multidisciplinary field that applies information engineering to the acquisition, storage, retrieval, and use of health-related data. It has traditionally drawn on institutional sources such as electronic health records, laboratory systems, and imaging archives. Increasingly, clinically relevant data originate outside the hospital, in wearable, implantable, ambient, and handheld devices that record physiological and behavioural signals in everyday settings. Applying IoT principles to these devices has given rise to the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), a connected infrastructure of medical devices, sensors, software applications, and services that exchange data with healthcare information systems (Islam, Kwak, Kabir, Hossain, & Kwak, 2015, Dimitrov, 2016). Typical IoMT deployments include continuous glucose monitors, ambulatory electrocardiography patches, pulse oximeters, smart inhalers, fall detectors, and connected infusion pumps. They are used in chronic disease management, post-operative recovery, elderly assistance, and fitness and wellness. The IoMT differs from general-purpose IoT in ways that raise the engineering stakes. First, many medical signals are time-critical. A delayed or lost arrhythmia alert can have consequences that a delayed thermostat reading cannot, so latency, reliability, and quality of service become safety properties as well as performance metrics. Second, the data are highly sensitive. Health records are consistently among the most valuable and most frequently breached categories of personal data, and regulatory regimes such as HIPAA in the United States and the GDPR in the European Union impose stringent obligations on confidentiality, integrity, and consent. Third, the devices are severely resource constrained. Sensor nodes must often run for months or years on coin-cell batteries, fit within the body or on the skin, and tolerate the poor propagation conditions of the human body, which absorbs and shadows radio-frequency energy (Movassaghi, Abolhasan, Lipman, Smith, & Jamalipour, 2014). Fourth, the ecosystem is heterogeneous. Devices from many vendors, using different protocols and data models, must interoperate with gateways, cloud platforms, and clinical systems. Together these characteristics mean that the properties of the IoMT as a whole are bounded by the properties of its lowest-level communication links. Those links are provided mainly by Personal Area Networks PANs). A PAN interconnects devices within the immediate vicinity of a person, typically within a range of about 10 m, and in the IoMT it forms the first hop of a layered architecture. Sensors measure changes in physical, chemical, or physiological stimuli and transmit them over the PAN to a personal gateway such as a smartphone, a home hub, or a bedside unit. Local area networks (LANs) and wide area networks (WANs) then carry the data to clinicians, caregivers, insurers, researchers, and analytics services. Choices made at the PAN layer determine achievable data rates, which range from a few kilobits per second for slowly varying vital signs to several megabits per second for multichannel electroencephalography or streaming audio. They also determine energy consumption, coexistence behaviour in the crowded However, 2.4 GHz [11] band, network topology and scalability, and the security mechanisms available to protect data at its point of origin. A subset of PANs, Body Area Networks (BANs), is designed [19] specifically for devices on, in, or around the human body, with requirements [24] for extremely low power, minimal interference with tissue, and strict limits on radiated energy (Chen, Gonzalez, Vasilakos, Cao, & Leung, 2011; Movassaghi et al., 2014). Despite the importance of this layer, the literature on IoMT remains uneven. Existing surveys have concentrated on application-level services, cloud and big-data analytics, or security and privacy frameworks, usually treating the underlying wireless technologies as a background detail (Islam et al., 2015). Conversely, the wireless sensor network and BAN literature offers detailed protocol-level analyses, but it rarely connects them to the requirements of deployed healthcare products or to the commercial landscape in which clinicians and system architects must decide. As a result, practitioners and researchers entering the field have no consolidated account that relates PAN standards to the characteristics of medical data, the requirements of IoMT applications, and the offerings of current vendors. The standards themselves are also evolving quickly. Bluetooth Low Energy, for example, has progressed through several specification revisions that changed its throughput, range, and mesh [35] capabilities, so earlier comparisons are partly outdated. This chapter addresses that gap by characterizing the PAN landscape that underpins the IoMT. However, We pursue three research questions. (RQ1) Which PAN standards are most widely used in academic prototypes and commercial IoMT products, [7] and [12] how do they [36] compare in data rate, range, power consumption, topology, and security provisions? RQ2) How do BANs, and the IEEE 802.15.6 standard in particular, extend or diverge from general-purpose PAN technologies in meeting the constraints of body-centric medical sensing? (RQ3) How are these technologies currently embedded in IoMT applications and vendor offerings, and what open challenges does this reveal for real-time operation, security, and privacy? The chapter makes four contributions. First, it provides a structured comparative analysis of three PAN standards that dominate current practice, Bluetooth (including Bluetooth Low Energy), [2] ZigBee built on IEEE 802.15.4, and ANT/ANT+. The analysis uses a common set of quantitative criteria, including nominal physical-layer data rates from roughly 250 kbps to 2 Mbps, typical communication ranges of 10 to 100 m, and duty-cycle-dependent energy profiles. Second, it examines BANs as a distinct class of PAN, reviewing their architecture, tiered communication model, and the particular demands [25] of in-body, on-body, and off-body channels. Third, it surveys prevalent IoMT application areas and maps each to the PAN technologies and vendor products that realise it, so that technical characteristics can be read against real deployments. Fourth, it synthesises cross-cutting challenges, namely real-time performance, security, privacy, interoperability, and energy efficiency, and identifies directions for future research and standardisation. The remainder of the chapter proceeds as follows. We first describe the layered IoMT architecture and the role of the PAN within it. We then analyse the selected standards [2] and BANs in turn, survey applications and vendors, and conclude with a discussion of open issues. Study design and scope We conducted a structured narrative survey of the technologies that form the personal-area layer of the Internet of Medical Things IoMT). The design follows the guidance for [6] systematic reviews in software and systems engineering Kitchenham & Charters, 2007) and borrows the transparency conventions of the PRISMA statement (Moher et al., 2009). We did not attempt a formal meta-analysis because the primary literature reports heterogeneous metrics under non-comparable experimental conditions. Instead, we combined a protocol-driven literature review with a normative comparison of published standards and a catalogue of commercial IoMT offerings. The review addressed three questions. (RQ1) Which short-range wireless standards underpin personal area networks (PANs) in healthcare, and what are their physical-layer and medium-access characteristics? (RQ2) How do body area networks (BANs) extend or specialize these standards for on-body and implanted sensing? (RQ3) Which IoMT application classes and vendors currently use these technologies?
