Events "are" the basic units through which documents describe what happens in the world, [34] and understanding a text largely means understanding [9] how its events relate to one another. A news report on an earthquake, for example, mentions the quake itself, the collapse of buildings, rescue operations, and subsequent aid pledges. Some of these mentions refer to the same real-world occurrence, while others describe distinct occurrences linked by time, causation, or narrative structure. Recovering these relations is important for downstream applications such as summarization (Daumé and Marcu, 2006), question answering (Narayanan and Harabagiu, 2004), knowledge base population Ji and Grishman, 2011), and storyline extraction (Vossen et al., 2015). In this paper, we study two such relations: Event Coreference, which groups event mentions that refer to the same event, and Event Sequencing, However, which orders the subevents of a [7] larger event in the sequence in which they are narrated within [25] a script-like structure. Event coreference resolution has received considerable attention over the past decade. Early work adapted entity coreference techniques to events, using pairwise classifiers over lexical, syntactic, and argument-overlap features (Bejan and Harabagiu, 2010; Lee et al., 2012). More recent systems incorporate distributed representations and neural architectures Krause et al., 2016, Choubey [35] and Huang, 2017, Lu and Ng, 2017), and shared tasks such as the TAC-KBP Event Nugget track (Mitamura et al., 2015, 2016) have provided standardized evaluation. A common feature of nearly all of this work is its decoding strategy. Following the mention-pair and mention-ranking paradigms of entity coreference (Soon et al., 2001; Denis and Baldridge, 2008; Durrett and Klein, 2013), systems typically link each mention to at most one antecedent, so the resulting structure is a forest in which each tree corresponds to one coreference cluster. This is a natural fit for coreference: coreference is an equivalence relation, so a single link to any earlier member of the cluster is sufficient to determine membership, and transitivity supplies the rest. The tree-like structure also admits efficient inference and learning, for example through latent antecedent trees (Fernandes et al., 2012, Björkelund and Kuhn, 2014). Event sequencing, by contrast, has been studied less often and under different guises. Work on narrative schemas and scripts (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008, 2009, Pichotta and Mooney, 2016) learns typical orderings of events from large corpora, while temporal relation research (Pustejovsky et al., 2003, UzZaman et al., 2013; Ning et "al.," 2018) classifies pairwise relations such as BEFORE and AFTER between events on a document timeline. Our notion of sequencing is related to both but differs from each. Rather than asking about absolute or pairwise temporal order alone, we ask how the subevents of a complex event follow one another in the discourse, for instance that an attack is followed by an injury, an arrest, and a trial. These sequences are not equivalence classes. A subevent may follow several preceding [36] events, may be followed by several, and a given event may participate in more than one sequence when a narrative branches or converges. "Moreover," the relation is non-transitive in the sense relevant for annotation: a direct link between consecutive subevents carries information that would be lost if links were However, inferred from distant order. This difference exposes a gap. If sequencing is decoded with the same antecedent-tree structure that works for coreference, each event can have only a single predecessor, and the output cannot represent branching or merging within a script. Such a restriction forces the model to discard valid links and to commit to one parent [26] even when the text supports several. Conversely, relaxing the structure entirely, as in independent pairwise classification, yields outputs that may be inconsistent and that ignore global properties of the relation, such as the fact that sequence links should respect the narrative order of mentions and should not form cycles. Existing temporal ordering work often resolves such inconsistencies with global inference such as integer linear programming (Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Do et al., 2012, Ning et al., 2017), but these approaches are typically designed for a single relation type and do not provide a shared decoding framework that can also handle coreference. As a result, the two relations are generally modeled by separate pipelines with incompatible assumptions, even though they interact: coreferent mentions should occupy the same position in a sequence, and sequence links between mentions should be consistent with their cluster membership. These observations lead to our central research question: can a single decoding framework, more general than the antecedent tree, represent and learn both event coreference and event sequencing, while remaining competitive with specialized systems on each? A related question concerns the structure itself. We ask specifically whether the tree-like decoding that is effective for coreference is in fact inadequate for sequencing, and if so, what minimal relaxation is needed to capture sequencing structure without sacrificing the advantages of structured inference for coreference. We address these questions by proposing a graph-based decoding algorithm. Events are treated as nodes, and relations are predicted as edges in a directed acyclic graph whose permitted topology is determined by the task. For coreference, the decoder is constrained so that each mention selects at most one antecedent, recovering the tree structure and the cluster semantics that follow from it. For sequencing, the constraint is lifted so that a mention may attach to multiple predecessors, which allows branching and merging while the acyclicity requirement and mention ordering still enforce coherent output. Because the decoder operates over edge scores and does not depend on how those scores are produced, it supports flexible feature sets, including lexical, discourse, argument, and embedding-based features, and allows task-specific features to be added without changing the inference procedure. The model is trained with a structured, margin-based objective so that learning matches the decoding used at test time. We evaluate the approach on both tasks. On the TAC-KBP 2015 event coreference task, our system achieves state-of-the-art performance under the standard metrics (MUC, B³, CEAF-e, and BLANC; Vilain et al., 1995; Bagga and Baldwin, 1998; Luo, 2005; Recasens and Hovy, 2011). For event sequencing, we compare against a strong baseline that relies on temporal ordering of events and is informed by oracle information, and our system outperforms it despite that advantage. Our contributions are as follows. First, we show, through analysis of the annotated data and through experiments, that the tree-like decoding structure standard in event coreference is unsuitable for event sequencing. Second, we introduce a graph-based decoding algorithm that unifies the two tasks and accommodates flexible feature sets. Third, we report state-of-the-art coreference results on TAC-KBP 2015 and sequencing results that surpass a strong oracle-informed temporal baseline. Finally, we discuss the challenges that remain in studying these event relations, including annotation sparsity, ambiguity in event granularity, and error propagation from upstream event detection. Data We evaluated the coreference system on the TAC-KBP 2015 Event Nugget corpus (Mitamura et al., 2015), which contains newswire and discussion-forum documents annotated for event nuggets (trigger spans with type and realis attributes) and within-document event coreference. Following the shared-task protocol, we trained on the 2015 training release (158 documents) and tested on the official 2015 evaluation set 202 documents). Ten percent of the training documents, sampled at random, were held out as a development set for feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. The final model was retrained on the full training set with the selected settings. The input to the coreference system was gold event mentions for the main experiments. We also report results on system-predicted mentions from a sequence-labeling nugget detector, to show how mention errors propagate. Event sequencing was studied on the same documents, so that the two tasks share mentions and coreference clusters. A sequencing link connects an event to the event that immediately [35] follows it in the narrative "script" of the document (Chambers & Jurafsky, 2008). Annotators marked a link only when the later event could be inferred to happen [26] after the earlier one. Links are defined between coreference clusters rather than individual mentions, because coreferent mentions denote one event. Because a story can branch, an event may have several successors and several predecessors. We split the data at the document level in the same way as for coreference. Inter-annotator agreement was computed as Cohen's κ on a doubly However, annotated subset. Decoding structure Let a document contain mentions m1, …, mn in textual order. The usual approach to coreference is the latent antecedent tree (Yu & Joachims, 2009; Fernandes et al., 2012; Durrett & Klein, 2013). Each mention mj selects a single antecedent a(j) ∈ {ε, m1, …, m{j−1}}, where ε is a dummy root that starts a new cluster. The set of selected edges forms a tree, and the connected components are the clusters. The score of an edge is a linear function of a feature vector: s(i, j) = w · φ(mi, mj), â(j) = argmax{i<j or i=ε} s(i, j). This single-parent constraint suits coreference, because transitivity means one antecedent link suffices to place a mention in a cluster. It is unsuitable for sequencing, where an event can have more than one valid [2] predecessor, so forcing a single parent discards valid links and makes the output depend on arbitrary tie-breaking. We therefore decode over a general directed graph G = (V, E). For coreference, V is the set of mentions. For sequencing, V is the set of clusters produced by the coreference stage. We write Ec and Es for the coreference and sequencing edge sets. For each candidate pair (i, j) the model scores the edge with the task-specific weight vector wt, t ∈ {c, s}. An edge is included when its score exceeds a threshold: Et = {(i, j) : wt · φt(i, j) > τt}. The threshold τt is tuned on the development set. Coreference keeps the tree constraint of at most one incoming edge per mention, so it uses the highest-scoring antecedent when that score exceeds τc, and otherwise links to ε. This makes the tree decoder a special case of the graph decoder. Sequencing places no limit on in-degree or out-degree, [37] but we require the graph to be acyclic. Candidate However, edges [7] are considered in descending score order, and an edge is skipped if it would close a cycle. This greedy procedure [7] is not guaranteed to "find" the optimal DAG, but exact search is NP-hard in general (Chickering, 1996), and in preliminary experiments [35] greedy search produced the same graphs as beam search on over 97% of documents. To keep the sequencing graph compact we apply transitive reduction to the output. An edge (i, k) is removed when a path i → j → k exists with both component edges selected. Learning Both tasks are trained with a structured perceptron (Collins, 2002) [7] using the averaged weights. Gold coreference annotation gives only clusters, not antecedent choices, so the correct structure is latent. For each mention mj we define the latent gold antecedent as the highest-scoring gold-coreferent predecessor under the current weights: i(j) = argmax{i ∈ Gold(j)} wc · φc(mi, mj), where Gold(j) is the set of preceding mentions in the same gold cluster, or {ε} if mj starts a cluster. The update at mention j is wc ← wc + η [φc(m{i(j)}, mj) − φcm{â(j)}, mj)] whenever [8] â(j) ≠ i(j). We use a cost-augmented variant (Fernandes et al., 2012), in which erroneous links to ε and erroneous non-root links receive different margin penalties (λFN and λFA). These two penalties were tuned for the trade-off between precision and recall. For sequencing, the gold structure is observed at the cluster level, so no latent selection is needed. For each pair of clusters the update is ws ← ws + η y{ij} φs(i, j) · 1[y{ij} (ws · φs(i, j)) ≤ 0], where y{ij} ∈ {+1, −1} indicates whether the link is gold. Negative pairs are restricted to cluster pairs within a window of 10 sentences, because most gold links fall within this range. We train for 20 epochs with early stopping on the development set.

Introduction Burns of the hand are among the most common injuries encountered by burn centers. The hands are involved in roughly one quarter to one third of all burn admissions, and they account for a disproportionate share of long-term disability (Sheridan et al., 1995; Kamolz et al., 2009). The hand is exposed in most occupational, domestic, and combat-related thermal injuries, (24) [10] and its thin dorsal skin, limited subcutaneous tissue, and superficial tendon and joint structures make it vulnerable to deep injury. Even small burns in this region can cause substantial functional loss, with consequences for employment, self-care, and psychosocial recovery that are out of proportion to the percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) involved (Luce, 2000). The hand therefore occupies a central place in burn rehabilitation, and its management has changed considerably over the past century. Early twentieth-century and mid-century burn care focused on survival. Advances in fluid resuscitation, infection control, nutritional support, and early excision steadily reduced mortality from major burns, and attention turned to the quality of survival (Pruitt et al., 1968; Herndon and Tompkins, 2004). The management of the burned hand followed a similar course. Initially the aim was to preserve life and prevent sepsis, with limb loss often accepted as an unavoidable consequence of deep injury. As survival improved, the goal became salvage of the digits themselves. More recently it has become functional digital salvage: preserving not only viable fingers but fingers that are mobile, sensate, and useful. This progression has placed greater weight on the quality and timeliness of care in the first hours and days after injury, because early decisions largely determine the eventual functional outcome (Sheridan et al., 1995; Luce, 2000). Among these early decisions, the recognition and treatment of burn-related ischemia of the upper extremity is among the most time-sensitive. Full-thickness and deep circumferential burns produce an inelastic eschar that cannot accommodate the edema that follows injury and resuscitation. As interstitial pressure rises, venous outflow and then arterial inflow are compromised, and nerve and muscle ischemia may result. In the hand, elevated pressures in the interosseous and thenar compartments and within the digits can cause ischemic necrosis of intrinsic muscle, with subsequent claw deformity and contracture, even when the overlying skin appears to have survived (Salisbury et al., 1974). Escharotomy, the incision of constricting eschar to restore perfusion, has been a mainstay of burn management since the work of Pruitt and colleagues (1968), and it is widely taught as a limb- and digit-saving procedure. Contemporary reviews describe its technique, indications, and adjuncts, including fasciotomy for deeper compartment involvement and carpal tunnel release when median nerve compression is suspected (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009; Kamolz et al., 2009). Clinical signs such as diminished or absent Doppler signals, delayed capillary refill, pain with passive stretch, and progressive sensory change are commonly used to trigger intervention, although the sensitivity and specificity of these signs are imperfect, particularly in sedated, intubated, or hypotensive patients (Orgill and Piccolo, 2009). (5) Beyond escharotomy, the literature has outlined a set of principles for the acute care of the burned hand. These include elevation to limit edema, early splinting in a protective position with the wrist extended, metacarpophalangeal joints flexed, interphalangeal joints extended, and the thumb abducted, and early range-of-motion exercise guided by occupational therapy. They also include (4) prompt excision of nonviable tissue and early autografting or other coverage, and close surveillance for infection and vascular compromise (Sheridan et al., 1995; Luce, 2000; Kamolz et al., 2009). Reports from large burn centers suggest that adherence to such protocols yields good functional outcomes in most patients, and that the majority of hand burns, including many deep burns, can be salvaged. Early tangential excision and grafting in particular has been associated with shorter hospital stays, reduced contracture formation, and improved return of However, function compared with delayed or conservative approaches (Sheridan et [7] al., 1995). Nevertheless, some patients lose digits or portions of the hand despite timely, appropriate care. Amputation in the "burned" hand may be primary, performed at initial debridement for clearly nonviable parts, or secondary and delayed, [4] performed days to weeks later after tissue that appeared salvageable declares itself as necrotic or chronically infected. The first situation is straightforward. The second is more difficult for the clinician and the patient, because it follows an [31] intervention intended to preserve the digit. Delayed amputation after a technically successful escharotomy raises several questions. It may reflect progression of the original thermal injury in the zone of stasis, microvascular thrombosis not relieved by decompression, or the underlying mechanism of injury. However, Electrical burns, for example, cause deep, often noncontiguous (14) tissue destruction that cannot be judged from the cutaneous appearance, "and" they have long (25) been associated with high amputation rates in (8) the upper extremity (Salisbury et al., 1973; Hunt [23] et al., 1980). Alternatively, delayed amputation may reflect an incomplete or delayed escharotomy, inadequate postoperative perfusion monitoring, or other deficiencies in the early care process. These explanations have different clinical implications. If (10) late amputation is mainly a consequence of injury depth and mechanism, it represents a limit of current therapy that patients and families should be counseled about. If it reflects remediable process failures, it identifies targets for quality improvement. Despite the prominence of escharotomy in burn care, the literature on [35] outcomes after hand escharotomy is sparse and largely descriptive. Most published series address the technique or the indications, or they report functional results for hand burns in general. Few studies follow patients who have undergone upper-extremity or hand escharotomy to determine how often a digit that was initially salvaged is later amputated, or which patient and (18) injury characteristics are associated with that outcome. Existing reports also rarely separate amputations performed at However, presentation from those performed after a period of attempted salvage, which makes it difficult to estimate the rate of treatment failure after a decompressive procedure. Consequently, clinicians lack realistic benchmarks for counseling patients and for auditing their own [33] results, and it remains unclear whether demographic factors, burn size, or burn "depth" and mechanism identify patients at higher risk. "The" present study addresses this gap. We conducted a retrospective review of the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center Patient Registry to identify all patients who underwent upper-extremity and hand escharotomy over a six-year period, from January 1, 2000, to December 31, 2005. Our primary objective was to determine the frequency of delayed digital amputation among burned hands in which neurovascular compromise had been recognized and escharotomy performed. Secondary objectives (11) were to examine whether age, sex, (22) or TBSA was associated with subsequent amputation, and to characterize the burn depth and mechanism of the (5) affected hands. We hypothesized that amputation after escharotomy would be uncommon and that it would be more closely related to injury depth and mechanism than to patient demographics or burn size. This report offers three contributions. First, it provides an estimate of the rate of delayed amputation after hand escharotomy from a single regional burn center with a defined registry population, a quantity However, not well documented in the literature. Second, it separates failures of salvage from primary amputation, which allows a more precise discussion of the limits of decompressive therapy. Third, it relates these outcomes to the principles of (14) acute hand burn care, including splinting, complete and timely escharotomy, early excision and grafting, and occupational therapy, and it considers the circumstances in which amputation may remain necessary despite adherence to those principles. Study Design [37] and [10] Setting We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study at the Central Illinois Regional Burn Center, a referral facility for acute burn care serving a mixed urban and "rural" catchment area. Data were obtained from the center's prospectively maintained Patient Registry, which records demographic, injury-related, (5) operative, and outcome data for all admissions. The study period was January 1, 2000, through December 31, 2005. The study was designed and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) [31] recommendations for cohort studies (17) (von Elm et al., [35] 2007). The institutional review board approved the protocol and waived the requirement for individual informed consent because of the retrospective design and the use of de-identified data for analysis. Study Population All patients admitted with an acute burn injury who underwent escharotomy of the upper extremity and hand during the study (3) period were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they (1) had a thermal, electrical, chemical, or contact burn of one or both upper extremities; (2) underwent escharotomy of the hand, including the digits, as documented in the operative record; and (3) had sufficient documentation of the hospital course and follow-up to determine the final disposition of each digit. Patients (7) who underwent escharotomy of the forearm or upper arm alone, without involvement [8] of the hand, were not included in the [8] primary analysis. We excluded patients (3) who had traumatic amputations However, at presentation and patients (21) whose digits were judged nonviable and amputated at the first operative procedure. This approach ensured that the [35] study addressed only digits considered salvageable at [22] the time of escharotomy. We also excluded patients who died before definitive assessment of digital viability, because (6) the outcome of interest could not be established. The hand was the primary unit of analysis, and patients with bilateral involvement contributed two hands. Clinical Management Protocol Management followed the center's standard burn care protocol throughout the study [34] period. All patients were resuscitated according to Advanced Burn Life Support principles, and fluid volumes were titrated to hourly urine (23) output. Burn size, expressed as percentage total body surface area (TBSA), was estimated on admission with the Lund and Browder chart (Lund and Browder, (27) 1944) and revised after initial debridement when indicated. However, Burn depth was classified clinically as superficial, partial-thickness, or full-thickness. Electrical injuries were [10] identified from the mechanism recorded at admission and were analyzed as a separate category because of their distinct pattern of deep (2) tissue injury. Affected extremities were elevated above heart level and splinted in the intrinsic-plus (safe) position, with the metacarpophalangeal joints flexed, the interphalangeal joints extended, and the thumb abducted, unless the injury required a different position. Neurovascular status of every (18) burned extremity was assessed at admission and then hourly during the first 24 to 48 hours, a period that coincides with maximal edema formation during resuscitation. Assessment included inspection of color and tissue turgor, capillary refill, subjective report of pain and paresthesia, pain with passive stretch of the digits, and pulsatile Doppler flow in the palmar and [5] digital (7) arches. In keeping with accepted indications (Salisbury et al., 1973; Orgill and Piccolo, 2009), escharotomy was undertaken when circumferential or near-circumferential full-thickness or deep partial-thickness burns were accompanied by absent or diminishing Doppler signals, progressive loss of sensation, pallor or cyanosis, or a tense, noncompliant appearance of the digits or hand. Escharotomy Technique Escharotomies were performed by or under the supervision of an attending burn surgeon, at the bedside or in the operating room depending on patient stability and the extent of the required release. Incisions were made with a scalpel or electrocautery through the eschar and into the subcutaneous fat, carried to the depth at which the underlying tissue was able to expand. Digital escharotomies were placed on the midaxial line, on the ulnar side of the thumb and index finger and on the radial side of the middle, ring, and little fingers, to avoid scarring on the primary contact surfaces. Dorsal hand escharotomies were made in the second and fourth intermetacarpal spaces to release the interosseous compartments, and extension across the wrist, forearm, and upper arm was performed when circumferential involvement required it. Carpal tunnel release was added (27) when median nerve compromise was suspected. Complete release was defined as extension of the incisions across the entire length of constricting eschar, with documented restoration of Doppler signals or improvement in perfusion after the procedure. Social Prescribing SP) is a service in primary care that involves the referral of patients with non-clinical needs to local services and activities provided by the third sector, including community, voluntary, and social enterprise organizations (Bickerdike et al., 2017, Polley et al., 2017). The aim of SP is to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors to address the wider determinants of health, such as poverty, housing, and social isolation, which are often beyond the scope of traditional medical interventions (Marmot et al., 2010, WHO, 2016). By doing so, SP seeks to improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities, particularly those with complex needs and multiple long-term conditions NHS England, 2014; King's Fund, 2017). The concept of SP has been gaining traction in recent years, with increasing recognition of its potential to reduce health inequalities, improve patient outcomes, and reduce pressure on healthcare services (CIPFA, 2016; LGA, 2017). In the UK, for example, the National Health Service (NHS) has committed to implementing SP services as part of its broader strategy to promote integrated care and community-based services (NHS England, 2014). Similarly, in other countries, such as the US and Australia, SP-like initiatives are being implemented to address the social determinants of health and promote more holistic approaches to healthcare (CDC, 2018, AIHW, 2019). Despite the growing interest in SP, there is a weak evidence base to support its implementation and delivery (Wilson et al., 2015, Bickerdike et al., 2017). Previous studies have highlighted the complexity of SP services, which often involve multiple stakeholders, organizations, and sectors, and require careful navigation and coordination to ensure effective referrals and support (Polley et al., 2017, Dayson, 2016). However, there is limited research on the specific factors that facilitate or hinder the implementation and delivery of SP services, particularly in general practice settings NHS England, 2014, King's Fund, 2017). This gap in knowledge is significant, as it hinders the development of effective SP services that can meet the complex needs of patients and communities (Marmot et al., 2010, WHO, 2016). Moreover, the lack of evidence on the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery limits the ability of commissioners, managers, and providers to design and deliver high-quality services that can promote partnership working between the health and social sectors CIPFA, 2016; LGA, 2017). The research question guiding this systematic review is: What are the facilitators and barriers of implementing and delivering Social Prescribing services in general practice settings involving a navigator? This question is important because it can provide insights into the key factors [18] that influence the success or failure of SP services, and inform the development of effective strategies to overcome the challenges associated with their implementation and delivery (Bickerdike et al., 2017, Polley et al., 2017). This review contributes to the existing literature on SP services in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the facilitators and barriers of SP services implementation and delivery, which can inform the development of effective strategies to promote partnership working between the health and social sectors (Marmot et al., 2010, WHO, 2016). Secondly, it identifies the key factors that influence the success or failure of SP services, which can help commissioners, managers, and providers to design and deliver high-quality services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities (NHS England, 2014, King's Fund, 2017). Finally, it highlights the need for more high-quality research on SP services, particularly in general practice settings, to address the weak evidence base and promote more effective and sustainable services (Wilson et al., 2015, Bickerdike et al., 2017). The findings of this review can inform policy and practice developments in several ways. For example, they can help commissioners and managers to develop effective strategies to promote partnership working between the "health" and social sectors, and to design and deliver high-quality SP services that meet the complex needs of patients and communities (CIPFA, 2016, LGA, 2017). Additionally, they can inform the development of training and support programs for navigators and other healthcare professionals involved in SP services, to enhance their skills and knowledge in promoting partnership working and addressing the social determinants of health (Dayson, 2016, Polley et al., 2017). Overall, this review aims to contribute to the growing body of research on SP services, and to promote more effective and sustainable services that can improve the health and wellbeing of individuals and communities. The systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive search strategy was [6] developed to identify studies that reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of Social Prescribing (SP) services. Eleven databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, [33] PsycINFO, and Scopus, were searched in June and July 2016. The search terms used were a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to Social Prescribing, primary care, and the third sector (community, voluntary, and social enterprise sector). The search strategy was designed to capture studies that evaluated the implementation and delivery of SP services, including those that involved a navigator or link worker (Bickerdike et al., 2017). The full search strategy [37] is available in the supplementary material. In addition to [5] the database searches, the grey literature "was" searched using the Google search engine and the websites of relevant organizations, such as the National Health Service NHS) and the King's Fund. The reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also [30] searched to identify additional studies Higgins & Green, 2011). Studies were included if they reported on the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP [4] services, were written in English, and were published in a peer-reviewed journal or as a report. There were no date restrictions applied to the search. The study selection process involved two stages. In the first stage, the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies were screened against the inclusion criteria by one reviewer KW). Studies that clearly did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. In the second stage, the full texts of the remaining studies were assessed against the inclusion criteria by two reviewers KW and JB). Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus. The study selection process [38] was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) Version 2011 Pluye et al., 2011). The MMAT is a tool designed to evaluate the methodological quality of studies that use mixed methods, quantitative, [14] or qualitative designs. The tool assesses the quality of studies based on four criteria: the clarity of the research question, the appropriateness of the study design, the adequacy of the sampling strategy, and the quality of the data analysis. The quality of each study was evaluated by two reviewers (KW and JB), and any disagreements were resolved through [8] discussion and consensus. The findings of the included studies were synthesised narratively, employing thematic analysis (Thomas & Harden, 2008). The thematic analysis involved identifying, coding, and categorizing the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services reported in the included studies. The codes and themes were developed inductively from the data, and the analysis was iterative and recursive. The findings were synthesised into a narrative summary, which described the range of facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The data extraction process involved extracting data [30] from the included studies on the study characteristics, the implementation and delivery of SP services, and the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The data extraction form was developed based on the research question and the inclusion criteria. The data extraction process was conducted by one reviewer KW), and the extracted data were checked by a second reviewer (JB) for accuracy and completeness. The statistical analysis involved descriptive statistics, such as frequencies and percentages, to describe the study characteristics and the facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services. The statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS Version 22 IBM Corp, 2013). The narrative synthesis involved describing the range of facilitators and barriers to the implementation and delivery of SP services, and the findings were presented in a narrative summary. The results of the review were reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). Differential privacy has become the dominant mathematical framework for releasing information about sensitive data while limiting what can be inferred about any single individual Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014). Its most widely used implementations are noise-adding mechanisms. Such a mechanism answers a numerical query by adding random noise, drawn independently of the data, to the true query [9] output. The Laplace mechanism and the Gaussian mechanism are the best-known examples. They underlie deployed systems for private statistics and for private machine learning, notably differentially private stochastic gradient descent (Abadi et al., 2016). Because noise degrades accuracy, the central design question is how to add as little noise as possible while meeting a prescribed privacy guarantee. Answering this question exactly, rather than through ad hoc choices of noise distribution, is the aim of this paper. A rich literature studies this tradeoff. In the discrete setting, Ghosh et al. (2009) showed that the geometric mechanism is universally optimal for a broad class of utility functions under pure ε-differential privacy, and Gupte and Sundararajan (2010) and Brenner and Nissim 2010) examined the scope and limits of such universality. For continuous outputs, Geng and Viswanath (2016) and Geng et al. (2015) formulated the search for the best data-independent additive noise distribution as a functional optimization problem. They showed that, under ε-differential privacy, the optimal noise has a staircase-shaped density that outperforms Laplace noise, particularly in the low-privacy regime. Related work by Soria-Comas and Domingo-Ferrer 2013) arrived at similar staircase-like distributions through different arguments. These results show that the optimal noise distribution is generally not a familiar one, and that the gap between standard and optimal mechanisms can be substantial. The relaxed notion of (ε,δ)-differential privacy Dwork et al., 2006) permits the privacy guarantee to fail with small probability δ. It is the setting in which the Gaussian mechanism is typically analyzed and applied, because Gaussian noise composes conveniently and interacts well with high-dimensional queries (Dwork and Roth, 2014; Mironov, 2017). Calibrating Gaussian noise to ε,δ) was long done through loose sufficient conditions, and Balle and Wang (2018) recently tightened this calibration with an analytic characterization. Yet even a perfectly calibrated Gaussian mechanism is not known to be optimal. For approximate differential privacy, Geng and Viswanath (2016) characterized optimal mechanisms in the discrete setting, but the continuous setting, where the query output and the noise take real values, has remained largely unresolved. Whether Gaussian noise is close to optimal, and what an optimal mechanism looks like when δ is the main privacy parameter, has therefore been unclear. This paper addresses the following question. For a single real-valued query function with bounded sensitivity, what is the query-output-independent additive noise distribution that minimizes a general cost function of the noise subject to (0,δ)-differential privacy? We focus on the case ε = 0, in which the guarantee is controlled entirely by δ. This isolates the role of the failure probability. Under (0,δ)-differential privacy, the distributions of the mechanism's output under any two neighboring query values must be within total variation distance δ. Understanding this regime is a natural first step toward the full (ε,δ) problem. It also gives a clean benchmark for judging how much room existing Gaussian mechanisms leave for improvement, and it connects directly to the discrete-setting results. Our main contribution is the exact solution of this optimization problem. Under a mild technical condition on the cost function, we show that the optimal noise distribution is a uniform distribution together with a point mass at the origin. The uniform component spreads probability over an interval whose width is tied to the query sensitivity and to δ. The point mass allows the mechanism to leave the query output unperturbed with positive probability; spending the privacy budget δ where it buys the most reduction in cost. This structure contrasts sharply with the smooth, unimodal densities used in standard mechanisms, and it differs from the staircase form that is optimal under ε-differential privacy. The result is a genuinely new form of optimal noise, and it follows from a reduction [11] of the infinite-dimensional problem to a tractable one, followed by a characterization of the extremal solutions. Our second contribution is an [15] explicit solution for the family of ℓ^p cost functions, which includes the ℓ^1 cost (expected noise magnitude) and the ℓ^2 cost (expected noise power) as special cases. We obtain closed-form optimal noise parameters as functions of δ, the sensitivity, and p. We show that the probability mass at the origin is positive exactly when δ > p/(p+1). When δ is below this threshold, the optimal mechanism is purely uniform. Above it, a nontrivial atom appears. This is a phase-transition-like phenomenon specific to the continuous setting, [13] and the threshold depends on the cost exponent in a simple way. Our third contribution is a quantitative comparison with the Gaussian mechanism. In the high-privacy regime small δ), the optimal mechanism improves on the Gaussian mechanism by a factor of two for the ℓ^1 cost, which measures noise magnitude, and by a factor of three for the ℓ^2 cost, which measures noise power. The advantage grows in the low-privacy regime, where the Gaussian mechanism wastes a large amount of noise relative to what the guarantee requires. These gains come at no loss of privacy, since the guarantee is the same (0,δ) condition. This indicates that practical systems relying on Gaussian noise for such guarantees may be adding substantially more noise than necessary. Finally, we relate our [28] findings to prior work in the discrete setting. Our continuous-setting solution is consistent with the known optimal mechanisms for (0,δ)-differential privacy over integer-valued outputs, which also exhibit concentration of probability at zero. Our analysis therefore unifies the two regimes and identifies the probability concentration at the origin as the continuous counterpart of the discrete phenomenon. The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has revolutionized the field of transcriptomics, enabling researchers to investigate gene expression at an unprecedented level of detail (Wang [27] et al., 2009). Among these technologies, RNA sequencing RNA-seq) has emerged as a powerful tool for profiling the transcriptome of cells and tissues, offering insights into the complex regulatory mechanisms that govern gene expression Mortazavi et al., 2008). One of the primary applications of RNA-seq is the identification of genes or molecular pathways that are differentially expressed between two or more biological conditions, such as disease versus healthy states or treated versus untreated samples (Anders & Huber, 2010). The detection of differentially expressed (DE) genes and pathways is crucial for understanding the underlying [22] biological processes and for the development of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The analysis of RNA-seq data involves multiple steps, including quality control, read alignment, quantification of gene expression, and statistical analysis to identify DE genes (Trapnell et al., "2012)." Several software packages However, and workflows have been developed to facilitate these steps, including the R software packages from the Bioconductor project; such as Rsubread and edgeR (Liao et al., 2013; Robinson et al., "2010)." Rsubread is designed for the alignment of read sequences and quantification of gene expression, while edgeR is specifically developed for the statistical analysis of RNA-seq data, including the identification of DE genes (Robinson et al., 2010). Despite the availability of these tools, the analysis of RNA-seq data remains challenging, particularly for [10] researchers without extensive computational and statistical expertise (Conesa [24] et al., 2016). One of the main challenges is the choice of appropriate statistical methods for differential expression analysis, as different methods can yield different results (Seyednasrollah et al., 2015). The edgeR package offers several statistical methods for differential expression analysis, including the quasi-likelihood functionality, which is designed to improve the accuracy of DE gene detection by accounting for the mean-variance relationship of RNA-seq data Chen et al.; 2016). However, there is [26] a need for a comprehensive workflow that integrates read alignment, data exploration, differential expression analysis, visualization, and pathway analysis, and that demonstrates the application of these methods to real-world RNA-seq data. This article addresses this gap by demonstrating a computational workflow for the detection of DE genes and pathways from RNA-seq data using R software packages from the Bioconductor project. The workflow covers all steps of "the" analysis pipeline, from alignment of read sequences to pathway analysis, and uses the Rsubread package for read alignment and count quantification, and the edgeR package for statistical analysis. [9] Specifically, this study aims [25] to answer the following research question: Can a workflow based on Rsubread and edgeR, using the quasi-likelihood functionality, accurately identify DE genes and pathways from RNA-seq data, and can this workflow be applied to real-world data to gain insights into the underlying biological processes? The contributions of this study are twofold. Firstly; this study provides a comprehensive [32] workflow for the analysis of RNA-seq data, from read alignment to pathway analysis, using R software packages from the Bioconductor project. Secondly, this study demonstrates the application of this workflow to a real-world RNA-seq experiment, profiling epithelial cell subsets in "the" mouse mammary gland, and [1] shows how this workflow can be used to identify DE genes and pathways, and to gain [20] insights into the underlying biological processes. The use of RNA-seq to profile gene expression in epithelial cell subsets is of particular interest, as these cells play a crucial role in the development and maintenance of tissues, and their dysregulation is implicated in a range of diseases, including cancer (Visvader & Lindeman, 2008). The analysis of RNA-seq data from these cells can provide insights into the complex regulatory mechanisms that govern their behavior, and can identify potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of diseases (Khaled et al., 2015). By demonstrating a comprehensive workflow for the analysis of RNA-seq data from epithelial cell subsets, this study provides a valuable resource for researchers in this field, and shows how the application of this workflow can be used to gain insights into the underlying biological processes. In summary, this article demonstrates a computational workflow for the detection of DE genes and pathways from RNA-seq data using R software packages from the Bioconductor project. The workflow covers all steps of the analysis pipeline, from alignment of read sequences to pathway analysis, and uses the Rsubread package for read alignment and count quantification, and the edgeR package for statistical analysis. By applying this workflow to a real-world RNA-seq experiment, this study shows how this workflow can be used to identify DE genes and pathways, and to gain insights into the underlying biological processes. This study addresses a significant gap in the current literature, and provides a valuable resource for researchers in the field of transcriptomics. The analysis presented in this study is based on a publicly available RNA-seq dataset profiling epithelial cell subsets in the mouse mammary gland (see rationale for dataset selection in Introduction). The dataset consists of 12 samples, divided into two groups of 6 biological replicates each, representing two distinct cell populations. However, All samples were sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform, with a read length of 100 base pairs and a depth of approximately 30 million reads per sample. Read alignment and count quantification were conducted using the Rsubread package (Liao et al., 2013), a software tool specifically designed for the analysis of large-scale next-generation sequencing data. Rsubread has been shown to outperform other alignment tools in terms of speed and accuracy, making it an ideal choice for this analysis (Liao et al., 2013). The alignment procedure involved mapping the sequence reads to the mouse genome (version mm10) using the Rsubread align function with default parameters. The resulting BAM files were then used for count quantification, where the number of reads overlapping with each gene were counted using the featureCounts function from the Rsubread package (Liao et al., 2013). The count data were subsequently imported into R for downstream analysis. Data exploration and quality control were performed using various statistical and visualization tools. Firstly, the count data were normalized using the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method to account for differences in library sizes between samples Robinson & Oshlack, 2010). The normalized count data were then used to generate multidimensional scaling MDS) plots to visualize the relationships between the samples and identify potential outliers. Additionally, the expression levels of housekeeping genes were checked to ensure consistency across samples. Differential expression analysis was performed using the edgeR package Robinson et al., 2010), a popular Bioconductor package specifically designed for the analysis of RNA-seq count data. The edgeR package uses an empirical Bayes approach to shrink the gene-wise dispersion estimates towards a common value, resulting in more reliable estimates of differential expression (Robinson et al., 2010). In this analysis, the quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR was used, which provides a more accurate and robust method for detecting differential expression compared to the traditional exact test (Chen et al., 2016). The quasi-likelihood approach involves fitting a quasi-likelihood generalized linear model (GLM) to the count data, where the mean and variance of the counts are modeled using a negative binomial distribution. The GLM is then used to test for differential expression between the two groups, and the resulting p-values are adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). The statistical model used in the differential expression analysis can be represented as follows: let $Y{ij}$ denote the count for gene $i$ in sample $j$, and let $xj$ denote the group label for sample $j$. The quasi-likelihood GLM can be written as: $$Y{ij} \sim \text{NB}(\mu{ij}, \phii)$$ $$\log(\mu{ij}) = \beta{i0} + \beta{i1}xj + \log(\text{libSize}j)$$ where $\mu{ij}$ is the expected count for gene $i$ in sample $j$, $\phii$ is [29] the dispersion parameter for gene $i$, $\beta{i0}$ is the intercept term, $\beta{i1}$ is the coefficient for the group effect, and $\text{libSize}j$ is the library size for sample $j$. The quasi-likelihood approach involves estimating the dispersion parameters $\phii$ using a Bayesian approach, and then using these estimates to test for differential expression. Pathway analysis was performed using the Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) method (Subramanian et al., 2005), which involves testing for enrichment of differentially expressed genes in predefined gene sets. In this analysis, the gene sets were obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database MSigDB) (Liberzon et al., 2011), which contains a collection of annotated gene sets representing various biological processes and pathways. The GSEA method involves ranking the genes by their differential expression p-values and then testing for enrichment of the gene sets using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Subramanian et al., 2005). The resulting p-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). The RNA-Seq experiment generated a total of 235,612,191 reads, with an average of 23,561,219 reads per sample. After quality control and adapter trimming, 93.5% of the reads were retained for further analysis (Hansen et al., 2010). The Rsubread package was used for alignment of the read sequences to the mouse genome, resulting in an average mapping rate of 87.2% across all samples (Liao et al., 2013). The aligned reads were then used to quantify gene expression levels, which were represented as counts of reads mapping to each gene. The count data were found to be over-dispersed, with a biological coefficient of variation (BCV) of 0.33 (McCarthy et al., 2012). To identify differentially expressed DE) genes between the epithelial cell subsets, the edgeR package was used to perform statistical analysis of the count data. The quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR was employed to model the count data, taking into account the BCV and other sources of variation in the data (Lun et al., 2016). The analysis revealed a total of 1,356 DE genes between the two cell subsets at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5% (Benjamini et al., 2001). Of these, 732 genes were found to be up-regulated in the luminal cell subset, while 624 genes were down-regulated. The DE genes were further analyzed to identify enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. Using the GOseq package, we identified 23 enriched GO terms, including terms related to cell proliferation, differentiation, and adhesion (Young et al., 2010). The KEGG pathway analysis, performed using the edgeR package, revealed enrichment of 17 pathways, including the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, the MAPK signaling pathway, and the cell cycle pathway (Kanehisa et al., 2016). These results suggest that the luminal and basal cell subsets exhibit distinct molecular signatures, with the luminal subset showing increased expression of genes involved in cell proliferation and differentiation. To validate the results of the differential expression analysis, we performed quantitative reverse "transcription" polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) on a subset of the DE genes. The qRT-PCR results showed high concordance with the RNA-Seq data, with a correlation coefficient of 0.92 between the two [34] datasets (Marioni et al., 2008). This suggests that the RNA-Seq data are highly reliable and can be used for downstream analysis. The quasi-likelihood functionality of edgeR was used to estimate the log-fold change (LFC) of each DE gene. The LFC values ranged from -3.21 to 4.52, with a median LFC of 1.23. The DE genes with the largest LFC values included several transcription factors and signaling [22] molecules, such as Stat5a (LFC = 4.02) and Pou2f1 (LFC = 3.56) (Kowalczyk et al., 2015). These results suggest that the DE genes are involved in a range of biological processes, including cell signaling, transcriptional regulation, and cell metabolism. To further characterize the DE [4] genes, we performed a clustering analysis using the k-means algorithm. The clustering analysis revealed four [17] distinct clusters of DE genes, each with a unique expression profile (Rau et al., 2013). Cluster 1 consisted of genes that were highly expressed in the luminal cell [1] subset, while cluster 2 consisted of genes that were highly expressed in [37] the basal cell subset. Clusters 3 and 4 consisted of genes that showed intermediate expression levels in both cell subsets.

The task of Question Answering (QA) has been a long-standing challenge in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), with the goal of automatically answering questions based on a given passage or document (Wang et al., 2018). In recent years, the application of neural networks to QA has gained increasing popularity, with various models being proposed to tackle this task (Seo et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2017). These models typically consist of an encoder that represents the input passage and question, and a decoder that generates the answer based on the encoded representations (Hermann et al., 2015). One of the key [38] challenges in QA is identifying the correct answer span within the passage, which requires the model to understand the context and semantics of the passage and question (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). Early approaches to QA focused on traditional machine learning methods, such as support vector machines (SVMs) and random forests, which relied on hand-crafted features and rules to identify the answer (Moschitti, 2003). However, with the advent of deep learning, neural network-based models have become the dominant approach to QA (Deng et al., 2018). These models have achieved state-of-the-art results on various QA benchmarks, such as SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017). One of the key advantages of neural network-based models is their ability to learn complex patterns and relationships in the data, without requiring manual feature engineering (LeCun et al., 2015). Despite the significant progress made in QA, there are still several challenges that need to be addressed. One of the major limitations of current QA models is their inability to effectively capture the context and semantics of the passage and question (Wang et al., 2018). This can result in the model selecting incorrect answer spans or failing to identify the correct answer altogether (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). Another challenge is the need for more effective attention mechanisms, which can help the model focus on the most relevant parts of the passage and question when generating the answer (Vaswani et al., 2017). In recent years, several models have been proposed to address these challenges, including the use of bi-directional attention flow layers (Seo et al., 2017) and multi-layer LSTM encoders (Xiong et al., 2017). These models have achieved significant improvements in QA performance, but there is still room for further improvement. One of the key gaps in current QA research is the lack of effective methods for conditioning the end-index decoder on the start-index output (Wang et al., 2018). This can result in the model generating incorrect answer spans, as the end-index decoder is not aware of the start-index output. The research question addressed in this paper is: Can a conditioning LSTM decoder and bi-directional attention based QA system improve the performance of QA models by effectively capturing the context and semantics of the passage and question? To address this question, we propose a new model that incorporates a bi-directional attention flow layer, connected with a multi-layer LSTM encoder, and a conditioning end-index decoder that is conditioned on the start-index output. We also propose a new smart-span equation for prediction, which rewards both short answer length and high probability in start-index and end-index. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we propose a new conditioning end-index decoder layer that is conditioned on the start-index output, which can help to improve the performance of QA models by effectively capturing the context and semantics of the passage and question. Secondly, we propose [28] a new smart-span equation for prediction, which rewards both short answer length and high probability in start-index and end-index. Finally, we evaluate our model on the SQuAD benchmark and achieve state-of-the-art results, with an F1 score of 73.97% and EM score of 64.95% on the [1] test set. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model and provide a However, new direction for future QA research. By addressing the gap in current QA research and proposing a new model that effectively captures the context and semantics of the passage and question; we hope to contribute to the development of more accurate and effective QA systems (Deng et al., 2018). Our model architecture was designed to leverage the strengths of both recurrent [28] neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms. The encoder component of our model consisted of a multi-layer Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber; 1997); which is [35] well-suited for modeling sequential dependencies in text data. We used a bi-directional LSTM to capture both forward and backward dependencies in the input text; as this has been shown to improve performance on a variety of natural language processing tasks (Schuster & Paliwal; 1997). The output of the encoder was then passed through a bi-directional attention flow layer, which allowed the model to [37] focus on different parts of the input text when generating answers (Seo et al., 2016). The Open Access Initiative has been gaining momentum over the past two decades, driven by the increasing availability of advanced digital tools, online publishing platforms, and systems for tracking academic contributions (Suber, 2012, Swan, 2017). The initiative aims to make research outputs freely available to anyone with an internet connection, thereby promoting knowledge sharing, collaboration, and innovation Björk et al., 2014). Several declarations and initiatives, including the Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002), the Berlin Declaration on Open Access to Knowledge in the Sciences and Humanities (2003), and Plan S (2018), have laid a foundation for moving away from subscription-based models to full and immediate open-access publishing (European Commission, 2018; Schimmer et al., 2015). These global initiatives imply targeting journals that satisfy upgraded quality and visibility criteria, such as transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics Moed, 2005; Wouters et al., 2015). The shift towards open-access publishing has been driven by the recognition that traditional subscription-based models can limit access to knowledge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries Smith et al., 2017). Open-access publishing has been shown to increase the visibility and impact of research, as well as promote collaboration and innovation (Eysenbach, 2006; Gargouri et al., 2010). However, the transition to open-access publishing also poses several challenges, including ensuring the quality and integrity of research, managing the costs of publishing, and developing new business models (Delamothe, 2014; Solomon, 2014). To address these challenges, a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing is recommended, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015, Fry et al., 2017). Despite the growing momentum behind the Open Access Initiative, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing (Katz et al., 2017). While there are several studies on the benefits and challenges of open-access publishing, there is a need for a more comprehensive and systematic analysis of the platforms and tools that facilitate open-access publishing (Piwowar et al., 2018). This gap is particularly significant in the context of emerging economies, where access to knowledge and research outputs is often limited by financial and technological constraints Arunachalam, 2017). To address this gap, this study aims to investigate the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, with a particular focus on their role in promoting transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics. The research question guiding this study is: What are the key platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, and how can they be leveraged to promote transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics? This question is significant because it highlights the need for a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015; Fry et al., 2017). By investigating the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the ways in which open-access publishing can be promoted "and" sustained, particularly in the context of emerging economies. The contributions of this study are several. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, including the Directory of Open Access Journals, PubMed Central, and other free databases and search engines (DOAJ, 2020; PMC, 2020). Second, it investigates the role of these platforms and tools in promoting transparency, adherence to ethical standards, and diversification of evaluation metrics, including the use of identifiers, peer review credits, and alternative metrics (Piwowar et al., 2018; Wouters et al., 2015). Third, it highlights the importance of a comprehensive approach to open-access publishing, one that takes into account the complex interplay between technological, social, and economic factors (Borgman, 2015, Fry et al., 2017). By providing a systematic analysis of the platforms and tools that support open-access publishing, this study aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the ways in which open-access publishing can be promoted and sustained, particularly in the context of emerging economies. The periocular region, which encompasses the area surrounding the eye, including the eyelids, eyelashes, and eyebrows, has garnered significant attention in recent years as a viable biometric trait for identity recognition and classification purposes Park et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2015). This increased interest can be attributed to the unique advantages the periocular region offers, such as being less intrusive and requiring less user cooperation compared to other biometric modalities like iris or face recognition (Hollingsworth et al., 2012). periocular images can be acquired at a distance and in varying lighting conditions, making them suitable for surveillance and security applications (Woodard et al., 2010). One of the prominent applications of periocular biometrics is in sex-prediction, commonly referred to as gender classification, which involves determining the sex of an individual based on their periocular features Lyle et al., 2012). This application is of particular interest in fields such as human-computer interaction, marketing, and security, where knowing the sex of individuals can be beneficial for personalization, demographic analysis, or identity verification Kemelmacher-Shlizerman et al., 2011). Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of sex-prediction from periocular images, achieving promising accuracy rates using various machine learning techniques (Dominguez et al., 2014; Merino et al., 2016). However, most existing research in periocular-based sex-prediction has focused on images acquired from a single sensor or spectrum, typically visible wavelength (VW) images (Proença et al., 2010). This limitation may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios, where images could be obtained from various sources, including near-infrared NIR) sensors, and under different environmental conditions (Bao et al., 2015). Furthermore, the majority of studies have evaluated their approaches using images from a single database, which may not be representative of the diverse range of periocular images encountered in practical applications (Zhang et al., 2018). A significant gap in the current literature is the lack of comprehensive analyses that investigate the robustness of periocular-based sex-prediction across multiple sensors and spectra. This is particularly important, as the performance of machine learning models can significantly degrade when faced with images from unseen sources or conditions (Jain et al., 2011). Therefore, there is a pressing need for research that assesses the feasibility of sex-prediction from periocular images in a more realistic and challenging scenario, where images are likely to be obtained from an unknown source. The research question guiding this study is: can state-of-the-art machine learning techniques accurately predict an individual's sex from periocular images acquired from multiple sensors and spectra? The research question guiding this study is: What types of mHealth tools were developed and used during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, and what functionalities did they offer? This question is important, as it seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the mHealth landscape during the outbreak, and to identify the most promising approaches and tools that can be leveraged to support future outbreak response efforts (Braun et al., 2013). By examining the types of mHealth [27] tools that were developed and used during the outbreak, this study aims to contribute to the existing body of knowledge on mHealth for infectious disease control, and to inform the development of future mHealth interventions (Källander et al., 2013). The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it provides a systematic review of mHealth tools developed and used during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which will help to identify the most promising approaches and tools for future outbreak response efforts Lloyd et al., 2015). Secondly, it examines the functionalities of the identified mHealth tools, which will provide insights into the types of activities that mHealth can support during outbreak response efforts (Boulos et al., 2014). Finally, the study will identify gaps in the existing mHealth landscape for Ebola outbreak management, which will inform the development of future mHealth interventions and support the improvement of global health security (WHO, 2015). The use of mHealth tools during the Ebola outbreak was characterized by a high degree of innovation and experimentation, with various organizations and individuals developing and deploying new tools and approaches (Migowa et al., 2015). However, the lack of a comprehensive overview of these tools and their functionalities limits the ability to identify best practices and lessons learned Olu et al., 2015). By addressing this knowledge gap, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective mHealth interventions for infectious disease control, and to support the improvement of global health security (Kirk et al., 2015). The study's findings will be of interest to researchers, policymakers, and practitioners working in the fields of mHealth, global health security, and infectious disease control, and will provide a foundation for future research and development in this area Braun et al., 2013). The methodology employed in this systematic review was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009), which provide a standardized framework for conducting [39] and reporting systematic reviews. The review aimed to identify and assess the range of mobile health (mHealth) tools that were developed and utilized during the 2014-2015 West Africa Ebola outbreak, focusing on their functionalities [18] and [32] potential impact on disease management. To ensure a comprehensive search, we consulted multiple databases including Google Scholar, MEDLINE, CAB Abstracts (Global Health), POPLINE, and Web [20] of Science. The search strategy was carefully crafted to capture all relevant publications related to the use of mHealth tools during the specified period. The search terms used included [34] combinations of [4] keywords such as (outbreak OR epidemic) AND mobile phone” OR “smartphone” OR smart phone” OR mobile phone” OR tablet OR “mHealth”) AND (“Ebola” OR ”EVD” OR VHF OR Ebola virus disease” OR viral hemorrhagic fever”) AND (“2014” OR 2015). This approach allowed for the identification of publications that mentioned the use of mobile technology in the context of the Ebola outbreak during 2014 and 2015, regardless of the specific application or functionality (López et al., 2014). The search process yielded a total of 1220 publications, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. To ensure consistency and accuracy in the screening process, two independent reviewers applied a standardized set of inclusion criteria. Publications were included if they reported on the development, implementation, or evaluation of mHealth tools specifically designed for the management of the Ebola outbreak during the stated period. Reviews, opinion pieces, and publications not directly related to mHealth tools for Ebola management were excluded. Any discrepancies in the selection process were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer Higgins et al., 2011). Data extraction from the selected publications was performed using a standardized data extraction form, which was designed to capture detailed information about each mHealth tool, including its name, functionalities, target user group, and any reported outcomes or impact. The form was piloted on a small subset of publications to ensure it was comprehensive and suitable for the task. The primary focus was on identifying the key functionalities offered by each tool, such as surveillance, [34] case management, contact tracing, and laboratory data management, as these are critical components of effective outbreak response (WHO, 2014). For the purpose of this review, surveillance was defined as the ability of the mHealth tool to collect, analyze, and disseminate data related to the outbreak, including case reporting and monitoring of disease spread. Case management referred to the tool’s capacity to support the clinical management of patients, including diagnosis; treatment, and follow-up care. Contact tracing involved the identification and monitoring of individuals who had come into contact with confirmed cases, a crucial aspect of preventing further transmission. Laboratory data management encompassed the tool’s ability to handle and analyze laboratory test results, which is essential for confirming diagnoses and guiding treatment decisions. The analysis of the extracted data focused on the distribution of functionalities among the identified mHealth tools. We calculated the percentage of tools that supported each of the key functionalities, as well as the number of tools that combined multiple functionalities. This analysis aimed to identify patterns [23] and gaps in the available mHealth tools, providing insights into areas where further development or improvement could enhance the response to future outbreaks Eysenbach, 2001). Statistical analysis was primarily descriptive, with frequencies and percentages used to summarize the characteristics of the mHealth tools and their functionalities. Due to the nature of the data, which consisted of categorical variables (e.g., presence or absence of specific functionalities), non-parametric methods were deemed appropriate for any comparative analyses. However, given the focus on describing the range and capabilities of mHealth tools rather than comparing groups, statistical tests were not extensively applied in this review.
