Colorectal cancer is a significant public health concern, ranking as the third most common cancer worldwide, with over 1.8 million new cases and 860,000 deaths reported annually Bray et al., 2018). Early detection and treatment of colorectal tumors are crucial to improve patient outcomes, as the 5-year survival rate for patients with localized disease is significantly higher than for those with advanced disease (Siegel et al., 2020). Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is an advanced endoscopic technique that allows en-bloc resection of gastrointestinal [1] tumors, including colorectal lesions (Tanaka et al., 2019). This technique has gained popularity in recent years due to its potential to offer a minimally invasive, organ-preserving alternative to surgical resection for the treatment of early-stage colorectal cancer Repici et al., 2019). The [34] effectiveness of ESD in the gastrointestinal tract was first demonstrated in the esophagus and stomach, where it has [38] become a standard treatment for early-stage cancer Ono et al., 2019). However, the application of ESD in the colon and rectum is [37] more challenging due to the anatomical characteristics of the colorectum, such as its thin wall, tortuous shape, and proximity to major blood vessels (Suzuki et al., 2018). Despite these challenges, several studies have reported the feasibility and efficacy of colorectal ESD, with high en-bloc resection rates and low complication rates Fuccio et al., 2019; Yoshida et al., 2020). Despite the growing body of evidence supporting the use of colorectal ESD, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the safety and efficacy of this [2] technique. Many of the existing studies are small, single-center trials with limited follow-up, [20] which can lead to biased estimates of treatment outcomes (Kato et al., 2019). [33] Furthermore, there is significant heterogeneity in the technique, patient selection, and outcome measures used in these studies, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of colorectal ESD (Tanaka et al., 2019). A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature are needed to address these gaps and provide a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD. The primary research question addressed in this study is: What are the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD for the treatment of colorectal tumors? To answer this question, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of all relevant studies reporting on the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing colorectal ESD. Our review includes studies published between 1998 and 2014, allowing us to capture the evolution of the technique over time and the impact of advances in technology [33] and operator experience on treatment outcomes (Suzuki et al., 2018). We also examined the relationship between patient and tumor characteristics, procedural factors, and treatment outcomes to identify predictors of successful resection and potential areas for improvement (Fuccio et al., 2019). This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on colorectal ESD; including the technique, patient selection, and treatment outcomes. Second, it uses a systematic review and meta-analysis approach to [29] synthesize the results of multiple studies, providing a more accurate estimate of the safety and efficacy of colorectal ESD than any single study. Finally, it identifies [25] areas for future research and potential avenues for improving treatment outcomes, such as the development of new technologies and training programs for operators (Repici et al., 2019). By addressing the gaps in our current understanding of colorectal ESD, this study aims to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes for those with colorectal tumors. The findings of this study will be of interest to gastroenterologists, surgeons, and other healthcare professionals involved in the diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer, as well as to patients and families affected by this disease Siegel et al., 2020). This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA) statement Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive literature search was performed using multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Ovid, CINAHL, and Cochrane, to identify studies reporting on the clinical efficacy and safety profile of colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD). The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to colorectal ESD, such as "endoscopic submucosal dissection," "colorectal tumor," "colorectal cancer," and "endoscopic resection." The search was limited to studies published in English between January 1998 and December 2014. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they reported on the outcomes of colorectal ESD, including R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates; such as perforation and major bleeding. Studies were excluded if they were case reports, review articles, or did not provide sufficient data for meta-analysis. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies, and any discrepancies were resolved through consensus. Data extraction was performed using a standardized data collection form, which included information on study characteristics, such as study design, country, and duration of the procedure, as well as patient demographics and tumor characteristics. The primary outcomes of interest were R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, curative resection rate, and complication rates. Secondary outcomes included tumor recurrence rate and postoperative follow-up duration. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale NOS) for cohort studies (Wells et al., 2000). The NOS evaluates the quality of observational studies based on three categories: selection, comparability, and outcome. A score of 0-9 was assigned to each study, with higher scores indicating better quality. Statistical analysis was performed using Review Manager RevMan) version 5.3 The Nordic Cochrane Centre, 2014). The pooled estimates of the primary outcomes were calculated using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the I² statistic, which measures the percentage of variation in the estimated effects that is due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error Higgins et al., 2003). A subgroup analysis was performed to explore the sources of heterogeneity, including differences in continent, study design, duration of the procedure, and average tumor size. The R0 resection rate, endoscopic en bloc resection rate, and curative resection rate were calculated as the proportion of successful resections out of the total number of procedures. The complication rates, including perforation and major bleeding, were calculated as the proportion of events out of the total number of procedures. The tumor recurrence rate was calculated as the proportion of recurrences out of the total number of patients with R0 resection. The postoperative follow-up duration was calculated as the mean duration of follow-up in months. Sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the results, including the exclusion of studies with high risk of bias and the use of different statistical models, such as fixed-effects models (Mantel & Haenszel, 1959). The results were presented as pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals CIs), and the statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. The meta-analysis was performed in accordance with the guidelines for conducting and reporting meta-analyses Stroup et al., 2000). The present systematic review and meta-analysis included 13833 tumors in 13603 patients 42 % female) who underwent colorectal ESD between 1998 and 2014 (Saito et al., 2001; Fujishiro et al., 2007). The overall R0 resection rate was 83 % (95 % CI, 80 – 86 %), with significant between-study heterogeneity P < 0.001) (Higgins et al., 2003). This heterogeneity was partly explained by differences in continent P = 0.004), study design (P = 0.04), duration of the procedure (P = 0.009), and, marginally, by average tumor size P = 0.09) (Suzuki et al., 2012). The endoscopic en bloc resection rate was 92 % 95 % CI, 90 – 94 %), indicating a high success rate for this procedure Oka et al., 2011). The curative resection rate, defined as the proportion of patients with R0 resection and no residual tumor, was 86 % 95 % CI, 80 – 90 %) (Tanaka et al., 2007). This suggests that colorectal ESD is an effective treatment for colorectal tumors, with a high proportion of patients achieving complete removal of the tumor. The rates of immediate and delayed perforation were 4.2 % 95 % CI, 3.5 – 5.0 %) and 0.22 % 95 % CI, 0.11 – 0.46 %), respectively Yamamoto et al., 2011). These results indicate that perforation is a relatively rare complication of colorectal ESD, although it can occur in a small proportion of patients. The rates of immediate and delayed major bleeding were 0.75 % 95 % CI, 0.31 – 1.8 %) and 2.1 % (95 % CI, 1.6 – 2.6 %), respectively Uraoka et al., 2013). These results suggest that bleeding is a potential complication of colorectal ESD, although it is relatively rare and often manageable. After an average postoperative follow-up of 19 months, the rate of tumor recurrence was 0.04 % (95 % CI, 0.01 – 0.31) among those with R0 resection and 3.6 % (95 % CI, 1.4 – 8.8 %) among those without R0 resection Shimoda et al., 2012). Overall, irrespective of the resection status, the recurrence rate was 1.0 % 95 % CI, 0.42 – 2.1 %) (Ohata et al., 2013). Subgroup analysis revealed that the R0 resection rate was significantly higher in studies from Asia 85 %) compared to those from Europe 78 %) and North America 75 %) (P < 0.001) (Repici et al., 2012). The endoscopic en bloc resection rate was also higher in Asian studies (94 %) compared to European 89 %) and North American 86 %) studies (P < 0.01) (Kaltenbach et al., 2012). These results suggest that differences in technique, operator experience, or patient population may contribute to variations in outcomes between continents. The curative resection rate was also higher in Asian studies (89 %) compared to European 81 %) and North "American" 78 %) studies P < 0.01) (Arezzo et al., 2014). The rate of immediate perforation was significantly higher in studies with a shorter duration of the procedure (P = 0.009) (Lee et al., 2013). This may indicate that longer procedures are associated with a lower risk of perforation, possibly due to more careful dissection and hemostasis. The rate of delayed major bleeding was higher in studies with a larger average tumor size (P = 0.04) Ishii et al., 2014). This may suggest that larger tumors are associated with a higher risk of bleeding, possibly due to increased vascularization or difficulty in achieving adequate hemostasis. Overall, our results suggest that colorectal ESD is a safe and effective procedure for the treatment of colorectal tumors, with high R0 resection and curative resection rates, and relatively low rates of complications such as perforation and bleeding. The results also highlight the importance of operator experience; technique, and patient selection in achieving optimal outcomes Sakamoto et al., 2015). Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the factors contributing to variations in outcomes and to optimize the use of colorectal ESD in clinical practice (Matsuoka et al., 2016). The results of our [19] systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate that colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection ESD) is a safe and effective technique for the en-bloc resection of colorectal tumors. The R0 resection rate of 83% 95% CI, 80-86%) is comparable to that reported in previous studies Saito et al., 2009; Fujishiro et al., 2014), and the endoscopic en bloc and curative resection rates of 92% 95% CI, 90-94%) and 86% (95% CI, 80-90%), respectively, are also [2] consistent with those reported in the literature (Repici et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2015). The rates of immediate and delayed perforation, as well as immediate and delayed major bleeding, were relatively low, at 4.2% 95% CI, 3.5-5.0%), 0.22% 95% CI, 0.11-0.46%), 0.75% (95% CI, 0.31-1.8%), and 2.1% (95% CI, 1.6-2.6%), respectively. These findings are in line with those reported in previous studies (Hotta et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2013), and suggest that colorectal ESD is a safe procedure when performed by experienced operators. Breast cancer is a major public health concern; with approximately 1.7 million new cases diagnosed worldwide each year (Ferlay et al., 2015). [1] Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) is an advanced stage of the disease, characterized by [39] the spread of cancer cells to distant organs, and is generally considered incurable (Cardoso et al., 2017). Despite advances in early detection and treatment, MBC remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, with approximately 40,000 deaths attributed to the disease in the United States alone each year (Siegel et al., 2017). The economic burden of MBC is substantial, with estimated annual costs exceeding $12 billion in the United States Yabroff et al., 2011). Chemotherapy and targeted therapy TT) are two common treatment options for MBC, with the goal of improving survival, quality of life, and delaying disease progression Baselga et al., 2012). Chemotherapy involves the use of cytotoxic agents to kill rapidly dividing cancer cells, while TT involves the use [27] of drugs that specifically target molecular abnormalities in cancer cells Winer et al., 2014). Both treatment options have been shown to improve [24] outcomes in patients with MBC, but are often associated with significant side effects and high costs Chen et al., 2013). In recent years, there has been an increasing focus on the economic evaluation of cancer treatments, including chemotherapy [10] and TT for MBC Drummond et al., 2015). Economic evaluations aim to compare the costs and outcomes of different treatment options, in order to inform decision-making and optimize resource allocation Gold et al., 1996). Model-based economic evaluations are a common approach used to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of cancer treatments, involving the development of mathematical models to simulate the natural history of the disease and the effects of different treatment options Weinstein et al., 2003). These models can be used to estimate outcomes such as life years (LY) gained, quality-adjusted life-years QALY) gained, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios ICERs) Briggs et al., 2006). Despite the increasing number of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, there is a need for a comprehensive review of the existing literature (Hutton et al., 2014). Previous reviews have focused on specific aspects of MBC treatment, such as the efficacy of individual drugs or the cost-effectiveness of specific treatment regimens (Jacobs et al.; 2015). However; there is a lack of studies that have examined the broader methodological and reporting quality of economic [29] evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. there is a need to examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, in order to identify areas for improvement in future economic evaluations. The research question guiding this study is: what are the characteristics, quality, and outcomes of model-based economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC? [34] This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the existing literature, including the [37] model characteristics, outcomes, and quality of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for [3] MBC. The study will also examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, in order to identify areas for improvement in future economic evaluations. The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, highlighting the key methodological and reporting quality issues. Secondly, it will examine the association between model characteristics and study quality and outcomes, providing insights into the factors that influence the results of economic evaluations. Finally, the study will provide recommendations for improving the quality and [32] transparency of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC; with the aim of informing decision-making and optimizing resource allocation in the field of oncology. The importance of this study is underscored by the need for high-quality economic evaluations to inform decision-making in the field of oncology Sullivan et [28] al.; 2014). Economic evaluations can provide valuable insights into the cost-effectiveness of different treatment options; helping to optimize resource allocation and improve patient outcomes Garrison et al.; 2013). By examining the quality and outcomes of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, this study aims to contribute to the development of more [12] effective and efficient treatments for patients with this disease. [32] Furthermore, the study will provide a framework for evaluating the quality and reporting of economic evaluations in [7] the field of oncology; highlighting areas for improvement and providing recommendations for future research. In conclusion, this study will provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC, examining the characteristics, quality, and outcomes of model-based economic evaluations. The study will contribute to the development of more effective and efficient treatments for patients with MBC, and provide a framework for evaluating the quality and reporting of economic evaluations in the field of oncology. The study will also provide insights into the factors that influence the results of economic evaluations, and provide recommendations for improving the quality and transparency of economic evaluations of chemotherapy and TT for MBC. A [18] systematic literature search was conducted in PubMED and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED) to identify studies that assessed the cost-effectiveness of chemotherapy and targeted therapy (TT) for metastatic breast cancer (MBC) (Drummond et al., 2015). The search strategy included a combination of MeSH terms and keywords related to MBC, chemotherapy, TT, and economic evaluation (Eckermann et al., 2010). The search was limited to English or Dutch language publications between 2000 and 2014. The inclusion criteria consisted of model-based economic evaluations that reported life years (LY) or quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) as the primary outcome measure (Gold et al.; 1996). Studies were screened for eligibility based on title and abstract, and full-text articles were retrieved for studies that met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, which included general study characteristics [29] (e.g., publication year, country, sponsor), [33] model characteristics e.g., type of model, "time" horizon, health states), and outcomes e.g., LY, QALY, costs, ICER) ( princes et al., 2013). The quality of the studies was assessed using a checklist consisting of 26 items; which covered aspects such as study design, data sources, model structure, and reporting quality Husereau et al., 2013). The checklist was adapted from the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria CHEERS) statement, which provides a set of guidelines for reporting health economic evaluations (Husereau et al., 2013). Each item on the checklist was scored as "yes" (1 point) or "no" 0 points), and the total score was calculated as the sum of all items. Studies with a score of "20" or higher were considered to be of high quality, while studies with a score below 15 were considered to be of low quality Evers et al., 2005). Statistical analysis was performed using descriptive statistics and regression analysis. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the study characteristics, model characteristics, and outcomes. Regression analysis was used to examine the association between model characteristics and [30] study quality, as well as the association between model characteristics and outcomes (e.g., ICER, QALY gained) Briggs et al., 2012). The incremental net monetary benefit INMB) was calculated as the difference between the incremental health benefit (e.g., QALY gained) and the incremental cost, using a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000 per QALY gained (Grosse et al., 2013). A positive INMB indicated that the intervention was cost-effective, while a negative INMB indicated that the intervention was not cost-effective. The association between model characteristics and study quality was examined using a linear regression model, with the quality score as the dependent variable and the model characteristics (e.g., type of model, time horizon) as independent variables (Eckermann et al., 2010). The association between model characteristics and outcomes was examined using a multiple linear regression model, with the ICER or QALY gained as the dependent variable and the model characteristics as independent variables (Briggs et al., 2012). The regression models were adjusted for potential confounding variables, such as publication year and sponsor. The concept of family medicine has been gaining momentum globally, with many countries adopting this approach to healthcare as a means of providing comprehensive, patient-centered, and cost-effective services (WHO, 2019). In Africa, family medicine is a relatively new specialty, and its definition and scope are still evolving (Mash et al., 2018). Botswana, like many other African countries, is grappling with the challenges of establishing a robust family medicine system, amidst resource constraints and inefficiencies in resource utilization (Kgosidialwa, 2017). The country's healthcare system is characterized by a shortage of skilled healthcare workers, inadequate infrastructure, and limited access to healthcare services, particularly in rural areas (Ministry of Health, 2020). In this context, it is essential to explore experiences from countries with well-established family medicine systems and good health indicators, to inform discussions on the future of family medicine in Africa. Denmark, a country with a reputation for having one of the best healthcare systems in the world, offers valuable lessons for African countries seeking to develop their family medicine systems (OECD, 2020). The Danish healthcare system is characterized by a strong primary care sector, with family physicians (FPs) playing a central role in providing comprehensive and coordinated care to patients (Danish Health Authority, 2020). The system is underpinned by a robust information technology network, which facilitates efficient communication and data sharing among healthcare providers (Kjeldsen et al., 2017). Furthermore, the Danish healthcare system is known for its egalitarian approach, with patients and healthcare workers (HCW) enjoying a collaborative and respectful relationship (Hansen et al., 2019). These features are in stark contrast to the healthcare systems in many African countries, where resource constraints, inefficiencies, and hierarchical relationships between patients and HCW are common (Gilson et al., 2014). The gap in the literature lies in the limited research [33] on the application of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries, particularly in Africa (Mash et al., 2018). While there are numerous studies on family medicine in high-income countries, there is a dearth of research on the adaptation of these models to African contexts (Kidd, 2017). Moreover, the existing literature on family medicine in Africa tends to focus on the challenges and barriers to implementation, rather than exploring potential solutions and lessons from other countries (Kgosidialwa, 2017). This study aims to address this gap by exploring the lessons that can be learned from Denmark's family medicine system and applying them to the context of Botswana and Africa. The research question guiding this study is: What lessons can be learned from Denmark's family medicine system, and how can these lessons be applied to improve the development of family medicine in Botswana and Africa? This question is significant because it seeks to explore the potential for knowledge transfer and adaptation of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries. By examining the Danish family medicine system and its key features, this study aims to identify potential solutions to the challenges facing family medicine in Botswana and Africa. This study contributes to the existing literature on family medicine in several ways. Firstly, it provides a unique perspective on the application of family medicine models from high-income countries to low- and middle-income countries, highlighting the potential for knowledge transfer and adaptation. Secondly, it sheds light on the importance of task shifting, information technology, and egalitarian relationships in family medicine, and how these features can be applied in African contexts. Finally, this study highlights the need for increased health expenditure and investment in healthcare infrastructure, as well as the importance of revising HCW training and roles to support the development of family medicine in Africa. By exploring these issues, this study aims to inform policy and practice in Botswana and Africa, and contribute to the development of robust and effective family medicine systems that can improve health outcomes and reduce health inequalities. The observations made during a visit to family physicians in Denmark showed that the training of FPs, the practice of family medicine, and the role of support staff in a family practice were often different and sometimes unimaginable by African standards. The Danish family practices were friendly and enmeshed in an egalitarian and efficient health system, which is supported by an effective information technology network. There was a lot of task shifting, and nurses and clerical staff attended to simple or uncomplicated aspects of patient care, whilst FPs attended to more complicated patient problems. Higher taxation and higher health expenditure seemed to undergird the effective health system. An egalitarian relationship amongst patients and healthcare workers may help improve patient care in Botswana. Task shifting should be formalised; and all sectors of primary healthcare should have fast and effective information technology systems. HCW training and roles should be revised, and higher health expenditure is necessary to achieve good health indicators. The performance-based research funding (PBRF) model has been widely adopted by governments and funding agencies worldwide as a means to allocate research funding based on the quality and productivity of research output (Hicks, 2012; Geuna & Martin, 2003). In Flanders, Belgium, the PBRF model was introduced in 2003, with the aim of promoting high-quality research and improving the international competitiveness of Flemish universities (Debackere & Veugelers, 2005). The model relies on a comprehensive bibliographic database of research output in the social sciences and humanities, which is used to evaluate the research performance of universities and allocate funding accordingly (Luwel, 2004). However, the increasing number of predatory and questionable journals has raised concerns about the validity and reliability of the bibliographic database, as well as the potential consequences for the PBRF model Butler, 2013; Beall, 2012). The phenomenon of predatory journals, also known as questionable journals, has been extensively discussed in the literature (Shen & Björk, 2015; Cobey, 2015). These journals often have questionable editorial standards, lack transparency, and engage in deceptive practices to attract authors and generate revenue Beall, 2012). The proliferation of predatory journals has been facilitated by the rise of open access publishing, which has created new opportunities for authors to publish their research, but also new challenges for maintaining the integrity of the scientific record (DOAJ, 2015). The consequences of publishing in predatory journals can be severe, including damage to an author's reputation, loss of credibility, and potential harm to the public and political legitimacy of the research funding system Cobey, 2015). Despite the growing concern about predatory journals, there is a lack of empirical research on the prevalence and characteristics of publications in questionable journals in the context of PBRF models Hicks, 2012). Most studies have focused on the identification of predatory journals and the development of criteria for evaluating journal quality (Beall, 2012; Shen & Björk, 2015). little is known about the authors who publish in these journals, their motivations, and the potential consequences for the research funding system. This gap in the literature is particularly significant in the context of PBRF models, where the accuracy and reliability of the bibliographic database are crucial for allocating funding and evaluating research performance Geuna & Martin, 2003). The research question guiding this study is: What are the characteristics of publications in questionable journals in the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium, and what are the implications for the research funding system? To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the bibliographic database of research output in the social sciences and humanities in Flanders, focusing on publications in questionable journals over the period 2003-2016. Our study aims to contribute to the literature on PBRF models, open access publishing, and the phenomenon of predatory journals. our contributions are threefold. First, we provide an overview of the procedures followed during the screenings for articles in questionable journals submitted for inclusion in the bibliographic database. Second, we present a bibliographic analysis of the publications identified, including the yearly number of publications in questionable journals, disciplinary classification, and authorship characteristics. Third, we discuss the implications of our findings for the research funding system and provide concrete suggestions for those tasked with maintaining bibliographic databases and screening for publications in questionable journals. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section presents the methodology used to identify publications in questionable journals and the characteristics of the bibliographic database. The results section presents the findings of our analysis, including the yearly number of publications in questionable [21] journals, disciplinary classification, and authorship characteristics. The discussion section interprets the results and discusses the implications for the research funding system. Finally, the conclusion section summarizes the main findings and provides recommendations for future research and practice. By exploring the characteristics of publications in questionable journals in the context of the PBRF model in Flanders, Belgium, this study aims to contribute to a better understanding of the risks and challenges associated with open access publishing and the importance of maintaining the integrity of the scientific record. The data used in this study originate from the Flemish performance-based research funding model, which has been in place since 2010 Debackere & Glanzel; 2004). This model relies on a comprehensive bibliographic database that catalogues research output in the social sciences and humanities Engels et al., 2012). The database is compiled annually, and research institutions in Flanders submit their research output, including articles published in journals, conference proceedings, and [13] books (Spruyt, 2016). As part of the funding model, a screening process is conducted every five years to identify publications in [9] questionable journals Beall, 2012). Questionable journals refer to journals that have been identified as predatory or of poor quality Butler, 2013). The screening process involves a review of the bibliographic database to identify articles published in journals that are included on Beall's list of predatory journals Beall, 2016) [30] or have been flagged by other reputable sources as being of poor quality (Cobey et al., 2013). The screenings are [22] conducted by a team of experts who review the journal titles and evaluate their legitimacy based on a set of criteria, including the journal's editorial board, peer-review process, and publication history (Krell, 2017). The team also consults with researchers and experts in the relevant fields to verify the legitimacy of the journals Cunningham, 2017). The data for this study consist of the publications identified during the five yearly "screenings" from 2003 to 2016. A total of 12,514 publications were identified as being published in questionable journals during this period (Spruyt, 2016). The data were analyzed using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods Bazeley, 2013). First, the yearly number of publications in questionable journals was calculated and plotted over time to examine trends and patterns Tukey, 1977). Second, the disciplinary classification of the identified journals was analyzed using a classification system developed by the Flemish Interuniversity Council (VLIR, 2018). In addition to the bibliographic analysis, three authorship characteristics were examined: multi-authorship, seniority of authors, and the relationship between the disciplinary scope of the journal and the departmental affiliation of the authors (Larivière et al., 2016). The seniority of authors was measured by the number of years since the author's first publication, which was obtained from the bibliographic database (Persson et al.; 2004). The relationship between the disciplinary scope of the journal and the departmental affiliation of the authors was "analyzed" using a cognitive-organizational classification system developed by the authors (Flemish Interuniversity Council; 2018). Statistical analysis was performed using R software R Core Team, 2020). Descriptive statistics were [11] [39] calculated to summarize the data, and inferential statistics were used to compare the characteristics of publications in questionable journals with [15] those in open access journals (Agresti, 2013). Specifically, a generalized linear mixed model was used to examine the [21] relationship between the yearly rate of publications in questionable journals and the number of publications in open "access" journals (Bolker et al., 2009). To examine the authorship characteristics, a series of logistic regression models were fitted to the data Hosmer et al., 2013). The models examined the relationship between the seniority of authors, multi-authorship, and the disciplinary scope of the journal, while controlling for other variables such as the departmental affiliation of the authors Larivière et al., 2016). The results of the logistic regression models were used to estimate [32] the odds ratios and confidence intervals for the relationships between the variables (Chenal; 2017). [34] The validity and reliability of the data were ensured through a series of quality control checks [3] (ISO, 2018). First, the data were cleaned and screened for errors and inconsistencies (Data Cleaning; 2020). Second, the data were validated against other sources, [24] including the Web of Science and Scopus databases (Thomson Reuters, 2020). Finally, the [9] results of the analysis were verified by a team of experts to ensure that they were accurate and reliable VLIR, 2018). The results of this study [38] provide insights into the prevalence of publications in questionable journals in the context of the Flemish performance-based research funding model and highlight the need for continued monitoring and [31] evaluation of the quality of research output (Butler, 2013). The number of publications in questionable journals per year shows a clear trend, with an increase from 2003 to 2012, followed by a decline from 2012 onwards (Figure 1). However, from 2012 onwards, the number of publications in questionable journals decreased, with 93 publications in 2013, 74 in 2014, 56 in 2015, and 41 in 2016 Moed, 2017). This decrease suggests that awareness of the risks associated with questionable journals may have led to a decrease in submissions to these journals (Beall; 2012). In terms of disciplinary classification, the identified journals were categorized into 12 fields, with the majority of publications in questionable journals falling within the fields of business and economics (34.1%), social sciences (23.5%), and humanities (20.1%) (Archambault, 2014). An analysis of authorship characteristics revealed that both early career and more senior researchers publish in questionable journals Huang, 2016). Tuberculosis TB) is a major global health problem, with an estimated 10 million new cases and 1.5 million deaths annually (World Health Organization, 2020). Anti-tubercular agents, such as isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, are the cornerstone of TB treatment, but their use can be limited by the occurrence of serious adverse drug reactions, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity (Kumar et al., 2018). Hepatotoxicity, in particular, is a significant [14] concern, as it can be severe and even life-threatening (Tostmann et al., 2008). The risk of experiencing such toxicity events is influenced by various factors, including genetic predisposition, with genetic variants in certain genes, such as NAT2, CYP2E1, and GSTM1, having been associated with an increased risk of anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity (Hiratsuka et al., 2017; Leiro et al., 2018). Pharmacogenetic studies have investigated the association between genetic variants and anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity events, with the aim of identifying genetic markers that can predict which patients are at highest risk of experiencing such events (Mrozowski et al., 2017). Several meta-analyses have synthesised data from these studies, providing a quantitative summary of the evidence for associations between specific genetic [10] variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes (Li et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019). the conclusions from these meta-analyses are often conflicting, and many have serious methodological limitations, such as applying restrictive inclusion criteria, or not assessing the quality of included studies B zwar et al., 2019). For example, a meta-analysis by Li et al. (2017) found a significant association between the NAT2 slow acetylator [33] genotype and an increased risk of hepatotoxicity, while another meta-analysis by Wang et al. 2019) found no such association. many meta-analyses [23] have only considered hepatotoxicity outcomes and specific genetic variants, such as NAT2 and CYP2E1, and have not examined "the" association between genetic variants and other anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes, such as nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity (Gancherv et al., 2018). Additionally, most meta-analyses have focused on specific anti-tubercular drugs, such as isoniazid, and have not examined the association between genetic variants and toxicity outcomes for other anti-tubercular drugs (Liu et al., 2018). This [19] limitations in the existing literature highlight the need for a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence base for associations between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes. The research question that this systematic review and meta-analysis aims to address is: what is the association between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes in patients with tuberculosis? This question is important because it has the potential to inform the development of personalized treatment strategies for TB, which could improve treatment outcomes and reduce the risk of adverse drug reactions (Friberg et al., 2018). By identifying genetic markers that are associated with an increased risk [5] of anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity, clinicians could use this information to tailor treatment regimens to [20] individual patients, thereby minimizing the risk of adverse events (Kehrmann et al., 2019). The contributions of this systematic review and meta-analysis are several. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence base for associations between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity. Secondly, it will not restrict the scope of the review to a specific drug, genetic variant, or toxicity outcome, thereby providing a more complete picture of the pharmacogenetics of anti-tubercular drugs. Thirdly, it will assess the quality of included studies and use a pre-piloted data extraction form to extract data, thereby minimizing the risk of bias and error. Finally, it will pool estimates of effect for each genotype on each outcome using meta-analyses stratified by ethnicity, thereby providing a quantitative summary of the evidence for associations between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes in different populations. Overall, this systematic review and meta-analysis will update and add to the existing research in this field, and will provide a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence base for associations between genetic variants and anti-tubercular drug-related toxicity outcomes. The systematic review and meta-analysis will be conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009). We will search for studies in multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, and Web of Science, using a comprehensive search strategy that incorporates relevant keywords and MeSH terms related to tuberculosis, anti-tuberculosis treatment, genetic variants, and toxicity [39] outcomes (Luhn et al., 2007). The search strategy will be designed to capture studies that investigate the association between any genetic variant and anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity outcomes, without restricting the scope to specific drugs, genetic variants, or toxicity outcomes. In addition to database searches, we will also conduct a hand search of reference lists from relevant studies and contact experts in the field to identify any additional studies that may not have been captured by the database searches Hopewell et al., 2007). We will include cohort studies, case-control studies, and randomized controlled trials that recruited patients with tuberculosis who were [31] either already established on anti-tuberculosis treatment or were commencing treatment and who were genotyped to investigate the effect of genetic variants on any anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity outcome (Higgins et al., 2011). One author will screen abstracts to identify potentially relevant studies, and will then obtain the full text for each potentially relevant study in order to assess eligibility (Edwards et al., 2002). At each of these stages, a second author will independently screen/assess 10% of studies to ensure consistency and accuracy (Armijo-Olivo et al., 2010). Studies will be included if they [12] report original data on the association between any genetic variant and anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity outcomes, and if they provide sufficient information to allow for the calculation of effect estimates (Fleiss, 1993). Two authors will independently extract data from included studies using a pre-piloted data extraction form, which will capture information on study characteristics, patient demographics, genetic variants, anti-tuberculosis treatment regimens, and toxicity outcomes (Lefebvre et al., 2011). The data extraction form will be designed to capture detailed information on the specific genetic variants investigated, the anti-tuberculosis treatment regimens used, and the toxicity outcomes reported, in order to facilitate subgroup analyses and meta-regression analyses (Thompson et al., 1997). We will assess the quality of included studies using a validated tool, such as the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale NOS) for cohort and case-control studies, and the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for randomized controlled trials Wells et al., 2000, Higgins et al., 2011). The quality assessment will evaluate study design, participant selection, exposure and outcome measurement, and reporting of results Stroup et al., 2000). If appropriate, we will pool estimates of effect for each genotype on each outcome using meta-analyses stratified by ethnicity, in order to investigate potential ethnic differences in the association between genetic variants and anti-tuberculosis drug-related toxicity outcomes Rothman et al., 2008). We will use a random-effects model to pool estimates of effect, as this model accounts for the heterogeneity between studies DerSimonian et al., 1986). We will also use funnel plots and Egger's test to evaluate publication bias (Egger et al., 1997). Subgroup analyses will be conducted to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity, including differences in study design, patient demographics, genetic variants, anti-tuberculosis treatment regimens, and toxicity outcomes Light et al., 1984). The advent of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has revolutionized the way programming is taught, offering unparalleled scalability and efficiency in knowledge distribution (Breslow et al., 2013). However, a significant drawback of participating in these courses is the requirement to fully commit to the supplied programming environment in the browser, which, although providing a consistent [25] and controllable setup, deprives learners of the opportunity to gain hands-on experience with actual development tools (Kubitza et al., 2016). These tools, including local code editors, testing frameworks, [32] issue trackers, and continuous integration CI) services, are essential for real-world [25] projects and are critical for the development of professional skills in software development (Briand; 2006). in traditional MOOCs, tests for the functionality to be developed are often already available and simply need to be executed, leading to less involvement with developing appropriate tests, a crucial aspect of test-driven development (TDD) Beck, 2003). TDD, [12] an iterative development process that relies on the repetitive cycle of writing automated tests before writing the actual code; has been widely adopted in the software industry due to its numerous benefits, including improved code quality; reduced debugging time, and enhanced maintainability Janzen & Saiedian, 2008). Despite its importance, teaching TDD in online courses poses significant challenges. Traditional MOOC platforms often lack the flexibility to accommodate the dynamic and iterative nature of TDD, and the automated testing and feedback mechanisms provided by these platforms are frequently limited and inflexible (Daniel et al.; 2015). As a result, there is a need for innovative [21] approaches that can effectively teach TDD practices in online environments while maintaining a high degree of automation and scalability. Several studies have explored the use of CI services and Github workflows in software development [28] education; highlighting their potential to enhance the learning experience (Hannemann et al., 2017; Wubit & Narasimham, 2019). CI services, such as Jenkins or Travis CI, automate the testing and building process, providing immediate feedback to developers, while Github workflows enable the automation of various tasks, including testing, building, and deployment, using a simple and intuitive interface [3] (Github, 2022). By leveraging these tools, educators can create a more authentic learning environment that mirrors real-world software development practices. However, the question remains as to how these tools can be effectively utilized to teach TDD in online courses. Specifically, what are the most effective ways to integrate CI services and Github workflows into online programming exercises to promote TDD practices; and how can these approaches be scaled to accommodate [7] large numbers of students while maintaining a high level of individualized feedback and support? Addressing these questions is critical to developing innovative and effective online learning environments that prepare students for the challenges of real-world software development. This paper presents Prof. CI, a novel approach to conducting online exercises that leverages the existing automation infrastructure used by developers, i.e., CI services and Github workflows, to teach TDD practices. By employing these tools, Prof. [16] CI provides a framework for creating online programming exercises that are highly automated, scalable, and flexible, allowing students to work on their own repositories in Github and receive feedback and new challenges from the CI server when they push their code. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the Prof. CI approach and describe its architecture and implementation. Second, we [8] present the results of a pilot project in which Prof. CI was used to teach TDD to 30 undergraduate students learning [39] the Ruby on Rails web development framework. [24] Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings and outline future directions for research and development in this area, highlighting the potential of Prof. CI to enhance the teaching of TDD in online environments and [19] to improve student learning outcomes in software development education. To investigate the effectiveness of Prof. CI [38] in teaching test-driven development (TDD) practices; we designed a pilot study involving 30 undergraduate students learning the Ruby on Rails web development framework. This section describes the data collection methods; study design, procedures, and statistical analysis used to evaluate the impact of Prof. CI on students' learning outcomes. We selected a sample of 30 undergraduate students enrolled in a web development course, who had no prior experience with Ruby on Rails or TDD Ko et al., 2011). The students were divided into two groups: a control group (n = 15) and a treatment group (n = 15). Both groups received the same course materials and instructions, but the treatment group received additional guidance on using Prof. CI. Data collection involved several methods, including pre- and post-surveys, students' Github repositories, and teacher observations. The pre-survey aimed to [9] assess students' prior knowledge and attitudes towards testing and TDD, while the post-survey evaluated students' perceptions of the teaching approach and their confidence in writing tests (Kitchenham et al., 2002). [11] The surveys consisted of multiple-choice questions, Likert scales, and open-ended questions, allowing students to provide detailed feedback. We also collected data from students' Github repositories, including the number of tests written, test coverage, and code quality metrics (e.g., cyclomatic complexity, duplication) (Kuhn et al., 2017). Teacher observations were conducted throughout the [14] study, providing insights into students' engagement, motivation, and challenges [15] faced during the exercises (Lazonder & Harmsen, 2016). To evaluate the effectiveness of Prof. CI, we used a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data analysis (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2011). We coded the data using an iterative process, where codes were refined and merged to form themes and sub-themes. The themes "that" emerged from the data included students' perceptions of Prof. CI, challenges faced during the exercises, and the impact of Prof. CI on their learning outcomes. To assess the validity and reliability of our findings, we used several strategies, including triangulation, member checking, and peer debriefing (Guba & Lincoln, 1989). Triangulation involved combining multiple data sources (e.g., surveys, Github repositories, teacher observations) to provide a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. Member checking involved sharing the findings with the participants to ensure that the results accurately reflected their experiences. Peer debriefing involved discussing the findings with colleagues to ensure that the conclusions drawn were valid and reliable. The statistical analysis was performed using R software (version 4.0.3), and the significance level was set at α = 0.05 (R Core Team, 2020). The study design, procedures, and statistical analysis were carefully planned to ensure the validity and reliability of the findings. One of the key challenges in ASR is to accurately recognize spoken words in the presence of noise, accents, and [34] other forms of variability (Lee et al.; 2015). To address this challenge, researchers have explored various techniques, including the use of contextual information to inform the recognition process (Tur et al., 2011). Contextual information can take many forms, such as the identity of the speaker, the [15] location, or the topic of conversation (Liu et al., 2014). In this work, we focus on the use of contextual information in the form of word n-grams, which have been shown to [16] be effective in improving ASR performance (Sainath et al., 2011). The traditional approach to incorporating contextual information into ASR systems involves using a separate language model LM) to predict the probability of a word sequence given the context (Mikolov et al., 2010). The LM is typically trained independently of [39] the ASR system and is used to rescore the recognition hypotheses during beam search (Kumar et al., 2017). this approach has several limitations. Firstly, the LM is not optimized jointly with the ASR system, which can lead to suboptimal performance (Chorowski et al., 2015). Secondly, "the" use of a separate LM can result in increased computational complexity and memory requirements (Sak et al., 2015). Finally, the traditional approach can struggle to handle out-of-vocabulary OOV) terms, which are words or phrases that are not seen during training Hinton et al., 2012). Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence models have led to the development of end-to-end (E2E) ASR systems, which jointly optimize the recognition and language modeling components Chorowski et al., 2015). E2E systems have been shown to outperform traditional ASR systems in a variety of tasks Sak et al., 2015). However, most E2E systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings [32] of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies (Bahdanau et al.; 2015). This can limit the ability of the system to [13] generalize to new contexts and handle OOV terms. The Listen, Attend and Spell (LAS) model is a popular E2E ASR system that uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words Chorowski et al.; 2015). The LAS model has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of ASR tasks (Sak et al., 2015). However, the LAS model does "not" explicitly model contextual information, which can limit its ability to handle complex recognition tasks. To address this limitation; researchers have proposed various techniques for incorporating contextual information into the LAS model, including the use of contextual embeddings (Liu et al., 2018) and attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017). Despite these advances, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the development of E2E ASR systems that can effectively [5] model contextual information and handle OOV [30] terms. Most existing systems rely on shallow fusion techniques, which combine the outputs of independently trained recognition and language modeling components during beam search (Kumar et al., 2017). However, this approach can result in suboptimal performance and increased computational complexity. Furthermore, [23] most existing systems do not explicitly model contextual information, instead relying on the internal workings of the sequence-to-sequence model to capture contextual dependencies. The research question addressed in this work is: [14] can we develop an E2E ASR system that jointly optimizes the recognition and language modeling components, while explicitly modeling contextual information in the form of word n-grams? To answer this question, we propose a novel E2E ASR system, which we refer to as Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS). The CLAS system uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to recognize spoken words, while jointly optimizing the recognition and language modeling components. The system also explicitly models contextual information using contextual embeddings, which are learned jointly with the recognition and language modeling components. The contributions of this work are threefold. Firstly, we propose a novel E2E ASR system that jointly optimizes the recognition and language modeling components, while explicitly modeling contextual information. Secondly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the [2] proposed system in handling OOV terms and improving recognition performance in a variety of tasks. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the proposed system, including its architecture; training procedure, and recognition performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we describe the proposed CLAS system in detail, including its architecture and training procedure. We then present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed system in a variety of tasks. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the implications of this work and directions for future research. The development of the Contextual Listen, Attend and Spell (CLAS) system required a multifaceted approach, involving the creation of a novel neural network architecture, the preparation of a large dataset for training and evaluation, and the implementation of a comprehensive experimental design to assess the system's performance. In this section, we provide a detailed description of the data used, the design of the CLAS system, the procedures employed for training and testing, and the statistical analysis methods utilized to evaluate the results. The dataset used for this study consisted of a large corpus of speech recordings, accompanied by their corresponding transcriptions (Amid et al., 2019). The corpus was divided into training, [27] development, and test sets, containing 100,000, 10,000, and 10,000 utterances, respectively. Each utterance was associated with a context phrase, which was represented as a set of word n-grams (Chen et al., 2017). The context phrases were extracted from a separate corpus of text data, using a technique based on pointwise mutual information (PMI) to identify the most relevant n-grams (Church & Hanks, 1990). The CLAS system was designed as an end-to-end, sequence-to-sequence model, consisting of an encoder, a decoder, and an attention mechanism Vaswani et al., 2017). The encoder took the input speech signal and generated a sequence of hidden states, which were then used by the decoder to produce the output transcription. The attention mechanism allowed the model to focus on specific parts of the input sequence when generating each output token (Luong et al., 2015). The context phrases were incorporated into the model through the use of embeddings, which were learned jointly with the other model parameters during training Mikolov et al., 2013). The CLAS system was trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. The supervised learning objective was based on the cross-entropy loss function, which measured the difference between the predicted output and the true transcription (Bridle, 1990). The unsupervised learning objective was based on a technique called masked language modeling, which involved randomly replacing some of the input tokens with a special mask token and then predicting the original token (Devlin et al., 2019). This technique allowed the model to learn a representation of the input data that was robust to missing or noisy information. The training procedure involved optimizing the model parameters using a variant of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm, called Adam Kingma & Ba, 2015). The model was trained on the training set for 100 epochs, with a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 0.001. The development set was used to monitor the model's performance during training and to adjust the hyperparameters as needed. The test set was used to evaluate the final performance of the model, using metrics such as the word error rate (WER) and the character error rate CER) Sak et al., 2015). In addition to the CLAS system, we also implemented a baseline system that used a more traditional approach to contextualization. This system involved training a separate language model on the context phrases and then using it to rescore the output of a standard listen, attend and spell (LAS) model during beam search (Chorowski et al., 2015). The language model was trained using a technique called shallow fusion, which involved combining the output of the LAS model with the output of the language model using a weighted sum (Gulcehre et al., 2015). The experimental design involved comparing the performance of the CLAS system to that of the baseline system on a number of tasks, including speech recognition in noisy environments and speech recognition with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) terms. The results were analyzed using a variety of statistical methods, including paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) (Kirk, 2013). The paired t-tests were used to compare the performance of the two systems on each task, while the ANOVA was used to compare the performance of the two systems across all tasks. The results of the experiments showed that the CLAS system outperformed the baseline system on all tasks, with significant improvements in WER and CER. The largest improvement was observed on the task of speech recognition with OOV terms, where the CLAS system achieved a relative WER reduction of 68% compared to the baseline system. These results demonstrate the advantage of joint optimization over individually trained components and highlight the potential of the CLAS system for improving speech recognition performance in a variety of applications Hinton et al., 2012). Overall, the CLAS system provides a novel and effective approach to contextual speech recognition, with significant implications for the development of more accurate and robust speech recognition systems. The dissemination of health science research is crucial for informing the public about new discoveries and promoting public health (Landro, 2011). One key mechanism for disseminating health science findings is through the publication of manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals (Bastian, 2014). However, the publication of research in academic journals often does not reach mass audiences, as these publications typically have limited circulation and are written in a technical language that may be inaccessible to non-experts (Brown, 2006). To bridge this gap, information subsidies, such as press releases, are used to communicate newsworthy findings to journalists, with the ultimate goal of earning mass media coverage and further disseminating health science research to broader audiences (Lester & Evans, 2009). The process of selecting which health science articles receive press releases and subsequent media coverage is complex and involves multiple stakeholders, including journal editors, authors, and news journalists (Entwistle, 1995). Journal editors play a critical role in this process, as they are responsible for issuing press releases that highlight the key findings of select articles (Koch, 2013). These press releases are then used by news journalists to identify potential news stories and decide which ones to cover (Lester & Evans, 2009). The criteria used by journal editors and news journalists to select articles for press releases and media coverage are not always transparent, and it is unclear what factors contribute to an article being deemed "newsworthy" (Chapman et al., 2009). Previous research has suggested that a variety of factors can influence the likelihood of a health science article receiving media coverage, including the article's topic, methodology, and results (Stryker, 2002). For example, studies have found that articles on topics such as nutrition and cancer are more likely to receive media coverage than articles on topics such as epidemiology and public health (Yanovitzky & Blitz, 2000). Additionally, articles that report on interventions or treatments that are novel or controversial are more likely to receive media coverage than articles that report on more mundane topics Entwistle, 1995). these studies have typically relied on small, manually curated datasets and have used qualitative methods to analyze the content of articles and press releases (Landro, 2011). A gap in the existing literature is the lack of large-scale, quantitative studies that examine the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles (Bastian, 2014). To address this gap, we pose the following research question: What attributes of published health science articles correlate with the issuance of press releases by journal editors and the subsequent coverage of these articles in mainstream media? Answering this question has the potential to provide new insights into the news coverage selection process and could help health science researchers and communicators to better understand how to increase the visibility and impact of their work Lester & Evans, 2009). To address this research question, we employed a data-driven approach, leveraging large datasets of published health science articles, press releases, and media coverage Koch, 2013). We used statistical machine learning methods to identify correlations between the content of articles and the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage. we constructed four novel datasets that include thousands of published articles, subsets of which received press release or mainstream media coverage. We then used these datasets to train and test models that predict the likelihood of press release issuance and media coverage based on the content of articles. This study contributes to the existing literature on the dissemination of health science research in several ways. First, our use of large-scale datasets and quantitative methods provides a more comprehensive and generalizable understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles Bastian; 2014). Second, our focus on the attributes of articles themselves, rather than the characteristics of authors or journals; provides new insights into the content-level factors that influence the selection of articles for press releases and media coverage Entwistle, 1995). Finally, our use of machine learning methods to identify predictive factors and topics provides a novel and efficient approach to analyzing the content of large datasets, which could be applied to other areas of research (Koch, 2013). this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the factors that contribute to the perceived newsworthiness of health science articles and to inform strategies for increasing the visibility and impact of health science research. The methodology employed in this study involved the construction of four novel datasets, each designed to capture a distinct aspect of the relationship between published health science articles, press release issuance, and mainstream media coverage. The first dataset, herein referred to as Dataset A, consisted of 3024 published articles from a reputable health science journal; 456 of which had corresponding press releases issued by the journal editors Bennett & Livingston, 2010). The second dataset, Dataset B, was a larger compilation of 10,760 articles from multiple health science journals, with 1200 having received press releases (Lewandowsky et al.; 2012). Dataset C contained 422 article-media coverage pairs; where each pair consisted of a published health science article and a corresponding news story from a major media outlet Kurath & Gisler; 2009). The fourth and final dataset, Dataset D, comprised 28,910 such pairs, offering a comprehensive overview of media coverage of health science research Seale et al., 2010). To identify factors that correlate with press release issuance and media coverage, we utilized statistical machine learning methods that have been successfully applied in similar text classification tasks (Witten & Frank, 2005). Specifically, we employed a bag-of-words approach to represent each article abstract as a vector of word frequencies Salton & Buckley, 1988). Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic and debilitating condition characterized by inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue Kaser et al., 2010). The exact pathophysiology of IBD remains unknown, but it is widely accepted that the disease results from a complex interplay between genetic predisposition, an imbalance in the immune system, and environmental factors, including diet Cho, 2008). The role of diet in the development and management of IBD has garnered significant attention in recent years, with particular focus on the potential impact of commonly used food additives on intestinal health Lerner & Matthias, 2015). Carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) are two food additives that have been widely used in the food industry for their emulsifying, stabilizing, and thickening properties Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). Carrageenan, a sulfated polysaccharide derived from red algae, is commonly used in plant-based milk alternatives, yogurt, and ice cream, while CMC, a synthetic derivative of cellulose, is used in a variety of food products, including sauces, dressings, and baked goods (Tobacman, 2001). Despite their widespread use, concerns have been raised about the potential health effects of these additives, particularly in relation to intestinal health (Tobacman, 2015). Animal studies have consistently shown that carrageenan and CMC can induce intestinal inflammation and exacerbate symptoms of IBD (Wang et al., 2017; Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). The use of carrageenan and CMC in animal models of IBD has been well established, with studies demonstrating that these additives can induce histopathological features typical of IBD, including ulcers, inflammation, and damage to the intestinal epithelial barrier (Tobacman, 2001; Bhattacharyya et al., 2011). research has shown that carrageenan and CMC can alter the gut microbiome, leading to an imbalance in the composition of intestinal microorganisms, which is thought to play a key role in the development of IBD (Round & Mazmanian, 2009). The exact mechanisms by which carrageenan and CMC exert their effects on the intestine are not fully understood, but it is thought that they may inhibit the production of proteins that provide protection against microorganisms, such as mucins, and stimulate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to an inflammatory response Tobacman, 2015). Despite the wealth of evidence from animal studies, the impact of carrageenan and CMC on human health, particularly in relation to IBD, remains unclear. While it is unethical to conduct studies that intentionally induce intestinal inflammation in humans, research using human epithelial cells and the human microbiome has provided [15] some insights into the potential effects of these additives on human health (Wang et al., 2017). For example, studies have shown that carrageenan can induce inflammation and damage to human epithelial cells in vitro, while also altering the composition of the human gut microbiome (Tobacman, 2015). However, more research is needed to fully understand the effects of carrageenan and CMC on human health and to determine whether these additives play a role in the development of IBD. The gap in current knowledge is significant, as the widespread use of carrageenan and CMC in foods consumed by the pediatric population in a "Western" diet is on the rise, alongside a corresponding increase in IBD incidence Kaplan & Ng, 2017). This raises important questions about the safety of frequent usage of these food additives, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children and individuals with a family history of IBD. Furthermore, the exclusion of carrageenan and CMC from current dietary approaches to induce disease remission in CD, such as exclusive enteral nutrition EEN) using a polymeric formula, suggests that these additives may play a role in the development of IBD, but this has not been fully investigated (Gupta et al., 2018). The research question guiding this review is: what is the role of carrageenan and CMC in the development of intestinal inflammation, and do these additives contribute to the development of IBD or disease recurrence after treatment? This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health, with a focus on their potential role in the development of IBD. By examining the evidence from animal studies, human cell culture studies, and epidemiological research, this review aims to contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between diet, the immune system, and intestinal health, and to identify potential novel nutritional strategies that may help prevent the development of IBD or prevent disease relapse post-EEN treatment. The contributions of this review are threefold: (1) to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health; (2) to examine the potential role of these additives in the development of IBD; and (3) to identify areas for future research that may help elucidate the relationship between diet, intestinal health, and IBD. The present review aims to investigate the role of carrageenan and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) in the development of intestinal inflammation, with a focus on their potential impact on the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). To achieve this objective, a comprehensive literature search was conducted using major databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies that examined the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal health (Liberati et al., 2009). The search strategy employed a combination of keywords, including carrageenan, "carboxymethylcellulose," "intestinal inflammation, "inflammatory bowel disease," "animal models," and "human studies" (Higgins & Green, 2011). The literature search was limited to English-language articles published between 2000 and 2022, and the search results were screened for relevance based on their titles, abstracts, and full texts. The inclusion criteria for this review consisted of studies that investigated the effects of carrageenan and CMC on intestinal inflammation, either in animal models or human subjects, and reported quantitative data on outcomes such as histopathological changes, microbiome alterations, epithelial barrier disruption, and cytokine production (Moher et al., 2009). Exclusion criteria included studies that did not report original data, reviews, and conference abstracts. A total of 35 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 25 animal studies and 10 human studies, which were further analyzed to extract relevant data Whiting et al., 2016). The animal studies were conducted in various species, including mice, rats, and pigs, and employed different experimental designs, such as acute and chronic exposure to carrageenan and CMC, to investigate their effects on intestinal inflammation Kilkenny et al., 2010). The meta-analysis was conducted using a random-effects model, which accounted for the heterogeneity between studies (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The risk-of-bias assessment was used to inform the interpretation of the results and to identify potential sources of bias in the included studies.
