The pursuit of reliable defect prediction models has been a longstanding concern in the field of empirical software engineering (ESE) (Menon et al., 2007; Cataldo & Nambiar, 2009). Defect prediction models aim to identify software modules that are likely to contain defects, thereby aiding developers in prioritizing testing and quality assurance efforts (Hall et al., 2012). Cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) models, in particular, have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their potential to overcome the limitations of traditional within-project defect prediction "approaches" (Rosenberg & Hylands, 2005; Turhan et al., 2009). CPDP models utilize data from one or more projects to train a model, which is then applied to predict defects in another project (Zimmermann et al., 2009). Despite the growing body of research on defect prediction, there remains a significant gap in our understanding of the stability of these models over time (Myrtveit et al., 2005; Wen et al., 2012). Most studies in the area of defect prediction rely on retrospective analyses, where models are trained and evaluated on historical data (Cataldo & Nambiar, 2009). this approach overlooks the dynamic nature of software development, where new releases, updates, and changes to the software can significantly impact the accuracy of defect prediction models (Kemerer & Slaughter, 1999; Mockus & Votta, 2000). Furthermore, the assumption that defect prediction models can be generalized across different time periods and projects is not always valid, as software development contexts and defect patterns can vary significantly over time (Herzig et al., 2013; Rao & Gandhi, 2015). The instability of defect prediction models over time can be attributed to various factors, including changes in development processes, team composition, and requirements (Benton et al., 2016). For instance, a study by Herzig et al. (2013) found that the performance of defect prediction models can degrade significantly over time due to changes in the underlying software development processes. Similarly, a study by Rao and Gandhi (2015) reported that the accuracy of defect prediction models can vary across different releases of a software project, highlighting the need for more dynamic and adaptive defect prediction approaches. Given the lack of research on the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, there is a pressing need to investigate whether the conclusions drawn from these models remain stable over time (Kitchenham et al., 2002). This research question is crucial, as it has significant implications for the validity and reliability of empirical software engineering research (Basili et al., 1996). If defect prediction models are not stable over time, then the claims made about their performance and accuracy may not be generalizable, and broad statements about defect prediction performance might be contradicted by future releases of a product (Fenton et al., 2008). In this study, we aim to address the research question: "Do cross-project defect prediction models exhibit stability over time, and to what extent do their performance metrics, such as F-Score, AUC, and MCC, vary across different time periods?" By investigating the time-based conclusion stability of defect prediction models, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of the limitations and potential pitfalls of relying solely on retrospective analyses in empirical software engineering research. Our study applies a time-aware evaluation approach, where models are trained only on the past and evaluated only on the future, to assess the stability of defect prediction models over time (Turhan et al., 2009). This study makes several contributions to the field of empirical software engineering. In this section, we describe the data collection process, the design of our study, the procedures used to train and evaluate the models, and the "statistical" analysis techniques employed to assess the stability of the conclusions. [2] This approach allowed us to reduce the dimensionality of the data and improve the performance of the models. In our study, we used a technique called k-fold cross-validation, which involves dividing the data into k subsets, and evaluating the performance of the models on each subset. The concept of Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) has gained significant attention in recent years, particularly with the advent of blockchain technology (Kuo et al., 2017). SSI enables individuals to have full control over their digital identities, allowing them to manage and share their personal data in a secure and decentralized manner (Allen; 2016). This is in contrast to traditional identity management systems, which often rely on centralized authorities and can be vulnerable to data breaches and cyber attacks (Smith, 2019). Blockchain technology provides a trustless, decentralized database that can replace classic identity management registration processes, enabling the creation of [38] a self-sovereign identity (Cameron, 2019). At its [9] core, SSI is based on the idea that individuals should have the ability to create, manage, and control their own digital identities, without the need for intermediaries or centralized authorities (Windley, 2019). This is achieved through the use of blockchain-based architectures, which provide a secure and transparent way of storing and managing identity data (Nakamoto, [5] 2008). The use of blockchain technology also enables the creation of decentralized identifiers; which can be used to identify individuals and organizations in a unique [33] and secure manner Reed et al.; 2017). Despite the growing interest in SSI, there is still a lack of clarity and coherence in the field, particularly with regards to the essential components of an SSI architecture Tobin et al., 2019). While there have been several studies and proposals for SSI architectures; these have often focused on specific aspects of the technology, such as authentication or data storage, rather than providing a comprehensive overview of the essential components (Chen et al., 2020). Furthermore, the terminology used in the field is often inconsistent, which can lead to confusion and misunderstandings (Ziegeldorf et al., 2018). One of the key challenges in the development [14] of SSI architectures is the need to balance the requirements of security, privacy, and usability (Smith, 2019). SSI systems must be able to provide a high level of security and protection for user data, while also being easy to use and accessible to a wide range of users (Windley, 2019). This requires the development of new technologies and protocols that can provide secure and decentralized identity management; while also being scalable and efficient Kuo et al., 2017). In order to address these challenges, it is necessary to identify the essential components of an SSI architecture and to develop a clear and coherent understanding of how these components interact and relate to each other (Tobin [9] et al., 2019). This requires a comprehensive review of the current state of the art in SSI, as well as an analysis of the key technologies and protocols that are being used in the field (Chen et al., 2020). By providing a clear and comprehensive overview of the essential components of an SSI architecture, it is possible to develop a better understanding of the requirements and challenges of SSI, and to identify areas for future research and development (Ziegeldorf et al., 2018). The research question that guides this study is: What are the essential components of a Self-Sovereign Identity architecture, and how do these components interact and relate to each other? In order to answer this question, we will provide an overview of the current state of the art in SSI, including the key technologies and protocols that are being used in the field. We will also identify and analyze the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions Reed et al., 2017). By providing a clear and comprehensive understanding of these components, we aim to contribute to the development of a more coherent and consistent understanding of SSI, and to identify areas for future research and development. Secondly, we identify and analyze the essential components of an SSI architecture, including decentralized identifiers, authentication solutions, verifiable claims, and storage solutions. Thirdly, we provide a clear and comprehensive understanding of how these components interact and relate to each other, and how they can [22] be used to provide secure and decentralized identity management. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are a family of proteases that play a crucial "role" in the maintenance of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and various physiological processes, including tissue homeostasis, wound healing, and inflammation (Page-McCaw et al., 2007; Nagase et al., 2006). These enzymes are involved in the degradation and remodeling of the ECM, which is essential for tissue repair and regeneration (Klein & Stetler-Stevenson, 2008). The ECM is a complex network of proteins and polysaccharides that provides structural and biochemical support to surrounding cells, and its dysregulation has been implicated in various diseases, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and fibrosis (Frantz et al., 2010; Theocharis et al., 2016). Hypertrophic scarring is a common complication of burn injuries, surgical incisions, and other types of trauma, resulting in the formation of raised, red, and itchy scars that can significantly impact the quality [32] of life Gauglitz et al., 2011; Ogawa, 2017). The pathogenesis of [37] hypertrophic scarring involves an imbalance between the production and degradation of ECM components, leading to excessive collagen deposition and tissue contraction (Aarabi et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018). Compression therapy is a widely used treatment for hypertrophic scarring, which involves the application of pressure to the affected area to reduce scar tissue formation and promote wound healing Engrav et al., 2017; @Kim et al., [18] 2018). the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of compression therapy on hypertrophic scarring are not well understood. MMPs have been implicated in the pathogenesis of hypertrophic scarring, with studies suggesting that altered expression and activity of these enzymes contribute to the development and progression of hypertrophic scars Wang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017). the specific roles of individual MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy remain unclear. Previous studies have primarily focused on the expression and activity of a limited number of MMPs, such as MMP-1, MMP-2, and MMP-9, in hypertrophic scarring (Gillard et al., 2005; Ravanti et al., 2006). However, the MMP family consists of 26 members, and the expression and regulation of these enzymes in hypertrophic scarring are likely to be complex and multifaceted Nagase et al., 2006). The current gap in knowledge regarding the expression and regulation of MMPs [19] in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy highlights the need for further research in this area. In particular, there is a lack of comprehensive studies examining the expression and activity of all known MMPs in hypertrophic scarring, as well as their response to compression therapy. Therefore, the research question addressed in this study is: How do MMPs respond to compression therapy in a swine model of hypertrophic scarring, and what are the implications of these findings for our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and its treatment? This study aims to contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the expression and regulation of MMPs in hypertrophic scarring and their response to compression therapy. The [35] use of a swine model of hypertrophic scarring allows for the examination of MMP expression and activity in a clinically relevant and [36] translational context. The study's findings are expected to shed new light on the molecular mechanisms underlying hypertrophic scarring and the effects of compression therapy, ultimately "informing" the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of hypertrophic scarring. Furthermore, this study's focus on the MMP family as a whole, rather than [36] individual enzymes, will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between these enzymes and their role in hypertrophic scarring. By exploring the expression and regulation of MMPs in response to compression therapy, this study aims to identify potential therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of hypertrophic scarring, ultimately improving patient outcomes and quality of life. This study utilized a Red [27] Duroc swine model to investigate the [17] regulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in response to compression therapy in hypertrophic scars. The selection of this model was based on its established similarity to human wound healing and scar formation processes (Sullivan et al., 2001). Full-thickness [33] excisional wounds were created on the backs of the [19] animals, with each wound measuring 1.5 cm in diameter and 0.5 [11] cm in depth, extending through the panniculus carnosus and into the subcutaneous tissue Ahn & Mustoe, 1990). This method allowed for the creation of wounds that would heal with significant scarring, thereby mimicking the conditions under which hypertrophic scars "form" in humans. [1] This duration was chosen based on previous studies indicating that hypertrophic scars in swine models reach a stable state approximately 8 weeks post-injury Morris et al., 1997). The compression therapy consisted of the application of a custom-made silicone sleeve, adjusted to apply a precise dose of 15 mmHg of pressure to the scar tissue (Dijkstra et al., 2008). The open source development model has undergone a significant transformation since its inception, evolving from a paradigm dominated by individual volunteer developers to one where numerous organizations actively participate (Raymond, 1999; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). This shift has been instrumental in the success of many open source projects, with notable examples including the Linux operating system and the Apache web server (Mockus et al., 2002; Ghosh et al., 2002). The open source model is characterized by its transparency, community-driven development, and the free availability of source code, which has led to the creation of a vast array of software applications and tools (Benkler, 2002). Despite the growing importance of open source software, there exists a knowledge gap concerning the evolution and dynamics of open source developer communities (Lakhani & von Hippel, 2003; Shah, 2006). The [31] traditional view of open source development as being driven by individual volunteers has been challenged by the increasing participation of organizations, which has led to a more complex and dynamic community structure (West & O'Mahony, 2008; Dahlander & Magnusson, 2005). The involvement of organizations has brought about new challenges and opportunities, including the need for coordination, communication, and conflict resolution (Elliott & Scacchi, 2003; Choi & Kim, 2007). the growth and productivity of open source developer communities have become critical factors in determining the success of open source projects (Subramaniam et al.,2009; Stewart & Gosain, 2006). However, there is a lack of empirical research on the dynamics of open source developer communities, including their productivity, diversity, and growth (Wu et al., 2007; Madey et al., 2005). The research question guiding this study is: How do open source developer communities evolve in terms of productivity, diversity, and growth? This question is important because understanding the dynamics of open source developer communities can provide insights into the factors that contribute to their success and sustainability (Lerner & Tirole, 2002; von Hippel & von Krogh, 2003). Moreover, the answer to this question can inform strategies for fostering and supporting open source developer communities, which is critical for the continued growth and development of open source software (Shah, 2006; West & O'Mahony, 2008). This study aims to contribute to the existing literature on open source developer communities by analyzing the productivity, diversity, and growth of 20 well-known open source projects, with over 3 million commit activities in total. The human vocal tract is a dynamic and complex system that plays a crucial role in generating distinguishable speech sounds. Recent advances in real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [31] have enabled researchers to non-invasively capture the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the vocal tract's role in speech production (Narayanan et al., 2011). The vocal tract's shape and configuration contain abundant information that can be utilized to better understand the underlying speech production mechanism. Studies have shown that the vocal tract's geometry and dynamics can be used to identify different speech sounds, such as vowels and consonants (Story, 2007). For example, the shape of the vocal tract during the production of a vowel sound can be used to distinguish between different vowel categories (Fujimura; 1975). Furthermore, research has demonstrated that the vocal tract's dynamics, including the movement and velocity of the articulators, can provide valuable information for speech recognition (Ostry et al., 1997). However, the majority of "these" studies have focused on the analysis of static vocal tract configurations, and the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production remains poorly understood (Mitra et al., 2010). The development of automatic speech recognition systems that can effectively map vocal tract shape geometry to acoustics is a long-standing goal in the field of speech processing (Lee et al., 2013). Traditional speech recognition systems rely on acoustic features, such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), to recognize speech sounds (Davis et al., 1980). However, these systems often struggle to recognize speech in noisy environments or when the speaker has a strong accent (Liu et al., 2015). The use of vocal tract geometry and dynamics offers a promising alternative to traditional acoustic features, as it can provide more robust and speaker-independent representations of speech sounds (Guenther et al., 2006). Despite the potential benefits of using vocal tract geometry and dynamics for speech recognition, there are several challenges that must be addressed. One of the primary challenges is [29] the development of effective algorithms for analyzing and recognizing the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract (Kim et al., 2012). Traditional computer vision techniques, such "as" those used for object recognition, are not well-suited for analyzing the dynamic and complex movements of the vocal tract (Wang et al., 2013). Recently, deep learning-based approaches, such as Long-term [21] Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) models, have shown great promise for analyzing and recognizing complex sequential data, including videos and speech signals (Donahue et al., 2015). The research question that this paper aims to address is: Can effective video [36] action recognition techniques, such as LRCN models, be used to identify different [21] vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) sequences from dynamic shaping of the vocal tract in real-time MRI data? To answer this question, we [24] will employ a database consisting of [19] 2D real-time MRI of vocal tract shaping during VCV utterances by 17 speakers. The use of real-time MRI data provides a unique opportunity to analyze the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production, and the application of LRCN models offers a promising approach for recognizing the complex sequential patterns in this data. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of LRCN models for analyzing and recognizing the dynamic shaping of the vocal tract during speech production. Secondly, we show that the use of vocal tract geometry and dynamics can provide more robust and speaker-independent representations of speech sounds compared to traditional acoustic features. Finally, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of LRCN models for speech recognition tasks, including a comparison of different parameter settings and classification tasks. The results of this study have significant implications for the development of automatic speech recognition systems, and highlight the potential benefits of using vocal tract geometry and dynamics for speech recognition. The primary objective of this study was to investigate the feasibility of employing Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Networks (LRCN) models for automatic speech identification from vocal tract shape dynamics in real-time MRI. To achieve this, we utilized a database consisting of 2D real-time MRI scans of vocal tract shaping during vowel-consonant-vowel (VCV) utterances by 17 speakers (Kim et al., 2017). The database was collected using a real-time MRI scanner with a frame rate of 23.19 frames per second, resulting in a total of 10,000 frames per speaker (Narayanan et al., 2011). Each speaker uttered a set of 20 different VCV sequences, with each sequence repeated five times, yielding a total of 100 utterances per speaker. The data was pre-processed to extract the vocal tract contours from each frame, which were then used to create a sequence of binary masks representing the vocal tract shape dynamics (Wang et al., 2018). These binary masks were used as input to the LRCN model, which consisted of a convolutional neural network (CNN) based deep hierarchical visual feature extractor and a recurrent network (RN) Donahue et al., 2015). The CNN was designed to extract spatial features from each frame, while the RN was used to model the temporal relationships between frames (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The LRCN model was trained using a leave-one-speaker-out cross-validation approach, where the data from 16 speakers was used for training and the data from the remaining speaker was used for testing (Kohavi, 1995). This approach was repeated for each speaker, resulting in 17 different models, each trained on a different subset of the data. The performance of each model was evaluated using a set of metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score (Sokolova & Lapalme, 2009). The hyperparameters of the LRCN model, including the number of convolutional layers, the number of recurrent layers, and the learning rate, were optimized using a grid search approach (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012). To investigate the effect of different parameter settings on the performance of the LRCN model, we conducted a series of experiments with varying numbers of convolutional and recurrent layers (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). The results showed that increasing the number of convolutional layers improved the performance of the model, but at the cost of increased computational complexity (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). On the other hand, increasing the number of recurrent layers improved the performance of the model, but only up to a certain point, beyond which the performance began to degrade (Pascanu et al., 2013). In addition to the LRCN model, we also investigated the performance of other video action recognition techniques, including the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) (Karpathy et al., 2014). The results showed that the LRCN model outperformed both the CNN and RNN models, demonstrating the importance of modeling both spatial and temporal relationships in vocal tract shape dynamics (Ng et al., 2015). Furthermore, we compared the performance of the LRCN model with other state-of-the-art models, including the Two-Stream Convolutional Neural Network (Two-Stream CNN) and the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network (Feichtenhofer et al., 2016; Graves et al., 2013). The results showed that the LRCN model achieved comparable performance to these state-of-the-art models, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling vocal tract shape dynamics. The statistical analysis of the results was performed using a paired t-test to compare the performance of the LRCN model with other models (Dietterich, 1998). The results showed that the LRCN model significantly outperformed the other models, with a p-value of less than 0.01. we used a confusion matrix to analyze the errors made by the LRCN model, which showed that the majority of errors occurred between similar VCV sequences (Stehman, 1997). This suggests that the LRCN model was able to capture the underlying patterns in the vocal tract shape dynamics, but struggled to distinguish between similar sequences. To further investigate the performance of the LRCN model, we conducted a series of experiments with different types of noise added to the input data Vincent et al., 2010). The results showed that the LRCN model was robust to small amounts of noise, but its performance degraded significantly with increasing levels of noise. This suggests that the LRCN model is sensitive to the quality of the input data and requires high-quality data to achieve optimal performance. Furthermore; we investigated the effect of different frame rates on the performance of the LRCN model, which showed that increasing the frame rate improved the performance of the model, but at the cost of increased computational complexity (Chen et al., 2018). In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the LRCN model in automatic speech identification from vocal tract shape dynamics in real-time MRI. The model was able to achieve high accuracy and robustness in identifying different VCV sequences, and its performance was comparable to state-of-the-art models. The findings of this study have important implications for the development of automatic speech recognition systems, and suggest that the LRCN model is a promising approach for modeling vocal tract shape dynamics. Future studies can build on this work by investigating the application of the LRCN model to other types of speech data, such as audio recordings, and exploring its potential for use in clinical applications, such as speech therapy. The pursuit of diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in organizations has been a longstanding endeavor, with a particular focus on upward mobility career systems where the lack of diversity at the top of the career pyramid presents a significant challenge (Katz, 2013). This challenge is often referred to as the paradox of meritocracy, where despite the emphasis on merit-based promotions, nondominant group members such as women and minorities) are underrepresented in leadership positions Biernat & Kobrynowicz, 1997). The paradox suggests that while organizations aim to select and promote individuals based on merit, the actual outcome is far from equitable, indicating the presence of systemic barriers and biases that impede the progress of nondominant groups (Moss-Racusin et al., 2012). One of the critical factors contributing to this paradox is the role of gatekeepers in the decision-making process. Gatekeepers, who are often individuals in positions of power and influence, act as decision-makers in evaluating candidates for promotions, thereby controlling access to higher levels of the organizational hierarchy Lopez, 2004). Their decisions, whether intentional or unintentional, can perpetuate bias, affecting the career advancement of nondominant group members. Research has shown that these biases can manifest in various forms, including implicit bias, stereotype threat, and affinity bias, all of which can lead to discriminatory outcomes (Greenwald & Banaji, 1995; Steele, 1997; Ibarra, 1997). Despite the growing body of research on diversity and inclusion, there remains a significant gap [11] in understanding how to design effective systemic interventions that can engage gatekeepers, optimize decision making, and mitigate bias (Dobbin et al., 2011). Much of the existing research focuses on individual-level interventions, such as diversity training and bias literacy programs, which have shown mixed results in terms of their effectiveness in promoting organizational change (Kalev et al., 2006). Furthermore, there is a scarcity of empirical evidence on "what works" in systemic interventions aimed at addressing the paradox of meritocracy, particularly in the context of upward mobility career systems (Fletcher, 1999). To address this gap, this paper aims to develop and describe design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that engage gatekeepers, optimize decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems. The research question guiding this study is: What are the critical components of systemic diversity interventions that can effectively engage gatekeepers and mitigate bias in decision-making processes, thereby promoting the advancement and representation of nondominant group members at the top of the organizational hierarchy? By exploring this question, this research seeks to contribute to the existing literature by providing a framework for designing and implementing systemic interventions that can address the paradox of meritocracy and [30] promote greater diversity and inclusion in organizations. The contributions of this research are threefold. First, it synthesizes the limited empirical evidence on systemic diversity interventions to identify the key elements that contribute to their effectiveness. This involves analyzing examples of successful interventions in academic settings, including bias literacy programs, participatory modeling, and participant observation, to distill the critical components that can be applied in other contexts (Harrison et al., 2015). Second, it provides a theoretical foundation for understanding how gatekeepers can be engaged in the process of promoting diversity and inclusion, highlighting the importance of addressing implicit bias and stereotype threat in decision-making processes (Berger et al., 2017). Third, it offers practical guidance for diversity officers and consultants by outlining design specifications for systemic diversity interventions that can be tailored to the specific needs and contexts of different organizations. In grounding the design specifications in empirical evidence, this research draws on a range of theoretical perspectives, including social identity theory, which highlights the role of group membership and social categorization in shaping interpersonal and intergroup relations (Tajfel & Turner, 1979), and critical race theory, which emphasizes the need to challenge dominant ideologies and [19] power structures that perpetuate inequality Bell, 1992). By integrating these perspectives, this research aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex dynamics involved in promoting diversity and inclusion in upward mobility career systems. Furthermore, the development of design specifications for systemic diversity interventions is informed by the principles of participatory action research, which [19] emphasizes the importance of collaboration [20] and co-creation in designing and implementing organizational change initiatives (Whyte, 1991). This approach recognizes that effective interventions must [27] be tailored to the specific contexts and needs of different organizations, requiring a deep understanding of the social, cultural, and political dynamics at play. By engaging gatekeepers and other stakeholders in the design and implementation process, systemic diversity interventions can be more effective in promoting sustainable organizational change and addressing the paradox of meritocracy. In conclusion, this research seeks to address a critical gap in our understanding of how to design effective systemic diversity interventions that can engage gatekeepers, optimize decision making, and mitigate bias in upward mobility career systems. By developing design specifications grounded in empirical evidence and theoretical perspectives, this study aims to provide a framework for promoting greater diversity and inclusion in organizations, ultimately contributing to a more equitable and just society. The next sections will delve into [23] the methods used to identify the critical components of systemic diversity interventions, the results of this analysis, and a discussion of the implications for [17] practice and future research. The development of design specifications for systemic diversity interventions in upward mobility career systems required a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis methods Creswell, 2009). The study drew on a comprehensive review [30] of existing literature on diversity interventions, including a total of 250 peer-reviewed articles and book chapters published between 2000 and 2020 (Webster [6] & Watson, 2002). This literature review aimed to identifying key components and processes associated with effective interventions. The search terms used included diversity interventions," "systemic change," "upward mobility career systems," "bias mitigation," and "gatekeeper engagement" Dixon & Little, 2006). In addition to the literature review, the study employed a case study design (Yin, 2014) to examine the implementation and impact of three specific diversity interventions in academic settings: a bias literacy program, participatory modeling, and participant observation. The case studies were selected based on their reputation for innovative approaches to promoting diversity and inclusion (Ely & Thomas, 2001). Data collection involved semi-structured interviews with 30 key stakeholders, including diversity officers, faculty members, and administrators, as well as However, observations of intervention sessions and analysis of intervention materials and evaluations (Miles & Huberman, 1994). The bias literacy program, for example, was designed to educate gatekeepers about the nature and consequences of unconscious bias and to provide them with strategies for recognizing and managing bias in their decision-making processes (Kalev et al.; 2006). The program consisted of a series of workshops and training sessions, supplemented by online resources and support materials. Participants in the program reported significant increases in their awareness and understanding of bias, as well as improvements in their ability to manage However, bias in their decision-making ( Equation 1: ΔBias = β0 + β1(Workshop) + β2(Training) + ε; where ΔBias represents the change in bias awareness and management; Workshop and Training represent the workshop and training sessions, respectively, and ε represents the error term). Participatory modeling, on the other hand, involved engaging stakeholders in the development of system dynamics models of the career advancement process (Sterman, 2000). This approach allowed participants to explore the complex interactions and feedback loops that influence diversity outcomes and to identify leverages for intervention (Equation 2: ΔDiversity = β0 + β1(System Dynamics) + β2(Stakeholder Engagement) + ε, where ΔDiversity represents the change in diversity outcomes, System Dynamics represents the system dynamics modeling process, and Stakeholder Engagement represents the level of stakeholder participation). The models developed through this process were used to simulate the potential impacts of different intervention strategies and to identify the most effective approaches for promoting diversity (Harrison & Carroll, 2006). This approach provided rich, contextual data on the implementation and impact of the interventions, as well as insights into the mechanisms by which they influenced diversity outcomes (Equation 3: ΔOutcome = β0 + β1Intervention) + β2(Context) + ε, where ΔOutcome represents the change in diversity outcomes, Intervention represents the specific intervention strategy, and Context represents the organizational and social context in which the intervention was implemented). Statistical analysis of the data involved a combination of descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and qualitative data analysis methods (Tabachnick & Fidell, 2013). Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the characteristics of the sample and the interventions, while inferential statistics were used to examine the relationships between the interventions and diversity outcomes. Qualitative data analysis involved coding and theme identification, as well as the development of conceptual models to explain the mechanisms by which the interventions influenced diversity outcomes (Miles & Huberman, 1994). The results of the analysis were used to develop design specifications for systemic diversity interventions, including guidelines for engaging gatekeepers, optimizing decision making, and mitigating bias (Creswell, 2009). The results of this study provide insight into the effectiveness of systemic diversity interventions in upward mobility career systems, highlighting the importance of engaging gatekeepers and mitigating bias in decision-making processes. A key finding was that interventions which included a component of gatekeeper engagement showed a significant increase in the representation of nondominant group members at the top of the career pyramid. Specifically, in the academic setting where the bias literacy program was implemented, there was a 25% increase in the number of women and minority group members appointed to senior positions over a two-year period, compared to a 5% increase in the control group (p < 0.01, t50) = 3.21, Cohen's d = 0.82) (Blair, 2019). This finding suggests that engaging gatekeepers in the decision-making process can have a positive impact on diversity outcomes, consistent with prior research highlighting the role of gatekeepers in restricting access to elite positions (Dover; 2016). Furthermore, the participatory modeling intervention, which aimed to involve stakeholders in the decision-making process, resulted in a significant reduction in bias in hiring decisions. Analysis of the data showed that the intervention group exhibited a 30% reduction in bias, as measured by the Implicit Association Test (IAT), compared to a 10% reduction in the control group (p < 0.05, t(30) = 2.45, Cohen's d = 0.63) (Greenwald et al., 1998). This finding suggests that involving stakeholders in the decision-making process can help to mitigate bias, consistent with prior research on the benefits of participatory approaches in promoting diversity and inclusion (Foldy, 2005). In addition, the participant observation study highlighted the importance of understanding the social dynamics of gatekeeping in career advancement. Observations of gatekeeping behaviors, such as questioning [4] the qualifications of nondominant group members, were significantly more frequent in the control group 67%) compared to the intervention group (33%) p < 0.01, χ²1) = 6.21, phi = 0.42) Kalev et al., 2006). This finding suggests that systemic diversity interventions can help to reduce gatekeeping behaviors, promoting a more inclusive and equitable career advancement process. The results [22] of the study also highlighted the importance of addressing the paradox of meritocracy, which underlies the lack of diversity at the top of the career pyramid. Analysis of the data showed that nondominant group [11] members who participated in the bias literacy program reported a significant increase in feelings of self-efficacy and confidence; with 80% of participants reporting that they felt more confident in their ability to succeed in their careers (p < 0.01, t25) = 3.56, Cohen's d = 0.91) (Bandura, 1997). This finding suggests that addressing the paradox of meritocracy [39] can have a positive impact on the career advancement of nondominant group members, consistent with prior research highlighting the negative impact of meritocratic ideologies on diversity outcomes (Castilla & Benard; 2010). In terms of the design specifications for systemic diversity interventions, the results of the study suggest that a comprehensive approach is needed, one that includes engaging gatekeepers, mitigating bias, and addressing the paradox of meritocracy. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are widely recognized as essential tools for synthesizing evidence from multiple studies to inform decision-making in various fields, including healthcare, education, and social sciences (Higgins & Green, 2011). These reviews involve the identification, evaluation, and synthesis of all relevant studies on a specific research question, using clearly defined methods to minimize bias (Moher et al., 2009). However, the process of conducting systematic reviews can be complex, particularly when dealing with multiple data sources for individual trials. A single trial may be reported in multiple sources, such as journal articles, conference abstracts, and study protocols, which can lead to differences in the reported results, methods, and conclusions (Egger et al., 2003). The use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews is not a new phenomenon, but it has become increasingly common with the growing number of studies being published and the ease of access to various sources of information Song et al., 2010). For example, a study may be reported in a journal article, a conference abstract, and a clinical trial registry, each providing different levels of detail and potentially conflicting information (Zarin et al., 2011). The selection of which sources to use can significantly influence the results of systematic reviews, and therefore, it is essential to develop practical guidance on how to handle multiple data sources (Gøtzsche & Hróbjartsson, 2010). Despite the importance of this issue, there is a lack of clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Previous studies have highlighted the potential problems associated with using multiple data sources, including inconsistencies in reporting, selective reporting, and publication bias (Dwan et al., 2013). However, these studies have not provided comprehensive guidance on how to address these issues in practice. The current guidelines for systematic reviews, such as the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statement, provide some guidance on reporting, but do not specifically address the issue of multiple data sources Moher et al., 2009). The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to investigate the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews and to develop practical guidance for reviewers (personal communication). The study involved a comprehensive review of the literature, as well as a survey of systematic review authors and a case study of a sample of systematic reviews. The results of the MUDS study highlighted the complexity of the issue and the need for clear guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews. The study found that the selection of sources can influence the results of systematic reviews, and that reviewers often lack clear [2] protocols for handling multiple data sources (unpublished data). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can systematic reviewers use multiple data sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results? This question is critical because the use of multiple data sources can introduce bias and errors into systematic reviews; which can have significant consequences for decision-making (Ioannidis, 2005). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to reduce the risk of bias and errors in systematic reviews and to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized. The contributions of this paper are several. First, we provide a comprehensive review of the literature on the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, highlighting the potential problems and challenges associated with this issue. Second, we present the results of the MUDS study, which provides new insights into the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews. Third, we develop practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources in systematic reviews, based on the results of the MUDS study and the literature review. This guidance includes recommendations on how to specify which sources to use, how to link individual trials with multiple sources, how to extract trial characteristics from multiple sources, and how to prespecify outcomes and results to examine in the review and meta-analysis. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the conduct of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and provide recommendations for future research in this area. In terms of the theoretical framework underlying our research, we draw on the concept of "research waste," which refers to the waste of resources, time, and effort in conducting research that is not useful or relevant Chalmers & Glasziou, 2009). We argue that the use of multiple data sources in systematic reviews can contribute to research waste, and that clear guidance on how to use these sources can help to reduce this waste. We also draw on the concept of "evidence-based medicine," which emphasizes the importance of using the best available evidence to inform decision-making (Sackett et al.; 1996). By developing practical guidance on how to use multiple data sources, we aim to improve the quality of the evidence synthesized in systematic reviews, and to promote evidence-based decision-making. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the issue of multiple data sources in systematic reviews, and presents practical guidance on how to use these sources in a way that minimizes bias and ensures the accuracy and reliability of the results. The guidance presented in this paper has the potential to improve the quality of systematic reviews and meta-analyses; and to promote evidence-based decision-making in a range of fields. The Multiple Data Sources in Systematic Reviews (MUDS) study was designed to investigate the impact of using multiple data sources on the results of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The study used a combination of empirical research and expert consensus to develop practical guidance for reviewers. In this section, we describe the data, design, procedures, and statistical analysis used in the MUDS study. The MUDS study included a total of 50 systematic reviews, each with multiple data sources. Error detection is a crucial step in data preprocessing, as it directly affects the quality and reliability of downstream data analysis and machine learning (ML) models (Hellerstein, 2008). Errors in data can arise from various sources, including human mistakes, sensor malfunctions, or data integration issues (Dasu & Johnson, 2003). Traditional error detection methods rely on hand-crafted rules, which can be time-consuming to develop and maintain, especially for large and complex datasets (Hogan, 1997). Furthermore, these methods often struggle to detect errors that are not anticipated by the rules, leading to poor recall and precision (Rahm & Do, 2000). In recent years, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising approach for error detection, as it can learn to recognize patterns in data and detect errors without requiring explicit rules (Berti-Equille et al., 2011). However, ML-based error detection models require large amounts of labeled training data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain, especially for datasets with complex error patterns Kuang et al., 2018). To address this challenge, researchers have explored active learning and ensemble-based methods, which can reduce the need for labeled data by selectively sampling the most informative instances or combining the predictions of multiple models (Lewis & Gale, 1994; Melo et al., 2017). Nevertheless, these methods still require a significant amount of human involvement, either in the form of labeling data or designing complex models. Few-shot learning, which involves training ML models with only a few examples, has gained significant attention in recent years (Fei-Fei et al., 2006). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can we develop a few-shot learning framework for error detection that requires minimal human involvement and can detect errors with high precision and recall? To answer this question, we need to address two key challenges: 1) developing an expressive model that can learn rich representations of errors, and (2) designing a data augmentation strategy that can generate additional training data with minimal human supervision. Our key insight is to learn data augmentation policies from the noisy input dataset in a weakly supervised manner, which allows us to leverage the structure of the data to generate new training examples (Peng et al., 2019). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce a novel few-shot learning framework for error detection, which combines an expressive model with a data augmentation strategy to detect errors with high precision and recall. The extraction of local features from images has been a fundamental problem in computer vision for several decades (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). Local features are used to describe small regions of an image, and they have numerous applications in various computer vision tasks such as object recognition Lowe, 2004), image matching (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005), and 3D reconstruction (Szeliski, 2010). The precise location of these features is crucial in many applications, particularly in 3D reconstruction problems where the accuracy of the features directly affects the quality of the reconstructed model Fua, 1997). Over the years, various methods have been proposed to extract local features, ranging from handcrafted methods to deep-learning-based approaches. Initially, local features were extracted using handcrafted methods, which relied on carefully designed algorithms to detect and describe regions of interest in an image (Harris & Stephens, 1988; Lowe, 1999). These methods, such as the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) (Lowe, 2004) and the Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) Bay et al., 2008), were widely used in various computer vision applications. handcrafted methods have several limitations, including their sensitivity to affine transformations and their inability to capture complex patterns in [19] images Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). Furthermore, the design of handcrafted features requires a deep understanding of the underlying image formation process and the characteristics of the features being extracted (Lazebnik et al., 2005). To overcome the limitations of handcrafted methods, researchers began to explore the use of classical machine learning techniques to learn local features from data (Csurka et al., 2004). These methods, such as the Bag-of-Words (BoW) model (Sivic & Zisserman, 2003), used machine learning algorithms to learn a dictionary of visual words from [27] a set of training images. The learned dictionary could then be used to represent new images as a collection of visual words. However, these methods had limited success in computer vision tasks, particularly in applications that required precise feature localization (Mikolajczyk & Schmid, 2005). In recent years, deep-learning-based methods have revolutionized the field of computer vision, including the extraction of local features Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 1998), have been used to learn local features from large datasets of images. These methods, such as the DeepDesc Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) and the LIFT (Yi et al., 2016), have shown impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including object recognition and image matching. However, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction also raises several challenges, including the need for large amounts of labeled training data and the computational complexity of the methods (Rosten & Drummond, 2006). The evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods has been driven by the need for more robust and accurate feature extractors. However, despite the significant progress made in this area, there is still a need for a comprehensive review of the existing methods and their performance on various benchmarks. Furthermore, the use of deep-learning-based methods for local feature extraction raises several questions, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function on the performance of the method. In this paper, we aim to address these questions and provide a comprehensive overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Our research question is: How have local features evolved from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, and what are [5] the key factors that affect their performance in various computer vision tasks? To answer this question, we will first review the existing literature on handcrafted and classical machine learning-based methods for local feature extraction. We will then discuss the recent advances in deep-learning-based methods and their applications in various computer vision tasks. Finally, we will evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and discuss the challenges and limitations of these methods. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive review of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods. Secondly, we discuss the key factors that affect the performance of local feature extractors, including the importance of the network architecture, the role of pre-training, and the impact of the loss function. Finally, we evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art methods on various benchmarks and provide insights into the challenges and limitations of these methods. Our paper will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in [9] the field of computer vision, and "will" help to advance the state-of-the-art in local feature extraction and related applications. One of the seminal studies in this area was conducted by Haaland (1999), who mapped the dental hygiene literature using Bradford's Law of Scattering, a method for analyzing the distribution of cited references across different journals (Bradford, 1934). Haaland's study examined a three-year sample of cited references from core dental "hygiene" journals and identified a core set of journals that accounted for a significant proportion of citations Haaland, 1999). However, this study is now over two decades old, and the dental hygiene literature has undergone significant changes since then, with the advent of online publishing, the proliferation of open-access journals, and the [12] increasing importance of interdisciplinary research Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). The lack of up-to-date information on the dental hygiene literature creates a significant gap in our [19] understanding of the field, with implications for librarians, researchers, and practitioners seeking to navigate the vast array of available resources (Whitmore, 2003; Munn, 2015). Specifically, the absence of current data on journal publication patterns, citation trends, and database coverage hinders the development of effective collection development strategies, user education programs, and research agendas (Johnson, 2017; Peterson, 2019). the rapid evolution of the dental hygiene literature, driven by advances in technology, changes in clinical practices, and shifting research priorities, underscores the need for a comprehensive update of Haaland's study Neylon, 2017; Wouters, 2017). This study aims to address this gap by asking the following research question: What are the current characteristics and trends of the dental hygiene literature, and how have they changed since Haaland's 1999 study? To answer this question, this study will employ a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative [16] analysis of cited references with qualitative examination of journal publication patterns and database coverage. By analyzing a three-year sample of cited references from core dental hygiene journals, this study will identify the core set of journals that account for the majority of citations, estimate the coverage of major databases, and examine the patterns of citation across different formats and publication years (Bradford, 1934; Haaland, 1999). The contributions of this study are several. Firstly, this study [13] will provide an updated mapping of [14] the dental hygiene literature, revealing changes in journal publication patterns, citation trends, and database coverage over the past two decades Haaland, 1999, Whitmore, 2003). This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis techniques to update Haaland's 1999 dental hygiene mapping study (Haaland, 1999). The research design involved a retrospective analysis of cited references from a three-year sample of core dental hygiene journals, as well as a survey of major databases to determine indexing coverage. The study's methodology was guided by Bradford's Law of Scattering, which states that a core of journals produces a significant proportion of the literature in a given field, with the number of journals decreasing as the number of relevant articles increases (Bradford, 1934). To identify the core dental hygiene journals, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Journal Citation Reports (JCR) database, which provides a list of journals ranked by impact factor and subject category (Garfield, 2006). The search was limited to journals classified under the subject category "Dentistry, Oral Surgery, and Medicine." The top 20 journals with the highest impact factors in this category were selected for inclusion in the study, as they are likely to be the most widely read and cited in the field (Braun & Glänzel, 1990). These journals were then manually reviewed to ensure they were indeed focused on dental hygiene, resulting in a final sample of 15 core journals. Cited references from the selected journals were collected over a three-year period 2015-2017) using a combination of manual and automated methods. Manual data collection involved reviewing each issue of the selected journals and recording the references cited in each article, while automated data collection utilized citation extraction software to gather references from online versions of the journals (Wallace & Boynton, 2006). The cited references were then categorized into five formats: journal articles, books, government publications, conference proceedings, and internet sources. This categorization scheme was based on previous studies of citation patterns in the health sciences Lancaster & Smith, 2006) and was designed to capture the range of sources cited in dental hygiene research. The categorized references were then analyzed according to Bradford's Law of Scattering, which involves dividing the references into zones based on their frequency of citation Bradford, 1934). Zone 1 consists of the core journals that produce the largest number of relevant articles, while Zone 2 and Zone 3 consist of journals that produce fewer relevant articles. The number of journals in each zone was calculated, as well as the percentage of total citations accounted for by each zone. This analysis allowed for the identification of the most influential journals in the field of dental hygiene and the characterization of changes in citation patterns over time. In addition to the analysis of cited references, a survey of major databases was conducted to determine the indexing coverage of dental hygiene journals. The databases surveyed included CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, which are among the most comprehensive databases in the health sciences (Haynes et al., 2006). The survey involved searching each database for the core dental hygiene journals identified in the study and recording the number of journals indexed in each database. This information was used to estimate the overall indexing coverage of dental hygiene journals and to identify areas where coverage may be lacking. The [26] sharing of health data is essential for advancing medical research, improving patient outcomes, and reducing healthcare costs (Friedman et al.; 2010). Despite the importance of addressing the tension between access and privacy in health data sharing, there is currently a [17] lack of effective solutions that balance these competing interests (Ohm, 2010). This question is significant because it highlights [18] the need for innovative solutions that can facilitate the sharing of health data while protecting [20] patient privacy and confidentiality. The proliferation of online review platforms has led to an overwhelming amount of user-generated content, making it increasingly difficult for consumers to discern relevant and useful information (Papenko and Gelbukh, 2017). To combat this issue, compact and concise forms of reviews, commonly referred to as tips, have emerged as a valuable means of conveying essential information about products or services (Kumar and Sharma, 2018). Despite their growing importance, tips have [10] received relatively little attention from researchers, with the majority of existing work focusing on the analysis and generation of full-length reviews (Azimen et al., 2019). This dearth of research on tips generation is particularly surprising, given the significant potential benefits of automatically generating high-quality tips, including improved user experience, increased customer engagement, and enhanced decision-making (Liu et al., 2019). One key factor that has been overlooked in existing research on tips generation is the importance of incorporating persona' information, which captures the intrinsic language style of users or the distinct characteristics of product items (Bao et al., 2019). Persona information can be used to personalize the tone, language, and content of generated tips, making them more relatable, engaging, and relevant to individual users (Kim et al., 2018). For instance, a user who frequently uses humorous language in their reviews may appreciate tips that are equally humorous, while a user who values conciseness may prefer tips that are brief and to the point (Wang et al., 2019). Similarly, product items with distinct characteristics, such as a luxury brand or a niche product, may require tips that reflect their unique features and tone (Lee et al., 2020). The lack of consideration for persona information in existing tips generation research is a significant gap, as it neglects the complex and nuanced relationships between users, products, and language (Chen et al., 2019). Existing approaches to tips generation have primarily focused on exploiting syntactic and semantic features of text data, without accounting for the variation in language style and tone that arises from differences in user and product personas (Zhang et al., 2018). This oversight can result in generated tips that are generic, impersonal, and fail to resonate with target users, ultimately undermining their effectiveness and usefulness (Liu et al., 2018). To address this gap, the research question guiding this study is: How can persona information be effectively incorporated into a tips generation framework to produce personalized, engaging, and relevant tips that capture the unique characteristics of users and product items? This question requires the development of a novel framework that can model and represent persona information, and integrate it into a tips generation component to produce high-quality tips. This study aims to contribute to the existing body of research on tips generation by proposing a persona-aware tips generation framework that leverages adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE) for persona modeling, and incorporates persona embeddings and sentiment information into a recurrent neural networks (RNN) based tips generation component. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, we propose a novel framework for persona-aware tips generation that exploits the persona information of users and product items to produce personalized and engaging tips. Secondly, we design a persona memory component that stores persona-related words for users and items, and uses a Pointer Network to retrieve these words when generating tips. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness [39] of our framework, using quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis to demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches to tips generation (Huang et al., 2020). By addressing the gap in existing research and providing a novel solution to the challenge of persona-aware tips generation, this study aims to make a significant contribution to the field of natural language processing and human-computer interaction. To investigate the task of persona-aware tips generation, we propose a multi-component framework that integrates adversarial variational auto-encoders (aVAE) for persona modeling, a persona memory for storing persona-related words, and a recurrent neural network (RNN) based tips generation component. In this section, we outline the data collection, design of the framework, procedures for training and testing, and statistical analysis. The dataset used in this study consists of tips and reviews from a popular online review platform, which includes 100,000 users and 10,000 items (Kang et al., 2019). Each user has an average of 50 reviews, and each item has an average of 100 reviews. The tips are truncated to 50 words, and reviews are truncated to 500 words. We preprocess the data by tokenizing the text, removing stop words, and converting all text to lowercase (Mikolov et al., 2013). We split the dataset into training (80%), validation (10%), and testing (10%) sets. Our framework consists of three main components: persona modeling using aVAE, persona memory, and tips generation using RNN. For persona modeling, we use aVAE to learn the latent variables that capture the intrinsic language style of users and items (Kingma & Welling, 2014). The aVAE model consists of an encoder network that maps the input text to a latent space and a decoder network that generates text from the latent space. We use a Gaussian mixture model as the prior distribution for the latent variables (Dilokthanakul et al.; 2016). The persona embeddings are obtained by sampling from the latent space using the reparameterization trick (Kingma & Welling, 2014). To design the persona memory, we use a dictionary-based approach to store persona-related words for users and items (Miller et al., 2016). We select the top 100 words with the highest TF-IDF scores for each user and item, which are then stored in the persona memory. The persona memory is used to retrieve persona-related words during tips generation. We use a Pointer Network to select the relevant words from the persona memory (Vinyals et al., 2015). For tips generation, we use an RNN-based approach with a sequence-to-sequence architecture (Sutskever et al., 2014). The encoder takes the item description and user's persona embedding as input, and the decoder generates the tips. [33] We use a attention mechanism to focus on the relevant parts of the item description and persona embedding during generation (Bahdanau et al., 2015). The persona embeddings and sentiment information are incorporated into the decoder to generate tips that reflect the user's language style and sentiment towards the item. We train the framework using a multi-task learning approach, where the aVAE model is trained to minimize the reconstruction loss, and the RNN-based tips generation component is trained to minimize the cross-entropy loss (Rennie et al., 2017). We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 128. We train the framework for 100 epochs and evaluate the performance on the validation set after each epoch. To evaluate the performance of the framework, we use automatic metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR, which measure the similarity between the generated tips and the ground truth tips (Papineni et al., 2002; Lin, 2004; Lavie & Agarwal, 2007). We calculate the average rating and standard deviation "to" measure the consistency of the ratings. The increasing amount of data being published on the Web in the form of RDF (Resource Description Framework) datasets has led to a [28] growing need [38] for interoperability among these datasets (Bizer et al., 2009). achieving interoperability is challenging due to semantic heterogeneity, which refers to the differences in the meaning and interpretation of data across different datasets (Shvaiko & Euzenat; 2013). These differences arise from various factors, including context-specific requirements, different data modelling decisions, domain-specific purposes, and technical constraints Halevy et al., 2006). As a result, integrating and querying data from multiple sources becomes a complex task, requiring significant effort and expertise (Lenzerini, 2002). The problem [4] of semantic heterogeneity is exacerbated by the fact that different RDF publishers and knowledge domains often use different vocabularies, ontologies, and data models to represent their data (Heath & Bizer, 2011). This makes it difficult to establish links between datasets, which is essential for querying and accessing the data in a meaningful way (Berners-Lee, 2006). The Vocabulary of Interlinked Datasets (VoID) is an attempt to address this issue by providing a set of terms and patterns for describing and linking RDF datasets (Alexander et al.; 2009). VoID has limitations, as it primarily focuses on describing the structure and content of individual datasets, rather than providing a mechanism for linking them (Tran et al., 2013). To address the challenge of semantic heterogeneity and improve interoperability among RDF datasets, researchers have proposed various approaches, including data integration (Lenzerini, 2002), ontology alignment (Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2013), and link discovery (Volz et al., 2009). However, these approaches often require significant manual effort, are time-consuming, and may not be scalable to large numbers of datasets (Halevy et al., 2006). Furthermore; even if the problem of semantic heterogeneity is solved, querying and accessing the data of distributed RDF datasets on the Web is still not straightforward (Berners-Lee, 2006). This is because understanding how these datasets can be related or linked, and consequently, queried, is a complex and fastidious process (Heath & Bizer, 2011). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can we enhance the interoperability [38] of RDF datasets by introducing virtual links between resources from different datasets, and what benefits can be achieved by using these links? To answer this question, we propose to extend the existing VoID by introducing new terms and patterns, including the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns. A virtual link [26] is a connection between resources, such as literals and IRIs (Internationalized Resource Identifier), with some commonality, where each of these resources is from a different RDF dataset (Volz et al.; 2009). These links are required to understand [24] how to semantically [36] relate datasets and to enable querying and accessing the data in a meaningful way (Berners-Lee; 2006). The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns as an extension to VoID; which enables the creation of virtual links between resources from different RDF datasets. Second, we describe the benefits of using virtual links to improve interoperability between heterogeneous and independent datasets, including improved query "performance," increased data reuse, and enhanced data integration. Third, we exemplify and apply our approach to multiple world-wide used RDF datasets, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposal. By addressing the challenge of semantic heterogeneity and improving interoperability among RDF datasets; our work has the potential to facilitate the creation of a more integrated and coherent Web of Data (Heath & Bizer, 2011). The use of virtual links to enhance interoperability among RDF datasets is a novel approach that has not been extensively explored in the literature. While there have been efforts to develop link discovery algorithms and ontology alignment techniques, these approaches often focus on establishing links between datasets based on semantic similarity or equivalence Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2013). In contrast, our approach focuses on creating virtual links between resources from different datasets based on commonalities, such as shared concepts, entities, or relationships (Volz et al., 2009). This approach has the potential to enable more flexible and dynamic querying and accessing of data from multiple sources, and to facilitate the creation of new applications and services that rely on integrated data from diverse sources (Berners-Lee, 2006). In conclusion, the problem of semantic heterogeneity among RDF datasets is a significant challenge that hinders the integration and querying of data from multiple sources. The proposed extension to VoID, including the concept of Virtual Link Set and data model patterns, has the potential to address this challenge by enabling the creation of virtual links between resources from different datasets. The benefits of using virtual links, including improved query performance, increased data reuse, and enhanced data integration, make our approach an attractive solution for improving interoperability among RDF datasets. The remainder of this paper will provide a detailed description of our approach, including the design and implementation of the Virtual Link Set concept and data model patterns, and the application of our approach to multiple world-wide used RDF datasets.
