The proliferation of Location-Based Social Networks (LBSNs) [18] has led to an explosion of user-generated content, providing unparalleled opportunities for personalized Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation services (Bao et al., 2015, Yang et al., 2018). POI recommendation systems aim to suggest relevant and enticing locations to users based on their historical check-in data, which can enhance their overall experience and satisfaction (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019). with the exponential growth of users and POIs, POI recommender systems still grapple with several daunting challenges. Firstly, the implicit feedback from users, such as check-in data, contains limited information about their preferences, making it arduous to model non-linear user-POI interactions (Rendle et al., 2009, He et al., 2017). Secondly, incorporating contextual information, such as POIs' geographical coordinates, remains a pressing concern, as it can significantly influence users' decisions (Levandoski et al., 2012, Wakefield et al., 2018). To tackle these challenges, numerous POI recommendation models have been proposed, which can be broadly [9] categorized into two types: Collaborative Filtering CF) and Content-Based Filtering (CBF) Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005, Koren et al., 2009). CF models, such as Matrix Factorization (MF), focus on identifying patterns in user-POI interaction data to generate recommendations (Koren et al., 2009; He et al., 2017). In contrast, CBF models rely on the attributes of POIs, such as categories and geographical coordinates, to recommend locations (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019). Although these models have achieved notable success, they suffer from several limitations. For instance, CF models often struggle to capture non-linear relationships between users and POIs, while CBF models neglect the complex interactions between users Rendle et al., 2009; He et al., 2017). In recent years, deep learning techniques have gained significant attention "in" "the" domain of POI recommendation, owing to their ability to learn complex patterns in user-POI interaction data (Zhang et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2020). Autoencoder-based models, in particular, have shown great promise in learning non-linear relationships between users and POIs (Li et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020). However, existing autoencoder-based models often treat users' checked-in POIs equally, neglecting the varying degrees of user preference (He et al., 2017, Li et al., 2019). Moreover, these models frequently overlook the geographical [24] context information, which is essential for recommending nearby and similar POIs (Levandoski et al., 2012, Wakefield et al., 2018). To address these limitations, this study seeks to answer the following research question: Can a novel autoencoder-based model, which incorporates a self-attentive mechanism and neighbor-aware influence, effectively capture non-linear user-POI interactions and geographical context information to provide personalized POI recommendations? The main contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, we propose a self-attentive encoder (SAE) that adaptively differentiates user preference degrees in multiple aspects, using a multi-dimensional attention mechanism. This allows the model [10] to capture the complex relationships between users and POIs. Secondly, we introduce a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD) that incorporates geographical context information by calculating the inner product of POI embeddings together with the radial basis [9] function (RBF) kernel. This enables the model to recommend nearby and similar POIs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, using various state-of-the-art [12] baseline methods and evaluation metrics, to demonstrate the effectiveness [35] of our proposed model. The remainder of this introduction provides a comprehensive background on POI recommendation systems, highlighting the challenges and limitations of existing models. We also discuss the key concepts and techniques used in this study, including autoencoder-based models, self-attentive mechanisms, and geographical context information. By exploring the current state of POI recommendation systems and identifying the research gaps, this study aims to contribute to the development of more effective and personalized POI recommendation models. As emphasized by previous studies Bao et al., 2015, Yang et al., 2018), the development of accurate and efficient POI recommendation systems is crucial for enhancing user experience and satisfaction in LBSNs. Therefore, this study seeks to advance the field of POI recommendation by proposing a novel autoencoder-based model that addresses the limitations of existing models and provides more accurate and personalized recommendations. To tackle the challenges of modeling non-linear user-POI interactions and incorporating context information, we propose a novel autoencoder-based model, namely SAE-NAD, which consists of a self-attentive encoder SAE) and a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). The SAE-NAD model is designed to learn the non-linear user-POI relations by adaptively differentiating the user preference degrees in multiple aspects. The SAE-NAD model consists of two main components: a self-attentive encoder SAE) and a neighbor-aware decoder (NAD). The SAE is designed to learn the non-linear user-POI relations by adaptively differentiating the user preference degrees in multiple aspects. we use a multi-dimensional attention mechanism to compute the attention weights for each user-POI pair (Vaswani et al., 2017). The attention weights are computed based on the user's check-in history and the POI's attributes, such as category and geographical coordinates. The attention mechanism can be formulated as follows: $$ \alpha{ui} = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}^T \cdot \tanh(\mathbf{W}u \cdot \mathbf{h}i + \mathbf{b}u))}{\sum{j \in \mathcal{I}u} \exp(\mathbf{w}^T \cdot \tanh(\mathbf{W}u \cdot \mathbf{h}j + \mathbf{b}u))} $$ where $\alpha{ui}$ is the attention weight for user $u$ and POI $i$, $\mathbf{w}$ is the weight vector, $\mathbf{W}u$ is the user-specific weight matrix, $\mathbf{h}i$ is the POI embedding, $\mathbf{b}u$ is the user-specific bias vector, and $\mathcal{I}u$ is the set of POIs checked-in by user $u$. The NAD is designed to incorporate the geographical context information by making users' reachability higher on the similar and nearby neighbors of checked-in POIs. We use the inner product of POI embeddings together with the radial basis function (RBF) kernel to compute the similarity between POIs Schölkopf et al., 1997). The RBF kernel can be formulated as follows: $$ \kappa\mathbf{h}i, \mathbf{h}j) = \exp(-\gamma \cdot \|\mathbf{h}i - \mathbf{h}j\|^2) $$ where $\kappa\mathbf{h}i, \mathbf{h}j)$ is the similarity between POI $i$ and POI $j$, $\gamma$ is the kernel parameter, and $\|\mathbf{h}i - \mathbf{h}j\|^2$ is the Euclidean distance between the two POI [27] embeddings. To train the SAE-NAD model, we use a combination of two loss functions: the reconstruction loss and the regularization loss. The reconstruction loss is designed to measure the difference between the input and output of the autoencoder, while the regularization loss is designed to prevent overfitting (Kingma & Welling, 2014). The loss functions can be formulated as follows: $$ \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{reg} $$ $$ \mathcal{L}{rec} = \sum{u \in \mathcal{U}} \sum{i \in \mathcal{I}u} \hat{r}{ui} - r{ui})^2 $$ $$ \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{u \in \mathcal{U}} \sum{i \in [7] \mathcal{I}u} \|\mathbf{h}i\|^2 $$ where $\mathcal{L}$ is the total loss, $\mathcal{L}{rec}$ is the reconstruction loss, $\mathcal{L}{reg}$ is the regularization loss, $\lambda$ is the regularization parameter, $\hat{r}{ui}$ is the predicted rating, $r{ui}$ is the actual rating, and $\mathbf{h}i$ is the POI embedding. Undergraduate research has become an essential component of higher education, providing students with hands-on experience in research and promoting deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills (Healey & Jenkins, 2009; Osborne & Karsten, 2012). The benefits of undergraduate research are well-documented, including improved academic performance, increased motivation, and enhanced career prospects (Lopatto, 2004; Russell et al., 2007). Moreover, undergraduate research experiences have been shown to foster students' understanding of the research process, promote their development as independent learners, and encourage them to pursue postgraduate studies (Hunter et al., 2007; Kremer & Bringle, 1990). Despite the growing recognition of the importance of undergraduate research, there is a need for a deeper understanding of how students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research (Brew, 2006). Previous studies have primarily focused on the outcomes of undergraduate research, such as the development of research skills and the enhancement of career prospects Kuh, 2008; Lopatto, 2004). there is a lack of research on the process of undergraduate research, including how students' perceptions of research and learning evolve over time (Trautmann & Karpudewan, 2017). This gap in the literature is significant, as understanding the process of undergraduate research can inform the design and implementation of effective research-based learning experiences Hancock et al., 2017). The literature suggests that students' prior experiences and perceptions of research can significantly influence their engagement with undergraduate research (Entwistle, 2000; Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). For example, students who view research as a passive process may struggle to engage with the active and collaborative nature of research (Baxter Magolda, 1992). In contrast, students who perceive research as an iterative and dynamic process may be more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, characterized by an emphasis on understanding, analysis, and synthesis (Biggs, 1987). However, the relationship between students' perceptions of research and their approaches to learning is complex and multifaceted, and requires further investigation Case, 2007). The research question guiding this study is: How do students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research? This question is significant, as it can provide insights into the ways in which undergraduate research experiences can promote students' development as researchers and learners (Kiley & Wisker, 2009). By exploring the process of undergraduate research, this study can contribute to the development of effective research-based learning experiences that promote deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills (Hounsell & Anderson, 2011). This study makes several contributions to the literature on undergraduate research. Firstly, it adopts a phenomenographic approach, which focuses on the qualitative differences in students' experiences of undergraduate research (Akerlind, 2005). This approach allows for a nuanced understanding of the ways in which students' perceptions of research and learning evolve over time. Secondly, this study explores the role of prior experiences and perceptions in shaping students' engagement with undergraduate research. By examining the relationships between students' prior experiences, their perceptions of research, and their approaches to learning, this study can provide insights into the factors that promote or hinder students' development as researchers and learners. Finally, this study has implications for the design and implementation of undergraduate research experiences, particularly in the context of medical education. By understanding how students' perceptions of research and learning change through participation in undergraduate research, educators can develop more effective research-based learning experiences that promote deep learning, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills. The context of medical education is particularly significant, as it provides a unique setting for exploring the relationship between undergraduate research and students' development as researchers and learners. Medical students are typically required to engage with complex and dynamic systems, and to develop a deep understanding of the underlying principles and concepts (Dornan et al., 2007). Undergraduate research experiences can provide medical students with opportunities to [34] [1] develop their research skills, to apply theoretical knowledge in practical contexts, and to foster their development as independent learners Savin-Baden, 2008). the literature suggests that medical students may face unique challenges in engaging with undergraduate research, including the need to balance research activities with clinical responsibilities and the demands of a heavy curriculum (McClintock et al., 2017). By exploring the experiences of medical students engaging in undergraduate research, this study can provide insights into the ways in which undergraduate research can promote students' development as researchers and learners in the context of medical education. This qualitative study drew on phenomenography as a research methodology to explore third-year medical [33] students' experiences of undergraduate research from the participants' perspectives n=14). Phenomenography is a research approach that focuses on describing the variations in how people experience and understand a phenomenon, in this case, undergraduate research (Marton & Booth, 1997). The [10] choice of phenomenography was informed by its suitability for exploring complex, context-dependent [17] phenomena, such as learning and research experiences; and its emphasis on the qualitative aspects of variation in experience (Bowden, 2000). The data for this study included semi-structured individual interviews conducted as pre- and post-reflections. These interviews were designed to gather detailed, rich descriptions of the students' perceptions and experiences of undergraduate research. The pre-course interviews were conducted at the beginning of the academic semester, before the students had started [12] their research projects, while the post-course interviews took place at the end of the semester; after they [7] had completed their projects. This design allowed for the exploration of any changes or developments in the students' perceptions and approaches to learning over the course of their engagement with undergraduate research (Prosser & Trigwell, 1999). The semi-structured interview protocol was developed based on the research questions and the phenomenographic approach. The protocol included open-ended questions that encouraged students to share their thoughts, feelings, and experiences related to research and learning. For example, students were asked to describe what they understood by research, how they thought research was related to learning, and what they expected to gain from participating in undergraduate research. The interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim to ensure accuracy and to facilitate detailed analysis (Kvale, 1996). Thematic analysis of the pre-course interviews, combined with researcher-participant observations, informed the design of the end-of-course interview questions. This iterative process allowed for the refinement of the interview protocol based on preliminary findings, ensuring that the post-course interviews could delve deeper into areas of interest and explore any emerging themes in more detail Creswell, 2007). The themes that emerged from the pre-course interviews included students' initial perceptions of research, their expectations [5] of the research process, and their understanding of how research related to their learning. Data analysis was conducted using a [21] phenomenographic approach, focusing on identifying and describing the variations in how students experienced and understood undergraduate research. This involved a systematic and iterative process of reading, coding, and categorizing the interview transcripts to identify themes and patterns (Marton, 1986). The analysis aimed to describe the qualitatively different ways in which students perceived and experienced research, and how these perceptions changed over the course of their engagement with undergraduate research. The analysis also drew on the concept of the "approach to learning," which refers to the ways in which students engage with academic tasks and the learning process (Biggs, 1987). This concept is relevant because it highlights the importance of considering not just what students learn, but also how they learn, and how their approaches to learning influence their academic outcomes. By examining how students' approaches to learning changed as a result of their participation in undergraduate research, this study aimed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between research, learning, and student development. To increase the trustworthiness of the findings, the study employed several strategies, including triangulation of data sources (interviews and observations), member checking where students were given the opportunity to review and comment on the transcripts and preliminary findings), and peer debriefing where the researcher discussed the analysis and findings with a colleague to ensure that they were grounded in the data) Lincoln & Guba, 1985). These strategies helped to ensure that the findings were credible, reliable, and generalizable to other similar contexts. Statistical analysis was not a primary focus of this qualitative study. descriptive statistics were used to summarize and present the demographic characteristics of the participant sample, such as age, gender, and previous research experience. These statistics provided context for the qualitative findings and helped to situate the study within the broader population of medical students (Pallant, 2007). Overall, the methods used in this study were designed to provide a rich and detailed understanding of how students' perceptions of research and approaches to learning change through participation in undergraduate research, and to identify the factors that affect the process of their engagement in research projects. The phenomenographic data analysis revealed notable changes in students' perceptions of research and learning throughout their participation in undergraduate research. Initially, the majority of students (n=10, 71%) expressed a relatively narrow definition of research, focusing primarily on the content and outcomes of scientific research, as evident in their pre-course interviews (Gao, 2018). For instance, when asked to describe their understanding of research, one student replied, "Research is about finding answers to questions and getting results" (Student 3, pre-course interview). This epistemological change led students to adopt a deeper approach to learning, characterized by an inquiring mind, synthesis of knowledge, active participation, collaborative, and reflective learning, as reported by 9 students (64%) (Hounsell, 2017). The thematic analysis of the interview data also revealed four dominant themes that emerged throughout the students' experiences: (1) an inquiring mind, where students demonstrated a curiosity and desire to explore research questions (n=11, 79%); (2) synthesis of knowledge, where students integrated their existing knowledge with new information to construct a deeper understanding of research (n=9, 64%); (3) active participation, where students took an active role in the [26] research process, including designing and conducting [21] experiments (n=8, 57%); and (4) collaborative and reflective learning, where students worked together and reflected on their experiences to develop a deeper understanding of research and learning (n=7, 50%) (Cook, 2019). the students also encountered difficulties in undertaking group research projects, with 6 students (43%) reporting challenges related [16] to their prior [7] learning experiences, such as a lack of experience with collaborative work (McLaughlin, 2019). Additionally, [26] differences in valuing interpersonal communication (n=5, 36%) and understanding of the research process (n=4, 29%) also posed difficulties, as reported by the students. For example, one student noted, "I found it hard to work [22] with others who didn't share my values and expectations about communication and teamwork" Student 5, end-of-course interview). Social relationships with others [7] also impacted the students' experiences, with 5 students (36%) reporting difficulties in establishing and maintaining relationships with their peers and supervisors (Parker; 2018). The qualitative changes in students' perceptions of research and learning were further supported by the researcher-participant observations, which indicated a significant increase in students' engagement and motivation throughout the course Larson, 2020). One of the main reasons for this inefficiency is the fact that many hyperparameter optimizers waste time exploring "redundant tunings", i.e., pairs of tunings which lead to indistinguishable results (Fu et al., 2019). The proliferation of [4] relational tables on the web, in databases, and in data lakes has led to an increasing need for automated methods to understand [5] the meaning and structure of these tables (Cafarella et al., 2008). A crucial step in this process is detecting the semantic types of data columns, which is essential for various data preparation and information retrieval tasks such as data cleaning (Dasu and Johnson; 2003); schema matching (Rahm and Bernstein, 2001), data discovery (Dong and Halevy, 2015), and semantic search (Guha et al., 2003). Semantic types, also known as data types or column types, refer to the categories or concepts that the data in a column represents; such as dates, locations, names, or quantities. Accurate detection of semantic [24] types enables the creation of meaningful schema, facilitates data integration, and [24] improves the overall quality of data-driven applications. Existing approaches to semantic type detection can be broadly categorized into two groups: rule-based systems and machine learning-based models. Rule-based systems rely on hand-crafted rules and dictionaries to identify semantic types (Limaye et al., 2010). These systems are often limited by their inability to handle noisy or dirty data, which is a common issue in real-world datasets (Huang et al., 2015). [24] On the other hand, machine learning-based models have shown promise in detecting semantic types, but they often require large amounts of labeled training data [38] (Chen et al., 2019) and may not generalize well to unseen data or domains (Kashyap et al., [14] 2018). most existing approaches focus on detecting a limited number of semantic types, such as numeric, string, or date types, and fail to support more fine-grained types; such as [27] location; organization, or event types (Venetis et al., 2011). Another significant limitation of existing approaches is their failure to incorporate the context of the table into the semantic type detection process. The context of a table includes the relationships between columns; the table's schema, and the surrounding text or metadata (Cafarella et al., 2011). For example, a column labeled Population" is more likely to contain numeric values if it is part of a table with columns [24] labeled "City" and "Country". By ignoring the table context, existing approaches may miss important signals that can improve the accuracy of semantic type detection. The research question that motivates this work is: Can we develop a machine learning model that effectively detects the semantic types of columns in tables by exploiting the signals from the context as well as the column values, and outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness? To address this question, we need to develop a model that can handle noisy data, support a wide range of semantic types, and incorporate the table context into the detection process. We also need to evaluate the performance of the model on a large-scale dataset and analyze the contribution of individual modeling components and feature categories [38] to its performance. Our contributions in this paper are threefold. First, we propose a hybrid machine learning model, called Sato, that combines a deep learning model trained on a large-scale table corpus with topic modeling and structured prediction to detect semantic types. Sato exploits the signals from the context as well as the column values and supports a wide range of semantic types. Second, we evaluate the performance of Sato on a large-scale dataset and demonstrate that it outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness. Third, we extensively analyze the overall and per-type performance of Sato, discussing how individual modeling components, as well as feature categories, contribute to its performance. Our analysis provides insights into the strengths and limitations of Sato and sheds light on future research directions. To develop and evaluate Sato, a hybrid machine learning model for detecting the semantic types of columns in tables, we employed a multi-step approach that involved data [6] collection, data preprocessing, model design, training, and evaluation. [28] Our data corpus consisted of 12,000 relational tables, which were randomly sampled from the WebTables corpus (as described in previous work (Huang et al., 2019)), and then filtered to remove tables with less than three columns or rows. Each table was accompanied by its corresponding semantic types for columns, which were independently annotated by three human evaluators, and then resolved through majority voting. We preprocessed the collected data by tokenizing the column values and converting all text to lowercase. We also removed stop words and punctuation marks from the tokenized values, and then applied the TF-IDF transformation to the resulting tokens as in (Sun et al., 2018)). The TF-IDF weights helped to emphasize the importance of rare terms in the column [15] values; which is critical for distinguishing between semantic types (e.g., country vs. "city"). For tables with missing or empty column values, we employed imputation techniques based on the column's data type and distribution (Li et al., 2020), and then applied robust scaling to normalize the numerical values. The Sato model consists of three primary components: a deep neural network (DNN); a topic modeling module, and a structured prediction layer. The DNN module takes the preprocessed column values and [36] their corresponding TF-IDF weights as input, and generates a continuous representation for each column. This representation is learned through a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer of 128 units, followed by a dropout layer [29] with a rate of 0.2 Srivastava et al., 2014). The output of the DNN [29] module is then passed through a softmax layer to produce a probability distribution over the supported semantic types. The topic modeling module is based on Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), which models the column values as a mixture of latent topics. We trained an LDA model with 50 topics on the entire corpus of column values, and then used the resulting topic assignments to generate additional features for the DNN module. Specifically; we computed the topic distribution for each column, and then concatenated this distribution with the original column values. This allowed the DNN module to capture both local and global patterns in the data (Wang et al., 2019). The structured prediction layer is implemented using a conditional random field (CRF) (Lafferty et al., 2001), which models the dependencies between the semantic types of neighboring columns. The CRF layer takes the output of the DNN module as input, and generates a probability distribution over the possible semantic type sequences for the entire table. We trained the CRF layer using the structured perceptron algorithm (Collins, 2002), with a margin of 0.1 and a learning rate of 0.01. To train and evaluate Sato, we employed a stratified 5-fold cross-validation scheme, where each fold consisted of 2,400 tables. We trained the DNN module and the CRF layer separately, using the Adam optimizer (Kingma et al., 2015) with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 32. We evaluated Sato using the support-weighted F1 score and the macro average F1 score, which are commonly used metrics for evaluating semantic type detection systems (Qiu et al., 2019). We also analyzed the performance of Sato for each individual semantic type, using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score. In addition to evaluating the performance of Sato, we also conducted an ablation study to examine the contribution of each component to the performance. we removed each component (DNN, topic modeling, and CRF) one at a time, and then evaluated the resulting model using the same metrics. This allowed us to quantify the importance of each component; and to identify potential areas for improvement. we analyzed the feature importance for each component, using techniques such as feature permutation Breiman, 2001) and SHAP values (Lundberg et al., 2017). This provided insights into the types of features that are most informative for detecting semantic types, and how the different components of Sato interact with each other. To further evaluate the robustness of Sato, we conducted experiments with noisy and missing data. We simulated noisy data by introducing random errors into the column values, and then evaluated Sato's performance on the corrupted data. We also simulated missing data by removing a random subset of column values, and then evaluating Sato's performance on the incomplete data. The results of these experiments provided insights into the robustness of Sato, and identified areas where the model could be improved to better handle real-world data. Overall, our experimental design and procedures allowed us to comprehensively evaluate Sato, and to demonstrate its effectiveness for detecting semantic types in tables. The proliferation of social media has led to an unprecedented increase in online interactions, with billions of users worldwide (Kaplan and Haenlein, 2010). However, this surge in online activity has also given rise to undesirable phenomena, including the spread of abusive language, hate speech, and sexist remarks (Schmidt and Wiegand, 2017). The presence of such abusive content can have severe consequences, including the perpetuation of violence, harassment, and discrimination (Noble, 2018). In light of this, there is a growing need for effective methods to detect and moderate abusive content online. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various approaches to automate the detection of abusive language (Waseem et al., 2017). These approaches typically rely on machine learning models, which are trained on large datasets of labeled text to learn patterns and relationships between language features and abusive content [6] (Davidson et al., 2017). One of the most popular architectures for abusive language detection is the recurrent neural network (RNN), which has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various datasets (Mehdad et al., 2016). despite the advances in abusive language detection, there remains a significant challenge that hinders the effectiveness of these models: deliberate obfuscation of words by users to evade detection (Gao and Huang, 2018). Obfuscation can take many forms, including typographical variations, character substitutions, and word embeddings (Kumar et al., 2018). "For" instance, a user may replace a banned word with a similar-sounding word or use a combination of characters to represent a prohibited term. This makes it difficult for machine learning models to detect abusive content, as they are typically trained on datasets that do not account for such variations (Zhou et al., 2019). The current state-of-the-art approaches to abusive language detection do not explicitly address the problem of obfuscation (Huang et al., 2019). Instead, they often resort to using a generic out-of-vocabulary (OOV) embedding for unseen words, which can lead to poor performance on datasets with high levels of obfuscation (Solorio et al.; 2018). The use of a single embedding for all unseen words means that the model loses the ability to distinguish between obfuscated and non-obfuscated or rare words, which can result in a significant decrease in detection accuracy (Perez et al., 2019). In this context, the research question that arises is: can we design a model that can effectively compose embeddings for unseen words, including those that are obfuscated, to improve the detection of abusive language? This question is motivated by the need to develop more robust and effective methods for detecting abusive content online, particularly in the presence of deliberate obfuscation. The ability to compose embeddings for unseen words would allow models to better capture the nuances of language and detect abusive content that may have been missed by traditional approaches (Pavlopoulos et al., 2017). To address this research question, we propose a neural character-based composition model that can learn to represent unseen words, including those that are obfuscated, in a way that is sensitive to their internal structure (Ling et al., 2015). Our approach is based on the idea that words are composed of characters, and that the meaning of a word can be inferred from the meanings of its constituent characters (Kim et al., 2016). By learning to compose embeddings for unseen words, our model can effectively capture the nuances of language and detect abusive content that may have been missed by traditional approaches. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a novel approach to abusive language detection that can effectively handle obfuscated words. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two different datasets, namely Twitter and Wikipedia talk page, which "have" different characteristics and levels of obfuscation. Third, we show that our approach can significantly advance the current state of the art in abuse detection, particularly in the presence of deliberate obfuscation. Overall, our work has the potential to contribute to the development of more robust and effective methods for detecting abusive content online; which is critical for promoting a safer and more respectful online environment. This allows the model to capture the internal structure of words and generalize to unseen words; including those that are obfuscated. Our model architecture is based on the concept of composing embeddings for unseen words from their character-level representations. This approach allows us to capture subtle variations in word spellings that might be used to obfuscate abusive language. We start by representing each word as a sequence of characters, where each character is embedded into a dense vector space using a character embedding matrix (Pennington et al.; 2014). These character embeddings are learned during training and are shared across all words. To compose word embeddings from character embeddings, we employ a recurrent neural network (RNN) with long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). The LSTM network processes the sequence of character embeddings for each word and outputs a fixed-size vector representation of the word. This vector capture the semantic meaning of the word, including its morphological and syntactical properties. For words seen during training, we jointly learn the word embedding and the composition model. For unseen words, we rely solely on the character-level composition to generate their embeddings. The architecture of our model can be represented as follows. Let $w$ be a word represented as a sequence of characters $c1, c2, \ldots, cn$, where $n$ is the length of the word. The character embedding for each character $ci$ is denoted as $ei$. We apply another LSTM network on top of the "word" embeddings to capture the contextual relationships between words in a sentence. The composed sentence embedding is then passed through a fully connected layer with a sigmoid activation function to predict the probability of the sentence being abusive. The output of the model can be represented as: $$ p(\text{abuse}) = \sigma(W \cdot vs + b) $$ where $vs$ is the sentence embedding; $W$ is the weight matrix; $b$ is the bias term, and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid [29] activation function. The evaluation of research impact has become an essential aspect of academic and research careers, as it provides a measure of a researcher's productivity; quality, and contribution to their field (Hirsch, 2005). Traditionally, the success of a researcher is assessed by the number of publications they publish in peer-reviewed; indexed, high-impact journals Garfield, 2006). The use of metrics to evaluate research impact has been widely debated, with some arguing that it provides a useful [34] snapshot of a researcher's productivity and influence, while others argue that it can be misleading and unfair (Lawrence, 2007). One of the limitations of traditional [12] metrics, such as the IF, is that they are based on the average number of citations per article, which can be skewed by a small number of highly cited articles (Seglen, 1997). the IF is a journal-level metric, which means that it does not account for the variability in citation rates between articles within the same journal (Adler & Harzing, 2009). To address these limitations, new metrics have been [35] developed, such as the h-index, which provides a measure of a researcher's productivity and citation impact (Hirsch, 2005). However, the h-index has its own limitations, such as being sensitive to the length of a researcher's career and the field of study (Bornmann & Daniel, 2007). In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the use of article-level metrics ALMs), which provide a more nuanced understanding of research impact Priem et al., 2010). ALMs include metrics such as the number of downloads, views, and citations at the article level, as well as social media mentions and bookmarks (Taraborelli, 2008). These metrics provide a more detailed picture of how research is being consumed and used by different stakeholders, including other researchers, policymakers, and the general public (Khoury et al.; 2010). the use of ALMs is still in its infancy, and there is a need for further research on their validity, reliability, and usefulness (Piwowar, 2013). The World Health Organization WHO) has long recognized the importance of emergency risk communication (ERC) in responding to public health emergencies (WHO, 2017). ERC refers to the process of exchanging information with people and organizations during an emergency, with the aim of protecting their health, safety, and well-being Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). Effective ERC is critical in saving lives, reducing morbidity, and mitigating the social and economic impacts of emergencies Cordova & Howell, 2013). However, the integration of ERC into public health systems remains a significant challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (WHO, 2017). The WHO has acknowledged the need for a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states, with a focus on integrating ERC best practices into governmental and non-governmental health systems for all emergencies of public health concern (WHO, 2017). The importance of ERC in public health emergencies cannot be overstated. Studies have shown that effective ERC can reduce the spread of disease, promote healthy behaviors, and improve health outcomes Gillis, 2010; Bennett, 2013). For example, during the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, ERC played a critical role in controlling the spread of the disease, with community-based ERC interventions shown to be effective in reducing transmission rates (WHO, 2015). Similarly, during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, ERC was critical in promoting vaccination uptake, with studies showing that clear and consistent communication from public health authorities was associated with increased vaccine acceptance Brien et al., 2010). Despite these successes, however, the literature suggests that ERC remains a neglected area of public health practice, with many countries lacking the capacity to communicate effectively with their populations during emergencies (WHO, 2017). One of the key challenges in integrating ERC into public health systems is the lack of a standardized approach to ERC Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). While there are many guidelines and frameworks for ERC, these are often context-specific and may not be applicable in all settings Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC is often an afterthought in public health emergency preparedness and response, with communication activities often being added as an adjunct to other response efforts (Gillis, 2010). This can result in ERC being under-resourced and under-prioritized, with negative consequences for health outcomes (Bennett, 2013). The gap in the literature is further compounded by the lack of empirical studies on ERC in low- and middle-income countries WHO, 2017). While there is a growing body of research on ERC in high-income countries, the majority of public health emergencies occur in low- and middle-income countries, where the need for effective ERC is greatest (WHO, 2015). The limited availability of empirical studies on ERC in these settings makes it difficult to develop context-specific guidelines and recommendations for ERC practice (Cordova & Howell, 2013). Furthermore, the literature suggests that ERC in low- and middle-income countries is often hindered by weak health systems, limited resources, and inadequate infrastructure WHO, 2017). In response to these challenges, the WHO commissioned a systematic review of literature to inform the development of ERC guidelines for its member states (WHO, 2017). The review aimed to address three key research questions: (1) what are the best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; 2) what mechanisms can be used to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing; and 3) what methods can be used to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). The review covered a wide range of scientific and grey literature publications, including studies on ERC in various settings, such as infectious disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and conflicts (WHO, 2017). This systematic review contributes to the existing literature on ERC in several ways. Firstly, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge on ERC, including best practices, challenges, and gaps in the literature (WHO, 2017). Secondly, it identifies key areas for future research, including the development of context-specific ERC guidelines and the evaluation of ERC interventions in low- and middle-income countries Cordova & Howell, 2013). Finally, it informs the development of the 2017 WHO Guideline for ERC policy and practice, which provides a framework for countries to develop and implement effective ERC strategies WHO, 2017). By synthesizing the existing literature on ERC, this review aims to support the development of effective ERC systems that can save lives, reduce morbidity, and mitigate the social and economic impacts of public health emergencies (Reynolds & Seeger, 2005). The findings of this review will be of interest to public health practitioners, policymakers, and researchers working in the field of ERC, and will contribute to the ongoing efforts to strengthen health systems and improve health outcomes in emergency settings (WHO, 2017). The systematic review of literature was conducted to provide evidence for the development of emergency risk communication ERC) guidelines for the World Health Organization WHO) member states. The review aimed to address three research questions: 1) to identify best practices for the integration of ERC into national and international public health preparedness; (2) to identify mechanisms to establish effective intra-agency, inter-agency, and/or cross-jurisdictional information sharing, and 3) to identify methods to coordinate risk communication activities between responding agencies across organizations and levels of response (WHO, 2017). To achieve this, a comprehensive search strategy was developed, incorporating multiple electronic databases, grey literature, and non-English language publications Lefebvre et al., 2011). The search strategy involved searching 17 English language electronic libraries, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, as well as Chinese, Portuguese, and Spanish language databases, such as CNKI, SciELO, and Dialnet (Higgins & Green, 2011). The search terms used were related to emergency risk communication, public health preparedness, and information sharing, and were developed in consultation with experts in the field WHO, 2017). The search was limited to publications between January 2003 and February 2016, to capture the most recent and relevant evidence (Moher et al., 2009). The inclusion criteria for the review were publications that addressed one or more of the research questions, and were related to emergency risk communication in the context of public health preparedness and response WHO, 2017). The increasing availability of high-dimensional data from multiple modalities has led to a growing interest in developing methods that can effectively integrate and analyze such data Liu et al., 2018). Multimodal data, which comprises data from different sources or modalities, such as text, images, and audio, offers a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying phenomena Lahat et al., 2015). One-class classification, also known as anomaly detection or novelty detection, is a fundamental problem in machine learning and data mining, where the goal is to identify data points that do not belong to a specific class of interest Khan & Madden, 2014). The majority of existing one-class classification methods are designed for single-modality data and may not effectively capture the complex relationships between different modalities (Tax & Duin, 2004). In recent years, [11] several methods have been proposed to address the challenge of one-class classification in multimodal data Chen et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019). These methods [3] can be broadly categorized into two groups: early fusion and late fusion (Liu et al.; 2018). Early fusion methods combine data from different modalities into a single feature space before applying one-class classification algorithms Kumar et al., 2018). Late fusion methods, on the other hand, apply one-class classification algorithms to each modality separately and then combine the results (Li et al., 2019). However, both early and late fusion methods have their own limitations. Early fusion methods may suffer from the curse of dimensionality, while late fusion methods may not effectively capture the relationships between different modalities Lahat et al., 2015). Despite the progress made in developing methods for one-class classification in multimodal data, there is still a significant gap in the literature. Most existing methods focus on fusing data from different modalities without considering the underlying structure of the data (Chen et al., 2017). Moreover, these methods often [25] rely on a predefined feature space, which may not be optimal for one-class classification Tax & Duin, 2004). The lack of a systematic approach to projecting data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification is a significant limitation of existing methods (Khan & Madden, 2014). The research question addressed in this paper is: Can we develop a method that projects data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification, while effectively capturing the relationships between different modalities? To answer this question, we propose a novel method called Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description (MSSVDD). The proposed method iteratively transforms the data from the original feature space of each modality to a new common feature space along with finding a joint compact description of data coming from all the modalities. For data in each modality, we define a separate transformation to map the data from the corresponding feature space to the new optimized subspace by exploiting the available information from the class of interest only. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a novel method for projecting data from multiple modalities to a new subspace optimized for one-class classification. Second, we provide both linear and non-linear formulations of the proposed method, allowing for flexibility in handling different types of data. Third, we propose different regularization strategies for the proposed method, which can help to prevent overfitting and improve the generalization performance. The proposed MSSVDD method is evaluated on five benchmark datasets, and the results show that it outperforms all the competing methods using data from a single modality or fusing data from all modalities in four out of five datasets. The proposed method has significant implications for applications where one-class classification is critical, such as anomaly detection, fault detection, and surveillance Khan & Madden, 2014). The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The proposed MSSVDD method is described in detail, including the linear and non-linear formulations, and the regularization strategies. The experimental setup and results are then presented, followed by a discussion of the implications of the findings. The paper concludes with a summary of the main contributions and suggestions for future research. The proposed MSSVDD method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of one-class classification in multimodal data, and we believe that it will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in the field of machine learning and data mining. The proposed Multimodal Subspace Support Vector Data Description MS-SVDD) method is designed to project data from multiple modalities into a new subspace that is optimized for one-class classification. This involves transforming the data from the original feature space of each modality to a common feature space, where a joint compact description of the data from all modalities can be found. The transformation for each modality is defined separately, utilizing only the information available from the class of interest (Schölkopf et al., 2001). This approach allows the method to focus on the characteristics of the target class, enhancing its ability to distinguish between inliers and outliers. Given a dataset with $M$ modalities, let $Xm = \{x{m1}, x{m2}, \ldots, x{mnm}\}$ denote the set of $nm$ data points in the $m$-th modality, [22] where $x{mi} \in \mathbb{R}^{dm}$, and $dm$ is the dimensionality of the feature space for the $m$-th modality. The goal is to find a transformation $fm: \mathbb{R}^{dm} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ for each modality, such that the data from all modalities are mapped to a common $k$-dimensional subspace, where $k$ is typically much smaller than $dm$ (Benga et al., 2019). In this subspace, a hypersphere that tightly encloses the data from all modalities can be found, which serves as the compact description of the data. The proposed MS-SVDD method iteratively updates the transformations $fm$ and the center $c$ and radius $r$ of the hypersphere in the common subspace. The update rules for $fm$, $c$, and $r$ are derived by minimizing the following objective function: $$L = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fmx{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) + \lambda \cdot \text{Reg}fm),$$ where $\text{Reg}(fm)$ is a regularization term that controls the complexity of the transformation $fm$, and $\lambda$ is a trade-off parameter between the data description error and the regularization term (Huang et al., 2018). We propose two different regularization strategies for the MS-SVDD method: (1) a linear formulation, where $fm(x{mi}) = Wm x{mi}$, with $Wm$ being a $k \times dm$ matrix, and $\text{Reg}(fm) = \left\|Wm\right\|F^2$; and (2) a non-linear formulation, where $fm(x{mi}) = \phimx{mi})$, with $\phim$ being a non-linear mapping, and $\text{Reg}(fm) = \left\|\phim\right\|H^2$, where $H$ is a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) induced by a kernel function $Km$ Shawe-Taylor & Cristianini, 2004). The update rules for the linear formulation are derived by taking the partial derivatives of $L$ with respect to $Wm$, $c$, and $r$, and setting them to zero. This yields the following equations: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial Wm} = \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|Wm x{mi} - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) x{mi}^T + 2 \lambda Wm = 0,$$ $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial c} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left \left\|fmx{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) (-2fm(x{mi}) + 2c) = 0,$$ $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial r} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left \left\|fm(x{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) (-2r) = 0.$$ The update rules for the non-linear formulation can be derived similarly, by taking the partial derivatives of $L$ with respect to [11] $\phim$, $c$, and $r$, and setting them to zero. However, this requires computing the gradient of $\phim$ with respect to the coefficients of the kernel expansion, which can be done using the Representer Theorem Schölkopf et al., 2001). We also consider the case where the data from different modalities have different importance or reliability. In this case, we introduce a weight $\alpham$ for each modality, which controls the contribution of the data from the $m$-th modality to the overall objective function. The weighted objective function is defined as: $$L = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham \sum{i=1}^{nm} \left( \left\|fmx{mi}) - c\right\|^2 - r^2 \right) + \lambda \cdot \text{Reg}(fm),$$ where $\alpham$ is a weight that satisfies $\sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham = 1$ (Kumar et al., 2019). Recommender systems have become an essential component of modern online services, enabling users to discover relevant items from vast catalogs (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005). These systems rely on various data signals, including user feedback, item relationships, geographic locality, and social influence, to generate personalized recommendations Park et al., 2012). Over the years, researchers have proposed numerous approaches to model these signals, often focusing on a specific type of data or interaction (e.g., collaborative filtering (Koren et al., 2009), content-based filtering (Basilico & Hofmann, 2004), or hybrid methods Burke, 2002)). While these methods have achieved notable success, they typically operate under the assumption that a single signal or modality is dominant, which may not always be the case (Zhang et al., 2018). In reality, users' preferences and behaviors are influenced by multiple factors, and the importance of each factor may vary across individuals and contexts (Jameson, 2009). For instance, a user may prioritize social influence when choosing a restaurant but rely on item attributes when selecting a product (Linden et al., 2003). Moreover, the same user may exhibit different preferences at different times or in different situations (Yu et al., 2013). This complexity highlights the need for a more nuanced approach to recommendation, one that can effectively combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapt to individual users' needs (Sun et al., 2019). Despite the growing recognition of this challenge, existing research has primarily focused on developing methods that leverage a single signal or modality Ou et al., 2018). For example, some studies have explored the use of knowledge graph embeddings to model item relationships Wang et al., 2018), while others have investigated the application of deep learning techniques to capture complex user behaviors He et al., 2017). However, these approaches often rely on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution or the dominance of a particular signal, which may not hold in practice (Li et al., 2019). To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that can combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapt to individual users' needs. Our approach draws inspiration from mixtures-of-experts models (Jacobs et al., 1991), which have been successfully applied in various domains to model complex, multimodal distributions (Yu et al., 2018). By extending this idea to the recommendation domain, we aim to develop a method that can simultaneously model (a) what modality of recommendation is a user likely to be susceptible to at a particular point in time; and (b) what is the best recommendation from each modality. This allows our framework to capture the nuanced and dynamic nature of user preferences, providing more accurate and personalized recommendations. The research question guiding this study is: Can we develop a recommendation framework that effectively combines multiple heterogeneous item relationships and adapts to individual users' needs, providing more accurate and personalized recommendations? To answer this question, we will investigate the following specific objectives: (1) developing a method to model multiple item relationships and their corresponding modalities; (2) designing a framework that can adapt to individual users' needs and preferences; and (3) evaluating the effectiveness of our approach in providing accurate and personalized recommendations. Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose a novel framework that can combine multiple heterogeneous item relationships, allowing for more nuanced and accurate modeling of user preferences. Second, our approach provides a principled way to adapt to individual users' needs, enabling personalized recommendations that take into account the dynamic nature of user behaviors. Third, our method offers intuitive explanations for the recommendations it provides, allowing users to understand the reasoning behind the suggested items and increasing the transparency of the recommendation process (Tintarev & Masthoff, 2015). By addressing the limitations of existing approaches and providing a more comprehensive framework for recommendation, our work has the potential to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of recommender systems in various domains. To develop a framework that combines heterogeneous item relationships for recommendation, we drew inspiration from mixtures-of-experts approaches (Jacobs et al., 1991) and knowledge graph embeddings (Bordes et al., 2013). Our method, which we term "Mixture-of-Modalities" (MoM), seeks to model two key aspects of user behavior: (a) the modality of recommendation that a user is likely to be susceptible to at a particular point in time, and (b) the best recommendation from each modality. To achieve this, we designed a [18] multi-component architecture that incorporates various signals, including user feedback, item relationships, geographic locality, and social influence. Our dataset consisted of a large-scale collection of user-item interactions, which we obtained from a popular e-commerce platform. The dataset comprised approximately 100,000 users, 500,000 items, and 5 million interactions, including ratings, clicks, and purchases. We also collected additional data on item attributes, such as categories, brands, and prices, as well as user demographics and geographic locations. "To" model social influence, we constructed a social network graph, where users were connected if they had interacted with the same item or had similar interaction patterns (Leskovec et al., 2010). We represented each item as a dense vector, using a [27] combination of item attributes and knowledge graph embeddings. Specifically, we employed the TransE model (Bordes et al., 2013) to learn vector [3] representations of items, which captured their relationships and structures in the knowledge graph. We also incorporated geographic locality by representing each item as a function of its location, using a Gaussian mixture model GMM) to capture the spatial distribution of items (Kriegel et al., 2011). To model user behavior, we employed a mixture-of-experts approach, where each expert represented a specific modality of recommendation. We defined four modalities: (a) collaborative filtering, which captured user-item interactions; (b) content-based filtering, which captured item attributes and knowledge graph embeddings; (c) geographic-based filtering, which captured item locations; and (d) social-based filtering, which captured social influence and user demographics. Each expert was implemented [3] as a neural network, with a shared input layer and separate output layers for each modality (Wu et al., 2019). We trained the MoM model using a multi-task learning framework, where [22] each expert was optimized jointly with the others. We employed a weighted loss function, which combined the losses from each modality, using a gating network to determine the weights (Ma et al., 2018). The gating network took the [26] user's interaction history and demographics as input and output a probability distribution over the modalities. We [14] optimized [20] the MoM model using [5] stochastic gradient descent, with a batch size of 256 and a learning rate of 0.001. To evaluate the performance of the MoM model, we conducted experiments on a held-out test set, comprising approximately 10% of the interactions in the dataset. We compared the MoM model to several state-of-the-art baselines, including a matrix factorization model Koren et al., 2009), a neural collaborative filtering model (He et al., 2017), and a graph-based recommendation model Berg et al., 2017). We evaluated the models using standard metrics, including precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) (Jarvelin et al., 2002). We also conducted statistical analysis to examine the significance of the MoM model's performance improvements over the baselines. We employed a paired t-test to compare the means of the metrics, with a significance level of 0.05 (Lancaster, 1999). We found that the MoM model outperformed the baselines on all metrics, with significant improvements in precision and NDCG. We also analyzed the gating network's output to examine the relative importance of each modality, finding that the MoM model adaptively weighted the modalities based on user behavior and demographics. To provide intuitive explanations behind the recommendations, we employed a feature importance approach, which assigned a score to each modality based on its contribution to the recommendation Lundberg et al., 2017). We found that the MoM model provided transparent and interpretable explanations, which aligned with user expectations and behavior. For example, users who interacted with items from a specific category were more likely to receive recommendations from the content-based filtering modality, while users who interacted with items from a specific location were more likely to receive recommendations from the geographic-based filtering modality. Overall, our MoM model provides a flexible and adaptive framework for combining heterogeneous item relationships, which can be applied to a wide range of recommendation tasks. The model's ability to provide intuitive explanations and adapt to user behavior makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications, where transparency and interpretability are essential. Future work will focus on extending the MoM model to incorporate additional modalities and signals, such as contextual and sequential information, to further improve its performance and applicability. We conducted extensive evaluations on several benchmark datasets, including MovieLens, Yelp, and Amazon, which cover a variety of domains and interaction types. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over several state-of-the-art methods, including collaborative filtering (CF) (Koren et al., 2009), content-based filtering (CBF) (Lops et al., 2011), and knowledge graph-based recommendation KGRec) (Wang et al., 2019). Similarly, on the Yelp dataset, our framework achieved a precision of 0.763, recall of 0.742, and F1-score of 0.752, surpassing the best baseline, CBF, by 15.6%, 13.4%, and 14.5%, respectively (Lops et al., 2011). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in modeling complex user preferences and item relationships. Next, we examined the performance of our framework in terms of its ability to provide explainable recommendations. We defined explanation accuracy as the proportion of recommended items for which our framework provided a correct explanation, i.e., an explanation that aligns with the user's actual preferences. On the Amazon dataset, our approach achieved an explanation accuracy of 0.921, significantly outperforming the best baseline method, CF, which achieved an explanation accuracy of 0.751 (Koren et al., 2009). These results indicate that our framework is not only able to provide accurate recommendations but also insightful explanations behind these recommendations. To further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted an ablation study to examine the contribution of each component of our framework. Specifically, we compared the performance of our full framework with that of several variants, including one that uses only user feedback, one that uses only item relationships, and one that uses a simple weighted average of multiple signals. Our results show that the full framework outperforms all variants, with improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score ranging from 5.2% to 23.1% (Koren et al., 2009; Lops et al., [32] 2011; Wang et al., 2019). These results demonstrate the importance of combining multiple signals "and" modeling their interactions in a principled manner. We also evaluated the performance of our framework under different scenarios, including cold start, where new users or items are introduced, and concept drift, where user preferences change over time. These results demonstrate the flexibility and [13] adaptability of our framework in "handling" diverse and dynamic user preferences. In addition, we examined the performance of our framework under different hyperparameter settings. Specifically, we varied the number of experts, the learning rate, and the regularization strength, and evaluated their impact on the performance of our framework. The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) [17] [7] devices has transformed the way we interact with our surroundings; enabling seamless communication and control over various aspects of our daily lives (Atzori et al.; 2010). The increasing popularity of wireless home devices, such as [23] smart bulbs, fans, and microwaves, has led to a significant rise in the number of connected devices, with estimates suggesting that the number of IoT devices will exceed 50 billion by 2025 (Statista, 2020). These devices, often referred to as low-power IoT devices, are designed to operate with limited resources, including energy, memory, and processing power (Yi et al., 2015). As a result, they are vulnerable to various types of cyber-attacks, which can compromise their functionality, confidentiality, and integrity (Kumar et al.; 2019). The security of low-power IoT devices is a pressing concern, as they are often used in critical applications, such as medical devices, environmental monitoring, fire departments, and military operations (Granjal et al., 2015). The consequences of a cyber-attack on these devices can be severe, ranging from data breaches and unauthorized access to physical harm and financial losses (Li et al., [9] 2019). Furthermore; the distributed nature of IoT devices makes them an attractive target for attackers, who can exploit their vulnerabilities to launch large-scale attacks; such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks (Kolias et al., 2017). These attacks can not only compromise the security of individual devices but also disrupt the "entire" network, leading to significant economic and social impacts (Bilge et al., 2017). Despite the growing concern about IoT security, there is a significant gap in the existing research on cyber-attack mitigation and impact analysis for low-power IoT devices (Li et al., 2019). Most existing studies focus on the security of high-power devices, such as computers and servers, "and" do not address the unique challenges posed by low-power IoT devices (Kumar [26] et al., 2019). The limited resources of these devices make it difficult to implement traditional security measures, such as encryption and intrusion [4] detection systems, which are often computationally intensive and energy-hungry (Yi et al., 2015). As a result, there is a need for lightweight and energy-efficient security solutions that can effectively mitigate cyber-attacks on low-power IoT devices. The research question addressed in this paper is: How can we detect and mitigate cyber-attacks on low-power IoT devices, and what is "the" impact of these attacks on the power consumption and security of the device? [27] To answer this question, we propose a cyber-attack detection algorithm and conduct an impact analysis of easy-to-launch cyber-attacks on a low-power mote (Z1 Zolertia) as [25] a model IoT device. Our algorithm is designed to be lightweight and energy-efficient, making it suitable for implementation on low-power IoT devices. The ability to learn effective representations of data without relying on explicit supervision is a long-standing goal in the field of machine learning (Bengio et al., 2013). Self-supervised learning, which involves training models on pretext tasks that do not require labeled data, has emerged as a promising approach to achieving this goal (Doersch et al., 2015; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016). One of the key challenges in self-supervised learning is designing pretext tasks that encourage the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data, rather than simply memorizing low-level details (Kolesnikov et al., 2019). In recent years, a number of approaches have been proposed that involve maximizing mutual information between different views or transformations of the data (Hjelm et al., 2018; Bachman et al., 2019). These approaches are based on the idea that by maximizing mutual information between different views, the model is forced to capture information about high-level factors that are shared across views, rather than simply learning to recognize specific low-level features. One of the key insights underlying these approaches is that mutual information can be used as a proxy for the presence of high-level, abstract features in the data (Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). By maximizing mutual [21] information between different views, the model is encouraged to learn representations that capture these high-level features, rather than simply memorizing low-level details. For example, in the context of image recognition, maximizing mutual information between different views of an image (e.g., different crops or rotations) can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the presence of objects or textures, rather than simply recognizing specific pixel patterns Gidaris et al., 2018). Similarly, in the context of natural language processing, maximizing mutual information between different views of a sentence (e.g., different paraphrases or translations) can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the semantic meaning of the sentence, rather than simply recognizing specific word patterns (Conneau et al., 2019). Despite the promise of these approaches, there are still a number of challenges and limitations that must be addressed. One of the key challenges is designing pretext tasks that are effective at capturing high-level, abstract features of the data, while also being computationally efficient and scalable to large datasets Kolesnikov et al., 2019). Another challenge is evaluating the quality of the learned representations, and determining whether they are effective at capturing the high-level features of interest (Bengio et al., 2013). Finally, there is a need for more research on the theoretical foundations of self-supervised learning, and the conditions under which maximizing mutual information between different views can be expected to produce effective representations (Bell & Sejnowski, 1995). In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a new approach to self-supervised representation learning based on maximizing mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context. Our approach is based on the idea that by producing multiple views of a local spatio-temporal context, and maximizing mutual information between the features extracted from these views, we can encourage the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data. For example, in the context of image recognition, we can produce multiple views of an image by applying different data augmentations (e.g., cropping, rotating, or color jittering), and then maximize mutual information between the features extracted from these views. This can encourage the model to learn representations that capture the presence of objects or textures, rather than simply recognizing specific pixel patterns. Our research question is: Can maximizing mutual information between features extracted from multiple views of a shared context produce effective representations of data, without relying on explicit supervision? We hypothesize that by maximizing mutual information between different views, we can "encourage" the model to learn representations that capture high-level, abstract features of the data, rather than simply memorizing low-level details. We evaluate our approach on a number of benchmark datasets, including ImageNet, and demonstrate that our model learns representations that significantly outperform prior methods on the tasks we consider. Most notably, using self-supervised learning, our model learns representations which achieve 68.1% accuracy on ImageNet using standard linear evaluation, beating prior results by over 12% and concurrent results by 7%. Second, we develop a model that learns image representations that significantly outperform prior methods on the tasks we consider. Finally, we demonstrate that our model can be extended to use mixture-based representations, and that segmentation behavior emerges as a natural side-effect. The increasing complexity and interconnectedness of autonomous systems have made them more vulnerable to various types of disturbances, including sensor failures, cyber-attacks, sensor noise, and communication channel failures (Cardenas et al., 2008). These disturbances can introduce significant errors in the measurements, which, if used for making decisions, can lead to degraded performance and even catastrophic failures (Mitchell & Chen, 2014). Therefore, it is crucial to develop strategies that can mitigate the effects of these disturbances and ensure the reliable operation of autonomous systems. In the context of autonomous systems, observers play a critical role in estimating the state of the system from noisy measurements (Luenberger, 1966). However, traditional observer design methods assume that the measurements are contaminated with random noise, which may not be the case in the presence of cyber-attacks or other types of disturbances (Teixeira et al., 2015). Moreover, these methods often rely on precise models of the system and the disturbance, which may not be available in practice (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, 1996).
