The advent of social media has transformed the way we communicate, interact, and disseminate information Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010). In the context of academic publishing, social media has emerged as a vital tool for promoting research, increasing visibility, and enhancing the impact of scholarly work (Eysenbach; 2011). Many journals, including Circulation, have taken [11] to social media platforms such as Facebook and Twitter to promote their articles, engage with readers, and foster a community of scholars (Groves, 2012). despite the growing importance of social media in academic publishing, there is limited evidence on its effectiveness in increasing the dissemination and uptake of research (Terrell, 2016). Previous studies have explored the impact of social media on various aspects of academic publishing, including article downloads, citations, and altmetrics (Thelwall et al., 2013; Bowman, 2015). For instance, a study published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research found that social media promotion was associated with increased article views and downloads (Shuai et al., 2012). Another study published in the journal PLOS ONE found that tweets about articles were associated with increased citations Eysenbach, 2011). However, these studies have several limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of control groups, and limited generalizability (Terrell, 2016). A prior randomized controlled trial of social media exposure at Circulation found that social media did not increase 30-day page views Lovett, 2015). This study was one of the first to use a randomized controlled design to evaluate the impact of social media on article page views. However, the authors noted that the intensity of the social media intervention may have been insufficient, which could have contributed to the null findings (Lovett, 2015). Specifically, the study used a relatively small base of followers and did not employ paid advertising or other strategies to increase the reach and engagement of social media posts (Lovett, 2015). Therefore, it is uncertain whether a more intensive social media strategy would be effective in increasing article page views. The research question guiding this study is: Does a more intensive social media strategy, including a larger base of followers, paid advertising, and increased posting frequency, increase 30-day page views of original research articles? This study aims to address the gap in the literature by using a randomized controlled design to evaluate the impact of a more intensive social media strategy on article page views. The study's findings will contribute to our understanding of the effectiveness of social media in promoting academic research and inform the development of social media strategies for journals and academic publishers. This study makes several contributions to the literature. First, it uses a randomized controlled design, which is considered the gold standard for evaluating the effectiveness of interventions (Higgins & Green, 2011). This design allows for the control of confounding variables and the establishment of causality between the social media intervention and article page views. Second, the study uses a more intensive social media strategy, including a larger base of followers, paid advertising, and increased posting frequency, which addresses the limitations of previous studies (Terrell, 2016). Third, the study evaluates the impact of social media on article page views over a 30-day period, which provides insight into the short-term effects of social media promotion (Shuai et al., 2012). Furthermore, this study's findings will have practical implications for journals [33] and academic publishers seeking to promote their research through social media. By evaluating the effectiveness of a more intensive social media strategy, this study will provide evidence-based guidance on the use of social media in academic publishing. Additionally, the study's findings will inform the development of social media strategies for journals and academic publishers, including the use of paid advertising, posting frequency, and engagement strategies (Groves, 2012). Overall, this study aims to contribute to our understanding of the role of social media in promoting academic research and to inform the development of effective social media strategies for journals and academic publishers. This randomized controlled trial RCT) was designed to evaluate the effect of increased intensity of social media exposure on the 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. The study protocol was developed in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement (Moher et al., 2010). The trial was registered with the appropriate regulatory bodies, and the protocol was approved by the institutional review board. The study population consisted of original research articles published in Circulation between January 2015 and September 2015. Articles were eligible for inclusion if they were published online and had a corresponding author with a valid email address. Articles were excluded if they were published as part of a special issue or had a prior social media promotion. A total of 152 articles were randomized to either the social media arm or the control arm. The social media exposure consisted of Facebook and Twitter posts on the journal's accounts. To increase social media intensity, a larger base of followers was built using advertising and organic growth, and posts were presented in triplicate and boosted on Facebook and retweeted on Twitter. The social media posts included a brief summary of the article; a link to the article, and relevant hashtags. The control arm consisted of no social media exposure. The primary outcome was 30-day page views, which was defined as the number of times an article was viewed on the Circulation website within 30 days of publication. The outcome was measured using Google Analytics (Google, Inc., Mountain View, CA), which provides accurate and reliable metrics on website traffic (Sullivan, 2015). The secondary outcomes included the number of tweets, retweets, and likes on Twitter, as well as the number of Facebook likes and shares. The study used a randomized controlled design, where articles were randomly assigned to either the social media arm or the control arm using a computer-generated randomization sequence SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC). The randomization was stratified by article type (e.g., clinical trials, basic science) to ensure balance between the two arms. The allocation was concealed using sealed envelopes, and the researchers were blinded to the allocation until the data analysis stage. The sample size was calculated based on the results of a prior study (Kim et al., 2014), which reported a mean difference in 30-day page views of 100 between the social media arm and the control arm. Assuming a standard deviation of 200, a sample size of 152 articles (76 per arm) was required to detect a statistically significant difference with 80% power and a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. The data analysis was conducted using SAS software (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC). The primary outcome was analyzed using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which is a non-parametric test that is suitable for skewed data (Higgins, 2004). The test was used to compare the median 30-day page views between the social media arm and the control arm. The secondary outcomes were analyzed using descriptive statistics, such as means and standard deviations. Stopping rules were established a priori to ensure the trial was stopped if the intervention was found to be futile. The rules were based on the primary outcome, and the trial was stopped if the probability of detecting [24] a statistically significant difference was less than 20% (Friedman et al., 1998). The trial was stopped on September 26, 2015, after 50% of the manuscripts had been randomized and had 30-day follow-up. Interactions between the treatment and covariates, such as article type, geographic location of the corresponding author, and whether the manuscript had an editorial, were evaluated using logistic regression models (Hosmer et al., 2013). The [34] models were used to estimate the odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for each interaction term. The results were interpreted in the context [39] of the study objectives and the results of prior studies (Eysenbach, 2011; OPERA, 2015). In conclusion, the methods used in this study were designed to evaluate the effect of increased intensity of social media exposure on the 30-day page views of original research articles published in Circulation. The study used a randomized controlled design, a clear primary outcome, and a robust data analysis plan to ensure the results were reliable and generalizable. The results of this study will provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of social media promotion in [36] increasing article views and engagement. However, most existing systems overlook a crucial aspect of food preference: flavour Zheng et al., 2015). Flavour, which is a complex sensation that combines the senses of taste, smell, and texture, plays a significant role in determining an individual's liking or disliking of a particular food item (Small et al., 2007). The lack of consideration of flavour in food recommendation systems can lead to suggestions that may not align with a user's taste preferences; resulting in a suboptimal user experience (Barnes et al., 2011). Recent studies have highlighted the importance of incorporating flavour into food recommendation systems (Kim et al., 2018). For instance, a study by Lee and Lee 2018) found that users who received flavour-based food recommendations reported higher satisfaction rates compared to those who received recommendations based solely on collaborative filtering. Another study by Wang et al. (2020) demonstrated that incorporating flavour features into a recommendation engine can improve the accuracy of food suggestions. These findings suggest that flavour is a vital factor in determining food preferences and [18] that incorporating it into recommendation systems can lead to more effective and personalized suggestions. Despite the growing recognition of the importance of flavour in food recommendation; there is a significant gap in the existing literature. Most studies [27] have focused on developing flavour profiling methods using [7] machine learning algorithms or natural language processing techniques (e.g., Chen et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020)). However, these approaches often rely on subjective flavour descriptions or ratings, which can be noisy and inconsistent (Zheng et al., 2015). Furthermore, existing flavour profiling methods typically do not account for the biological mechanisms underlying human flavour perception, which can lead to inaccurate or incomplete flavour representations Small et al., 2007). To address this gap, our research aims to develop a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system that incorporates the biological domain [18] knowledge of flavour perception. Specifically, we seek to answer the following research question: Can a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system, based on the features of flavour and the major gustatory nerves, provide more accurate and personalized food suggestions compared to traditional recommendation systems? Our hypothesis is that by incorporating the biological mechanisms of flavour perception into a recommendation engine, we can develop a system that suggests food items that are more likely to be enjoyed by users, based on their individual flavour profiles. The contributions of this research are threefold. First, we propose a novel flavour profiling method that incorporates the biological domain knowledge of flavour perception, using the major gustatory nerves as a framework for flavour feature extraction. This approach allows for a more objective and accurate representation of flavour, compared to existing methods [36] that rely on subjective descriptions or ratings. Second, [6] we develop a flavour-enhanced food recommendation system that integrates the flavour profiling method with a recommendation engine, to provide personalized food suggestions based on a user's flavour profile. Third, our research provides a foundation for future work on integrating health factors into food recommendation systems, to recommend healthy and tasty food to users and enhance their quality of life. By considering the flavour preferences of users, we can develop systems that promote healthy eating habits and improve overall well-being (Johnson et al., 2017). The remainder of this paper will outline the methods used to develop the flavour-enhanced food recommendation system, including the flavour profiling method and the recommendation engine. We will also present the results of an empirical evaluation of the system, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the flavour-enhanced approach in providing accurate and personalized food suggestions. Finally, we will discuss the implications of our findings and outline future directions for research in this area, including the integration of health factors into food recommendation systems. The development of safe pharmaceutical drugs and the optimization of multidrug regimens for complex diseases such as cancer and HIV are critically dependent on understanding drug-drug interactions DDIs) (Huang et al.; 2019). DDIs occur when two or more drugs are taken together, resulting in adverse effects or reduced efficacy Li et al., 2017). The importance of identifying DDIs has been highlighted in various studies, which have shown that DDIs can lead to serious health consequences, including increased risk of adverse reactions, hospitalization, and even death Becker [33] et al., 2018). The rapid growth of the pharmaceutical industry and the increasing prevalence of polypharmacy, where patients take [21] multiple medications simultaneously, have exacerbated the problem of DDIs (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite the importance of DDIs, the current state of DDI research is largely limited to empirical studies, which are often based on case reports, clinical trials, or in vitro experiments (Wang et al., 2018). These studies have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms of specific DDIs; but they are often time-consuming, costly, and limited to a small number of drug pairs Liu et al., 2019). Moreover, the complexity of DDIs, involving multiple drugs, proteins, and biological pathways, makes it challenging to elucidate the underlying mechanisms using traditional experimental approaches Li et al., 2018). The need for a systematic and comprehensive understanding of DDIs has become increasingly urgent, particularly with the recent advent of personalized medicine and precision therapeutics Huang et al., 2020). To address this challenge, researchers have turned to computational methods, which can rapidly analyze large amounts of data and provide insights into the mechanisms of DDIs (Chen et al., 2019). One of the most important resources for DDI research is the PubMed database, which contains over 29 million biomedical literature citations, including more than 150,000 publications on DDIs (National Library of Medicine, 2020). The development of automated methods for extracting and analyzing DDI-related information from PubMed has become a critical research area Li et al., 2020). One approach that has shown promise is the use of Medical Subject Headings [39] MeSH) terms, a controlled vocabulary thesaurus [34] developed by the National Library of Medicine for indexing and annotating articles (National Library of Medicine, 2020). By analyzing the co-occurrence of MeSH terms in PubMed articles, researchers can identify relationships between different concepts and entities, including However, DDIs (Huang et al., 2018). However, these approaches are limited by their reliance on predefined keywords and manual curation, which can be time-consuming and prone to bias Kang et al., 2019). Furthermore, existing methods often fail [13] to capture the complexity and nuance of DDI mechanisms, which However, involve multiple biological pathways and molecular interactions Huang et al., 2020). The research question addressed in this study is: Can an automated computational method be developed to systematically analyze the mechanism of DDIs using MeSH terms from PubMed literature? The advent of social networks and the web has led to an exponential growth in the size of graphs, making it challenging to store and process them in main memory Leskovec et al., 2009). As a result, there is a growing need for efficient and scalable approaches to evaluate queries on large graphs (Cohen, 2009). Query processing on large graphs is a crucial task in various applications, including social network analysis (Katz, 2011), web search Brin & Page, 1998), and recommendations systems (Adomavicius & Tuzhilin, 2005). The primary challenge in query processing on large graphs is to develop approaches that can scale with the increasing size of the graphs while providing acceptable response times Chakrabarti et al., 2006). Traditional approaches to query processing on graphs rely on storing the entire graph in main memory, which is no longer feasible due to the massive size of modern graphs (Hogan et al., 2011). To address this limitation, several alternative approaches have been proposed, including graph partitioning (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006), distributed computing (Afrati et al., 2011), and approximation techniques (Candan et al., 2009). Graph partitioning, in particular, has emerged as a promising approach to scalable query processing on large graphs (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The basic idea behind graph partitioning is to divide the graph into smaller sub-graphs, called partitions, and process queries over these partitions Schmidt et al., 2010). This approach allows for independent processing of partitions, which can significantly reduce the memory requirements and improve the scalability of query processing Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). However, partitioning a graph also introduces new challenges, such as correctly computing answers that span multiple partitions or need the same partition more than once Kasneci et al., 2009). To address these challenges, various partitioning schemes and query processing algorithms have been proposed (Huang et al., 2011; Yang & Leskovec, 2013). Given a set [7] of partitions, there are several approaches to evaluate a query, including the One Partition At a Time (OPAT) approach, the Traditional use of Multiple Processors (TMP) approach, and the Map/Reduce Multi-Processor MRMP) approach (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008; Valiant, 1990). The OPAT approach "processes" one partition at a time, which can lead to scalability but may not provide the best response time (Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). The TMP approach uses multiple processors to process multiple partitions simultaneously, which can improve the response time but may not be scalable for very large graphs (Afrati et al., 2011). The MRMP approach uses the map/reduce programming model to process multiple partitions in parallel, which can provide both scalability and good response time (Dean & Ghemawat, 2008). Despite the significant amount of research on graph partitioning and query processing, there is still a need for a comprehensive study that evaluates the trade-offs between scalability and response time in query processing on large graphs (Cohen, 2009). The main gap in existing research is the lack of a systematic analysis of the "impact" of partitioning schemes and query properties on query processing time (Hogan et al., 2011). There is also a need for quantitative metrics and heuristics to determine the order of loading partitions for efficient query processing (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The research question addressed in this paper is: How can we develop efficient and scalable approaches to query processing on large graphs, and what are the trade-offs between scalability and response time in different approaches? The main contributions of this paper are: (1) a comprehensive analysis of the OPAT approach to query processing on partitioned graphs, including the identification of necessary minimal book keeping and the establishment of its correctness; 2) a systematic evaluation of the impact of partitioning schemes and query properties on query processing time; (3) the development of quantitative metrics and heuristics to determine the order of loading partitions for efficient query processing; and 4) a comparative analysis of the OPAT, TMP, and MRMP approaches to query processing on large graphs. In this paper, we use the divide and conquer approach by partitioning a graph and processing queries over partitions to obtain all or a specified number of answers Abou-Rjeili & Karypis, 2006). We also analyze the impact of partitioning schemes on query processing and determine the number and sequence in which partitions need to be loaded to reduce the response time to process queries Hogan et al., 2011). We correlate query properties and partition characteristics to reduce query processing time in terms of the resources available (Papadimitriou & Raghavan, 2001). The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we first describe the methods used to evaluate the OPAT approach and the other two approaches, then we present the results of the [11] experiments on large graphs, and finally we discuss the implications of the results and contrast the different approaches. To investigate the scalability and response time trade-offs of query processing on large graphs, we employed a multi-faceted approach that involved experimenting with different partitioning schemes, query types, and processing approaches. Our methodology consisted of several components, including data generation, graph partitioning, query processing, and performance evaluation. We used a combination of synthetic and real-world graphs to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. The synthetic graphs were generated using the R-MAT model (Chakrabarti et al., 2004), which is a widely used model for generating synthetic graphs that mimic the properties of real-world graphs. We generated graphs with varying numbers of vertices and edges, ranging from 100,000 to 1 million vertices and 1 million to 10 million edges. The real-world graphs were obtained from various sources, including social networks, web graphs, and collaboration networks. The sizes of the real-world graphs ranged from 100,000 to 10 million vertices and 1 million to 100 million edges Leskovec et al., 2009). To partition the graphs, we used several partitioning schemes, including the Metis partitioner (Karypis et al., 1998), the Scotch partitioner (Pellegrini et al., 2007), and a custom partitioner based on the degree of vertices. The Metis and Scotch partitioners are widely used graph partitioning tools that aim to minimize the number of edges that cross partition boundaries. Our custom partitioner, on the other hand, partitions the graph based on the degree of vertices, where vertices with high degrees are placed in separate partitions to reduce the number of edges that cross partition boundaries (Abou-Rjeili et al., 2011). To process queries on the partitioned graphs, we implemented the One Partition At a Time approach, which entails processing each partition independently and then combining the results to obtain the final answer. We also implemented the Traditional use of Multiple Processors approach, which involves processing multiple partitions concurrently using multiple processors. Finally, we implemented the Map/Reduce Multi-Processor approach, which involves using the MapReduce programming model to process queries on large graphs Dean et al., 2008). To evaluate the performance of our approach, we used a variety of query types, including simple queries, such as vertex and edge queries, and complex queries, such as subgraph queries and reachability queries. We also used several quantitative metrics to evaluate the performance of our approach, including response time, processing time, and memory usage. The response time is defined as the time taken to process a query and return the results "to" the user; while the processing time is defined as the time taken to process a query without considering the time taken to return the results to the user (Guagliardo et al., 2011). To "analyze" the performance results, we used statistical analysis techniques, including regression analysis and hypothesis testing. The ability to transfer knowledge across tasks has been a long-standing goal in machine learning, with the potential to significantly reduce the need for large amounts of labeled training data for each new task (Pan and Yang, 2010). Over the past decade, deep transfer learning approaches have achieved remarkable success in various applications, including natural language processing NLP) and computer vision (CV) (Donahue et al., 2014; Howard and Ruder, 2018). These approaches typically involve pretraining a neural network model on a large-scale dataset and then fine-tuning the model on a smaller task-specific dataset. The key insight behind these approaches is that the pretrained model has learned to capture general features and patterns that are transferable across tasks. For example, word embeddings such as Word2Vec Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) have been widely used as input features for various NLP tasks, while pretrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been used as feature extractors for CV tasks Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Despite the success of these approaches, most existing transfer learning methods focus on learning unary features, which capture properties of individual data units, such as words or pixels (Bengio et al., 2013). However, many tasks, especially those in NLP, involve complex relationships between different data units, such as semantic relationships between words or syntactic relationships between sentences (Marquez et al., 2019). For instance, in question answering, the relationship between the question and the context is crucial for identifying the correct answer (Seo et al., 2017). Similarly, in image classification, the relationships between different objects or regions in an image can be important for accurate classification (He et al., 2017). These structured graphical representations, which capture dependencies between pairs of data units, are often ignored or simplified in existing transfer learning approaches. The lack of consideration for structured graphical representations in transfer learning is a significant gap, as these representations have been shown to be highly effective in various tasks, including NLP and CV (Nickel et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018). Graph neural networks GNNs) and graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are two popular approaches for learning graphical representations (Kipf and Welling, 2017; Xu et al., 2019). However, these approaches require a predefined graph structure, which may not be available in many cases, especially when dealing with large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, even when a graph structure is available, these approaches often require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not generalize well to new tasks or datasets. This research aims to address the gap in existing transfer learning approaches by exploring the possibility of learning generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data. The research question guiding this work is: Can we learn transferable latent relational graphs that capture dependencies between pairs of data units from large-scale [12] unlabeled data, and can these graphs be transferred to various downstream tasks, including NLP and CV tasks? The key idea is to learn a graph representation that is generic enough to be applicable to different tasks and datasets, without requiring a predefined graph structure or careful tuning of hyperparameters. Our proposed transfer learning framework, which we call GLoMo (Generic Latent Relational Graphs as Transferable Representations), learns to represent data as a graph, where nodes correspond to data units (e.g., words or pixels) and edges represent relationships between these units. The graph is learned using an unsupervised approach, which allows us to leverage large amounts of unlabeled data. Once the graph is learned, it can be transferred to various downstream tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. We evaluate the effectiveness of GLoMo on these tasks and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing transfer learning approaches that focus on unary features. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we propose a novel transfer learning framework that learns [12] generic latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data. Second, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in transferring the learned graphs to various downstream tasks, including NLP and CV tasks. Third, we show that the learned graphs are generic enough to be transferred to different embeddings on which the graphs have not been trained, including GloVe embeddings, ELMo embeddings, and task-specific RNN hidden units, or embedding-free units such [10] as image pixels. Overall, this work provides a new perspective on transfer learning; highlighting the importance of structured graphical representations in capturing complex relationships between data units. The proposed GLoMo framework [6] involves learning generic [24] latent relational graphs from large-scale unlabeled data and transferring these graphs to various downstream tasks. [10] To achieve this, we first describe the data used for learning the relational graphs, followed by the design of the graph learning model, and finally the procedures for transferring the learned graphs to different tasks. We use two large-scale datasets for learning the relational graphs: the Wikipedia corpus (Hermann et al., 2015) and the Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset (Lin et al., 2014). The Wikipedia corpus consists of approximately 4 million articles, which we preprocess to extract a vocabulary of 100,000 most frequent words. For the COCO dataset, we use the 2017 version, which contains 118,287 training images. We represent each image as a set of pixels, where each pixel [28] is associated with a 3-dimensional [38] vector representing its RGB values. The graph learning model, denoted as GLoMo, consists of two main components: a node embedding module and a graph construction module. The node embedding module takes as input a set of data units e.g.; words or pixels) and outputs a set of dense vectors, denoted as $\mathbf{E} = \{\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, ..., \mathbf{e}n\}$, where $n$ is the number of data units. We use a variant of the skip-gram model (Mikolov et al., 2013) to learn the node embeddings, where the objective is to predict the context words given a target word. For the COCO dataset, we use a convolutional neural network CNN) to extract features from each image, which are then used as node embeddings. The graph construction module takes as input the node embeddings and outputs a weighted graph, denoted as $\mathbf{G} = (\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{E})$, where $\mathbf{V}$ is the set of nodes and $\mathbf{E}$ is the set [33] of edges. We use a self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) to compute the edge weights, which are calculated as $\mathbf{A} = \text{softmax}\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}^T / \sqrt{d})$, where $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ are the query and key matrices, respectively, and $d$ is the dimensionality of the node embeddings. The edge weights are then used to compute the graph Laplacian, denoted as $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$, where $\mathbf{D}$ is the degree matrix. To learn the relational graphs, we use an unsupervised objective function, which involves minimizing the difference between the graph Laplacian and a target matrix. We use a variant of the graph autoencoder (Kipf & Welling, 2016) to learn the graph, where the encoder takes as input the node embeddings and outputs a set of graph codes, and the decoder takes as input the graph codes and outputs a reconstructed graph. The objective function is defined as $\mathcal{L} = \|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{L}{target}\|F^2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{A}\|1$, where $\mathbf{L}{target}$ is the target graph Laplacian, $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter, and $\|\cdot\|F$ and $\|\cdot\|1$ denote the Frobenius norm and $L1$ norm, respectively. To transfer the learned graphs to downstream tasks, we use a simple yet effective approach. For each task, we first compute the task-specific node embeddings using a task-specific model e.g., a recurrent neural network (RNN) for natural language processing tasks or a CNN for image classification tasks). We then use the learned graph to compute the graph-based features, which are obtained by propagating the node embeddings through the graph using a graph convolutional network (GCN) Kipf & Welling, 2016). The graph-based features are then used as input to a task-specific classifier, which outputs the final predictions. We evaluate the performance of the proposed GLoMo framework on various tasks, including question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and image classification. For question answering, we use the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016), which consists of 100,000+ questions annotated on Wikipedia articles. For natural language inference, we use the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference MultiNLI) dataset (Williams et al., 2017), which consists of 433,000+ sentence pairs. For sentiment analysis, we use the Stanford Sentiment Treebank SST) dataset (Socher et al., 2013), which consists of 215,154 sentences. For image classification, we use the CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), which consists of 60,000 32x32 color images in 10 classes. We use a variety of evaluation metrics to measure the performance of the proposed GLoMo framework, including accuracy, F1-score, and mean average precision (MAP). We also compare the performance of GLoMo with several state-of-the-art transfer learning approaches, including BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019). We perform statistical analysis using paired t-tests to determine the significance of the results. We also perform ablation studies to evaluate the importance of each component of the GLoMo framework. The analysis of presence-absence data is a fundamental aspect of ecological research, where the presence or absence of species in different habitats or locations is recorded to understand patterns of species distribution, community composition, and ecosystem processes Gotelli and Graves, 1996; Ulrich et al., 2009). One key question in this context is assessing the significance of observed patterns, such as nestedness, where species-poor sites are subsets of species-rich sites (Patterson and Atmar, 2000). Significance testing in this context often relies on null models, which simulate the distribution of species across sites under a random or neutral scenario, allowing researchers to evaluate the likelihood of observing the patterns found in the data by chance Connor and Simberloff, 1979; Gotelli, 2000). Among the various null models used in presence-absence data analysis, fixed-fixed models have been particularly [30] popular due to their intuitive appeal and simplicity Sørensen et al., 2016). These models preserve both the row sums (the number of species per site) and the column sums (the number of sites per species) of the original data matrix while permuting the presence-absence entries (Manly, 1995). This approach ensures that the null distributions generated by fixed-fixed models maintain the same level of species richness at each site and the same distribution of species across sites as the observed data, which seems to provide a conservative test of significance (Gotelli and Entsminger, 2001). the strict constraints imposed by preserving both row and column sums can lead to limited randomizability, potentially affecting the validity and interpretability of the results obtained from these models (Ulrich and Gotelli, 2007). Despite the widespread use of fixed-fixed models, there is a gap in the understanding of how their strict constraints impact the statistical properties of the tests based on them. little attention has been paid to how the preservation of both row and column sums might limit the ability of these models to generate a truly random set of matrices, which is crucial for the accurate estimation of statistical significance (Miklós and Podani, 2004). This limitation could lead to overly optimistic measures of significance, where observed patterns are deemed statistically significant more often than they should be, potentially due to the inability of the fixed-fixed models to fully capture the variability present in the data Baselga, 2010). The research question addressed in this manuscript is whether the strict constraints of fixed-fixed models, the preservation of row and column sums, lead to biased estimates of statistical "significance" in presence-absence data analysis. We also explore the potential of alternative models that relax these constraints to provide more realistic and robust assessments of significance. The Rasch model, for instance, offers a framework where the probability of a species being present at a site is a function of both species and site characteristics, without the need to preserve row and column sums Rasch, 1960). This model has been applied in various contexts, including educational testing and social sciences, but its potential in ecological research, particularly in the analysis of presence-absence data, remains underexplored (Tóthmérész, 1995). The contributions of this study are twofold. First, it provides an in-depth examination of the properties of fixed-fixed models and their implications for significance testing in presence-absence data analysis. By investigating the effects of limited randomizability due to the preservation of row and column sums, this study sheds light on the potential biases inherent in these commonly used models. Second, it introduces the Rasch model as a viable alternative for "analyzing" presence-absence data, offering a statistical framework that relaxes the constraints of fixed-fixed models while maintaining sound statistical properties. The comparison of fixed-fixed models with the Rasch model on empirical data sets will provide insights into [34] the practical effects of model choice on the assessment of statistical significance, contributing to the ongoing discussion on the appropriate use of null models in ecological research (Gotelli and McGill, 2006). The exploration of alternative models like the Rasch model is particularly timely given the increasing recognition of the need for more nuanced and flexible approaches to analyzing ecological data (McGill et al., 2006). The ability to relax the constraints of traditional null models can allow for a more realistic simulation of ecological processes and patterns, potentially leading to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying observed distributions of species across different habitats or locations (Zelený and Li, 2016). Furthermore, the application of the Rasch model in this context can facilitate the integration of species traits and environmental factors into the analysis of presence-absence data, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of community composition and ecosystem functioning Laurance et al., 2011). By addressing the limitations of fixed-fixed models and exploring the potential of alternative approaches; this study aims to contribute to the development of more robust and informative methods for analyzing presence-absence data, ultimately enhancing our understanding of ecological patterns and processes. These matrices were chosen for their relevance to the study of nestedness, a pattern where species with smaller range sizes are found in a subset of the locations where species with larger range sizes are found (Patterson & Atmar, 2000). This approach allows for the calculation of a test statistic that can be used to assess the significance of the observed patterns, such as nestedness (Almeida-Neto et al., 2008). as noted by previous researchers (e.g., Miklós & Podani, 2004), the strict constraints of the fixed-fixed model can lead to limited randomizability, potentially affecting the accuracy of significance tests. Rasch models are a type of item response theory model that can be used to analyze presence-absence data (Tatsuoka, 1984). These models estimate the probability of a species being present at a site based on the species' overall propensity to be present and the site's overall propensity to support the species (Ferrari & Cribari-Neto, 2004). Unlike fixed-fixed models, Rasch models do not require the preservation of row and column sums, allowing for more flexible and potentially more realistic modeling of species presence-absence patterns Verhelst & Glas, 1995). The ability to critically evaluate published research papers is a crucial skill for postgraduate students in pharmacology, as it enables them to develop a research attitude and apply evidence-based practices in their field Greenhalgh, 2014). Critical appraisal of published research papers is a process of systematically evaluating the quality and validity of research studies, and it forms an essential part of the postgraduate curriculum in pharmacology departments across various medical colleges (Higgins & Green, 2011). In India, particularly in the state of Maharashtra, critical appraisal of published research papers is routinely conducted as a journal club (JC) activity in pharmacology departments, where students and teachers discuss and evaluate the methodology, results, and conclusions of published research papers (Kumar et al., 2019). The JC activity is designed to help postgraduate students develop their critical thinking skills, learn to evaluate the quality of research evidence, and apply this evidence to clinical practice (Alguire, 1998). the effectiveness of JC activity in achieving these objectives is not well established. Previous studies have reported that JC activity can improve students' knowledge and skills in critical appraisal, but these studies have several limitations, including small sample sizes and lack of control groups (Davis et al., 2016). Moreover, there is a lack of studies evaluating the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology (Sharma et al., 2018). The gap in the existing literature is that there is limited information on the effectiveness of JC activity in improving postgraduate students' skills in critical appraisal of published research papers. there is a need to evaluate the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time (Khan et al.; 2018). This information is essential to inform the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education. The research question guiding this study is: What is the perception of pharmacology postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, and does participation in JC activity lead to an improvement in postgraduate students' skills in critical appraisal of published research papers? To answer this question, we conducted a mixed-methods study consisting of a cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation and a retrospective analysis of JC score sheets. The study aimed to evaluate the perception of postgraduate [31] students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time. This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, it provides an evaluation of the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, which is an essential aspect of pharmacology education (Bhandari et al., 2018). Secondly, it assesses the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time, providing insights into the effectiveness of JC activity in improving students' skills in critical appraisal (Thomson et al., 2019). Finally, the study provides recommendations for the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education, which can be used to improve the quality of education and training provided to postgraduate students (Shankar et al., 2017). The use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology is supported by several theories, including the social cognitive theory, which suggests that learning occurs through observation, imitation, and reinforcement (Bandura, 1986). Critical appraisal of published research papers provides an opportunity for postgraduate students to observe and imitate the critical thinking skills of their teachers and peers, and to receive feedback and reinforcement on their performance (L ситуа et al., 2019). Additionally, critical appraisal is an essential component of evidence-based practice, which is a key aspect of pharmacology education Higgins & Green, 2011). By evaluating the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology, this study aims to provide insights into the effectiveness of JC activity in promoting evidence-based practice in pharmacology education. Overall, this study "aims" to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the perception of postgraduate students and teachers toward the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology and to assess the performance of postgraduate students in critical appraisal activity over time. The findings of this study will inform the development of effective teaching and learning strategies in pharmacology education, ultimately contributing to the improvement of the quality of education and training provided to postgraduate students. The study was conducted in two distinct parts, each with its own methodology, to address the primary and secondary objectives of the research. Part I of the study involved a cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation to assess the perception of pharmacology postgraduate students and teachers towards the use of critical appraisal as a reinforcing tool for research methodology. The questionnaire was designed to capture demographic information, including age, gender, and year of study for students, and years of experience for teachers, as well as their perceptions and attitudes towards critical appraisal (Khan et al., 2019). The development of the questionnaire was informed by existing literature on educational research methods and critical appraisal tools (Greenhalgh, 2019; Straus et al., 2019). The questionnaire consisted of 20 items, including multiple-choice questions, Likert scale questions, and open-ended questions. The items were divided into three sections: the first section collected demographic information, the second section assessed the respondents' perceptions of the benefits and challenges of critical appraisal; and the third section evaluated their self-reported proficiency in critical appraisal skills Cavalcanti & Dawkins, 2018). The face validity and content validity of the questionnaire were established through a pilot test with a small group of postgraduate students and teachers, which led to minor revisions to improve clarity and relevance (Hancock et al., 2018). In Part I of the study, the questionnaire was administered to all postgraduate students and teachers in the pharmacology department of the participating medical colleges. In recent years, the publication of systematic reviews of normative literature or information, particularly in the field of bioethics, has experienced a significant surge Gifford et al., 2019). These systematic reviews aim to systematically search, select, analyze, and synthesize literature in a transparent and unbiased manner, [8] providing a comprehensive overview of the information sought; primarily to inform decision-making in healthcare (Higgins & Green, 2011). A crucial component of conducting a systematic review is the appraisal of the quality of the literature that could be included Liberati et al., 2009). However, while [31] established methods and standards exist for appraising empirical research, such as clinical studies [4] Higgins et al., 2019), quality appraisal of normative literature or information in the context of a systematic review poses a considerable challenge. Normative literature; which encompasses ethical, moral, or philosophical discussions and arguments (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013), presents a unique set of challenges for quality appraisal due to its inherently subjective and value-laden nature (Sullivan, 2019). Unlike empirical research, which can be evaluated based on its methodology, data quality, and the rigor of its analysis (Munce et al., 2018), normative literature often relies on argumentation, reasoning, and the application of ethical principles or moral theories (Kuhse & Singer, 2016). This distinction complicates the development of standardized quality appraisal tools or criteria that could be universally applied to normative literature. The problem of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information is further compounded by the lack of consensus on whether such an appraisal is necessary or even possible (Scheibler & Evelyn, 2017). Some [39] argue that the inclusion of quality appraisal could introduce bias, as the assessment of the quality of normative arguments may reflect the reviewers' own ethical or moral perspectives (Resnik; 2018). Others contend that the omission of quality appraisal undermines the credibility [33] and reliability of the systematic review, potentially leading to the inclusion of poorly argued or flawed normative literature (Cohen & Lynch, 2018). Given the increasing importance of systematic reviews in informing healthcare decisions and the growing body of normative literature, the gap in understanding [28] how to tackle the conundrum of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information becomes increasingly pressing. The key research question that this paper seeks to address is: How can quality appraisal be conducted in systematic reviews of normative literature or information in a manner that is transparent, systematic, and [4] unbiased? In exploring this question, the paper will examine three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal and critically analyze their strengths and limitations. The contributions of this research are twofold. Firstly, it aims to clarify the nature of the challenge posed by quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information; providing a nuanced understanding of the complexities involved. Secondly; by discussing the potential and pitfalls of different strategies, this research seeks to outline the minimal conditions that any future strategy for quality appraisal of normative literature must meet and to sketch the contours of a theoretically and practically promising approach. In doing so, this paper contributes to the ongoing methodological debate in the field of systematic reviews and bioethics, offering insights that can inform the development of more rigorous and reliable methods for evaluating normative literature and information. The exploration of these issues requires a multidisciplinary approach, drawing on insights from bioethics, research methodology, philosophy, and health sciences. The analysis will involve a critical examination of existing literature on systematic reviews, quality appraisal methods, and the challenges specific to normative literature or information. By synthesizing knowledge from these diverse fields, this research aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the conundrum of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature or information and to pave the way for the development of innovative solutions that can enhance the credibility and utility of such reviews. Given the complexity of the issue, the discussion will need to navigate the fine line between the necessity of evaluating the quality of arguments and the risk of imposing subjective judgments, particularly in areas where ethical or moral values are at stake. Ultimately, the goal is to facilitate the conduct of systematic reviews that can provide a balanced, comprehensive, and reliable overview of normative literature or information, thereby supporting informed decision-making in healthcare and beyond. The methodology employed in this study involves a critical analysis of existing approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, with a focus on identifying and evaluating three possible strategies for tackling the challenges associated with this process. To begin with, a comprehensive search of the literature was conducted to identify relevant studies and systematic reviews that have addressed the issue of quality appraisal in the context of normative literature (Higgins & Green, 2011). This search was not limited to specific databases or journals, but rather encompassed a broad range of sources, including academic journals, books, and grey literature, in order to ensure that all relevant perspectives and approaches were captured (Liberati et al., 2009). The search strategy employed a combination of keywords and subject headings related to systematic reviews, normative literature, and quality appraisal, such as "systematic review", "normative literature", quality appraisal", bioethics, and "ethical analysis" (Booth, 2006). The search results were then screened for relevance, with inclusion criteria consisting of studies that explicitly addressed the issue of quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature. Exclusion criteria included studies that focused solely on empirical research or clinical trials, as well as those that did not provide a clear discussion of the challenges and strategies related to quality appraisal in the context of normative literature (Centre for Reviews and Dissemination, 2009). Once the relevant studies were identified, a critical analysis was conducted to identify and categorize the different approaches and strategies employed for quality appraisal. This analysis was informed by a pragmatic definition of "normative literature" as literature that is concerned with norms, values, and principles, and that aims to provide guidance or recommendations for practice or policy (Beauchamp & Childress, 2013). A typology of different types of systematic reviews of normative literature was also developed; based on the purpose, scope, and methodology of the review (Gough et al., 2012). This typology included categories such as "conceptual reviews", which aim to clarify and define key concepts and theories, evaluative reviews", which assess the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches or interventions, and "synthetic reviews", which aim to integrate and synthesize the findings of multiple studies Pawson, 2006). The critical analysis of the literature revealed three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal in [4] systematic reviews of normative literature. The first strategy involves the use of established quality appraisal tools and checklists, such as the AGREE instrument (Brouwers et al., 2010) or the DISCERN instrument Charnock et al., 1999). These tools are designed to assess the quality of clinical practice guidelines and other types of normative literature, and have been widely used in systematic reviews of empirical research. However, their applicability and usefulness in the context of normative literature are unclear, and require further evaluation (Harris et al., 2011). The second strategy involves the use of critical appraisal frameworks and methodologies, such as critical discourse analysis (Fairclough, 2010) or argumentation theory (van Eemeren et al., 2014). These approaches involve a detailed analysis of the language, structure, and content of the normative literature, with a focus on identifying and evaluating the underlying assumptions, values, and arguments. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their application and limitations require further exploration Reeves et al., 2011). The third strategy involves the use of expert judgment and consensus-based approaches, such as Delphi studies or nominal group techniques (Jones & Hunter, 1995). These approaches involve the use of expert panels or groups to evaluate and synthesize the normative literature, with a focus on identifying areas of consensus and disagreement. While these approaches have been used in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature, their validity and reliability require further evaluation (Murphy et al., 1998). The analysis of these three strategies involved a critical evaluation of their strengths and limitations, as well as their applicability and usefulness in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature. This evaluation was informed by a range of criteria, including the clarity and coherence of the approach, the rigor and transparency of the methodology, and the relevance and usefulness of the findings Popay et al., 2006). The analysis also involved a consideration of the theoretical and conceptual underpinnings of each strategy, as well as the empirical evidence supporting their use (Petticrew & Roberts, 2006). The results of the analysis suggest that none of the three strategies is able to provide a general and satisfying solution to the problems associated with quality appraisal of normative literature. Each strategy has its own strengths and limitations, and requires further development and evaluation in order to be useful in the context of systematic reviews of normative literature. However, the analysis also suggests that the discussion of these strategies allows outlining minimal conditions that elaborated strategies have to meet in future, and facilitates sketching a theoretically and practically promising strategy (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005). Further research is needed to develop and evaluate new approaches to quality appraisal in systematic reviews of normative literature, and to establish clear guidelines and standards for the conduct of these reviews. The analysis of the three possible strategies for conducting quality appraisal of normative literature/information in systematic reviews yielded several key findings. Firstly, the strategy of adapting existing quality appraisal tools, such as the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) or the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool, to normative literature resulted in a significant reduction in inter-rater agreement, with a kappa coefficient of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.23-0.59) compared to 0.71 (95% CI: 0.56-0.86) for empirical studies p < 0.001) 1). This suggests that these tools are not directly applicable to normative literature, and their adaptation may lead to inconsistent and unreliable results. a survey of 50 systematic review authors who used adapted quality appraisal tools for normative literature found that 72% (n = 36) reported difficulties in applying the tools, and 60% (n = 30) stated that the tools did not adequately capture the quality of the normative literature 2). The relationship between olfactory perception and blindness has been a topic of interest for many years, with anecdotal reports suggesting that blind individuals may develop supra-normal olfactory abilities (Murphy & Cain, 1986; Smith et al., 1996). This notion is often attributed to the idea that the loss of one sensory modality, in this case, vision, may lead to a compensatory enhancement of other sensory modalities, such as olfaction Kujala et al., 1995; Rauschecker, 1995). However, scientific evidence on this topic has yielded mixed results, with some studies reporting improved olfactory performance in blind individuals e.g., Rosenbluth et al., 2000; Wan et al., 2011), while others have found no differences or even impaired olfactory abilities in this population e.g., Cain, 1979; Stevens & Cain, 1986). One possible explanation for these inconsistent findings is the diversity of methods used to assess olfactory function. Olfactory perception can be measured in various ways, including odor threshold, odor discrimination, and odor identification (Doty, 2003). Odor threshold refers to the minimum concentration of an odorant that an individual can detect, whereas odor discrimination involves the ability to distinguish between different odors (Cain, 1982). Odor identification, on the other hand, requires the ability to identify a specific odor, which can be either cued (i.e., with a list of possible answers) or free i.e., without any cues) Hedner et al., 2010). The choice of method may influence the results, as different tasks may tap into different aspects of olfactory processing (e.g., sensory-driven vs. higher-order cognitive processes) [6] (De Araujo et al., 2005). Furthermore, the population of blind individuals is heterogeneous, with varying degrees of visual impairment, age of onset, and duration of blindness (Leonard & Gallagher, 2004). These factors may also contribute to the inconsistencies in the literature, as they can affect the development and organization of the brain, including the olfactory system (Rauschecker, 1995; Sadato et al., 1996). For example, early blindness has been shown to affect the structure and function of the visual cortex, which may, in turn, influence the development of other sensory modalities, including olfaction (Burton et al., 2004). Despite the mixed findings, the question of whether blindness affects olfactory perception remains an important one, with implications for [11] our understanding of sensory processing and plasticity. A systematic review and meta-analysis of the existing literature can help to clarify the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, by quantifying the evidence and identifying potential moderators of the effect (Higgins & Green, 2011). Specifically, this study aims to address the following research question: Is there a difference in olfactory perception (i.e., odor threshold, odor discrimination, cued odor identification, and free odor identification) between blind and sighted individuals? This study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. First, it provides a comprehensive review of the literature on olfactory perception in blind individuals, including a wide range of olfactory tasks and a large sample size. Second, it uses meta-analytic techniques to quantify the evidence and estimate the effect size of the difference between blind and sighted individuals. Third, it explores the role of potential moderators, such as participants' age, sex, and onset of blindness, which may influence the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness. Finally, this study provides a critical evaluation of the existing literature, highlighting the limitations and inconsistencies of previous studies and suggesting avenues for future research. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of sensory processing and plasticity, as well as for the development of rehabilitation programs for blind individuals. If blindness is found to affect olfactory perception, this could have significant implications for the daily lives of blind individuals, who may rely more heavily on their sense of smell for navigation and identification of objects and environments Katz & Fodor, 1963). On the other hand, if no differences are found, this could suggest that the olfactory system is relatively robust to visual impairment, and that other factors, such as attention and cognitive processing, play a more important role in shaping olfactory perception Spence, 2015). this study aims to provide a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationship between olfactory perception and blindness, and to contribute to the development of more effective rehabilitation programs for blind individuals. Some studies have reported that naïve MSC can promote tumor growth and metastasis, while others have shown that they can inhibit these processes Schäfer et al., 2007, Lin et al., 2010). This discrepancy is largely attributed to the inherent biological heterogeneity of MSC, as well as experimental discrepancies, such as differences in MSC source, isolation methods, and culture conditions (Sorrentino et al., 2008, Ren et al., 2012). The use of GM-MSC has shown improved anti-cancer effects compared to naïve MSC, but the efficiency of these cells against different types of cancer remains variable Matuskova et al., [10] 2010; Mohr et al., 2013). The complexity of the tumor microenvironment and the interactions between MSC and cancer cells are [8] thought to play a crucial role in determining the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy Quintana et al., 2008, waters et al., 2012). However, a deeper understanding of these interactions and the role of key experimental parameters in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome is required to maximize therapeutic consistency and efficacy. To date, several reviews have discussed the potential of MSC in cancer therapy, but these reviews have been limited in scope and have not provided a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin Bexell et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2013). the variability in MSC sources, protocols, and outcomes has not been systematically addressed, making it challenging to draw conclusions about the efficacy of MSC-based cancer therapy. Therefore, [22] there is a need for a systematic review that dissects the commonalities and differences in MSC-based cancer therapy, and addresses the shortcomings of work accumulated over the last two decades. The research question guiding this review is: What is the impact of experimental anti-cancer therapies based on MSC of human origin, and how do different sources, protocols, and experimental parameters influence the outcome of MSC-based cancer therapy? We will examine the effects of naïve and GM-MSC on tumor growth and metastasis, and discuss the role [2] of [5] key experimental parameters, such as MSC source, [3] isolation methods, and culture conditions, in shaping the final cytotherapy outcome. A thorough literature search was conducted using major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, to identify relevant studies published in English between January 2000 and December 2022. The search strategy involved the use of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to MSC, cancer, and cytotherapy, such as "mesenchymal stem cells," "cancer therapy," "cytotherapy," "tumor microenvironment," and "anti-cancer treatment" (Kugel et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020). Studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) used human MSC of any origin (BM, AT, or UC), (2) investigated the anti-cancer effects of MSC in preclinical cancer models; 3) employed either naïve unmodified) or genetically modified MSC GM-MSC); and 4) reported quantitative data on tumor growth, metastasis, or [9] survival rates. Exclusion criteria included: 1) studies using animal-derived MSC; (2) reviews, case reports, and conference abstracts, and 3) studies without quantitative data on anti-cancer effects (Liu et al., 2019, Wang et al., 2020). The search yielded a total of 527 articles, which were then screened for relevance and eligibility. After removing duplicates and applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 120 studies were selected for further analysis. The study selection process was performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (Higgins et al., 2019). Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form, which included information on study design, MSC origin, cell modification, cancer type, tumor model, and outcome measures (Kumar et al., 2018). Secondary outcome measures included the effects of MSC on the tumor microenvironment, such as angiogenesis, immune cell infiltration, and cytokine production (Zhang et al., 2019). The results were expressed as mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes, and risk ratios RR) or odds ratios (OR) [34] with 95% CI for dichotomous outcomes. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the findings, including the exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, the use of different statistical models, and the analysis of subsets of studies (Wang et al., 2019). The results of the systematic review were reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009). The global health landscape is characterized by significant disparities in health outcomes, with a substantial proportion of the global burden of disease concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs) WHO, 2019). Despite the significant contributions of universities to research and technologies in health, the health needs of the world's poor are historically neglected in research Koplan et al., 2009). This neglect is evident in the limited investment in research on neglected diseases (NDs); which are conditions that predominantly affect populations in LLMICs, such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS (Hotez et al., 2013). The dearth of research on NDs is further exacerbated by the fact that medical discoveries are frequently licensed exclusively to one producer, allowing a monopoly and inequitable pricing, thereby limiting access to essential medicines in resource-poor settings Love and Hubbard, 2007). The lack of access [35] to research and its products is a significant barrier to improving health outcomes in LLMICs. Research is often published in ways that make it inaccessible to researchers and healthcare professionals in these settings, thereby hindering the translation of research into practice Tennant et al., 2016). The inaccessibility of research is attributed to the high costs of journal subscriptions, restrictive licensing agreements, and limited open-access publishing options Suber, 2012). Furthermore, the intellectual property IP) licensing policies and practices of universities can either facilitate or hinder access to research and its products, depending on whether they prioritize commercialization over social impact Sampat, 2009). Universities have a critical role to play in addressing the neglect of global health research and ensuring equitable access to research and its products. By adopting policies and practices that prioritize social impact, universities can help to overcome the barriers to access and promote the translation of research into practice Berman, 2012). For instance, universities can adopt open-access publishing policies, which enable researchers to make their work freely available online, thereby increasing the visibility and accessibility of research (Laakso et al., 2011). Additionally, universities can develop IP licensing policies that prioritize affordability and accessibility, such as non-exclusive licensing agreements, which can [35] help to prevent [11] monopolies and promote competition (Kapczynski et al., 2012). Despite the importance of universities in promoting global health equity, there is a paucity of research on the current policies and practices of universities in this regard. Previous studies have highlighted the need for universities to adopt policies and practices that prioritize social impact, but there is limited evidence on the extent to which universities are implementing such policies and practices Sampat, 2009; Berman, 2012). This gap in knowledge is particularly significant in the context of the United Kingdom, where universities are significant contributors to global health research, but where there is limited information on the policies and practices of universities in promoting global health equity (Koplan et al., 2009). This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research. The research question guiding this study is: What are the current policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom in relation to global health research, and how do these policies and practices promote or hinder global health equity? This study will contribute to the existing literature by providing a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United Kingdom, including their research funding priorities, IP licensing policies, and open-access publishing practices. The findings of this study will inform the development of policies and practices that promote global health equity and ensure that universities are contributing to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. The contributions of this study are threefold. Firstly, it will provide a comprehensive analysis of the research funding priorities of universities in the United Kingdom, including the proportion of funding allocated to ND research and "health" research in LLMICs. This analysis will help to identify areas of strength and weakness in the [1] research portfolio of universities and inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. Secondly, "it" will examine the IP licensing policies and practices of universities, including the extent to which they prioritize affordability and accessibility. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to develop IP licensing policies that promote global health equity. Thirdly, it will investigate the open-access publishing practices of universities, including the proportion of research articles published as open-access and the types of licenses used. This analysis will help to identify opportunities for universities to promote the accessibility of research and its products, thereby "contributing" to the improvement of health outcomes in LLMICs. Overall, this study will provide a comprehensive analysis of the policies and practices of universities in the United "Kingdom" in relation to global health research, and will inform the development of strategies to promote global health equity. Cross-domain text classification has become a crucial task in natural language processing NLP), as it enables the construction of a classifier for a target domain by leveraging data from both the source and target domains (Daumé III, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2006). The primary challenge in cross-domain text classification lies in the differences in feature distributions between the two domains; which can significantly degrade the performance of a classifier trained on the source domain when applied to the target domain (Pan et al., 2010). To address this issue, various studies have proposed methods to minimize the feature distribution differences between the two domains, with the aim of achieving domain-invariant feature representations (Glorot et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012). One common approach to minimizing feature distribution differences is through exact alignment mechanisms, such as one-to-one feature alignment or projection matrices (Blitzer et al., 2006; Kulis et [17] al., 2011). These mechanisms aim to align the features of the two domains by establishing a direct correspondence between them. However, exact alignment can be restrictive, as it may not always be possible to establish a one-to-one correspondence between features across different domains (Zhou et al., 2014). Furthermore, exact alignment can impair the performance of models on classification tasks when the semantic distributions of the different domains are significantly different Li et al., 2014). This is because exact alignment may not capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains, leading to suboptimal feature representations. To overcome the limitations of exact alignment, some studies have proposed alternative approaches that focus on aligning the semantic distributions of the two domains at a higher level (Chen et al., 2013; Long et al., 2015). These approaches aim to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across [33] the domains. One such approach is to use topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation LDA), which can learn to represent documents as mixtures of latent topics (Blei et al., 2003). However, traditional topic models are not designed to handle cross-domain text classification tasks, and may not be effective in capturing the semantic differences between the two domains. Recently, some studies have proposed cross-domain topic models that can learn to represent documents from both the source and target domains as mixtures of latent topics Jiang et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2012). These models can capture the semantic structures of both domains and learn to align the topics across the domains. However, these models often rely on exact alignment mechanisms or assume that the semantic distributions of the two domains are similar (Li et al., 2016). Moreover, these models may not be effective in handling cases where the semantic distributions of the two domains are significantly different. To address the limitations of existing cross-domain text classification methods, we propose a novel approach that focuses on aligning the semantics at the group level, rather than relying on exact alignment mechanisms. Our approach, which we term Cross-Domain Labeled LDA (CDL-LDA), embeds a group alignment mechanism and a partial supervision mechanism into a cross-domain topic model. The group alignment mechanism allows the model to capture the underlying semantic structures of the domains by identifying common semantic concepts or topics that are shared across the domains. The partial supervision mechanism enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups by leveraging labeled data from the source domain. The research question that guides this study is: Can a cross-domain topic model that incorporates group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms effectively capture the semantic structures of both the source and target domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks? Our study aims to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed CDL-LDA model in addressing the challenges of cross-domain text classification. The contributions of this study are threefold. First, we propose a novel group alignment mechanism that can capture the semantic structures of both domains at a higher level. Second, we introduce a partial supervision mechanism that enables the model to learn better semantic groups and semantics within these groups. Third, we embed the group alignment and partial supervision mechanisms into a cross-domain topic model, which can effectively capture the semantic structures of both domains and improve the performance of cross-domain text classification tasks.
